World.title: How a Democrat in Michigan rocked the party days before the US midterms
World.content:
Haley Stevens, a sitting Democratic congresswoman, stood alongside the Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.

It was a surprise appearance that saw Stevens endorse the Republican candidate in the state's crucial US Senate contest, instead of her fellow Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

BBC's Nada Tawfik was in Detroit, Michigan where the party spat unfolded.

Read the full story here.

Follow our coverage of the US midterm elections here.

World.title: Trump makes final campaign push in final weekend before election
World.content:
Trump has been campaigning non-stop across the country ahead of the election - even in areas that were once thought to be safe Republican strongholds.

Throughout the weekend, Trump made the case for his party at rallies in Kansas, Florida and Iowa as well as at tele-rallies for candidates in states including Michigan, Ohio and Pennsylvania.

In previous years, Trump easily won Florida, Iowa and Kansas - once considered reliably Republican states - but the president's visits there in the final days of his election drive highlighted just how competitive these states have become in determining control of Congress.

Trump told supporters he had transformed the country, saying Democrats had left the US in a "dark age" but under his command, "we quickly turned it into the golden age of America".

Trump is facing a backlash over the cost of living. Prices have gone up, particularly for fuel, groceries and health care, since the war in Iran began over eight months ago. At these rallies, Trump appeared to have two aims: to change the subject from those issues and use fear to turn out the Republican vote.

At rallies in Florida and Iowa, he highlighted his policies on trade and immigration and said if Democrats were given power, they would "open the border", "bankrupt your family", "take away your guns" and "mutilate your children". He played video montages of Democrats criticising ICE and supporting transgender rights.

In the room at the rallies, supporters cheered, but there has also been disquiet among some Republicans over Trump's appeal with more moderate voters.

World.title: Nine killed as small jet crashes on Florida street
World.content:
A business jet crashed in a neighbourhood in Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people on board, the US transport secretary has said.

The crash happened near Cresthaven, some nine miles (14 km) from Mar-a-Lago, President Donald Trump's resort in the wealthy enclave of Palm Beach County, around 12:50 EST (17:50 GMT).

Images show a large crater in the middle of a multi-lane road, with fire and debris from the Learjet 60 aircraft scattered across it, but nobody on the ground was hurt.

The aircraft had departed from Austin, Texas, and was headed to the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a statement.

World.title: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
World.content:
Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (Â£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.

The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.

Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack.

The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.

Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."

There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.

Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.

The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with âthe fallout of the attack.

Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.

Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.

"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.

"The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.

World.title: Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
World.content:
Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff to pay for a sharp rise in its fuel costs which have surged following the US-Israel war with Iran.

The carrier said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.

Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be â¬2bn (Â£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and said it expects European airfares to increase to help cover the cost.

But it said that was unlikely to be enough and, among a number of measures, it is looking into "temporary pay freezes". The BBC has contacted Unite, the union which represents Ryanair employees, for comment.

The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to â¬2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to higher fuel costs jumped by 15%.

Ryanair said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" â in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices â the cost of the remainder had doubled.

Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the war in the Middle East, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.

Ryanair's chief executive, Michael O'Leary, said last month he expects the firm and other airlines to increase fares by 15% to 20% next year.

He said at the time: "You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe in the next 12 months.

"The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don't think it will be."

Ryanair said it was weighing up freezing pay as "maturing labour agreements" - multi-year wage deals with unions - come to to an end.

It also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions.

World.title: China state broadcaster pulls La Liga matches following Mbappé joke
World.content:
China's state broadcaster CCTV did not air a Real Madrid match on Sunday, despite the club's star striker Kylian MbappÃ©'s apology for his "ill-judged" remarks on the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong.

MbappÃ© drew huge backlash after saying the meme "that makes [him] laugh the most" was the one in which his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao.

China Media Group, CCTV's parent organisation, said last Tuesday it would suspend broadcasts of Spanish football La Liga matches following the furore, which also led to MbappÃ© being dropped by several Chinese brands.

China's foreign ministry had said it took MbappÃ©'s apology "seriously". Real Madrid and La Liga have also apologised.

China Media Group had earlier demanded apologies from the three parties, calling them "an absolute prerequisite" for moving past the incident.

It has acknowledged the apologies, but has not commented on how long the broadcast blackout will last.

MbappÃ©, who reportedly made his remark about the meme on French talk show The Bridge, apologised later on Tuesday.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," he had said.

The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his having overseen one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.

Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, died in 1976.

During his rule he oversaw the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society.

This is not the first time Beijing has suspended sports broadcasts over political sensitivities.

It pulled NBA games for a year from October 2019 after Daryl Morey, the general manager of Houston Rockets, tweeted in support of Hong Kong protesters during widespread pro-democracy protests in the city.

Morey backtracked on his comment after fierce criticism from Chinese fans, sponsors and commercial partners.

"I have had a lot of opportunity since that tweet to hear and consider other perspectives," Morey later wrote.

"I have always appreciated the significant support our Chinese fans and sponsors...I would hope that those who are upset will know that offending or misunderstanding them was not my intention."

Real Madrid beat Racing Santander 3-0 in Sunday's match, with goals from MbappÃ©, Jude Bellingham and Yan Diomande.

World.title: France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
World.content:
Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.

An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.

The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.

Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.

Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.

Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.

There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.

World.title: Popular Australian children's author jailed over child exploitation offences
World.content:
Australian children's author Craig Silvey has been sentenced to seven months in jail for possessing and distributing child exploitation material.

In handing down her sentence, Judge Hayley Cormann called Silvey's actions "repulsive" and "degrading".

In January, Silvey was arrested after police raided his home in Western Australia and seized several electronic devices. In May, the 44-year-old pleaded guilty to possessing and distributing child exploitation material and in October he was jailed pending his sentencing.

The father-of-three is best known for his award-winning young adult novel Jasper Jones and children's book Runt, both of which were later made into movies.

"You have devastated and betrayed the trust of thousands of people, and you've let entire communities down," Cormann said on Monday, according to WA Today.

Police said Silvey had online chats, in which he discussed child exploitation, open at the moment they turned up to raid his house.

In them, the court heard, Silvey had described himself as "extremely open minded" and "obsessed with taboos".

He'd discussed his sexual interest in children as young as five with another user of a pornography site, and detectives found images and videos of other adults abusing children on his devices.

He was initially charged with four offences, but prosecutors later dropped two.

Prosecutors said Silvey contributed to the "cycle of abuse" victimising the children in the images, and argued a harsh sentence was required.

However, the author's defence lawyer said he did not have a "sexual interest in children" and was seeking out "the most depraved material" as a form of "emotional" self harm.

"His behaviour provided temporary relief from psychological agitation," Eloise Barker said.

She said Silvey had displayed genuine remorse for his offending, and that his high profile and the resulting media scrutiny - which lead to his former partner and children relocating interstate - was already a form of punishment.

Judge Cormann did not accept many of her arguments, and said Silvey's offending was extremely serious.

"These children, the victims of this type of offending, are real and are traumatisedâ¦ the consequences for them from these abuses are long lasting and very, very traumatic," she said, according to The Australian.

Silvey was sentenced to seven months in jail, backdated to 22 October. He is eligible for parole.

Silvey's coming-of-age novel Jasper Jones sold more than half a million copies and was awarded the Book of the Year Award by the nation's peak publishing body in 2010.

The novel, set in Western Australia with two teenage boys as the main characters, was also shortlisted for the International Dublin Literary Awards and the Miles Franklin Literary Award.

It was later turned into a film starring Toni Collette and Hugo Weaving in 2017 as well as a stage play.

Another of his acclaimed works is 2022's Runt, about the adventures of an 11-year-old girl and her stray dog and set in the Australia outback. It was also adapted for film in 2024, featuring Celeste Barber.

Since his arrest, publishers and book shops have pulled his works from shelves while schools in some states have removed Jasper's books from teaching lists.

World.title: Sowore releases video of alleged attackers, alleges erased CCTV footage in Ekiti
World.content:
Omoyele Sowore, the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), has released a video purportedly showing individuals he identified as participants in the attack on his team in Ado-Ekiti, Ekiti State, last Friday.

In a post announcing the development on X, the Sahara Reporters publisher described the video as a breakthrough in identifying those involved in the attack. He, however, called for an independent investigation to establish the identities and roles of the individuals shown.

The video appears to show some men wielding cutlasses and sticks during a confrontation, while another person dressed in a black suit is seen being dragged. Several bystanders are also visible watching the incident.

Mr Sowore also alleged that CCTV recordings from Tawakalitu Restaurant, where the incident occurred on 30 October, had been erased after police officers and operatives of the State Security Service (SSS) also known as the Department of State Services (DSS), allegedly took possession of the surveillance equipment.

“The breakthrough comes amid disturbing revelations that CCTV recordings from Tawakalitu Restaurant, where the attack occurred, have reportedly been completely erased after police officers and the DSS took possession of the equipment and took it to Government House only to return it this evening without any images,” he alleged in an X post.

He further sstated that the CCTV equipment was subsequently returned to the restaurant management without the recorded footage.

“Tawakalitu Restaurant management reportedly confirmed that a DPO returned the CCTV equipment, but the recordings had been completely wiped. The management refused to identify the officer responsible for returning the equipment. This is an indication of a coordinated cover-up by the police hierarchy in Ekiti State,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The latest allegations came three days after Mr Sowore accused suspected political thugs of attacking him and members of his team in Ado-Ekiti. The Ekiti State Police Command had disputed his account, describing the incident as an “altercation” with some individuals at a restaurant.

In an earlier statement, the police command said officers rescued Mr Sowore after receiving information about the incident and that he sustained minor injuries. The command also said the Commissioner of Police, Michael Falade, had ordered a discreet investigation to establish what happened and identify those responsible.

Mr Sowore said he contacted Mr Falade, the Divisional Police Officer (DPO) of Ado-Ekiti Central Police Station, Mustapha Mohammed, and the Rapid Response Squad commander to request an update on the investigation.

He claimed the officers told him there was no complainant because he had not submitted a written statement.

Mr Sowore questioned this explanation, arguing that the police had already intervened in the incident.

“The officers claimed there was “no complainant” because I had not submitted a written statement, despite police rescuing the victims, taking them to their hospital, arresting suspects, and recovering weapons, stolen phones, and other devices,” he said.

Mr Sowore called on the police and the SSS to release the CCTV footage from the restaurant, saying it could help establish what happened during the incident.

He also demanded the removal of the state Commissioner of Police and other officers he accused of mishandling the investigation.

PREMIUM TIMES contacted the Ekiti State Police Command’s Public Relations Officer (PPRO), Sunday Abutu, by phone to seek his response to the allegations. However, he asked the reporter to call back in the afternoon.

“I will get back to you, please,” he said. “Call me around 12:00 p.m.”

World.title: Dakar 2026 YOG: Kuti bounces back with victory over Tunisian opponent
World.content:
Nigeria’s Matthew Kuti revived his hopes of reaching the knockout stage of the men’s singles table tennis event at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games with a 3-1 victory over Tunisia’s Youssef Aidli on Sunday.

The Nigerian recovered from an opening-day defeat to Hong Kong’s Li Ki Ho to beat Aidli 11-8, 11-8, 9-11, 11-7, keeping his campaign alive at the Dakar Expo Centre in Senegal.

Kuti, Nigeria’s deputy captain and reigning African Youth Cup champion, had endured a difficult start to his Group C campaign, losing 3-0 (11-4, 11-4, 11-3) to Li, whose attacking game proved too strong for the Nigerian.

However, he responded positively against Aidli, winning the first two games before the Tunisian reduced the deficit by taking the third. Kuti regained control in the fourth game to seal an important victory.

The result leaves the Nigerian needing one more win to secure qualification for the knockout stage, with his final group match against Italy’s Francesco Travesan scheduled for Monday.

The top two players in the four-man group will advance to the next round.

Speaking after his victory, Kuti acknowledged the quality of opposition at the Games but expressed confidence in his ability to overcome the Italian.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“It has not been easy for us here in Dakar because everybody is at their best and we are all aiming for the knockout stage. I hope I can raise my game against the Italian,” he said.

Meanwhile, Kuti and his compatriot, Favour Ojo, suffered an early exit from the mixed doubles event after losing to their Thai opponents in the round of 16 on Saturday.

Ojo also failed to progress in the women’s singles event after suffering a 3-1 defeat to Egypt’s Yara Elbadawy in her second group match.

The loss followed her opening group-stage defeat, ending her hopes of reaching the knockout rounds.

With Ojo’s campaign over, attention will now turn to Kuti’s decisive encounter against Travesan as the Nigerian seeks to keep his medal hopes alive in Dakar.

World.title: Sultan Muhammadu Sa’ad Abubakar III: Twenty years of a reign shaped by destiny, By Samuel Aruwan
World.content:
Today, 2 November 2026, Sultan Sa’ad marks exactly twenty years on the throne. He is the Sultan with the longest reign in this century and, by commonly accepted reign dates, ranks third in length of reign in the history of the Sultanate. During 2027, he is expected to surpass Sultan Muhammadu Bello and move into second place, behind only his father.

When little Sa’ad, the prince who would become Sultan Muhammadu Sa’ad Abubakar III, was born on Friday, 24 August 1956, to Sultan Siddiq Abubakar III and Hajiya Fadimatu Binta Abubakar, neither his father, who was 53, nor his mother nor anyone in the Sultanate could have known what Allah had written for him. No one could have foreseen that he would become a military officer, serve across Nigeria and beyond, and return decades later as the twentieth Sultan of Sokoto. As he marks twenty years on the throne, the course of that journey can be seen more clearly. The throne was not the visible destination of his childhood. That knowledge belonged to Allah alone.

If any of Sultan Abubakar III’s sons appeared close to the throne, it was Sultan Sa’ad’s much older brother, Sultan Muhammadu Maccido, who was 30 when Sultan Sa’ad Abubakar III was born. Sultan Maccido became their father’s trusted aide and one of the principal contenders when Sultan Abubakar III died in 1988. Destiny first turned elsewhere with the emergence of Sultan Ibrahim Dasuki. Eight years later, Sultan Maccido was appointed Sultan. He reigned for a decade before dying with his son, Senator Badamasi Maccido, and grandson in the ADC Airlines Flight 53 crash of 29 October 2006.

Sultan Sa’ad’s mother lived to witness his accession, a blessing denied his father and brother. Hadijatu Kubbura died months before Sultan Abubakar III became Sultan in 1938, while Sultan Maccido’s mother, Hauwa, died before his accession in 1996. Sultan Abubakar III was 35 when his paternal uncle and guardian, Sultan Hassan Dan Mu’azu, died on 31 May 1938. Still grieving both his mother and the uncle who had raised him and prayed that he would succeed, he became the seventeenth Sultan on 17 June 1938.

Sultan Sa’ad did not rise through the conventional hierarchy of palace and district titles, but he was never a stranger to the Sultanate. He witnessed at close quarters how his father administered its affairs and accompanied him on journeys to Maiduguri, Kaduna and elsewhere, observing his engagement with governments, traditional rulers, religious authorities and diverse communities. His apprenticeship began at his father’s side and continued through national service.

His entry into the Army was unexpected. After performing well in his West African School Certificate examination, he appeared destined for further study. Soldiering was not his youthful ambition, and he had not joined Barewa College’s Student Cadet Force. His direction changed after General TY Danjuma visited Sokoto and urged Sultan Abubakar III to encourage educated northern youths to join the Army after the Civil War. Deciding that the response should begin at home, Sultan Abubakar III ensured that seven eligible young men from his household applied to the Nigerian Defence Academy (NDA). All sat the entrance examination, three reached the interview stage, but only Sultan Sa’ad succeeded.

He entered the NDA on 30 June 1975 as a member of the 18th Regular Combatant Course and was commissioned a second lieutenant on 17 December 1977. Posted to the Armoured Corps, he held command, operational, staff and diplomatic appointments, including service in Chad and Sierra Leone. He rose to brigadier general and served as Nigeria’s Defence Adviser to Pakistan. The prince who left Sokoto returned as a commander, peacekeeper and diplomat.

Following Sultan Maccido’s death, Sultan Sa’ad hurried from Jos to Sokoto to join the royal family in receiving condolences. Nothing publicly suggested that he was returning to seek the throne. The contenders included older traditional titleholders and public servants from distinguished branches of the ruling family. His military career had kept him outside the traditional hierarchy, making his selection surprising to many. On Thursday, 2 November 2006, the grieving younger brother was announced as Sultan.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He was formally installed and presented with the staff of office on Saturday, 3 March 2007. The ceremony drew President Olusegun Obasanjo and traditional rulers from across Nigeria. Sultan Sa’ad renewed his pledge to uphold equity, fairness and justice, moving from military command to moral leadership sustained by credibility, restraint and persuasion.

When Sultan Sa’ad ascended the throne, several revered monarchs who had interacted with Sultan Abubakar III were still reigning. They included Emir Ado Bayero of Kano, Emir Shehu Idris of Zazzau, Shehu Mustapha Umar El Kanemi of Borno, Lamido Aliyu Mustapha of Adamawa, Oegwam Oegworok Gwamna Awan, Attah Aliyu Obaje of Igala and Aku Uka Shekarau Angyu Masa Ibi Kuvyon II of Wukari. Sultan Sa’ad engaged them in his own right, while their memories of his father provided a living connection between the two reigns. Emir Ado Bayero and Shehu Mustapha were among the rulers who attended his formal installation in 2007.

Two decades later, Sultan Sa’ad occupies the senior position once held by those older monarchs. Rulers who came to their thrones after him include Emir Umar Faruq Umar of Daura, Emir Abdulmumini Kabir Usman of Katsina, Oegwam Oegworok Ufuwai Bonet, Shehu Abubakar Garbai El Kanemi of Borno, Lamido Muhammadu Barkindo Aliyu Mustapha of Adamawa, Emir Rilwanu Suleiman Adamu of Bauchi, Emir Muhammadu Sanusi II of Kano, Emir Abubakar Shehu Abubakar III of Gombe, Emir Ahmed Nuhu Bamalli of Zazzau, Attah Matthew Alaji Opaluwa of Igala and Aku Uka Manu Ishaku Ada Ali of Wukari. Sultan Sa’ad has become a dean and senior reference point among them, offering experience, institutional memory and counsel. The prince who sat among rulers who knew his father now guides a younger generation of monarchs.

What appeared unplanned was preparation by another route. Sultan Sa’ad carried an established philosophy of leadership into a new age. During the upheavals of 1966, Sultan Abubakar III shuttled between Kaduna and Lagos, consulting leaders and helping to calm the country while mourning his kinsman and counsellor, Sir Ahmadu Bello. He condemned violence, discouraged reprisals and opposed taking the law into private hands. In his broadcast of 17 June 1966, he reassured frightened communities, asked people from other provinces not to leave the North and invited those who had fled to return. He deployed his moral authority in defence of peace and national unity.

Sultan Abubakar III’s accommodation of religious difference was also evident in his dealings with Christian missions. In “Sir Siddiq Abubakar III, 17th Sultan of Sokoto,” Alhaji Shehu Malami devotes a section to those relations. Mukhtar Umar Bunza and Jamilu Shehu provide an example in their 2018 study, “Sudan Interior Mission: An Evangelical Operation for a Unique Task in Northern Nigeria to 1960.” Drawing on a colonial record preserved at the National Archives, Kaduna, they state that when Christian boys began attending the Sokoto Native Authority School, Sultan Abubakar III paid for their Bibles. The gesture, entirely consistent with his Islamic convictions, reflected his willingness to accommodate the religious needs of Christians under his authority.

His openness was equally evident across ethnic lines. In “Indigeneity, Ethnicity and Federalism,” published in “Transition Without End,” Daniel C. Bach recounts the story of Alhaji Mamman Dike, known as Deke, an Igbo man born in Asaba. Other accounts identify him as Dike Okwuosa. After bringing the first motorcar to the Native Authority workshop during the reign of Sultan Muhammadu Maiturare, from 1915 to 1924, Deke entered palace service and served successive Sultans. Sultan Abubakar III valued him because “he could keep secrets,” made him his most trusted servant and entrusted him with the keys to his private apartments. Deke married two Hausa women, had eleven children, remained in Sokoto throughout the Civil War and died there on 22 May 1990. His life showed how trust, loyalty and belonging could transcend ethnic origin.

The tradition continued with Sultan Muhammadu Maccido, who maintained a close friendship with Chief Joe Ifedobi, the Okosisi of Akpo. Published recollections state that Chief Ifedobi drove him to the airport shortly before his appointment as Sultan was announced in 1996. Their friendship endured until Sultan Maccido’s death in 2006.

Sultan Sa’ad has carried that inheritance into a different age. His father taught that faith, education, productive work, justice, security and social welfare belonged together, and that material progress without discipline, tolerance and humility was incomplete. Sultan Sa’ad has applied those principles in democratic Nigeria, working with Muslim and Christian leaders, governments, security authorities and communities across ethnic and regional boundaries, despite exercising no executive power.

His twenty years have spanned the administrations of Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar’Adua, Goodluck Jonathan, Muhammadu Buhari and Bola Ahmed Tinubu. If Sultan Abubakar III preserved the Sultanate through colonial rule, independence, coups and eight federal administrations, Sultan Sa’ad has sustained its moral authority through terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, violence between farmers and herders, communal conflict and political division. Like his father in the 1960s, he has not been absent from Nigeria’s most difficult national conversations.

He has repeatedly condemned Boko Haram, banditry and violence committed in the name of religion. Following the killing of Deborah Samuel in Sokoto in May 2022, the Sultanate Council condemned the act as unjustifiable and demanded that the perpetrators face justice. The principle was unmistakable. No allegation permits a mob to become accuser, judge and executioner. Every grievance must be subjected to the law, irrespective of the religion of the accused or the victim.

My encounters with Sultan Sa’ad span nearly two decades. I began covering him as a journalist in 2007 at meetings of the Northern Governors’ Forum, the Northern Traditional Rulers Council and Jama’atu Nasril Islam. I also recorded and reported his BBC and VOA Hausa interviews, particularly on security. Our paths crossed again in 2015 and continued throughout my decade of service in different capacities in the Kaduna State Government. That contact revealed the consistency of his concern for peace, security, religious harmony and national unity.

His campaign for peace has also travelled abroad. I was with Sultan Sa’ad at the 2022 International Ministerial Conference on Freedom of Religion or Belief in London, where he joined religious leaders, rights advocates and government representatives in advancing religious tolerance. As President General of the Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs and joint chairman of the Nigeria Inter Religious Council, he has worked with successive leaders of the Christian Association of Nigeria. The armoured officer now influences through consultation, restraint and persuasion.

The anniversary carries a rare historical distinction. Sultan Abubakar III’s reign of more than fifty years remains the longest in Sokoto’s history, while Sultan Muhammadu Bello ruled for approximately twenty and a half years in the nineteenth century. Today, 2 November 2026, Sultan Sa’ad marks exactly twenty years on the throne. He is the Sultan with the longest reign in this century and, by commonly accepted reign dates, ranks third in length of reign in the history of the Sultanate. During 2027, he is expected to surpass Sultan Muhammadu Bello and move into second place, behind only his father.

After twenty years on the throne, Sultan Sa’ad stands at the intersection of palace and barracks, mosque and interfaith table, inherited authority and democratic citizenship. Events he did not arrange redirected his life. His father’s response to General Danjuma’s appeal took him into the Army. Military service prepared him for unforeseen responsibilities. His brother’s death brought him home to mourn, only for the kingmakers to entrust him with the Sultanate.

The child whose future only Allah knew served at home and abroad before returning to continue an old legacy in a democratic era. What seemed unplanned was destiny unfolding in its appointed time.

Allah Ya ja zamanin Amirul Muminin!

Samuel Aruwan is a postgraduate student at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria.

World.title: TRIBUTE: Chief C.O. Adebayo: Remembering a true hero one year after
World.content:
Some people leave lasting marks, memories, and imprints on our lives. The late Chief Cornelius Olatunji Adebayo, former university lecturer, Second Republic governor of Kwara State, Senator, former minister of communications, and later transportation, a formidable figure of the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO), a leading voice for Afenifere, the Middle Belt Forum, and the Movement for National Reformation (MNR), amongst others, was one such person. He lived a purposeful life, defined by integrity, humility, and commitment to lofty ideals. He walked tall, carrying himself with grace, dignity and quiet self-confidence. One year later, I’m still trying to come to terms with the reality of his passing. Chief C.O. Adebayo, popularly known as C.O., left a lasting legacy. A year after his interment, we remember an elder statesman who meant so much to many people.

If you were an itinerant journalist covering politics in the early 1990s, you might well have encountered Chief C.O. Adebayo. I first met him 34 years ago at his Ilorin GRA home. I had gone to interview him as a member of the editorial team at the Lagos-based Classique magazine. I was excited to interview him. His handshake was firm, and he radiated warmth. His smile was infectious. He did not shy away from expressing his progressive views. During the interview, he spoke with clarity, precision, eloquence and coherence, so much so that I was at home with him. He was a consummate communicator and a great repository of knowledge. So, what began 34 years back as a journalistic encounter evolved into an enduring, lifelong bond until his passing last year. I have many fond memories of him. He had great oratorical skills- always delivering his points with clarity, excellent diction and rhythm. His simplicity was disarming. He was entirely without airs. There was never a time you visited C.O. Adebayo that he wouldn’t see you off, extend his customary friendly parting handshake!

I vividly remember the last time I saw him: in 2021, four years before his passing, when I visited him in his Abuja home. I had gone to check on him upon learning that he hadn’t been quite well. That afternoon, I met him with one of his daughters. He was his usual self- straightforward, attentive and jovial. As I sat with him that day, my mind went back to decades past when he was very active politically-with a commanding personality. We spent so much time together reminiscing on certain political developments and the state of the nation. He said he was very delighted and proud to see my name among those nominated by the then President, Muhammadu Buhari, as Ambassadors-designate. He promised to visit me in Bangkok, Thailand. Even then, I suspected he might not visit because of his age and the rigours of such a long trip. He was a visionary who gave his all to several organisations, including NADECO, MNR, Afenifere, and the Middle Belt Forum.

In fact, Chief Adebayo was a thought leader, a progressive compass, and a calming presence in turbulent times. Apart from being a towering figure in NADECO’s battle for the restoration of late Chief M.K.O. Abiola’s electoral mandate, C.O. Adebayo was a pivot in Afenifere, the Middle Belt Forum, and the MNR, respectively. An inimitable hero, a voice of reason and courage, late C.O. Adebayo exemplified exceptional integrity, uncommon moral force, and an extraordinary sense of both courage and compassion. His depth of thought, word choice, and unique storytelling style set him apart. He communicated his views with a peculiar ease and poise. Throughout my association with him, beginning in the early 1990s, he always evinced great wisdom, logic, strength of character and conviction.

Chief C.O. Adebayo’s insights were always pertinent, especially his vehement opposition to military rule and his call for Nigeria’s restructuring. His decency, affable disposition, and his inclination to counsel (freely) younger professionals like myself naturally drew us very close. Thus, a sustained relationship emerged that lasted for more than three decades. He was a go-to person on happenings in the defunct Social Democratic Party (SDP). Because of our closeness, he wrote me a letter from Calabar prison, where the regime of late General Sani Abacha detained him in 1994 after his frontline role in NADECO. The Calabar prison letter was more than a personal account of his experience. It is on record that C.O. Adebayo declined a ministerial offer from the regime of late General Sani Abacha. As a journalist covering politics, C.O. Adebayo drew me close, and I became one of the media foot soldiers in the battle for June 12 and democracy. He was one of the preeminent progressive voices who greatly helped me in my early days in journalism, serving as a reservoir of information. His media-friendly disposition during those turbulent years of the Babangida and Abacha regimes also helped those of us who yearned for the news behind the news! Chief Adebayo was congenial, and, to boot, exceptionally media savvy. His depth of thought, rich sense of intellectual wit, and openness drew some of us to him, and his Lagos home became a meeting place for thoughtful political engagement.

We remember him today as a statesman who positively impacted many. He was deeply genial, with an astute, quick-witted intellect. He was an Iroko whose unwavering commitment, courage, and intellectual acuteness inspired admiration and hope. He was straightforward, pragmatic and bold. His influence spanned politics, leadership, public service, community service, the Middle Belt Forum, the Yoruba nation, Kwara and Kogi States, and more. His accomplishments were remarkable. A scholar who was a Senator and governor at a young age! He was Minister of Transportation and Communications at different times. A lecturer at the University of Ife, head of the English Department at Kwara State College of Technology, and Commissioner for Education in the old Kwara State, respectively, at an early stage. There is no doubt that C.O. Adebayo was one of our nation’s most consequential statesmen and illustrious reformists who stood on the side of the people during the tempestuous years of military dictatorship.

His voice on pressing national issues was unequivocal. At the core of his political philosophy was a call to restructure Nigeria. In an interview in 2016, he was quoted as saying: “There are nations, and I am talking about the conventional sense of the word nation, in the sense that Yorubaland is a nation. There are smaller ones, and there are bigger ones. Who wants to be together? My people in Kwara want to be part of the Yoruba nation within a federation. And so long as they have such desires, they must be addressed. And if they are not addressed, the people are not happy. They are not getting what they believe they need to stay happy within the federation…Power is too heavy in the hands of the Federal Government in Nigeria. There must be devolution. Before devolution, there must be restructuring to stem the oppression of minorities within a unit. My position remains what you’ll expect it to be.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He added: “With all modesty, I was one of the leaders of the Middle Belt Forum, and I remain one of the leaders of the forum. I was at one point chairman of the political forum of Afenifere; I remain a very strong believer in Afenifere and of course, the Yoruba nation. I believe Kwara wants and deserves the best share of whatever this country has to offer. So, beginning at home, we were talking restructuring.…I was secretary of the National Reformation Movement. And what the NADECO was about is restructuring of Nigeria…”

He was a quintessential leader, an iconic statesman whose deeds and reputation transcended many jurisdictions. He was also a man of incredible resilience and strength, confronting various challenges with grace and courage. Born on February 24, 1941, in Igbaja, in present-day Kwara State, Adebayo attended Oke-Onigbin Provincial Secondary School before progressing to Barewa College. He graduated from Ahmadu Bello University in 1967 and later attended the University of Ghana, Legon, where he earned his Master’s degree. He was a versatile personality whose rich service record spanned academia, governance, parliament, community service, and the pro-democracy movement.

Chief C.O. Adebayo was a colossus, a torchbearer, a shining star from Oke-Onigbin, Isin Local Government in Igbomina land, Kwara State, who shone brilliantly throughout his 84 years. His accomplishments and enduring influence remain a legacy for generations to come. One year later, as we remember the iconic and heroic Chief C.O. Adebayo, widely known as C.O., I find solace in the comforting words of Clare Harner, the American poet, whose poem in 1934 entitled “Do Not Stand at My Grave and Weep,” remains soothing:

“Do not stand at my grave and weep. I am not there.

I do not sleep. I am a thousand winds that blow.

I am the diamond glints on snow.

I am the sunlight on ripened grain.

I am the gentle autumn rain when you awaken in the morning hush.

I am the swift uplifting rush of quiet birds in circled flight.

I am the soft stars that shine at Night.

Do not stand at my grave and cry. I am not there.

I did not die.”

In the blueness of our beautiful skies and oceans, and in the warmth and brightness of our tropical weather, we remember C.O. Adebayo as a patriot, a forthright public-spirited leader who was deeply committed to the restructuring of Nigeria, democracy, rule of law, and a new nation built on federalism that recognises the diversity of its peoples. His exemplary accomplishments will continue to serve as a guiding light in an era of vanishing dedication to noble ideals.

Ambassador Oma Djebah, a frontline diplomat-journalist and member of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council, is a former Delta State Commissioner for Information and erstwhile Nigeria’s Ambassador to Thailand, with concurrent accreditation to the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP) and Myanmar.

World.title: Tinubu granted rare access inside Ka’abah, reaffirms commitment to Nigeria
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has reaffirmed his commitment to Project Nigeria and his determination to build a prosperous nation, invest in the future of young Nigerians, and pursue development in line with the will of Almighty Allah and the people’s aspirations.

The president stated this on Monday while reflecting on his spiritual journey to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to perform Umrah, during which the Custodian of the Holy Mosques of Makkah and Madinah, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, granted him a rare privilege of leading Nigeria’s delegation to pray inside the Holy Ka’abah.

At the Ka’abah, President Tinubu offered prayers of gratitude to Almighty Allah for the privilege of serving as Nigeria’s President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces.

Sheikh Dahlulah Muthawal of Masjid al-Haram led the president into the Ka’abah.

President Tinubu thanked the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, for granting him and members of his Nigerian delegation the opportunity to enter the Holy Ka’abah in Makkah and offer prayers to Almighty Allah.

The president described the honour as a historic and deeply cherished spiritual experience, reflecting the longstanding bonds of friendship, mutual respect and cooperation between Nigeria and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

“I want to say a big thank you for the faith, for the recognition. I can’t believe the fencing of the Ka’abah is in Green-White-Green, which reminds us of the Nigerian identity.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I thank the Crown Prince and all the administrators of the holy land. I thank them for the hospitality and recognition given to me as the leader of the delegation and the country.

“We are all facing challenges and hostility around us. We will overcome them with faith in God Almighty. I’m grateful forever. I thank the king and the royal crown prince.

“It is an honour that I enjoyed, and it is gracious of them to have allowed me to enter inside the Ka’abah. This is history,” the president said.

President Tinubu said he asked Allah for wisdom and resilience to continue serving Nigerians, and expressed confidence that his prayers have been answered.

“Well, I asked for wisdom and resilience to continue to serve the people. I know that prayer has been granted. Before the 2023 election, I did the same thing. I asked Allah to bless my Umrah then, and He did. And I promised that I would come back to thank Him,” the president said.

Reflecting on the message from the Holy Qur’an in Surah Aal-Imran, Verse 26, which affirms that Almighty Allah is the owner of all sovereignty, granting power and authority to whom He wills and taking them away from whom He wills, the president said power is a trust that must be exercised responsibly, with humility and in the service of the people, recognising that no position of authority is permanent and that ultimate sovereignty belongs to Almighty Allah.

“There is no other God but Almighty Allah. He is the giver and the taker. He owns power and authority. He says, ‘ If I give you, use it well. If you don’t use it in accordance with my dictates, I can take it from you and give it to another person. I am the only One who has that authority,” the president said, quoting the words of the Qur’an.

President Tinubu said faith in Allah had strengthened his conviction that his emergence as Nigeria’s leader was an extraordinary blessing that must be matched with dedicated service to the country.

“I have faith in that, and I believe extremely well that He has done me and my country a great favour. Out of many millions of people, to be the President and Commander-in-Chief is a favour that only Almighty God can do to a human being,” he stated.

President Tinubu emphasised that his commitment to Project Nigeria had become even stronger, assuring Nigerians of his resolve to pursue policies and programmes that would promote prosperity, national development and shared progress.

“My commitment to Project Nigeria is higher. I am determined to usher in prosperity and fully develop the country, consistent with the wish of Allah and the support of the people.

“It is important to put Allah first, then move on. Follow your conscience. Follow the right path that will lead Nigeria to that greatness,” the president said.

On the nation’s economic outlook, President Tinubu expressed optimism about the progress made under his watch, describing the economic foundation as solid and the country’s emergence from a difficult period as encouraging.

“The foundation is solid, and the economy has come out of the dark tunnel. This is inspiring,” he said.

He maintained, however, that nation-building requires sustained investment in young Nigerians’ future, noting that today’s leaders’ decisions will determine how future generations remember them.

“We need to build a future for our youth. If we don’t invest in their future, how do we want to be remembered as leaders 50 years from now? That’s the main thing. So this is a rare privilege to lead the country,” the president added.

President Tinubu reiterated that his administration would remain focused on strengthening the country’s economic foundations, expanding opportunities for young people and creating the conditions necessary for Nigerians to realise their potential.

The president thanked Almighty Allah for the opportunity to lead Nigeria and reaffirmed his determination to justify the confidence the Nigerian people have placed in him through purposeful leadership and an enduring commitment to national progress.

Apparently seized by emotions, Minister of Justice Lateef Fagbemi, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare Ali Pate, Governors of

Borno, Sokoto, Jigawa, Kaduna, Yobe and Kwara States as well as captains of industry, including Chairman of BUA Abdulsamad Rabiu and CEO of Oando Wale Tinubu, expressed gratitude to Allah and the president for allowing them to enter and pray with him in the most holy mosque and sacred ground in Islam.

Bayo Onanuga

Special Adviser to the President

(Information & Strategy)

November 2, 2026.

World.title: Access Bank appoints new deputy managing director, executive director
World.content:
Access Bank Plc has appointed Oluseyi Kumapayi as Deputy Managing Director, African Subsidiaries, and Olanrewaju Bamisebi as Executive Director, Information Technology and Digitalisation, as the lender moves to strengthen its operations, profitability and technology-driven services.

The appointments, which took effect on 27 and 28 October, respectively, followed the approval of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), according to a regulatory filing by Sunday Ekwochi, the Group Company Secretary.

Commenting on the appointments, the Group Chairman of Access Holdings, Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede, said the decisions reflected the group’s strategic priority of translating its extensive banking presence across Africa and beyond into improved performance, operational efficiency and stronger shareholder returns.

“Access Holdings has built a substantial banking franchise across Africa and beyond. Our strategic priority is now to translate that scale into superior performance, greater efficiency, stronger returns on capital and sustainable value for shareholders,” Mr Aig-Imoukhuede said.

He said Mr Kumapayi’s elevation would strengthen the group’s efforts to improve the performance of its African subsidiaries, while Mr Bamisebi’s appointment would bring technology leadership closer to the bank’s operations, customers and commercial priorities.

The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Access Bank, Roosevelt Ogbonna, said the lender was focused on building a more productive, efficient and profitable institution through better utilisation of its capital, technology and established market presence.

He said the bank would prioritise improving returns across its African subsidiaries, simplifying technology platforms, strengthening operational reliability and accelerating innovation to improve customer experience at a lower cost.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Access Holdings said the appointments were part of its transition from a strategy focused on scale to one centred on value creation, profitability, capital efficiency and sustainable shareholder returns.

The group said its priority, having established a significant banking presence across Africa and selected international markets, was to maximise the value of its existing operations through improved subsidiary performance, disciplined capital allocation and technology-driven productivity.

It added that transferring executive responsibility for Information Technology and Digitalisation from the holding company to Access Bank was intended to integrate technology transformation more closely with banking operations, customer service, revenue generation and cost management.

The group said the move would accelerate digital transformation, simplify operating platforms, strengthen resilience and improve execution across its banking operations.

Profiles

Mr Kumapayi was elevated from his previous position as Executive Director, African Subsidiaries, which he had held since November 2020.

He has over 25 years of banking experience spanning financial management, strategy, risk management, treasury and business development.

He joined Access Bank in 2002 and served as Group Chief Financial Officer between 2007 and 2020, where he contributed to strengthening the bank’s financial management and supporting its strategic development.

In his new role, he will retain responsibility for the bank’s African subsidiaries, with an expanded mandate to improve profitability, capital productivity, operational performance and cross-border business integration.

He will also support the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer in the broader leadership and strategic management of the bank.

Mr Kumapayi is a Fellow of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria. He holds an Executive MBA from IMD, Lausanne, and an Executive Master’s degree in Digital Transformation and Innovation Leadership from IE University, Madrid. He also holds degrees from the Universities of Lagos and Ibadan.

Olanrewaju Bamisebi

Meanwhile, Mr Bamisebi joined the board of Access Bank from Access Holdings, where he previously served as Executive Director, Information Technology and Digitalisation.

He has over 20 years of experience in technology transformation, digital banking, enterprise systems and operational management across the financial services industry and other sectors.

Before joining Access Holdings, he held senior positions at Equity Group Holdings Limited, including Group Director, Information Technology and Operations, and Managing Director of Finserve Africa.

He also served as Group Chief Information Officer at Diamond Bank, alongside other technology leadership positions at major Nigerian institutions.

In his new role, Mr Bamisebi will lead Access Bank’s technology and digitalisation strategy, focusing on improving operational efficiency, modernising technology platforms, strengthening cybersecurity and accelerating digital solutions to improve customer experience.

He holds a bachelor’s degree in Computing and Information Technology from the University of Derby and an MBA from Durham Business School. He is also an alumnus of the Cambridge Judge Business Senior Management Programme.

World.title: ₦70k transport allowance: Relief for some, questions for all, By Posi Olatubosun
World.content:
Ultimately, a short-term allowance should be weighed against the more lasting alternatives available: a sustainable wage framework, targeted cash transfers for vulnerable households in the informal economy, and cheaper mass transport that lowers costs for every commuter. Relief for public servants is welcome, and labour has negotiated hard for it. A country where most workers have no employer to bargain on their behalf needs a wider safety net. The task is to turn a six-month concession into a lasting framework: fair wages, targeted support for the vulnerable and cheaper transport for all.

₦70,000 a month will ease the commute for civil servants. What about the trader, the okada rider and the farmer?

That is the question raised by the Federal Government’s agreement with organised labour to pay a monthly transport intervention of ₦70,000 to public service workers across all levels for six months, beginning in November. The same agreement provides for arrears of the peculiar allowance, backdated to 1 May, to be paid in three monthly installments, and for minimum wage negotiations to begin immediately. The deal followed weeks of pressure from the Nigeria Labour Congress over the pump prices of petrol, wages, tax relief and unpaid allowances. It may avert a strike and bring genuine relief to many households. But it also raises important questions about fairness, fiscal cost and what happens when the six months end.

The workers’ case is strong. Since the removal of petrol subsidy in May 2023, transport has become one of the heaviest burdens on household budgets. Earlier this year, civil servants in Abuja told the News Agency of Nigeria that commuting now consumes more than half of their salaries, with some daily fares more than doubling. Inflation has eased to 14.63 per cent, but food inflation remains close to 20 per cent, and the earlier surge in prices has not been reversed. Notably, the new allowance equals the ₦70,000 national minimum wage agreed in 2024.

For the lowest-paid public servants, it effectively doubles their monthly income for six months. That is significant relief. Precision matters, however. An allowance of this kind is not a wage increase, and it is not targeted at a need. It is a temporary, flat payment to a defined group of employees. Its value lies in speed and simplicity, but those same features shape its limitations. The test is whether it is the best use of scarce public resources to cushion hardship, and whether it is affordable for every tier of government that it covers.

The first concern is fairness. Public servants are an important constituency, but they are a small portion of Nigeria’s entire workforce. The majority of Nigerians earn their living in the informal economy as traders, artisans, commercial drivers, farmers and casual labourers. Many of them face the same transport costs with less job security and no employer to negotiate on their behalf. Critics, including opposition presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar, have already asked what the arrangement offers the millions of people without formal jobs. The question deserves a serious answer. Relief that reaches only those with a payslip risks widening the gap between the formal and informal economy.

The fourth concern is the cliff edge. The agreement does not state what happens after six months. Temporary payments have a way of becoming permanent expectations, especially in an election season. If the allowance ends abruptly in April 2027, just weeks after the general elections, workers will face a sharp fall in income. If it is extended, it becomes a recurrent commitment without a clear funding source.

The second concern is cost. The agreement has not been accompanied by a published estimate of its total cost. Simple arithmetic shows why one is needed. Every one million beneficiaries would cost ₦70 billion a month, or ₦420 billion over six months, before the peculiar allowance arrears are added. Nigeria is already spending heavily on debt service, which reached ₦5.28 trillion on domestic debt alone in the first half of 2026. The president has also asked the National Assembly to approve a new external borrowing plan of about $20.5 billion. In that context, citizens are entitled to know how the allowance will be funded, whether it is provided for in the budget, and what spending, if any, will be reduced to accommodate it.

The third concern pertains to the states. The agreement covers public service workers across all levels, which presumably includes the state and local governments. Their finances vary widely. Some states have already raised their minimum wages well above ₦70,000; others still struggle to pay salaries on time. Experience suggests caution. In 2023, when the Federal Government agreed to a ₦35,000 wage award for its workers, states were divided over whether they would follow. An allowance that some states pay and others cannot would create new grievances and possibly fresh industrial disputes.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The fourth concern is the cliff edge. The agreement does not state what happens after six months. Temporary payments have a way of becoming permanent expectations, especially in an election season. If the allowance ends abruptly in April 2027, just weeks after the general elections, workers will face a sharp fall in income. If it is extended, it becomes a recurrent commitment without a clear funding source. Either outcome needs to be planned for now, not improvised later.

The fifth concern is the wider economic effect. Putting additional cash into the hands of public servants will support spending in markets, shops and transport services, which is welcome for small businesses. But if the payments are financed by borrowing rather than savings or reallocated spending, they add to demand at a time when inflation, though easing, remains high, and pre-election spending is already expected to rise. The Central Bank cut its policy rate in September partly because price pressures were moderating. A sizeable fiscal injection without a clear funding source could complicate that progress and make further easing harder. That would ultimately hurt the same workers through higher prices and dearer credit.

…payment systems must be secure. Nigeria’s payroll has long been vulnerable to ghost workers and padded nominal rolls. Before the first installment is paid, federal and state authorities should verify beneficiaries through existing payroll and identity systems, so that the money reaches genuine workers, rather than leak through fraud. Independent audits after each payment cycle would strengthen confidence further.

None of this means the allowance is wrong. It means it should be seen as a bridge, not a destination. The more durable solutions lie elsewhere.

First, the minimum wage negotiations now beginning offer an opportunity to agree on a sustainable framework. Wages linked to productivity and reviewed regularly would protect workers more reliably than periodic emergency payments. Second, relief for the informal majority should come through targeted cash transfers. The National Social Register already provides a platform for this. Making it accurate, transparent and timely would allow government to support vulnerable households, regardless of where they work. This is the approach that the IMF has repeatedly recommended. Third, the root cause, the cost of moving people and goods, must be addressed directly. Expanding CNG-powered mass transit, improving urban rail and road networks, and encouraging competition in fuel supply would lower transport costs for everyone, not just salaried workers.

A cheaper commute benefits the trader and the farmer as much as the civil servant. Fourth, transparency should accompany every intervention. The government should publish the expected cost, the number of beneficiaries and the funding source, and report on disbursement. Public confidence depends on seeing that relief is honestly accounted for. Fifth, payment systems must be secure. Nigeria’s payroll has long been vulnerable to ghost workers and padded nominal rolls. Before the first installment is paid, federal and state authorities should verify beneficiaries through existing payroll and identity systems, so that the money reaches genuine workers, rather than leak through fraud. Independent audits after each payment cycle would strengthen confidence further. Every naira lost to an inflated payroll is a naira that could have supported a vulnerable household outside the public service.

Ultimately, a short-term allowance should be weighed against the more lasting alternatives available: a sustainable wage framework, targeted cash transfers for vulnerable households in the informal economy, and cheaper mass transport that lowers costs for every commuter. Relief for public servants is welcome, and labour has negotiated hard for it. A country where most workers have no employer to bargain on their behalf needs a wider safety net. The task is to turn a six-month concession into a lasting framework: fair wages, targeted support for the vulnerable and cheaper transport for all. That would be a relief worth celebrating.

Posi Olatubosun is a UK-based academic faculty member in accounting and finance.

World.title: NASS Roundup: Rising school fees, insecurity, poor telecom network, other stories from House of Reps
World.content:
Lawmakers move to halt school fee increases, probe NELFUND impact

The House on Tuesday urged the federal government to halt recent increases in tuition fees and other mandatory charges by public tertiary institutions, warning that the development could undermine the objectives of the Nigeria Education Loan Fund (NELFUND).

The call followed a motion moved by Ifeoluwa Ehindero (APC, Ondo), who said some public universities, polytechnics and colleges of education had increased their fees by more than 100 per cent.

He argued the increases could widen inequalities in access to education and make it harder for students from low-income families to benefit from the federal government’s student loan scheme.

The lawmakers urged the Federal Ministry of Education and the National Universities Commission to engage institutions’ management on suspending the increases and reviewing their tuition structures.

The House also mandated its Committees on University Education, Federal Polytechnics and Higher Technical Education, and Federal Colleges of Education to investigate the extent and justification for the increases.

Reps insist telecom operators’ CEOs must appear over poor services

The House Ad Hoc Committee on Telecommunications Service Quality rejected a request by the Association of Licensed Telecommunications Operators of Nigeria (ALTON) to allow its Chairman, Gbenga Adebayo, to represent telecommunications companies at its investigation into poor network services.

The committee, chaired by Olumide Osoba (APC, Ogun), insisted that the chief executives of MTN Nigeria, Airtel Nigeria, Globacom, Mafab Communications and other operators must appear individually to explain persistent complaints about dropped calls, poor internet connectivity, failed airtime and data transactions, and inadequate network coverage.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The committee gave the executives until 4 November to appear, warning that noncompliance could attract warrants of arrest.

The lawmakers argued that the operators held individual licences and should be directly accountable for service quality.

The investigation comes amid persistent subscriber complaints. Figures cited during the proceedings showed that the four major operators recorded a combined 413,587 consumer complaints in the first half of 2026.

Lawmakers seek security, humanitarian intervention after Taraba killings

Following the deadly bandit attack on Binnari community in Karim Lamido Local Government Area of Taraba State, the House on Thursday called for urgent security and humanitarian interventions for affected communities.

The lawmakers adopted a motion moved by Mohammed Audu (APC, Taraba), who said between 57 and 60 people reportedly died in the 23 October attack.

According to the lawmaker, the attackers opened fire on residents and traders at a community market, killing 10 people at the scene. In contrast, several others reportedly drowned in a river as they fled.

The House urged the federal government to strengthen intelligence-sharing among security agencies in Taraba, Plateau and Bauchi states and called on relevant humanitarian agencies to provide relief materials to affected families.

It also called for the completion of the abandoned Wase-Karim Lamido road project, which lawmakers said would improve access for security personnel responding to attacks.

The House referred the motion to the Committees on the North-East Development Commission, Works, and the National Emergency Management Agency for further legislative action.

Kaduna Polytechnic gets 72-hour ultimatum to explain falling revenue, pension deductions

The House Committee on Federal Polytechnics and Higher Technical Education gave the management of Kaduna Polytechnic 72 hours to submit financial records following concerns about declining internally generated revenue and the remittance of statutory deductions.

During an oversight visit to the institution on 28 October, the committee, chaired by Fuad Laguda (APC, Lagos), questioned why the polytechnic’s internally generated revenue fell from ₦1.478 billion in 2023 to ₦1.398 billion in 2024 and ₦1.332 billion in 2025 despite an increase in student enrolment.

The lawmakers also demanded documentary evidence showing that approximately ₦1.3 billion deducted as pension contributions had been remitted to the appropriate authorities.

They further sought explanations on the payment of death benefits to the families of more than 30 employees reportedly deceased between 2023 and 2025.

The Rector, Suleiman Umar, represented by the Deputy Rector (Academic), Aliyu Usman, denied any default in pension remittances and assured the committee that the requested documents would be submitted within the stipulated period.

The committee said it would review the documents before determining whether the institution had complied with its financial and statutory obligations.

Transparent rules for electric, CNG vehicle imports

The House also called on the federal government to establish a transparent regulatory framework for importing electric vehicles (EVs), compressed natural gas (CNG) vehicles and other clean mobility equipment into Nigeria.

The resolution followed a motion moved by Ademorin Kuye (APC, Lagos) on 27 October.

Mr Kuye argued that although the government had introduced fiscal incentives, including import duty and tax reliefs, to encourage investment in cleaner transportation technologies, the policy required clear regulations to ensure local investment and consumer protection.

Under the proposed framework, companies seeking approval to import the vehicles would be required, where applicable, to establish certified maintenance centres, provide genuine spare parts and warranty support, and employ and train qualified Nigerian technical personnel.

They would also be expected to invest in electric vehicle charging infrastructure or CNG refuelling facilities and comply with relevant safety, environmental and technical standards.

The House urged the National Automotive Design and Development Council, the Bureau of Public Procurement, the Standards Organisation of Nigeria and the Nigeria Customs Service to develop objective criteria for approving importers.

It mandated the relevant House committees to monitor implementation and report back within four weeks for further legislative action.
