World.title: Entering Holy Kaaba with Tinubu a blessing beyond measure – Abdul Samad Rabiu
World.content:
Billionaire industrialist and Chairman of BUA Group, Abdul Samad Rabiu, has described his entry into the Holy Kaaba alongside President Bola Tinubu as a rare spiritual privilege and an experience he would cherish for the rest of his life.

Rabiu disclosed this in a Facebook post on Sunday night, sharing a photograph of himself with Tinubu

He wrote, “Some moments in life are beyond words, moments that touch the soul and remain forever engraved in the heart.

“Alhamdulillah, today I was profoundly humbled and blessed to be among those granted the extraordinary honour of entering the Holy Kaaba alongside His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR.

“It was a once-in-a-lifetime blessing, an honour beyond measure, and a moment of divine grace that will remain etched in my heart for as long as I live.”

Rabiu said his prayers at the sacred site extended beyond himself and his family to Nigeria, expressing hope for lasting peace, unity and prosperity in the country.

He added, “In that most sacred of places, my thoughts and prayers were not only for myself and my family, but for our entire nation.

“May Almighty Allah accept our prayers and bless our beloved nation with lasting peace, unity, and prosperity.”

Rabiu was among the delegation that accompanied Tinubu to Makkah for Umrah, the lesser pilgrimage, on Friday, which included Oando Group Chief Executive Officer, Wale Tinubu, state governors and other senior government officials.

Speaking at a dinner hosted for members of the delegation in Makkah on Saturday, Rabiu pledged the continued support of the business community for the administration and thanked the president for the rare spiritual opportunity.

Tinubu had also told journalists after performing the Umrah that he felt fulfilled, describing the experience as spiritual.

World.title: African players in Europe: Defender Hakimi’s historic hat-trick
World.content:
PSG’s Moroccan defender #02 Achraf Hakimi (R) celebrates with teammates after scoring his team’s fifth goal during the French L1 football match between Le Havre Athletic Club and Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) at Stade Oceane in Le Havre, north-western France on October 30, 2026. (Photo by Guillaume SALIGOT / AFP)

Reigning African Footballer of the Year and Paris Saint-Germain defender Achraf Hakimi claimed a first career hat-trick at the weekend in a 5-1 Ligue 1 rout of bottom club Le Havre.

Meanwhile, Nicolas Jackson continued to defy critics from a difficult spell at Chelsea by scoring his eighth goal in 12 appearances for Aston Villa, who drew 1-1 with Fulham.

AFP Sport highlights African headline-makers in the major European leagues:

FRANCE

ACHRAF HAKIMI (Paris Saint-Germain)

Morocco captain Hakimi was involved in all five goals as defending European champions and Ligue 1 leaders PSG inflicted a seventh defeat in nine matches on Le Havre. Apart from his hat-trick, he set up goals for Mika Godts and Senny Mayulu.

ENGLAND

NICOLAS JACKSON (Aston Villa)

In-form Jackson scored again, but it was not enough for Unai Emery’s men to defeat struggling Fulham. The Senegal international coolly slotted home from Johan Manzambi’s pass for a fifth Premier League goal in his last five games.

TAIWO AWONIYI (Coventry City)

Awoniyi netted his first league goal for Coventry in a 3-1 win over Sunderland that hauled the Sky Blues out of the relegation zone. The Nigerian made the most of his first start since September as he won possession himself before surging into the Sunderland box and firing into the bottom corner.

SPAIN

YAN DIOMANDE (Real Madrid)

Ivory Coast teenager Diomande completed the scoring before half-time as Real Madrid triumphed 3-0 at Racing Santander in La Liga. The record signing by the 15-time European champions lashed home from the edge of the box after 37 minutes.

ITALY

M’BALA NZOLA (Cagliari)

Angolan Nzola gave mid-table Cagliari the lead midway through the first half, but Serie A pacesetters Lazio hit back to win 2-1 in Rome. Nzola struck from the edge of the six-yard box to net in successive matches for the first time in 70 months.

GERMANY

SERHOU GUIRASSY (Borussia Dortmund)

His second-half goal put Borussia on track for an impressive 2-2 Bundesliga draw at leaders Bayern Munich. After Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane missed a penalty, Dortmund went to the other end of the pitch and Guirassy equalised. It brought the goal tally of the Guinea striker in all competitions to eight this season.

IBRAHIM MAZA (Bayer Leverkusen)

Leverkusen were outplayed by Stuttgart in a 4-2 defeat, but Maza left the pitch with his head held high. After the Algeria midfielder showcased his stunning dribbling, he scored after 79 minutes with an unstoppable header.

BILAL EL KHANNOUSS (Stuttgart)

El Khannouss provided the creative spark as Stuttgart snapped a run of poor form to win at Leverkusen. The Moroccan scored with a superb low shot early in the second half and helped create Stuttgart’s fourth for Ermedin Demirovic.

World.title: Tinubu reaffirms commitment to Project Nigeria
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu

President Bola Tinubu has reaffirmed his commitment to Project Nigeria, pledging to build a prosperous nation, invest in youths and pursue development guided by Almighty Allah and Nigerians’ aspirations.

The president stated this on Monday while reflecting on his spiritual journey to Saudi Arabia for the lesser Hajj, during which he was granted the rare privilege of praying inside the Holy Ka’abah.

King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, granted the President and members of his delegation access to the sacred structure in Makkah.

At the Ka’abah, Tinubu offered prayers of gratitude to Almighty Allah for the privilege of serving as Nigeria’s president and commander-in-chief of the armed forces.

Sheikh Dahlulah Muthawal of Masjid al-Haram led the President into the Ka’abah.

Tinubu thanked King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for granting him and members of his delegation the opportunity to enter the Holy Ka’abah and offer prayers.

He described the honour as historic and a deeply cherished spiritual experience, reflecting the longstanding bonds of friendship, mutual respect and cooperation between Nigeria and Saudi Arabia.

“I want to say a big thank you for the faith, for the recognition. I can’t believe the fencing of the Ka’abah is in green-white-green, which reminds us of the Nigerian identity.

“I thank the Crown Prince and all the administrators of the Holy Land. I thank them for the hospitality and recognition given to me as the leader of the delegation and the country.

“We are all facing challenges and hostility around us. We will overcome them with faith in God Almighty. I’m grateful forever. I thank the King and the royal Crown Prince.

“It is an honour that I enjoyed, and it is gracious of them to have allowed me to enter inside the Ka’abah. This is history,” he said.

The president said he prayed for wisdom and resilience to continue serving Nigerians, expressing confidence that Almighty Allah had granted his request.

“Well, I asked for wisdom and resilience to continue to serve the people. I know that prayer has been granted. Before the 2023 election, I did the same thing.

“I asked Allah to bless my Umrah then, and He did. And I promised that I would come back to thank Him,” the President said.

Reflecting on Surah Aal-Imran, Verse 26 of the Holy Qur’an, the President said sovereignty belonged ultimately to Almighty Allah, who grants and withdraws power.

He said the message underscored the need for leaders to exercise authority responsibly, with humility and in the service of the people.

“There is no other God but Almighty Allah. He is the giver and the taker. He owns power and authority.

“He says, ‘If I give you, use it well. If you don’t use it in accordance with my dictates, I can take it from you and give it to another person. I am the only one who has that authority.”

Tinubu said his faith had strengthened his conviction that becoming Nigeria’s leader was an extraordinary blessing that must be matched with dedicated service.

“I have faith in that, and I believe extremely well that He has done me and my country a great favour.

”Out of many millions of people, to be the President and Commander-in-Chief is a favour that only Almighty God can do to a human being,” he stated.

The president said his commitment to Project Nigeria had become stronger, assuring Nigerians of his determination to pursue policies that would promote prosperity and shared progress.

“My commitment to Project Nigeria is higher. I am determined to usher in prosperity and fully develop the country, consistent with the wish of Allah and the support of the people.

“It is important to put Allah first, then move on. Follow your conscience. Follow the right path that will lead Nigeria to that greatness,” he said.

On the economy, Tinubu expressed optimism about the progress recorded under his administration.

“The foundation is solid, and the economy has come out of the dark tunnel. This is inspiring,” he said.

He said nation-building required sustained investment in young Nigerians, stressing that present leadership decisions would shape how future generations remembered them.

“We need to build a future for our youth. If we don’t invest in their future, how do we want to be remembered as leaders 50 years from now? That’s the main thing. So this is a rare privilege to lead the country,” the president added.

Tinubu reiterated his administration’s commitment to strengthening the economy, expanding opportunities for young people and creating conditions for Nigerians to realise their potential.

He thanked Almighty Allah for the opportunity to lead Nigeria, pledging to justify the confidence reposed in him through purposeful leadership and sustained commitment to national progress. (NAN)

World.title: Sultan Turbans two sons, Murtala Dan’Iyan as Dallatun Sokoto
World.content:
By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto

SOKOTO — The Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III, has conferred traditional titles on two of his sons, Alhaji Murtala Abdulkadir Dan’Iyan Jarman Sokoto and 10 other distinguished Nigerians in recognition of their contributions to humanity and community development.

The ceremony, held on Sunday at the Sultan’s Palace in Sokoto, also witnessed the turbaning of two biological sons of the Sultan. Alhaji Abubakar Sadiq was turbaned Sarkin Dawakin Tsakar Gida, while Alhaji Shehu Abubakar received the title of Fagacin Sokoto.

The event marked the climax of a three-day programme organised by friends, associates and well-wishers of the new Dallatun Sokoto to celebrate his elevation into the traditional institution of the Sokoto Caliphate.

It attracted traditional rulers, politicians, senior government officials, Islamic scholars, business executives and community leaders from within and outside Nigeria.

Among those honoured were Alhaji Abubakar Hussain, who received the title of Sarkin Bai; Alhaji Aminu Isa-Buhari, Danmalikin Sokoto; Professor Mansur Ibrahim, Danmasanin Sokoto; and Professor Ishaq Oloyede, Kuliyan Sokoto.

Others were Dr Peter Igoh, Kakakin Daular Usmaniya; Representative Almustapha Rabah, Bauran Sokoto; Dr Balarabe Kakale, Wakilin Makarantar Daular Usmaniya; Alhaji Bello Abbas, Wakilin Tarihin Daular Usmaniya; and Alhaji Gandi Umar, Sarkin Galmar Sarkin Musulmi.

Speaking at the ceremony, the Sultan described the turbaning as a historic occasion organised by the Sultanate Council to recognise individuals whose contributions and achievements in their respective fields had distinguished them as worthy ambassadors of the Caliphate.

He said the traditional institution would continue to recognise and honour sons and daughters of the Caliphate who demonstrated commitment, integrity and outstanding performance in their various endeavours.

The monarch, however, reminded the new title holders that their elevation should not be regarded merely as a ceremonial honour but as a call to greater service and responsibility to their communities and society.

He urged them to remain their brothers’ keepers, promote peace, unity and peaceful coexistence, and offer constructive ideas to strengthen harmonious relationships within the Caliphate, Sokoto State and Nigeria.

In separate interviews after the ceremony, prominent personalities described the new Dallatun Sokoto as humble, honest and trustworthy, citing his philanthropic activities and readiness to assist people across religious, ethnic and social divides.

A father figure and mentor to the new title holder, Alhaji Umarun Kwabo AA Jarman Sokoto, described him as loyal, humble and dependable, saying his commitment to the service of God and humanity had earned him the confidence of those around him.

“I am optimistic that Dallatun Sokoto, Alhaji Murtala Abdulkadir Dan’Iyan Jarman Sokoto, will wear the shoes and crown in the service of God and humanity,” Kwabo said.

He expressed confidence that his protégé would sustain the values of service, loyalty and compassion associated with the traditional institution.

Also speaking, the Minister of Labour and Employment, Alhaji Muhammad Maigari Dingyadi, Katukan Sokoto, described the new Dallatun Sokoto as a trustworthy and loyal personality whose humanitarian activities had demonstrated his worthiness for the title.

Dingyadi said the honour was well deserved, adding that his consistent commitment to philanthropy and community service had earned him widespread admiration and made his elevation a source of pride to the people of Sokoto State.

The ceremony highlighted the role of the Sokoto Caliphate’s traditional institution in recognising contributions to society and encouraging service, unity and community development.

World.title: Trump says ‘at some point’ US will have to give Iran ‘the hammer’

World.title: 2027: Bury differences to re-elect Tinubu, Otu – Governor’s wife tells APC women
World.content:
….Betta Edu: We won’t repeat 2023 mistakes

By Ike Uchechukwu, Calabar

The wife of Cross River State Governor, Mrs Eyoawan Bassey Otu, has urged All Progressives Congress (APC) members to put aside their grievances, reconcile and unite ahead of the 2027 general elections, saying party cohesion is crucial to securing victory for President Bola Tinubu and Governor Bassey Otu.

Mrs Otu made the appeal at the weekend in Calabar during a meeting of the Women Mobilisation Directorate of the APC Campaign Council, organised ahead of the party’s rally in the state.

The meeting was held at the instance of the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu.

Addressing the gathering, the governor’s wife urged party members to let go of past disagreements and focus on the task ahead.

“Whatever has been bothering us, whatever has been our pain, let’s bury the hatchet and move on,” she said.

She stressed that the party’s immediate political objective should be the re-election of Tinubu and her husband in 2027.

Citing Ephesians 2, Mrs Otu urged members who felt offended or sidelined to remain committed to doing what was right, irrespective of how others treated them.

“Whether they love you or not, just keep doing the right thing. At the appropriate time, the reward will come,” she said.

The governor’s wife also highlighted her interventions in the health sector, disclosing that her free medical outreach had conducted more than 2,000 surgeries across 12 editions in three years.

She said the 13th edition of the programme was scheduled for the following week.

“My best might not be good enough for you, but I am trying my utmost best,” she said, explaining that her interventions were intended to bridge gaps in healthcare delivery while the governor focused on administration and infrastructure development.

Mrs Otu urged APC women to take the campaign to their homes, churches, markets and neighbourhoods, noting that their familiarity with residents placed them in a good position to drive grassroots mobilisation.

“Talk to your neighbours about APC. Your faces have been sold. They know you already,” she said.

Also speaking, former Minister of Humanitarian Affairs, Dr Betta Edu, who is Co-Director of the APC Women Mobilisation Directorate, declared that the party would not repeat the mistakes it made during the 2023 elections.

Edu commended the First Lady for empowering women and noted the increase in female representation in the Cross River State House of Assembly.

“I remember the days there was only one woman in the House,” she said.

She told the women that their commitment to the party would be measured by their performance at the polling units, rather than assurances and promises.

“There is only one line of authority in Cross River State. Our leader is Governor Bassey Otu, and his dear wife. What they tell me to do is what I will go and do,” she said.

Edu called for intensive grassroots mobilisation through door-to-door campaigns, church gatherings, prayer meetings and market engagements.

“We don’t even have up to 80 days for this election. It’s serious business. If you don’t organise up to 200 votes, know that you have failed yourself.

“Let’s not repeat the mistakes of 2023. We must ensure we win all the LGAs, 18 out of 18, for President Tinubu and Governor Otu,” she said.

World.title: Tinubu: I Remain Committed To Building A Prosperous Nigeria
World.content:
.Appreciates God for obliging him rare favour and privilege to lead Nigerians

.Thanks King Salman for granting him access to Ka’abah

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

President Bola Tinubu on Monday reiterated his commitment to Project Nigeria and his determination to build a prosperous nation, invest in the future of young Nigerians, and pursue development in line with the will of Almighty Allah and the people’s aspirations.

The President stated this while reflecting on his spiritual journey to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to perform Umrah, during which the Custodian of the Holy Mosques of Makkah and Madinah, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, granted him a rare privilege of leading Nigeria’s delegation to pray inside the Holy Ka’abah.

At the Ka’abah, Tinubu offered prayers of gratitude to Almighty Allah for the privilege of serving as Nigeria’s President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces.

Sheikh Dahlulah Muthawal of Masjid al-Haram led the President into the Ka’abah.

Tinubu thanked the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, for granting him and members of his Nigerian delegation the opportunity to enter the Holy Ka’abah in Makkah and offer prayers to Almighty Allah.

The President described the honour as a historic and deeply cherished spiritual experience, reflecting the longstanding bonds of friendship, mutual respect and cooperation between Nigeria and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

His words: “I want to say a big thank you for the faith, for the recognition. I can’t believe the fencing of the Ka’abah is in Green-White-Green, which reminds us of the Nigerian identity.

“I thank the Crown Prince and all the administrators of the holy land. I thank them for the hospitality and recognition given to me as the leader of the delegation and the country.

“We are all facing challenges and hostility around us. We will overcome them with faith in God Almighty. I’m grateful forever. I thank the King and the royal Crown Prince.

“It is an honour that I enjoyed, and it is gracious of them to have allowed me to enter inside the Ka’abah. This is history.”

Tinubu said he asked Allah for wisdom and resilience to continue serving Nigerians, and expressed confidence that his prayers have been answered.

According to him: “Well, I asked for wisdom and resilience to continue to serve the people. I know that prayer has been granted. Before the 2023 election, I did the same thing. I asked Allah to bless my Umrah then, and He did. And I promised that I would come back to thank Him.”

Reflecting on the message from the Holy Qur’an in Surah Aal-Imran, Verse 26, which affirms that Almighty Allah is the Owner of all sovereignty, granting power and authority to whom He wills and taking them away from whom He wills, the President said power is a trust that must be exercised responsibly, with humility and in the service of the people, recognising that no position of authority is permanent and that ultimate sovereignty belongs to Almighty Allah.

“There is no other God but Almighty Allah. He is the giver and the taker. He owns power and authority. He says, ‘ If I give you, use it well. If you don’t use it in accordance with my dictates, I can take it from you and give it to another person. I am the only One who has that authority,” the President said, quoting the words of the Qur’an.

Tinubu said faith in Allah had strengthened his conviction that his emergence as Nigeria’s leader was an extraordinary blessing that must be matched with dedicated service to the country.

“I have faith in that, and I believe extremely well that He has done me and my country a great favour. Out of many millions of people, to be the President and Commander-in-Chief is a favour that only Almighty God can do to a human being,” he stated.

The President emphasised that his commitment to Project Nigeria had become even stronger, assuring Nigerians of his resolve to pursue policies and programmes that would promote prosperity, national development and shared progress.

“My commitment to Project Nigeria is higher. I am determined to usher in prosperity and fully develop the country, consistent with the wish of Allah and the support of the people.

“It is important to put Allah first, then move on. Follow your conscience. Follow the right path that will lead Nigeria to that greatness,” Tinubu said.

On the nation’s economic outlook, the President expressed optimism about the progress made under his watch, describing the economic foundation as solid and the country’s emergence from a difficult period as encouraging.

“The foundation is solid, and the economy has come out of the dark tunnel. This is inspiring.”

He maintained, however, that nation-building requires sustained investment in young Nigerians’ future, noting that today’s leaders’ decisions will determine how future generations remember them.

“We need to build a future for our youth. If we don’t invest in their future, how do we want to be remembered as leaders 50 years from now? That’s the main thing. So this is a rare privilege to lead the country,” he added.

Tinubu reiterated that his administration would remain focused on strengthening the country’s economic foundations, expanding opportunities for young people and creating the conditions necessary for Nigerians to realise their potential.

The President thanked Almighty Allah for the opportunity to lead Nigeria and reaffirmed his determination to justify the confidence the Nigerian people have placed in him through purposeful leadership and an enduring commitment to national progress.

Apparently seized by emotions, Minister of Justice Lateef Fagbemi (SAN), his Health and Social Welfare counterpart, Prof Ali Pate, Governors of Borno, Sokoto, Jigawa, Kaduna, Yobe and Kwara States as well as captains of industry, including Chairman of BUA, Abdulsamad Isiaka Rabiu and CEO of Oando, Wale Tinubu, expressed gratitude to Allah and the President for allowing them to enter and pray with him in the most holy mosque and sacred ground in Islam.

World.title: Insecurity: As 30 State Houses of Assembly Okay State Police…
World.content:
With 30 State Houses of Assembly endorsing state police, Nigeria moves closer to decentralised policing. But constitutional approval, operational legislation, funding, safeguards and implementation challenges remain critical to success, writes Sunday Aborisade.

Nigeria’s decades-long debate over the establishment of state police appears to be approaching a decisive turning point, following the endorsement of the proposed constitutional amendment by no fewer than 30 State Houses of Assembly.

The development, announced by the Senate Leader, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, represents a significant milestone in efforts to decentralise the country’s security architecture and introduce a policing arrangement that allows state governments to establish their own police services alongside the existing federal structure.

For a country grappling with banditry, kidnapping, terrorism, communal conflicts and other violent crimes, the proposed reform has far-reaching implications for national security, federalism and the protection of lives and property.

However, beyond the excitement generated by the legislative breakthrough, Nigerians must understand two separate but interconnected initiatives: the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, which seeks to provide constitutional authority for state police, and the proposed National Policing Bill, 2026, which will establish the operational, administrative and regulatory framework.

While the former provides the constitutional foundation, the latter prescribes the institutional arrangements, standards and safeguards required to implement the reform.

This distinction is important because approval of the constitutional amendment does not automatically authorise governors to recruit police officers, establish commands or commence independent policing operations.

Advocates of state police have consistently argued that Nigeria’s centralised policing structure has become inadequate for a federation of its size, population and security complexities.

They maintain that a single national police organisation cannot always respond effectively to the peculiar security challenges confronting communities across 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

State governments, being closer to their communities, are considered better positioned to identify local threats, understand the terrain, communicate in indigenous languages and develop intelligence networks capable of preventing criminal activities.

Opponents, however, fear that governors could turn state police formations into instruments of political intimidation, persecution of opponents and suppression of dissent. Others question the financial capacity of several states to maintain properly equipped and professionally trained police organisations.

Despite these concerns, the National Assembly has taken the process considerably further.

The Senate passed the State Police Constitution Alteration Bill on June 24, 2026, while the House of Representatives approved it on July 23. Following the passage by both chambers, the Clerk to the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, transmitted the proposal to the 36 State Houses of Assembly on September 16 for consideration and approval.

Under Section 9(2) of the 1999 Constitution, an alteration requires resolutions from not less than two-thirds of all State Houses of Assembly. With 36 states, the constitutional requirement is 24.

On October 23, the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill announced that the required threshold had been achieved. Six days later, on October 29, Bamidele disclosed that the National Assembly had received formal reports indicating that at least 30 state assemblies had endorsed the amendment.

Although the constitutional requirement had already been satisfied upon securing 24 approvals, the additional endorsements provide a broader political foundation for the proposed reform.

Bamidele, who is also Vice Chairman of the Senate Committee on the Review of the 1999 Constitution, described the development as a historic breakthrough.

He said the National Assembly intended to complete the outstanding legislative procedures and transmit the amendment to President Bola Tinubu for assent latest by December 2026.

The remaining procedures include the consideration and collation of reports from the state legislatures and the passage of the necessary resolutions by both chambers before transmission to the President.

The Senate Leader stressed that the proposed reform was not intended to establish state armies or weaken the Federal Government’s authority. Rather, it would create state-led, community-based policing arrangements operating within constitutional safeguards, professional standards, oversight mechanisms and human rights protections.

Perhaps the most important issue in the ongoing debate is the distinction between the constitutional amendment and the National Policing Bill.

The Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, provides the legal authority for Nigeria to move from its existing centralised police arrangement towards a dual structure comprising the Federal Police Service and State Police Services.

In practical terms, it removes the constitutional obstacles preventing individual states from establishing their own police organisations.

The National Policing Bill, on the other hand, will provide the operational framework, including recruitment requirements, training procedures, institutional responsibilities, accountability mechanisms, funding arrangements and minimum professional standards.

This means constitutional permission does not automatically translate into operational readiness.

The Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, chaired by the President’s Chief of Staff, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, was established to develop the comprehensive legislative framework.

On October 19, the group submitted the draft National Policing Bill, 2026, alongside 29 consequential amendment bills, to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting review and validation.

The proposed legislation is expected to address existing legal provisions designed around a single national police organisation that may become inconsistent with the introduction of state police services.

The official National Policing Bill information portal explains that the constitutional amendment is enabling and phased.

Under the proposed arrangement, a state may possess the constitutional authority to establish its police service but cannot commence operational policing until it has enacted the necessary state legislation and obtained certification that it meets the national minimum standards prescribed by an Act of the National Assembly.

Consequently, the constitutional amendment and the National Policing Bill must progress together. One establishes the legal foundation, while the other provides the institutional machinery for implementation.

The proposed arrangement will introduce two levels of police administration: the Federal Police Service, retaining responsibility for national policing functions and federal offences, and individual State Police Services established by states that satisfy the necessary legal, administrative, operational and financial requirements.

The intention is to enable state police officers to respond more directly to security threats within their jurisdictions, while federal police retain responsibilities requiring national coordination.

These include terrorism, organised crime, federal offences and security challenges extending beyond individual state boundaries.

The final legislation will determine the precise division of responsibilities and command structures.

Cooperation will also be essential. Kidnapping incidents involving the movement of victims or suspects across state boundaries, for instance, will require coordinated operations between affected state police formations and federal security agencies.

Similarly, organised criminal networks operating across several states cannot be effectively confronted without intelligence sharing, integrated criminal information management and clearly defined command responsibilities.

The success of the proposed system will therefore depend on cooperation rather than competition between the different levels of policing.

One of the strongest objections to state police has been the fear that governors could deploy the new institutions against political opponents, critics and democratic activities.

These concerns cannot be dismissed, particularly in a political environment where relationships between state governments and opposition parties are often characterised by intense rivalry.

For this reason, the proposed National Policing Bill places considerable emphasis on accountability, independent oversight, professional standards and human rights protection.

Its framework identifies critical areas requiring regulation, including recruitment, vetting, training, discipline, complaints management, firearms control, financial sustainability and institutional supervision.

It also envisages independent oversight arrangements and state-readiness certification before any state police service can commence operations.

Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Lateef Fagbemi, had earlier emphasised that the proposed legislation was intended to prevent state police from becoming instruments of political persecution.

For the reform to enjoy public confidence, state police institutions must remain accountable to the Constitution and the law rather than the personal interests of governors or political office holders.

Independent complaints mechanisms, transparent recruitment, professional discipline and judicial oversight will therefore be indispensable.

Another major challenge concerns the financial implications of establishing and maintaining state police organisations.

Nigeria’s 36 states have different revenue profiles, economic capacities and competing development priorities.

While some may possess the resources to establish modern police formations, others could struggle to finance recruitment, training, salaries, pensions, equipment, vehicles, communication facilities and operational accommodation.

Establishing a police organisation goes beyond recruiting officers and providing uniforms. It requires sustainable funding, continuous professional development, adequate equipment and institutional structures capable of maintaining acceptable operational standards.

The National Policing Bill is expected to address these concerns through provisions dealing with sustainable financing, national standards and possible grant support.

Importantly, states that are not immediately ready to establish their own police services are expected to continue benefiting from the Federal Police.

This phased arrangement is intended to prevent the reform from creating security gaps in states that cannot immediately establish independent police formations.

Nevertheless, the National Assembly must ensure that the final legislation clearly defines funding responsibilities and transparent criteria for determining when a state is financially and institutionally ready.

Without such provisions, decentralised policing could create significant disparities in security capacity across the federation.

Developments surrounding state police have also acquired a political dimension ahead of the 2027 general election.

Speaking when members of the Arewa Revival Project, a northern youth organisation with membership across the 19 northern states, visited him in Abuja, Senate President, Senator Godswill Akpabio expressed optimism that Nigeria could soon embrace decentralised policing.

He disclosed that about 30 state assemblies had endorsed the constitutional amendment, describing the development as an important step towards improving national security.

Akpabio also used the occasion to canvass support for President Tinubu’s re-election, urging the northern youths to mobilise grassroots backing for the administration.

His remarks reflected the growing intersection between governance, security reforms and electoral politics as political parties and their supporters prepare for the next general election.

However, the proposed establishment of state police should be treated as a national institutional reform rather than a partisan political achievement. Its ultimate success or failure will affect Nigerians irrespective of their political affiliations or the parties controlling their respective states.

With the constitutional threshold achieved, attention will now shift to the outstanding legislative and executive responsibilities.

First, the National Assembly must complete the collation and consideration of reports received from the State Houses of Assembly. Both chambers must then pass the necessary resolutions before transmitting the constitutional amendment to the President for assent.

Bamidele has indicated that the National Assembly intends to conclude these procedures by December 2026.

Second, the Presidential Working Group must complete the review and validation of the National Policing Bill and its accompanying consequential amendments before the proposed legislation undergoes the necessary executive and legislative processes.

Third, the National Assembly must scrutinise the operational framework, particularly its provisions on federal and state jurisdictions, recruitment, funding, oversight, intelligence sharing, human rights and accountability.

Fourth, individual states will be expected to enact enabling laws and demonstrate their readiness to establish police services.

This means that even after the constitutional amendment and National Policing Act have been completed, the commencement of operations will depend on each state’s compliance with prescribed conditions.

Consequently, some states may establish their police services earlier than others, depending on their financial and institutional preparedness.

Interestingly, Bamidele’s address at the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies, Kuru, went beyond the state police debate to raise another important question about the quality of lawmaking in Nigeria.

He argued that the performance of the 10th National Assembly should not be judged principally by the number of bills passed into law but by their measurable impact on citizens.

He cited legislation on student loans, minimum wage, taxation, social investment, electoral administration, cybercrime, insurance and regional development commissions as examples of the Assembly’s legislative interventions.

The Senate Leader, however, acknowledged that good laws alone cannot guarantee good governance. Legislation, he argued, must be relevant, evidence-based, implementable, adequately funded, properly administered, effectively monitored and periodically reviewed.

That argument is particularly relevant to the state police initiative.

Nigeria has enacted several laws and established numerous institutions, but implementation has frequently remained a major challenge.

The establishment of state police must therefore not become another constitutional milestone celebrated primarily through speeches, ceremonies and political declarations.

Its real value will be determined by whether it reduces criminal activities, improves intelligence gathering, strengthens community confidence and makes the protection of lives and property more effective.

The National Assembly must ensure that the final legislation establishes measurable performance standards and mechanisms for holding federal and state police authorities accountable. Governors, on their part, must demonstrate that their commitment to state police goes beyond the political attraction of controlling another security institution.

Ultimately, the endorsement of the constitutional amendment by at least 30 state assemblies represents an important development in Nigeria’s search for a more responsive security architecture.

But the journey is not over. The constitutional amendment must be completed, the National Policing Bill must become law, states must establish the necessary institutions and the prescribed safeguards must be enforced.

For Nigerians, the central expectation is straightforward: a policing system that responds faster to emergencies, understands local security challenges, prevents crimes more effectively and protects citizens without fear or favour.

The real measure of this reform will not be the number of state police commands established or officers recruited, but whether Nigerians can live, work, travel and conduct their daily activities with greater security and confidence.

World.title: Poultry Division without a hen
World.content:
One of the most funnily memorable stories I ever heard from a state governor was in 2001, when then Borno State Governor Mala Kachallah paid us a visit at New Nigerian, where I was the editor. He had left his state capital, Maiduguri in some turmoil because the state NLC branch was demanding implementation of the newly approved national minimum wage. The governor said BOSG was handicapped because it had the second largest number of civil servants in Nigeria, 30,000, so he had to retrench some workers before he could implement the new wage. NLC rejected that option. To give us an idea of the problem he faced, Kachallah said, “The Poultry Division of the Borno State Ministry of Agriculture; their last hen died in 1981, but they have 571 staffers, and every year they bring a promotion list.”

Eleven years later, I heard a slightly different complaint from Borno State Governor Kashim Shettima. In response to Boko Haram attacks, he had banned motorcycles from Maiduguri streets and instead bought 5,000 tricycles, all of which were sold to beneficiaries at a discounted price, to be paid for instalmentally. Many beneficiaries turned around, sold them at an even lower price and squandered the money. The governor was unhappy; he wondered if such attitude can happen anywhere else. I said, “Sir, take heart. I don’t know about the South, but in almost every Northern state, the same thing will happen if you sell anything on loan at a discounted price.”

The Kachallah/Shettima worry in Borno reminded me of what then Niger State Governor Musa Inuwa told me in 1993. He had proposed to retrench some skilled civil servants and instead get for them bank loans to set up businesses. They rejected the plan and threatened to go on strike. Inuwa said, “Niger State Scholarships Board has eight typists but only three typewriters. Niger State Ministry of Works has 60 skilled artisans, carpenters, electricians and plumbers who are not doing any work. They are to be found sitting in front of the ministry’s premises, and small thing they will say “Strike! Strike!”

I used to think that governors are well fed, but on two occasions I encountered a hungry governor. In 1993, Governor Musa Inuwa gave me an 8am appointment in Minna but when I arrived at his office, he had a sudden visitor in Abia State Governor Dr. Ogbonnaya Onu. I had to wait for two hours until he escorted Onu out of town. When I was ushered into his office, he apologized for keeping me waiting, said we should proceed with the interview, even though he had not eaten his breakfast. So I said, “Sir, please have your breakfast. I will wait in CPS’s office.” He was very grateful!

In 2002, Jigawa State Governor Ibrahim Saminu Turaki arrived very late for an interview at New Nigerian. An hour into the interview, he suddenly said he was very hungry, and asked if the man who used to sell roasted meat at nearby NEPA roundabout was still there. Staffers rushed out and brought hot roasted meat. The governor retreated into the MD’s office, ate his fill, and returned to continue the interview.

Most memorable was Abacha-era Works Minister Major General Abdulkarim Adisa’s press conference in Abuja. A reporter audaciously asked him why he awarded contracts only to his friends. The rambunctious Adisa said, “Those who say I give contracts only to my friends, I pray to God to make them minister so that they will give contracts to their enemies.”

In 2000AD, as Editor of New Nigerian, I accompanied my managing director Dr. Omar Faruk Ibrahim to Sokoto to pacify Governor Attahiru Bafarawa. He was very angry because, in our inside page, his picture was used to illustrate a story about a Sokoto magistrate court that convicted two homosexuals. Bafarawa was certain that New Nigerian’s Sokoto reporter planted it that way to embarrass him. We struggled to convince him that the reporter was far away from the production center and could not possibly know how a sub editor carelessly designed that page.

In 1991, very fresh into my journalism career as a Citizen magazine reporter, I was in Katsina to interview military governor Colonel John Yahaya Madaki. As we sat in the visitors’ room, Madaki saw us on a CCTV camera. He stormed out, chased away a woman and a male contractor, then came for me and said, “Who are you?” His Chief Press Secretary Abubakar Yar’adua quickly intervened and said he brought me. I was ushered into the office and sat in the conference area. Madaki left his desk, came near me and sat on the center table, his starched khaki menacingly rubbing my leg. I was young and audacious then, so I said, “Sir, please sit down on the chair.” The Jungle Expert exploded; “This is my office! I will sit down where I want! If you don’t want, pack your things and go!” But we had a rich two-hour interview.

My next explosive gubernatorial interview came 18 years later, with Adamawa State Governor Murtala Nyako in Abuja. Two of us were ushered to the dining table where the governor sat. Looking at the other man, he said, “Girigiri [Second Republic Senator Girigiri Lawan of Yobe], I asked you to come because I am going to talk to this journalist, and I do not trust him.” Turning to me, he said, “You, you hate the people of Adamawa State!” I quickly replied, “Sir, I was born in Adamawa State.” “It’s a lie!” “It is true!” “When?” “In Northern Nigeria. My father was the D.O in Mubi.” Nyako then changed tack and said, “I know why you are mischievous. It is because your family’s cattle have finished. There is no person more evil than a Fulani man whose cattle has finished.” I said, “Sir, my grandfather left behind many cows.” “How many?” I said, “Up to 30.” He said, “My father left behind 15,000 cows!”

Katsina State Governor Umaru Musa Yar’adua was one of the gentlest governors I interviewed, in 2001. I [audaciously] asked him why he drove a car with three commissioners to go on a condolence visit, why he stopped at a roadside kiosk to buy cigarettes, and why, as governor, he prayed under a Tsamiya tree instead of entering the Friday mosque to pray beside the Emir. Malam Umaru looked at me quietly and said, “I have been praying under that tree for 18 years. Why should I enter the mosque and pray beside the Emir, only to come out again one day when I am no longer the governor and resume praying under that tree? You see, all these things, my fear is for women and children. Me, any day I lose privileges, I can adjust, but when women and children are used to something, they find it difficult to adjust. It is the cause of the corruption all around.”

In 1992, I interviewed Sokoto State Governor Malam Yahaya Abdulkarim and asked him about a protracted quarrel between himself and Senator Garba Ila Gada. The governor looked at me and said, “Turn off your tape recorder.” He then said, “You know the real reason for this quarrel between me and him? It is because he wants this chair.”

I once asked former Abia State governor and then ANPP national chairman Dr. Ogbonnaya Onu about the fiasco at ANPP’s 1999 Kaduna convention, when he was nominated as presidential candidate and then substituted with AD candidate Olu Falae. Onu laughed heartily and said, “My brother, it is something you do not wish to happen even to your worst enemy.”

In 2001, Kogi State Governor Abubakar Audu invited me to Lokoja to mark two years of his administration. When I was ushered in, he said no interview until I first toured his projects. His Chief Press Secretary then grabbed a car and we charged through the state until well after dusk, inspecting roads, housing projects, the Audu Oyigi eye hospital and the then new Abubakar Audu University at Ayingba. On our way back I told the CPS that I was really impressed with what I saw. So he said, “When we go to see Oga, please praise him! My Oga likes praise. Please praise him very well, and agbada will flow!”

Small fry like me, I once found myself settling a quarrel between two governors. Former Zamfara State governor Senator Ahmed Sani came to my Abuja office in 2009 and said, “I come to report your friend [his successor, Governor Mahmud Aliyu Shinkafi].” He told me that he went to Government House to see the governor, was told that he was praying in the mosque, so he waited for him in his office. After a very long wait, he asked what was delaying the governor’s return, and the office messenger told him that when the governor heard that Yarima was waiting for him in the office, he summoned his car to the mosque and sneaked away.

I then sent a message to Governor Shinkafi and said “Sir, Yarima has reported you to me.” The very gentle Shinkafi replied that he will be in Abuja in two days and will send for me, which he did. I told him what Yarima said, and he said, “Yarima was wrong!” That there was going to be an ANPP primaries contest in Bakura LGA, and he asked Yarima who was his preferred candidate, but he said both men were the same to him. The two men went for the primaries and after one of them won, Yarima said he preferred the other one. “That was why I went away.”

For the first [and possibly the last] time in my life, I found myself scolding a sitting governor. I said, “Sir, you made a mistake by going away. As the Governor, you should have stayed and told him firmly that he was wrong. But by sneaking away, you spoilt the case.”

World.title: Our Commitment to Ndi Enugu: The Journey So Far
World.content:
GUEST COLUMNIST BY PETER MBAH

First let me begin by giving my profound gratitude to the entire Management and Staff of Godfrey Okoye University and its other collaborators for this excellent forum – and the opportunity it offers for an enriching dialogue.

My dear people of Enugu State, I want to begin today by asking you to remember something.

Think back to May 2023, when we first assumed office. Think about the condition of our state, the difficulties we faced, and the expectations we had gradually learned to live without.

I want us to be honest about that period, because unless we remember where we began, it becomes difficult to appreciate the distance we have travelled.

There was a time when Monday was no longer an ordinary working day in Enugu. Shops remained closed. Roads were deserted. Parents were afraid to send their children to school. People who depended on their daily earnings had to surrender an entire day’s income because others had decided they should remain indoors.

Consider what that meant for a woman selling food in the market. Her customers were at home, her produce was deteriorating, and the money she needed to support her family would not be earned that day.

Or the young man who had borrowed money to start a business, only to discover that one working day in every week had effectively been taken away from him.

Our children who lost a whole academic year before their compulsory external exam paper fell on a Monday. That was the reality we inherited.

Our roads were in poor condition. Public services had deteriorated. Many schools were struggling to provide the kind of education our children deserved. Our health facilities needed substantial investment.

And Enugu, a city that had once been the natural centre of commercial, political and cultural life across the region, was gradually losing that position.

Businesses were looking elsewhere. Major events were moving to other cities. Our airport had barely two incoming flights a day. Perhaps the greatest danger was that we might begin to accept these conditions as normal. Because when people live with the same difficulties for long enough, their expectations begin to change. They stop asking what is possible and concentrate instead on getting through the day. I knew we could do better.

I had spent much of my working life building businesses, dealing with challenges and making decisions about the future. I understood that Enugu possessed enormous resources, but I also knew that those resources would achieve very little unless we created the conditions for people to use them.

Our greatest resource was already here: the people of Enugu. What was missing was a clear direction, the determination to pursue it, and a government prepared to take responsibility for the results.

When I presented my original Statement of Purpose, I set out an ambition that some people considered almost impossible. We proposed to grow Enugu’s economy from approximately $4.4 billion to at least $30 billion within eight years, making our state one of Nigeria’s three leading economies.

We also committed ourselves to the long-term ambition of eliminating poverty. Those were enormous goals. I knew that. But I wanted us to understand the scale of the change required.

An economy cannot grow substantially if businesses cannot operate safely, if electricity is unreliable, if roads are impassable, or if young people leave school without the skills they need.

These problems are connected. They have to be addressed together. So, we began by identifying the foundations of a functioning state: security, education, healthcare, infrastructure, productive industries and institutions capable of delivering results.

And we made some difficult choices. We committed an unusually large share of our resources to education because we recognised that the future of Enugu would depend upon the abilities of its children.

We began restoring security and normal economic activity. We invested in roads and transport, planned improvements to healthcare and set about attracting the businesses and industries that would create employment.

I also knew that government itself had to change. For too long, public announcements had been treated as achievements. A project could be celebrated at its commencement and then disappear from public attention.

I wanted a different standard.

If we promise a school, people should be able to visit it. If we announce a road, they should be able to travel on it. If we say that public services are improving, citizens should be able to tell us whether that is true.

This is why accountability, measurable performance and public participation were written into our original Statement of Purpose. We were asking the people of Enugu to place their confidence in a programme of substantial change. We therefore had an obligation to demonstrate, through our work, that their confidence was justified.

Distinguished Guests, Today, I can stand before you and point to changes that have taken place across our state.

One of the earliest and most important was the restoration of normal activity on Mondays. I remember how deeply the sit-at-home restrictions had affected people’s lives. The fear was real, and the economic consequences were considerable.

Today, people are going about their business with a freedom that had been denied to them for far too long. A trader can plan a full working week. Children can attend school. Businesses can receive customers, move goods and keep their employees working.

It may seem strange that we should celebrate something as ordinary as being able to go to work on Monday. But anyone who lived through those years understands its importance.

Security gave us a foundation upon which other changes could begin.

We turned our attention to the condition of our roads and the movement of people around the state.

Road construction is often discussed in kilometres and contract values. Most people experience it rather differently. They know the road that used to damage their vehicles, the journey that took too long, or the difficulty of getting produce from a farm to a market.

These are the experiences that matter. We have undertaken substantial road development and begun introducing a more organised transport system, including new buses and terminals.

Our ambition is to make movement around Enugu safer, more comfortable and more dependable, while connecting communities to the opportunities being created across the state.

The same thinking informs our work in aviation. When we assumed office, Enugu had barely two incoming flights a day. In our recent review, we counted more than fifteen.

That change tells us something about the renewed interest in our state. Through Enugu Air and our wider aviation plans, we want to strengthen the connections between Enugu, the rest of Nigeria and international markets.

A businessperson should be able to reach customers and partners without unnecessary difficulty. Investors should be able to visit our state. People who have made their lives elsewhere should find it easier to return, visit family and participate in our economy.

Of course, improved air travel alone will not transform the life of someone living in a rural community. But a growing economy needs these connections, and our responsibility is to ensure that the opportunities they generate reach much further.

That brings me to education. I have always believed that the most important investment we can make is in the abilities of our children.

Consider the world into which a child entering school today will eventually graduate. Technology is already changing the way people work. Some occupations will disappear, others will be transformed, and entirely new industries will emerge. That child needs an education that prepares them to think independently, solve problems, communicate well and adapt to circumstances we cannot yet predict. This is the thinking behind our 260 Smart Green Schools, designed to bring a new standard of education to every ward in Enugu State. We want children in our rural communities to have access to the kind of learning opportunities that parents might once have believed were available only in the most privileged schools.

Imagine what that could mean for a family whose children are the first generation to receive such an education. A daughter might develop the skills to build an agricultural business using modern methods. A son might become an engineer, a software developer or a skilled technician. Another child might become a teacher or a healthcare professional and return to serve the community in which they grew up.

We cannot know exactly what each child will become. But we can give them a stronger foundation from which to choose. That is why education occupies such a central place in our development programme. And we must ensure that the economy grows alongside it. There would be little satisfaction in educating a generation of talented young people if they could find no opportunity to put their abilities to work.

Our plans for agriculture, industry, technology, energy and commerce are intended to create those opportunities.

Take agriculture: Enugu has fertile land, experienced farmers and communities with generations of knowledge about food production.

Yet many farmers still struggle with poor access to equipment, storage, processing facilities and markets. They work hard, take considerable risks and often receive too little of the final value of what they produce.

We want to build an agricultural economy in which more of that value remains here. Think of a farmer who grows cassava. If the crop can be processed locally, it creates work beyond the farm. Someone operates the equipment. Someone maintains it. Someone packages the finished product. Others transport and sell it.

The income generated by that activity can support families and create further businesses within the community. Now imagine similar opportunities developing around other crops and agricultural products across Enugu. That is the practical meaning of agricultural industrialisation.

Our plans for energy and industrial development follow the same logic. Reliable electricity can change the prospects of a small business. A tailor can work more efficiently. A food processor can preserve produce. A manufacturer can operate equipment without constantly depending on expensive alternative power.

We have set out major ambitions for increasing electricity generation and attracting industrial investment because these are essential to the kind of economy we want to build. Some of these undertakings are long-term. Their benefits will develop over several years, and we must be realistic about the work involved. But we cannot afford to postpone them.

I also want to speak about healthcare. For a parent with a sick child, the most important question is whether good medical attention is available when it is needed.

For an expectant mother, it is whether she can receive proper care during pregnancy and childbirth.

For an elderly person, it is whether treatment can be obtained without travelling an unreasonable distance or placing an impossible burden on the family.

These are the circumstances against which our healthcare investments must be judged.

We have been working to improve primary healthcare facilities and strengthen services across the state. We are also investing in the wider systems needed to make healthcare more effective.

There is still work ahead, particularly in ensuring that improvements reach every community. And I want to acknowledge that openly. I know that some people listening today are already experiencing the benefits of the changes we have made. Others are still waiting for a road to be completed, a facility to become fully operational, or a new economic opportunity to reach their community.

I understand that frustration. A government must be judged by the experiences of all its citizens, including those who have yet to see the full benefit of its work. That is why our programme must continue, and why we must remain willing to listen and make corrections.

Now consider the larger investments we are pursuing. We are working to expand Enugu’s aviation connections, develop tourism destinations, attract major hospitality investment, improve electricity supply and create new areas for business and residential development.

Some people will understandably ask what these projects have to do with their daily lives. It is a fair question. A new hotel can bring visitors and create demand for food, transport, maintenance, laundry, construction and many other services. A tourism destination can support local businesses. Better electricity can make investment in manufacturing more attractive.

But government must do more than hope that these benefits spread. We must help our people acquire the skills, access the finance and establish the businesses that allow them to participate. A large project should create possibilities for many smaller enterprises. That is how economic development begins to reach into households and communities.

We have made substantial progress in restoring Enugu’s position as a place where people want to live, work, invest and visit.

The changes are visible, and the scale of our ambition is becoming clearer. We should take pride in what has been achieved, while recognising how much remains to be done.

My fellow citizens, there is a reason I have spent time today looking back at where we began and examining the progress we have made.

I want us to understand the opportunity now before us. We are living through a period of extraordinary change. Technology is reshaping industries across the world. The way food is produced, goods are manufactured, businesses are managed and knowledge is shared is changing faster than at any previous point in our lives. The opportunities created by these changes are considerable, but they will not be distributed equally. Places that invest in education, infrastructure, skills and productive enterprise will be better prepared to benefit. Those that fail to prepare may find themselves falling further behind. This matters enormously for Enugu.

We have a young population, talented people, valuable natural resources and a long history of enterprise. We also have a generation of children growing up at a time when the possibilities available to them could be greater than anything their parents experienced.

But those possibilities depend upon the choices we make now. A young person who wants to establish a business needs more than encouragement. They need access to skills, customers, finance and dependable infrastructure.

A farmer who wants to increase production needs practical support and a market in which the additional effort can be rewarded. A community that wants better healthcare or education needs functioning institutions and a government that responds to its concerns. These are the connections we must strengthen in the years ahead.

Our Statement of Purpose was built around the ambition of creating a productive economy and improving the lives of our people. That remains our direction. The next phase must deepen the work already begun, bring projects into full operation and extend their benefits to communities that are still waiting. We must also create more opportunities for our young people to participate in the industries of the future.

The development of technology, modern agriculture, manufacturing, tourism and other productive sectors will require a workforce with new capabilities. Our schools, training institutions, businesses and government agencies must work together to develop them.

There is urgency in this work because time matters. A child who receives a poor education today cannot simply recover those years later. A business that closes because it cannot operate may never reopen. A talented young person who leaves because there is no opportunity at home may build their future somewhere else.

We cannot afford to lose another generation of potential. And this is why the moment before us is so important. The foundations we have begun to establish give us an opportunity to move faster and achieve more. The decisions we make over the coming years will determine how widely the benefits of this transformation are shared and how firmly they become established.

I believe Enugu is capable of becoming one of the great centres of economic and social progress in Nigeria. But that future will depend upon the continued effort of government, the confidence of investors, the enterprise of our businesses and the participation of our people.

Which brings me to the most important invitation I want to make today.

My dear people of Enugu, when we began this journey, I asked you to believe that our state could become something greater. Today, I am asking you to become more deeply involved in making that future a reality. Government can create the conditions for progress, but the energy that sustains it comes from the people. It comes from the teacher who takes responsibility for the children in her classroom, the business owner who trains young employees, the farmer who introduces a better method of production, and the community that comes together to solve a problem.

It also comes from citizens who ask difficult questions, demand accountability and contribute their ideas to the decisions that affect them. I want that relationship between government and citizens to grow stronger.

Our original Statement of Purpose committed us to transparent government, measurable performance and public participation. These commitments matter because people are more likely to take responsibility for something when they understand it and have a meaningful voice in shaping it.

When a new school opens in your community, I want you to regard its success as a shared responsibility. The government must provide the facilities, teachers and resources. Parents and community leaders also have an important part to play in supporting the children who attend it.

When a new road connects your community to a market, I want us to consider the businesses and opportunities that connection could support.

When an investment creates the possibility of employment, I want our young people to be ready with the skills and determination to take advantage of it.

And when government falls short, I want citizens to speak up and help us identify what needs to improve. This is how a stronger relationship between the people and their institutions is built. I am particularly conscious of the responsibility we carry towards the next generation. Our children will inherit the state we leave behind. They will live with the consequences of our decisions, our investments and the opportunities we either created or failed to recognise.

And I believe that when they look back upon this period in Enugu’s history, they should be able to say that something important happened here. That a generation of people looked honestly at the condition of their state, decided it could do better and began the difficult work of changing its future. That the progress continued because people across Enugu chose to participate.

We have already seen what can happen when a state begins to regain its confidence. People return to their businesses. Investment begins to grow. New institutions emerge. Young people see possibilities that were previously difficult to imagine.

There is a growing sense that Enugu is moving forward again. But the greatest part of this journey is still before us. I spoke earlier about the dawn. In May 2023, we stood at the beginning of a new day. There was uncertainty about what lay ahead, but we knew that the time had come to change direction.

Today, the first light has given way to morning. We can see the work taking shape around us, and we can begin to appreciate the scale of what is possible. We are now in the heat of the morning, when the real labour of the day must be done. And I want every citizen of Enugu to recognise the importance of this hour.

Because history sometimes gives a people an opportunity to change the direction of their future. Such opportunities do not remain open indefinitely.

The world is moving quickly, and we must be prepared to move with it.

This is one moment in the long history of Enugu. This is a moment of extraordinary possibility for our people. And I believe this is the moment we must seize. The work we have begun needs the commitment of all of us.

I ask you to bring your ideas, your skills, your enterprise and your experience into the life of our state. Take an interest in what is happening in your community. Help us identify problems and develop practical solutions. Encourage our young people to learn, create and build their futures here.

We have the opportunity to leave something of lasting value to those who come after us: A state with stronger institutions, a more productive economy, better opportunities for its children and communities whose people can take pride in what they have achieved together.

That is the Enugu I want us to build. And I believe we have reached the point in our history when we can begin to make that ambition real.

My fellow citizens, the morning is upon us. There is much work ahead, and I am ready to continue that work with you.

Ndi Enugu, Tomorrow Is Here.

Thank you.

Mbah, Govenor of Enugu State, presented the manifesto performance scorecard at Godfrey Okoye University, Enugu

World.title: Kwankwaso, Yusuf: South Must Retain Power in 2027
World.content:
Igbo torn between emotion and reason, declares Soludo

Says those who couldn’t defeat Tinubu out of power won’t do so now

Unites APGA, APC, PDP, Accord in Anambra for president’s re-election

Akpabio: Akwa Ibom’ll deliver South-South’s highest votes to Tinubu

Urges APC factions to unite

Deji Elumoye, Sunday Aborisade in Abuja, David-Chyddy Eleke in Awka and Ahmad Sorondinki in Kano

The Vice Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Rabiu Kwankwaso; Kano State Governor, Abba Kabir Yusuf, and Personal Assistant to the President on Radio and Broadcast (Office of the Vice President), Hajya Rahma Abdulmajid, yesterday insisted that the South should retain power in 2027, warning against breaking the existing rotational arrangement between the North and the South.

While Kwankwaso warned former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) against disrupting the zoning arrangement, Yusuf and Abdulmajid argued that allowing the South to complete its eight-year tenure was necessary for national stability, reciprocity and peaceful coexistence.

Also yesterday, Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, said the Igbo were torn between emotion and reason ahead of the 2027 elections, urging them to support President Bola Tinubu’s re-election, while Senate President Godswill Akpabio assured that Akwa Ibom State would deliver the highest votes for the President in the South-South.

It’s Still Turn of South in 2027, Kwankwaso Warns Atiku, ADC

Kwankwaso has warned Atiku not to disrupt the zoning system by contesting, urging him to allow the system to continue by supporting Mr. Peter Obi to complete the remaining tenure belonging to the South.

Kwankwaso, who stated this during an interactive session with journalists at his residence in Kano, yesterday, also warned the ADC against causing confusion over the rotational presidency between the North and the South.

He said even though zoning was not enshrined in the constitution, common sense dictates that if one part of the country rules for two terms, the other region should be allowed to take over.

According to the former governor, fielding any candidate from the North would not help the country’s peaceful coexistence but will rather create confusion and disharmony among Nigerians.

“Atiku should not disrupt the system by contesting at this point in time. He should allow the system to continue by supporting Peter Obi to complete the remaining tenure belonging to the South.”

Kwankwaso recalled how he contested for president three consecutive times but decided to abandon his ambition to allow the Southern part of the country to produce Mr. Peter Obi.

“What is happening in the ADC will not help us. Some people want to create confusion by bringing a candidate from the North, knowing full well that it is still the turn of the South. After Obi presidency, it will return to the north.

“I sacrificed my ambition for Peter Obi because he is credible and from the South. We share common goals and ideology. We are strong and can manage the affairs of this country with ease,” he added.

The Kwankwasiyya leader stressed that for the Nigerian system to be balanced, Obi from the South should be given the opportunity to steer the affairs of the presidency.

Yusuf, Presidential Aide Insist on Power Rotation

Specifically, the Presidency justified the existing power rotation between the North and the South by urging the North to honour the current eight-year tenure being served by the South to completion, in the interest of reciprocity and national stability.

It said Nigeria’s national stability hangs by a slender thread, demanding that the North honour the unwritten power rotation pact and allow the South to complete its full eight-year tenure, warning that breaking this foundational trust could jeopardise the country’s unity.

Personal Assistant to the President on Radio and Broadcast (Office of the Vice President), Hajya Rahma Abdulmajid, stated this in Kano during the Grand Inauguration & Strategic Media Awards Ceremony of Matan Arewa 4 Tinubu Again (MATA).

According to her, Nigeria’s power rotation arrangement was not a sectional concession but a reciprocal compact that has stabilised the Fourth Republic.

In a veiled reference to Atiku, who she recalled attended and participated in the famous Kaduna meeting where the power rotation agreement was reached, Abdulmajid argued that the North cannot sacrifice the stability of Nigeria for the ambition of one man.

Tracing the origin to Kaduna, she noted that when military rule ended, patriots negotiated a framework for unity, maintaining that, “present in that room was Atiku Abubakar himself, as later confirmed by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), George Akume.

“Chief Sunday Awoniyi, the great Northern elder, stood up in 1998 and declared that the North should not field a candidate, in order to heal the wounds of June 12 and soothe the pain of the South.”

She further listed other patriots who shaped the understanding to include Dr. Chuba Okadigbo, speaking for the South; Alhaji Abubakar Rimi, speaking for the North; Dr. Alex Ekwueme, and Dr. Okwesilieze Nwodo.

Insisting on the power rotation arrangement, the Presidency said, “In 1999, when the guns of military rule finally fell silent, this nation did not just switch governments—we made a sacred promise. Our founding patriots gathered in Kaduna with one urgent, defining question echo-chambered in their minds: How do we keep Nigeria one?

“And from that sacred deliberation came a compact: not a sectional concession, but a reciprocal agreement. This gentleman’s agreement decreed that power must rotate between North and South every eight years—an arrangement to guarantee fairness, to ensure stability, and to guarantee that no Nigerian ever feels like a stranger in his own country.”

On how the arrangement worked, Abdulmajid said it survived because it was honoured.

“This is not fiction. This is our history. And how did it work? It worked because we honoured it. In 1999, we gave it to the South—Chief Olusegun Obasanjo, eight years, from 1999 to 2007. Then we gave it to the North: Umaru Musa Yar’Adua in 2007. But death, a painful death, cut his tenure short in 2010.

“His vice, Goodluck Jonathan from the South, took over. The North felt cheated. The North said our turn was not complete, and that agitation was legitimate. What happened? In 2015, power returned to the North. The late former President Muhammadu Buhari, eight full years, 2015 to 2023! The sequence was restored! The principle survived,” she stated.

The Presidency contended that the agreement was a two-way street and the North has already taken its full benefit.

“My people, listen to me. The agreement is reciprocal; it is a two-way street. The North has already taken its full benefit after eight solid years under Buhari. You cannot eat your cake and still demand another man’s cake,” Abdulmajid said.

The presidential aide stressed that stability requires reciprocity, recalling that the current President, a Southerner, worked tirelessly for the late General Muhammadu Buhari to emerge victorious when the North demanded power must return after Jonathan’s tenure.

“That same logic applies today. You cannot abandon a principle when it becomes inconvenient. If you do, you tell the world that the agreement was never a principle at all—merely a temporary tactic. And if we destroy trust today, what will we use to negotiate tomorrow? Let us be honest. Much of this noise against the South completing its term is not a matter of principle. It is personal ambition,” she queried.

Attributing opposition to the South completing its term to personal ambition, Abdulmajid said, “Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar tells us zoning is “self-defeating.” But he participated in and benefited from zoned arrangements in 2015 and 2019 when they favored his ambition! When rotation opened the door for him, it was acceptable. When it stands in his way, it becomes “intellectually dishonest.”

“Shall we sacrifice Nigeria’s stability for one man’s ambition? The North’s genuine interest is not served by that; the North’s interest is stable inclusion. The guarantee that power will return to you only lives if we honour the compact today.”

The Presidency appealed to the North not to break the sacred promise that binds nation, urging the people of the region to rise together and complete the Southern tenure, describing it as not merely an election.
