The discrepancy between the 14 suspects recorded as booked into custody and the 10 named in the release entry also raises questions about the subsequent status of the other suspects. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Sakaja said a June 2025 enforcement notice adds another dimension to the questions surrounding the property and the enforcement of planning regulations.

The notice, issued by Nairobi City County over alleged construction works undertaken without the required development permission, cited the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, 2019, and county by-laws.

It directed the recipient to stop the works and remove the development described as illegal, warning that the County could undertake the required action and recover the costs if the directives were not followed.

The notice also provided for an appeal to the County Physical and Land Use Planning Liaison Committee.

Sakaja clarified that approval to change a property’s use from private to commercial-cum-residential does not amount to approval of architectural plans authorising construction.

He said the County approved the change of use but did not approve the architectural plans, yet construction proceeded.

I have seen some people peddling a fake approval document alleging that the Eastleigh development was approved. It is telling that this is the same document that the Eastleigh developer used to get NCA approval. They allege that the development was approved in January of 2024. This is not true. The application for development as shown below was made in November of 2024, it could not have been approved in February of the same year. Also, there is a difference between a change of user approval and a development approval. The developer applied for change of use from residential to residential & commercial in August of 2024. Change of user was approved in October of 2024. Development approval has never been granted. The developer went on to build with impunity and without building approvals despite enforcement action by the county and arrests. — Sakaja Arthur Johnson (@SakajaJohnson) October 25, 2026

“If the building had been approved for construction, I would have named the officers who approved it so that action could be taken against them,” he said.

Sakaja, in his argument, said the current arrangement creates a gap between enforcement and prosecution, leaving counties dependent on other agencies after taking action against alleged offenders. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Under his proposal, appropriately authorised county prosecutors would be able to pursue qualifying county offences through the courts, subject to the law and the constitutional authority of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

He said county prosecutors previously had a better understanding of technical offences involving planning, construction and other county regulations, enabling them to handle such cases more directly.

“We want to be able not only to enforce regulations and make arrests, but also to take offenders to court and prosecute them. When counties had prosecutorial powers, we had prosecutors who understood the nature and seriousness of county offences and could ensure that appropriate legal action was taken,” he said.

World.title: Pregnant woman rescued from collapsed Eastleigh building
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya Red Cross workers after rescuing a man who trapped in the rubble.

A pregnant woman was on Saturday evening rescued from the multi-storey building that collapsed in Nairobi’s Eastleigh estate on Friday, October 23 and rushed to the Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) for treatment.

She is the second person to rescued as earlier in the afternoon the Kenya Red Cross society announced the rescue of a man from the ill-fated building.

The man was also taken to KNH for treatment with the society saying that the rescue followed hours of work put in by the search and rescue multi-agency team.

“After hours of painstaking work alongside multi-agency partners, our search and rescue teams in Eastleigh brought a trapped man out of the rubble,” said Red Cross.

The rescue comes even as the fate of six people who were reported missing on Friuday remains unknown with rescue teams still continuing with the search at the site of the collapsed building along Yusuf Haji Avenue.

The society said that 66 of the 67 construction workers who were at the site had been traced and accounted for but the search continues for people who may have been near the site of the collapsed building.

The development comes as police announced that they had launched a manhunt for the for the owner and contractor of a building.

Police spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga said that officers had launched a probe in collaboration with relevant bodies to establish the cause of the collapse and determine criminal liability.

“Any individual or entity found culpable of negligence or of violating building regulations will face the full force of the law,” he said in a statement.

Nyaga called on members of public to stay completely clear of Yusuf Haji Avenue and 9th Street to give access to heavy excavators, specialised canine units and rescue personnel to perform their duties.

Earlier Saturday, at least 31 families reported their relatives missing as coordinated rescue efforts entered their second day.

No deaths have been reported so far.

The National Construction Authority (NCA) on Friday evening identified the developer, contractor, architect and structural engineer listed for the collapsed building.

The Authority has faced scrutiny over its oversight role, as Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja said the project had failed to comply with construction guidelines.

He said the county had forwarded relevant information to the Directorate of Criminal Investigations for further investigation.

In a statement, the NCA said the building was registered on July 30, 2025, as a proposed development on 9th Street in Eastleigh.

It identified 9th Street Plaza Limited as the developer and Stromax Holdings E.A. Limited as the contractor.

Emmanuel Mwangi Maina was listed as the project architect, while Joseph Muturi Mugu was named as the structural engineer.

World.title: Democratic leaders enter the midterms ‘confident and paranoid’
World.content:
Virginia Beach, Virginia —

No part of a rolling, decadelong existential crisis is ever easy, even when things seem on the cusp of going well — and especially when Democrats have had their hopes raised and dashed so many times.

“It’s a little bit of deja vu,” said Elaine Luria, who in 2018 flipped Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District in the Democratic midterm wave during Donald Trump’s first term, held onto it in a squeaker in 2020 to help make up a slim majority, lost it in 2022 as part of Republicans winning their own small majority, and is now running to get it back.

“If you see how people are feeling today, the energy on the ground — the second time around living through this hell of the Trump administration … people want change,” Luria said. “They can’t take it anymore.”

The path to a Democratic majority runs through this district, Luria said onstage in the small theater of Batten University. Early voting data suggests Democrats are outperforming Republicans. The energy within the party is bubbling.

Internal polls described to CNN have Democratic leaders already smiling about how the midterms seem to be ending, even as they will bare-knuckle through the results as they come in Tuesday. They will enter the midterms with a 9-point advantage over Republicans in the generic congressional ballot, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls.

“Republicans are closing talking about ballrooms and backsides. That’s the disarray the Republicans are in,” said New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader who joined Luria on Saturday, taking a swipe at Trump’s remake of the White House and his reviews of Republican physiques.

After Jeffries spoke, the crowd filed out grabbing signs and other campaign material, heading out to knock a few more doors. Jeffries was heading to a plane to try to save the seat of Rep. Shomari Figures, whose Alabama district Republicans targeted after the Supreme Court’s decision hollowing out the Voting Rights Act this spring.

“There are going to be so many close races that you can’t predict — my guess is at least 20, the loser will get 49% — so it’s just going to be difficult to predict,” said Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia as he left the Luria rally, describing himself as upbeat but unsure.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen chaired the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm in 2018, when the party successfully defended several Senate seats it had been projected to lose while falling short of a majority. The Maryland senator said those elections were dominated by distraught Democrats talking about “the resistance.”

This year, as he’s been out campaigning from New Mexico to Georgia to New Hampshire, Van Hollen said, he’s been seeing a broader turn from those who backed Trump for a second term because they wanted the lower prices and end to foreign wars he promised.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen speaks at the Capitol on March 18 in front of a memorial of shoes representing those killed in the US strike on an Iranian school. Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images for Win Without War

“This time what’s different is on these promises that candidate Trump made that helped him win votes among his coalition, he’s done a 180,” Van Hollen told CNN.

Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor and congressman who helped oversee the campaigns that led to the midterms romp during George W. Bush’s second term, said the sense he’s getting from voters is different from 2006. He believes there is a backlash from Americans enraged by corruption, particularly among Black and Latino voters.

In 2006, “the emotion was disappointed, tired,” Emanuel said. “Here, it’s anger and bitterness. And that tells you something about the motivation.”

That doesn’t mean Emanuel is going into Tuesday fully confident that the polls aren’t missing the level of support for Trump and Republicans and that turnout won’t bring surprises as the precinct breakdowns come in.

“I keep checking to make sure we’re not all talking to each other. So I’m walking around looking for anything, ‘Please give me a negative,’” Emanuel said. To his fellow Democrats anxious that they’re about to be disappointed again, Emanuel added, “You might be right, but you may want to use that energy in a productive way rather than sitting around. Text, email, phone call, stand in the middle of the highway. I don’t care what you do, but just use it. There’s nothing productive getting done by being sitting there and being nervous.”

Operatives in both parties have been stunned at the cynicism coming across in focus groups, spanning every geographic, demographic, age and political category. Politics is, to many, seen as a game for the insiders in a world that looks more and more like a playground for the rich and powerful, with everyone else left behind while their costs go up and their lives get worse.

The candidates are hearing it all on the trail, in supermarket aisles, or when showing up to vote early themselves. Anger, disappointment, abandonment — that’s what’s coursing through American voters as they head to the polls.

Will Democrats make the most of the moment?

“Confident and paranoid” is how Washington state Rep. Suzan DelBene, the chair of the House Democrats’ campaign arm, described her mindset going into Tuesday.

Netting the three seats that would put her party in the majority seems a given to DelBene — but then again, she went through the final days of the election two years ago, when the majority also felt in reach. The paranoia, she says, comes from the ways she can see Trump trying to interfere with the election results.

Democratic supporters cheer as former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks at a rally with Sen. Jon Ossoff in Atlanta on October 29. Megan Varner/Getty Images President Donald Trump pauses as he speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on October 30. Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

DelBene ticked through conversations she’s been having on the trail, from an early voting center in an Ohio district that Democrats believe they can hold to a Meals on Wheels location in an Arizona district they are hoping to flip. At every stop, she says, the economic pain is palpable. At every stop, she tries to get voters to believe that Democrats are ready to come in with some real solutions.

Voting early last week, Cleveland Mayor Justin Bibb said he talked to a woman who was lamenting how the price of her groceries and prescriptions have gone up. She brought her whole family with her to the polling place. To her, that seemed like the only thing to do. But Bibb said he’s worried Democrats gleeful about big wins are going to misunderstand why she and others bothered to give voting one more chance.

He understands the cynicism out in the country, Bibb said. He hopes other Democrats do too, and he’s already starting to organize with fellow mayors on how to press Washington, DC, to respond if and when the results come in as he’s hoping.

“We can’t miss this moment with just hearings and impeachment proceedings,” Bibb said. “People need to see their pocketbooks improve.”

Before anyone starts counting committee chairmanships, Van Hollen said, first they need to actually win. As he stumps around the country, the senator often ends by telling the story of the 2017 races for the Virginia House of Delegates. At the end, control was decided by one seat, and the election of that seat was a tie, leaving it decided under state law by a game of chance —in the case, drawing slips of paper out of a bowl. Republicans won.

“I would not rely on these polls,” Van Hollen said. “My plea is: Don’t take anything for granted, don’t let control come down to one campaign.”

That can be hard for the voters and candidates and leaders alike. DelBene says she’s been spending the final stretch of the campaign doing a lot of pep talks.

“It’s a very stressful time. Folks are tired. They’ve been working incredibly hard,” DelBene said. “I have a lot of conversations with folks just to say, ‘Keep going.’ The one thing about an election is: There is an end date.”

World.title: Brazil’s left reinvented the right’s online playbook. It helped Lula win
World.content:
For three weeks in October, Veridiana Cunha became a so-called “soldier” for a digital army fighting to reelect Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Every few minutes, the 48-year-old would interrupt her day job in São Paulo as a copy editor and check WhatsApp for new instructions. She even reactivated an Instagram account she hadn’t used since 2022 and learned how to post on X for the first time for the cause.

“I’d edit a text, then go to the army. Edit another text, then go to the army,” she told CNN of a WhatsApp channel, led by Congressman André Janones, that became a virtual campaign headquarters during the final weeks of Brazil’s presidential campaign.

Cunha was one of millions of Brazilians who joined the channel called “Lula’s Army.” Their mission: to reverse Lula’s first-round defeat on October 4 to the right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, scion of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

And they succeeded. Lula won the election on October 25, which analysts partly attribute to the eleventh-hour strategy of harnessing a digital playbook long associated with Brazil’s right of using WhatsApp to amplify political messaging and mobilize voters.

From coordinated social media campaigns to reclaiming national symbols, the online strategy mobilized many to vote for Lula, in an effort that experts say offers a striking example of how the Brazilian left learned to fight the right on its turf.

Millions of “soldiers,” one command

WhatsApp is a powerful force in Brazilian politics. Jair Bolsonaro’s successful presidential campaign in 2018 was supported by extensive networks of private groups that spread videos, political messages and disinformation.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers’ Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, speaks as he celebrates with Andre Janones, a member of the Chamber of Deputies of Brazil, after winning the presidential runoff election, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 25. Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

But ahead of the October 4, first-round vote, Lula’s campaign had struggled to compete with the right’s digital operation. While Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign had long made social media a central part of its strategy, Lula’s team underestimated its importance, according to Lucas Fernandes, a political analyst at BMJ Consultores Associados.

“The right understood this and applied it on several fronts, not just to Flávio’s candidacy, while the left failed to make that transition,” Fernandes said, highlighting social media as one of the key factors for Flávio’s victory in the first round.

That changed after Lula’s defeat when Janones, 42, emerged as a central figure in this new playbook.

The congressman for the state of Minas Gerais created the WhatsApp channel in April. After Lula’s first-round loss to Bolsonaro, Janones transformed it into a virtual command center, issuing coordinated instructions to supporters who were suddenly confronting the possibility of losing the presidency.

Viktor Chagas, a professor at Fluminense Federal University who researches political communication, described Janones as a politician who “fights the far right with the same resources it uses,” resorting to emotionally charged messages, aggressive language and, at times, content of dubious origin.

It was a strategy he deployed on the channel, which saw it swell from 50,000 followers before the first-round vote to nearly 11 million in three weeks as Janones rallied supporters to help Lula stage a historic comeback.

From anti-system figure to digital general of Lula

Within Congress, Janones is known for his combative style, which he dubbed “cultural Janonism,” adopting tactics associated with Bolsonarism, according to Chagas. This included provocative language, emotionally charged posts, and attacks on his adversaries. It also turned Janones into a polarizing figure, who last year was suspended by Congress for three months for offensive statements against another combative lawmaker, the right-wing politician Nikolas Ferreira.

Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers’ Party (PT) candidate for re-election, alongside Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, gestures as he addresses supporters after his victory in the presidential runoff election, at Paulista Avenue, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 26. Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

Through videos, audio messages and social media posts, Janones instructed his followers to promote hashtags, comment on livestreams, share videos, like posts, publish photos making the “L” hand gesture in support of Lula, and recruit new members.

He called for a panelaço — a traditional Brazilian form of protest in which people bang pots and pans — during Flávio Bolsonaro’s highly anticipated interview on TV Globo, as a way to boycott the broadcast. Janones also urged supporters to avoid commenting on opponents’ posts, warning that engaging with their content could inadvertently boost its visibility through social media algorithms.

The pace was so intense that Janones went so far as to condemn resting unless the “soldier” could find a replacement for the “missions.” On October 17, he wrote on the channel: “If there is a substitute soldier, the change is authorized. Pass him the cell phone. Rest and come back in ten minutes.”

Chagas described the strategy as a form of “gamification,” which fostered a sense of collective purpose. According to the academic, that structure gave progressive digital activism a level of coordination that had been absent even during Lula’s successful campaign in 2022.

Bolsonaro’s strategy focused on disseminating content from a few major influencers, while “Lula’s Army” had a centralized command that instructed its members to create and disseminate their own content as well as official lines.

Janones not only told them what to share but taught them how to do it, experts noted.

Leonardo Magalhães Firmino, chief executive of research firm IPSE Global, compared the method to training thousands of small social media managers.

But the rise in online activity also raised concerns about misinformation. In one widely circulated image by the left, Brazilian soccer legend Ronaldo appears to be wearing a national team jersey bearing Lula’s ballot number, 13, and making the “L” gesture. The image was manipulated by artificial intelligence and posted by a Colombian artist, according to Brazilian fact-checking outlet Agência Lupa. Ronaldo’s representatives said it had been used without his authorization.

While Janones’ tactics tend to pursue democratic ends, Chagas argues that they could also degrade public debate by reducing complex political discussions to a constant confrontation.

CNN reached out to Janones, who has previously denied spreading disinformation, for comment.

Brazil’s right-wing senator and presidential candidate for the Liberal Party (PL) Flavio Bolsonaro reacts after knowing the first results in the presidential runoff election, in Brasilia, on October 25, 2026. Pablo Porciuncula/AFP/Getty Images

On the channel, Janones called himself “general,” assigned daily “missions” to Lula’s supporters, and urged them to take the campaign beyond their own social media.

The tactics frustrated Bolsonaro’s supporters. On October 11, a supreme court judge ordered the suspension of the WhatsApp group following a complaint by Bolsonaro’s campaign for alleged disinformation. The decision was later overturned.

Did the “army” change the outcome of the election?

Lula’s victory was decided by factors beyond the digital battle: electoral participation, the redistribution of votes from eliminated candidates, and geographical changes in support for candidates.

But Janones’ online mobilization was fundamental to Lula’s victory, says Firmino.

“I have no doubt. Without that, I don’t think the comeback would have happened,” he told CNN. “He organized the militancy, he gave them a method. I think that’s the main point.”

According to Firmino, the right underestimated Janones’ strategy, saying that he only spoke with Lula supporters. But that was the point: the goal was to speak directly with the “soldiers” who were already converted, not the undecided.

The “soldiers” were the ones who would take the message beyond the channel and to their family, friends, undecided voters, and those thinking about abstaining, he said.

‘I managed to change a vote’

For Cunha, the missions meant much more than a political cause. Her mother, a longtime Lula supporter, became seriously ill in August and she spent weeks by her side in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais, so she did not vote in the first round. Back in São Paulo for work, she needed a distraction and a purpose, which she found in digital mobilization.

“The Army saved Brazil, it saved Lula and it saved me a little too,” she said. Participating in the campaign allowed her to feel closer to her mother and continue fighting for a cause they both shared.

But one of her greatest satisfactions came on election day, when a friend, who was thinking of abstaining, finally went to the polls and voted for Lula. “I managed to change a vote,” Cunha said.

No one can determine how many stories like hers translated into additional votes on a national scale. But for Cunha, the victory had an unexpected consequence: After three weeks spent almost entirely campaigning, getting back to normal proved harder than she imagined.

“I think we’re living through a kind of post-traumatic stress from the Army, like we’ve really gone to war,” she said. “We’re exhausted, but we want more missions. We feel like we can conquer the world.”

World.title: Germany blames infiltrators as Gen Z protests turn violent
World.content:
Cost-of-living protests in Germany turned violent on Saturday evening with police using water cannons to disperse crowds and masked rioters smashed shop windows, as officials warn the day of rallies organized by a youth-led movement was infiltrated by extremist factions.

Saturday’s action across Germany, organized by the ‘Gen Z has got this!’ movement, railed against the high cost of living, underfunding in education, environmental concerns and a potential reintroduction of mandatory military service. It follows a wave of similar protests which have swept Europe, including significant unrest in France, which saw a third straight weekend of rallies.

Despite organizers calling for the protests to remain peaceful, violence broke out in some German cities, most notably in Frankfurt and Cologne. Police used water cannons while masked protesters smashed shop windows.

Speaking to German tabloid Bild, Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt said that “violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from migrant communities” hijacked the peaceful protests, without elaborating further.

The interior minister for the state of Hesse, which includes Frankfurt, warned that “around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists” infiltrated the city’s protest as the evening descended into violence and looting.

“It is shameful how this event here in Frankfurt has ended,” Roman Poseck said.

Police use a water cannon against protesters in Frankfurt on Saturday night. Florian Wiegand/picture-alliance/dpa/AP A person tries to break a store window in Frankfurt amid the youth-led protests on Saturday. Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters

Poseck said he was determined the violence that has rocked France would not be replicated in Germany.

“We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” he said, according to Reuters. “France must not be held up as a model in this regard.”

In Frankfurt, police said Molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency personnel and shop windows were smashed. Officers arrested a suspect and seized two weapons after windows were broken at a gun shop. According to German news magazine Der Spiegel, several people broke into shops in downtown Frankfurt and over 30 people had been temporarily detained in city by the late evening.

Police in Cologne said water cannons were used after some protesters set off fireworks during a march in the city center. “Our measures are directed against troublemakers and violent individuals – not against peaceful participants,” the police said in a statement.

In Hamburg, riot police responded after barriers were set on fire and emergency service workers were attacked. “There has been an increase in incidents of emergency personnel being pelted with pyrotechnics and construction (materials) … our riot police are taking immediate action against this,” the police said.

Berlin police wrote on X that 27 officers in the German capital had sustained minor injuries and just under 60 people had been detained for offenses including property damage, assault, and resistance against emergency forces.

The movement’s organizers have sought to distance themselves from the ensuing violence. “We had no influence on what happened after the demonstrations ended,” a spokesperson from their press team was quoted by Der Spiegel as saying.

Fires burn in Frankfurt amid riots in the city center on Saturday night. Andreas Arnold/picture-alliance/dpa/AP

Organizers of ‘Gen Z has got this!’ planned the day of action to coincide with Halloween, to maximize turnout and visibility. According to the organization, 120,000 people attended the protests across Germany on Saturday.

“We are young people who no longer want to watch decisions being made about our future without us,” the movement states on its website.

Speaking for his reasons for joining the movement, an 18-year-old student protester in Munich told Reuters, “The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us.” In the eastern city of Dresden, demonstrators held placards reading, “The rich want war, the youth want a future!” and “You’ve screwed up – Gen Z will sort it out.”

Europe-wide protests

More nationwide protests from the Yellow Vests movement took place in France on Saturday, in what was billed as the third act of demonstrations, following earlier protests on October 17 and 24.

This time, however, they were more scaled down than before. The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people protested across the country on Saturday, with 70,000 turning up in Paris; a significantly smaller number than the 550,000 who demonstrated on October 17 and the 410,000 who showed up last week.

The French protests were mostly peaceful, except for a few incidents. The Interior Ministry said in a statement that “radical elements at the tail end of the processions” in several cities. including Bordeaux, Toulouse, Rennes, Lille, Nantes, Marseille, and Lyon, “attempted to enter city centers with the intent to cause damage and engage in looting.”

Protests over soaring housing costs also swept Portugal and Italy on Saturday. In the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, thousands marched to demand Portugal’s center-right government withdraw a rental bill they say will worsen the country’s housing crisis.

In Italy, protests largely led by student groups and workers rallied against inflation, stagnant wages and unaffordable housing in cities including Turin, Bologna and Milan.

World.title: The huge stakes of an unusually momentous midterm election
World.content:
Midterm elections are always a verdict on a sitting president. But the 2026 edition could become something rarer and more significant — a catalyst that points the way to a new political era.

Tuesday’s election is critical for Trump’s presidency and legacy. It could either sustain the MAGA movement’s decadelong grip on national life or initiate its decline. It could result in redemption for Democrats two years after their crushing defeat in the last presidential election. And in both parties, it will demarcate the opening chapters of the 2028 presidential race.

The midterms are the first chance for voters to place some constitutional restraints on a freewheeling president who has the most aggressive view of executive power in modern times.

If Democrats win back the House of Representatives or the Senate on Tuesday, Trump will face a seismic tide of investigations: into his conduct; his Cabinet; alleged government corruption; his legacy construction spree; turmoil at the Pentagon; and his own fortune, which has swelled since he returned to the White House.

More broadly, the election is also a referendum on nearly two divisive years in which Trump has sought to dismantle swaths of the federal government and used the power of his office to target political enemies. Abroad, he’s replaced traditional global leadership with America First nationalism while starting a new Middle East war; fraternizing with Russian and Chinese dictators; and carrying out extrajudicial killings of alleged traffickers in the Pacific and Caribbean.

But Democrats also have a lot at stake as they tried to repair a brand tarnished by high inflation and lax border security under President Joe Biden’s administration and the chaos of his aborted reelection bid.

For voters to trust them again, they must prove they’re more than just anti-Trump; they must deliver results at a frantic political moment and despite a president who will put up ferocious resistance. Failure would invite voters’ wrath in 2028.

Election Day could also turn into a crucible for US democracy itself. Trump has already challenged the conduct of elections in Alaska and California and drawn comparisons to his effort to overturn the 2020 election by signaling last week that he’d accept the results of the midterms only if he deems them fair.

But most importantly, the elections are a chance for politicians to listen to the people whom they often seem to forget they serve. Millions of Americans are desperate for relief from the costs of food, housing and healthcare and feel rising anxiety about the possible impact of AI on their job security.

President Donald Trump takes the stage during a campaign rally at the Ocean Center Arena on October 30, 2026 in Daytona Beach, Florida. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Trump’s strange campaign

Trump is the most unorthodox president of modern times. But his decision to make the election about his performance amid a deeply unpopular war and boiling public dissatisfaction with his decisions was iconoclastic even for him.

His erratic final pitch, delivered on a journey through wobbling GOP districts in red states, touched on almost everything but the economic issue voters care about most. He boasted about the new ballroom he’s building at the White House; bizarrely lauded the backside of Ohio Sen. John Husted; and lashed out with some of the most explicit anti-Muslim and bigoted rhetoric of any US election campaign.

On Sunday, the president shrugged off polls showing Democrats heavily favored to recapture the House and threatening multiple Republican senators in states he won by wide margins, instead promising a triumph for the GOP on Tuesday night.

“A vote for any Democrat anywhere in the country is a vote to put a deranged group of extremists into power and it could really hurt us, and we are not going to let anything hurt us, because we have the greatest country right now,” Trump said in Iowa. House Speaker Mike Johnson, at Trump’s side, vowed, “We are going to win and shock the world on Tuesday night. I believe it.”

But if voters react badly to Trump’s depiction of a new economic “golden age” and evident indifference to their struggles, he will be consigned to a lonely political plight — shocking even for a man once subject to multiple criminal cases. His self-themed campaign would make it an unusually personal blow, especially if his handpicked Senate candidates lose in states like Texas and Georgia. The idea that Trumpism has permanently changed politics would be called into question, and the GOP would be plunged into soul-searching over its future direction.

And next year, the isolation would become more acute under the relentless pressure of Democratic investigations after the end of a rubber-stamp Republican Congress.

A Democratic victory would turn into a fateful test

A good night for Democrats would count as a political earthquake only two years after Trump staged one of history’s greatest comebacks by beating Democratic nominee Kamala Harris to win a nonconsecutive second term.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris shakes hands on the rope line during a campaign event on the campus of Clark Atlanta University, Thursday, October 29, 2026, in Atlanta. Mike Stewart/AP

Yet even if the party were to win both chambers, Trump will still enjoy considerable clout, including with expansive constitutional authority to conduct foreign policy. The president’s history of spurning checks and balances means he’d fight any attempt by Democrats in Congress to rein in his powers, with showdowns likely over the war, budgets and policy-making.

But if Democrats rack up the net gain of four seats needed to win the Senate, they will acquire the ability to block Trump’s campaign to complete his conservative transformation of the judiciary and potentially to fill any new Supreme Court vacancy.

And any potential Democratic majorities could also challenge Trump on his conduct of the war with Iran — which he is waging without congressional authorization — and funding for military operations if he has failed to end the conflict by the time new lawmakers are seated on January 3.

“Right now, (it) is about stabilizing the country itself and providing some check against not just an out-of-control presidency and a corrupt presidency but everyone’s costs,” Democratic Sen. Brian Schatz told CNN’s Kasie Hunt last month. “Diesel, gasoline agricultural products, consumer products … everything is up, and I think people want to see us do not everything but a few things that will take the pain out of what they’re experiencing.”

But while the loss of Congress could turn Trump into a lame duck, he’s unlikely to act like one. The history of his first term suggests pitched legal battles over congressional subpoenas and attempts by Democratic investigators to penetrate deep into the administration and trawl for evidence in his family finances.

The president’s veto power, and the requirement for 60 votes to pass major legislation in the Senate, means Trump will be able to temper Democratic hopes for sweeping change.

Lessons for 2028 are already being drawn

The midterm results will also shape the 2028 presidential race likely to explode into life as soon as the votes are counted.

A huge GOP defeat could raise doubts about whether Trumpism will outlast Trump’s political career. Potential presidential candidates such as Vice President JD Vance would confront the delicate task of separating themselves politically from a president who remains a hero to the grassroots but who, according to polls, has lost the rest of the country’s confidence on almost every issue.

Vice President JD Vance speaks during an event with President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House on October 20, 2026. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Democrats lining up for a tilt at their party’s presidential nomination will parse midterm results for winning messages. Key figures such as Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro could enhance credentials with thumping reelection wins.

The election aftermath is sure to reignite the party’s debate over ideology. If progressive candidates like Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed win their races, movement leaders such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will argue the country is ready to embrace more left-wing policies on healthcare and the economy.

The schism between progressives and moderates burst into the open on Sunday when defeated Michigan Democratic primary candidate Haley Stevens sensationally endorsed Republican nominee Mike Rogers over El-Sayed, ostensibly amid a clash over Israel.

Midterms polls also show limited public confidence that Democrats can meaningfully reorient the nation. A 2026 victory would therefore turn into a 2028 audition.

“The Democrats have to prove in 2027 they have won,” former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel told CNN’s Brianna Keilar last week. “I’m for comprehensive hearings, follow the money, everything. Venezuela … the Russian money, the oil, all these deals,” said Emanuel, a possible 2028 Democratic presidential primary candidate.

“But if you don’t do ethics reform, you haven’t delivered change. … If you don’t deliver a rise in the minimum wage, you haven’t addressed affordability.”

This is the risk for Democratic leaders: Trump’s intractability and veto power could reduce them to passing endless affordability bills that go nowhere. That won’t impress angry voters.

But that’s for next year, if Democrats win.

The last rites of the midterms must first play out. And Trump still doesn’t seem to get the message. In a telling symbol of obliviousness, he’ll deliver his closing argument in Washington on Monday at the National Mall’s Reflecting Pool, which was just repaired at great expense and which showcases his legacy fixation.

With millions of Americans in need of tangible economic relief, the event may deliver an eloquent explanation of why Trump and the GOP risk a painful reckoning on Election Day.

World.title: Despite government ban, tree-felling persists across Egypt
World.content:
In the heart of the countryside, once lush and verdant, the landscape now groans from trees felled by merciless deforestation.

Despite a prime minister’s decree banning it, the crime of indiscriminate logging continues to spread across several governorates.

Along the Mit Ghamr–Banha road, Al-Masry Al-Youm on Saturday observed two vehicles loaded with freshly cut tree trunks. Although they passed through security checkpoints at Sarhagt al-Kubra and Kafr Shukr, no one stopped the vehicles to inquire about the origin of the timber or its destination.

The trucks eventually turned onto a secondary agricultural road before reaching the regional highway.

Local citizen, Mohamed Shaaba spotted a vehicle on the Mansoura road carrying a large quantity of felled trees.

He posted a photograph on his personal social media page, commenting: “Right now, on Mansoura–Aga road, there is a truck loaded with cut trees—and no one is asking where they came from or where they are headed!”

A timber merchant in Qalyubiya, Saeed al-Sayed, confirmed that trees cut down in the Gharbiya, Daqahliya, and Qalyubiya governorates are being transported to charcoal kilns scattered throughout the villages of Mit Ghamr and Kafr Shukr.

The charcoal produced there is intended for export—a trade that intensifies during winter months. Currently, these kilns are operating at full capacity to produce charcoal before the onset of the rainy season, Sayed said.

He added: “Every year, during September and October, charcoal kilns become active, and trees are cut down—both in fruit orchards and along some streets. This year, however, social media has fueled public outrage.”

In the Gharbiya Governorate, many residents, from the village of Dima (in the Kafr al-Zayat district), the city of Tanta, and the villages of Mahallat Marhoum and Barma in the Tanta area, have complained about the ongoing felling of trees and the destruction of greenery across various areas in these and neighboring villages.

A resident of Tanta, Mohsen Ramadan, remarked: “The state is making efforts to stop the tree-cutting by filing official reports, but those responsible carry out their work at night, evading the notice of the authorities.”

An official source at the Ministry of Local Development and Environment said that the minister has issued strict orders to the governors to crack down on the indiscriminate felling of trees and to address any violations.

These instructions include seizing vehicles loaded with cut trees, verifying the origin of the timber, and holding those responsible for the felling, as well as those in charge of the area where it occurred, accountable.

The source added: “According to the minister’s directives, no tree may be cut down without a permit. Vehicles transporting such trees must carry a copy of the permit; anyone failing to produce one will face legal action.”

He noted that there is a ministerial initiative underway to introduce urgent amendments to the Environmental Law.

These amendments aim to explicitly criminalize indiscriminate and unregulated tree-felling.

Furthermore, efforts are being directed toward a reforestation drive, which includes implementing a plan to double vegetation cover and expand green spaces across all governorates, a move intended to improve environmental quality and bolster the state’s efforts in addressing climate change.

The Cairo Governorate issued a statement encouraging citizens to plant trees in front of their own homes and shops, while ensuring a spacing of four to five meters between each tree.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Amr Adib lashes out over Egypt’s stray dog ​​crisis
World.content:
Media personality Amr Adib has revisited the issue of stray dogs on Sunday following the death of a young girl who was mauled to death by dogs late in October.

During his program “al-Hekaya,” (the story) on MBC Masr channel, Adib questioned how the debate has persisted without any clear solution being reached.

He noted that the issue of stray dogs frequently resurfaces in public discourse.

Adib highlighted a societal divide: one group opposes the culling of dogs, viewing it as an unacceptable act, while another group considers the presence of these animals on the streets a danger to citizens, especially children, due to the risk of bites and attacks that can sometimes prove fatal.

“Is there no middle ground? Is there no clear solution to this problem?”, he asked.

He added that some view expenditures aimed at managing the stray dog ​​population as a waste of resources, especially since the dogs remain on the streets, until a tragic incident occurs, bringing the issue back into the spotlight.

World.title: Cobra sightings on the rise in Egypt’s residential areas
World.content:
Cobra sightings have been on the rise in Egypt’s residential areas, sparking panic amongst citizens.

The Head of the Central Administration for Nature Reserves at the Ministry of Environment, Mohamed Youssef, explained that research has determined that the appearance of dangerous animals in populated areas is typically the result of factors such as environment changes displacing them.

During a phone-in with the program “Hadith al-Qahira” (Cairo Talk), Youssef added that the emergence of animals in areas inhabited by humans requires an examination of the specific circumstances surrounding each case, and that one should not rush to conclusions regarding the reasons for their presence.

Cobras are highly sensitive to the temperature of their surrounding environment; they may move about in search of warmth, food, or shelter, he noted.

Changes in environmental conditions can drive these animals to leave their usual habitats.

Instead, they should promptly notify the relevant authorities, such as the Civil Defense, emergency services, or the governorate’s operations center.

World.title: Egypt’s temperatures to continue rising on Monday
World.content:
The Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) expects temperatures to continue rising across most regions on Monday.

The weather will be hot during the day in most areas, and very hot in the southern parts of Upper Egypt, while turning cooler at night and during the early morning hours across most parts of the country.

In Greater Cairo and Lower Egypt, maximum temperatures are expected to reach between 31C and 32C, with minimums ranging from 19C to 20C.

Along the northern coasts, the maximum will range between 28C-31C, with minimum temperature between 18C ​​and 22C.

In northern Upper Egypt, maximum temperatures are forecast to be between 32C-34C, with minimums between 18C ​​and 19C.

Southern Upper Egypt will experience the highest temperatures, with maximums reaching between 36C and 37C, and minimums ranging from 19C to 22C.

Meteorological forecasts indicate the possibility of light, intermittent rain across parts of the northern coastal governorates and the northern Lower Egypt.

Winds are expected to pick up, reaching speeds of 30-40 km/h, affecting areas along the northwestern coast, the Western Desert, and exposed parts of Greater Cairo, Lower Egypt, the Suez Canal cities, and Upper Egypt.

These winds may occasionally stir up sand and dust.

Additionally, low-level clouds may form in scattered areas across Greater Cairo, the southern Lower Egypt, and the Suez Canal cities, potentially resulting in a light, inconsequential drizzle in some locations.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Liberia: Senator Amara Konneh Wants Port Operators Summoned Over Delays; NPA’s MD Dukuly: “We Are Working on Dredging and Expansion”
World.content:
MONROVIA – Seen from the beaches of Monrovia, the problem is easy to spot. On a grey afternoon this week, several cargo ships sat at anchor on the horizon off Liberia’s capital. They were waiting for a berth at the Freeport of Monrovia, the country’s main gateway for imported food, fuel, building materials and consumer goods.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Video footage seen by FrontPageAfrica shows at least five vessels anchored in a line offshore. A frayed Liberian flag flaps on a wooden pole in the foreground, and fishing canoes sit on the beach.



For Liberian importers, those waiting ships mean money lost. Business owners say every day a container spends at sea pushes up their costs, and those costs end up in the prices ordinary Liberians pay at the market.

Now the issue has reached the Liberian Senate. In an October 25, 2026 letter to President Pro-Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence, Senator Amara M. Konneh of Gbarpolu County asked the Senate to summon port operators and government agencies. They would appear before the full Senate, sitting as a Committee of the Whole, to explain what he called “protracted delays of containers, high transaction costs, and their impact on businesses and consumer prices.”

‘Over 30 days at sea’

Konneh is a former Minister of Finance and Development Planning. He wrote that “serious and persistent complaints” from the business community, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), had reached lawmakers over the past several months.

According to the Senator, importers and shipping agents report that containers bound for Liberia now spend “an average of over 30 days at sea” before berthing in Monrovia. He said most of these vessels are being routed to and held at ports in neighbouring Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana.

The letter gives two alleged causes. The first is a lack of yard space at the Freeport to hold more containers. The second is that larger vessels cannot berth because dredging of the port basin and channel has been “prolonged.”

Responding to the concerns, National Port Authority (NPA) Managing Director Sekou Dukuly told FrontPageAfrica: “We are working on dredging and expansion.” He did not give a timeline or say what the work would cost.

“These delays are severely hurting business inventories, tying up working capital, leading to stock-outs, and imposing heavy demurrage costs,” Konneh wrote. Demurrage is the daily penalty shipping lines charge when containers are held beyond an agreed period. In a small, import-dependent economy like Liberia’s, such costs are rarely absorbed by businesses. They are passed on to shoppers.

A ‘multiplicity of opaque’ fees

The Senator also pointed to costs that importers face once their goods reach the dock. He said businesses carry “a multiplicity of opaque transaction costs and fees.” He named APM Terminals, MEDTECH Scientific Limited, Global Tracking and Maritime Solutions (GTMS) and “other actors in the supply chain” as the bodies charging them.

APM Terminals, part of the Danish shipping group A.P. Moller-Maersk, operates the Freeport’s container terminal under a long-term concession agreement with the Government of Liberia. MEDTECH and GTMS provide services in Liberia’s cargo-clearance chain. “These charges are being passed on to consumers,” Konneh wrote.

Falling inflation, but prices still high

The Senator’s main economic argument is a puzzle many Liberians will recognise. On paper, the economy is improving. In practice, market prices have barely moved.

Konneh noted that headline inflation has fallen to 4.6 percent and that the Liberian dollar has gained against the US dollar. Both signal progress under the Government’s economic stabilisation programme, backed by an International Monetary Fund (IMF) Extended Credit Facility. Even so, he wrote, “consumer prices remain stubbornly high.”

He argued that problems at the port “are potentially a major driver of these sticky prices.” That, he said, risks “negating the gains” of the reform programme.

If the problems are not fixed urgently, the letter warned, they “will continue to undermine private sector competitiveness, discourage investment, and erode the purchasing power of ordinary Liberians.”

Seven bodies named

Konneh asked that the following appear before Plenary to respond to the allegations and present solutions:

* The National Port Authority (NPA)

* APM Terminals Liberia

* MEDTECH Scientific Limited

* Global Tracking and Maritime Solutions (GTMS)

* The Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA), Customs Department

* The Ministry of Commerce and Industry

* The Brokers Union / Customs Brokers Association of Liberia

Lawmakers want clarity on four things: the current state of dredging, the berthing and yard capacity problems, the full schedule of fees charged at the port, and the immediate and medium-term steps being taken to clear congestion and reduce costs for Liberian businesses.

“I pray that Plenary will accord this matter its urgent and kind consideration,” the Senator wrote.

Calls for concession reform

Outside the Senate, some Liberians have been pressing for changes to how the Freeport is run. They are making three demands.

First, they want the Government to review, fix and extend the APM Terminals concession, so the company can invest more money in yard expansion and equipment.

Second, they want the Government to review, negotiate and sign a proposed US$230 million concession from Moroccan port operator Marsa Maroc. That deal would allow the company to build a new multipurpose terminal with three berths and compete with APM Terminals.

Third, they want dredging obligations written into the financial model of both concessions, to ensure the port basin and channel are dredged regularly and on time. Lack of dredging is one of the causes Konneh’s letter blames for the delays.

Why it matters beyond Liberia

Liberia imports most of what it consumes, including much of its rice, the national staple. Congestion at its main port affects more than a single industry. It reaches every household.

The complaints also matter for the region. If, as the letter alleges, Liberia-bound vessels are queuing at Abidjan and Tema, then delays in Monrovia are adding to pressure on West Africa’s wider shipping network, at a time when governments across the region are trying to attract investment and lower the cost of trade.

It was not immediately clear when the Senate would take up the request. Beyond Dukuly’s brief comment on dredging and expansion, the NPA did not respond to the Senator’s other concerns, including yard space, delays at sea and port fees. As of press time, APM Terminals Liberia, MEDTECH and GTMS had not publicly responded to the allegations in the Senator’s letter.

World.title: Liberia’s Cancer Fight: Survivors Walk, Push For Early Detection And Care
World.content:
MONROVIA — Benejane Shaw remembers exactly what the word did to her. “When they told me breast cancer, I broke down, I shed tears,” she said, “because as far as I’m concerned, when they say you have cancer, it’s a death sentence.”

By Rodney D. Sieh

On Saturday, Shaw took part in a breast cancer awareness walk to show that it need not be. She had surgery on March 3, 2025, followed by ten cycles of chemotherapy. “God first, JFK second, and Dr. Deddeh Supuwood,” she said, naming the capital’s John F. Kennedy Medical Center and the oncologist she credits with her recovery. “I’m a living testimony that early detection saves lives.”



She was among the survivors who spoke at the walk, the annual awareness campaign of the Liberia Cancer Resource Initiative (LCRI), a Liberian group focused on breast and cervical cancer. October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month worldwide, and Saturday was its final day.

A Walk for the Living

Among those who spoke was Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe, a lawyer and former presidential candidate, who tied the disease to the country’s governance problems. “Corruption starts with C. Cancer starts with C,” he said. “We have to sweep the two Cs from Liberia. When we sweep corruption, we sweep cancer successfully.”

Florence B. Tugbeh, a survivor, describing the toll of treatment and her recovery, says, “Anyone who says cancer cannot be healed is lying.”

The day’s most vivid testimony came from another survivor, Florence B. Tugbeh, who described the toll of treatment and her recovery. “Anyone who says cancer cannot be healed is lying,” she said. “When you looked at my palm, it used to be black like fire coals. But see me now. I got body, I got hair. I never had hair, but now I can shake my head.” She thanked supporters in Liberia and abroad, including the President and his wife, and asked for help for Dr. Supuwood to continue her studies.

For LCRI Executive Director Christine E. Brooks-Jarrett, the walk was “a demonstration of solidarity and collective action.” The campaign exists to educate the public, “break the stigma surrounding cancer and encourage women to prioritize their health and get screened,” she said. But a month is not enough: “Cancer awareness must be a year-round effort.”

Planning time was short this year, she said, yet turnout was encouraging. Participants praised the organization and the souvenirs and welcomed the extra activities after the walk. “The games and dry rice added spice to the fun,” she said, referring to a Liberian rice dish served at the event.

“Saving a Whole Family”

For Dr. Deddeh Supuwood, the fight is personal. A medical oncologist at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center, she is also president of the Liberia Medical and Dental Association and a statutory council member of the Liberia Medical and Dental Council. She lost her own mother to breast cancer.”Since I returned from school, I have dreamed of helping as many women as I can,” she said. “I couldn’t do it for my mother, so seeing survivors now and hearing their stories brings me joy. When you save one woman’s life, you are probably saving a whole family.” Watching patients “go from hopeless to hopeful,” she said, has been humbling. “My ultimate dream is that no Liberian woman should easily die from breast cancer.”

Benejane Shaw, another survivor, said, “I’m a living testimony that early detection saves lives.”

The dream has a hard number attached to it. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in Liberia, with an estimated 885 new cases and 421 deaths in 2024, according to the International Agency for Research on Cancer, the World Health Organization’s cancer research arm. That is roughly 48 deaths for every 100 women diagnosed. Because Liberia has no population-based cancer registry, these are modeled estimates rather than a head count, and the true toll is likely to be uncertain in both directions.

Cancer in Liberia, by the Numbers

An estimated 4,217 Liberians were diagnosed with cancer in 2024 and 2,745 died of it, according to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), in a country of about 5.6 million people. Women carry the heavier burden: 2,628 new cases and 1,605 deaths, against 1,589 cases and 1,140 deaths among men.

The burden is growing. The WHO’s 2020 Country profile, built on 2018 data, counted 2,808 cases and 2,223 deaths. Measured against that, estimated cases are up about 50 percent and deaths about 23 percent, while the population grew roughly 14 percent over the same period (4.9 million in 2019). Population growth explains part of the rise, but the two sets of estimates come from different editions and methods, so they show a direction rather than a precise trend.

Five cancers account for more than half of the toll, and most of them can be caught earlier or prevented:

The death-to-case ratios tell their own story. Liver cancer is the deadliest by that measure: 283 deaths against 315 new cases, nearly nine in ten. Cervical cancer, which is largely preventable through HPV vaccination and screening, still kills an estimated 345 women a year.

Hope Meets a Thin Health SystemThe survivors on Saturday were the fortunate ones. The WHO’s 2020 profile found Liberia had no radiotherapy machines, no radiation oncologists, no mammography equipment and no national breast or cervical cancer screening program. The country has also never had a population-based cancer registry, which is why its numbers remain estimates. Hospital leaders say a cobalt radiotherapy machine at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center was destroyed during the civil war, the two conflicts that convulsed Liberia between 1989 and 2003.

Dr. Deddeh Supuwood, the fight is personal. A medical oncologist at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center, she is also president of the Liberia Medical and Dental Association and a statutory council member of the Liberia Medical and Dental Council.

Things are changing, slowly. In July 2025, Liberia broke ground on its first national radiotherapy center at the Kennedy hospital, with support from the International Atomic Energy Agency, and received its first mammography unit. The government has since brought two more mammography machines, digital X-ray and ultrasound equipment and an MRI machine, worth $100,000 in all. Most of it sits at the Kennedy hospital, and experts warn that only a fraction of women will be able to reach it.

That hospital is the country’s only public facility offering specialized cancer treatment, and its patients arrive from all 15 counties. Many come late, when treatment is costlier and less likely to work. In June 2026, officials handed over a consignment of chemotherapy drugs after shortages left patients on waiting lists, with partial treatment, or sent to buy drugs from private pharmacies. “Cancer treatment has been a challenge as many patients are unable to pay,” the hospital’s chief medical officer, Dr. J. Emmanuel Tamba, said. A 42-year-old breast cancer patient who had to pause chemotherapy put it more plainly: “My children and I were deciding what to sell next.” One survivor told the Observer she paid $500 a week for a year, mostly through donations from family, church and friends.

Brooks-Jarrett said LCRI knows the walk is only a start. “We recognize that there is more to be done,” she said, and the group remains committed to “advocating for better access to screening and treatment.” Then she made the point that Shaw, Tugbeh and Supuwood had made in their own ways: “Every Liberian has a role to play, because the fight against cancer requires collective and sustained action.”

World.title: Liberia: NPP Chairman Moves to Install ‘Political Leader’ at December Convention as Embattled Standard Bearer Jewel Howard-Taylor Fights Drug Charges
World.content:
MONROVIA – The leadership of the National Patriotic Party (NPP) has unveiled a plan that critics say would quietly strip former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor of control of the party at the very moment she faces the gravest challenge of her political life: a drug trafficking and money laundering prosecution.

By Rodney D Sieh

In a message circulated to partisans, NPP National Chairman Atty. George Sylvester Mulbah Sr. said there would be no Standard Bearer election at the party’s December convention. Instead, delegates will elect a “political leader” who will have no right to contest the presidency.



Mulbah said the decision rests on what he called the 2016 Bomi amendment to the party’s constitution. He said the political leader post would cease to exist once the party elects a Standard Bearer for the 2029 elections.

The chairman also declared that “every official has lost tenure” and that partisans would elect new officers at the December convention — a statement critics read as including Howard-Taylor, who has held the Standard Bearer post.

Delegates capped at three per district

Mulbah’s message came in response to complaints from partisans about the size of the delegation to the convention. He said the party’s National Executive Committee (NEC) voted at its last meeting to send three delegates from each district, and that the minutes of that meeting are clear on the matter.

With Liberia’s 73 electoral districts, that would put the number of voting delegates at roughly 219.

The chairman said he would address NPP partisans in the United States virtually on Sunday, November 1, and wished partisans “a peaceful convention in December.”

‘No such position’

Critics within the party have rejected the plan outright. A senior partisan opposed to the move told FrontPageAfrica there is no political leader position in the NPP’s constitution or by-laws.

The partisan said the Bomi amendment Mulbah is relying on was never printed or circulated to members, and accused former Secretary General Andrew Peters of keeping it secret.

Peters is a longtime figure in the party’s factional battles. He was aligned with former Chairman James Biney in the protracted fight against Howard-Taylor for control of the NPP, a dispute that split the party, ended up before the National Elections Commission and reached the Supreme Court.

Earlier warnings of a Koung takeover

The chairman’s announcement deepens a crisis FrontPageAfrica first reported on October 21, when party insiders alleged that the fight over the December convention was about more than the calendar.

“I think a few at the top want to use this impasse to sell the NPP to Vice President Jeremiah Koung,” a senior party source said at the time, speaking on condition of anonymity. Koung’s office did not respond to FrontPageAfrica’s request for comment then.

A group calling itself the Concerned Partisans of the National Patriotic Party (CP-NPP), led by Emmanuel Goll, had already called for the convention to be postponed. The group said holding it now showed a lack of sensitivity to Howard-Taylor’s arrest and indictment, and could feed public perceptions that the case against her is politically motivated.

The CP-NPP argued that under Article V, Section 5.22(VII) of the party’s 2004 Constitution, the Standard Bearer remains in office until the next National Convention, which it says is not due until 2029. It noted that a December date fits the party’s Biennial Convention, not a National Convention, and questioned why the leadership reportedly presented the gathering to the National Elections Commission as a National Convention.

The group also questioned why the December meeting appeared designed to replace the sitting Standard Bearer with a political leader — exactly what Mulbah has now announced.

The CP-NPP further accused Senator Biney, who chairs the Senate Committee on Executive, of influencing a faction of the executive committee to push for the convention in pursuit of his own ambition to become political leader. Biney did not respond to FrontPageAfrica’s inquiry for that story.

The group conceded that many party officials have served beyond their terms because of the long internal crisis, but argued that if they can remain in office until a proper convention elects successors, the Standard Bearer should be allowed the same.

The drug case

Howard-Taylor, who served as Vice President from 2018 to 2024 under former President George Weah, was arrested at Roberts International Airport on August 19, 2026.

Prosecutors have charged her with drug trafficking, money laundering, criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation, criminal solicitation, and the unlicensed importation, sale, distribution and transportation of controlled substances.

The case followed the July 21 seizure of nearly four metric tons of cocaine valued at about US$317 million in Duazon, the largest drug bust in Liberia’s history. The government’s case covers the period from 2021 to August 2026 and centers on her alleged meetings and financial dealings with people investigators describe as members of a transnational trafficking organization, including an alleged US$15,000 payment in August 2026. Prosecutors do not allege she physically handled cocaine.

She was initially committed to the Monrovia Central Prison after the Monrovia City Court refused her lawyers’ request that she remain in hospital. Criminal Court “C” later granted her compassionate release to receive medical care at her residence under strict restrictions. A Montserrado County grand jury indicted her and others on October 7.

Howard-Taylor denies the allegations. Her family and legal team have proclaimed her innocence and said the defense will move directly to trial. She is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

A familiar fight

The latest maneuvering revives one of the longest-running feuds in Liberian party politics. Howard-Taylor and Biney fought for years over who controls the party founded by her ex-husband, former President Charles Taylor, with expulsions, counter-expulsions and rival conventions.

Mulbah himself has openly clashed with Howard-Taylor. In April 2025, he branded her “rebellious” after she endorsed the CDC-backed candidate in the Nimba County senatorial by-election, and said the party would focus on rebranding and electing new leadership ahead of 2029.

For Howard-Taylor’s supporters, the timing of the December convention — and a leadership post they say does not exist in the party’s founding documents — looks less like reform and more like an effort to settle old scores while she is unable to fight back.

World.title: Liberia: Orange Rings Up US$35.7M for Gov’t as Lonestar Drops Off LRA Top-10 List
World.content:
MONROVIA – Orange Liberia has paid the Government of Liberia US$35,666,986 so far this year, making it the fourth-largest revenue contributor in the country, according to Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA) figures as of October 31, 2026.

Only ArcelorMittal Liberia, Bea Mountain Mining Company and the Civil Service Agency rank higher. Orange sits ahead of fuel importers, the operator of the Freeport of Monrovia, the country’s main brewery and its maritime registry.

Its closest rival, Lonestar Cell MTN, is nowhere on the list. Lonestar was Liberia’s first GSM operator and for years its largest. Its absence raises fresh questions about the health of a company whose parent, South Africa’s MTN Group, has openly weighed selling it.



Orange’s Biggest Month

October was Orange’s biggest month of the year. The company paid US$6,275,560 in October alone, second only to Bea Mountain Mining Company’s US$16.6 million and well ahead of ArcelorMittal Liberia’s US$2.7 million.

That payment is almost double Orange’s monthly average. From January through September, the company paid about US$29.4 million, or roughly US$3.3 million a month.

Lonestar’s absence puts a ceiling on what it paid. The tenth-ranked contributor for the year, The LISCR Trust Company, paid US$11,952,270, and tenth place for October went to Monrovia Breweries at US$1,281,300. If Lonestar is listed as a single taxpayer, it paid less than both amounts. That means Orange paid at least three times as much as Lonestar this year, and nearly five times as much in October.

Orange’s payments this year also exceed those of APM Terminals Liberia, which runs the Freeport (US$16.6 million), Monrovia Breweries (US$14.0 million) and LISCR (US$12.0 million).

What the Figures Don’t Show

The LRA lists “consolidated” payments and does not break them down. For a telecom company, that total can include corporate income tax, the 15 percent Goods and Services Tax (GST) on telecom services, which customers pay and the company passes on, payroll taxes withheld from staff, and other levies.

This means the figures cannot be used to work out how much Orange earns. A dollar of GST a customer pays on airtime is counted the same way as a dollar of Orange’s own profit tax.

Orange has not published its Liberia revenue for this year. In 2019, during its fight with the Liberia Telecommunications Authority (LTA) over surcharges, Orange’s then general manager, Mamadou Coulibaly, put the company’s turnover at US$63.1 million. A separate figure in FrontPageAfrica’s reporting at the time was US$93.3 million.

Lonestar: First on the Air

Lonestar Cell was set up in 2000 by Beirut-based Investcom and went on air as Liberia’s first GSM network. It started with 17 towers linking Monrovia and surrounding areas, and began hiring in 2001.

MTN Group took control in 2006 when it bought Investcom, and the company became Lonestar Cell MTN. Liberian businessman Benoni Urey, through PLC Investments, holds a significant minority stake and chairs Lonestar Communications Corporation. In 2011 Lonestar held an estimated 48 percent of the market, the largest of any operator.

In May 2023, MTN said it was considering selling its operations in Liberia, Guinea and Guinea-Bissau. Bloomberg later reported that MTN was in advanced talks with Axian Telecom. The three markets made up just 1.6 percent of MTN’s group revenue in 2022.

Lonestar denied in November 2023 that it was leaving. “Lonestar is not exiting from Liberia,” corporate communication manager Lisa White said at the time. In 2024 MTN sold its Guinea and Guinea-Bissau units to Telecel. Liberia stayed in its portfolio.

At its 20th anniversary, Lonestar reported about 1.8 million subscribers. Its MTN Mobile Money arm has reported 1.28 million subscribers. At the LRA’s most recent taxpayer awards, held this year, Lonestar MTN Mobile Money was named the top contributor in digital finance.

Orange: From Cellcom to Market Leader

Orange Liberia began life as Cellcom Liberia, which was founded in 2003 and backed by the U.S.-based investment firm YCF Group. Cellcom was an early mover on 4G data in Liberia.

In January 2016, France’s Orange Group announced it would buy 100 percent of Cellcom Liberia through Orange Côte d’Ivoire. The price was not disclosed. Orange inherited about 1.4 million subscribers and rebranded the network as Orange Liberia in 2017.

By May 2025, Orange said it had more than 3 million subscribers. That month it opened the Orange Icon16 Building, a US$10 million headquarters, and CEO Jean Marius Yao pledged US$200 million in network investment over six years. Orange Money passed 1 million subscribers in March 2025 and now holds its own LTA license as a separate company.

The LRA has repeatedly ranked Orange among its top taxpayers. Orange was the highest domestic taxpayer in fiscal year 2016/2017 and took bronze for 2023. At this year’s awards, it took the overall Gold Award, ahead of Monrovia Breweries and ArcelorMittal Liberia.

A Price War and a Regulator

The rivalry has drawn the regulator in more than once. In 2019 and 2020, both companies fought LTA surcharges on voice and data, and the Supreme Court upheld the surcharges. In a joint April 2020 letter, Orange and Lonestar said they could not pay, warning the charges could mean less investment and downsizing, or lead their parent companies to judge the Liberian businesses unsustainable.

In June 2024, Orange made Orange Money transfers free. That same month, the LTA fined both operators US$300,000 each, citing a floor-price violation and refusal to submit revenue data. “A shrinking telecom landscape is called predatory pricing,” acting LTA chairperson Abdullah Kamara said.

New rules this year require the operators to spin off mobile money into separate companies. That could matter for the tax rankings: if Lonestar’s network and its mobile money arm pay taxes separately, each would appear on the LRA list on its own.

FrontPageAfrica has reached out to Lonestar Cell MTN, Orange Liberia and the LRA for comment on the figures, including what Lonestar paid this year, whether MTN still plans to sell, and what share of Orange’s payments is GST collected from customers.

World.title: Final Verdict: Swiss Supreme Court Upholds Alieu Kosiah’s 20-Year Sentence for Lofa War Crimes
World.content:
Court clears ex-ULIMO commander of crimes against humanity but leaves sentence intact

Monrovia – Former ULIMO commander Alieu Kosiah will serve the full 20 years in prison for atrocities committed in Lofa County during Liberia’s civil war, after Switzerland’s Federal Supreme Court upheld his war crimes conviction in a ruling made public Friday.

By Rodney Sieh



The decision makes final the first war crimes conviction ever handed down by a Swiss civilian court. It is also the first conviction anywhere of a Liberian for war crimes committed during the country’s two civil wars, which ran from 1989 to 2003 and killed an estimated 250,000 people.

Kosiah was found guilty of crimes committed in Lofa between 1993 and 1995, including killing civilians and ordering their killing, rape, using a child soldier, ordering pillage, cruel treatment of civilians, and desecrating the body of a dead civilian through an act of cannibalism.

The Appeals Chamber of Switzerland’s Federal Criminal Court had found that those crimes alone would justify 150 years in prison. The sentence was reduced to 20 years, the maximum allowed under Swiss law.

Crimes Against Humanity Charge Thrown Out

In a partial win for the defense, the Supreme Court acquitted Kosiah of crimes against humanity, a conviction the Appeals Chamber added in 2023. The court ruled that the crimes against humanity provision, which entered Swiss law in 2011, cannot be applied to acts committed between 1993 and 1995.

The acquittal does not affect his 20-year sentence or his expulsion from Switzerland once he has served it.

Lawyers for the victims welcomed the final conviction but criticized the acquittal.

“Today the survivors of Alieu Kosiah’s crimes have final justice, more than 30 years after they suffered and twelve years after his arrest,” said Alain Werner, Director of Civitas Maxima, the Geneva-based group that represents victims in the case. “When this case began, it was often their word against his, about events during a brutal and traumatic civil war. Today Switzerland’s highest court has confirmed that they were believed.”

Werner said his team was “deeply disappointed” by the acquittal, arguing that civilians in Lofa were deliberately targeted — killed, raped, looted and forced to carry loads for fighters — in a widespread and systematic attack.

“What happened in Lofa between 1993 and 1995 is the very definition of a crime against humanity,” he said.

Twelve Years in Detention

Kosiah settled in Switzerland in the late 1990s and was arrested in November 2014 after Liberian victims filed a criminal complaint through their lawyers. He has been in detention ever since.

Survivors traveled from Liberia to testify against him during the investigation and at both of his trials.

The case was built with the help of the Global Justice and Research Project (GJRP), a Liberian organization that has documented civil war crimes for more than a decade. Together, Civitas Maxima and GJRP have contributed to six criminal trials in four countries linked to Liberia’s civil wars, resulting in five convictions.

‘Our People Should Not Have to Keep Looking to Europe’

The ruling once again throws a spotlight on Liberia’s failure to try its own war criminals. More than two decades after the war ended, no war crimes trial has been held on Liberian soil. Armed groups recruited more than 21,000 children during the conflict.

Liberia has committed to establishing a War and Economic Crimes Court, but the court has yet to hear a case.

GJRP Director Hassan Bility thanked Swiss authorities for more than ten years of commitment that allowed Liberian survivors to take part directly in the trials, but said justice should be delivered at home.

“These crimes were committed in Liberia by a Liberian against Liberians, and the judgment was delivered thousands of miles away,” Bility said. “Our people should not have to keep looking to Europe or the United States for justice. It is more than time for these trials to take place in Liberia, and for the War and Economic Crimes Court to start its work.”
