World.title: Liberia: Bong County’s New Road Machines Could Open the Way from Farm to Market, Says EPA Boss Yarkpawolo
World.content:
GBARNGA, Bong County – The arrival of 30 pieces of heavy earthmoving equipment in Bong County is being greeted as a turning point for the county’s farmers, traders and rural families. The head of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) says the machines could turn isolation into opportunity.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo, the EPA Executive Director and a son of Zota District, said the yellow machines carry meaning far beyond the construction work they are expected to do. In his view, passable roads sit at the heart of food security, farm income and the daily survival of rural households.



In a statement marking the arrival, Dr. Yarkpawolo commended President Joseph Nyuma Boakai for placing roads at the center of his administration’s agenda. He argued that the initiative could begin to ease transportation problems that have long held back farming and trade in Bong, one of the country’s most important agricultural counties.

He leaned on a saying the President is known for: that people cannot eat a road, yet a road is what allows people to eat. “People do not eat road, but it is road that can make people eat,” he recalled. According to the EPA chief, the line captures what farmers across rural Liberia live with every season.

Farmers in Bong, he explained, put months of labor and money into growing rice, cassava, vegetables and plantains. But the work does not end at harvest. Getting crops out of the village and into a market is often the harder part, and where roads have deteriorated, that journey can fail altogether.

The rainy season makes matters worse. Mud, washed-out surfaces and damaged crossings can cut off whole farming settlements, leaving vehicles unable to reach them. Produce waiting by the roadside may rot before a buyer ever sees it, and the farmer absorbs the loss. “A farmer can grow rice, cassava, vegetables, and plantains, but without a reliable road to the market, that harvest may spoil before it can be sold,” he said.

The damage, Dr. Yarkpawolo noted, does not stop with the farmer. Market women struggle to get supplies, traders lose business, and families in towns and cities pay more because the cost of hauling food over bad roads gets passed along at the market stall.

That is why, he said, agriculture and infrastructure should not be treated as two separate items on the government’s to-do list. “A road connects the hands that grow our food to the households that need it,” he stated. He added that it also lets farmers earn the money to feed, educate and uplift their children.

Roads, he stressed, are also lifelines to schools and clinics. Children in remote communities can find it hard to reach the classroom, and patients needing urgent care may not reach a hospital in time when the only route is barely passable. More dependable roads throughout the year, he said, would ease those burdens. “Beyond food, better roads can help children reach school, patients reach hospitals, and businesses reach new customers,” he said.

His comments come amid an ongoing national conversation about road development and economic recovery, especially in rural counties where farming remains a main source of work and income. In Bong, many households rely on farming and small-scale trading to get by, and weak road links have historically made it harder to move goods and reach basic services.

Dr. Yarkpawolo believes sustained rehabilitation of rural roads could open doors for residents who have waited years. Farmers who can move crops quickly and cheaply stand a better chance of earning enough to enlarge their farms, buy inputs and improve conditions at home.

Traders would gain too. With better roads, he said, they could reach more villages, buy directly from producers and carry goods to bigger markets. Stronger ties between farmers and city consumers could also help bring down some of the transport costs that keep market prices high.

For Zota District and other rural parts of Bong, the stakes are personal.

“Today, as Bong County’s yellow machines arrive home, I welcome them with pride as a son of Bong,” he declared. He said the machines offer farmers, market women and cut-off communities a chance to turn isolation into access and hard work into income.

Yet the EPA chief was clear that delivery is not the same as results. He warned that the arrival of equipment does not fulfill the government’s responsibility, and called for practical steps to keep the machines running and ensure they produce measurable benefits.

Maintenance, he said, must be a priority. Without disciplined management and steady attention to servicing and operating needs, the machines’ usefulness will fade.

He also urged fairness in deployment, insisting that communities facing the toughest travel problems should get a real share of the benefit.

“Their arrival must now translate into results. We must maintain the machines, deploy them fairly, and ensure they serve the communities that need them,” he said.

Dr. Yarkpawolo said the program should not be judged by the number of machines parked in Bong, but by what changes on the ground. “Their true value will be measured in roads made passable, travel made easier, and livelihoods improved,” he said. Road work, in his words, must deliver tangible gains: easier movement, better market access and more earning opportunities for rural households.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-Mayor Jefferson Koijee Hands Over Disputed Sinkor Property to VP Koung, Vows Political Fight Continues
World.content:
The former mayor, who served under the administration of ex-President George Manneh Weah, used the statement to renew allegations of political persecution against the administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Vice President Koung.

Former Monrovia City Mayor Jefferson T. Koijee says handing over the 19th Street premises does not amount to surrender or an admission of guilt, accusing the Boakai-Koung administration of political persecution while declaring 2029 as his political destination.

Former Monrovia City Mayor Jefferson T. Koijee says he has officially handed over a disputed property on 19th Street, Coleman Avenue, in Sinkor, to Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung following an intervention by his spiritual adviser, Pastor Philemon A. Tarpeh.

In a public statement, Koijee said the decision was driven by his faith and commitment to peace, insisting that relinquishing the premises should not be interpreted as an admission of wrongdoing or a retreat from his political struggle.



“I have chosen peace. My faith remains unshaken. 2029 is our destination,” Koijee declared, signaling his intention to remain politically active ahead of the next presidential election.

The former mayor, who served under the administration of ex-President George Manneh Weah, used the statement to renew allegations of political persecution against the administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Vice President Koung.

At the center of his argument is the ownership dispute surrounding the Sinkor property.

Koijee recalled that on September 18, 2018, then Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, Mo Ali, publicly alleged that he had acquired a house valued at US$250,000 in less than nine months.

According to Koijee, the allegation followed him for years and was repeatedly used to portray him as corrupt.

However, he said a writ of summons issued by the Monrovia City Magisterial Court on October 13, 2026, identifies Vice President Koung as claiming the same property.

He questioned how the property could have been attributed to him in 2018 but is now being claimed by the Vice President.

“So which lie were they telling then, and which lie are they telling now?” Koijee asked, challenging the government to explain the circumstances surrounding the competing claims.

He said the Boakai-Koung administration owes the Liberian public an explanation, although the competing ownership claims and the legal status of the property remain matters requiring clarification through the appropriate legal process.

Koijee also revisited the international sanctions announced against him on December 8, 2023, saying his political opponents celebrated the development as the end of his political career.

He claimed that the sanctions resulted in repeated visa denials and other restrictions but credited Pastor Tarpeh’s prayers and spiritual support for helping him overcome the difficulties.

“The man they buried is still standing,” he said, invoking biblical passages to reinforce his message of resilience and faith.

The former mayor further rejected allegations linking him to criminal activities, including murder, accusing the current administration of using state institutions and public platforms to tarnish his reputation.

Koijee argued that despite nearly three years of accusations, authorities had failed to prove the allegations against him in court.

“They called me a criminal. They called me a murderer,” he said. “For almost three years the Boakai-Koung regime has controlled the police, the prosecutors, and the microphones, and not one case has been proven against me.”

He challenged the government to produce evidence supporting the allegations, including financial records and properties allegedly linked to him.

However, his claims about the absence of proven cases do not, on their own, establish that all allegations against him are unfounded. The specific status of any investigations or proceedings would need to be established through official records.

In defending his public service record, Koijee cited his tenure as Monrovia City Mayor, arguing that he prioritized public service over personal comfort.

He said he continued using an official vehicle purchased by his predecessor rather than requesting a new one, adding that he nearly lost his life in an accident involving the same vehicle on June 16, 2018.

Koijee maintained that throughout his six years as mayor, he never purchased a new official vehicle for himself and challenged critics to verify the claim through records at City Hall.

He also directed questions at Chairman George Sylvester Mulbah, demanding clarification over his alleged relationship with the Office of the Vice President.

“Seven statements, and still no answer. Are you employed in the Office of Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung? Yes or no?” Koijee asked.

He did not provide further details about the seven statements referenced in his challenge.

Despite handing over the disputed premises, Koijee said he would continue advocating for what he described as constitutional governance, independent courts and equal justice.

He framed the property handover as a decision to avoid confrontation rather than a withdrawal from the political arena.

“They can take a property, but they cannot take my voice, my faith, or the people’s hunger for change,” he declared.

Koijee concluded by reaffirming his political ambition ahead of the 2029 elections, describing the next presidential contest as the destination of his ongoing political struggle.

“I have handed over the premises. I have not handed over the truth,” he said.

The property dispute, the circumstances surrounding its handover and the competing claims of ownership are likely to remain subjects of public interest as the political exchanges between the former mayor and the current administration continue.

World.title: Liberia: STAND Slams Boakai-Koung Over Poverty, CBL Pay Disparities; Demands Probe Into President’s Son
World.content:
MONROVIA-The Solidarity & Trust for a New Day (STAND) has accused the Boakai-Koung administration of failing ordinary Liberians while allowing wide salary disparities within government, and reiterated call for an independent investigation into drug trafficking allegations involving Joseph Boakai Jr.

By Jaheim T. Tumu – [email protected]

STAND said the government’s billion-dollar budget has not translated into meaningful relief for citizens struggling with poverty, poor public services and economic hardship.



It also questioned why senior Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) officials reportedly receive substantial salaries and allowances while some lower-paid public workers face salary reductions.

In a statement issued, STAND Chairman Mulbah K. Morlu Jr. said the government’s approach to public spending and accountability reflects what the group described as a growing gap between the privileges enjoyed by senior officials and the difficulties facing ordinary citizens.

“Despite boasting of a billion-dollar budget, the government has failed to translate increased public spending into meaningful relief for ordinary Liberians,” STAND said.

STAND argued that nearly three years into the Boakai-Koung administration, many Liberians continue to struggle to meet their basic needs, while public schools and healthcare services remain inadequate.

STAND Questions CBL Pay Packages

STAND cited reported compensation packages at the Central Bank of Liberia as an example of what it considers unequal treatment within the public sector.

According to the group, some senior CBL officials reportedly receive monthly salaries of US$14,000, along with US$15,000 in housing allowances.

The statement also cited a reported compensation package of approximately US$29,000 per month disclosed by a nominee for CBL deputy governor, Euphemia G.T. Swen-Monmia

STAND contrasted those figures with the case of a Governance Commission employee who, it said, faces demotion and a salary reduction from approximately US$1,281.91 to US$900 per month.

The group argued that the contrast raises questions about the government’s commitment to shared sacrifice at a time when many workers are struggling financially.

“This situation is neither a shared sacrifice nor a genuine Rescue Mission; it’s a two-tier system that punishes the underprivileged while shielding privilege,” STAND stated.

The group called on the Civil Service Agency, Governance Commission, Central Bank and Legislature to explain the reported disparities and subject public-sector salaries, allowances and benefits to an independent review.

It also demanded that any decisions found to be unlawful or improperly authorized be corrected and those responsible held accountable.

The compensation figures and employment decision cited by STAND were not independently verified in its statement.

Demands Drug Investigation Into President’s Son

Beyond economic concerns, STAND reiterated its call for an independent investigation into drug trafficking allegations involving Boakai Jr. arguing that political and family connections should not determine how the law is applied.

The group questioned what it described as the government’s failure to demonstrate the same urgency in addressing allegations against the President’s son as it has shown in pursuing drug-related charges against former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor.

“If one witness’s testimony provides probable cause to prosecute Mrs. Taylor, why should Jojo Boakai be above arrest and prosecution when a drug cartel has publicly accused him?” STAND asked.

Morlu, STAND Chairman asserted that substantial evidence exists against Jojo Boakai and challenged the government to demonstrate that justice is being applied equally.

STAND also called on President Boakai to justify Taylor’s continued detention and show that family connections do not exempt anyone from the law.

The allegations against Jojo Boakai have not been independently established by the statement. STAND’s claims do not, by themselves, establish criminal wrongdoing, and any investigation or prosecution must be based on evidence and due process.

STAND Calls SPARK Foundation a ‘Humanitarian Fraud’

STAND also criticized the launch of Jojo Boakai’s SPARK Foundation, describing it as a “Humanitarian Fraud” and arguing that philanthropy should not replace accountability.

“Philanthropy cannot replace accountability, and a foundation cannot serve as a shield against scrutiny,” the group said.

The organization alleged that the foundation could be used to create a humanitarian image for the President’s son while questions surrounding the reported US$317 million drug case remain unresolved.

It further raised questions about whether the foundation could be financed with drug proceeds or taxpayers’ funds. However, the statement provided no independently verified evidence establishing that either source was used.

STAND called for the allegations to be investigated independently, insisting that no charitable initiative should place anyone beyond legitimate scrutiny.

The group said it condemns crime and does not seek to protect anyone accused of wrongdoing, but wants the law applied equally to all Liberians.

Group Warns of Civil Disobedience

STAND warned that the government’s response to allegations of corruption, selective justice and economic exclusion could determine its next course of action.

The group said the administration’s continued failure to address allegations involving powerful officials and the President’s son could become grounds for targeted civil disobedience conducted within the confines of the law.

It announced plans to make a broader declaration in the coming days, promising to challenge what it described as the administration’s “Rich Family-First” approach to governance.

STAND also criticized the Legislature, accusing lawmakers of failing to exercise effective constitutional oversight and neglecting the economic struggles of ordinary Liberians.

The group said it intends to confront lawmakers over alleged corruption and political patronage, arguing that the Legislature must hold public officials accountable rather than allow alleged abuses of power to go unchecked.

STAND called on reform-minded groups to unite and pursue lawful means of demanding greater transparency, accountability and fairness in government.

The group warned that corruption, economic exclusion and declining public confidence could threaten Liberia’s stability and democracy.

World.title: Football icon Freddie Mwila dies at 80
World.content:
Zambian football is mourning following the death of former national team captain and coach Freddie Mwila Snr.

Family spokesperson Lillian Kalikeka has confirmed to FAZ Media that Mwila, 80, died at Maina Soko Medical Centre in Lusaka around 01:00 hours on Monday after suffering a stroke.

Kalikeka said funeral gathering is being held at the family home in Mapepe Farms.

Mwila remains one of the most decorated figures in Zambian football history, both as a player and coach.

As a player, he featured for Rhokana United, now Nkana, before becoming one of the first Zambians to play professional football abroad when he joined American side Atlanta Chiefs in 1967.

He later had a stint with English side Aston Villa, paving the way for future generations of Zambian footballers to play abroad.

As a coach, Mwila etched his name in continental football history when he led Power Dynamos to the 1991 African Cup Winners’ Cup – making Power the first Southern African club to win a continental title.

He also coached the Zambia and Botswana national teams, and several local clubs including Zanaco, Lusaka Dynamos, Nkwazi and Circuit Chiefs.

Mwila is remembered for his contribution to the development of the game spanning over five decades, nurturing talent and raising Zambia’s profile on the international stage.

FAZ and the football family are expected to announce funeral and burial arrangements in due course.

World.title: “Africa’s newest dictator”: Leaders demand apology as Khama row over HH escalates
World.content:
Former Botswana President Ian Khama is facing a growing backlash in Zambia after describing President Hakainde Hichilema as “Africa’s newest dictator”. Members of Parliament, State House and governance experts have demanded that he withdraw the remark and apologise. They describe his comments as careless, reckless and unfounded. The row has quickly grown into one of the most heated exchanges between Zambia and a former regional leader in recent years. It has also opened a debate at home, with some opposition voices saying the remarks should not be brushed aside.

The controversy began in Botswana’s Ntlo ya Dikgosi, the House of Chiefs, where Mr Khama sits as a traditional leader. During a session in Gaborone, he asked Botswana’s Minister of International Relations whether the government regretted sending a representative to President Hichilema’s inauguration. In framing the question, he labelled the Zambian leader “Africa’s newest dictator”. The Minister, Dr Phenyo Butale, defended Botswana’s attendance. He said Botswana must keep good neighbourly relations and cannot engage with other countries if it stays away.

Mr Khama did not back down. In a later media interview, he repeated his description of President Hichilema as a dictator. He went further, accusing the Zambian Government of manipulating elections, persecuting opposition politicians and abusing political activists. His comments come amid continuing political and legal disputes after Zambia’s general election on 13 August, including the detention of several opposition figures. The Zambian Government has rejected the characterisation of its record.

State House Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka was among the first to respond. He questioned Mr Khama’s conduct and pointed out that the former Botswana leader had previously visited State House and held talks with President Hichilema. Mr Hamasaka said he found it hard to understand how someone who had engaged the President in that way could now call him a dictator. UPND Lusaka Province Secretary James Sichomba described the remarks as misleading and hypocritical. He cited Zambia’s election to the United Nations Human Rights Council for 2027 to 2029, the abolition of the death penalty and the expansion of free education as evidence of the country’s democratic progress.

Member of Parliament Judith Kabemba has now called on Mr Khama to withdraw his remarks and offer an unreserved apology to President Hichilema and the people of Zambia. Ms Kabemba described the statements as unfortunate, reckless and unbecoming of a former head of state. She said leaders of Mr Khama’s standing are expected to champion diplomacy, statesmanship and respect for democratic institutions. She said President Hichilema’s political career has been defined by respect for constitutional processes and democratic principles. She pointed to his decision to pursue power through successive elections and lawful means over many years.

“Unlike the characterisation being advanced against our President, Mr Hichilema has consistently demonstrated his commitment to patriotism, democracy and constitutionalism,” Ms Kabemba said.

Governance expert and human rights advocate Wesley Miyanda has also condemned the remarks. He described them as unfortunate, misplaced and harmful to the strong political, social and economic ties between Zambia and Botswana. Mr Miyanda said Zambia has earned international recognition as one of Africa’s most peaceful and stable democracies. He said the country has an enviable record of conducting credible elections and facilitating peaceful transfers of power. That record, he said, should command respect across the region.

Livingstone MP Mr Mayangwa said Mr Khama should reflect on his own governance record before attacking President Hichilema. He described the President as a democratically elected leader whose administration is focused on economic recovery. He said the Government has worked to restore investor confidence and create opportunities for national development. He said the President’s record should be judged on those results. He said it should not be judged by commentary from across the border.

Not everyone has dismissed Mr Khama’s comments. Socialist Party president Fred M’membe said that while the language used by a foreign former head of state is a matter for regional reflection, the substance of the criticism should not be casually brushed off. He argued that the remarks reflect concerns his party has raised about the state of democracy in Zambia. His position puts him at odds with the ruling party and its allies. It also shows how quickly a diplomatic spat has become part of Zambia’s domestic political debate.

Mr Khama served as President of Botswana from 2008 to 2018 and remains an outspoken voice on regional politics. Zambia and Botswana share a border at Kazungula, where the two countries jointly built the Kazungula Bridge across the Zambezi River. Botswana’s current government has made clear through its minister that it values good relations with Lusaka. For now, Zambia’s leaders want one thing from Mr Khama: a withdrawal and an apology. Whether he responds will decide whether the row fades or deepens.

World.title: ZPL partners with ZIT in a five year agreement
World.content:
Zambia Premier League (ZPL) has partnered with ZIT in a five-year agreement to introduce ZPL Smart Football, a digital platform that will improve club administration, player development and fan engagement.

Zambia Premier League Head of Communications, Christina Zulu says the initiative is part of the league’s efforts to professionalise and commercialise football through technology and innovation.

Zulu said the platform will provide clubs with digital tools for player profiling, squad management, match preparation, performance analysis and financial management.

She said ZPL Smart Football will also strengthen relationships between clubs and supporters through digital memberships, fantasy football competitions, player statistics and interactive match day experiences.

Zulu added that the platform’s sponsorship portal will create opportunities for businesses to reach football audiences through digital advertising.

She said the partnership is expected to contribute to the development of a more connected, data-driven and commercially sustainable football ecosystem in Zambia.

World.title: ZCSA to catch-up on mobile money scams
World.content:
The Zambia Cyber Security Agency (ZCSA) has intensified public awareness efforts to keep up with the evolving difficulty of mobile money scams and account hacking.

ZCSA Director of Research, Education and Awareness, Edgar Mlauzi, said scammers have developed advanced social engineering tactics that go around safety measures put in place and breach security to trap victims.

Mr Mlauzi said the agency is targeting behavioral change among end-users as a key strategy to curb scams and hacking.

“We continuously educate end users, so that whatever prompt you receive, you should stop, think, verify, then act,” he said.

Mr Mlauzi said the agency is committed to strengthening the country’s digital security through stricter requirements for institutions designated as Critical Information Infrastructure.

He noted that these institutions will be required to conduct vulnerability assessments, undergo annual cybersecurity audits and implement security measures to protect their systems against cyberattacks, fraud and data theft.

“Mobile money providers will also be required to have stringent policies and controls in place,” he said.

He further called upon members of the community and the media, stating they play a vital role in cyber conduct while emphasizing that cyber security is everyone’s responsibility.

World.title: ICGLR calls for audit of mineral supply chains
World.content:
The International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) has called for strict auditing of mineral supply chains to prevent illicit minerals from entering the formal market and strengthen the credibility of the regional certification mechanism.

Speaking at the close of the 30th Audit Committee meeting in Lusaka, Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Permanent Secretary, Hapenga Kabeta said the committee plays a critical role in authenticating mineral certificates and ensuring that minerals traded across the region are legally sourced.

Dr Kabeta was speaking in a speech read for him by Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Director Artisanal Small Scale Mining, Brighton Kateka.

Dr Kabeta urged auditors to thoroughly examine every stage of mineral production and transportation, emphasising that no individual or player in the mineral supply chain should be exempted from scrutiny.

“Promoting responsible mining is important because it will help our minerals to earn more, no one is exempted from scrutiny,” Dr Kabeta said.

And ICGLR Deputy Executive Secretary, Yassir Mohammed said that mineral resources should serve as catalysts for peace, prosperity and development rather than sources of conflict.

Ambassador Mohammed has called on member states to strengthen regional cooperation, promote responsible mineral sourcing and support artisanal and small-scale miners.

Meanwhile, Zambia’s ICGLR National Coordinator, Christopher Sitwala noted that mining remains a government priority over the next five years.

“With increased investment in brownfield and greenfield projects, streamlined licensing processes and formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining operations,” Mr Sitwala said.

Mr Sitwala added that government remains committed to ensuring that mining activities are legal, formal, commercially viable and safe while curbing illegal exploitation of natural resources.

Meanwhile, ICGLR committee Chairperson, Philiph Kiplangat said the three-day meeting has provided an opportunity to examine third-party audit reports, assess progress among member states and identify areas requiring improvement.

Engineer Kiplangat said that the effectiveness of the certification mechanism depends on translating audit findings into practical improvements on the ground.

The three-day meeting brought together representatives of ICGLR member states and cooperating partners, including GIZ and IMPACT, in efforts to improve accountability and transparency in the regional mineral trade.

World.title: Magistrate laments declining family support in society
World.content:
Mkushi Magistrate Felix Lukonde has expressed concern over the apparent lack of family support for a 47-year-old woman with a history of mental health challenges.

Beatrice Chewe is accused of assaulting Bertha Kangwa and has been charged with one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, contrary to Section 250 of the Penal Code Act, Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia.

She has pleaded not guilty to the charge.

During the court proceedings, Magistrate Lukonde expressed concern that Chewe’s siblings and daughters had reportedly not attended court to support her since the matter began.

He said the woman had not chosen her condition and deserved care and support from her family.

“She did not want or choose to be in this condition,” Magistrate Lukonde said.

The court heard that a mental state examination conducted on Chewe indicated that she had a mild mental health problem and also reportedly to have suffered postpartum psychosis many years ago.

Ms Chewe, who is reportedly homeless and sleeps at the market, told the court that she owns a house in the Kawama area of Mkushi District.

The court also heard that she sometimes became violent.

Magistrate Lukonde questioned the apparent absence of her relatives, saying she had been alone throughout the proceedings.

He urged families to look after their vulnerable relatives, emphasising the importance of compassion and collective responsibility.

“We are a family, and families should look out for each other,” he said.

Magistrate Lukonde has acknowledged the Department of Social Welfare’s effort of contacting one of Chewe’s brothers to establish family support

The magistrate’s remarks highlighted concerns about the welfare of vulnerable people and the importance of family involvement in ensuring they receive appropriate care and support.

The matter has been adjourned to 4th November, 2026.

World.title: Medical expert cautions the public on mental health
World.content:
A medical expert and psychiatric clinician has urged the public to prioritise early medical intervention and personal acceptance in mental health as essential tools in combating cultural stigma and preventing relapse.

Speaking in an interview in Lusaka today, Aaron Chishimba highlighted that stress impacts every stage of life, ranging from academic pressure in young adults to job loss and family breakdown later in life.

Mr Chishimba challenged cultural misconceptions, stressing that the human brain is a physical organ prone to diseases and that behavioral changes are medical symptoms rather than manifestations of witchcraft.

The medical expert warned that unaddressed psychological strain within households easily disrupts children’s emotional development thereby contributing directly to the rising number of youths living on the streets.

Mr Chishimba recommended that families should be empathetic and create firm boundaries to avoid enabling behavior while seeking immediate professional medical care if they are manage domestic mental health crises effectively.

He noted that accessible, affordable psychiatric evaluation and treatment remain available national wide through specialised regional facility annexes, such as Chinama mental Hospital.

Meanwhile, Clinical Neuropsychologist, Aaron Bwembya explained that mental health conditions stem from an interplay of factors, including early childhood trauma, toxic relationships, parental rejection, and social media pressure, which trigger anxiety and substance abuse.

“Over 80 percent of individuals living with mental health conditions reside in low- and middle-income countries, where poverty creates immense barriers to care,” Mr Bwembya explained.

He also highlighted how economic hardships restrict access to basic needs.

“To combat this threat, communities, workplaces, and families must adopt compassionate, non-stigmatising language that empowers individuals to seek help and rebuild their lives,” he stated.

World.title: Leaders demand apology as backlash grows over Khama’s remarks on HH
World.content:
Political leaders and governance stakeholders have mounted a strong defence of President Hakainde Hichilema against remarks attributed to former Botswana President Ian Khama. They describe the remarks as careless and unfounded. The backlash follows comments Mr Khama allegedly made in a recent radio interview, in which he described President Hichilema in an undiplomatic manner. Government officials and other stakeholders have challenged the former Botswana leader to retract his remarks and apologise. The row has drawn in members of Parliament, governance experts and human rights voices.

Member of Parliament Judith Kabemba has called on Mr Khama to withdraw his remarks and offer an unreserved apology to President Hichilema and the people of Zambia. Ms Kabemba described the statements as unfortunate, reckless and unbecoming of a former head of state. She said leaders of Mr Khama’s standing are expected to champion diplomacy, statesmanship and respect for democratic institutions. She said comments of this kind undermine the dignity expected of those who have held the highest office in their countries. Her call was among the strongest from Zambia’s political establishment.

Ms Kabemba said President Hichilema’s political career has been defined by respect for constitutional processes and democratic principles. She pointed to his decision to pursue power through successive elections and by lawful means. He contested several general elections before winning the presidency in 2021. He was re-elected in the August 2026 general election. Ms Kabemba said that record directly contradicts the picture painted by Mr Khama.

“Unlike the characterisation being advanced against our President, Mr Hichilema has consistently demonstrated his commitment to patriotism, democracy and constitutionalism,” Ms Kabemba said.

Governance expert and human rights advocate Wesley Miyanda has also condemned the remarks. He described them as unfortunate, misplaced and harmful to the strong political, social and economic ties Zambia and Botswana have enjoyed for many years. Mr Miyanda said Zambia has earned international recognition as one of Africa’s most peaceful and stable democracies. He said the country has an enviable record of conducting credible elections and facilitating peaceful transfers of power. He said that record should command respect from leaders across the region.

Livingstone MP Mr Mayangwa said Mr Khama should reflect on his own governance record before attacking President Hichilema. He described President Hichilema as a democratically elected leader whose administration is focused on economic recovery. He said the Government has worked to restore investor confidence and create opportunities for national development. He said the President’s record should be judged on those results. He said it should not be judged by commentary from outside the country.

Mr Khama served as President of Botswana from 2008 to 2018. Since leaving office, he has been an outspoken commentator on politics in Botswana and the wider region. Zambia and Botswana share one of the shortest borders in the world at Kazungula, where the two countries jointly built the Kazungula Bridge across the Zambezi River. The bridge has become a symbol of regional cooperation and a key link for trade between Southern African countries. Relations between Lusaka and Gaborone have generally been warm and cooperative.

Neither the Government of Botswana nor Mr Khama had publicly responded to the calls for an apology at the time of writing. The remarks appear to have been made in a personal capacity rather than as a statement of Botswana’s official position. That distinction matters for diplomatic relations between the two countries. Still, criticism from a former head of state carries weight across the region. The strength of the reaction in Zambia shows how seriously the remarks have been taken.

For President Hichilema’s supporters, the episode is a chance to restate the democratic credentials that underpin his administration. For the region, it is a reminder that former leaders’ words can strain relations between neighbours. Zambia’s leaders have made their position clear: they want the remarks withdrawn and an apology issued. Whether Mr Khama responds will decide whether the row fades or deepens.

World.title: South Africa: Rigging Claims, Xenophobia Raise Fears of Polling Station Tensions
World.content:
Cape Town — Days before South Africans vote in the local government elections on Wednesday 4 November 2026, social media is carrying unverified claims of election rigging alongside posts that blame foreign nationals. This has raised concerns about the potential for online hostility to spill into real-world tensions.

The Centre for Analytics and Behavioural Change (CABC), through its High-Risk Events Monitoring programme, logged 79 potentially harmful posts between 22 and 29 October. This included allegations of electoral fraud, hate speech and calls that could incite violence.

One post urged people to gather at voting stations to stop foreign nationals from voting. Of the 79 posts, 51 were tagged as misinformation or disinformation, 33 as hate speech and 12 as incitement to violence. The categories overlap, so a single post can fall into more than one. The posts attracted approximately 546,600 views, 29,600 likes, 4,100 shares and 1,350 comments across platforms.

According to CABC, the wider conversation was much larger.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Over the eight days to 29 October, the CABC recorded more than 15,310 mentions of the elections from 6,426 unique authors, with volumes rising steadily from 25 October.

Illegal immigration was the leading topic.

The organisation found that conversations about illegal immigration were largely driven by frustration with government immigration policies and perceptions among some users that protests against immigration were being silenced. Elements of collective blame directed at foreign nationals were also identified. Users were angry about the government's immigration policy and what they saw as an attempt to silence protests on the issue.

The monitoring also reported on the mobilization of foreign nationals to campaign for political parties, with concerns that immigration related grievances could fuel tensions around the electoral process.

Most of the South African conversations were critical of the ruling political parties, with users expressing concern over the ongoing struggles facing citizens. Other posts criticised governing parties or focused on the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) and its preparations.

Election-related discussions increased steadily from 25 October, with a spike of approximately 1,000 additional mentions on 26 October.

The quietest day was 24 October, with 1,253 mentions, which the CABC said coincided with Economic Freedom Fighters ( EFF) leader Julius Malema's campaigning in Mpumalanga, where he put "unemployment and poor service delivery at the centre of his party's election campaign."

The highest volume of mentions was recorded on 27 October, reaching 2,615. According to the CABC, this increase was driven partly by debates between the African National Congress (ANC) and the Democratic Alliance (DA) over housing delivery in Cape Town.

The ANC's mayoral candidate argued that the party had a stronger housing delivery record, claiming it had "delivered more housing in that period than the DA has in 20 years".

According to CABC, the log records approximately 546,600 views, 29,600 likes, 4,100 shares and 1,350 comments across entries with available metrics.

Three narratives driving online hostility

The CABC identified three recurring narratives in the online conversation: allegations of election rigging, xenophobic claims linking foreign nationals to electoral manipulation, and calls that could translate online hostility into confrontation at polling stations.

The first centres on distrust in the IEC and the credibility of the electoral process.

Several users cast doubt on the IEC and the credibility of results before voting took place. One post claimed the ANC had already voted on behalf of citizens and offered what it presented as proof of ANC–IEC collusion. The CABC logged 95,500 views for it. Another user suggested that a delay in announcing results would allow them to be doctored. Other posts alleged the IEC was compromised or asked whether an ANC or DA victory could occur without rigging.

The CABC said these posts show how suspicion of election administration is being expressed "as specific, but unverified, allegations". It stressed that criticism or distrust alone is not necessarily misinformation.

"Distrusting an institution is not misinformation. Posting specific accusations with nothing behind them is," said CABC. "Claims that the count is rigged hand people a ready-made explanation for any result they dislike. When those claims are tied to foreign nationals, they can send people to a polling station looking for someone to blame."

CABC warned that unsubstantiated rigging allegations could undermine confidence in election results, particularly when used to explain outcomes that political supporters or voters may dislike.

The second narrative links foreign nationals to alleged electoral manipulation and political advantage.

One user claimed the ANC was replacing South Africans with foreign nationals, using a derogatory term for migrants. Another alleged that Home Affairs was issuing identity documents to foreign nationals in Cape Town, a post with 35,000 logged views. A third claimed migrants would be used to dilute South Africans' votes and rig elections.

The CABC said the common thread is "an unsubstantiated suggestion that immigration and documentation are tools for manipulating the electorate". It warned that this framing risks confusing immigration status with eligibility to vote and reinforcing hostility towards migrant communities.

Close 

The third narrative raised concerns about the possibility of online allegations translating into confrontation at voting stations.

Some posts went beyond claims of unfairness to calls for direct action. One user urged South Africans to gather at voting stations on 4 November to prevent foreign nationals from voting for the ANC and the EFF, a post with 3,366 logged views. Another warned that foreign nationals were allegedly being mobilised to campaign for a political party.

The CABC said these examples "do not establish organised intimidation or impending violence". However, they illustrate how unverified claims about migrant participation might be translated into confrontational activity near polling stations. Lawful observation and political mobilisation, it said, must be distinguished from threats, discriminatory targeting and interference with voters.

In its conclusion, the organisation warned that allegations of electoral fraud and xenophobic narratives could reinforce one another.

"The clearest risk is not proof of widespread manipulation, but the possibility that unverified claims weaken confidence in electoral processes and encourage hostility towards perceived foreign voters," reported the CABC.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 2, 2026
World.content:
Sudan's El Fasher Remains a Ghost Town One Year After RSF Takeover

One year after the capture of El Fasher, North Darfur, by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the city remains largely deserted, with survivors and aid workers reporting widespread destruction, fear, and ongoing human rights abuses. Thousands of residents are still missing, and others are believed to be detained in overcrowded prisons where torture, disease and inhumane conditions have been reported. 40,000 to 60,000 people are estimated to have returned or visited the city. Many are still reluctant to return because of the trauma, the insecurity, and the fear that new arrivals have taken their homes. International investigators have documented mass killings and sexual violence during the siege. The UN estimates that around 6,000 people were killed. However, researchers believe the actual death toll could be significantly higher.

HRW Accuses Zambian Forces of Abductions, Torture and Crackdown on Critics



Human Rights Watch has accused Zambian security forces of forcibly disappearing, arbitrarily detaining and abusing opposition members, journalists, lawyers and government critics following the August 2026 general elections. The organisation documented 14 apparent cases of enforced disappearances, 61 cases of alleged abuse in custody and 71 cases of potentially politically motivated arrests or prolonged detention without charge. Several detainees have reportedly faced beatings, torture, restricted access to lawyers and medical care, while opposition figures, including leader Brian Mundubile, have been charged with treason. Human Rights Watch has called on President Hakainde Hichilema's government to end the crackdown, release those arbitrarily detained and investigate alleged abuses, including the controversial killing of former government minister Mutotwe Kafwaya during a security raid.

Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed Sends Cabinet Ministers for Military Training

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put cabinet ministers and senior government officials through military training. He said that military discipline can help strengthen leadership and advance national development. Images shared on social media show ministers, including Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba, participating in exercises at the Hurso military training centre. Abiy said that military institutions can teach discipline, patriotism, teamwork and accountability, helping create leaders capable of achieving the country's development ambitions. The unusual initiative comes as Ethiopia faces ongoing conflicts in Tigray, Amhara and Oromia, as well as heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea. Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

Gauteng Shuts 20 Liquor Outlets in GBV Crackdown

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi said that the province has shut down 20 liquor outlets following more than 7,300 inspections as part of efforts to tackle gender-based violence and protect women and children. The province plans to deploy 1,022 response teams across 122 high-risk areas and recruit an additional 56 social workers to support victims and survivors. Authorities are also strengthening specialised sexual offences courts, victim-friendly facilities, shelters and security measures, while municipalities work to address crime hotspots. However, Lesufi acknowledged that progress remains slow, with only 21 of the 67 government instructions to combat violence against women and children completed. 38 remain underway and eight have yet to begin.

DR Congo Hunger Crisis to Worsen, With 30 Million at Risk

More than 28.8 million people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo are expected to face acute food insecurity through December, according to the latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) assessment. The crisis is being driven by ongoing conflict and displacement in the east, rising food and fuel prices, disease outbreaks, including the expanding Ebola epidemic, and climate-related shocks. North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri remain the worst-affected provinces, with more than 10 million people experiencing high levels of food insecurity. The situation is expected to worsen between January and June 2027 when the number of people facing acute hunger could reach 30.3 million, including 4.2 million in emergency conditions.

Close 

Malawi's President Says He Remained in Control During South Africa Stay

Malawi President Peter Mutharika has assured citizens that he remained in full control of government during his three-week private leave in South Africa, maintaining regular contact with ministers, government officials and his party. Mutharika dismissed concerns about his absence. He said that the country remained under control and that any challenges were largely political. His return comes as Malawi faces foreign currency shortages, a fuel crisis and frequent power cuts. His absence also sparked speculation about his health on social media, although he did not directly address the rumours. He called for national unity and urged Malawians to work together for the country's progress.

World.title: South Africa: Police Step Up Security Ahead of Election Voting - South African News Briefs - November 2, 2026
World.content:
press review

Police Step Up Security Ahead of Election Voting

Western Cape police have said that they are ready to ensure safe and secure local government elections, with special voting starting, reports EWN. Provincial Police Commissioner Sizakhele Dyantyi said security has been strengthened in identified hotspots, particularly Cape Town, Knysna and Vredenburg, amid concerns over gang violence and political killings. Police officers have been deployed to these areas under an operational plan approved by the National Joint Operational and Intelligence Structure (NatJoints).

Cat Matlala Attempted Murder Trial Resumes



The attempted murder trial of businessman Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala and four co-accused is set to resume at the Johannesburg High Court following a three-week recess, reports SABC News. Matlala is accused of orchestrating three failed assassination attempts targeting his former girlfriend Tebogo Thobejane, businessman Joe Sibanyoni and music producer DJ Vettys between 2022 and 2024. Proceedings will continue with a trial-within-a-trial as alleged hitman Musa Kekana challenges the admissibility of evidence obtained following his 2024 arrest, while the State has accused him of tailoring his testimony.

Cape Town Assures Langa Commuters Amid CATA Suspension

The City of Cape Town has assured Langa residents that the six-month suspension of the Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association (CATA) Langa Inter-township Taxi Association will not disrupt commuter services, reports EWN. The suspension follows an investigation that found the association had allowed route invasions, failed to control its members and was linked to violence. Taxi services are expected to resume normally after violence claimed about a dozen lives and disrupted operations. Meanwhile, the Western Cape High Court has interdicted CATA and the Cape Organisation for the Democratic Taxi Association (CODETA) from engaging in violence or interfering with public transport, with safety officials remaining on high alert.
