World.title: Kenya: Ebola Update - 46 Contacts Set for Release Tuesday, Five Patients Await Second Tests
World.content:
Health workers in protective gear inside the Ebola treatment centre at Buniaâs referral hospital in Ituri province, eastern DRC, October 2026.

Nairobi — The government is expected to release 46 people who have been under quarantine over the Ebola outbreak on Tuesday,, as it intensifies diplomatic efforts to persuade Saudi Arabia to lift travel restrictions imposed on the country.

The planned discharge will follow the completion of the mandatory 21-day monitoring period by the contacts, provided they remain free of symptoms.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said the government was also optimistic that five of the seven patients still receiving treatment would be discharged alongside the contacts after returning a second negative Ebola test.

The five patients had already tested negative once and were scheduled for another test on Monday, November 2, before a final decision on their discharge.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The planned releases will add to the 20 contacts who were discharged on October 26 after completing 21 days of monitoring without developing symptoms.

This would bring the number of people released from quarantine to 66, marking another milestone in Kenya's efforts to contain the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak.

The Ministry of Health says all 135 contacts linked to the initial imported case have been identified and traced, with 118 placed under quarantine as part of containment measures.

Kenya has reported nine confirmed infections, including two deaths, with all subsequent infections linked to the initial case involving a Kenyan national who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda.

The eight secondary infections involved four healthcare workers and four close family members of the initial patient.

Duale said Kenya had not recorded a new confirmed infection since October 19, adding that there was no evidence of transmission beyond the identified cluster.

The government maintains that the outbreak has remained contained through contact tracing, isolation, laboratory testing and enhanced surveillance at points of entry.

Meanwhile, Kenya has stepped up diplomatic engagement with Saudi Arabia following the Kingdom's decision to suspend travel and visa services involving the country over concerns about the Ebola outbreak.

Saudi Arabia announced the restrictions on October 30, barring its citizens from travelling to Kenya and suspending the issuance of all categories of visas to Kenyan travellers.

The restrictions also prohibit entry into Saudi Arabia for travellers arriving from Kenya, including those transiting through other countries if they have been in Kenya within the preceding 21 days.

In response, the Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs formally protested the decision, describing the restrictions as disproportionate and unsupported by the prevailing epidemiological situation in Kenya.

In a diplomatic communication dated October 30, Nairobi urged Riyadh to review and immediately lift the measures, warning that they could disrupt travel, trade, tourism and employment opportunities between the two countries.

Kenya also asked Saudi Arabia to provide the World Health Organization (WHO) with scientific justification for the restrictions within 48 hours, in accordance with the International Health Regulations.

The government further indicated that it would raise concerns over the restrictions with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

Health authorities have argued that Kenya's containment efforts should be supported through international cooperation rather than blanket travel restrictions.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale maintained that the measures imposed by Saudi Arabia did not reflect the progress made in containing the outbreak.

Kenya is particularly concerned about the potential economic implications of the restrictions, given that Saudi Arabia hosts a significant number of Kenyan migrant workers and remains an important destination for Kenyan travellers.

Close 

The restrictions could also affect students, business travellers, tourists and religious pilgrims seeking to travel to the Kingdom.

Saudi Arabia, however, has said its decision was informed by epidemiological assessments conducted by its public health authorities to prevent the virus from spreading across its borders.

The government has not indicated when the restrictions will be lifted.

Kenya's Ministry of Health has continued to urge the public to remain vigilant while reassuring communities that the confirmed infections have remained within one identified transmission cluster.

The World Health Organization has supported Kenya's containment efforts and recommended evidence-based measures, including surveillance, contact tracing and screening at points of entry, rather than travel restrictions.

Kenya's planned November 3 discharges are expected to provide another indication of progress in the country's response to the outbreak.

World.title: South Africa: Gauteng Shuts Down 20 Taverns in Fight Against Violence
World.content:
Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi says authorities shut down 20 liquor outlets after 7,322 inspections as part of a crackdown on alcohol-related violence.

The province plans to deploy 1,022 teams across 122 dangerous areas and hire 56 more social workers to help victims of violence.

Gauteng has shut down 20 liquor outlets and is preparing to send 1,022 response teams into some of the province's most dangerous communities to protect women and children.

Premier Panyaza Lesufi announced the measures on Sunday, 1 November, as the province steps up its fight against gender-based violence and the killing of women.

Police and inspectors have already carried out 7,322 inspections at liquor outlets across Gauteng.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

They issued 459 notices to businesses breaking the rules and referred another 566 outlets for further inspections.

Authorities also carried out 41 joint operations targeting liquor businesses.

Lesufi said police would continue going after illegal taverns, repeat offenders and businesses selling alcohol outside permitted hours.

"Enforcement operations will continue to target unlicensed liquor outlets, repeat offenders and illegal trading beyond permitted hours as part of broader efforts to address alcohol-related violence," he said.

The crackdown follows President Cyril Ramaphosa's instructions on 29 September to speed up investigations into rape, murder and other serious crimes against women and children.

Gauteng has identified 122 high-risk areas where response teams will be deployed.

The province has also singled out 10 police stations with the highest numbers of reported rape cases for special attention.

These include Rietgat, Alexandra, Mamelodi, Diepsloot, Ivory Park, Dobsonville, Midrand and Tembisa.

Lesufi said the province would bring in another 56 social workers to help victims and survivors.

Seven specialised Sexual Offences Courts and 144 victim-friendly facilities will also receive more support.

The province's 19 Medical Legal Clinics will help protect evidence needed to investigate crimes and bring offenders to court.

Gauteng currently has 18 shelters with 363 beds for people escaping violence, as well as seven Thuthuzela Care Centres.

Support services have helped tens of thousands of people over the past six months.

New systems for referring victims to support services have also been introduced at all 43 courts dealing with protection orders.

Lesufi said technical problems with the e-Panic Button application had been fixed, while more security cameras had been added to help keep communities safe.

Municipalities are also being told to clean up dangerous public spaces.

In Johannesburg, officials have identified crime hotspots and are preparing 10 previously hijacked or illegally occupied buildings for public use.

Tshwane has cleared overgrown bushes around dangerous public transport stations.

Ekurhuleni has inspected all its taxi ranks and identified broken security cameras that need repairs.

Municipalities on the West Rand have identified dangerous buildings and neglected public areas.

Safety checks are between 60% and 80% complete in most municipalities. Officials plan to address urgent dangers within 90 days.

But Lesufi admitted that much work remains.

Close 

Of the 67 instructions issued to tackle violence against women and children, only 21 have been completed.

Another 38 are still being carried out, while eight have not yet started.

The province is also struggling with delays in forensic testing and outstanding criminal cases.

Lesufi said officials would meet every week to check progress and hold departments and municipalities accountable.

"Protecting our women and children is an absolute priority that demands immediate action, as delayed justice is no justice at all," he said.

He also called on communities to help fight violence.

"The fight against GBVF requires sustained government action, effective law enforcement and active participation from communities and all sectors of society."

World.title: Zambia: Widespread Repression in Post-Election Crackdown
World.content:
Opposition and Critics Forcibly Disappeared, Arbitrary Detained, Beaten

Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members, lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August.

The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices.

The authorities should immediately halt the crackdown, allow access to lawyers and medical care to detainees, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses.

(Johannesburg) - The Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities have also yet to credibly explain or investigate the killing of an opposition leader in contested circumstances.

"Zambia's government should break this dangerous cycle of repression," said Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at Human Rights Watch. "The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces."



President Hakainde Hichilema was reelected in the August 13 election, which observers said was marred by irregularities such as a suspension of counting and limited fundamental freedoms. From August 24 to 28, the authorities suspended judicial services and prevented legal challenges to the presidential election results, closing and cordoning off court premises. Zambian police stated that the closures were an "intelligence-led and preventive measure," without providing details.

Human Rights Watch documented 14 cases in August that appear to have been enforced disappearances, in which the authorities refused to reveal the situation and whereabouts of a detained person. Several of these people were initially forcibly disappeared for days. Victims, family members, and lawyers said that the military held some of them.

Human Rights Watch also documented 61 cases in which detainees or their lawyers and relatives allege that they were beaten or otherwise violently abused during their arrest, in detention, or both. Eighteen have been charged with treason, with two also facing sedition charges. In many cases, the people detained were never charged with a crime while in others, the charges against them appear to be politically motivated. The government has not disclosed how many people were arrested during the crackdown or the charges against them, prompting concerns that the number of people detained is higher than presently known.

Human Rights Watch has also documented two cases in which the Zambia-based relatives of government critics living abroad say government authorities harassed and threatened them.

The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices, Human Rights Watch said. On September 11, the government announced the cancellation of six government critics' passports, including that of an academic, Sishuwa Sishuwa, for "security reasons."

On August 14, security forces raided the home of the Tonse Alliance opposition leader, Brian Mundubile, in a suburb of Lusaka, the capital. Opposition members present allege that security forces killed a former government minister, Mutotwe Kafwaya, during the raid. Inspector General of the Zambia Police Service Graphel Musamba said members of a "joint intelligence-led operation" were met with "gunfire and resistance from unknown individuals" that "prompted officers to return fire," and that Kafwaya had been killed in the process. Kafwaya's fate was not known until August 19, after his wife filed a habeas corpus petition to compel authorities to disclose his whereabouts, bring him before court, and show sufficient and lawful cause for his continued detention.

Public officials made contradictory statements about the raid and who was responsible for it. On August 15, the Zambia Information and Communications Technology Authority (ZICTA) sent out a text message to all registered phones in Zambia stating: "Beware of false reports of shootings and abductions. Stay calm and peaceful." The Ministry of Information and Media dismissed reports of the raid and shooting as "disinformation intended to alarm and mislead the public."

The police also issued a media statement denying that there had been a raid and that Mundubile was in police custody. Police Inspector General Musamba later admitted that there had been a "joint security-led intelligence operation" at Mundubile's home.

Mundubile, who was later arrested and charged with treason, stated in a High Court petition that Human Rights Watch has seen that he saw a member of the military fatally shoot Kafwaya.

Given the conflicting statements by government officials about who was responsible for the raid on Mundubile's home and the circumstances surrounding Kafwaya's killing, Zambian authorities should institute an independent, impartial, and thorough investigation into the matter, Human Rights Watch said.

Detainees have implicated Zambia's military in arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Forty-three opposition members acting as election monitors were detained on August 14. Their lawyer said their whereabouts had been unknown for eight days and that the police had denied holding them. When a lawyer finally saw them, he told Human Rights Watch that "most of them were swollen and had terrible injuries, including broken bones. They said they had been brutalized by the military." Their lawyers filed a habeas corpus application and, on September 10, a court in Lusaka ordered their immediate release.

Under Zambian law and international human rights law, all detainees have the right to due process, including to be promptly informed of the charges against them, to have access to counsel if charged with a crime, to have their detention reviewed by a judge, and to be presumed innocent. They should also have access to adequate medical care and be able to communicate with their families.

In a September 2 call, the United Nations special rapporteur on the rights to freedom of assembly and of association said that the authorities should "release all political detainees, respect fundamental freedoms, and restore democratic accountability." The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said in response that the call was "inaccurate, undiplomatic and falling short of the standards of objectivity, moderation and discretion expected of UN mandate holders."

The ministry said that being a member of opposition party "does not place a person beyond the reach of the law, nor does it convert a criminal suspect into a political detainee... The government is committed to ensuring that these protections are respected in every case, and Zambia's courts are open to test them."

Zambia will serve as a member of the UN Human Rights Council for the 2027-2029 term. As a council member, Zambia is expected to "uphold the highest standards in the promotion and protection of human rights."

"The Zambian government's needs to end its brazen human rights crackdown," Budoo-Scholtz said. "Leaders in Southern Africa and Zambia's development partners should encourage President Hichilema to restore the rule of law and ensure that civic and political spaces are protected."

Enforced Disappearances, Including by Military Personnel

Human Rights Watch documented 14 cases of apparent enforced disappearances of opposition members and supporters, including some in which the authorities denied holding people who were later produced after habeas corpus applications.

The authorities claimed to have arrested 11 men during the August 14 raid on Mundubile's home.

Lawyers and family members of seven of the men said that they were made to lie down and were beaten using fists, rifle butts, and sticks, kicked by men in military uniform, then blindfolded and driven away in military vehicles. Victims and witnesses identified members of Zambia's military through their uniforms and military vehicles.

During the same raid, security forces picked up several opposition members and supporters and forcibly disappeared them for days before family members or their lawyers found them. They included Bishop Trevor Mwamba, an opposition leader; Patrick Mwansa, a leading opposition campaigner; and security aides Jackson Mutyoka, Bernard Chewe, Brazil Soko, Francis Mulenga, and Richard Banda.

According to their lawyers and court documents seen by Human Rights Watch, the men were taken to a "military command center" where they were "screened and processed" then detained in "various police stations around Lusaka." Lawyers and family members said they went around police stations in Lusaka looking for the detainees, but authorities denied holding the men. However, some were found days later at the same stations where the police had denied holding them.

Mwansa's family said he had a broken finger and swollen face when they finally located him four days later in Lusaka's Central Police Station. On September 6, Mwansa was moved to a maximum security prison in Kabwe, 150 kilometers from Lusaka, and has not yet received medical treatment, a family member said.

The family of Bishop Mwamba, president of the opposition United National Independence Party, who was also picked up during the raid at Mundubile's home, said they searched for him in police stations in and around Lusaka for four days before locating him at Matero Police Station. Earlier, including on the day he was located, officers at Matero Police Station had denied holding Mwamba.

"He had spent days without food and without taking his prescription medication," the relative said. "The police had first denied [holding him] but we insisted to see him, because we had received an anonymous tip informing us that he was at Matero. When they brought him out and we asked what he was arrested for, police said they had no charge for him 'because he was brought in by the military who asked us to keep him in the cells for them."'

On August 30, when the family took food and pain killers to Benard Chewe at Kabwata Police Station, where he had been detained, officers there told them that he had been moved but claimed that they did not know where. When the family traced him two days later to Mwembeshi Correctional Facility on the outskirts of Lusaka, they were denied access.

Men in unmarked vehicles who introduced themselves as "state intelligence officers" picked up Harry Findlay, a Lusaka businessman and opposition supporter, from his residence on August 4, a family member said. Neither his lawyer nor family had access to him, and the authorities did not inform them of his whereabouts. Findlay's lawyers sent two letters to Zambian authorities, on August 7 and August 17, requesting his whereabouts and calling for his immediate release and access to doctors, lawyers, and family.

On August 20, Findlay was taken to court under a judge's order to inquire into the legality of his detention. On August 29, he was charged with treason and moved to Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison, where he remains without trial.

All the men detained in the August 14 raid were eventually charged with treason and remain in detention without having appeared in court. Human Rights Watch believes that in these cases, Zambian authorities are using treason charges, which are nonbailable, and sedition, which carries a heavy penalty, to stifle dissent and political opposition.

On August 27, police arrested Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, and subsequently also charged them with treason and seditious practices. The charge sheet, which Human Rights Watch has seen, alleges that Mundubile and Zulu went on Facebook live on August 14 stating that the opposition had won the election. The government alleges that this was meant to "raise discontent or disaffection among the people of Zambia."

On September 22, the Law Association of Zambia raised concerns about prolonged detentions without court appearances. Zambia's Human Rights Commission on September 3 said it was following 84 election-related detainees whose cases it cast as part of a "disturbing pattern of prolonged detention, delayed notification of charges, restricted access to family and legal representation and failure to bring detainees before a competent court without undue delay."

Abuse and Ill-Treatment in Custody

Human Rights Watch documented that 61 people had been mistreated in custody by reviewing court documents and interviewing family members.

Lawyers for the 43 opposition members acting as election monitors who were detained on August 14 said that state security agents kicked and beat them and denied them food during the first 8 days of their 21-day detention.

Lawyers representing 18 detainees accused of treason state in court documents that the detainees were abused and assaulted in custody and denied medical attention. The lawyers also said 10 of the 18--George Chisanga, Patrick Mwansa, Trevor Mwamba, Francis Mulenga, Brazil Soko, Jackson Mutyoka, Bernard Chewe, Richard Banda, Emmanuel Mulenga, and Darius Mwila--had been restricted from accessing their lawyers or family members.

In a court petition filed on September 11, Ezra Topola, Dickson Tembo, and Victor Muzyamba alleged that security personnel waterboarded them and suspended them from a metal bar and beat them. Findlay alleged that he was kept in solitary confinement in Mwembeshi Correctional Facility and denied access to his prescription medication. Mwansa alleged that he suffered serious injuries, including cuts to his face and a fracture on his hand, but was denied access to medical attention.

Family members told Human Rights Watch that when they found Mutyoka on August 17 at Lusaka's Central Police Station, three days after military detained him at Mundubile's home, he showed signs of having been physically abused. "When we saw him, his face was swollen, he was coughing blood and was limping," a relative said. "He said they had been made to lie down in the yard of Mundubile's home and beaten using rifle butts and whips by masked men in military unform. All he wanted was to see a doctor, but that request was denied and, to this day, he has not been seen by a doctor."

When Chewe's family members found him at Kabwata Police Station three days after he was taken from Mundubile's home, they said that he too showed signs of physical abuse. "He had a swollen forehead, busted lips, and complained of body pains," a relative said. "He said he had been assaulted by the military at their headquarters before they took him to the police station."

Lawyers for Chewe, Mutyoka, and Soko at Mwembeshi Correctional Facility said that Zambia Army Special Forces personnel interrogated them and that on September 10, authorities moved the three to Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison without informing family or lawyers.

On October 27, family members said medical doctors have not yet seen the three despite urgent letters written on September 9, seen by Human Rights Watch, to the commissioner of the Zambia Correctional Service and the officer-in-charge of Mwembeshi Correctional Facility.

Eight election monitors for the opposition, men aged 21 to 26, said a group of armed soldiers wearing uniforms and masks jumped over the perimeter wall into a house in Lusaka's Emmasdale township on August 15 around 8 p.m., where the monitors were meeting. They said the armed soldiers dragged them out of the house, kicked them with boots, and beat them with fists and sticks.

They were forced into a military truck and taken away but could not identify where they were held. For the next three days, security forces beat them several times a day, demanding confessions that they belonged to "Brian Mundubile's militia." All eight were released on August 18 without charge.

Human Rights Watch has also examined a petition filed on September 11 by lawyers for the 18 accused of treason that implicates the army in interrogations and abuse of detainees. In the petition, lawyers allege that special forces personnel led by Gen. Moses Shapwaya threatened and intimidated some of the detainees in prison to force them to incriminate Mundubile and Zulu.

Arbitrary Arrests and Detention

From court records and interviews with victims, family, and lawyers, Human Rights Watch documented 71 cases in which opposition members and supporters, as well as government critics, were arrested on charges that may be politically motivated or held in prolonged detention without charge. These include the 43 election monitors and 17 musicians and comedians who were detained after performing at an opposition rally, among others.

The arrest of the 43 monitors came after the opposition leader stated that he planned to challenge the election result in court, while the government accused him of plotting an insurgency. In an electoral court challenge, the monitors would have been potential witnesses for the opposition's case. After their 21 days in detention without charge, the court ruled that their arrest was unjustified and ordered their immediate release.

Human Rights Watch interviewed a 44-year-old Lusaka mathematician who was hired to tally numbers for a potential court challenge to President Hichilema's election. He said that on August 15 at about 9:30 p.m., about eight armed men who identified themselves as intelligence and police officers broke into his house and harassed him. They demanded access to his phone and laptop, he said, and to know who was funding the court challenge.

He said they dragged him outside, put him into a vehicle, and took him to the police headquarters in Lusaka, where he was interrogated further about the election petition. The next day, he was transferred to Ridgeway Police Station, where he spent 18 days without being charged. On August 28, his lawyer filed a habeas corpus application in the Lusaka High Court, which Human Rights Watch has seen. Five days later, police charged him with a misdemeanor offense and released him the same day.

Before the election, on August 5, a group of 17 people were arrested after performing at an opposition rally in Mongu, Western province. Police detained them for over two weeks on what was initially said to be a traffic offense of travelling in a vehicle without numbered plates, a lawyer familiar with the case told Human Rights Watch.

Close 

The lawyer said that the group's arrest and prolonged detention were politically motivated because of their vocal and visible mobilization for the opposition. Police later charged and prosecuted the 17 for "riotous assembly or behavior." In a court document seen by Human Rights Watch, the state alleges that the 17 did "unlawfully assemble and begun to execute a common purpose by a breach of peace and the terror of the public." A court released them on bail on August 30, after over three weeks in detention.

Driven into Hiding

Human Rights Watch interviewed seven people, including lawyers and a journalist, who said they had fled their homes because they believed they had been targeted for arrest in the days after the August 13 election. A lawyer and a journalist showed Human Rights Watch messages on their phones alerting them that they were on a "wanted list." Some left and others were in hiding within the country.

A statement by seven international lawyers' associations said some lawyers involved in preparing or lodging election-related legal challenges had fled Zambia due to threats to their safety.

A lawyer said that he went into hiding on August 15 after scores of security agents came to his home and office. The lawyer had been acting on behalf of Tonse Alliance, including working on a court petition to challenge President Hichilema's election. "There was no reason for the security agents to chase me in that manner," he said. "If the police wanted me for any reason, they should have alerted me, and I would have presented myself with my legal representatives."

Mulenga Kapwepwe, an opposition leader who worked closely with Mundubile and Zulu, said she went into hiding on August 15 after confidential sources alerted her that she was "on a wanted list." "I have had to rearrange my life," she said. "Many of my colleagues are in detention charged with treason, and I have been warned that the moment I come out of hiding, I will be targeted."

On August 17, a journalist who runs an investigative journalism website and has previously been detained for his journalism crossed the border into a neighboring country hours before security agents went to his house looking for him. "My website was following up on the raid at Mundubile's house," he said. "That is when I received messages on my phone saying: 'Stop what you are doing. We are coming after you.' I was once arrested and detained without charge for nearly two weeks. I know what these people are capable of. So, fearful for my life, I left."

While he was fleeing, the journalist said, he received a call from a family member that about five people who identified themselves as officers from Office of the President were at his house looking for him. They told his family that he was wanted for sedition.

Harassment of Family Members

Human Rights Watch documented two cases in which the authorities allegedly harassed and threatened the Zambia-based family members of government critics living abroad.

Police allegedly detained two siblings of a well-known diaspora critic of the government and harassed their 76-year-old father, demanding that their sibling abroad, who runs a popular social media page with hundreds of thousands of followers, take down material critical of the government.

One sibling was detained in a 3 a.m. raid on their home, in which armed police officers demanded access to their phones and laptop, a close source said, adding that one of the police officers "had a gun and said: 'This is a high security operation." The officers said the foreign-based sibling's "political commentary was 'a problem' and that they needed it to stop." The authorities allegedly demanded the removal of specific videos as a condition for their release. In one of these videos, the social media personality demanded an independent inquiry into the August 14 killing of Kafwaya.

In another case, a government critic in the United States with investments in Zambia said that three men who identified themselves as intelligence officers from the Office of the President approached family members in Zambia days after the election and threatened to "squeeze" her businesses if she continued to criticize President Hichilema's administration on social media. "They told my sister, a civil servant, that she risked losing her job if I did not tone down my criticism," the critic said.

World.title: Malawi: Mutharika Says He Ran Govt From South Africa, Nobody Should Complain
World.content:
President Peter Mutharika has told Malawians that he kept full control of government during his three weeks of private leave in South Africa, and that nobody should complain.

In an interview with State House press officer Cathy Maulidi, released by government in a video clip, Mutharika spoke on camera at State House (Kamuzu Palace), accompanied by First Lady Gertrude Mutharika.

He said he had stayed in close contact with ministers and officials in charge of government, and with the party.

"Everything is under control. Nobody should complain," he said.

He acknowledged that there had been "a few things" to deal with, but dismissed them as politics.

"In general, I want Malawians to know that I was in full control of the country and the government," he said.

Mutharika also thanked the people who had sent him messages while he was away, and said he had missed the country and its affairs.

He said he was glad to see "a little progress".

He returns to a country still struggling with a shortage of foreign currency, a fuel crisis and frequent power cuts.

Rumours about his health spread on social media during his absence. The clip does not address them directly.

The president closed with a call for national unity, borrowing a Kenyan phrase. "Let's go on together as a country. They say in Kenya, harambee, which means let's pull together for the sake of our nation," he said.

World.title: Sudan: A Year After the Fall of El Fasher, Sudan's War Has Left a Ghost Town in Its Wake
World.content:
A year after paramilitary forces at war with the Sudanese army captured the strategic city of El Fasher, survivors and aid workers report that the capital of North Darfur state remains largely abandoned. Some residents are too scared to return, while thousands are still missing - many held in deplorable conditions in overcrowded prisons.

On 26 October, 2025, after 500 days of siege, El Fasher fell to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), an armed group that has been fighting Sudan's army since April 2023.

It marked one of the darkest chapters of the conflict. The paramilitaries pledged to "cleanse" the city and explicitly called for the elimination of non-Arab communities - notably the semi-nomadic Zaghawa and the Fur, Darfur's largest ethnic group.



International investigators have found evidence of widespread atrocities, including mass killings and sexual violence. The United Nations has estimated that some 6,000 people were killed, but researchers studying satellite imagery suspect the death toll is much higher - in the tens of thousands.

According to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), nearly 100,000 people managed to flee. Thousands more civilians are missing, having died while trying to escape or been captured by the RSF.

In January, under the supervision of the city's new authorities, humanitarian organisations were able to visit El Fasher for the first time since the paramilitaries seized control. They described "a ghost town, with few civilians remaining".

Contested repopulation

"My house was destroyed," says Salwa, who did not want to be identified by her full name. Born in El Fasher, she fled a few days before the city fell.

"They smashed everything and threw all our things into the street. My father's house is still standing, but they've put people we don't know in it."

Like many residents who fled, she believes the new authorities are seeking to replace the city's original inhabitants - mainly Zaghawa and Fur - with members of nomadic Arab tribes, from which the RSF draws its leadership and most of its fighters.

Sudan's RSF paramilitaries accused of crimes against humanity in El Fasher

"They're bringing in people from outside and giving them our homes. They're even giving them documents to prove they're the owners. These people will never leave. On top of that, they're filming them for propaganda and claiming that the residents of El Fasher have returned."

Tasis, a coalition of civilian and armed groups led by the RSF and governing in parallel from the city of Nyala in South Darfur, has called for displaced residents to go back to El Fasher and says it is helping civilians to return.

"These aren't residents of El Fasher, but people who were brought in to repopulate the city," Salwa protests.

Lingering trauma

Solidarités International, a French humanitarian organisation that has returned to work in El Fasher, estimates that between 40,000 and 60,000 people have either returned or come and go regularly, out of a pre-war population of at least 300,000.

"They come to seek aid, to see their neighbourhood, their home. They've heard that an NGO is here, that the paramilitary-linked government's humanitarian aid office is organising food distributions," Renaud Douci, the organisation's field coordinator in Sudan, told RFI.

But returnees are often put off by what they find, he said. "When the market where you used to get food is now a meagre affair with a few stalls and exorbitant prices, those aren't conditions under which you can return with your family."

Others are kept away by the memory of the siege. "For now, because of the trauma and violence of those 500 days, people don't feel at all ready to return," Douci said.

Women victims of Sudan's war bear scars of 'indescribable' violence

Laura Mills, a researcher at Amnesty International, shares his assessment. "Only a fraction of the population has returned; people are too afraid," she told RFI.

"Humanitarian workers tell us there are pockets of houses still standing. And between each pocket, the streets are deserted. The city is still abandoned."

For her, the hesitation is understandable. "The residents of El Fasher are traumatised by what they've been through. Why would they return when the paramilitaries are still there and have never been held accountable for their actions? Why return when you risk being arrested and tortured at any moment?"

Prison of horror

The RSF took thousands of people prisoner during the capture of El Fasher: not only members of the armed forces but civilians - soldiers' families, teachers, doctors, journalists, civil society activists and others they accused of supporting the Sudanese army.

Ibrahim (not his real name), a journalist with El Fasher Radio and Television, was taken by the paramilitaries a few weeks before the city fell, according to his wife, who wanted to remain anonymous.

"One morning he went out to look for food, because at the time there was nothing left to eat. He left in the morning and didn't come back that evening or the next day," she told RFI.

His wife believed he was wounded or dead until she learned that he had been captured by the RSF and sent to Dagris, a notorious prison outside Nyala that has been described as a "site of horror".

"The conditions were terrible," she said. "The detainees were crammed into small cells. Sometimes they would go entire weeks without seeing the sun. Occasionally, they'd be taken outside so they could air their belongings, dry their clothes and get rid of insects and fleas. And their toilets were right inside the cells. The sanitary conditions there are disgusting."

Sick, emaciated and having lost his sight in one eye, Ibrahim was finally released nine months later upon payment of $2,000. Numerous accounts report demands for ransom are common.

US has 'alienated' Sudan's army in 'complex war', analyst tells RFI

'They took my family'

According to human rights organisations, between 13,000 and 19,500 people were being held at Dagris earlier this year - several times the prison's official capacity of 4,500.

Zamzam, a journalist originally from the El Fasher region who now lives in exile, says her relatives were among them, arrested as punishment for her coverage of the conflict.

Close 

"The RSF contacted me to tell me to stop writing, they even offered me money. But I refused, so they took my family," she told RFI.

Her cousin, a doctor at a hospital in El Fasher who chose to stay throughout the offensive, remains incommunicado. Zamzam has heard only that he is working in construction.

"They use prisoners as labourers in construction, to do laundry, to clean the homes of RSF fighters' families," she claimed.

Sudan's war reshapes loyalties as civilians see 'no option' but the army

Conditions at Dagris prison are inhumane and in some cases life-threatening, according to Mohamed Faisal, a member of the Sudan Doctors Network.

"The detainees have no rights and no contact with their families," he said. "The cells are overcrowded. There are lots of diseases, such as cholera and dengue fever, and we are seeing a sharp rise in mortality. A few months ago, there were four deaths every week. And when prisoners die, their families aren't even notified."

An estimated 73 medical personnel are being held in Dagris and Kober, another prison in South Darfur, the network believes. Several journalists are also detained, including Muammar Ibrahim, a correspondent for Al Jazeera's Arabic news channel who had been covering the conflict since it began in April 2023.

Today, Darfur is almost entirely under the control of the paramilitary forces. The fighting has shifted to the Kordofan region, where the UN has warned El Fasher's grim history could be repeated.

This article was adapted from the original version in French by Alexandra Brangeon.

World.title: GIANNO CALDWELL: I fled California. Steve Hilton gives voters golden opportunity to stay
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

I lived in Los Angeles from 2017 until May 2020, two months into the LA shutdown, and by the end I barely recognized it. The city I had moved to for its energy and opportunity was starting to look like Gotham City. Tent cities spread across Los Angeles. Break-ins and violent crime climbed. When COVID-19 arrived, the people running California seemed far more interested in policing masks on the beach than policing the streets. So, I left for Miami because Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis governed his state with sanity.

I was blessed. I could leave. Millions of Californians can't, and they shouldn't have to.

Six years later, California Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton is giving Californians a reason to stay.

CA POST EDITORIAL BOARD: VOTE HILTON FOR CALIFORNIA GOVERNOR OVER ESTABLISHMENT HACK BECERRA FOR REAL CHANGE

What was once a great state has turned into a hellhole for too many of its own citizens. Working families pay some of the highest gas prices in America, and have for over a decade, along with some of the highest housing costs anywhere. Small businesses are drowning in fees and regulation. Homeless encampments, open drug use and crime have become normal in a state that used to draw people from around the world. After 16 years of one-party rule in Sacramento, Californians deserve to ask a simple question: What are the results? Unfortunately, a state in decline.

Hilton has proven over and over again that he is the person voters should entrust to succeed Democrat Gavin Newsom as governor of California. I must admit, I am impressed by what he has done as a candidate. I've known Steve since our days together at Fox News. Even then, he wasn't interested in cable-news shouting matches. He wanted to talk about solutions, and that's exactly the candidate he has become.

NEWSOM UNDER FIRE AS CALIFORNIA GAS TAX HIKE SENDS PUMP PRICES EVEN HIGHER

Just look at the campaign he's run. It has been focused and substantive. In an era when too many candidates run on slogans and grievance, Hilton has put real plans on the table. He wants no state income tax on the first $150,000 a Californian earns. He has a plan to get gas to $3 a gallon by eliminating the state gas tax, repealing the Low Carbon Fuel Standard and producing more of our own oil here at home.

On housing, he would streamline building codes and rein in the lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act that are routinely used to stop housing from ever getting built.

STEVE HILTON LAUNCHES AD MOCKING XAVIER BECERRA'S '36 YEARS' AS A CAREER POLITICIAN IN CALIFORNIA GOV RACE

You can disagree with any one of those ideas. But you can't say he hasn't approached the issues with gravitas.

On top of that, he's outworked his opponent. Since the June primary, Hilton has campaigned all over California, while Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former Health and Human Services secretary under President Joe Biden, has kept a low profile as if he doesn't have to compete for every vote. When the Los Angeles Times hosted a candidate forum this month, Hilton showed up and answered tough questions on homelessness, housing and climate. Becerra didn't attend.

HOUSING FIRST IS A DISASTER. I SAW SACRAMENTO'S HOMELESS CHAOS FIRSTHAND

Public safety is the work I've given my life to. As founder of the Caldwell Institute for Public Safety, I fight for victims and for communities left behind when leaders refuse to enforce the law. That work is exactly why I personally support Steve Hilton's candidacy, and why I believe he is the right choice for California.

Hilton has said plainly that crime in California is out of control and that a lack of consequences has demoralized police officers and residents alike. He is calling for a tougher approach to crime and stronger support for law enforcement. On homelessness, he would enforce the law against street encampments while expanding mental health and addiction treatment, so people actually get help instead of being left on the sidewalk.

CALIFORNIA DEM, FORMER LA MAYOR VILLARAIGOSA ADMITS TRUMP'S NOT TO BLAME FOR STATE’S HOMELESSNESS, COST CRISES

And he has earned the endorsement of Yolo County District Attorney Jeff Reisig, the architect of Proposition 36, the tough-on-crime measure that nearly 70% of California voters passed to restore consequences for repeat theft and drug crimes. Sacramento has looked the other way on this for years. Hilton won't.

In an era when too many candidates run on slogans and grievance, Hilton has put real plans on the table. He wants no state income tax on the first $150,000 a Californian earns. He has a plan to get gas to $3 a gallon by eliminating the state gas tax, repealing the Low Carbon Fuel Standard and producing more of our own oil here at home.

California's problems aren't red or blue. When you're paying six bucks a gallon, nobody's asking whether you're a Democrat or a Republican. Same goes for a young family priced out of a starter home, or a small business owner who gave up on Sacramento's rules.

STEVE HILTON BLASTS DEMOCRATS FOR MAKING CALIFORNIA UNAFFORDABLE AFTER 16 YEARS OF UNCHECKED POWER

Hilton understands this better than most because of where he comes from. His parents fled communism in Hungary. He knows what it looks like when government grows so large that it stops serving the people and starts ruling them. That perspective is exactly what California needs after a decade and a half of Sacramento telling people what to drive, what they're allowed to build and how much more they'll have to pay for it.

California has elected Republican governors before, from Ronald Reagan to Arnold Schwarzenegger, when voters were ready for a change. The polls say Hilton is the underdog. But I've seen enough elections to know the polls don't vote. People do.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

I left California in 2020 because I didn't believe officials would ever change course. Steve Hilton has given me a reason to believe the Golden State can shine again. On Tuesday, Nov. 3, Californians have a real choice. I hope they make it count.

World.title: REP BRIAN MAST: We are protecting our troops from having our own tech used against them
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The key objective in economic warfare is to do more harm to your enemy than you do to yourself, and President Donald Trump is doing what every American president should do: putting America first and making sure the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) cannot use our own resources against us.

Let’s be clear about what we are dealing with. The CCP is not our friend. It is a strategic adversary that wants to weaken the United States, challenge our military and place itself in leadership around the world. China is pouring resources into the technologies that will define the next generation of warfare. It wants more advanced weapons, better targeting systems, stronger cyber capabilities and every technological advantage it can get its hands on. And you better believe they will buy, cheat and steal their way to getting it, so in no way should we, the United States of America, be helping them get there faster.

For too long, American capital and expertise have found their way into Chinese companies developing technologies with military applications. And for anyone to argue that every part of China’s economy isn’t linked directly to the CCP military clearly hasn’t been paying attention. That is a serious national security failure. We should never allow our investments, our ingenuity or our world-class research to give the CCP an advantage over the United States.

TRUMP'S QUIET CHINA WINS ARE MORE IMPORTANT THAN XI'S EMPTY STATE VISIT

That’s why I couldn’t be happier to see the Trump administration propose new rules to put an end to Chinese infiltration. By strengthening restrictions on investments that could help build China's military-industrial base, the administration is taking meaningful action to protect the technologies that keep America strong. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the administration deserve a huge amount of credit for advancing these protections and working to ensure that American money does not end up strengthening our greatest foreign adversary.

The COINS Act was a great step forward to provide a stronger foundation for preventing American investment from supporting sensitive technologies in countries that threaten our national security. Now, we are making sure those protections have teeth.

CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE

We are closing loopholes, addressing the ways financial and professional services can help Chinese companies advance and ensuring that restrictions keep pace with the technologies Beijing is trying to acquire.

Because this is not just about money. It is about American lives.

I served in the Army. I know what it means to put on a uniform and accept the responsibility of defending this country. To pray that our military is better and stronger than our enemy’s.

But our service members don’t get to choose whether the enemy they face has better technology. And we should never ask them to confront an adversary that we helped make stronger.

BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN

Think about the consequences. Every technological advantage China gains can make it harder for our troops to detect a threat, defend against an attack, protect their communications or accomplish their mission and come home safely. When the CCP develops more capable weapons and more advanced military systems, it is our service members who may ultimately have to face them.

Our troops should never have to face a more powerful Chinese military because American dollars helped build it.

We are closing loopholes, addressing the ways financial and professional services can help Chinese companies advance and ensuring that restrictions keep pace with the technologies Beijing is trying to acquire. Because this is not just about money. It is about American lives.

That is why we cannot afford to be careless about where American money goes. We cannot warn the American people about China's military buildup with one hand while allowing our capital and expertise to help finance it with the other. Protecting our national security means making difficult decisions, confronting uncomfortable realities and refusing to let short-term financial interests come before the safety of the American people.

We also need to recognize that this competition is about more than the next investment or the next regulation. It is about who will control the technologies that shape the future on and off the battlefield. Artificial intelligence (AI), advanced semiconductors, quantum computing and other critical technologies will determine economic strength and military power for generations to come.

CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS

America has the talent, the resources and the ingenuity to lead that race. But we cannot win if we keep handing our advantages to the Chinese Communist Party. We have the responsibility to protect our breakthroughs, strengthen our defense industrial base and make sure American innovation serves American interests.

It’s for this very reason I have been so passionate about passing legislation to do these very things. During this Congress, we in the House Foreign Affairs Committee have been staunch supporters of codifying the president’s AI Action Plan with legislation such as AI OVERWATCH Act, the MATCH Act and the Remote Access Security Act, to strengthen oversight of advanced AI chip exports, close loopholes in semiconductor equipment controls, and prevent China from bypassing our safeguards through remote access to sensitive technology.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

We cannot let the CCP exploit gaps in our laws to get the chips, equipment and computing power it needs to strengthen its military. If we close one door but leave another wide open, China will always find a way through and it will mean dangerous consequences for the U.S. on the other side.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

I applaud President Trump for taking action to protect America's technological edge and for recognizing that we cannot allow the Chinese Communist Party to exploit our own success against us.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM REP. BRIAN MAST

World.title: How to watch critical 2026 midterm election races in TX, OH, MI, WI, GA, IA, NV, ME and FL
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Control of Congress is on the line Tuesday as voters decide pivotal Senate and House races across the country, while closely watched contests for governor will shape the political landscape in key states during President Donald Trump's second term.

Republicans are fighting to defend their congressional majorities as Democrats seek gains in battlegrounds from Texas and Georgia to Michigan and Maine. Open seats, vulnerable incumbents and competitive statewide races have put nine states at the center of the fight for power in Washington and state capitals.

With races stretching across multiple time zones, here are the key contests to watch, when polls close and how to follow live results as Election Night unfolds.

SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY

Texas — Polls close at 8 p.m. ET, 9 p.m. ET in some areas

Texas voters face two major statewide showdowns, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton battling Democratic state Rep. James Talarico for the Senate seat held by outgoing Republican John Cornyn, while GOP Gov. Greg Abbott seeks a historic fourth term against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.

TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK

The Senate contest has emerged as an unusually competitive race in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988, pitting Paxton's conservative appeal and history of legal controversies against Talarico's campaign focused on political change.

Meanwhile, Abbott's reelection bid offers another test of Republican dominance, with border security, education and the economy shaping the fight over the state's future.

Ohio — Polls close at 7:30 p.m. ET

Ohio features a Senate rematch of sorts, with former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown seeking a return to Washington against Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vice President JD Vance's former seat. Brown is attempting a political comeback in a state that has shifted toward Republicans, while Husted seeks his first electoral victory for the Senate.

Husted's campaign also enlisted Ohio native and former NFL coach Jon "Chucky" Gruden for campaign appearances.

Voters will decide who succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy facing Democrat Amy Acton. Ramaswamy's campaign recently pulled a controversial ad featuring Acton's estranged mother after criticism from fellow Republicans, including DeWine.

Michigan — Polls close at 8 p.m. ET, 9 p.m. ET in some areas

Michigan's open Senate seat could prove pivotal to the balance of power in Washington, with former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers facing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the contest to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW

The Senate race has grown increasingly contentious as Rogers and Republican allies have raised allegations about El-Sayed's family's purported ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, citing old social media posts by his half-sister. El-Sayed has denied any connection to the organization and publicly disavowed it, while independent fact-checkers have found no evidence establishing his personal affiliation.

The state also features a gubernatorial showdown between Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican Rep. John James, testing whether Michigan voters will maintain Democratic control of the governor's office or turn to Republicans.

Wisconsin — Polls close at 9 p.m. ET

Wisconsin's open governor's race pits Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany against Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley as voters choose a successor to Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.

The contest centers on the state's political direction, including taxes, public spending and education, after Crowley defeated progressive state Rep. Francesca Hong in a crowded Democratic primary.

Georgia — Polls close at 7 p.m. ET

Georgia offers two major statewide contests, with Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defending his seat against Republican Rep. Mike Collins in a state Trump narrowly carried in 2024.

Ossoff's race will test whether Democrats can hold a Senate seat in a state that has delivered closely contested presidential and Senate elections, while the open governor's race between Republican businessman Rick Jackson and former Democratic Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will determine who succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp.

Iowa — Polls close at 9 p.m. ET

Iowa voters will decide whether Republicans can retain two major offices in a state Trump carried comfortably in 2024. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for the Senate seat being vacated by Republican Joni Ernst, while Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand faces Republican Zach Lahn in the open governor's race to succeed retiring longtime GOP Gov. Kim Reynolds.

Although the Hawkeye State has shifted toward Republicans in recent election cycles, Democrats previously enjoyed sustained statewide success through figures including former Sen. Tom Harkin and former Gov. Tom Vilsack.

The contests will test whether Democrats can regain ground, with affordability, agriculture and state economic policy among the central issues.

Nevada — Polls close at 10 p.m. ET

Nevada's marquee contest features Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo seeking another term against Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford.

The race will test whether Republicans can retain the governor's office in a state where Democrats have remained competitive in statewide elections, with housing affordability, education and public safety among the issues facing voters.

Lombardo, the former Clark County sheriff, defeated incumbent Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak in 2022, with Ford now hoping to hit the jackpot in Carson City.

Maine — Polls close at 8 p.m. ET

Maine's Senate race pits longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins against former Democratic state Senate President Troy Jackson in one of the country's most closely watched contests.

Collins is seeking another term in a blue-leaning state that supported Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Meanwhile, Jackson is attempting to turn Maine's Democratic presidential voting pattern into a Senate pickup after replacing Graham Platner, who withdrew as the Democratic nominee following a sexual assault allegation that he denied.

The contest will test Collins' longstanding crossover appeal and could have major consequences for the Senate's balance of power, as she remains New England's only Republican member of Congress.

Florida — Polls close at 7 p.m. ET, 8 p.m. ET in some areas

Florida voters will choose a successor to term-limited Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, with Republican Rep. Byron Donalds facing former Republican congressman turned Democrat David Jolly.

The race presents a contest over the future of Florida's government, including affordability, immigration and the direction of state policy.

Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, appointed to the seat vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, also faces DSA-affiliated Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon in a special Senate election, while competitive House contests could affect the national congressional picture.

World.title: EJ ANTONI: Overseas wars put affordability on hold, but that’s only temporary
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

American families aren’t imagining it: we’ve had affordability problems since at least 2022. The situation was improving markedly throughout last year, right up until this February, but overseas conflicts reversed some of that progress. Once the wars with Iran and in Ukraine conclude, affordability will start to improve again.

The cost-of-living crisis started during the Biden administration when prices rose so much faster than earnings that people’s paychecks shrunk in terms of their purchasing power. Although the average American’s weekly paycheck grew roughly 17% during President Joe Biden’s term, it bought about 4% less.

For many families, that meant canceling vacation plans or being unable to buy a newer vehicle. For others, it meant having to put some necessities — like rent, prescriptions and food — on credit cards. Even when inflation came down, families were still facing high costs since inflation is the rate of price increases, not the prices themselves.

DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

To add insult to injury, 40-year-high inflation prompted the fastest rise in interest rates in just as long. Not only did prices rise rapidly, but so did borrowing costs. That was a deadly one-two punch for homeownership affordability as higher home prices and mortgage interest rates combined to double the monthly payment on a median-priced home in just four years.

But affordability was improving after January 2025. Real (inflation-adjusted) weekly paychecks rose roughly 2% on average from January 2025 through February of this year. While not a windfall, it was still good progress and reversed half the cumulative losses from the Biden years as income growth outpaced inflation.

GEN Z IS WORKING HARD, BUT THE ECONOMY IS PUTTING THE AMERICAN DREAM OUT OF REACH FOR MANY

Tax and regulatory reform, along with sound energy policy, were spurring economic activity and wage growth while keeping inflation down. Then the Iran war broke out. Global energy markets specifically and supply chains broadly were severely disrupted, causing costs to skyrocket.

Oil prices quickly rose from $60 or $70 per barrel, depending on the market, to $100 or $120. Prices at the pump soon followed, but the energy shock is spilling over to more sectors of the economy with each passing day.

CHEVRON CEO WARNS IRAN CONFLICT HAS CREATED 'VERY REAL' THREAT TO GLOBAL OIL SUPPLIES AS GAS PRICES CLIMB

Energy is an input cost in every product and service consumers buy. Food at the grocery store was grown with diesel-powered tractors and fertilizer synthesized from natural gas. It was transported to the store on a truck, and maybe a train too, fueled by diesel. Prices for everything from airfares to plastics to manufactured goods are up because of the energy shock.

The reversal in progress on affordability is evident in housing too. Homeownership affordability hit a three-year high in February and, while still relatively low, marked a significant improvement from the record low in the Biden years. However, it’s fallen each month since then to the lowest level since July 2024 as interest rates ramped up.

THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE

Those higher mortgage interest rates are also a result of the current energy shock. When fuel supplies began falling, energy prices rose, and that in turn drove inflation expectations higher. Interest rates followed as lenders demanded a higher return for the anticipated inflation.

And the disruptions are not just from the Middle East, but Eastern Europe too. Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have exacerbated the shortage of oil and petroleum products, especially diesel. The result was higher prices and lower real earnings.

AMERICA'S TRUCKERS ISSUE DIRE WARNING AS SOARING DIESEL COSTS THREATEN 'DOMINO EFFECT'

However, unlike the runaway inflation that peaked in 2022 at an annual rate exceeding 9%, today’s higher prices are not from the government devaluing the currency by spending, borrowing and creating too much money. Rather, this is an energy shock that is causing countless prices to rise.

The difference in causation means there’s a different solution and a better outlook too. The affordability crisis was easing significantly until the energy shocks hit and those shocks came from overseas. There’s nothing wrong with the domestic fundamentals underpinning the American economy.

LEE ZELDIN: BIDEN'S ENERGY RULES COST BILLIONS. TRUMP'S EPA IS LOWERING COSTS

Investment is booming, the manufacturing sector is expanding at the fastest pace in at least four years, the private sector is adding jobs, AI is fueling productivity growth and earnings are still growing. Once the conflicts overseas are resolved, energy markets will begin to normalize and costs will start declining. Then the economy will be firing on all cylinders.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Just as higher energy prices are pushing up costs everywhere else, so will lower energy prices put downward pressure on consumer staples everywhere. Likewise, inflation expectations will fall, dragging interest rates back down and improving homeownership affordability. Falling prices and rising earnings mean more breathing room for families.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

None of this will happen overnight because supply chains take time to heal, but it’s crystal clear that once peace returns, affordability will follow. All the other pieces of the puzzle are already in place.

World.title: Mamdani says Trump agrees to grant visa so mother can attend funeral of teen killed in Bronx shooting
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that President Donald Trump has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a teenage immigrant from Ghana who was shot and killed last week in the Bronx.

"The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," Mamdani wrote Saturday on X. "Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment.

TRUMP LEAVES STAGE MID-SPEECH TO EMBRACE PARENTS OF 12-YEAR-OLD KILLED BY STRAY BULLET IN THE BRONX

Javits Frimpong, 15, was heading to school in a Bronx neighborhood shortly before 9:30 a.m. on Thursday when he was shot in the abdomen, according to New York City Police.

He was rushed to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead

No arrests have been made in connection with the shooting. The incident remains under investigation.

"All of New York City is mourning this tragedy," the mayor said.

Frimpong arrived in the Bronx from Ghana a year ago to stay with his father and begin a new life in the U.S., according to U.S. Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.

TRUMP, MAMDANI SET TO MEET AGAIN ON MAYOR’S HOME TURF AFTER MONTHS OF POLITICAL WHIPLASH

"Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him," Torres said. "Every child in the Bronx deserves to walk to school without fearing for their life, and no parent should ever have to endure what Javits’s father, Thomas, is enduring now."

Thomas Frimpong described his son as a quiet teenager. He told reporters that learned just days before the shooting that his son was being bullied at school.

"It was the principal who told me," Thomas Frimpong said. "He said two guys are disturbing my son so he has suspended the two guys. My son is at school. He’s innocent, so I call him. I talk with my son, he said 'dad, I’m okay.'"

Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said on X that Ghanaian officials in New York are coordinating with local authorities, adding that the foreign ministry "will work tirelessly with U.S. authorities to ensure justice is secured."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

He also said he welcomes Mamdani's intervention and Trump’s "timely decision" to grant a visa to the victim's mother.

"Madam Doris Adu Gyamfi’s pain as a loving mother is unimaginable and indeed everything must be done to ensure she is present to pay her respects," the foreign minister said.

The Ghanaian government "will take care of the full cost of Madam Adu Gyamfi’s travels and also stands ready to contribute towards a dignifying funeral," he added.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Philadelphia Eagles lose sixth straight as Washington Commanders score 27 unanswered points
World.content:
The Philadelphia Eagles are in free-fall. After building an early 10-0 lead, Philadelphia gave up 27 unanswered points in a 27-10 loss to the Washington Commanders on Sunday Night Football.

Philadelphia started fast. Jake Elliott hit a 40-yard field goal, and Saquon Barkley scored on a three-yard run after a Washington turnover. The Eagles never scored again. Washington took over behind Jayden Daniels and kicker Drew Stevens.

Stevens hit a 56-yard field goal late in the first quarter, Daniels found Stefon Diggs for an eight-yard score in the second, and Stevens added a 39-yard kick before halftime to put Washington up 13-10.

JALEN HURTS TO REPORTEDLY MISS REMAINDER OF NFL SEASON AFTER BLOOD CLOTS FOUND IN QUARTERBACK'S LUNGS

Philadelphia has no answers without Jalen Hurts. Tanner McKee looked like a backup all night, holding the ball, taking sacks, refusing to throw downfield and turning the ball over twice.

Without Hurts, Washington stacked the box and held Barkley to 30 yards on 13 carries.

The turning point came in the third quarter. Dorance Armstrong strip-sacked McKee, and Charles Omenihu recovered the fumble. Daniels hit Treylon Burks for 53 yards on the next play, setting up a 25-yard Stevens kick.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

When Philadelphia finally drove into scoring position in the fourth quarter, mental mistakes wiped it out. Elliott made an apparent 36-yard field goal to cut the deficit to three, but an illegal formation penalty on left tackle Jordan Mailata took the points off the board. Backed up five yards, Elliott missed wide right.

Washington closed it out. Stevens kicked a 42-yard field goal with 3:43 left. Commanders cornerback Rasul Douglas intercepted McKee on the next possession.

Rachaad White broke off a 33-yard run and scored from a yard out with 1:52 remaining, and Austin Ekeler ran in a two-point conversion to make it 27-10.

Daniels finished with 217 passing yards, one touchdown and no turnovers. Philadelphia has lost six straight games, falling to 2-6. Washington improves to 2-4-1, climbing out of last place in the NFC East.

World.title: Collins accuses Schumer of pushing attack ads filled with 'outright lies' in tight Maine race
World.content:

Sen. Susan Collins on Sunday blasted Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic Party over what she described as a wave of false attack ads targeting her and other Republican candidates, saying she has never seen a campaign with "so many outright lies."

She made the remarks during an interview with Fox News on Sunday, just two days before Election Day in Maine, where she is seeking reelection in a closely watched race against Democratic rival Troy Jackson. According to the latest Fox News poll, the two candidates are tied at 49%.

Collins accused Democrats of following "Chuck Schumer's playbook," pointing to attack ads she said were nearly identical to those targeting other Republican lawmakers.

MANCHIN CALLS SCHUMER 'CRAZY' FOR TRYING TO OUST GOP SENATOR IN CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN

"One of the outrageous, completely false ads against me had to do with Jeffrey Epstein. And it turns out, in talking to two of my colleagues who are in tough races, that they had virtually identical ads run against them. So this is part of Chuck Schumer's playbook," she said.

"There are a lot of differences between my opponent and me, but I've never seen a campaign with so many outright lies. It's very frustrating," she added.

Collins further accused Democrats of trying to shift the focus away from local issues and toward divisive national political battles.

"It's certainly an attempt by my opponent and Chuck Schumer and their allies to nationalize this race," she said.

SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY

Turning to her own campaign, Collins portrayed herself as a bipartisan lawmaker willing to work across party lines, arguing that the Senate needs more centrists as moderates increasingly leave Washington.

"Unfortunately, a lot of them have given up and retired or decided they just didn't want to run again. And that's one reason I am running again," she said.

"We need more people who are willing to work across party lines. That is really important," she said.

FOX NEWS POLL: NAIL-BITER IN MAINE SENATE RACE

She also described herself as the "most independent senator on either side of the aisle," pointing to her voting record and saying her decisions are based on what she believes is right, rather than who occupies the White House or what President Donald Trump supports.

"There's this phony figure out there that I voted with President Trump 95% of the time. That's based on a sample of only 30% of the votes. If you look at a broader sample of 90% of the vote, that drops significantly to like 72%. And I voted against the president's policies 138 times," she said.

While Jackson previously told Fox News that he believes he has a "good shot" at defeating Collins, the longtime Republican senator touted strong voter support and said she is more optimistic than ever about her reelection chances.

World.title: Missing Utah teen Kylie Arellano found safe in Oregon after 500-day search
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Utah teenager who vanished nearly a year and a half ago has been found safe in Oregon, ending a lengthy nationwide search that spanned more than 500 days.

Kylie Arellano, now 17, was last seen by her family on May 29, 2025, at their home in Garden City, Utah, when she was 15 years old.

Kylie's disappearance had triggered a wide federal and state investigation that led officials through dozens of unconfirmed sightings before culminating in her recovery on Sunday.

MISSING TEEN FOUND HIDING IN CONVICTED SEX OFFENDER'S CLOSET IN FLORIDA, SHERIFF SAYS

Law enforcement officers in Oregon, working directly with the FBI's Salt Lake City field office and the Rich County Sheriff's Office, safely recovered the teen, according to a law enforcement news release.

Kylie, they said, was found with a 39-year-old man in Oregon. The man was taken into custody without incident.

"The FBI and the Rich County Sheriff’s Office have been actively investigating this case for more than a year and pursuing every lead received from across the U.S. and in other countries.

FBI NABS MORE THAN 350 ALLEGED CHILD SEX ABUSE OFFENDERS

"As this case is ongoing, no further information will be released at this time," the FBI's Salt Lake City field office said in a statement on Sunday.

Federal authorities also credited the Oregon State Police, the FBI's Portland field office and the Utah Department of Public Safety for their assistance in the operation.

"Tonight, local police in Oregon brought a minor who had been missing for a year and a half to safety, acting on information provided by our FBI Salt Lake City Field Office," FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital.

"We are grateful she can return home, and we will continue working with our partners to hold those responsible accountable," Patel added.

MIKE WALTZ, TIM TEBOW LAUNCH EFFORT TO COMBAT ONLINE CHILD EXPLOITATION: 'IT'S HAPPENING IN THEIR BACKYARD'

"To anyone using gore groups to target and exploit children: the FBI and our partners are coming for you.

"We are using every tool at our disposal to combat nihilistic violent extremism, bring offenders to justice and protect America’s children."

Kylie Arellano’s grandmother also thanked the authorities for finding her. "THANK YOU for all you and your agents and teams are doing to find our baby girl, Kylie Arellano and bring her home!!!" she wrote on X.

According to a law enforcement source, the suspect allegedly met the teenager on Snapchat before her disappearance.

Last year, Rich County Sheriff Dale Stacey said detectives had chased reports of sightings across multiple states and urged the public to preserve any photographic or timestamped evidence.

TWO MISSING CHILDREN RESCUED FROM TRAILER AS POLICE ARREST BABYSITTER ON KIDNAPPING CHARGES

New details about the investigation had also emerged days before Kylie was found.

Unsealed search warrants reviewed by KUTV on Oct. 29 showed that investigators had previously scrutinized Kylie's mother, Stephanie Coleman, and questioned her about a 2024 allegation of physical abuse.

There were also questions about discrepancies involving missing text messages from the night Kylie vanished and suspicious marks in the home.

Coleman had denied having any role in her daughter's disappearance or abusing her, providing timestamped "good night" text messages from May 29, 2025.

She said the marks were caused by an injured cat and maintained that Kylie had likely been groomed and lured away by someone she encountered online, the outlet reported.
