Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before striking near the Palm Beach County roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining a crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.

Sponsor Message

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a "horrific tragedy." The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation, he said.

toggle caption i Mark Elias/AP

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed.

"It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis told reporters at the scene. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road."

Rain pounded the region on Sunday. A flood watch due to excessive rainfall was in effect through Monday afternoon, the National Weather Service said.

The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.

The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).

Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.

Sponsor Message

A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it smashed into the ground.

Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net.

"We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers.

But the situation rapidly deteriorated. After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate.

"We're descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed.

"We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. "We're going to crash into the ground."

Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said the jet was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.

Steve Arroyo, an aviation safety expert, said icing and turbulence could have been factors in the crash and may have caused the plane to stall while it was cruising at 34,000 feet (10,363 meters).

There are many potential factors and the NTSB will consider all of them, including how the pilot responded to the icing and turbulence reported over the radio. But investigators won't rule anything out at this early stage, he said.

The NTSB said investigators were expected to arrive at the crash site on Sunday and Monday. A media briefing is scheduled for Monday in West Palm Beach.

Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. The road will be closed until further notice, county officials said.

The crash occurred in Greenacres, Florida, according to Palm Beach County sheriff's officials. The city of 45,000 people is about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.

World.title: TD tried to make grieving mom pay $38K in student debt after daughter died of cancer
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Joyel Singfield co-signed her daughter’s TD student loan in 2020, it included life insurance. But after her daughter, Maari, died in 2025 of breast cancer, the bank told the mother the life insurance had expired, so she was on the hook for close to $40,000.

The bank told this grieving mother she owed $38K in student debt. She fought back | Go Public

Joyel Singfield struggles to hold back tears as she recounts losing her 30-year-old daughter Maari to breast cancer last year— and the bitter dispute with TD Bank that followed.

In 2020, Singfield co-signed a $40,000 TD student loan for Maari which included life insurance. She only learned after Maari's death that the insurance had expired, making her responsible for the $37,806 outstanding debt.

"It was honestly shocking," said Singfield, who lives in Gatineau, Que. "We committed to that loan in 2020 with insurance."

An internal TD investigation determined Singfield was on the hook for the full amount, plus growing interest. She fought back, battling the bank for more than a year-and-a-half. Following a Go Public investigation, TD backed down and wiped out the entire debt.

"I'm very relieved. I'm very grateful. I'm also a little bit disheartened at how this had to get to this point," Singfield said.

"Nothing can prepare you for the loss of a child. … That's what our family should have been focusing on."

Account handled properly, TD says

Singfield is one of tens of thousands of Canadians who launch complaints against their banks every year, often with large amounts of money at stake.

According to the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, financial institutions reported handling 236,324 customer complaints in the 2025–2026 fiscal year, with about 31 per cent not resolved to the consumer's satisfaction.

Unhappy customers can escalate complaints to the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments (OBSI), an independent resolution service funded by financial institutions. But a 2025 internal feedback survey of 1,598 Canadians who used OBSI found that only 20 per cent were satisfied with the outcome.

Maari Singfield passed away from cancer in January 2025 at the age of 30. (Submitted by Joyel Singfield)

Following TD's investigation, Singfield appealed to OBSI, which sided with the bank that she was liable for the debt. However, both agreed that TD should cover Singfield's $1,577 in unpaid interest and pay her $500 for distress.

"It's an insult," said Singfield, who rejected the offer. "Two thousand dollars doesn't even cover any of the pain and suffering that this has caused."

After Go Public got involved, TD cleared Singfield of all liability. Spokesperson Ashleigh Murphy said in an email that the bank handled the account appropriately, but decided to help Singfield due to her "difficult circumstances."

Got a story you want investigated? Contact Sophia and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

OBSI spokesperson John Bowes declined to comment citing "confidentiality obligations."

Go Public investigates

In 2020, Maari got a student line of credit to pursue a graduate degree in counselling psychology. In remission from breast cancer at the time, she secured life insurance as added protection for her mother as co-signer.

Maari graduated in 2023, and she died in 2025, at which point the bank went after Singfield for loan payments. She pushed back, convinced the loan was insured.

It took the bank seven months to officially clarify that the original insurance policy was automatically cancelled when Maari's student line of credit converted to a personal loan upon graduation.

Singfield insists the bank failed to notify her or Maari about the expired insurance, depriving them of the chance to renew the policy.

"We would have taken action for sure," she said.

TD shared with Joyel Singfield this letter it says it sent her daughter in 2023, which included details about the need to renew her life insurance. Go Public discovered the letter is undated, and TD could only provide an estimated mailing date of 'November 2023.' (TD Bank)

TD shared with Singfield a letter it claimed to have sent Maari in 2023 outlining the loan changes and insurance renewal requirement. But Go Public discovered the letter is undated, and TD could only provide an estimated mailing date of "November 2023."

"Undated letters are always viewed with suspicion by the courts," said Duff Conacher, co-founder of the citizen advocacy group Democracy Watch.

"You have to actually prove things, not just claim you did something."

Meanwhile, Go Public confirmed TD never sent the letter to Singfield — even though Canada's Bank Act requires banks to send co-signers separate loan notifications.

The bank said this is because Singfield opted out of receiving notifications. But Go Public challenged this after discovering the bank had sent her several notices regarding Maari's personal loan — just not the critical one with details about the need to renew the insurance.

"That's pretty damning," said Erik Knutsen, a law professor at Queen's University in Kingston, Ont. "I think as a bank, you cannot dig your way out of that one."

Shortly after Go Public presented its findings, TD cleared the entire debt — which had grown to $41,188.

Knutsen says it's disheartening that her dispute required media intervention, "which is essentially relying on public shame."

Do customers need help to pursue complaints?

Conacher says Singfield's case highlights the power imbalance when average customers battle big banks.

"You're up against the bank with a team of lawyers and unlimited resources to drag it out and argue their case," he said. "On the other side is the lowly consumer on their own."

OBSI spokesperson Bowes said that people who turn to OBSI don't require legal representation or specialized knowledge "to be assured of a fair outcome."

Conacher disagrees and offers as a solution Democracy Watch's long-standing proposal for Canada to establish a Financial Consumer Organization . It would advocate on behalf of customers involved in banking disputes, giving them "lawyer help, expert help," he said.

Help earlier would have been good, Singfield says.

"Too many people don't have the energy to fight something like this," she said. "I think that's really unfair."

World.title: 5 reasons why the Democrats might not take control of Congress in U.S. midterms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Political strategists of both main parties in the U.S. believe it’s almost certain the Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives from the Republicans in Tuesday's midterm elections.

The likelihood of the Democratic Party flipping the Senate, however, is another story.

In the House, non-partisan election-forecast websites such as Cook Political Report rate the Republicans as vulnerable in as many as 30 GOP-held seats. The Democrats need a net gain of merely three to get a majority.

Also, consider that the party of the sitting president has suffered a net loss of House seats in all but two midterm elections since the late 1930s, and that no U.S. president has gone into a midterm with a lower approval rating than what Donald Trump has right now.

But when it comes to the Senate, there are doubts the Democrats have a clear path to flipping the four states they need to reach the majority threshold of 51.

Here are five reasons why the Democrats may not wind up with control of both houses of Congress for the remainder of Trump‘s time in office.

WATCH | What a Democrat sweep of the midterms would mean for Trump and the GOP: How big Democrat wins in the midterms could impact Trump — and his party | Duration closed caption 4:57 With the 2026 U.S. midterm elections threatening Republican control of Capitol Hill, CBC’s Ellen Mauro breaks down how a shifting balance of power could challenge President Donald Trump’s agenda — and the key tools he can use to counter Democratic opposition.

1. The 2026 Senate map is tough for Democrats

Flipping the Senate this year was always going to be a tough haul for the Democrats, simply because of their limited opportunities to gain seats in this particular midterm.

Only one-third of Senate seats are up for grabs each election, because senators are elected to six-year terms.

Nearly all of the Republican-held seats the Democrats are seeking to flip are in states that Trump carried by at least 11 percentage points in 2024. (The only exceptions within easier reach are Maine and North Carolina.)

That means to get a majority, the Democrats must gain at least two states from a list that includes Ohio, Iowa, Texas, Alaska and Kansas.

That will require a giant swing toward the Democrats in states that have long been ruby red.

WATCH | Why Trump looms so large in the Texas race for U.S. Senate: What Texans on both sides really think of Trump | Duration closed caption 10:06 Texans have voted Republican for decades, but as many sour on the Trump agenda, Democrat James Talarico could flip the state's Senate seat. For the National, Paul Hunter talks to voters on both sides to see if the race is now a referendum on Donald Trump himself.

2. The polls could be off

There's been a well documented history of polling in the Trump era failing to measure the full extent of support for Republicans. On the final weekend before the 2024 presidential election, a poll in Iowa (by a pollster with a sterling reputation) showed Kamala Harris up by three points. Trump won the state by 13.

Polling firms have, over the years, adjusted their methods to try to compensate for the tendency of Democrats to be more likely than Republicans to answer polls.

They weight responses so samples better reflect the full demographics of who actually shows up at the polls, factoring in education, income and ethnicity. They ask respondents who they voted for in the last election to check the sample isn’t torqued toward one party or the other.

Polling is a science, but an inexact one, and it’s important to remember its limitations. One key limitation is that when two candidates are polling within the margin of error — say, a lead of just two percentage points — you really can’t say who’s winning.

Recent polls in the Senate races in Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Kansas have all shown results within the margin of error.

WATCH | Two Blocks from the White House answers your questions about the midterms:

3. So much depends on turnout

Voter turnout in midterm election years has historically lagged behind turnout in presidential election years. The key midterm challenge for each party, whether on the offensive or defensive, is getting their supporters simply to show up.

While polling broadly suggests registered Democrats are more enthusiastic about punishing Trump than the Republican base is defending him, Democratic candidates still need help from independent voters to win in toss-up races.

It's worth noting that the highest turnout for a midterm election since the First World War came in 2018, during Trump's first term.

One factor that could dampen a blue wave is whether the Democratic Party and its candidates made strong enough arguments for why Americans should vote for them, rather than simply relying on their desire to vote against the Republicans.

WATCH | 'Double haters,' fed up with both parties, could sway tight midterm races: They hate both U.S. parties. They could swing the midterms | Duration closed caption 7:52 In states like Arizona, some undecided voters have grown to dislike both major political parties. Rather than withdrawing altogether, these ‘double haters’ remain politically engaged and their votes could swing the U.S. midterms.

4. GOP money has flooded the airwaves

Extraordinary amounts of money have gone into campaign advertising this midterm cycle.

In just the competitive Senate races, Republicans and their affiliated political action committees (PACs) have spent some $1.2 billion US, outpacing Democrats by $237 million US, according to a Bloomberg analysis of ad-buying data from the consulting firm AdImpact.

Elon Musk alone has spent the staggering sum of nearly half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates in the midterms ($475 million US, reports the New York Times, $446 million US, according to the Guardian.)

The race to be come the next U.S. senator for Texas — between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico — is poised to become the most expensive non-presidential campaign in history, with s pending since the primaries already surpassing $500 million US, according to data compiled by AdImpact.

WATCH | Will young men support Republicans like they did with Trump in 2024?: 'I feel like I got duped': The young men turning on Trump | Duration closed caption 9:05 Young American men and conservative podcasters who supported U.S. President Donald Trump in 2024 are distancing themselves from his administration over unmet promises, a shift experts warn could decide key midterm races.

5. Democrat candidates could underperform

Don’t discount the possibility the Democrats could fall short in a state or two because their particular candidate fails to capture the full extent of the swing away from the Republicans elsewhere in the country.

In Maine, the Democrats had to scramble in July to nominate a candidate to replace Graham Platner, the oysterman who’d attracted national attention for his anti-establishment campaign only to be forced to resign amid allegations he’d sexually assaulted a former partner.

His replacement, Troy Jackson, is a logger who’s been a politician for 20 years and, while equally plain-spoken, lacks much of Platner's charisma.

Jackson is also battling a formidable opponent in Susan Collins, who has held this Senate seat for 30 years despite Maine’s history of voting Democrat for president.

Michigan is another state where the Democrat candidate is potentially at risk. Abdul El-Sayed, one of the most left-leaning Senate candidates the party is fielding this cycle, won the bitter nomination battle this summer to replace the retiring Gary Peters.

Trump has leaned into Islamophobic rhetoric to attack El-Sayed, repeatedly calling him a "jihadist" who's "on the side of the terrorists." The results on Tuesday will give some indication whether those attacks resonated with Michigan voters or repelled them.

World.title: 'We often try suicide:' The hidden cost of problem gambling in Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.

Dave, a retiree recovering from gambling addiction, says that when he was winning, he felt like a king, hooked by the prospect of wealth and recognition.

But he says like most gamblers, he "inevitably" started losing.

"Not only money — trust, people we care for, spouses, children, we lose the whole gamut. Everything that we built goes crumbling down," he told CBC News during a recent online Gamblers Anonymous meeting in Toronto.

"So we often try suicide, which I did try. I turned out to be an utter failure at that."

CBC reporter Dave Seglins speaks to a Gamblers Anonymous meeting in Toronto. (Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)

A CBC News investigation has found that at least 220 problem gamblers in Canada have died by suicide in the last decade, which includes a tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022.

But the national numbers are likely higher, as Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Nunavut don’t track gambling-related deaths, citing a lack of obvious indicators in most death investigations.

What’s more, no coroner in Canada has ever held an inquest into the issue — unlike in Australia and the United Kingdom, where inquests are being used to critically examine the gambling industry and the links between addiction and suicide.

'Misery and great harm'

A coroner in Australia delivered a scathing inquest report last month, calling for major industry reforms after investigating the suicide of 22-year-old Kyle Hudson.

Hudson opened online betting accounts after his 18th birthday and over four years, placed more than 10,000 bets, losing a cumulative $47,000 Cdn.

The morning he died, he had placed and lost bets worth $6,200.

Coroner Paul Lowrie concluded that Hudson’s preferred platform, SportsBet, ought to have detected his problem gambling.

"Kyle’s case reveals, in the sharpest relief, the human cost of online gambling," the coroner wrote. "It should be a clear signal that we cannot leave monitoring and intervention solely in the hands of the betting companies."

Kyle Hudson was 'a young man brimming with promise,' according to a coroner's report in Australia. He was working part-time while in his fourth year at university and loved sport. (ABC.net.au)

Hudson’s betting escalated and triggered 37 alerts on SportBet’s internal "Safer Gambling" monitoring system, the inquest heard.

The company sent him automated support emails and on multiple occasions called him to suspend his account, only to receive a call back from Hudson, who convinced them to reinstate it.

SportsBet also sent Hudson hundreds of bonus offers and inducements to continue playing, which the coroner found to be "contrary" to the company’s safer gambling programs.

"These products are carefully designed to keep gamblers engaged and active, and to extract net losses over time," Lowrie wrote.

"They are dangerous and capable of causing misery and great harm, especially for the young or those whose traits may make them more vulnerable."

SportsBet maintained during the inquest that Hudson did not have a gambling problem. That’s despite accounts from Hudson’s family, experts and analysis of the extent of his online gambling activity.

"It is chilling that this is SportsBet’s view," Lowrie concluded.

LISTEN | The Big Bet: Understood: The Big Bet 2:32 Introducing The Big Bet Once associated with bookies, organized crime, and backroom bets, sports betting is now one of the fastest-growing industries in North America. This is the story of how it went mainstream — and who’s paying the price. Four episodes, releasing weekly starting Monday, October 5, 2026.

Inquests examine gambling companies' player data

Charles Ritchie of Sheffield, England, who started the charity Gambling With Lives , says inquests are an important tool to change laws and cast light on the gambling industry.

He became an advocate after his 24-year-old son Jack took his own life in November 2017.

"We realized straight away that it was gambling that had killed him. It was there in his suicide note," Ritchie told CBC News, detailing how Jack had started gambling as a teen and got hooked online after a fluke win of 1,000 pounds ($1,870 Cdn) on an electronic gaming terminal.

Jack Ritchie’s online gambling addiction led to his death, a U.K. coroner found. (Leigh Day law firm)

Ritchie says an inquest into Jack’s death in 2022 validated that it was caused by gambling.

Beyond that, he says inquests have become a valuable tool for grieving families to hold companies accountable if they have failed to intervene in cases of addiction.

WATCH | Gambling apps can spot warning signs, says watchdog: Gambling apps can spot warning signs, says watchdog | Duration closed caption 1:07 Father who lost son to gambling suicide says betting companies must use player data to intervene and protect addicts.

After someone’s death, he says inquests can analyze the deceased’s behaviour using player data and banking records.

"When we look at those figures in the raw… Somebody is, at four o'clock in the morning, having hundreds of bets, is losing hundreds of pounds. You as a human being would say, ‘This is wrong. We need to intervene,’" he said.

"Gambling companies don't do that. And that has been found in so many of the inquests."

The U.K. has held inquests into the gambling deaths of, clockwise from top left, Arthur Soames, Jack Ritchie, Oliver Long, Gareth Evans, Luke Ashton, Ellen Mulvey and Lee Adams. (Leigh Day law firm)

No inquests in Canada

The U.K. has held seven gambling-related inquests since Jack Ritchie’s death inquiry in 2022, resulting in numerous recommendations to the government and the gambling industry.

Coroners and medical examiners in Canada have never undertaken a similar investigation.

CBC contacted chief coroners and medical examiners across Canada, who acknowledge not every jurisdiction tracks gambling suicides.

Nor do most coroners consider whether problem gambling was a contributing factor during suicide investigations. It can be hard to detect without an explicit suicide note.

People with gambling addictions tend to hide their problem from family and friends. Coroners don’t routinely probe a suicide victim’s financial records or online history to determine whether they had a gambling problem.

Journalist Rob Csernyik, author of A Losing Hand: The Human Cost of Canada’s Gambling Epidemic, says chief coroners pledged in 2003 to begin tracking the problem nationally. It has never happened.

"It's just something that hasn't been on the radar in many years in Canada, despite the expansion of gambling," Csernyik told CBC News.

Canada lacks data on gambling suicides, despite the expansion of online betting, says author and journalist Rob Csernyik. (Roger Cosman/CBC)

"I think that now with the larger push into legal gambling markets, that it's something we finally need to address."

Dr. Shawn Kelly says the tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022, the year the province legalized private online betting, worries him that we'll see an epidemic of addiction.

"This is the thing I’ve been fearful for," said Kelly, an adolescent addiction specialist in Ottawa.

He’s calling for much closer monitoring of problem gambling as well as restrictions on gambling advertising to curb gambling’s harms before they get worse.

"To me, it would be much too late to act when we had irrefutable evidence that our changes in gambling legislation have led to an increase in suicide amongst the vulnerable."

Dr. Shawn Kelly says the tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022 is a warning sign for public health officials. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

CBC asked Ontario’s Ministry of Health to comment on the rise in gambling addiction and related suicides in the province.

The minister’s press secretary deferred to Ontario’s Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Gaming, which oversees the province’s $3-billion-a-year online gambling market.

The Gaming Ministry did not address the rise in suicide rates but said in an email that since 2018, "our government has invested $421 million, including $70.1 million over the last year, in responsible gambling education, research and addiction treatment."

In the meantime, members at Gamblers Anonymous, a peer-to-peer support group with chapters around the world, are hoping more people who are struggling reach out for help.

Dan, who like Dave considered suicide, describes the group as a "big extended family."

"If I didn't find GA (Gamblers Anonymous), there's a very solid chance that either I'd be living on the streets, lost my home, marriage or even dead," he told CBC News. "That came across my mind many times."

WATCH | Gamblers Anonymous 'saved my life,' says recovering gambler: Gamblers Anonymous 'saved my life,' says recovering gambler | Duration closed caption 1:01 Dan from London, Ont., says he might have lost everything or wound up dead if not for regular meetings of Gamblers Anonymous.

Are you, or someone you know, suffering from gambling? Support is available.

World.title: Economic frustration set to boil over in midterm elections
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

American voters are headed to the polls for the U.S. midterms this week. Most are angry and frustrated about the state of the economy and the way Donald Trump has managed it.

If you want evidence of that dissatisfaction look no further than the University of Michigan's Index of Consumer Sentiment.

It shows consumer confidence is plummetting under Trump.

"Only three times since the 1970s have more than half of Americans said their government's doing bad job managing the economy. Right now it's at 74 per cent," said Kathryn Anne Edwards, a labour economist and policy consultant in Houston.

The index gauges consumer sentiment. It is lower today than it was during the toughest recessions in the 1980s or even the financial crisis in 2008-09.

And she says that survey is one of the biggest and longest standing bodies of economic data in the country. It's been going on since the 1940s. And it's been a monthly survey since 1978.

Edwards says these kinds of numbers show that on some fundamental level, the U.S. economy is failing American households.

"It's so completely unprecedented. It's really hard to put into words," said Edwards.

Those kind of plunges in consumer sentiment historically only happen in the deepest and darkest days of a recession.

And that's what's odd.

The U.S. economy is nowhere near a recession.

The latest GDP numbers out of Washington show the U.S. economy is the fastest growing economy in the Western world.

American GDP expanded by 3.8 per cent in the quarter running from July to September. (By comparison, Canada is on track for about a third of that growth.)

Retail sales were up. Investment in AI continues to churn ever higher. And stock markets are at an all-time high.

"GDP is growing above trend, consumer spending remains robust, layoffs trudge along at ultra-low levels, and we've seen a stable unemployment rate over the past year," wrote RBC's team of economists Mike Reid, Carrie Freestone and Imri Haggin.

But if the macro data is so good, why are voters so angry?

"For many voters, the economy is now synonymous with inflation, as rising prices outweigh job reports, housing affordability and stock market performance," wrote Francis Généreux, lead economist at Desjardins Group in a note to clients.

And those rising prices have been driven by two main things; tariffs and the U.S.-led war with Iran.

Gas prices shot up the day the war began. They have bounced around a little as talk of various ceasefires and deals come and go, but American drivers are paying far more at the pumps today than they were a year ago.

And gasoline prices are posted everywhere as drivers and pedestrians alike move through a neighbourhood. So even if you ride a bicycle to work, the increase in prices is incredibly hard to ignore.

Inflation in the U.S. has ticked up to 3.7 per cent, and economists warn it's not done climbing yet.

Yes, much of that increase is due to energy costs. But tariffs have contributed as well.

A recent report from the New York Federal Reserve found the cost of many everyday items would have declined last year were it not for Trump's tariffs.

Researchers looked at the 12-month change in consumer goods prices going back to the peak of the COVID-era surge in inflation. They showed price growth was still falling in 2024 and reversed in 2025.

"Our estimates attribute this increase to the tariffs: by February 2026, tariffs had contributed 2.9 percentage points to goods price inflation, and without them goods prices would have fallen slightly," wrote Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise and David E. Weinstein.

And Edwards says voters have followed the Trump administration's policy decisions and how they drive prices. She says there are two sharp drops in the consumer sentiment index. One when tariffs were introduced and the other when the war with Iran began.

"Americans get it. Tariffs have made their lives more expensive," she said.

And Americans will take that knowledge into the polling booth this week. If the polls hold, the midterms could lead to sweeping changes in the formation of Congress and who holds power on Capitol Hill.

But whether those newly elected Senate and House members actually take action to lower tariffs for Canadians is a different question altogether.

World.title: Hudson Williams talks tattoos, sex scenes, Connor Storrie with neurodivergent interviewers in The Assembly S2
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hudson Williams — whose own father is on the autism spectrum — rose to fame playing Shane Hollander, a world-class hockey player who is also on the spectrum, in Heated Rivalry.

So what did he say when he was invited to be questioned by a roomful of autistic and neurodivergent interviewers?

"I'm strapped in. My knees are bent."

The rules of The Assembly are as follows: "No subjects are out of bounds. No questions are off the table, and all might happen."

The first episode of Season 2 aired on CBC television last night and can still be viewed on Gem . To avoid spoilers, stream it now before reading any further.

The meaning behind one of his tattoos

Hudson Williams gives a bit of a tattoo tour at the start of his episode on The Assembly. As the room fills up, he shows the interviewers which ones were done by his tattoo-artist girlfriend, Katelyn Larson.

The cherries just above his left elbow, for starters. And higher up on his shoulder, the outline of a set of teeth.

It's the underbite of his late dog, Jesse Skywalker Williams, who died at 17 years old, he says.

"Whenever he looked at me, he had this little underbite smile," says Williams.

How Hudson Williams views his relationship with Connor Storrie

True to The Assembly's promise, one interviewer named Nate asks Williams what many people have been wondering but may have been too afraid to ask: "Did you ever feel something for Connor that was more than friendship?"

Williams says he and his Heated Rivalry co-star Connor Storrie are "platonic soulmates — just completely in love with each other."

But he makes it clear those feelings will never become romantic — not even if they cuddle for 10 hours straight. He says it's what makes their relationship stable and beautiful.

Though Williams does suggest it would be great to bring Storrie everywhere — even the shower.

"Someone needs to get my back. I wish Connor was just with me every day…. Because I have a loofah, but I can't reach. If I had Connor with me every day, he could just come in there."

In Season 2 of The Assembly, Williams answers questions about his Heated Rivalry co-stars and what it’s really like filming those steamy sex scenes. (CBC/Small Army Entertainment)

When the interview ends, that revelation inspires another member of The Assembly to share that he has a guy he loves too: his best friend Colin.

"That's lovely. It's so important to have that," Williams tells him.

He was 'pumped' for friends and family to watch Heated Rivalry sex scenes

Williams says he wasn't worried about those closest to him seeing the intimate scenes in Heated Rivalry.

In fact, he held a screening for the first episode and invited about a dozen friends plus his mom to watch it together, with the expectation it would be "the best friends-screening ever."

Any time a sex scene was coming up, Williams would tell his mom to cover her eyes. His friends all brought party horns, which they blew any time something provocative was happening on screen.

When the horns went silent, his mom knew it was safe to start watching again.

His controversial Victoria comment was taken out of context

When Williams was filming Yaga back in March, he described Victoria in a way that stirred up controversy online .

Specifically, he described it as "dead as f**k" and full of "old people."

The autistic and neurodivergent interviewers in The Assembly asked Williams a range of questions, including what his workouts were like and whether he ever caught feelings for his co-star Connor Storrie. (CBC/Small Army Entertainment)

An interviewer named Margot gives Williams the opportunity to set the record straight, and he takes it, telling her the quote was taken out of context.

"I was like, 'Oh my God, I'm doing so much better. I'm filming this show and I just love it. It's so great. I'm shooting in Victoria, which is like dead as f**k, old people, boring.' Like, I was using those adjectives to describe why I love it."

Williams says he never meant "old people" to be taken as an insult, but he's learning this is all part of being in the public eye.

Williams says he ignored ADHD symptoms

One of the questions Williams appears to appreciate most comes from an interviewer named Julia: "How do you feel like your Korean values have shaped your experience of having ADHD?"

Williams describes how for a long time he struggled to focus in class, and he says his background may have contributed to him ignoring symptoms or pretending they don't exist.

"I feel like a lot of the answer in Asian culture is just more discipline, more discipline…. Sometimes that can be good, but a lot of times it can look like denying a sensitive connection to yourself and a … kindness to yourself."

He tells The Assembly he now realizes ADHD isn't something he can fix simply by trying harder.

While he has taken medication for the condition before, he says he and his mother were initially reluctant. He then reveals he recently considered trying medication again, but "the Korean in me is like, 'Don't. Just focus, just don't do it. Just work harder.'"

Williams says he got goosebumps when some of the interviewers in The Assembly performed an a cappella version of All the Things She Said by t.A.T.u. — one of the songs included on the Heated Rivalry soundtrack. (CBC/Small Army Entertainment)

The episode ends with Williams sharing the Heated Rivalry message he hopes comes across most clearly:

"You deserve the best love story and the best romance story in your life — no matter who you are."

The episode is full of tender moments, and there are more to be seen in the longer producer's cut now streaming on Gem.

World.title: Crash that killed 4 teens in Puslinch, Ont., an 'unimaginable tragedy': police
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Four teenagers from the Greater Toronto Area were killed and two others were injured in a single-vehicle crash in Puslinch — a town southeast of Guelph. The vehicle left the road, struck a guardrail and fell into a ravine near Watson Road S. and Wellington Road 34. Ontario Provincial Police are investigating this collision. CBC’s Dale Manucdoc has more.

'Families forever changed,' OPP says after 4 teens killed in crash south of Guelph

A single-vehicle crash that killed four teens, aged 15 to 19, in Puslinch early Saturday was an "unimaginable tragedy," according to Ontario Provincial Police.

The dead included a 19-year-old man from Mississauga, a 19-year-old man from Brampton, a 17-year-old girl Mississauga and a 15-year-old girl from Milton, OPP Insp. Karen Medeiros said at a press conference Sunday.

"This is a devastating event that has impacted multiple families schools friend groups and communities across southern Ontario," she said.

A 17-year-old girl with life-altering injuries and a 16-year-old girl with non-life-threatening injuries, both from Mississauga, remain in hospital, Medeiros said.

A single-vehicle crash that killed four teens, aged 15 to 19, in Puslinch early Saturday was an "unimaginable tragedy," according to Ontario Provincial Police. (Diego Pizarro/CBC)

Officers were called to a rural area southeast of Guelph shortly after 1:30 a.m. Saturday. In the area of Watson Road S. and Wellington Road 34, a vehicle had left the road, struck a guardrail and fallen into a ravine, Medeiros said.

"Four young people have lost their lives in a matter of moments. Families have been forever changed and an entire community is searching for answers," she said.

She urged anyone with information or footage to contact the Wellington County OPP. Details that might seem insignificant could actually be valuable to investigators piecing together the circumstances of this tragedy, Medeiros said.

Roads remain closed due to the damaged guardrail and to ensure the safety of drivers in the area, she said.

Complex investigation ongoing: OPP inspector

Superint. Wendy Burrow expressed her condolences on behalf of the OPP for the lives lost in the crash, calling it an "unimaginable tragedy that claimed the lives of four young people."

"These young people will never have the opportunity to realize their hopes, dreams and aspirations that they envisioned for their futures," she said.

WATCH | 'Unimaginable tragedy,' OPP says, as 4 teens killed in car crash in southern Ontario: 'Unimaginable tragedy' as 4 teens killed in a fatal car crash in southern Ontario | Duration closed caption 2:15 A single-vehicle crash that killed four teens, aged 15 to 19, in Puslinch, Ont., early Saturday was an ‘unimaginable tragedy,’ according to the Ontario Provincial Police. Two other teens remain in hospital with life-altering and non-life-threatening injuries. Watson Road S. and Wellington Road 34 remain closed due to the damaged guardrail and to ensure driver safety in the area.Tags:

The OPP is supporting those affected by the crash and will ensure "every effort is made" to provide loved ones with answers on what happened, Burrow said.

The complex investigation is ongoing and officers are looking to determine what happened in the moments leading up to the crash, Medeiros said.

Investigators will look at whether speed and seatbelt use were factors, she said , adding that the vehicle was not believed to have had enough seatbelts for six people.

"Our responsibility is to ensure those answers are based on evidence, facts and a thorough investigation," Medeiros said.

She said police are urging all road users to be vigilant and travel safely. Burrow added that officers will remember this tragedy and work to make roads safer for everyone.

World.title: Carney has 'good conversation' with Trump on future of Canada-U.S. trade as midterms near
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he had a 'good conversation' with President Donald Trump on the future of Canada-U.S. trade — a move some political watchers say could be politically motivated as Trump faces a tough midterms fight, especially in border states where the trade war is unpopular.

Carney says he had a 'good conversation' on trade with Trump as midterms near

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he's had a "good conversation" with U.S. President Donald Trump on the future of Canada-U.S. trade, further adding their chat "builds on our recent constructive discussions" over the outlines of a possible trade deal.

"Our teams will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome," Carney said on social media on Sunday morning.

A senior Canadian source tells CBC News that it's unclear what form those talks will take, after earlier suggestions formal negotiations were set to begin again.

Autos are expected to remain a key sticking point, as they were last time in August before trade talks fell apart. That collapse prompted both countries to impose steep duties on one another.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday evening, Trump said that "we have the concept of a deal that's going to be great for our farmers, great for our country, and it will be fine for Canada."

A White House spokesperson said in a statement that "the Trump Administration welcomes continued engagement with Canada as we work toward finalizing the details of a deal that will deliver meaningful results for the American people."

WATCH | Canada not in a 'position right now' to agree to a U.S. trade deal, says Carney: Canada's not in a 'position right now' to agree to a U.S. trade deal: Carney | Duration closed caption 0:45 Asked about the possibility of a trade deal ahead of the U.S. midterms, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada 'will only entertain' a deal that suits Canadians.

Carney's comments on social media come days after he told reporters that Canada is not yet in a position to agree to a U.S. trade deal and that Ottawa is looking for the right agreement for Canadians.

"We think there's deals that are in the best interests of Canada, first and foremost, but also are in the interests of the United States. That's always been the case. We've been consistent," Carney said on Wednesday.

Over the final weeks of the U.S. midterm elections, Trump and other senior American officials have suggested progress was being made. But sources told CBC News last month that Canadian government officials have been informing industry groups a deal was unlikely before Tuesday's vote.

Sources also told CBC News that trade talks have intensified in recent weeks but that the conversations did not mean an agreement was imminent.

A source familiar with the discussions told Radio-Canada that "key elements" of the discussions remain unresolved and said, "We are not on the verge of an agreement just yet."

Trump's trade war on Canada has featured heavily in U.S. midterm discussions, as Democrats seize on his tariffs to prosecute a larger argument about his care for Americans' cost of living. Some Republican candidates have defended the duties, but others are distancing themselves.

Why talks broke down last time

After a flurry of negotiations in August, Canadian and American negotiators ultimately could not come to an agreement. Both countries, and their respective officials, blamed the other side for the collapse.

In the following weeks, Carney said one of the main reasons he walked away was because Washington demanded terms that would "destroy" big Canadian industries, including auto, steel and aluminum sectors.

U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick claimed that Canadian negotiators only brought up tariff relief on medium- and heavy-duty trucks at the last minute — and further alleged the Canadians did so to kill the deal.

WATCH | Canada's chief trade negotiator on auto discussions (from August): Charette says Canada consistently raised auto industry in U.S. trade negotiations | Duration closed caption 1:08 Speaking with CBC's Catherine Cullen on Friday, Canada's chief trade negotiator Janice Charette reacted to U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's claims that Canada had only raised concerns over medium- and heavy-duty trucks at the last minute. She said while it's true that Canada brought them up on the final Friday of trade negotiations, they 'also raised them on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.'

In an interview with The House, Canada's chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, said the Canadians raised the issue on "Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday."

Carney has also said that at the last minute, the U.S. took issue with Canadian rules that ensure French-language content is easy to find on streaming platforms, such as Netflix, and that the Americans tried to restrict Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries.

Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer quickly pushed back on Canada's claims about French-language discoverability, arguing the U.S. would not jeopardize a deal over that issue.

As for restrictions on Canada's future trade deals, Greer told CBC News in August that there was no requirement in the text, but rather the U.S. sought to discuss how Canada could align its tariffs so it doesn't become a back door for steel and aluminum from other countries.

A source has previously told CBC News that the U.S. wanted Canada to apply sectoral tariffs, primarily on steel and aluminum, to its trading partners, while countries that have a free trade deal with Canada would face tariffs on imports above 2025 levels.

In his social media post on Sunday, Carney described the possible "mutually beneficial trade deal" as one that would "create jobs for our workers, boost affordability for families, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty."

World.title: Staff walk out of Winnipeg restaurant, allege disrespect and discrimination
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

More than a dozen employees walked out of a Winnipeg restaurant this week after enduring what they describe as disrespectful treatment while on the job.

Servers, managers and kitchen staff allege they had no other option after concerns of routine disrespect at the Smitty's on St. James were not addressed, but the owners of the franchise said the situation is being mischaracterized.

Former general manager Ahadullah Khojazada says he reached his breaking point on Wednesday and quit after his concerns over the treatment of staff were ignored.

Since 2024, Khojazada said at least two staff members who oversee other employees have allegedly treated staff rudely, shared feedback on mistakes publicly and disregarded company rules.

"I've lost seven to eight managers working at this place. Nevermind the amount of servers or kitchen employees that I lost. All of them had the same complaint, they are disrespected or humiliated by [two employees]," Khojazada said.

"I cannot find the peace of mind. I don't want to work in a place where I'm disrespected."

According to Smitty's, 18 employees walked off the job, but five employees who left have since returned. (Santiago Arias Orozco)

According to Smitty's, the general manager was being investigated for misconduct at the time that he quit. The restaurant said two other managers then encouraged staff to leave the restaurant, and 18 employees walked off the job.

Khojazada denies he was under investigation.

Some of the staff gathered outside the business the next day to make their concerns known.

Shayna Curle and Sheridan Tait-Reaume, who both quit on Wednesday, said they also witnessed Indigenous customers being discriminated against while they were serving at the restaurant.

Other staff would not take tables where Indigenous families were sat, Curle said, with some making comments about their ability to pay or demanding Indigenous customers pay up front.

"They don't do that to white people. It's only ever with Indigenous customers," Curle said.

As an Indigenous person herself, Curle said it was "heartbreaking" to see.

"When people come in to dine, they want to be treated respectfully," Curle said.

Tait-Reaume said she doesn't think management should be letting the disrespect slide.

"It's honestly basic human decency that they have to provide," Tait-Reaume said. "Why make a code of conduct if you're not going to respect it?"

Curle said employees were also routinely charged for customers who left without paying.

Valarie Funk, co-owner of the St. James Smitty’s location, said in a statement the situation is being mischaracterized but they are not in a position to discuss specifics publicly.

Funk said there's no policy or direction suggesting some customers should be treated differently.

"We want to be clear that we do not tolerate racism, discrimination, or harassment of any kind," Funk said. "We have always believed that a workplace where every person feels respected and accepted is not just good practice, it is the only way to operate. These values are foundational to how we run our business and how we show up in our community."

Funk said they are following up at this location to make sure the policies are being carried out as intended.

As of Sunday, Funk said five employees who left have returned to their jobs.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Argentina’s Sea Lion case could founder on Falklands sovereignty, a legal expert warns
World.content:
Argentina’s Sea Lion case could founder on Falklands sovereignty, a legal expert warns

2nd Monday, November 2026 - 00:57 UTC Full article

The expert believes Argentina will pursue every legal, diplomatic and political avenue to block the project, and suggests that Milei may also be seeking to stir national pride ahead of the elections

Argentina’s case against the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands “could fall at the first hurdle”: the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, which cannot settle territorial sovereignty disputes, according to Australian law of the sea expert Donald R. Rothwell. The tribunal will hold hearings on Argentina’s request on November 10 and 11 in Hamburg.

In an analysis published by The Interpreter, the Lowy Institute’s publication, Rothwell, professor of international law at the Australian National University, notes that under Article 286 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea the tribunal is only competent to settle disputes “concerning the interpretation or application” of the treaty. Territorial disputes have traditionally fallen to the International Court of Justice.

The problem, he argues, is that Argentina’s case cannot be separated from the underlying question. “If the UK has sovereignty over the islands, then Sea Lion is a legitimate act of exploration and exploitation of the continental shelf. If the Argentine claim over the islands is valid, then the UK’s conduct is in breach of UNCLOS,” he writes. Argentina alleges that the UK is illegally exploiting the continental shelf, that the project will cause environmental damage and that issuing licences aggravates the dispute over the maritime areas. “Absent the underlying territorial dispute, these would all be legitimate issues for ITLOS determination,” the expert says.

Rothwell compares the case with the 2016 South China Sea arbitration, in which the Philippines “neatly sidestepped” the question of sovereignty over disputed features and focused on China’s maritime claims, so there was never a need to determine who owned what. That, he warns, will not be possible in the case of the South Atlantic islands. Even so, he acknowledges that the tribunal “has generally been reluctant to take a narrow view of its jurisdiction” and recalls that, in the maritime boundary dispute between Mauritius and the Maldives around the Chagos Archipelago, it reached a full determination even though sovereignty between Mauritius and the UK was not fully resolved at the time.

The legal expert believes Argentina will pursue every legal, diplomatic and political avenue to block the project, and suggests that President Javier Milei may also be seeking to stir national pride ahead of the 2027 elections. He adds that US President Donald Trump could intervene, unhappy at the limited British support over Iran; Washington officially remains neutral in the dispute, although Trump has said that position is “under review”. “London will inevitably robustly defend its position on all fronts,” Rothwell predicts, adding that if the case proceeds it will be historic: the first time any aspect of the dispute has gone before an international court.

Sea Lion, operated by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration, lies about 200 kilometres north of the archipelago. Argentina bases its claim on succession to Spanish rights and on its occupation of the islands between 1820 and 1833, when they were taken by the United Kingdom; London cites its continuous presence since then and the islanders’ right to self-determination, confirmed in the 2013 referendum by 99.8% of voters.

World.title: Cost-of-living protests spread across Europe with unrest in France and Germany
World.content:
Cost-of-living protests spread across Europe with unrest in France and Germany

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 15:52 UTC Full article

The protests began a month ago at a high school on the outskirts of Paris over the state of schools and widened to the cost of living

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of France and Germany on Saturday to protest against the cost of living and deteriorating public services, in mostly peaceful demonstrations that ended in clashes between police and masked groups in several cities. In France, where the third day of protests in a month took place, 565 people were arrested.

According to France’s interior ministry, some 320,000 people took part in about 150 demonstrations across the country, down from an estimated 410,000 the previous weekend. In Paris, 70,000 marched along boulevards on the outskirts to avoid the city centre, some in Halloween costumes. The protests, called by students, trade unions and former members of the “yellow vest” movement, passed off calmly until the end, when masked groups hurled paving stones at police in Paris, who responded with teargas and baton charges. There were also incidents in Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, where water cannon were used. Four police officers and a gendarme were injured in the capital. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who had deployed 70,000 officers, denounced an “extraordinary” level of violence and described a petrol bomb attack on a riot officer as “attempted murder”.

The protests began a month ago at a high school on the outskirts of Paris over the state of schools and widened to the cost of living. The first major day, on October 17, ended with the looting of hundreds of shops in several cities. Students announced new blockades of high schools and universities on Tuesday and Thursday, ahead of a trade union demonstration called for November 5.

In Germany, thousands of young people demonstrated in dozens of cities at the call of the group “Gen Z regelt!” (“Gen Z has got this”) “for education, health, the climate and an affordable life”. After largely peaceful marches, police used water cannon in Cologne against protesters throwing fireworks; in Frankfurt at least two shops were looted, according to a Reuters witness, and in Hamburg burning barricades were set up, according to the newspaper Bild.

There were also clashes in Tirana, the capital of Albania, at a new protest demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Police were on alert in Barcelona, over calls from an anonymous TikTok network, and in Italy, after recent clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

World.title: Argentine intellectuals reject the Falklands “national cause” amid escalating tensions with London
World.content:
Argentine intellectuals reject the Falklands “national cause” amid escalating tensions with London

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 14:48 UTC Full article

The dissenting voices come at a time of maximum tension

Nearly a hundred Argentine intellectuals, jurists, historians and politicians have signed a declaration rejecting the transformation of the Falklands dispute into a “national cause” that “admits no dissent”, and criticising Javier Milei’s government for acting with “flagrant opportunism” amid escalating tensions with the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project.

The declaration, entitled “Malvinas and dissent” and published in early October in the newspaper Perfil, is signed by, among others, jurist Roberto Gargarella, constitutional lawyer Daniel Sabsay, former justice minister Ricardo Gil Lavedra, former minister Graciela Fernández Meijide, economist Pablo Gerchunoff, writer Santiago Kovadloff and historians Luis Alberto Romero, Hilda Sabato and Federico Lorenz.

The signatories do not deny the dispute. They accept “the existence of this international disagreement”, with its “diplomatic and legal” dimensions, and acknowledge differing views among themselves, for example on whether the islanders should take part in any negotiations. But they warn that the issue “long ago ceased to be essentially a dispute and became a supposed national cause” that “admits no relevant dissent” and brands anyone who strays from it a “bad Argentine”. “The national cause is, in short, an abuse of state, political, social and cultural authority,” they argue. They particularly criticise Article 111 of the sovereignty defence bill, which in their view established “a vague criminal offence and the criminalisation of dissent”; the government acknowledged in mid-October that it would have to be removed. “On Malvinas, this is all we ask: that unanimity stop speaking in our name,” they conclude.

One of the signatories, Alejandro Cowes, who describes himself as a lawyer, went further in a text posted on Saturday in English and Spanish in a public Facebook group about the islands.
