Cowes accuses the government of using the “sacred national cause” as “a tool for internal state coercion and domestic political consumption” and revives Argentine political scientist Carlos Escudé’s thesis of the “malignant lie”: the idea that a tough policy will raise Britain’s costs, when to do so Argentina would have to multiply its own against a power with far greater resources. He criticises the sanctions on companies linked to hydrocarbon exploitation and the purchase of F-16 fighters, and concludes that the islands are British and that their inhabitants have “the inalienable right to self-determination”, a position not reflected in the collective declaration.

The dissenting voices come at a time of maximum tension. The sovereignty defence bill secured committee approval on October 27, after sanctions were narrowed in response to US objections, and the ruling party plans to debate it in the Chamber of Deputies on November 12. Two days earlier, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will hold the hearing in Hamburg on Argentina’s request to halt Sea Lion. Milei has reiterated that “the Malvinas are Argentine”, while ruling out “military solutions”.

The claim to sovereignty over the islands is enshrined in a transitional provision of Argentina’s Constitution and enjoys broad public support, as the declaration itself acknowledges.

World.title: Democrats seek to retake Congress in Tuesday’s US midterm elections
World.content:
Democrats seek to retake Congress in Tuesday’s US midterm elections

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 14:48 UTC Full article

Trump has headlined 28 rallies during the campaign, all in Republican-leaning states, urging supporters to vote “as if I were on the ballot”

The United States holds midterm elections on Tuesday in which the Democratic Party hopes to regain control of Congress, with the polls in its favour. At stake are all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats, in a vote shaping up as a test of Donald Trump’s second presidency.

Democrats lead Republicans by 51% to 42.6% on the generic ballot, according to a polling average from surveys collected by The New York Times. Polls suggest Republicans will lose the House and do not rule out their losing the Senate as well, a possibility considered remote before the summer. The Cook Political Report has moved races towards the Democrats in recent weeks, with close Senate contests in states such as Texas, Michigan, Kansas and Iowa.

Trump has headlined 28 rallies during the campaign, all in Republican-leaning states, urging supporters to vote “as if I were on the ballot”. Early voting has passed 51 million ballots, pointing to high turnout. Elon Musk has spent at least US$267 million supporting Republican candidates, according to The New York Times.

Polls list the cost of living, the war with Iran and immigration policy among voters’ main concerns, against a backdrop of low presidential approval ratings. Congress has an approval rating of 14%, one of the lowest recorded ahead of a midterm election. A Democratic majority in either chamber would allow the opposition to block White House initiatives and open investigations into the first half of the term.

Besides Congress, Americans will elect thousands of state and local officials and vote on hundreds of ballot measures, including a proposal to tax billionaires in California and a Montana initiative to curb the influence of undisclosed money in campaigns.

World.title: From Montevideo to Luján: Leo XIV’s tour of Uruguay and Argentina
World.content:
From Montevideo to Luján: Leo XIV’s tour of Uruguay and Argentina

31st Saturday, October 2026 - 01:14 UTC Full article

“It fills me with joy to return to the continent where I have lived so many moments of my life,” wrote the pontiff, who was born in Chicago and spent almost two decades as a missionary in Peru

Pope Leo XIV will begin a tour of South America in Montevideo on November 6 that will take him to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, with open-air Masses, meetings with Presidents Yamandú Orsi and Javier Milei, and events with young people, workers and prisoners. His stop in Argentina, from November 8 to 11, will be the first papal visit to the country since John Paul II’s in April 1987.

“It fills me with joy to return to the continent where I have lived so many moments of my life,” wrote the pontiff, who was born in Chicago and spent almost two decades as a missionary in Peru. “May this journey be an opportunity to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaim the Gospel with joy.” Leo XIV, 71, is recovering from lung cancer surgery on October 13; last week he cancelled a helicopter trip to Assisi as a medical precaution, but the Vatican has announced no changes to the tour.

Uruguay, November 6-8

The Pope will leave Rome on Friday 6 and land at Carrasco airport about eight and a half hours later. That afternoon, Montevideo’s Plaza Independencia will host the official welcome ceremony; he will meet Orsi and celebrate vespers at 7.05 p.m. in the Metropolitan Cathedral.

On Saturday 7 he will fly to Paysandú, on the border with Argentina, to celebrate Mass at 10 a.m. in Parque París Londres. Back in the capital, he will visit the parish of Our Lady of Guadalupe in the Casavalle neighbourhood, meet the education community at the Catholic University of Uruguay and lead a prayer vigil at 7 p.m. at the Centenario Stadium.

On Sunday 8 he will celebrate Mass at 10.30 a.m. in the city of Florida, in front of the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, Uruguay’s patron saint, on her feast day, a coincidence that was decisive in starting the tour there. At 3.10 p.m. he will leave for Buenos Aires.

Argentina, November 8-11

The Pope will land at Aeroparque Jorge Newbery on Sunday 8 at 4.30 p.m. After paying tribute at the monument to General San Martín, he will meet Milei at the Casa Rosada and, at 6.30 p.m., address authorities, civil society and the diplomatic corps at the Palacio Libertad.

On Monday 9 he will visit the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole and celebrate Mass at 11.30 a.m. at the Monument of the Spaniards in Palermo. In the afternoon he will meet trade unionists, business leaders and social movements at the Catholic University of Argentina, work being one of the themes of his pontificate, and leaders of other faiths at the Palacio San Martín, before celebrating vespers with the bishops at the Metropolitan Cathedral.

On Tuesday 10 he will travel to Córdoba, where he will celebrate Mass at 10 a.m. at the Military Aviation School and meet clergy at the cathedral. Back in Buenos Aires, he will lead a youth vigil at 8.15 p.m. at the Monument of the Spaniards.

On Wednesday 11 he will visit the Devoto prison complex and celebrate Mass at 10 a.m. at the Basilica of Our Lady of Luján, the country’s main shrine. The farewell is scheduled for 1.30 p.m. at Ezeiza, from where he will fly to Lima.

Argentina’s government declared the visit of national interest and set three public holidays: Monday 9 nationwide, Tuesday 10 in the city of Buenos Aires and Córdoba province, and Wednesday 11 in Buenos Aires province. Francis, the first Argentine pope, never returned to his country during his pontificate.

World.title: Specialised prosecutors appeal Milei’s dismissal in the $LIBRA case and seek to reopen it
World.content:
Specialised prosecutors appeal Milei’s dismissal in the $LIBRA case and seek to reopen it

30th Friday, October 2026 - 18:21 UTC Full article

According to the prosecutors, the investigation is not exhausted

Argentina’s Office of Administrative Investigations, a specialised prosecution service for crimes committed by public officials, has appealed the dismissal of charges against President Javier Milei, his sister and presidential chief of staff Karina Milei, and nine other defendants in the case over the $LIBRA cryptocurrency, and asked for the investigation to be reopened, arguing that key evidence is still missing.

The office, headed by prosecutor Sergio Rodríguez, joined the case and took over the criminal prosecution, which had been dropped by prosecutor Eduardo Taiano when he requested the dismissals later granted by federal judge Marcelo Martínez De Giorgi. Besides seeking to reopen the case, it filed a subsidiary appeal so that, if the request is rejected, the Federal Appeals Court can review the decision.

According to the prosecutors, the investigation is not exhausted. Pending steps include tracing the funds, recovering and analysing communications, investigating possible commercial agreements and examining the money movements linked to the case. They also question that the evidence was assessed piece by piece rather than as a whole, and argue that technical difficulties or incomplete responses cannot justify closing the case. They also propose examining whether the president’s conduct could amount to the crime of conflicts of interest in the exercise of public office.

The filing responds to a request from two organisations acting in the case as friends of the court, the Centre for the Investigation and Prevention of Economic Crime and the Institute of Comparative Studies in Criminal and Social Sciences, which had criticised Taiano’s handling of the case, including his refusal to summon Milei for questioning. The decision now rests with Federal Court No. 8, temporarily headed by Judge Daniel Rafecas while Martínez De Giorgi is on leave. The investors who lost money, removed from their role as plaintiffs, have also appealed and are awaiting a ruling from the Federal Court of Criminal Cassation.

In February 2025, Milei shared the $LIBRA cryptocurrency on X; its value soared and collapsed within hours, causing losses for thousands of investors. The president deleted the post, denied promoting the project and has rejected any wrongdoing.

World.title: Hackers steal US$6.3 billion in crypto from Binance in the sector’s biggest-ever heist
World.content:
Hackers steal US$6.3 billion in crypto from Binance in the sector’s biggest-ever heist

30th Friday, October 2026 - 18:18 UTC Full article

The Secret Service, the federal agency responsible for financial crimes, said it was “working around the clock” with the private sector “to identify, freeze, trace, and recover” the funds

Hackers stole about US$6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the world’s largest digital asset exchange, in the biggest theft in the sector’s history, which the US Secret Service is investigating with other agencies. Blockchain analytics firms point to a hacking group linked to North Korea, though there has been no official attribution.

Most of the theft took place in about 20 minutes from 20:05 GMT on Thursday, from the wallets Binance uses to process transactions, according to TRM Labs. Its chief policy officer, Ari Redbord, told the BBC that such speed “is the product of long preparation”: the attackers had funded an operator wallet 36 hours earlier and prepared in advance the signatures to authorise the transfers. According to TRM, they compromised the platform’s “signing infrastructure”.

Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng said the attack “was not carried out by one person”. The initial investigation pointed to an engineer’s laptop, but “additional points of breach” were later uncovered. The attackers exploited an Ethereum network mechanism known as EIP-7702 to gain control of a wallet without passing through normal approval controls, and used a “self-destruct mechanism” to erase their traces, according to Teng, who said customer losses would be covered by the company’s protection fund, a US$1 billion bitcoin reserve, and its own resources. Binance says it has begun recovering some funds. Withdrawals remain suspended and the company expects to resume them within about 40 hours; it will publish a full proof-of-reserves report on Monday.

The Secret Service, the federal agency responsible for financial crimes, said it was “working around the clock” with the private sector “to identify, freeze, trace, and recover” the funds, in coordination with the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia. The FBI said it was “aware of the incident”.

About half of the stolen assets were stablecoins that their issuers — Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture — have frozen. TRM estimates that about US$2.4 billion in bitcoin and ether is beyond reach, as no company can block them.

TRM Labs and Chainalysis said they had “high confidence” that the culprit is TraderTraitor, also known as Lazarus, a North Korea-linked group the FBI blamed for the theft of about US$1.5 billion from the Bybit exchange in 2025, until now the sector’s largest. Chainalysis detected Binance funds commingling with those from another recent attack attributed to North Korean actors. Pyongyang routinely denies involvement in such thefts. Bitcoin fell about 4% after news of the attack.

World.title: Leo XIV becomes the first pope to vote in a US election
World.content:
Leo XIV becomes the first pope to vote in a US election

30th Friday, October 2026 - 17:17 UTC Full article

The Chicago-born pope voted “as a citizen” and as he has done “whenever he has had the opportunity”, according to a statement from the Holy See press office

Pope Leo XIV has voted by mail in the US midterm elections to be held on November 3, making him the first pontiff to take part in an election in that country, the Vatican said on Friday.

The Chicago-born pope voted “as a citizen” and as he has done “whenever he has had the opportunity”, according to a statement from the Holy See press office. “In keeping with this well-established practice of civic participation, he sent his ballot by mail to Chicago,” the statement said, without indicating whom he voted for.

Robert Francis Prevost, as he was known before his election as pope in May 2025, spent almost two decades in Peru as a missionary and later as a bishop, and holds US and Peruvian citizenship. “The Holy Father also confirmed that during his years of residence in Peru he exercised his right to vote whenever he met the requirements to do so,” the Vatican said.

Leo XIV, 71, is recovering from lung cancer surgery on October 13. He is due to begin a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on November 6, running until November 17.

World.title: Cempasúchil: The flower that reunites lovers across life and death
World.content:
I heard the legend from a very early age: Xóchitl and Huitzilin met as children. They grew up and played together for years. Over time, an infinite love blossomed between them. When they came of age, they married and lived happily.

Their union, however, was not long for this world: As a warrior and leader of their people, Huitzilin had to leave for war. Xóchitl was left alone, hoping her husband would return one day. At that moment, Xóchitl didn’t know she would never see Huitzilin again.

This is the Mexica (better known as Aztec) legend of the cempasúchil, the “flower of the dead” in Mexican folk culture.

What is the legend of the cempasúchil flower?

According to the story, a few days after Huitzilin had gone to war, a soldier knocked on Xóchitl’s door. As she welcomed him in, she realized that the man was dressed in ceremonial attire to honor the dead. Ominous news was on his tongue: Her husband had died in battle.

Devastated by grief, Xóchitl decided to climb a high mountain to beg the sun god, Tonatiuh, to let her see Huitzin again. Seeing how distressed she was by her misfortune, Tonatiuh granted her a visit with her beloved.

He turned Xóchitl into a golden-orange flower that shed light during the nights. For months, the flower-woman remained closed, until a hummingbird landed on its stem.

Feeling the bird upon her, she recognized the soft touch of Huitzilin, who had been drawn to her by her scent. Instantly, the field surrounding her blossomed with an orange glow. Thousands of similar shoots emerged from the earth, illuminating the night with a radiance no one had ever seen before. Over the years, people began to call it cempoalxóchitl, or the 20-petaled flower.

What is the cempasúchil’s pre-Hispanic symbolism?

Etymologically, cempasúchil translates to “20-petaled flower,” based on the Náhuatl cempoalxóchitl. This term is composed of cempohualli, which translates as “20,” and xóchitl, or “flower.”

In traditional Mexica narratives, the flower’s intense yellow or orange color came directly from the sun. Cempasúchil’s golden-orange glow and unique aroma were said to guide departed souls back to a ceremonial banquet for them, prepared by their living relatives.

Hence, from time immemorial, the Tagetes erecta (the scientific name for the cempasúchil flower) has been used to decorate altars of the dead in different parts of Mexico, mainly during the first two days of November.

Cempasúchil flowers in the Day of the Dead festivities

Today, this plant, native to Mesoamerica, can be found growing wild in various ecosystems in Mexico. It’s also found in Central American countries, including Panama, Honduras and El Salvador. It can grow as tall as 1 meter, and its buds can reach 5 centimeters in diameter. This extremely versatile plant easily adapts to its surroundings, flourishing in temperate oak forests or in a tropical rainforest’s humidity.

Cempasúchil production in Mexico is primarily focused on the flower’s ceremonial purposes. In late October and the first days of November, the country is covered in an orange blanket of cempasúchil as people across Mexico invoke the spirits of their loved ones during Day of the Dead festivities.

Even centuries after the tradition began, cempasúchil flowers still brighten Mexicans’ altars, lighting the way back home for the souls of the departed so that, for just one night a year, we can see our loved ones again.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Baja man protests three-week CFE outage by hosting open bar in lobby
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

LA PAZ, Baja California Sur — Demonstrating remarkable civic resourcefulness in the face of infrastructure challenges, a local resident whose electricity was cut off for three weeks converted the customer service lobby of the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) into a temporary open-bar hospitality suite on Tuesday afternoon.

Equipped with a five-speed countertop blender, a sack of limes, coarse salt and bottles of tequila and damiana, the La Paz resident plugged directly into a primary outlet behind the ticket-dispensing kiosk, offering freshly blended margaritas to fellow customers waiting in line for billing dispute resolutions.

“If the federal grid cannot deliver electricity to my freezer, I must bring my ice to the grid,” said the resident, who noted that three weeks of unanswered service tickets and unkept reconnection promises had left his home appliances thoroughly non-functional. “The administrative process takes three hours anyway. It is simply good manners to offer refreshments while we wait for ticket number 47 to be called.”

CFE staff reportedly observed the operation with a mixture of bureaucratic neutrality and procedural deliberation, noting that while utility regulations prohibit unauthorized commercial vending in public facilities, current policy contains no explicit clause regarding the non-commercial distribution of frozen cocktails in waiting areas.

The impromptu tasting station quickly stabilized lobby morale, with several citizens in line offering to supply additional ice and fresh citrus in exchange for priority access to the blender’s frozen treats. One CFE employee estimated that the protest successfully reduced perceived wait times across the branch by about 40%, despite no change in actual ticket processing speed.

Utility representatives later confirmed that while the man’s power status remains under review, official policy guidelines are currently being evaluated to determine whether guest appliance usage in administrative lobbies constitutes a billable service tier.



The not-quite-so-powerless resident, meanwhile, promised to bring the rest of his kitchen appliances the following day if his service still hadn’t been reinstated.

World.title: In Tepoztlán, the dead get one more week to celebrate
World.content:
If you’ve ever seen Disney’s “Coco,” you’ll remember Miguel Rivera had to complete his journey from the Land of the Dead to the world of the living before the afterlife closed for another year. In Mexican culture, that’s usually one day after the veil between the two planes is lifted.

But in Tepoztlán, a Pueblo Mágico with mountains resembling the world of “Avatar,” the farewell to the dead doesn’t end on Nov. 2.

The dead linger for another week — and while they do, the celebration continues.

What is ‘La Octava’?

The term “La Octava” comes from Roman liturgy. It describes an eight-day cycle in which “the believer is turned from one bound to this world into one bound to heaven.”

The Catholic Church continues to celebrate octaves, such as the Octave of Christmas (Dec. 25 to Jan. 1) and the Octave of Easter, from Easter Sunday to Divine Mercy Sunday.

In Tepoztlán, people also commonly observe an octave after a death.

“When somebody dies, we hold a rosary for eight days, until, on the last day, we officially send the dead to the underworld,” says 78-year-old Thomas Muzquiz, a Tepozteco.

Thomas connects this Catholic practice with the celebration of Day of the Dead.

“When Catholicism was introduced to Mexico, it merged with Indigenous tradition,” he explains.

Day of the Dead beautifully fuses pre-Hispanic beliefs with Catholic observance. Food offerings, copal and flower trails coexist alongside processions of saints’ images and crosses.

But when we look behind the copal smoke and past the vivid decorations, we can see that Day of the Dead in Tepoztlán and its octave is more than just a remembrance of those who have passed.

It is about continuing to work on relationships and caring for one another, welcoming the deceased with love and respect: to hang out together, eat their favorite food and have a shot or two of their favorite mezcal, while mariachis set the tone for the night.

La Octava de Tepoztlán and pondering the meaning of death

In Tepoztlán, the first calling of the dead begins at midnight on Oct. 18. Churches across Tepoztlán ring their bells to remind residents that the dead are just around the corner. On Nov. 1 and 2, families welcome their deceased loved ones with offerings and flowers.

“We put cempasúchil out because it is believed to be the only flower the dead can see and smell,” adds Anabel Muzquiz, Thomas’ daughter and a professional tour guide.

But the welcome does not end on Nov. 2. Tepoztlán accommodates its deceased for another week.

On Nov. 8 and 9, one can still experience the spirit of Day of the Dead in Tepoztlán, when residents reunite for La Octava and finally send their deceased home. Nov. 8 is dedicated to children, while Nov. 9 marks the farewell to adults.

On Nov. 9, people gather at the cemetery to clean and decorate the graves of their dead kin. A procession of saints’ images from different barrios in Tepoztlán travels to the main cemetery in the town center for Mass and remembrance.

“There’s rice pudding, fruit or green mole, mezcal and coffee — whatever they liked,” says Elena, Thomas’ wife, describing the altars renewed on Nov. 9. “The children make little skulls out of chilacayotes and ask for sweets. There are mariachis, and there’s food.”

Walking the streets of Tepoztlán, visiting the different churches in the barrios or strolling around the cemeteries on Nov. 9 is a beautiful opportunity to experience the spirit of Day of the Dead apart from the big festivities and locura of the main event.

It invites people to reflect on their extraordinary relationship with the deceased and gives them another week to ponder the meaning of death, while copal smoke and cardboard skeletons fill the surroundings with humor and a sense of playfulness.

What makes Day of the Dead so peculiar in Morelos?

Other parts of Morelos, like Tepoztlán, are known for their elaborate rituals around Day of the Dead. The Indigenous community of Coatetelco, for example, has a tradition of hanging floating altars decorated with corn.

Its observances also begin in September, when the milpa yields its first corn harvest.

In her paper, “La fiesta: recreación de la cultura y la tradición,” anthropologist Dr. María Cristina Saldaña Fernández describes the Mesoamerican worldview underlying traditions of honoring the dead, in which duality — observed in day and night, cold and heat, life and death — played a fundamental role.

She also mentions how pre-Hispanic observances honoring the dead were connected to the agricultural calendar and coincided with the harvest.

This worldview understood life and death as a continuous process, like the germination, growth, death and return of crops, which can still be observed in Coatetelco and their corn-filled altars.



‘It’s becoming diluted, becoming more like Halloween’

However, although the cycle of life and death prevails, Day of the Dead celebrations, whether in Morelos or elsewhere, are subject to change.

“I remember how people used to light bonfires on every street corner to gather around,” says Thomas, remembering Day of the Dead in Santiago Tepetlapa some 70 years ago. “Back then, the chilacayote was the best. Now you see more mass-produced plastic pumpkins and costumes. It’s becoming diluted, becoming more like Halloween. It’s a different version now. Each generation changes things in response to its surroundings.”

According to Saldaña’s paper, politics, literature, media and cinema have also shaped the celebration, adding new elements while discarding others.

But even as La Octava changes, visitors can still respectfully join the festivities and bid farewell to the dead for another year — all while sipping their favorite mezcal, joining old friends and family, and building new relationships with the living and the deceased.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: From the archive: How Mexico’s Day of the Dead helps us remember the people we’ve lost
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in October 2019 — shows us how remembering lost loved ones can be a colorful celebration of life, love and the memories that keep them with us.

Day of the Dead is by far my favorite holiday in Mexico. My first experience with it was in 2002, when I was here as a university student.

The director of my study abroad program here in Xalapa piled a few of us into his pickup truck and we drove to Naolinco, a picturesque mountain town known for its leather products.

I was immediately enchanted. Altars were all over the place — in people’s homes, in public spaces, in restaurants and stores. As we walked along the street, people invited us into their homes for tamales, bread and homemade wine.

There were carolers at the cemetery. Carolers! With guitars! The brightly colored petals and exquisite smell of cempasúchil, “marigolds,” were everywhere.

Since then, Day of the Dead has caught on north of the border as well. Even before the popular movie “Coco” came out, the southern Texas city I return home to was starting to embrace its Mexican heritage in more expansive ways than it ever had before, with altars, decorated skulls and papel picado, “colorful tissue paper with designs,” suddenly appearing alongside Halloween decorations.

Who knew that the dead could bring us together?

Each year in my home we set up our altar with the same enthusiasm with which we decorate the Christmas tree. As the years pass and more people we know and love die, we’ve had to switch to a bigger table, as our collection of dead has grown.

My grandmother is there, as is my mother. Traditionally, the flower petals are to be sprinkled from the altar to the front door so that the dead can find their way back home from the other side to enjoy the offerings laid out for them.

My grandmother, in life, would not have appreciated her place on the altar. Like many Protestants of a certain age, she was suspicious of the “magical” elements mixed in with modern Catholicism.

Day of the Dead is, of course, a mixture of Catholic and Indigenous tradition, one that the Spaniards were only partially successful at co-opting. At least they got to move the dates to the ones they wanted. (I like to think that my grandmother, now on the other side, would be totally cool with it.)

Death is a universal reality, and all cultures have different ways of dealing with it. When I was growing up in central Texas, death was taboo, something no one wanted to talk about; it was sad at best and terrifying at worst.

Halloween was a time not to think about the dead we knew, but to have fun dressing up and getting candy (and subsequent cavities). When I learned later of the history of Halloween from pagan tradition to Catholicism’s version, All Saints’ Day, I felt decidedly more creeped out.

Why should we spend any time at all thinking about death? How uncomfortable!

How to confront death

My attitude since has evolved considerably. Now that I’m an adult, death has moved closer and closer to me in the form of the passing of actual people I’ve known and loved, and in the reality and certainty of my own mortality as the years go by.

I’m hopefully still a long way from it, but none of us really knows, do we? For something that’s such a firm fact of life, we sure do avoid thinking about it a lot.

Mexicans don’t (as much), and I think there’s something to be learned from that. We can accept that we’re going to die. We can paint skulls on our faces to remind all of us that life is for the living — that we won’t be around forever, so we’d better get to it!

What does Day of the Dead do for us? It keeps the memories of our loved ones alive. It keeps this culture alive and reminds us of the people we came from. Feel guilty about not thinking enough of your loved ones that have already passed on? Don’t: remembering to do that is built into an annual holiday here.

I am not religious myself. I don’t pretend to know what happens after death, though as an agnostic I fully expect that we simply cease to exist in the way a flame from a candle goes out. As Richard Dawkins has said, we know that consciousness is wrapped up in the brain, and we know that the brain rots, so I have no illusions.

To me, this news is not too disappointing, as I’m fairly certain that, as a dead person, I would not have the consciousness to care. Disappointing would be getting to that point of not existing and not having done anything worthwhile.

That said, I do believe that there is a way to keep our dead alive, and Day of the Dead helps us to do that. Because while they might not still be around, they live on in us, and this holiday helps us remember that in an active way. The ways they shaped us, influenced us, taught us and loved us live on.

Death is sad. We don’t usually wish for it, but learning to accept it and not fear it (at least not too much) is a worthy exercise. Celebrate, remember and love your dead. Sit and chat with them a while.

Share some hot chocolate, some tamales, some pan de muerto, play their favorite music, decorate your face the way their faces look now.

Welcome them back, at least for a couple of days, and celebrate your own beating heart.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Farewell to Cárdenas, a resignation at the INE and a record-breaking Catrina
World.content:
Listen to this article

The headlines of the week in Mexico began with news of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection in Brazil, which left President Claudia Sheinbaum “very happy” and, in her words, was “a breath of fresh air” for Latin America and the Caribbean.

But at home, Mexico’s governing political movement Morena suffered another setback as the resignation of National Electoral Institute (INE) president Guadalupe Taddei raised fresh doubts about the integrity of figures tied to the government, even as Sheinbaum insisted Morena is not to blame. Meanwhile, the opposition National Action Party (PAN) announced six presumptive gubernatorial candidates for the 2027 elections.

This week also brought the death of Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, a towering figure of Mexico’s democratic transition. And as the country heads into Day of the Dead (and Formula 1 Grand Prix) weekend, Sheinbaum called on new generations to preserve the holiday’s traditions.

Didn’t have time to catch Mexico’s top stories of the week of Oct. 26? Here’s what you missed.

Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas dies at 92

Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate and the son of President Lázaro Cárdenas, died in Mexico City on Wednesday. A member of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) for more than 30 years, he left the party in 1987 and ran in 1988 as the candidate of a left-wing coalition. He is widely believed to have won that election, but Carlos Salinas de Gortari was declared the winner. Cárdenas went on to co-found the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), contested the 1994 and 2000 elections, and served as Mexico City’s first elected mayor from 1997 to 1999.

Sheinbaum called him “a man of steadfast principles,” and Thursday’s mañanera centered on a tribute to him. Asked what he leaves the Mexican left, she answered: “Honesty and democracy.” A public tribute with his coffin present was set for Friday at the Palacio de Bellas Artes. His son Lázaro Cárdenas Batel is Sheinbaum’s chief of staff.

INE president resigns; Sheinbaum weighs in

Guadalupe Taddei announced her resignation as INE president on Sunday after media outlets, including Reforma, reported that companies tied to businessman José Alfredo Hernández Casillas, with whom she reportedly has a close personal relationship, won lucrative INE contracts. She is the first head of the INE or its predecessor, the IFE, to resign since 1990. The Federal Auditor’s Office has opened an investigation, and Taddei said: “Each allegation must be examined with evidence.”

On Monday, Sheinbaum called the resignation “good” and said an audit was needed. On Tuesday, she pushed back on journalist Carlos Loret de Mola’s claim that “Taddei is Morena,” noting that the Chamber of Deputies, not the president, chose Taddei, who was picked by lottery in 2023. By Thursday, Sheinbaum went further, saying she believes Taddei “betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico.” She also said her government will propose turning the state-run printer Talleres Gráficos de México into a state-owned company to supply most electoral materials. The INE’s focus remains the June 6, 2027, elections.

IMSS workers promised 8% raise

After weeks of protests, Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) director Zoé Robledo presented a plan of 12 actions in 120 days. It includes an 8% salary increase, permanent positions for almost 11,000 temporary workers, 2,500 new specialist doctors, more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys, and a push to guarantee medicines and clear the surgical backlog. Whether it satisfies workers, and ends shortages that have outlasted earlier government efforts, remains to be seen.

Dog poisonings rattle Condesa

Poison hidden in sausage left in and around Mexico City’s centrally located Parque España killed at least three dogs Tuesday, prompting an animal cruelty investigation. The toll later reached four. Attorney General Bertha Alcalde Luján said tests found methomyl, a highly toxic insecticide, in capsules placed inside the meat, and authorities recovered 14 suspect pieces.

On Friday, police arrested a 58-year-old man, identified as Salvador “N,” a block from the park after he resembled a person in images circulating on social media. He was detained for resisting arrest, and prosecutors cautioned that they had not yet established whether he was responsible. Residents are avoiding the park, and Cuauhtémoc borough Mayor Alessandra Rojo de la Vega urged pet owners not to let animals eat anything off the ground.

Guadalajara water plan and allegations of torture

On Wednesday, Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus announced a “historic agreement” with the federal government to invest 25 billion pesos (US $1.33 billion) in Guadalajara’s water infrastructure. The plan centers on two new aqueducts, from Lake Chapala and from the Calderón Reservoir, due by the end of 2028. The federal government will contribute 14.5 billion pesos and Jalisco 10.2 billion, and Lemus promised no new debt, privatization or rate increases. The announcement followed large protests demanding clean tap water.

The Oct. 11 protest in particular remains contentious. Two women, among around 10 people who have filed complaints with the Federal Attorney General’s Office, allege they were tortured by Jalisco state police. At least 39 people were arrested and dozens hurt. Lemus has conceded “serious mistakes” were made, Security Minister Juan Pablo Hernández denied ordering force and Sheinbaum has repeatedly denounced the alleged torture.

Citizen scientists make their mark

In Michoacán, residents who spotted unusual marks in a streambed led researchers to at least 50 dinosaur footprints near Apatzingán. The National Institute of Anthropology and History believes the Late Cretaceous tracks were left by three types of dinosaurs and says further study is needed to pin down species.

In Tabasco, residents of Barra de Santa Ana are working to restore coastal dunes. A 30-member community brigade trained by Eni Mexico and UNESCO will replant vegetation and install sand catchers. Erosion has hit 85% of the 30-kilometer coastline between Boca de Santa Ana and Boca de Panteones, and up to 3.5 meters of shoreline are lost each year.

Sheinbaum moves to keep Mexico’s masterpieces at home

Following the Gelman Collection controversy, Sheinbaum plans to strengthen the Monuments Law to prohibit the permanent export of privately owned works declared artistic or historical monuments. A preliminary draft was published Oct. 15. The change would reconcile the law with 10 presidential decrees protecting works by artists including Diego Rivera, Frida Kahlo and David Alfaro Siqueiros. The timing matters, as the Supreme Court is set to hear a challenge to the 1984 Kahlo decree.

Day of the Dead highlights

Mexico City’s cempasúchil production hit a record 10 million plants, up 53.8% from last year, grown mainly on Xochimilco’s chinampas.

The capital unveiled the world’s tallest Catrina in the Zócalo. At 33.4 meters, the papier-mâché figure tops Puerto Vallarta’s 2023 record holder and is the city’s fifth Guinness record this year. The offering is on display through Nov. 3.

At Friday’s mañanera, held amid marigolds and Catrina figures, Sheinbaum described the Mexican view of “death as part of life” and said the holiday has “recovered” from Halloween’s influence, partly thanks to films like “Coco.”

Economy: Exports surge, growth slows and India talks begin

Mexico’s economy grew 0.9% in the third quarter from the previous quarter, down from 1.4% but above the 0.7% economists expected. Year over year, growth of 3.2% was the largest in 12 quarters, helped by a weak third quarter in 2025.

Exports, meanwhile, reached US $77.79 billion in September, up 37.9% and the third-highest monthly total on record. Over the first nine months, exports rose 30.4% to $627.19 billion, driven by computer and electronic equipment sold to the United States amid an AI data center boom. Mexico posted a $9.25 billion trade surplus, but its oil deficit of $25.68 billion already exceeds the 2025 total.

On the trade front, Mexico and India signed terms of reference on Monday for negotiations on a preferential trade agreement. Merchandise trade between the two totaled $8.74 billion in 2024, and a Mexican business mission to India is under discussion for early 2027.

Charlyn Corral makes history at the Ballon d’Or

Pachuca forward Charlyn Corral, 35, won the Gerd Müller trophy for Best Striker of the Year at Monday’s Ballon d’Or ceremony, becoming the first Mexican woman to earn the distinction. She scored 49 goals in 49 matches for club and country and shared the honor with Harry Kane.

In her acceptance speech, she also asked the audience to recognize compatriot Scarlett Camberos, who was among the 30 nominees for the main award.

Looking ahead

Whether Jalisco’s 25 billion-peso water plan will be enough to keep Guadalajara’s streets calm is an open question. The two aqueducts are not due until the end of 2028, work “could” start next year, and the Oct. 11 allegations of police abuse remain under investigation, so residents may be left with promises rather than clean tap water for some time. On trade, Sheinbaum agreed with Donald Trump that a deal with the United States is “very close”, and on Wednesday she said talks were advancing as both sides weigh whether an interim agreement is possible before U.S. midterm elections next Tuesday, Reuters reported. Mexico is still seeking a “significant reduction” in U.S. tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, while Washington is pressing concerns over automotive content and Chinese investment.

Even a pre-election deal would leave questions for the next Congress, according to an opinion piece in The Hill by Duncan Wood and Ivan Zapien. They argue that a change in control of Congress would not end U.S. pressure on Mexico over trade, migration and security, but a Democratic House could summon officials, scrutinize the USMCA talks and push for tougher labor and environmental enforcement, while Republicans keep pressing on energy and China. Either way, they write, Mexico should expect to answer to more of Washington, more often, after the U.S. declined in July to extend the USMCA for another 16 years.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Why I’m grateful my son is getting the Halloween-Día de Muertos experience I never had
World.content:
The funny thing about growing up in California with Mexican immigrant parents is that you are perpetually intimate with, and distant from, your Mexican roots. Every holiday season, therefore, becomes a delightfully unique interpretation of both cultures mashed together.

Tamales wrapped in banana leaves and filled with turkey for Thanksgiving? Opening gifts at midnight for Noche Buena, and then again on Christmas morning? Getting your face smashed into a birthday cake?

These are all welcome in my life as a Mexican-American who must constantly toggle between my two identities on both soils.

Sometimes, though, one cultural norm or ideology can overtake the other, leaving one half egregiously overlooked, if not completely erased. For me, that has always been the case with Día de Muertos.

Halloween was the festive U.S. tradition my household embraced in its most suburbanized form: dressing up as Ninja Turtles, trick-or-treating with pumpkin-shaped buckets, and devouring pounds of Jolly Ranchers, fun-sized Snickers and M&Ms for weeks after.

I’ve never been the king of spooky season, but I’ve also never avoided it. As I grew older and met my wife, our family Halloween tradition became dressing up in custom-made outfits that reflected our personalities or the region we lived: two high school teachers dressed as our favorite punctuation marks; two Boston post-grads dressed as the local subway trains. (Spoiler: this year we are dressing up as Chedraui employees.)

And yet, despite traveling to Mexico regularly throughout my life, and having immigrant parents who spoke Spanish and were connected to their roots in Veracruz in different ways, I don’t have any real Día de Muertos memories from my childhood.

Finding the tradition

It wasn’t until the 2010s that I recall the concept entering mainstream culture in California and elsewhere beyond Mexico. For my wife and me — both as a couple, but also in our respective Mexican-American upbringings throughout the 1990s and 2000s — we never experienced our parents or family members building altars in our California homes. Not until maybe around Pixar’s “Coco” (2017), that is.

That tradition has quickly spread. Within the past decade, it has become more commonplace to see altares, ofrendas and Día de Muertos-themed households worldwide. Of course, it existed long before “Coco,” but it wasn’t as ubiquitous as it is today.

When my son was born in 2023, my wife and I had already spent significant time in Mexico, including traveling to Oaxaca for a month during Día de Muertos season and fully immersing ourselves in its wondrous spirit of parades, parties and gravesite visits.

We had learned, while exploring Mexico’s vast regional scenes and lodging with family members in various states across the span of multiple summers, about the importance of Día de Muertos as a form of intimate ancestral remembrance. In contrast to the candy-collecting rampage we’d always known the end of October to be, we’ve been able to incorporate those important elements of Día de Muertos into our lives — and in our son’s understanding of this time of the year.

Now, having fully transplanted our lives to Veracruz, we get to experience the best of both worlds as a young family: the playful, goofy costumery and decorations of Halloween, combined with the artisanal charms and spiritual connectivity of Día de Muertos.

I wouldn’t have it any other way.

Building core memories

Undoubtedly, our son’s autumnal memories will be completely different than ours: Instead of knocking on doors in a cul-de-sac with a group of neighborhood kids, he’s going to a field of cempasúchiles in a mountainous pueblo to get his photo taken on a horse that is whimsically painted like a calavera. Instead of visiting the pumpkin patch and riding a train through cornstalks and bales of hay, his abuela and bisabuelo are coming over to our house to eat pan de muerto and build a collective family altar with photos of family members that he, or even I, will never meet.

Each has their own joys and core-memory-building functions, and I enjoy them both. I hope he does, too.

It’s true that our current community doesn’t offer much traditional Halloween vibes, in the Americanized sense. You may see a decorative witch or black cat dangling from a window, here and there. Earlier this week, I walked past a large inflatable ghost on someone’s balcony, but it was awkwardly angled to avoid the mess of wires that complicate our narrow, colonial streets.

It’s just a different atmosphere in these smaller Mexican cities and towns, and the sidewalks don’t really allow for large groups of children to roam around without parents losing their minds over incessant traffic safety.

Trick-or-treating vs. Día de Muertos parades

In 2024, we flew to Mexico City for Halloween and Día de Muertos. It was noticeably different from our experience in Veracruz. A local group of parents organized families online for a neighborhood walk, with designated homes that had registered in advance, so we knew who would be giving out candy.

Similarly, we went to a mercado in Mexico City that weekend for a “calaverita” — a Mexican version of trick-or-treating, where kids dress up and go stall to stall asking for treats.

In those instances, my son, wife and I got to experience some of that old-school Americana by walking around Mexico City with strangers — some, but not all of them, international — and knocking on doors (or wandering shop aisles) together. That version of Halloween offers a communal, neighborly bonding that isn’t always seen during other holidays, which more often than not take place inside homes with close family members, rather than out in public and in the streets. We certainly could use more of it.

Then, there’s the other side of it all: attending a Día de Muertos parade and being part of a collective throng of spectators, while ceremoniously dressed performers and various forms of alebrijes dance, flutter and chant around you. (It’s worth noting that Día de Muertos parades, like the one in Mexico’s capital, are relatively new traditions in many areas; they weren’t commonplace when I was growing up, but are a part of Día de Muertos’ increasing popularity.)

I’m glad my son will get to be immersed in those cultural experiences in ways my wife and I weren’t for Halloween.

Fusing traditions in an ever-connected world

Having access to those dual experiences is a life hack, really. That’s not to say that Halloween has never existed in Mexico, or that Día de Muertos is nonexistent in California. In each case, the cultural traditions are becoming more fused than ever before, largely thanks to social media, travel access and other global factors.

You no longer have to be in Oaxaca’s Centro to experience Día de Muertos, nor do you have to reside in a U.S. suburb to appreciate Halloween. Depending on where you are, you may not be able to fully replicate the magic of the other — but you learn to salvage whatever aspects you can.

By being in Mexico, we are reminded that we will always have generous access to, and understanding of, both celebratory worlds. That’s ultimately the beauty of being a Mexican-American binational family, no matter the seasonal holiday or time of year.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Nigeria Business Activity Eases to 55.7
World.content:
File photo of farmland below a rocky hill in Taraba State, north-east Nigeria. Harvest-season farms like this are where bandits have struck in several states.

NIGERIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts What happened The Stanbic IBTC Bank Nigeria PMI fell to 55.7 in October from 56.4 in September.

The meaning Any reading above 50 means business conditions improved; this is the ninth straight month.

The catch Fuel costs pushed input prices to a four-month high, and hiring slowed.

Nigeria’s private sector kept growing in October 2026, but a little more slowly than in September, according to the monthly survey released on Monday 2 November 2026. The Stanbic IBTC Bank Nigeria PMI, a survey of purchasing managers at Nigerian firms in agriculture, manufacturing, services and wholesale and retail, slipped to 55.7 from 56.4.

For US readers, the number is a fast read on Africa’s most populous country, a market that sells oil and Eurobonds to American investors. A reading this far above 50 says demand is strong, while the rise in fuel-driven costs says inflation has not gone away.

Our earlier report on the September reading, a four-year high, shows where the index came from.

What Happened

The Stanbic IBTC Bank Nigeria PMI fell 0.7 points to 55.7 in October 2026, against 56.4 in September. The survey is compiled by S&P Global, a financial data company, for Stanbic IBTC, a Lagos-based bank and part of Africa’s Standard Bank Group.

A PMI, or purchasing managers’ index, asks company buyers whether orders, output, hiring and prices are higher or lower than a month earlier. A reading above 50.0 means conditions improved, and one below 50.0 means they worsened.

The release says new orders grew sharply for a ninth month in a row, only slightly more slowly than in September. Output also rose sharply in all four monitored sectors, a little less than in September.

What Drove the Reading

Firms told the survey that stronger customer demand and the launch of new products lifted new business. They also expect demand to keep improving, helped by planned advertising and business investment, although confidence eased slightly from September.

Employment rose only slightly, the slowest pace in three months. Agriculture and manufacturing added staff, while wholesale and retail and services cut jobs, and payrolls have grown every month since June 2025.

Companies kept buying inputs to meet orders and future projects, and supplier delivery times shortened for a fourth month. Backlogs of unfinished work fell for a third month, and by the most since January, which suggests firms are clearing orders faster.

The Trend in Recent Months

The index stood at 52.5 in July, 54.3 in August, 56.4 in September and 55.7 in October. September’s reading was the strongest in more than four years, so October’s dip is a step back from a peak rather than a break in the trend.

Business conditions have now improved for nine months in a row. The October figure is still well above the 54.0 recorded in October 2025.

The Price Problem

Input prices rose sharply, reaching a four-month high, and higher fuel costs were the main reason. Costs for transport, building materials and food also went up, while staff costs rose modestly.

Selling prices also rose at their fastest pace in four months. The increase was still weaker than the jump earlier this year after war broke out in the Middle East, according to the release.

What It Means for You

If you hold Nigerian Eurobonds, dollar bonds issued by the government, a strong PMI supports growth and tax revenue, while price pressure is one factor the central bank weighs on further interest rate cuts. A steady economy usually helps the naira, the local currency, but this survey does not measure the exchange rate, so treat it as one input and not a forecast.

US exporters selling machinery, food and equipment to Nigeria face a market where demand for inputs is rising, which is positive for orders. In our analysis, higher fuel costs can help Nigeria’s oil income when crude is expensive, but they raise costs for the businesses in this survey, which is why activity and inflation are moving up together.

Stanbic IBTC’s own commentary forecasts Nigerian growth of 4.27% in 2026 and 4.65% in 2027, after 4.16% in the first half of 2026. Those are the bank’s projections, not official statistics.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether October’s dip is a pause or the start of a slower trend, because one month cannot settle that. The survey also does not say how much of the rise in prices will carry into the official inflation figures for October.

Two things would change the picture: a fall in fuel prices would ease cost pressure and support activity, while a new jump in fuel costs would squeeze margins and could slow orders. The November survey, due in early December, will show which way it is going.

More: Nigeria news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is the Stanbic IBTC Bank Nigeria PMI?

It is a monthly survey of purchasing managers at Nigerian firms, compiled by S&P Global for Stanbic IBTC Bank. A reading above 50 means business conditions improved.

What Was the October 2026 Reading?

The index was 55.7, down from 56.4 in September. It was the ninth straight month above 50.

Why Did Prices Rise in October?

Higher fuel costs were the main driver, with transport, building materials and food also costing more. Input and selling prices both rose at four-month highs.

World.title: Maduro Long-Sentence Odds Climb to 39%
World.content:
Federal court buildings in Lower Manhattan, where Maduro’s case is pending. File photo.

Prediction Markets: Venezuela

Key Facts Prediction markets. Polymarket, a trading platform, 2 Nov, 4:25 a.m. ET: 60+ year sentence 39%, up 18 points in 7 days.

Context. No single trigger was reported. His judge died on 28 October; the new judge kept the schedule.

Thin market. About US$36,000 traded in 24 hours, US$1.03 million overall.

Next. Hearing on his head-of-state immunity claim 17 December 2026; jury trial 14 June 2027.

Traders now see a very long prison term for Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela’s ousted president, as more likely than a week ago. No new ruling explains it.

Bettors on Polymarket, a platform where users trade real money on outcomes, now give 39% to a sentence of 60 years or more for Maduro. A week earlier that outcome stood at about 21%.

For US readers, the price is a live read on how traders rate a case in a Manhattan federal court. It is a bet, not a forecast, and it says nothing about guilt: Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have pleaded not guilty.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket runs a market called “Maduro Prison Time?” It asks how long a sentence Maduro receives, if any. Prices at 4:25 a.m. ET on 2 November 2026:

60 years or more: 39.0%, up 3.5 points in 24 hours and 18 points in 7 days

39.0%, up 3.5 points in 24 hours and 18 points in 7 days No prison time: 42.0%, down 0.5 points in 24 hours and 11.5 points in 7 days

42.0%, down 0.5 points in 24 hours and 11.5 points in 7 days Under 20 years: 9.4%

9.4% 20 to 40 years: 6.0%

6.0% 40 to 60 years: 5.1%

The market has traded about US$1.03 million since it opened, but only about US$36,000 in the last 24 hours. It is thinly traded, so a few large bets can move the prices. We found no matching market on Kalshi, the exchange regulated in the US by the CFTC (the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal derivatives regulator).

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Why the Odds Moved

No single trigger was reported for the latest jump. Daily snapshots show the 60-year-plus price flat at about 21% from 26 to 29 October, then 28.5% on 30 October, 32% on 31 October and 39% today.

The only case news in that window is a change of judge. Alvin Hellerstein, the 92-year-old federal judge who handled the case, died on Wednesday 28 October. The case was reassigned the same day to Analisa Torres, a judge in Manhattan since 2013.

On Thursday 29 October, Torres ordered that all earlier decisions and deadlines stay in place. That keeps a hearing on 17 December 2026, where the court is due to hear the defence request that Maduro has sovereign immunity, meaning a head of state cannot be prosecuted by a foreign court. The jury trial stays set for 14 June 2027.

We earlier reported the other side of this market, when “no prison time” fell to 43% after the judge died. See our report on the 29 October move.

What the Charges Are

Maduro and Flores were flown to New York after a US military raid in Venezuela on 3 January 2026. They face charges that include conspiracy to commit narcoterrorism, conspiracy to import cocaine, weapons offences and, since an expanded indictment, conspiracy to commit torture. If convicted, Maduro could face a life sentence.

Both pleaded not guilty. Their lawyers argue that Maduro, as a head of state, is immune from prosecution, and the court has not ruled on that argument.

What It Means for US Readers

The case tests whether a US court can try a foreign leader who was seized by US forces. The immunity ruling is the first big legal test, and the judge has not decided it.

Traders still rate “no prison time” slightly ahead, at 42%, but the gap has narrowed fast. Only a court can decide, and the market stays open until 2028. Read more on our Venezuela page, in our latest Venezuela border report, and in the Latin America odds hub.

What Is Not Known

It is not known what drove the latest move. Nor is it known whether Torres will rule on immunity before the trial, or whether the 14 June 2027 date will hold.

A conviction would also not fix a sentence: a judge sets it later, and the market resolves only after that. The thin 24-hour volume means the price can reverse quickly. See all markets on our Prediction Markets hub.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do prediction markets say about Maduro’s sentence?

Polymarket gives a sentence of 60 years or more 39% and “no prison time” 42% at 4:25 a.m. ET on 2 November 2026. These are bets by traders, not a forecast by The Rio Times.

Why did the odds of a long sentence rise?

No single trigger was reported. The market moved after the death of the case’s judge on 28 October, but no new ruling or evidence explains the latest jump.

When is Maduro’s trial?

The jury trial is set for 14 June 2027 in Manhattan. A hearing on his sovereign immunity claim is set for 17 December 2026.

Who is the new judge?

Analisa Torres, a federal judge in Manhattan since 2013. She was assigned the case on 28 October 2026 after Judge Alvin Hellerstein died.

Does the market mean Maduro is guilty?

No. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have pleaded not guilty and are presumed innocent unless a court convicts them.

Sources: US District Court for the Southern District of New York (nysd.uscourts.gov) reassignment and scheduling orders of 28 and 29 October 2026; Polymarket and Kalshi public market data (read 2 November 2026, 4:25 a.m. ET). Prediction market prices are bets, not polls.

World.title: Grenada in Latin America, Role and Alliances
World.content:
GRENADA · LATIN AMERICA ROLE

Key Facts What it is Grenada is a Caribbean island state that sits inside Latin American and Caribbean diplomacy through CARICOM, CELAC and the OAS.

Why it matters A tiny state holds a full vote in several hemispheric bodies and keeps ties with Venezuela, Cuba, China and the United States at once.

The numbers About 117,400 people (Worldometer, October 2026) and nominal GDP of about US$1.42 billion in 2025 (Macrotrends).

The catch Citizenship by investment revenue fell from 14.7% of GDP in 2024 to 3.5% in 2025, according to the IMF.

What it means for you Expect a stable, tourism-led economy with an election on 5 November 2026, so check who holds office before you act.

The Grenada continent question has a short answer: Grenada is a Caribbean island state that belongs to Latin American and Caribbean bodies, yet we found no record of it in South American trade blocs. Its weight is small in numbers, but it holds a full vote in CARICOM, CELAC and the OAS.

Grenada is a Caribbean island nation of about 117,400 people as of October 2026. This guide explains where it fits in Latin America, which groups it joins, who its partners are and how it compares with its neighbours.

The regional agriculture institute CARDI at its test field in Barbados. File photo, 2010. Photo: CaribDigita, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Where Grenada Sits: Geography, Politics and Identity

Geographically, Grenada belongs to the Caribbean and not to the South American mainland. In diplomacy it is counted inside the wider Latin America and Caribbean region, which is why it takes part in groups such as the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC).

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Venezuela ranks 13th of 14 with 27.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (81); weakest: economic relationships (0). Alignment group: Closer to Beijing. Some pillar data are incomplete for Venezuela; see the index notes. WatchSovereign in selective default; inflation of 252%; public debt at 309% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Its head of state is the Governor-General, Dame Cécile La Grenade, who has held the post since 7 May 2013, according to Wikipedia and CARICOM. Its head of government is Prime Minister Dickon Mitchell of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), sworn in on 24 June 2022.

The NDC won nine of 15 seats in 2022, against six for the New National Party (NNP). Foreign policy sits with Joseph Andall, Minister for Foreign Affairs, Trade and Export Development.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Andall has said Grenada wants closer ties with Africa and with South and Central America. That fits a small country that spreads its partnerships widely, because it cannot rely on the weight of any single bloc.

The Numbers That Matter

Grenada had about 117,400 people in October 2026, a modelled estimate from Worldometer rather than an official count. The last full census confirmed in our research was in 2011, and the Central Statistical Office published parish counts in August 2024.

Nominal output was about US$1.42 billion in 2025, up 5.1%, according to the Macrotrends data aggregator. That places Grenada among the smallest economies in the hemisphere, although this guide did not compile a full ranking.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimated real growth of 4.4% for 2025, driven by investment and construction. We could not confirm a 2026 growth projection.

Indicator Value Owner and period Population 117,362 (modelled) Worldometers, mid-2026 Nominal GDP US$1.42 billion, up 5.1% Macrotrends, 2025 Real GDP growth 4.4% IMF estimate, 2025 Inflation, end-period 0.3% IMF, 2025 Primary deficit 3.2% of GDP IMF, 2025 Citizenship by investment revenue 14.7% of GDP, then 3.5% IMF, 2024 and 2025 Stayover tourist arrivals 54,565, up 12% Caribbean Tourism Organization, Q1 2026

The IMF says the fiscal rule was suspended for post-hurricane reconstruction. It expects a primary-balance floor of 1.5% of GDP to return from 2027, with a debt target of 60% of GDP by 2033.

Grenada has no national central bank and uses the Eastern Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB). The ECCB Monetary Council reappointed Governor Dr Timothy N. J. Antoine to a third five-year term from 1 February 2026.

The Malecón seafront in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, a larger Caribbean neighbour. Photo: -wuppertaler, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Regional Bodies: CARICOM, CELAC and the OAS

CARICOM and the Eastern Caribbean

Grenada is a member of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM), its main regional home. The 50th Heads of Government meeting ran from 24 to 27 February 2026, and the 51st from 5 to 8 July 2026.

Philip J. Pierre, Prime Minister of Saint Lucia, has chaired CARICOM since 1 July 2026. In July 2026 leaders, Grenada included, said third-country arrangements with the United States would be for transit, not settlement, according to the Gleaner.

Foreign-relations summaries also list Grenada in the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States, the Commonwealth and the Caribbean Development Bank. These memberships give it far more day-to-day influence than any Latin American bloc does.

CELAC

Grenada is a member of CELAC, a forum of Latin American and Caribbean states. Colombia’s Gustavo Petro handed the rotating presidency to Uruguay’s Yamandú Orsi at the X Summit in Bogotá on 21 March 2026, according to Colombia’s foreign ministry.

An emergency CELAC meeting on 4 January 2026, called over the US operation in Venezuela, ended without a joint declaration, according to Searchlight. The sources we read do not state Grenada’s position at that meeting.

CELAC is a door to Europe as well as to its neighbours for countries like Grenada.

The OAS, Mercosur, the Andean Community and SICA

Grenada is a member of the Organization of American States (OAS). Its 56th General Assembly met in Panama City from 22 to 24 June 2026, amid regional tensions over Nicaragua, Bolivia, Cuba and Venezuela.

We found no Grenadian statement from that assembly. We also found no record of Grenadian membership or association with Mercosur, the Andean Community or the Central American Integration System (SICA), which is an absence of evidence rather than a verified negative.

Alliances: Venezuela, ALBA, Cuba and China

Venezuela

Diplomatic relations with Venezuela date from 1977. Mitchell and Andall visited Caracas in April 2025 and signed a cooperation roadmap, according to Prensa Latina.

The United States seized Nicolás Maduro in early January 2026, and Delcy Rodríguez is now Acting President. In the days after the US operation, Mitchell said the events in Venezuela were “pushing the region into more instability”.

He added that “diplomacy, dialogue, negotiation and compromise are the only means” to resolve differences. Rodríguez later visited Grenada in April 2026, with talks on energy, agriculture, education and trade, according to Caribbean National Weekly.

ALBA, Cuba and China

Grenada joined ALBA, the alliance tied to Venezuela and Cuba, as a full member in December 2014. Venezuelan help has included PetroCaribe oil financing, a housing project and hospital rebuilding, but we did not check whether its ALBA status has changed.

Reporting from May 2019 put the PetroCaribe debt at EC$372.1 million, or 11.5% of GDP, according to Ministry of Finance figures. We could not confirm a current figure or any restructuring.

Cuba and Grenada established relations in 1979 and resumed them in 1994, according to a secondary source. Cuba, the United States, Venezuela and China all have embassies in Grenada.

Grenada switched recognition from Taiwan to the People’s Republic of China in 2005, though some sources say 2004, in exchange for aid including a cricket stadium. In January 2025 it affirmed the one-China principle, according to the Canada Caribbean Institute.

The skyline of Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, with the Caribbean Sea beyond. Photo: Jose Juan C, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Disputes and the Relationship with Washington

We found no active territorial dispute involving Grenada. Its public disagreements in the research concern policy rather than borders.

Grenada first rejected a US request to accept non-nationals for deportation, according to Caribbean National Weekly. On 30 January 2026 it signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding on possible transfers.

As reported, Grenada may accept or reject each case at its sole discretion, and Mitchell said Washington must pay all costs, including direct flights. We could not read the memorandum itself, so these details rest on press summaries.

Citizenship by investment (CBI) lets foreigners obtain citizenship through a qualifying contribution or property purchase. The IMF lists disruption to CBI and foreign direct investment among Grenada’s downside risks.

A US proclamation of 16 December 2025 placed partial visa restrictions on Antigua and Barbuda and on Dominica, and Grenada was not listed, according to the migration site Immigrant Invest. That comes from an industry source, so check the US State Department before relying on it.

How Grenada Compares with Its Peers

The closest peers are Dominica, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Antigua and Barbuda. We did not compile a full comparison of their output or debt, so this guide does not rank them.

The one sourced contrast is the US visa treatment above, where Antigua and Barbuda and Dominica faced restrictions and Grenada did not. The shared currency is a common thread, since Antigua and Barbuda’s Prime Minister Gordon Browne chaired the ECCB Monetary Council meeting reported on 14 February 2026.

Tourism is Grenada’s visible strength, with 54,565 stayover arrivals in the first quarter of 2026, up 12% on the first quarter of 2025, according to the Caribbean Tourism Organization via Caribbean Journal. Cruise figures from two reports could not be reconciled, so we do not cite them.

What It Means for Foreigners, and What to Watch

For investors and expats

The IMF lists tourism and import dependency, natural disasters, and disruption to CBI and foreign investment as downside risks. Low inflation and steady growth are the other side of the ledger.

Agent websites quote a National Transformation Fund contribution of US$235,000 for a family of up to four, and a real estate route from US$270,000 held for at least five years. These figures come from law-firm and agent sites, so check the official fee schedule before applying.

Mitchell attended the World Governments Summit in Dubai on 3 to 5 February 2026 and made an official visit to Qatar on 13 to 19 August 2026. Together with visa-waiver agreements with several African countries, this shows a government courting partners well beyond the hemisphere.

What to watch

Grenada votes on 5 November 2026 for 15 seats, and a party needs eight to govern. Mitchell called the vote almost a year before the October 2027 constitutional deadline, and 46 candidates are running.

Emmalin Pierre leads the NNP and is the first woman to take it into a general election, while Keith Mitchell is not standing after 42 years in Parliament. The NNP platform, Better Grenada, promises to cut corporate tax from 28% to 25%, and Peter David’s Democratic People’s Movement contests nine seats.

The only poll we found was a self-selected online survey, which is not representative and is no forecast. The result was unknown when this guide was written, so check who holds the foreign affairs portfolio afterwards.

Other markers include the CARICOM mid-year meeting, normally held in February, and the national budget, usually presented in the first quarter. We did not verify either date for 2027, so confirm them on official sites.

Related reading: Saint Lucia in Latin America Explained 2026; Moving to Antigua and Barbuda 2026, Step by Step; Moving to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines 2026, Step by Step; more from Caribbean.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Grenada part of Latin America?

Grenada is a Caribbean island nation, not part of the South American mainland. It takes part in Latin American and Caribbean diplomacy as a member of CELAC, the OAS and CARICOM. We found no record of membership in Mercosur, the Andean Community or SICA.

How big is Grenada’s population and economy?

Grenada has about 117,400 people as of October 2026, a modelled Worldometer estimate. Its nominal GDP was about US$1.42 billion in 2025, according to Macrotrends, and the IMF estimated real growth of 4.4% for that year.

Is Grenada a member of ALBA?

Grenada joined ALBA as a full member in December 2014. We did not check whether that status has changed, so confirm it before relying on it.

Will Grenada accept third-country deportees from the United States?

On 30 January 2026 Grenada signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding on possible transfers. As reported, it may accept or reject each case at its sole discretion, and Prime Minister Dickon Mitchell said the US must pay all costs.

Does Grenada recognise China or Taiwan?

Grenada switched recognition from Taiwan to the People’s Republic of China in 2005, though some sources say 2004. In January 2025 it affirmed the one-China principle, according to the Canada Caribbean Institute.

Who runs Grenada’s foreign policy in 2026?

Prime Minister Dickon Mitchell leads the government, and Joseph Andall is Minister for Foreign Affairs, Trade and Export Development. Both are incumbents in a caretaker period, because Grenada votes on 5 November 2026.

World.title: Saint Lucia in Latin America Explained 2026
World.content:
SAINT LUCIA · LATIN AMERICA ROLE

Key Facts What it is Saint Lucia is a small Caribbean state that reaches Latin America mainly through CARICOM, CELAC and the OAS.

Why it matters Prime Minister Philip J. Pierre has chaired CARICOM since 1 July 2026, and the island hosted its leaders on 5 to 8 July 2026.

The numbers The 2022 census counted 172,948 people, and the IMF projects growth of 2.0% for 2026.

The catch The region is split on Venezuela and Cuba, and the UK began requiring visas for Saint Lucians on 5 March 2026.

What it means for you Expect an open, tourism-led economy with its own diplomatic line, so check entry rules and regional politics before you invest or travel.

The Saint Lucia continent question has a short answer: the island is a Caribbean state that shapes Latin American diplomacy through CARICOM, not through the big South American blocs. In 2026 it holds the CARICOM chair, which gives a country of 172,948 people a louder voice than its size suggests.

Saint Lucia is a small parliamentary state whose Labour government was re-elected in December 2025. This guide explains its weight, its memberships, its alliances and its disputes, and what they mean for visitors and investors.

Ambergris Caye in Belize, on the western Caribbean rim. File photo, 2008. Photo: Asteiner, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Where Saint Lucia Sits in the Latin American Picture

Saint Lucia belongs to CARICOM, the Caribbean Community, a regional bloc whose leaders meet as a Conference of Heads of Government. Its foreign ministry lists CARICOM, the OECS (the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States) and CELAC as its regional integration pillars.

CELAC is the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, a political forum for governments on both sides of that divide. It has no common market, so its value lies in meetings, joint statements and the chance to sit beside much larger neighbours.

The research behind this guide found no evidence that Saint Lucia belongs to, or is associated with, Mercosur, the Andean Community or SICA. That is a finding of absence rather than a confirmed fact, so a reader who needs certainty should ask the foreign ministry.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.
