Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

The island also takes part in the Organization of American States (OAS), the hemisphere’s main political forum. This guide found no official 2026 source on Saint Lucia’s OAS work, and it names no representative for that reason.

The Numbers That Give Saint Lucia Its Weight

The 2022 census, published by the Central Statistical Office, counted 172,948 people, up from 166,526 in 2010. The census report is provisional, and average household size fell from 2.8 to 2.6 over the same period.

Indicator Figure Owner and period Population 172,948 Central Statistical Office, 2022 census (provisional) Population estimate About 0.183 million IMF country page, estimate Real growth 4.7% IMF Article IV, 2024 Projected growth 1.7% IMF Article IV, 2025 projection Projected inflation 0.8% IMF Article IV, 2025 projection Projected growth and inflation 2.0% and 2.5% IMF country page, 2026 projection IMF quota 21.4 million SDR IMF, as of 2026 Stopover visitors 228,091, up 2.5% Saint Lucia Tourism Authority, January to June 2026

An SDR is a special drawing right, the IMF’s own unit of account. Saint Lucia joined the fund on 15 November 1979, and its outstanding IMF purchases and loans stood at 19.26 million SDR on 31 March 2026.

The IMF Executive Board concluded the 2025 Article IV consultation, a routine health check of the economy, on 12 January 2026. It described a highly open economy driven by tourism and imports, and it recorded three consecutive primary surpluses.

This guide leaves out nominal GDP and the debt-to-GDP ratio, because the sources reviewed did not confirm them from primary data. The VON Radio outlet, reporting on regional statements, put public debt across the Eastern Caribbean Currency Union at 79.0% of GDP in 2025, down from 88.2% in 2020.

The regional agriculture institute CARDI at its test field in Barbados. File photo, 2010. Photo: CaribDigita, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

CARICOM and the OECS, the Home Base

Prime Minister Philip J. Pierre took the six-month rotating CARICOM chair on 1 July 2026. He succeeded Dr Terrance Drew of St Kitts and Nevis, and the chair is due to end on 31 December 2026.

Saint Lucia hosted the 51st Regular Meeting of CARICOM Heads of Government in Gros Islet from 5 to 8 July 2026, at Sandals Grande. The government’s agenda covered security, climate finance, food security, the Single Market, enlargement, foreign relations and reparations.

The Village Voice reported tensions before the meeting. It said the bloc was split over Cuba, that Trinidad and Tobago was absent from a statement condemning US measures, and that Trinidad and Tobago’s Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar doubted a second term for Secretary-General Dr Carla Barnett.

Secondary reports say leaders agreed to send aid to Cuba and to form a three-member committee on US ties. This guide could not find the official communiqué, so those points should be checked on the CARICOM website.

The OECS and the regional bank

Pierre hosted OECS Heads of Government in Saint Lucia on 13 January 2026 to discuss urgent regional and geopolitical matters, according to the Saint Lucia Star. The OECS gives the smaller islands a way to settle a common line before they meet the larger CARICOM members.

The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB) is led by Dr Timothy N. J. Antoine, a Grenadian economist. Its Monetary Council reappointed him for a third five-year term from 1 February 2026 to 2031, announced after its meeting on 13 February 2026.

CELAC and the OAS, Talking to the Larger Neighbours

Pierre and External Affairs Minister Alva Baptiste attended the eighth CELAC summit in St Vincent and the Grenadines in 2024. The Prime Minister’s office says he spoke there on behalf of Saint Lucia.

The tenth summit took place in Bogotá on 21 March 2026, according to the Colombian Foreign Ministry. Uruguay took over the pro tempore presidency, the rotating chair that organises the bloc’s work, and this guide could not confirm who represented Saint Lucia.

A CELAC emergency meeting on the US action in Venezuela ended without consensus, according to a Searchlight headline dated 9 January 2026. That outcome shows the limit of the forum, since a bloc of such different governments finds it hard to agree on force and sovereignty.

The Malecón seafront in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, a larger Caribbean neighbour. Photo: -wuppertaler, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Alliances and Disputes

Venezuela and the Lima Group

In 2021 Caribbean News Global reported that Baptiste announced Saint Lucia’s exit from the Lima Group, a bloc of governments critical of Caracas. The same report said Pierre pledged closer ties with Venezuela and a policy of non-interference.

The Bureau of the Conference of CARICOM Heads of Government, made up of Jamaica, Saint Kitts and Nevis and Saint Lucia, met on Saturday 3 January 2026 after US military action in Venezuela and issued its statement that day. It reiterated a call for peaceful dialogue through diplomatic channels.

This guide found no separate Saint Lucian government statement on the capture itself. Its line therefore appears to follow the CARICOM position, though that is an inference and not a declared policy.

Taiwan

Saint Lucia keeps diplomatic relations with Taiwan, which sets it apart from most of Latin America and makes it one of the few remaining Caribbean allies of Taipei. A Taiwanese naval training squadron of three ships and about 840 personnel visited Castries from 12 to 14 April 2026, the first such visit in 21 years.

Baptiste spoke at the visit, as did Taiwan’s ambassador, H.E. Nicole Su. The government described the visit as a reaffirmation of friendship, while the research found no comment from Beijing.

The United States, the UK and Peer Islands

A December 2025 US proclamation imposed visa restrictions from 1 January 2026 on Antigua and Barbuda and Dominica, citing their citizenship-by-investment programmes. Saint Lucia was not on that list, though the Saint Lucia Times reported that the island was told to move fast to avoid the same fate.

IMI Daily reported rising US visa denials for Saint Lucians, a claim this guide could not check against official data. Both outlets are secondary sources, so the trend should be read with care.

The United Kingdom imposed a visa requirement on Saint Lucians from 5 March 2026, with a transition period to 16 April 2026. The Home Office letter is dated 4 March 2026 and cited migration and border pressure and rising asylum claims.

The Government of Saint Lucia published a response to the decision. Reports say the Home Office also classed the citizenship-by-investment programme as high risk, a point the government has had to address.

This guide did not retrieve comparable GDP, debt or population data for Grenada, Dominica, St Vincent, St Kitts and Nevis or Antigua and Barbuda. A fair peer table needs IMF World Economic Outlook and ECCB figures, so none is offered here.

Politics, Tourism and the 2026 State of Play

Pierre’s Saint Lucia Labour Party won 14 of 17 House seats on 1 December 2025, according to Searchlight. It was the first consecutive re-election of a governing party since 2001, and Allen Chastanet of the United Workers Party leads the opposition after holding Micoud South.

Tourism is the economy’s main external link, and the 2026 data are mixed. Stopover arrivals reached 228,091 from January to June 2026, up 2.5% on 222,464 a year earlier, according to the Saint Lucia Tourism Authority.

April 2026 set a record for April stopovers, up 8.5% year on year, with Canadian visitors up 45.9% for the month. European stopover arrivals fell 15.9% to 22,073 in the first quarter, which CaribJournal called the Caribbean’s largest European drop.

June 2026 was slightly softer, with 33,340 stopovers against 33,646 in June 2025, a fall of 0.9%. This guide found no July to September data, and the IMF page says the authorities were still reviewing whether to publish the Article IV report.

What It Means for Foreigners and What to Watch

For travellers, the biggest change of 2026 is the UK visa rule, which affects Saint Lucians more than visitors to the island. Anyone planning business with Saint Lucian partners should check current entry rules in the UK, the US and elsewhere, because this guide could not confirm official fees or schedules.

For investors, the picture is a small, open, tourism-led economy with a stable government and a clear regional role. The risks are its exposure to visitor numbers, its high public debt as described in regional reporting, and scrutiny of citizenship-by-investment programmes.

Three dates are worth noting. Saint Lucia’s CARICOM chair ends on 31 December 2026, and the Caribbean Tourism Organization is due to hold its first Latin American Market Summit on the island on 5 and 6 May 2027, according to the Caribbean National Weekly.

CARICOM Heads of Government have normally met in late February or early March, but this guide could not confirm the 2027 date or host. It also found no confirmed dates for CELAC, OECS or ECCB meetings between November 2026 and April 2027.

Related reading: Moving to Antigua and Barbuda 2026, Step by Step; Moving to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines 2026, Step by Step; Who Runs Cuba in 2026? Raúl Castro and the US Murder Charge; more from Caribbean.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Saint Lucia part of Latin America?

Saint Lucia is a Caribbean state that takes part in Latin American diplomacy through CARICOM, CELAC and the OAS. This research found no evidence of membership in Mercosur, the Andean Community or SICA.

How many people live in Saint Lucia?

The 2022 census, published by the Central Statistical Office, counted 172,948 people, up from 166,526 in 2010. The census is provisional, and the IMF page uses an estimate of about 0.183 million.

Who leads Saint Lucia’s foreign policy in 2026?

Prime Minister Philip J. Pierre leads the government, and Alva Baptiste is Minister for External Affairs, International Trade, Civil Aviation and Diaspora Affairs. Pierre has also chaired CARICOM since 1 July 2026.

Does Saint Lucia recognise Taiwan?

Yes, Saint Lucia keeps relations with Taiwan. A Taiwanese naval squadron of three ships and about 840 personnel visited Castries from 12 to 14 April 2026, the first such visit in 21 years.

Do Saint Lucians need a visa for the UK?

Yes, the UK imposed a visa requirement from 5 March 2026, with a transition period to 16 April 2026. The Home Office cited migration and border pressure and rising asylum claims.

How is the Saint Lucian economy doing?

The IMF recorded growth of 4.7% in 2024 and projected 1.7% for 2025 and 2.0% for 2026. Stopover arrivals rose 2.5% to 228,091 from January to June 2026, according to the Saint Lucia Tourism Authority.

World.title: Cape Verde Neighbours in West Africa Explained 2026
World.content:
CAPE VERDE · WEST AFRICA

Key Facts What it is Cape Verde is an island state with no land borders, so its neighbours are sea neighbours, chiefly Senegal, Mauritania and Guinea-Bissau.

Why it matters Cape Verde has belonged to the regional bloc ECOWAS since 1977, yet its money and markets point north to Europe.

The numbers Europe took 95.4% of exports in 2025 (INE, the national statistics institute), and ECOWAS supplied about 5% of imports in one reported quarter.

The catch The planned Dakar to Praia sea link is targeted for the end of 2026.

What it means for you Treat Cape Verde as a Europe-facing economy with a West African political home, and check entry rules and sea-link news before planning regional trips.

Cape Verde neighbours are close on the map but modest in the ledger. This guide explains who they are, how the relationships work and where the island nation leads or follows.

Cape Verde is an Atlantic archipelago off the West African coast, with a population of 491,233 at the 2021 census. We cover borders, regional bodies, trade, migration, sea links and security, with figures dated as of 2 November 2026.

A freight train and travellers loading goods at Choum, northern Mauritania. File photo. Photo: Ben Kawam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

An Island Nation With Only Sea Neighbours

Cape Verde has no land borders, so its neighbours are reached by water or air. There are also no shared rivers, which removes the dam and basin disputes common elsewhere in West Africa.

The “shared infrastructure” story is therefore about ships, flights and maritime boundaries. Those links are thin today, and governments are still trying to strengthen them.

The sea boundaries are settled on paper. Cape Verde signed a delimitation treaty with Senegal on 17 February 1993, and it also has a treaty with Mauritania that includes a tripoint with Senegal.

The research reviewed found no documented dispute between Cape Verde and any neighbour. The date and text of the Mauritania treaty could not be confirmed, so we do not describe its terms.

ECOWAS: The Regional Home

ECOWAS, the Economic Community of West African States, is the main regional body. Cape Verde joined in 1977, and it is a party to the bloc’s free-movement protocol, according to a secondary source.

Senegal now holds both top ECOWAS posts. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye was elected chair of the Authority on 19 July 2026 at the 69th Ordinary Session in Sierra Leone, succeeding Julius Maada Bio.

General Birame Diop, a former Senegalese armed forces minister, was named Commission president for 2026 to 2030, succeeding Dr Omar Alieu Touray. He was due to take office in September 2026, though we could not confirm that he has started.

What Cape Verde Hosts and Pays

In January 2025 ECOWAS and Cape Verde’s ambassador, Belarmino Monteiro Silva, discussed the Community Levy, the 2026 elections and regional security. They also covered the ECOWAS Early Warning Centre in Praia and a pilot phase of a Praia, Dakar and Banjul sea link.

We could not read the communiqué of the July 2026 summit. We therefore cannot say what it decided about Cape Verde.

Aerial view of Nouakchott, Mauritania's capital, with a palm grove at the centre. File photo, 2017. Photo: Laminesall96, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Senegal: The Closest Partner

Senegal is the neighbour with the deepest ties. A Senegalese community lives in Cape Verde, and a Cape Verdean community lives in Senegal.

President José Maria Neves and President Faye met in Dakar on 16 July 2025, according to Le Soleil, a Senegalese daily. They stressed historical ties and shared political stability, and pledged to strengthen ECOWAS.

Le Soleil described the two countries as “two bastions of stability” for the bloc. Faye also attended the celebrations of Cape Verde’s 50th independence anniversary.

The two leaders announced the reactivation of a joint committee on the Dakar to Praia sea line, per Senego, a Senegalese news site. Cape Verde’s government changed in June 2026, and we found no reporting yet on its own stance towards Dakar.

Guinea-Bissau: The Sensitive Neighbour

Cape Verde and Guinea-Bissau share the liberation legacy of Amílcar Cabral. That history makes Bissau politics a delicate subject in Praia.

A coup on 26 November 2025 led ECOWAS, the African Union and the CPLP (the Community of Portuguese-Speaking Countries) to suspend Guinea-Bissau. We could not confirm a current date for elections there.

RTP, the Portuguese public broadcaster, reported that Neves said Cape Verde stayed out of direct mediation for historical reasons and preferred to work through ECOWAS. That article is undated and may refer to an earlier crisis, so it should not be read as a comment on the 2025 coup.

Guinea-Bissau is also the largest source of foreign residents in Cape Verde. That adds a human link to the political one.

Trade and Sea Links: Europe First

Trade with West Africa is marginal next to Europe. This is the key point for any investor weighing a Cape Verde base for regional business.

Measure Figure Source and period Exports 9.386 billion CVE, up 18.2% from 7.940 billion CVE INE via Inforpress, 2025 against 2024 Share of exports to Europe 95.4% (Spain alone 63.0%) INE via Inforpress, 2025 Imports 199.961 billion CVE, up 5.0% from 190.447 billion CVE INE via Inforpress, 2025 against 2024 Imports from ECOWAS 1.3 billion CVE (about €12m), up 43.1%, roughly 5% of 25.4 billion CVE Forbes África Lusófona, one quarter labelled Q1 2026, year unverified

In that same quarter Portugal supplied about 50% of imports, or 12.6 billion CVE, and the eurozone 68.1%.Sea links are the hoped-for fix.The Alkebulan Comimex group launched a private Dakar, Banjul and Praia freight line in October 2025, and its ship Djilor carried cement from Senegal and basalt from Cape Verde, according to Lusa, the Portuguese news agency.A separate ECOWAS Dakar to Praia link is targeted to start by the end of 2026.

People on the Move

The 2021 census counted 10,875 foreign residents, or 2.2% of 491,233 people, according to INE figures reported by Forbes África Lusófona. Guinea-Bissau accounted for about a third of foreign residents.

The same article suggests the Guinea-Bissau total could be near 10,000 once undocumented people are counted, but that estimate is unconfirmed.Every foreign visitor must pre-register on the EASE portal at ease.gov.cv, which is free, according to the 4sToGo travel site quoting official guidance.International flights carry an Airport Security Tax of 3,400 CVE (about €30.83), with exemptions for children under two and some other travellers.Entry rules have been changing, and secondary sources mention visa changes for some nationalities that we could not verify.

Check the immigration authority before you travel.

Where Cape Verde Leads and Follows

On security, Cape Verde is described by the US Africa Command and the Institute for Security Studies as unusually determined against cocaine smuggling. A US-funded Counter-Narcotics and Maritime Security Operations Center, which cost about $1.5m, supports that work.

We have no 2026 seizure statistics, so the record cannot be measured here. The Early Warning Centre in Praia adds a regional role in monitoring tensions.

On politics, the 17 May 2026 legislative election gave the PAICV party 37 of 72 seats on 48.04% of the vote, against 33 seats for the MpD party on 44.75%, per IPU Parline. Turnout was 46.46%, and the change of government followed peacefully.

As an editorial judgement, not a sourced finding, Cape Verde leads on stability and follows on trade volume. The World Bank reported GDP growth of 6.3% in 2025 and forecasts 4.8% for 2026, but also public debt of 100.7% of GDP in 2025.

What It Means for Foreigners and What to Watch

For investors, Cape Verde is a Europe-facing market with a West African political home. The ECOWAS trade share is small, so regional growth plans should be treated as ambition rather than present fact.

The government is led by Prime Minister and Finance Minister Francisco Carvalho. Manuel Augusto Lima Amante da Rosa holds the foreign affairs, communities and defence portfolio, according to Forbes África Lusófona.

The presidential election is set for 15 November 2026, and the Constitutional Court admitted five candidates on 21 September. They include Neves, who is seeking re-election, and Joana Gomes Rosa Amado of the MpD; a runoff would be needed if no one wins a majority, but we could not confirm its date.

Also watch the end-2026 target for the Dakar to Praia sea link. The new government’s programme may show its ECOWAS priorities.

Related reading: Benin Neighbours in West Africa Explained 2026; Mali and Its Neighbours in the Sahel Explained 2026; Idrissa Gueye Explained 2026: From Everton to Saudi Club Diriyah; more from Africa.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which countries are Cape Verde’s neighbours?

Cape Verde has no land borders, so its neighbours are sea neighbours, chiefly Senegal, Mauritania and Guinea-Bissau. It has maritime delimitation treaties with Senegal, signed on 17 February 1993, and with Mauritania.

Is Cape Verde a member of ECOWAS?

Yes, Cape Verde joined ECOWAS in 1977.

Does Cape Verde trade much with West Africa?

Not much. In 2025 Europe took 95.4% of exports according to INE, and ECOWAS supplied about 5% of imports in one reported quarter.

Is there a ferry between Cape Verde and Senegal?

A private freight line between Dakar, Banjul and Praia launched in October 2025. An ECOWAS Dakar to Praia link is targeted for the end of 2026.

Which foreigners live in Cape Verde?

The 2021 census counted 10,875 foreign residents, or 2.2% of the population. Guinea-Bissau was the largest group.

When is Cape Verde’s next presidential election?

The vote is set for 15 November 2026. The Constitutional Court admitted five candidates, and a runoff would be needed if no one wins a majority.

World.title: Benin Neighbours in West Africa Explained 2026
World.content:
BENIN · NEIGHBOURS

Key Facts What it is Benin is a coastal West African state whose port, roads and pipeline link it to Nigeria, Niger, Burkina Faso and Togo.

Why it matters The Port of Cotonou generates 45–50% of Benin’s fiscal revenue, according to La Nouvelle Tribune in October 2026.

The numbers The port handled 14.7 million tonnes in 2025, up 52% from 9.6 million tonnes in 2024.

The catch Niger’s side of the Malanville–Gaya border has been closed since the July 2023 coup, and no reopening was found through about August 2026.

What it means for you Cargo, travel and security conditions in Benin depend heavily on decisions taken in Abuja, Niamey, Ouagadougou and Lomé.

Benin neighbours include Nigeria, Niger, Burkina Faso and Togo, and each relationship shapes the country’s trade, security and politics. Nigeria is the largest partner, while Niger is the hardest to manage.

Benin is a coastal country whose port serves landlocked states to the north. This guide explains who its neighbours are, how trade, rivers and security tie them together, and what to watch.

Town hall of Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso's second city. File photo, 2013. Photo: Maarten van der Bent, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

A Small Country in a Crowded Neighbourhood

Benin is small, but it has a large job as a doorway to the sea. Its Port of Cotonou serves Benin’s own economy and also trucks heading inland to its northern neighbours.

The president is Romuald Wadagni, a former finance minister who won the 12 April 2026 election with more than 94% of the vote, according to election officials. He was sworn in on 24 May 2026 in Cotonou and succeeded Patrice Talon, who served from 2016 to 2026.

Foreign policy sits with Foreign Minister Corinne Amori Brunet, a former ambassador to France.Nigeria is the largest neighbour, and Niger is the most difficult.

Burkina Faso and Togo are partners on transport and security, and all four decide how freely goods, fuel and people move.

How the Present Pattern Formed

The turning point came on 26 July 2023, when a coup in Niger led to the closure of its border with Benin. Niger accused Benin of hosting French military infrastructure and jihadist bases, and Benin denied this.

The key crossing runs from Malanville in Benin to Gaya in Niger, over a bridge on the Niger River. According to Global Voices, Benin reopened its side in late February 2024, but Niger never opened the Gaya side.

A second shock came on 7 December 2025, when soldiers seized state television and announced Talon’s removal. At Benin’s request, Nigerian President Bola Tinubu sent Air Force jets and ground troops, according to Al Jazeera and Nairametrics.

The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), the regional bloc, then deployed standby-force personnel, according to Anadolu. Coverage described this as a first for Benin as a recipient of ECOWAS military support.

Sunrise at the Inata gold mine in northern Burkina Faso. File photo. Photo: darrylkeith, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Numbers That Matter

Most of Benin’s regional weight comes from its port and from the trade that crosses its borders. The table gathers the main figures, each with its owner and period.

Measure Figure Owner and period Port of Cotonou traffic 14.7 million tonnes, up from 9.6 million La Nouvelle Tribune, 2025 versus 2024 Transit share of port traffic 39.2% La Nouvelle Tribune, 2025 Port share of fiscal revenue 45–50% La Nouvelle Tribune, October 2026 Benin GDP growth forecast 7.0% for 2026 IMF, as reported by The Rio Times, 18 October 2026 WAEMU economic growth 6.7% in 2025, 6.4% projected for 2026 BCEAO

The port handled 14.7 million tonnes in 2025, up 52% from 9.6 million tonnes in 2024, according to La Nouvelle Tribune. Transit cargo made up 39.2% of that traffic.

Burkina Faso has become the leading transit partner, with nearly one million tonnes since 2025, mostly hydrocarbons, according to Benin Web TV. Niger’s traditional transit has declined, and oil keeps that link alive.

Lomé, Abidjan, Tema and Lagos all compete with Cotonou for the same cargo, according to AllAfrica in April 2025. Ecofin projects 16–16.5 million tonnes for 2026, and the port’s current stated target is 25 million tonnes a year, according to Le Matinal in October 2026.

Niger: The Hard Border and the Oil Pipeline

The border talks

On 2 June 2026 Wadagni met Niger’s head of state, General Abdourahamane Tiani, in Niamey. It was their first high-level meeting since the July 2023 coup, and the agenda covered security, the Malanville border, the pipeline and diplomatic relations.

The presidents created an expert committee with a 15-day deadline and agreed to relaunch their bilateral joint commission, according to Le Matinal. A joint communiqué on 16 June 2026 said the committees had finished a first cycle of work.

Benin Web TV reported that the committees concluded work in Cotonou on 21 June 2026, with no reopening date announced. No evidence of a reopening was found through about August 2026, so the border should be treated as closed on Niger’s side unless confirmed otherwise.

Before the closure, the Niamey-Route customs post handled heavy truck traffic, according to Ecofin on 5 June 2026. Exports to Niger included semi-milled rice, oilcake and raw sugar.

The pipeline that still links them

The crude pipeline runs from the Agadem field in Niger to the Sèmè-Kpodji terminal in Benin. It is described as 1,980 km long and is operated by China National Petroleum Corp. (CNPC), with exports starting in 2024.

Niger halted the pipeline in June 2024 amid the Niger–Benin border dispute, and on 19 August 2024 Benin’s Energy Minister Samou Adambi said loading of crude had started that morning. The line sits within a $4.6bn CNPC investment in Niger’s oil sector, and revenue repays a $400m oil-for-cash loan, according to Daba Finance.

Nigeria, Burkina Faso and Togo

Wadagni’s first official trip abroad was a visit to Abuja on 1 June 2026, where he met Tinubu, and it was the first stop of a regional tour that took him on to Ouagadougou, Niamey, Lomé and Abidjan and ended on 4 June. They discussed trade, energy, maritime security, cross-border crime and ECOWAS, and no major agreements were announced.

That visit built on a joint trade framework signed in August 2025 to remove cross-border barriers, according to Channels TV. The Seme-Krake Joint Border Post, on the coastal road to Lagos, opened in October 2018, according to ECOWAS.

Nigeria also helped route trade around the closed Niger border. On 9 February 2026 it reopened the Tsamiya–Kamba corridor in Kebbi State, closed since 2019, which lets trucks travel from Ségbana in Benin to Sabon Birni in Niger, according to AllAfrica.

In Ouagadougou on 2 June, Wadagni met Captain Ibrahim Traoré, and both stressed cooperation against terrorism and cross-border crime. According to Sidwaya, they called the Port of Cotonou strategic for Burkina Faso’s supplies and promised to speed up the fifth session of their Joint Cooperation Commission.

In Lomé on 3 June, Wadagni met Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, President of the Council in Togo. According to Koaci, they discussed trade, transport, cross-border security and defence.

Shared Roads, Rivers and Parks

The Abidjan–Lagos Corridor is a planned 1,028 km six-lane highway through Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria. AllAfrica reports a cost of about $16bn.

The Corridor Management Authority was launched on 25 June 2026.Sources disagree on when the road will operate, giving either 2030 or 2033.

Readers planning around it should check the ECOWAS highway site.The Nangbeto Dam on the Mono River is a joint Benin–Togo hydro project dating from 1987.

A Mono River Basin Authority was set up in 2014, and a basin master plan was reported on 29 June 2026, though dam releases can worsen floods.The W–Arly–Pendjari complex is a UNESCO World Heritage site shared by Benin, Burkina Faso and Niger, covering 1,714,831 ha in total.

African Parks has managed Pendjari since 2017, along with Benin’s part of W, while armed-group incursions since 2017 threaten the area, according to UNESCO.

Regional Bodies, Money and Security

Bridge between two blocs

Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have left ECOWAS and formed the Alliance of Sahel States, and relations between the blocs remain strained. Wadagni affirms Benin’s commitment to ECOWAS while seeking a rapprochement with the Sahel alliance, according to WAVN and Ecofin.

ECOWAS elected Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye as chair on 19 July 2026 at its 69th summit in Lungi, Sierra Leone. General Birame Diop of Senegal was named Commission president for 2026–2030, effective 1 September 2026.

Benin also shares the CFA franc and the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU) with Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Togo and Côte d’Ivoire. The regional central bank, the BCEAO, led by Governor Jean-Claude Kassi Brou, has kept its main rate at 3.00% since 16 March 2026.

The northern frontier

The government admitted that 54 soldiers were killed in an April 2025 attack claimed by JNIM, an Al-Qaeda-linked group, according to MyJoyOnline. Africanews reported that 15 soldiers died in the Kofouno attack of 4–5 March 2026.

ACLED data cited by AllAfrica shows attacks in the Benin–Niger–Nigeria triangle rose 86% from 2024 to 2025. Togo, Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana signed the Lomé Declaration on 4 July 2025, covering security and refugee protection.

What It Means for Foreigners and What to Watch

Visitors apply for entry through evisa.bj, the official portal run by the Direction de l’Emigration et de l’Immigration. The portal says yellow-fever vaccination documents are checked at entry points.

Shippers and investors should treat the Niger route as uncertain, and plan for transit through Nigeria or alternative ports. Anyone travelling in the far north should read their own government’s travel advice first, given the attacks described above.

The clearest signal to watch is whether Niger reopens the Gaya side of the border, and on what security terms. Also watch the new ECOWAS Commission under Diop and the new Abidjan–Lagos management authority.

The BCEAO’s Monetary Policy Committee met in March, June and September 2026, so a December meeting would fit the pattern. No date has been confirmed.

Related reading: Mali and Its Neighbours in the Sahel Explained 2026; Idrissa Gueye Explained 2026: From Everton to Saudi Club Diriyah; Central African Republic Explained, a Fragile Peace in 2026; more from Africa.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which countries are Benin’s neighbours?

Benin’s neighbours are Nigeria, Niger, Burkina Faso and Togo, the four countries President Wadagni visited in June 2026. Nigeria is the largest, and Niger is the most difficult.

Is the Benin–Niger border open?

Niger closed the border after its coup on 26 July 2023, and no reopening was found through about August 2026. Expert committees reported to both presidents in June 2026, but no reopening date was announced.

Why is the Port of Cotonou important to Benin’s neighbours?

It is a sea outlet for landlocked countries, and transit made up 39.2% of its 2025 traffic, according to La Nouvelle Tribune. Burkina Faso is now the leading transit partner, with nearly one million tonnes since 2025.

Is Benin still in ECOWAS?

Yes, and President Wadagni affirms Benin’s commitment to the bloc. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have left ECOWAS, and Benin seeks closer ties with them as well.

Who leads Benin and ECOWAS in 2026?

Romuald Wadagni has been Benin’s president since 24 May 2026. Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye became ECOWAS chair on 19 July 2026, and General Birame Diop leads the Commission from 1 September 2026.

Does Benin share a currency with its neighbours?

Benin uses the CFA franc with Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Togo and Côte d’Ivoire inside WAEMU. The BCEAO has held its main policy rate at 3.00% since 16 March 2026.

World.title: Bolivia Trade Surplus Passes US$2.2B
World.content:
Office towers in central La Paz, Bolivia. File photo: EEJCC / Wikimedia Commons, CC0. It does not show trade activity.

BOLIVIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts Power Index Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 28.4 points (October 2026 edition).

What is happening Bolivia’s exports beat its imports by US$2.24 billion in January to September, the INE says.

Why it matters Metal sales are earning the US dollars a cash-short Bolivia needs, and exports already top all of 2025.

The numbers Exports were US$10.35 billion and imports US$8.11 billion, with silver, gold and zinc leading.

What to watch Whether exports reach the US$13.65 billion record of 2022 by December, which needs US$3.30 billion more.

Bolivia has sold US$2.24 billion more abroad than it has bought this year, and its exports have already passed the whole of 2025. The gains come from silver, gold and zinc, and they follow 53 days of road blockades.

Bolivia ran a trade surplus of US$2,236.5 million in the first nine months of 2026, according to Bolivia’s INE, the national statistics institute. Exports reached US$10,350.2 million and imports US$8,113.7 million.

The figure matters to US readers because Bolivia, a landlocked Andean country, has been short of dollars. Silver, gold and zinc exports are one of its few reliable sources of them, as our report on the September surplus showed.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

In Plain English

A trade surplus means a country earned more from exports than it spent on imports. Bolivia’s gap is now large enough to matter for its dollar supply.

Exports Already Beat Last Year

Exports through September were about US$650 million, or 6.7%, above the roughly US$9.7 billion Bolivia sold in all of 2025. Exports in all of 2025 were US$9,702.1 million by the INE-based count, so nine months have beaten twelve.

Silver, gold and zinc led the gain, the INE data show.

A Recovery After the Blockades

The gains came despite 53 days of road blockades in May and June. Blockades shut highways and disrupted transport and supply chains across the country.

The surplus stood at US$1.67 billion at the end of June and US$1.92 billion at the end of July. September alone added US$183.4 million.

The Record Is Still Out of Reach

Bolivia’s export record is US$13.65 billion, set in 2022. The country needs another US$3,302.8 million in the last three months of the year to beat it.

That would take monthly exports of about US$1.10 billion. Exports averaged about US$1.15 billion a month so far this year, so the record is within reach but not secured.

What It Means for You

Investors in Bolivian bonds and mining companies get a better dollar picture than a year ago, because export earnings are rising. The wider economy is still weak, so a surplus does not mean a boom.

Travellers can read the Rio Times guide to La Paz for local context. More is on the Bolivia hub, and Bolivia Power Explained, Who Dominates in 2026 shows who holds power.

What Is Not Known

We did not find a breakdown of exports by destination in the figures we reviewed, so the share going to the United States is unknown. Nor is it clear how much of the mineral gain comes from higher prices and how much from higher volumes.

Whether exports can keep this pace in the last quarter depends on prices for silver, gold and zinc, and on whether the blockades return.

Frequently Asked Questions

How large is Bolivia’s trade surplus in 2026?

Bolivia ran a surplus of US$2,236.5 million from January to September 2026, the INE says. Exports were US$10,350.2 million and imports US$8,113.7 million.

What is Bolivia selling abroad?

Silver, gold and zinc led the export gains, the INE data show. Bolivia is a landlocked Andean country that depends on minerals and farm goods.

Have Bolivia’s exports passed last year’s total?

Yes, exports to September beat the US$9,702.1 million of all 2025 by about US$650 million, or 6.7%. The all-time record is US$13.65 billion, set in 2022.

Why does a trade surplus matter to Bolivia?

Bolivia has struggled with a shortage of US dollars. Export earnings are one way the country brings in hard currency.

Sources: Bolivia’s National Statistics Institute (INE), January to September 2026 foreign-trade data, published at the end of October 2026.

World.title: Mali and Its Neighbours in the Sahel Explained 2026
World.content:
MALI · SAHEL NEIGHBOURS

Key Facts What it is Mali’s relations with Burkina Faso, Niger, Algeria, Senegal, Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Mauritania and the regional bodies around them.

Why it matters Bamako is the capital of the Alliance of Sahel States, which Mali formed with Burkina Faso and Niger before leaving ECOWAS in January 2025.

The numbers The Dakar–Bamako railway is 1,286 km long, and UNHCR counted about 14,402 refugees identified in Mauritania’s Hodh Chargui region since the current influx began on 24 October 2025, according to its 21 May 2026 update.

The catch The al-Qaeda-linked group JNIM has blockaded fuel routes since 3 September 2025, and the blockade was reimposed in late April 2026.

What it means for you Visitors need a visa in advance, and the US State Department rates Mali Level 4, Do Not Travel.

Mali neighbours shape almost everything in the country, from the fuel in its tanks to the alliances of its generals. This guide explains who Mali’s partners and rivals are, how the links work, and what could change.

Mali is a Sahel state governed by a military-led transition and surrounded by countries that supply its ports, its trade routes and some of its threats. We cover the alliance it leads, the bodies it left, each key neighbour, and what it all means for foreigners.

How Mali Fits Into Its Neighbourhood

Mali depends on roads and rails through other countries to reach the sea. According to press reports, about 95% of its fuel arrives by road, much of it from Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire and Guinea.

Power sits with General Assimi Goïta, the transition president, whose mandate was extended by a revised Transition Charter that he promulgated on 8 July 2025. The Prime Minister is General Abdoulaye Maïga, in post since 21 November 2024, and Abdoulaye Diop is foreign minister.

Goïta took the defence portfolio himself after General Sadio Camara was killed in an attack on his home in Kati on 25 April 2026, as Al Jazeera reported.The political frame matters for neighbours.Al Jazeera reported in July 2025 that the revised Transition Charter gave Goïta a five-year presidential mandate, renewable, without an election, and no national vote is scheduled as of November 2026.

The Alliance of Sahel States: Where Mali Leads

The Alliance of Sahel States (AES) groups Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all governed by military leaders. Its roots lie in the Liptako-Gourma charter signed in Bamako on 16 September 2023.

The three governments signed a confederation treaty in Niamey on 6 July 2024 and left the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in January 2025. At the Bamako summit of 23 to 25 December 2025, Burkina Faso’s Captain Ibrahim Traoré took the rotating chair from Goïta for one year.

Africanews reported that the summit inaugurated an AES television channel and the BCID-AES bank. The AES investment bank, BCID-AES, was activated in Bamako on 23 December 2025 with reported capital of CFA 500bn, according to AllAfrica and Ecofin.

The bloc charges a 0.5% levy on imports from outside its territory, including from ECOWAS countries, AllAfrica reported in 2025. Trade among the three remains modest, and Apanews describes the integration as fragmented.

The joint force was first reported at 5,000 troops and later at 15,000 in mid-April 2026.

A freight train and travellers loading goods at Choum, northern Mauritania. File photo. Photo: Ben Kawam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ECOWAS and the Currency Union: A Split, Then Talks

Leaving ECOWAS did not cut every tie. We could not confirm the three AES states’ current status in the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU, or UEMOA in French).

ECOWAS said on 29 January 2025 that it would keep the free-trade zone and visa-free movement for AES citizens “until further notice”, Ecofin reported. That decision kept ordinary trade and travel moving while politics cooled.

Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye was elected chair of the ECOWAS Authority on 19 July 2026 and made a one-day working visit to Bamako on 28 July. AllAfrica reported that he told Goïta “nothing that could weaken Mali would come from Senegal” and urged dialogue, including on security along the Dakar–Bamako corridor.

Daily Trust reported a first ministerial meeting between ECOWAS and the AES in Dakar on 17 October 2026. It set up joint working groups to negotiate a cooperation deal on trade, movement of people and security, and no date was set for the next meeting.

Two other office holders are worth knowing. General Birame Diop of Senegal became ECOWAS Commission president around 31 August 2026, while the WAEMU Commission is led by a different Abdoulaye Diop, also Senegalese and not Mali’s foreign minister.

Neighbour by Neighbour

Algeria and Morocco

The rift with Algeria began on 31 March 2025, when Algeria shot down a Malian drone near Tinzaouaten, according to Hespress. Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso then recalled their ambassadors.

Mali filed a case at the International Court of Justice in September 2025, and the court said it could proceed only if Algeria accepted its jurisdiction, Asharq Al-Awsat reported. On 10 July 2026 the two countries announced they would restore ambassadors and reopen airspace after more than a year, according to AllAfrica, and we found no report that the case was withdrawn.

On 10 April 2026, Diop ended Mali’s recognition of the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, the claim to independence for Western Sahara. AllAfrica reported that Mali now backs Morocco’s autonomy plan, and no source we reviewed links this move to the Algeria dispute.

Senegal, Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire

Seneweb reported on 7 May 2026 that about 20% or more of the goods passing through the Port of Dakar are bound for Mali. Fuel, food and construction materials flow to Mali, while Mali sends out cotton, livestock and gold.

In January 2026, Mali and Guinea signed transit agreements for an alternative route to the sea, AllAfrica reported. The aim is to reduce reliance on Dakar and Abidjan.

Financial Afrik reported that Côte d’Ivoire’s President Ouattara received Guinea’s General Mamadi Doumbouya on 13 September 2026. We found no specific 2026 report on Mali’s relations with Côte d’Ivoire.

Mauritania, Niger and Burkina Faso

UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, counted about 14,402 refugees identified in Hodh Chargui in Mauritania since the current influx began on 24 October 2025. Only 484 arrived in the three weeks to 21 May 2026, because of movement restrictions inside Mali.

With Niger, led by General Abdourahamane Tchiani, and Burkina Faso, led by Traoré, Mali’s ties run mainly through the AES. We found no separate bilateral facts beyond the bloc, so we do not describe them here.

Aerial view of Nouakchott, Mauritania's capital, with a palm grove at the centre. File photo, 2017. Photo: Laminesall96, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Security That Crosses Borders

Since 3 September 2025, the al-Qaeda-linked Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) has blockaded fuel from Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire and Guinea, burning more than 300 tankers. Escorted convoys reached Bamako from late October 2025, the blockade eased early in 2026, and it was reimposed in late April.

On 25 April 2026, JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) attacked Bamako, Kati, Kidal, Gao, Mopti, Sévaré and Bourem, according to Al Jazeera. Russia’s Africa Corps withdrew from Kidal, Aguelhok, Tessalit and other northern posts between 27 April and 1 May, and Algeria reportedly mediated the Kidal withdrawal.

The army and Africa Corps re-entered Kidal on 6 October 2026 after the FLA left, according to Afrique Confidentielle and Studio Tamani. The FLA described its exit as a temporary withdrawal.

Fighting continued after the April offensive. The 2026 in Mali reference page lists attacks at Anéfis from 4 July, an ambush in Gao region that killed 50 or more soldiers and Africa Corps personnel, and an August garrison attack at San that killed about 40 militants and 10 soldiers.

Rails, Rivers and Gold

China Railway Construction Corporation (International) holds contracts to rebuild the 1,286 km Dakar–Bamako line, according to Railway Gazette. They are worth US$1.26bn on the Senegal side and US$1.47bn on the Mali side, and Ecofin reports the Dakar–Tambacounda section is about 90% rehabilitated.

In 2018 DP World, the port operator, signed a 20-year concession for a 1,000-hectare logistics hub outside Bamako. If the line and hub both work, Mali gains a second route that does not depend only on trucks.

The Niger Basin Authority covers nine countries and a 4,200 km river, according to Renewable Energy World. Sélingué dam sits on the Sankarani in Mali, Taoussa (25 MW) is in Mali, and Fomi (about 102 MW) is in Guinea, though we could not confirm dates or status from primary sources.

Mali also belongs to the OMVS, the Senegal River basin body, which Faye and Goïta discussed in Bamako. The river carries risk as well: a ferry disaster on the Niger in Timbuktu region in January 2026 killed 38 or more people.

Gold accounts for close to 80% of Mali’s exports, according to the IMF. Barrick and Mali reached an agreement in November 2025 to reopen the Loulo-Gounkoto mine, near the Senegal border on the Falémé River.

The Numbers That Matter

The table gathers the main figures with their owners and dates. Growth forecasts predate the April 2026 attacks and the renewed blockade, so they may prove too high.

Indicator Figure Owner and period Mali GDP growth forecast 5.5% for 2026, from 4.9% in 2025 IMF, via Bloomberg, December 2025 WAEMU-wide growth forecast 6.1% for 2026 BCEAO, via Financial Afrik, September 2026 Mali consumer prices Up 1.0% year on year INSTAT, April 2026 WAEMU-wide inflation 1.2% in July, 1.7% in August 2026 BCEAO, via Financial Afrik, September 2026 Main policy rate 3.00%, unchanged BCEAO, 9 September 2026 Gold share of exports About 80% Mining.com Dakar–Bamako rail contracts US$1.26bn (Senegal), US$1.47bn (Mali) Railway Gazette Malian refugees in Hodh Chargui About 14,400 UNHCR, 21 May 2026

The Banque Centrale des États de l’Afrique de l’Ouest (BCEAO) is the common central bank for WAEMU, so Mali sets no monetary policy of its own. Its committee is expected to meet again in December 2026, though the date is unconfirmed.

What It Means for Foreigners, and What to Watch

A visa is required and must be obtained in advance at a Malian embassy or consulate, and we found no e-visa. Third-party sites quote fees of about US$100, US$131 and US$165, so check the embassy’s own schedule.

In October 2025, Mali imposed a US$10,000 bond on US citizens, in reciprocity for a US bond list, according to buch-dein-visum.de. The US later removed Mali from that list, and we found no announcement that Mali ended its own bond.

The US State Department rates Mali Level 4, Do Not Travel, according to search summaries of its advisory. Investors should note that fuel, rail and port plans all run through neighbouring territory, so a blockade or a border dispute reaches Bamako quickly.

Several dates are worth tracking. Traoré’s year as AES chair ends in December 2026, the BCEAO committee meets in December, and INSTAT, the national statistics office, publishes prices around the 10th of each month.

The open questions are whether ECOWAS and the AES set a date for their next round, whether the Algeria thaw holds, and whether the Dakar–Bamako corridor stays open. A conservative reading is that cooperation on trade is advancing faster than cooperation on security.

Related reading: Idrissa Gueye Explained 2026: From Everton to Saudi Club Diriyah; Central African Republic Explained, a Fragile Peace in 2026; Chad Explained, the Landlocked Central African Power in 2026; more from Africa.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which countries are Mali’s closest partners?

Burkina Faso and Niger, which form the Alliance of Sahel States with Mali. Bamako is the bloc’s capital, and Burkina Faso’s Captain Ibrahim Traoré has chaired it since December 2025.

Is Mali still in ECOWAS?

No. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger left ECOWAS in January 2025. ECOWAS and the AES held a first ministerial meeting in Dakar on 17 October 2026 to prepare a cooperation deal.

Why did Mali and Algeria fall out?

The rift began when Algeria shot down a Malian drone near Tinzaouaten on 31 March 2025, according to Hespress. On 10 July 2026 the two countries announced they would restore ambassadors and reopen airspace after more than a year.

How does Mali get its fuel and goods?

Mostly by road through Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire and Guinea, with about 95% of fuel arriving that way. The Dakar–Bamako railway, a 1,286 km line being rebuilt, is meant to offer another route.

How many Malian refugees are in Mauritania?

UNHCR counted about 14,402 refugees identified in Hodh Chargui since the current influx began on 24 October 2025. Only 484 arrived in the three weeks to 21 May 2026, because of movement restrictions inside Mali.

Do foreigners need a visa for Mali?

Yes, and it must be obtained in advance at a Malian embassy or consulate, as we found no e-visa. The US State Department rates Mali Level 4, Do Not Travel, so check current advice before planning a trip.

World.title: US Midterm Vote Won’t Necessarily Lift Costa Rica’s 12.5% Tariff
World.content:
Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States could reshape the political climate around the 12.5% tariff Washington applies to many Costa Rican goods. But two international relations analysts say a change in control of Congress would not, by itself, bring that duty down. Voters on November 3 will choose all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 33 of the 100 Senate seats. Republicans currently control both chambers.

Analyst Carlos Murillo said the tariff is among the most sensitive issues for Costa Rica in the vote. He warned that President Donald Trump could rely on other legal instruments to keep his trade policy in place even if Congress or the courts push back, so a new majority would not automatically reverse measures that affect the country. What could change, Murillo said, is the political context in which those measures are applied.

The tariff took effect on July 24. It stems from investigations the Office of the US Trade Representative opened in March under Section 301 of US trade law into some 60 economies, over what Washington called insufficient efforts to block imports of goods made with forced labor. Costa Rica landed at the top of a range of 10% to 12.5%.

Coffee, pineapple, bananas, orange juice, plant cuttings, fruit and vegetable seeds, and certain refined sugars remain excluded, according to the Ministry of Foreign Trade (Comex). Trade Minister Indiana Trejos said at the time that Costa Rica respects labor rights and rules-based trade, and that her ministry would keep working with exporters and Washington to improve market access.

Nuria Marín, also an international relations analyst, described the midterms as a referendum on Trump’s presidency. She said Democrats have strong chances of retaking the House, while the Senate is harder to call. She put the president’s approval at around 30%, down from a peak of about 50% in March 2025, and said that level of support is not normal in the United States. Marín linked the slide to rising prices driven by tariffs and higher energy costs, which she said have squeezed household budgets for the same voters who backed Trump’s promise to fix the economy.

A Congress with more Democrats could tighten oversight of the president, particularly on trade, she said. But she cautioned that many decisions rest with the executive branch, so lawmakers would not be able to block everything. That limit extends to two other areas that matter to Costa Rica. In the analyst Marín’s view, a change in legislative control would not necessarily alter US migration policy or anti-drug cooperation directly, because both fall largely under the executive, where Trump retains broad powers.

Security ties between the two countries have been a recurring focus. US Ambassador Melinda Hildebrand met with representatives of the Supreme Court, the Public Ministry and the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) on September 30 and reaffirmed Washington’s commitment to fighting drug trafficking.

Murillo said Costa Rica has taken on significant commitments with the United States on policing, military and organized crime matters, which raises the stakes of any shift in US foreign policy or regional security priorities. He also pointed to fuel. Gasoline and diesel prices are a decisive issue for US voters because they hit family spending directly, he said. In Costa Rica, he added, local fuel prices are trending upward but have not yet fully reflected international increases because of the country’s price-setting system.

Murillo said the loss of a Republican majority could also sharpen confrontation between Trump and his opponents in Congress. Both analysts suggested that the policies with the most direct effect on Costa Rica, from the tariff to migration rules and security cooperation, will continue to be shaped largely by the White House rather than Capitol Hill, whatever the result on Tuesday.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Pesticide Problem and the Beauty of Backyard Gardening
World.content:
Isn’t it ironic that Costa Rica, our country famed throughout the world for its amazing flora and fauna, is also at or near the top worldwide for pesticide and herbicide use per unit of farmland? Ironic, and disgusting. And infuriating. Infuriating because this land is blessedly fertile. One can quite literally throw a few seeds into the ground and with a bit of care, watch plants come to life naturally. Home gardens flourish throughout the nation, and while all are not 100 percent organic, chemical use is typically minimal.

Of course, it is not the backyard planting responsible for the unwanted ranking. The main culprit is big agro. Multinational companies convert huge swaths of land into monoculture farms. Banana and pineapple plantations apply massive amounts of chemicals with names like mancozeb, glyphosate and ethoprophos in order to kill fungi, weeds, and anything else that might endanger the profitable yield of the valuable export crops.

I once spent a year in a small town in the southern zone of Costa Rica that was located in the heart of Del Monte’s pineapple plantations. The village was surrounded by a vast desert of pineapples. Almost everyone in the area worked for the company. Pay was minimal, but there were other benefits such as a free clinic for the laborers, a necessity due to the harsh labor-intensive work, that required long hours in the hot sun, and regular exposure to the variety of unhealthy chemicals used to ensure a steady supply of pineapples to sell worldwide.

There is an interesting parallel between this type of agriculture and the mega-resorts beginning to spring up in Costa Rica. Both are sources of steady employment for locals. Both are owned and operated primarily by outsiders. Both pay lip service to the environment. Mega resort developers will chop down trees, fill in mangroves, handle sewage and waste haphazardly, and either pay whatever fines come their way, or pay the right officials to look the other way.

Everywhere I have lived in Costa Rica, we have done our own small personal gardening. I live on a 700 square meter lot in a barrio of San Isidro de el General, about one mile uphill from downtown. On our lot we have all of the following: An avocado tree that has yielded hundreds of delicious fruits the past few years; a banana tree planted less than a year ago that recently provided our first regime; a vine that produces enormous chayotes; a lemon tree; a row of pineapples that was recently harvested, and mint and oregano plants.

And all of these have produced without the use of any type of lab-derived chemicals. This is why I take it personally. Ideally, we would all be taking advantage of the wondrous conditions available in Costa Rica for growing just about anything and caring for land while also reaping its benefits. Alas, we live in a world far from ideal, where production and profit are king.

Photos of what grows naturally in our backyard in a barrio in PZ, lemons, avocados, chayote, bananas, pineapple, oregano. Mint

World.title: Costa Rica Dollar Supply Hits Record 20 Years After Colón Devaluations Ended
World.content:
Costa Rica is marking 20 years since it abandoned the system of controlled devaluations that let the Central Bank weaken the colón against the U.S. dollar in small, predictable steps. The anniversary arrives as the foreign exchange market posts record dollar supply, keeping the exchange rate near its lowest level in two decades.

Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) President Róger Madrigal revisited the 2006 reform on Friday, Oct. 30, during the presentation of the institution’s October Monetary Policy Report. The weighted average exchange rate in the Foreign Currency Market (Monex) closed that day at ₡452.08 per dollar, about 35% below the record ₡696.76 set on June 21, 2022.

The BCCR board approved the change on Oct. 13, 2006, and it took effect four days later, ending the crawling peg the country had used since 1984. Under that system, the bank adjusted the rate in small daily increments, so the colón lost value against the dollar at a steady, predictable pace.

The 2006 reform replaced the peg with an exchange rate band. The dollar could move between a ceiling and a floor, and the Central Bank intervened when the rate reached either limit.

Costa Rica moved to the current managed float in February 2015. The rate is now set mainly by supply and demand, although the Central Bank can step in to prevent sharp swings. The shift also cleared the way for the inflation-targeting framework the bank formally adopted in 2018.

According to the October report, average daily dollar supply in the exchange market so far this year reached about $152.9 million, up from $134.9 million in the same period of 2025. Average daily demand rose from $108.1 million to $122.3 million, leaving a daily surplus of about $30.6 million.

Data presented Friday put the cumulative net result of the private exchange market at $6.41 billion over the first 209 business days of the year, compared with $5.53 billion in the same stretch of 2025. The BCCR attributed about 94.5% of the net surplus to companies operating under special trade regimes, chiefly free trade zones. Between January and August, those companies sold about $5.2 billion in foreign currency and bought $471 million, for net sales of $4.73 billion.

Free trade zone companies earn dollars by exporting medical devices, electronics and business services to international clients. They sell part of those dollars to pay salaries, suppliers and taxes in colones, and as more dollars reach the market, the exchange rate is pushed lower.

Foreign direct investment is another major source. It reached about $2.74 billion in the first half of 2026, 23.4% more than in the same period of 2025, according to an analysis by the Foreign Trade Promoter (Procomer) based on preliminary BCCR data. That figure excludes Heineken’s acquisition of FIFCO’s beverage, food and retail businesses, an extraordinary transaction that dominated first-quarter flows. The United States accounted for roughly 69% of the investment.

Tourism spending, remittances and income from services that Costa Rican companies sell abroad also add to the supply of foreign currency. A study published July 8, 2026, by ULACIT economist Stefan Krause Montalbert, which analyzed Monex data from 2015 to 2023, identified free trade zone activity, interest rate differentials and an improved perception of Costa Rica’s sovereign risk as drivers of dollar supply.

The surplus has also raised questions about whether illicit money is contributing. A national money laundering risk assessment commissioned by the General Superintendency of Financial Institutions (Sugef), dated November 2024 and published in April 2026, identified Costa Rica’s location along international drug trafficking routes as the country’s main threat.

The same assessment flagged the heavy movement and use of foreign currency in cash as a risk. Seizures have also climbed, with the Costa Rican Drug Institute (ICD) reporting ₡58.3 billion in colón-denominated seizures in 2024, compared with ₡1.76 billion in 2023. The impact on the exchange rate remains uncertain.

Economists have said there is not enough evidence to determine how much illicit money enters the foreign exchange market or whether the amounts are large enough to move the rate. The Central Bank has maintained that available information does not establish drug trafficking as the cause of the surplus. Its own figures identify special-regime companies as the dominant source of net dollar sales.

A stronger colón has uneven effects depending on whether people and businesses earn, save or spend in dollars. A lower exchange rate makes imported vehicles, electronics, machinery, raw materials and imported fuel cheaper in colón terms, although retail prices also depend on taxes, shipping costs and commercial pricing decisions.

Those effects help contain inflation by limiting price increases on imported goods. Costa Ricans who travel abroad or pay for services in dollars need fewer colones to do so, and borrowers who earn in colones but owe in dollars see their payments shrink in local currency terms. The pressure falls on those who earn in dollars and spend in colones. Hotels, tour operators, exporters and agricultural producers receive fewer colones for every dollar earned, even when sales hold steady, and exporters lose price competitiveness against rivals in other countries.

Households that receive salaries, pensions or remittances in dollars also see their purchasing power decline when they convert those earnings into colones. The surplus has kept the Central Bank active in the market. According to the October report, the BCCR bought about $5.21 billion in Monex during the period covered, or 63.4% of the amount traded, through stabilization operations, reserve accumulation and purchases to meet the foreign currency needs of the nonbank public sector.

Net international reserves reached about $20.22 billion as of Oct. 28, according to data presented Friday. Monex also set a record on Tuesday, Oct. 27, when trading reached $153.4 million, the largest single-day volume in the BCCR’s records. The Central Bank bought $52 million that day through stabilization operations and another $62.7 million to cover public-sector requirements.

Two decades after Costa Rica stopped devaluing the colón by design, its exchange rate is shaped increasingly by investment, exports and foreign currency flows. The stronger colón eases import costs and inflation but squeezes anyone whose income arrives in dollars, while questions about illicit funds keep financial oversight in focus.

World.title: Woman Accused of Forging Deeds to Take an American’s Property Deported to Costa Rica
World.content:
Two Costa Ricans wanted since 2016, including a woman suspected of using forged deeds and powers of attorney to take property and money from a U.S. citizen, have been deported from the United States and handed to Costa Rican judicial authorities, the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) reported Saturday.

Both were deported on Friday and arrived in Costa Rica after midday, according to the OIJ. Agents from the Interpol National Central Bureau in San José, which operates within the OIJ, detained them at the airport and brought them before the courts that had requested their arrest.

The 63-year-old woman is suspected of ideological falsification, use of a false document and simple robbery. According to the OIJ, in December 2016 she allegedly acted with other people to use false deeds and powers of attorney to take over properties belonging to a U.S. citizen and withdraw money from the victim’s bank accounts.

She also faces a separate, older allegation. Authorities say that in June 2014 she allegedly intercepted a person on a public street and took their cell phone, an account the OIJ described as preliminary. U.S. authorities detained Medina in February 2026 in Hampton Bays, New York, the OIJ said.

She was placed in immigration custody because she was apparently living in the United States without regular immigration status. The OIJ did not disclose the value of the properties or money involved, or the identities of any alleged accomplices. The man, a 54-year-old identified by his surname Grijalba, is suspected of involuntary manslaughter and causing involuntary injuries.

The OIJ says that in April 2016 he allegedly drove head-on into a motorcycle carrying two people in Sarapiquí, in Heredia province. One rider died at the scene and the other was taken to a medical center. Investigators later determined that he had left Costa Rica for the United States, according to the OIJ. He was detained in Monticello, Indiana, where he also apparently lacked regular immigration status.

Authorities did not say when that arrest took place or which U.S. agencies carried out either detention. Both suspects are presumed innocent, and neither has been convicted in the cases for which they were wanted. Costa Rican judicial authorities will now determine what precautionary measures apply while the investigations continue.

The transfers come amid a busy stretch of law enforcement cooperation between the two countries. Earlier this month, Costa Rica handed four suspects to the United States in three days, and has taken on a growing role in U.S. deportation efforts. In June, authorities also turned to Interpol after suspects left the country ahead of planned raids.

The allegations against Medina touch on a long-standing concern for anyone who owns property in Costa Rica but spends long periods away, as forged deeds and powers of attorney remain a known route for property registry fraud targeting absentee owners. Nearly a decade after the alleged events, both cases can now move forward in Costa Rican courts with the suspects here.

World.title: Wha Happen? 13 Patois Phrases for Costa Rica’s Caribbean Coast
World.content:
Most visitors arrive in Costa Rica armed with a few words of Spanish. Then they reach Puerto Viejo, Cahuita or Limón, someone greets them with a cheerful wha happen, and the phrasebook suddenly feels useless. Along the Caribbean coast, many families speak Mekatelyu, the local Patois known to linguists as Limonese Creole. The name comes from the phrase “make I tell you,” or “let me tell you.”

The language arrived with the Jamaican and other West Indian workers who came from the 1870s to build the railroad to the Caribbean and later stayed to work the banana plantations. Mekatelyu is an English-based creole closely related to Jamaican Patois, with African, Spanish and Caribbean influences.

It is spoken far more than it is written, so spellings vary from one person to the next. Whether Mekatelyu counts as a language or a dialect is a long-running debate, and linguists still do not fully agree. One handy rule unlocks a lot of words: the th sound mostly disappears. A soft th, as in think, becomes a t, so three is tree, thing is ting and thanks is tanks. A hard th, as in this, becomes a d, so this is dis, that is dat and though is doh.

Them becomes dem, which also does the job of making plurals. Di pickney dem means the children, and tree ting doh means three things, though. You do not need to be fluent. Locals appreciate the effort, and a few words go a long way at a soda, on a bus or at the beach.

A Mekatelyu starter kit

Wha happen: What’s up, or how are you. It is a greeting, not a sign that something went wrong.

What’s up, or how are you. It is a greeting, not a sign that something went wrong. Mi deh yah: I’m here, or I’m doing fine. The classic answer to wha happen.

I’m here, or I’m doing fine. The classic answer to wha happen. Aright: Alright, used for hello, goodbye, OK and everything in between.

Alright, used for hello, goodbye, OK and everything in between. Tank yu: Thank you.

Thank you. Weh yu deh?: Where are you? Useful when your friend says they are on the way.

Where are you? Useful when your friend says they are on the way. Soon come: I’ll be right there. On Caribbean time this can mean five minutes or two hours.

I’ll be right there. On Caribbean time this can mean five minutes or two hours. Likkle more: See you later.

See you later. Nyam: To eat. Wi a go nyam means we are going to eat.

To eat. Wi a go nyam means we are going to eat. Pickney: Child or children.

Child or children. Bredda and sista: Brother and sister, used for friends as much as family.

Brother and sister, used for friends as much as family. Mek wi go: Let’s go.

Let’s go. How much fi dis?: How much for this? Handy at a fruit stand or craft table.

How much for this? Handy at a fruit stand or craft table. Tek it easy: Take it easy, the unofficial motto of the coast.

Words for the table

Food has its own vocabulary too, and Caribbean cooking is where many visitors first hear it. Rice and beans is cooked in coconut milk, usually with red beans, and is not the same thing as gallo pinto, so do not confuse the two in front of a cook.

Rundown, called rondón in Spanish, is a rich coconut stew of fish or seafood and root vegetables. A patty, or patí, is a spicy turnover sold from coolers and bakeries all along the coast, and pan bon is a sweet dark bread with roots in the old West Indian kitchens.

A few tips

Speak slowly and smile, and do not worry about getting the accent right. Avoid imitating the accent as a joke, which can come across as mocking. If someone answers you in English, Spanish or Patois, follow their lead. Many people on the coast move between all three in a single conversation.

Most of all, listen. The best way to learn Mekatelyu is the way it has always been passed on, at a kitchen table, on a porch or with a calypso playing in the background. Limón calypso is now recognized as part of the country’s intangible cultural heritage and even appears on a new ₡100 coin, and events such as Puerto Viejo’s Wolaba Parade are a good place to hear all of it at once.

Mek wi go.

World.title: Fixing an Invoice in Costa Rica Can Now Reopen a Tax Return You Already Filed
World.content:
Starting today, fixing a mistake on an electronic invoice in Costa Rica can reopen a tax return you already filed. New invoicing codes from the Ministry of Finance took affect today and changes how you correct, cancel or replace an invoice. If you bill anyone in Costa Rica, whether you run a company, work freelance or rent out property, this applies to you.

The key change is timing as when you correct an invoice because of a material error, such as a wrong amount, the correction now belongs to the month the original invoice was issued, not the month you catch the mistake. So, an invoice from January that you correct in August sends you back to January. If the fix means you owed more tax that month, you pay the difference plus interest. If you paid too much, the difference becomes a credit in Tribu-CR, the tax administration’s online platform.

The point is to keep income and tax tied to the month they actually belong to. A correction filed months later could blur that line, and the new codes tell the tax administration exactly what kind of fix you made and which invoice it touches. Tax attorney Raymundo Volio said the update does not change tax rates or create new taxes, and is designed to improve tracking and the accuracy of the data.

Your invoices still run on version 4.4 of the electronic invoicing system, which became mandatory in September 2025. What changes today is the set of codes your billing software must use when it issues credit and debit notes. Three new codes cover material errors. One cancels an invoice (code 13), one corrects an amount (code 14) and one replaces an invoice entirely (code 15).

If you cancel an invoice and need to issue a new one, the replacement code must also be recorded so the two documents stay linked. Two more codes handle other situations. Code 16 is for replacing an invoice the tax administration rejected, and code 17 records a payment against an invoice through the electronic payment receipt.

An existing code for credit notes on tax exemptions granted after a sale has also been adjusted, and in that case the accounting effect lands in the month the credit note is issued. Silvia Castro, a tax partner at the firm Despacho Carvajal, said a correction that looks simple, like changing the amount on an invoice, can end up affecting taxes you already declared.

If you use private billing software, ask your provider whether the November codes are active. If an accountant handles your filings, ask how corrections will be flagged so the right months get amended. If you rarely correct or cancel invoices, you may notice little difference. The businesses that will feel it most are those that frequently adjust amounts, cancel sales or reissue rejected receipts.

The tax administration announced the changes on April 22 and let businesses switch early, so many billing platforms may already be updated. It is the latest in a series of moves to tighten tax monitoring, including a requirement for businesses to register the phone numbers they use to receive payments.

Another change is on the way. The National Registry plans to begin issuing new companies legal identification numbers that include letters, in a format such as 3-101-A00001. No start date has been set, though it is expected before the end of 2026. Invoicing systems will need to accept the new format, while existing companies keep their current numbers unless they request a change.

For anyone who invoices in Costa Rica, the practical step is the same. Make sure the software you bill with is current, and keep records that let you trace every correction back to the original sale. Questions about how a correction affects your tax obligations are best taken to an accountant.

World.title: Costa Rica Court Asked to Halt Shark Fishing Near Cocos Island
World.content:
A Costa Rican environmental attorney has asked a court to temporarily prohibit the capture of several types of sharks in waters surrounding Cocos Island, arguing that the government has failed to establish the fishing regulations needed to protect threatened marine species. Attorney Walter Brenes filed the request with Costa Rica’s Administrative Court, seeking an immediate suspension of both intentional shark fishing and the accidental capture of sharks during commercial fishing operations in the Bicentennial Marine Management Area.

The protected area surrounds Cocos Island, one of the most important marine conservation sites and a destination internationally known for its large populations of hammerhead sharks and other marine wildlife. At the center of the dispute is the absence of a specific fisheries management plan that would establish how commercial fishing can operate within the protected waters.

Brenes argues that without clear rules governing fishing activities, sharks remain vulnerable despite the area’s protected status. The request covers eight categories of sharks, including hammerheads, silky sharks, blue sharks, blacktip sharks, thresher sharks, Galápagos sharks, tiger sharks and shortfin makos.

Several of these species face serious conservation threats, particularly from commercial fishing operations that use longlines, which are fishing lines carrying hundreds or sometimes thousands of baited hooks. Although longlines are commonly used to catch tuna and other commercially valuable fish, sharks can also become hooked and brought aboard.

Brenes maintains that this type of fishing continues inside the marine management area without adequate safeguards for vulnerable species. He also questions provisions in the area’s general management plan that allow fishing activities in waters extending hundreds of meters below the surface.

According to the attorney, those rules fail to adequately protect sharks that regularly swim through the same depths where commercial fishing gear operates. He is also challenging portions of the general management plan, arguing that more of the protected area should be closed to fishing.

His proposal calls for substantially expanding the waters where fishing would be prohibited, although that remains part of the legal dispute rather than a requirement already accepted by authorities.

Costa Rica Already Faced a Court Order

The latest legal action follows a November 2025 ruling by Costa Rica’s Constitutional Chamber (Sala IV), which found that environmental authorities had failed to complete several measures required to manage Cocos Island and the surrounding marine protected area.

The court ordered the Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) and the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) to complete outstanding management and regulatory measures within 12 months of notification. Those requirements included a fisheries management plan for the Bicentennial Marine Management Area, rules governing public use and improvements to the resources available for conservation.

Although a general management plan for the marine area has since been published, Brenes argues that the separate fisheries plan remains unfinished. The distinction is important because the general plan establishes broad conservation objectives and zones where different activities may take place, while the fisheries plan is intended to provide more detailed rules for fishing operations.

The new court request seeks immediate protection for sharks while the dispute over those regulations is resolved.

A Critical Area for Sharks
