Cocos Island lies more than 500 kilometers (310 miles) off Costa Rica’s Pacific coast and is considered one of the most important locations in the eastern tropical Pacific for sharks, rays and other migratory marine animals. Its surrounding waters attract large schools of hammerhead sharks, making the island a major destination for scientific research and recreational diving.

In 2021, Costa Rica significantly expanded its marine protection around Cocos Island, creating a larger national park and the neighboring Bicentennial Marine Management Area, which covers approximately 106,000 square kilometers (40,900 square miles). The expansion was intended to protect marine biodiversity while allowing regulated activities in designated areas.

However, conservation groups have repeatedly raised concerns about how fishing is managed and monitored in those waters. Sharks are particularly vulnerable because many species grow slowly, mature relatively late and produce fewer offspring than other fish. Heavy fishing pressure can therefore take years or even decades to overcome.

Their movements also make protection difficult, since sharks regularly travel beyond the boundaries of national parks and other restricted areas. For Costa Rica, the issue goes beyond protecting individual animals. Sharks play an important role in maintaining healthy marine ecosystems, while Cocos Island’s wildlife has become part of the country’s international reputation as a leader in conservation and nature-based tourism.

The fishing industry also has an economic stake in the outcome, since restrictions on longline operations could affect access to commercially important fishing grounds.

Court Decision Still Pending

The new filing does not mean shark fishing has been prohibited in the Bicentennial Marine Management Area. A judge must first consider the request and determine whether temporary restrictions are justified while the underlying legal questions are examined. The outcome could influence how Costa Rica manages commercial fishing around one of its most important marine protected areas, particularly if the court requires additional safeguards before fishing activities can continue.

For now, the dispute highlights an unresolved question in Costa Rica’s marine conservation efforts: whether declaring an area protected is enough when the detailed rules governing fishing activities have yet to be completed.

World.title: Missing Caribbean Fishermen Found Alive in Colombia, Family Says
World.content:
Three fishermen from Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast who vanished at sea on Oct. 19 have been found alive in Colombia, a relative said Saturday, ending a 12-day search that drew in coast guard and air support from three countries. Rosemary Zárate, the aunt of one of the men, said that the three were very weak but already on dry land. No official statement on the discovery had been made public by Costa Rican authorities as of Saturday evening, and details of where and how the men were found had not been released.

The men were identified as Carlos Díaz, 27, a mechanic; Frederick Brown, 20, a hairdresser; and Michael González, 36. All three are from Cieneguita, a coastal community in the province of Limón. They left Cieneguita aboard the El Corrongo, a boat of about 10 meters (33 feet), at 3 a.m. on Monday, Oct. 19, and were expected back that evening. According to relatives, the engine had been giving trouble for days before the trip, and the crew carried food and water for a single day and no life jackets.

The crew later reported an engine failure and said they were stranded about 26 kilometers (16 miles) off the southern Caribbean coast, near the border with Panama. The first alert reached Panamanian authorities, who notified Costa Rica’s National Coast Guard Service. Commissioner Juan Carlos Alvarado, director of the National Coast Guard Service, said the search began the same day and continued without interruption. Coast guard boats from the Limón station patrolled the area while a U.S. aircraft flew overflights, with Panama’s National Aeronaval Service and the U.S. Joint Interagency Task Force South supporting the effort.

Search teams used a U.S. Coast Guard drift-modeling tool that weighs currents and wind to predict where a disabled vessel might travel. As the days passed, Alvarado warned that the search area was growing by the hour and did not rule out that the boat had drifted into international waters.

Relatives criticized the pace of the response during the search, saying they received few updates. Families also asked around coastal communities in Panama and Colombia for any sign of the men. Authorities are still looking into how the men reached Colombian territory and the condition of the boat, according to initial reports. No details on their return to Costa Rica have been announced.

It is the second time in roughly a month that Costa Rican fishermen have been found alive after drifting in the Caribbean. In late September, Panamanian authorities rescued three Costa Rican fishermen who had spent six days adrift.

World.title: Belize to study El Salvador’s anti-gang strategy as Minister Chebat acknowledges concerns over human rights
World.content:
Belize to study El Salvador’s anti-gang strategy as Minister Chebat acknowledges concerns over human rights

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Minister of National Security, Energy and Ports Michel Chebat has announced plans for Belizean officials to visit El Salvador to examine strategies used by that country to combat gang violence.

Speaking during Sunday’s emergency police briefing, Chebat said the government hopes to engage directly with Salvadoran authorities to better understand the policies and operations that contributed to the country’s reduction in gang-related crime.

The announcement comes as Belize faces a surge in deadly shootings and internal gang disputes.

When questioned about the human rights controversies surrounding El Salvador’s security policies, Chebat acknowledged that the circumstances confronting the two countries are different.

He said Belize would not necessarily adopt the same measures or implement them to the same extent.

Instead, the government hopes to identify strategies that could be adapted to Belize’s own legal and social circumstances.

El Salvador’s security crackdown under President Nayib Bukele has been credited with significantly reducing gang violence, although human rights organizations have raised serious concerns about arbitrary detention, due process and the treatment of detainees.

The possibility of adopting similar approaches in Belize has previously been examined by Breaking Belize News.

Chebat did not announce a specific date for the proposed visit.

World.title: Police say internal gang conflict behind Dodrick Madrill murder; surveillance technology helped identify suspects
World.content:
Police say internal gang conflict behind Dodrick Madrill murder; surveillance technology helped identify suspects

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police believe the murder of 19-year-old Dodrick Madrill on Freedom Street in Belize City was the result of an internal gang conflict, as investigators reveal that surveillance technology played a major role in identifying the suspects.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith provided the update during Sunday’s emergency briefing.

Madrill was murdered on Thursday, October 29, when a gunman opened fire on him while he was walking along Freedom Street.

Police have since jointly charged 31-year-old Emerson West and a 16-year-old boy with murder.

Smith revealed that the investigation was significantly advanced through footage captured by the Crime Fusion and Operations Centre, which recorded both the incident and its aftermath.

She explained that investigators believe Madrill’s murder resulted from an internal dispute within a particular gang.

Police also confirmed that only one individual discharged a firearm during the attack, although both accused persons have been charged with murder.

Smith declined to elaborate on the alleged roles of the two accused, explaining that the evidence would be presented during court proceedings.

Madrill’s murder preceded Friday’s Coastal Plain Highway quadruple homicide, which police have also attributed to an internal gang feud.

Two of the highway murder victims, Robert Gladden and Dayton Palacio, had previously faced firearm charges alongside Madrill in February 2025.

Police have not conclusively established whether the two murder investigations are directly connected.

West and the minor are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

World.title: Commissioner Rosado rejects allegations that police executed four men on Coastal Plain Highway
World.content:
Commissioner Rosado rejects allegations that police executed four men on Coastal Plain Highway

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Commissioner of Police Dr. Richard Rosado has strongly rejected allegations circulating on social media suggesting that police officers were responsible for Friday’s quadruple murder along the Coastal Plain Highway.

The Commissioner addressed the allegations during Sunday’s emergency police briefing after reporters questioned increased security operations along the highway.

Rosado explained that a specialized Highway Interdiction Team had been established to monitor the movement of suspected criminals through the relatively isolated corridor.

He confirmed that a vehicle checkpoint was being operated by police and security personnel in the area.

However, Rosado categorically denied suggestions that members of the security forces were involved in the October 30 massacre.

He defended the officers assigned to the highway operations, describing them as members of a vetted unit.

The Commissioner maintained that the highway operation was intended to prevent criminal activity and intercept individuals travelling through the area.

His comments came after social media speculation attempted to link the presence of heavily armed security personnel along the highway to the killings.

Police have instead attributed the quadruple murder to an internal gang dispute, based on intelligence gathered during the ongoing investigation.

World.title: Commissioner Rosado confirms internal gang feud behind Coastal Plain Highway quadruple murder
World.content:
Commissioner Rosado confirms internal gang feud behind Coastal Plain Highway quadruple murder

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Commissioner of Police Dr. Richard Rosado has revealed that intelligence gathered by investigators indicates that Friday’s quadruple murder along the Coastal Plain Highway resulted from an internal feud within a criminal gang faction.

Speaking during Sunday’s emergency police briefing, Rosado provided the clearest indication yet of what investigators believe motivated the October 30 massacre.

The attack claimed the lives of 33-year-old Lloyd Leslie, 23-year-old Robert Gladden, 23-year-old Dayton Palacio and 16-year-old David Usher.

The four were travelling in a red Ford Escape when they were ambushed by gunmen along the Coastal Plain Highway.

Three victims died at the scene, while Palacio subsequently succumbed to his injuries at the Southern Regional Hospital.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Gladden and Palacio had previously been charged alongside 19-year-old Dodrick Madrill in a February 2025 firearm and ammunition case.

Madrill was murdered on Freedom Street in Belize City just one day before the highway massacre.

The three men had appeared in court together after police discovered an unlicensed 9mm pistol and 13 live rounds of ammunition inside a Freedom Street residence.

Madrill pleaded guilty and accepted responsibility for the weapon, while Gladden and Palacio pleaded not guilty.

Rosado explained that internal disputes involving factions within the same gang have become increasingly difficult for police to contain.

His latest disclosure strengthens the possibility that the recent murders form part of a broader internal gang conflict, although investigators have not publicly established that all the killings were directly connected.

Police have not announced charges in connection with the quadruple murder.

World.title: Teashuan Kalym Jones charged with gang-related offence over rental vehicle used in Orange Walk armed robbery
World.content:
Teashuan Kalym Jones charged with gang-related offence over rental vehicle used in Orange Walk armed robbery

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged Belize City resident Teashuan Kalym Jones in connection with a vehicle allegedly used during the October 28 armed robbery at Julie’s Used Clothing in Orange Walk Town.

According to an official police update, Jones was arrested and charged at approximately 1:00 p.m. on Saturday, October 31.

He has been charged with participation in criminal activity in association with a gang.

During Sunday’s emergency police briefing, Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith explained that the charge stems from Jones’ alleged involvement in providing a vehicle used during the robbery.

Police confirmed that the vehicle was rented.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, armed men arrived at the used clothing establishment along the Belize–Corozal Road and robbed the proprietor before fleeing in a vehicle.

Investigators subsequently identified a vehicle of interest through surveillance technology and continued pursuing leads.

Smith said the case highlights growing concerns about the use of rental vehicles in criminal activities.

She explained that police have encountered numerous instances in which rented vehicles were allegedly used to facilitate serious crimes.

The government is now considering legislation aimed at strengthening recordkeeping requirements and accountability within the vehicle rental industry.

Jones is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

World.title: Five minors detained in connection with murder of 17-year-old Kevin Meraz in Punta Gorda
World.content:
Five minors detained in connection with murder of 17-year-old Kevin Meraz in Punta Gorda

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained five minors in connection with the murder of 17-year-old Kevin Camilo Meraz, who was stabbed during an altercation in Punta Gorda Town early Sunday morning.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith confirmed the detentions during an emergency press briefing on November 1.

According to police, Meraz was socializing with a group of approximately six persons when a dispute developed.

The confrontation reportedly escalated, resulting in Meraz being stabbed.

Investigators were subsequently informed that the teenager had arrived at the Punta Gorda Hospital seeking medical attention.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, the incident occurred shortly after midnight in the Cayetano Street area, and Meraz was pronounced dead at approximately 1:15 a.m.

Smith confirmed that all five persons detained in connection with the investigation are minors.

She could not immediately establish whether alcohol consumption contributed to the altercation and committed to obtaining additional information from investigators.

No charges had been announced at the time of the briefing.

The murder comes amid renewed national concern about the involvement of minors in serious criminal offences.

World.title: Herbert Belloso chased down and murdered in Ladyville; victim previously convicted of drug trafficking and detained in murder investigation
World.content:
Herbert Belloso chased down and murdered in Ladyville; victim previously convicted of drug trafficking and detained in murder investigation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have revealed new details surrounding Saturday’s murder of 31-year-old Herbert Belloso in Ladyville, including that he had previously been detained as a person of interest in another murder investigation.

Belloso, who was also sentenced to prison for drug trafficking in 2022, was reportedly pursued and shot after several armed men exited a vehicle near a store.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith told reporters during Sunday’s emergency police briefing that Belloso was murdered at approximately 11:15 a.m. on October 31 in the vicinity of Compassion Lane.

According to investigators, Belloso was at a store when a blue Chevrolet Equinox approached and stopped nearby.

Three men exited the vehicle, two of whom were armed.

Upon noticing the armed men, Belloso attempted to flee but was pursued and shot, sustaining fatal injuries.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, a source indicated that Belloso had been shot with a shotgun, sustaining a severe injury to his head.

During Sunday’s briefing, Smith declined to confirm the type of firearm used in the murder.

She also revealed that Belloso had previously been detained in connection with an earlier murder investigation in Ladyville.

However, investigators did not obtain sufficient evidence to charge him, although he remained a person of interest in that investigation.

Breaking Belize News has also confirmed that Belloso was previously convicted of drug trafficking in July 2022.

According to BBN’s July 28, 2022 court report, Belloso, who was 27 at the time, appeared before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court after police discovered 28.9 grams of crack cocaine concealed in his underwear.

Police had intercepted a Ford Ranger pickup in which Belloso and another man were travelling.

Belloso pleaded guilty to possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply, allowing the other accused to go free.

He was sentenced to two years at the Belize Central Prison and fined $10,000, which was to be paid by December 31, 2022, or he would face an additional three years in prison.

Meanwhile, police have identified a vehicle of interest in Saturday’s murder and are pursuing leads.

Smith said investigators have not conclusively established whether Belloso’s killing is connected to the earlier murder investigation or other recent shootings.

There is also no established connection between Belloso’s previous drug-trafficking conviction and his murder.

The investigation continues.

World.title: Police confirm Charles Nolberto murdered in Taylor’s Alley shooting; Charles Middleton and two others injured
World.content:
Police confirm Charles Nolberto murdered in Taylor’s Alley shooting; Charles Middleton and two others injured

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have officially confirmed that 31-year-old Charles Nolberto was murdered during Saturday night’s shooting in the Taylor’s Alley area of Belize City, while three other men sustained gunshot injuries.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith provided the confirmation during Sunday’s emergency police briefing, resolving conflicting reports that initially circulated about whether anyone had died.

The injured men include 29-year-old Charles Middleton and two others, ages Cesario Choco, 32, and Clifford Olivera, 43.

According to Smith, the attack occurred at approximately 7:10 p.m. on Saturday, October 31, while four men were socializing near Cemetery Road.

Investigators established through surveillance footage obtained from the Crime Fusion and Operations Centre that a black Chevrolet vehicle stopped in front of the group.

An individual inside the vehicle reportedly opened fire, fatally injuring Nolberto and wounding the three other men.

Police confirmed that all three surviving victims were in stable condition.

Smith revealed that investigators have identified a vehicle of interest and are actively searching for it.

Unlike the internal gang disputes being investigated in connection with other recent murders, police believe the Taylor’s Alley attack resulted from a conflict between opposing gangs.

Both Nolberto and Middleton were previously identified in BBN’s August 2024 coverage of alleged Taylor’s Alley gang affiliates detained during a state of emergency.

That report identified Nolberto and Middleton among several individuals detained under emergency measures following a deadly robbery in Belize City.

Their previous detention does not establish that either man was involved in that robbery or that Saturday’s shooting was connected to it.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: Glimmer of hope
World.content:
Merl Grove High School on Constant Spring Road, St Andrew (Naplhtai Junior)

A tenuous hope sparked at the weekend, following a decisive intervention by the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information, into the protracted five-year dispute that has shaken the

Merl Grove High School community.

The ministry’s Regional Educational Services, last Friday, mobilised an estimated 100 Merl Grove stakeholders and interested parties to the dispute which has pitted the school board, led by Chairman David Hall, against the principal of the institution, Dr Marjorie Fullerton.

Ahead of the meeting held under the theme ‘Restore, Rebuild, Renew’, the ministry advised the school to request parents to have their children study at home for the day, apparently to spare them any potential tension that could ensue.

But Jamaica Observer sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters, said in the hours before the gathering, the ministry turned down a request from the principal to have representatives accompany her to the meeting.

These would include her lawyer; the Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA); the Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS); a colleague school principal; and a human resource expert.

In particular, Fullerton wanted the school’s alumni association or alumni stakeholders to attend, “given the significant role that alumni continue to play in the development, support, and advancement of Merl Grove High School”, the sources said.

However, the ministry’s lead person explained that the discussions had not yet reached the stage where that level of representation was necessary but would be considered for the appropriate stage.

The meeting was being spearheaded by the ministry not as a formal hearing, but to allow internal stakeholders to express their concerns and work towards achieving a more harmonious and conducive environment, the sources told the

Observer.

In the end, the ministry agreed that the alumni representatives could attend as requested by Dr Fullerton. The newspaper also spotted two of her principal colleagues on the school compound Friday.

Adding a touch of drama to the day’s events, a group of teachers dressed in black carried out a silent protest on the campus.

The

Observer learned Sunday that the ministry would be reviewing the outcome of the discussions for a follow-up meeting to be decided. Some stakeholders said they were hopeful that the meeting would achieve a resolution but suggested that some of the issues were thorny and would require patience and a willingness to end the dispute.

“A lot of water has gone under the bridge. Egos were bruised and people felt that they were being slighted, hence the level of angst you are seeing,” a source, who attended the meeting, said.

The debacle at Merl Grove High School exploded into public view on September 10, 2021 after the controversial suspension of Principal Fullerton, whose appointment in 2015 set off a nasty struggle with Vice-Principal Loretta Ricketts.

What started off as a struggle between the two key leaders at the school, escalated into “all-out war” between the principal and Hall’s church-dominated school board which apparently sided with the vice-principal, resulting in the suspension and then dismissal of Dr Fullerton in 2022.

A March 2026 ruling by the Supreme Court of Jamaica, that Fullerton be reinstated, and intervention and prayers by the Assemblies of God church failed to douse the in-fighting, with Fullerton complaining that she been locked out of the school e-mail and the financial accounts, and not paid for the four years while she fought her dismissal in the courts.

Concerned about how the internal fight has been affecting students, the Merl Grove Parents Teachers’ Association (PTA) in September declared: “…whatever disagreements may exist between parents, the administration, or other stakeholders, students should never be made to carry the burden of those differences or be placed in circumstances where they feel caught between the adults responsible for their education and welfare”.

The JAPSS, worried about the circumstances under which Dr Fullerton had been working, last week entered the fray, requesting a meeting with the school board to seek a resolution.

“Our intention is to engage in a respectful and solution-oriented discussion with a view to exploring opportunities for mediation and facilitating an amicable and sustainable resolution that supports Dr Fullerton in the effective discharge of her duties, and advances the best interests of Merl Grove High and its wider community,” the JAPSS said.

For its part, the PTA urged the board of management and the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information “to move beyond informal interventions and undertake an objective and timely assessment of the present leadership situation”.

In summoning the stakeholders to Friday’s meeting, the ministry said: “Given the nature and frequency of the concerns raised by both parties in numerous e-mail communications, it is evident that substantive intervention is required to facilitate a resolution and strengthen the school’s governance and operational effectiveness.”

World.title: High-flying Tru-Juice take over JPL lead
World.content:
Promoted side Tru-Juice FC took over the lead in the Legend Jamaica Premier League on Sunday after beating Chapelton Maroons 1-0 at the Bramwell Clarke Sports Complex in Linstead, St Catherine.

The St Catherine-based team’s win, their third in a row, took them to 17 points, one more than Racing United who were the leaders going into the round but lost 3-4 to Treasure Beach. Meanwhile, 10 man Montego Bay United led twice but had to settle for a 2-2 draw with defending champions Portmore United at Jarrett Park.

Daniel Roberts scored a goal in second half time-added for Tru-Juice as they went atop the JPL leaderboard.

It was Roberts’ fourth goal of the season as Chapelton crashed to their third loss and stayed in eighth place.

At Ferdie Neita Park, Daniel Hardy scored his first hattrick to lead Treasure Beach to their first win of the season, edging Racing United in a seven-goal thriller.

Tajay Grant scored a brace for Racing who came back three times to tie up the scores but Hardy got the winner in time added at the end of the second half.

Hardy opened the scoring in the sixth minute but Grant drew Racing level in the 16th minute; Dahmani Miller restored the visitors’ lead in the 23rd minute but once again Grant drew the hosts level, this time from the penalty spot in the 28th minute.

Hardy scored his second to give his team the lead in the 66th minute and Racing managed once more to draw level when Nicholas Lawrence scored in the 86th minute.

Treasure Beach would not be denied however, and Hardy completed his hattrick late in the game to give the St Elizabeth-based club their first win of the season.

Despite being down to 10 players, MBU took the lead against the defending champions when Jordaine Fletcher pounced on a cross from Devonte Campbell and powered the ball past goalkeeper Robert Henry in the second minute of time added.

Portmore wasted little time getting the equaliser as Jevaughn Grant caught Barlett off his line a minute later and lobbed the ball over the head of the goalkeeper.

MBU retook the lead in the 59th minute when Fletcher repaid Campbell for his first half assist, sending him through to beat Henry from just inside the 18-yard box.

Demario Dailey however salvaged a point for Portmore when he capitalised on a mix-up in the MBU defense and scored from close range in the 77th minute.

Also on Sunday, Dunbeholden scored their second win, beating Humble Lion 3-0 with goals from Marlon Allen, Clive Wedderburn and Nevaun Turner.

Tivoli Gardens gifted Arnett Gardens before coming from behind to earn a 1-1 draw in their derby played at the Edwards Seaga Complex.

Arnett Gardens took the lead in the 64th minute though a Barrington Pryce own goal but Mickel Graham, who was a 67th minute substitute, scored the equaliser in the 88th minute.

Sunday’s Results

Montego Bay United-2 Portmore United-2

Racing United-3, Treasure Beach-4

Dunbeholden FC-3, Humble Lion FC-0

Tivoli Gardens FC-1, Arnett Gardens-1

Tru-Juice FC-1, Chapelton Maroons-0

– Paul Reid

World.title: Unstable weather expected across Jamaica beginning Tuesday
World.content:
Jamaicans are being advised to brace for unstable weather conditions beginning Tuesday.

According to the Meteorological Service of Jamaica, a broad Trough is expected to develop across Jamaica and the western Caribbean on Tuesday and will produce a large area of disorganised showers and thunderstorms across the region.

Consequently, the Met Office said, unstable weather conditions are expected across the island beginning Tuesday afternoon.

The forecast is for a gradual increase in cloudiness followed by intermittent showers and thunderstorms, which may be heavy at times, to affect most parishes through Saturday.

Sea conditions will also deteriorate in the vicinity of showers and thunderstorms. Fishers and other marine interests, especially inshore and offshore the south coast, should therefore exercise caution, the Met Office said.

The Meteorological Service said it will continue to monitor this system and update accordingly.

World.title: ‘Kicking and screaming!’
World.content:
THE 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) opens in St John’s, Antigua, today amid a deepening rift over slavery and reparation, with Caribbean leaders welcoming British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s openness to a formal apology for chattel slavery but firmly rejecting his dismissal of reparation as “not the right answer”, insisting that reparatory justice must remain at the heart of the talks.

Burnham’s position in an op-ed for The Guardian newspaper in England, days before his arrival in Antigua and Barbuda for the summit, was immediately seen by Dr Ralph Gonsalves, senior advisor and elder for The Repair Campaign, as Britain yielding to mounting international pressure to negotiate.

“They coming to the table, but they coming kicking and screaming,” Gonsalves, who served as prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines for 24 years, told the Jamaica Observer on Saturday.

“It’s a positive move, but we have to understand that this is only the commencement of the journey, and that they are coming kicking and screaming,” Gonsalves said.

At the same time, he said he expects that the tone of the discussions at the summit would be “respectful, frank, honest, and at times robust”.

Gonsalves said that while slavery and reparation were not formally on the CHOGM agenda, there is no doubt that the issues will be raised by Caribbean Community (Caricom) leaders, as well as their counterparts from Africa and India.

He pointed to the United Nations General Assembly adoption of a resolution on March 25, 2026, declaring the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement as “the gravest crime against humanity”, arguing that the matter had assumed global significance.

“This matter has gone beyond us. It is central to us, but it has gone beyond us. It’s the same way that there’s a tribal war between two sets of Slavic peoples

— Russians and Ukrainians

— but it has global implications,” Gonsalves told the Sunday Observer.

On Saturday, Caricom Chairman Prime Minister Philip J Pierre outlined in a statement that the regional bloc was ready to engage with the United Kingdom, but rejected Burnham’s position that reparation was not “the right answer”.

Burnham, who will attend the November 1-4 CHOGM, has said he is “open” to listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of Britain for its role in the slave trade, but ruled out considering financial reparation.

“I do not believe that is the right answer,” he wrote in The Guardian. “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

Burnham instead offered a “structured dialogue” with those affected by the slave trade, saying, “Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent, and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery

— and we can show leadership again today.

“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he added.

In his response, Pierre, the prime minister of St Lucia, said Burnham’s expression of personal sorrow and regret for the suffering caused by slavery and its continuing effects, together with his willingness to consider a formal apology on behalf of the British State, represented a significant development.

“No British prime minister has gone this far before. It would be wrong of us not to say so, and we welcome it in the spirit in which it appears to be offered,” Pierre said. “For more than a decade, this community has asked for exactly such a dialogue. We are ready to engage.”

However, the Caricom chair said the community did not accept the argument that reparations were inappropriate or that Britain’s responsibility had ended because present-day citizens had not personally participated in slavery.

“Reparatory justice has never been about individual guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions

— and that responsibility does not expire with the passing of generations,” he said.

Pierre pointed to Britain’s role in legislating for, protecting, and profiting from slavery, as well as its decision to compensate enslavers at Emancipation while formerly enslaved people received no land, wealth, or compensation.

He noted that the loan raised to compensate enslavers was still being repaid by British taxpayers until February 2015.

The consequences of slavery, he said, continue to be felt across the Caribbean through chronic disease, inequalities in education and opportunity, economies shaped by extraction, national debt, and vulnerability to economic and climate shocks.

Pierre said a formal apology would be an important first step, but argued that it must be accompanied by practical measures to address the lasting effects of slavery.

He pointed to Caricom’s 10-Point Plan for Reparatory Justice, which includes a formal apology, public health, education and training, cultural heritage restitution and reconnection, psychological rehabilitation, technology and innovation, entrepreneurship, debt cancellation, monetary compensation, and decolonisation.

He said the proposed dialogue must allow for discussion of every element of the plan, as well as reparation for the genocide of Indigenous Peoples and the harm caused to people brought from India and China to sustain colonial systems.

“A dialogue that begins by placing reparations outside the room cannot be a complete dialogue,” Pierre said.

The Caricom chair also acknowledged the United Kingdom’s initiative, to be led by former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, to restructure the debt of the poorest Commonwealth countries.

He said the community would examine the proposal seriously but cautioned that most Caricom member states were classified as middle- or high-income economies and were routinely excluded from concessional relief despite their vulnerability to climate and economic shocks.

“Any initiative that is to be meaningful for our region must measure vulnerability, not income alone,” he said, adding that debt relief could not be used as a substitute for reparatory justice.

Pierre said the Prime Ministerial Sub-Committee on Reparations, led by Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, and the Caricom Reparations Commission, chaired by Sir Hilary Beckles, were prepared to work with the British Government on the terms, agenda, and timetable for structured dialogue.

He said he looked forward to meeting Burnham in Antigua and Barbuda.

“Our ancestors did not receive justice in their lifetime. We owe it to them, and to the generations who will come after us, to see this work through

— with dignity, with patience, and with resolve,” Pierre said.

Jamaica’s Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness and Barbados’s head of Government Mottley also responded to Burnham’s comments.

“Jamaica takes note of news that the United Kingdom is now willing to engage meaningfully on the matter of reparatory justice,” Holness said in a statement.

“We are encouraged to learn that Prime Minister Burnham and his Government are open to listening to calls for a formal apology for chattel enslavement. We have always been open to having full and meaningful dialogue on this important issue. We welcome this development, coming in the wake of our legal petition which is now before the Privy Council. We look forward to the discussions and actions that will follow,” Holness said.

Mottley said her Government, “recognises and appreciates Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s acknowledgement that the transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of human beings, and his offer of a structured dialogue, including his openness to a formal apology”.

She said Barbados is committed to that dialogue and will take part in good faith as a member of Caricom.

“We also thank former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer who, in Samoa in 2024, joined fellow Commonwealth leaders in agreeing that the time had come for a meaningful conversation on reparatory justice. That decision opened the door to the process now before us,” Mottley said.

Stating that her country speaks on this matter with a particular memory, Mottley said that in 1661, under English colonial authority, the first comprehensive slave code in the English-speaking world was regrettably passed in Barbados.

“It defined African men, women, and children as non-human property and became the model for codes across the region and beyond. That system was built by law and enforced by the State,” she said.

“Dialogue matters because we are not yet on the same page on every element. On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully. Honest disagreement on some questions should not hold back progress on the many others where we can readily agree,” Mottley added.

She thanked Burnham and his Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband “for breaking new ground and recognising that this is the right thing and the moral thing to do by ensuring that we move to the next stage of engagement on this difficult and emotional issue”.

Gonsalves, too, pointed to the importance of dialogue as he recalled that in 2013 when he took the matter of reparation to Caricom all his colleagues were supportive.

“We set up the Prime Ministerial Sub-Committee on Reparations, we set up the Caricom Reparations Commission. We asked that national reparations commissions be set up in every country; we had the 10 Point Plan being devised and approved in 2014, and the show was on the road, so to speak. But some people said, ‘Man, this thing is a mirage, this is a fool’s errand,’ and so forth. But those of us who understood this issue, we knew,” Gonsalves said.

“Now Britain is saying they want to have a structured conversation and in that structured conversation, he’s open to the question of the apology, and to deal with matters looking forward in a number of areas

— debt relief, appropriate funding for this, that, and the other; and he recognised the horrors of slavery, and all the rest of it. So the British Government has come from a position of no apology to one where we will have this structured conversation,” Gonsalves told the Sunday Observer, adding that he expects “other things will emerge in the structured conversation”.

“So, they’re coming to the table kicking and screaming, but coming nevertheless,” he emphasised.

On Friday Britain’s King Charles III, who is on a Caribbean tour, arrived in Antigua where, as the head of the Commonwealth family of nations, he will preside over the four-day summit.

World.title: ‘Not an undercover PNP front’
World.content:
Fi We Children Foundation (FWCF) Youth Policy Committee members Jordaina Denton (left) and Antonio Davis at a Jamaica Observer Press Club meeting at the newspaper’s headquarters in St Andrew last Thursday.Photos: Garfield Robinson

DETERMINED to shake off accusations of political bias and being an organisation that exists mainly to criticise the Government, Fi We Children Foundation is insisting that its criticism of government decisions is driven by its commitment to protecting children’s rights and holding those in power accountable.

The foundation, which describes itself as a non-profit, non-partisan and youth-led organisation, says its public statements are only part of its work, which includes efforts to reduce violence in schools, improve children’s access to proper nutrition and give young people a greater role in decisions affecting their lives.

During a Jamaica Observer Press Club last Thursday, members of its Youth Policy Committee firmly rejected suggestions that the organisation is operating as an undercover political group, with attorney-at-law Antonio Davis saying its purpose is to give children and young people a voice in matters that directly affect them.

“So we would categorically state that we’re not a psyop [psychological operation]. We would categorically state that we’re not an undercover basis for the PNP [People’s National Party], or any party, really. But what it is really, is that I think this foundation gives children the platform.

“Many times, as young people, we’re in the driver’s seat and we’re just passengers watching life go by, and so this platform gives us an opportunity now to kind of hold on to the reins a little bit, hold on to the driving wheel a little bit, and have a voice… So I wouldn’t really say it’s just bashing the Government, but if we see something, then we say something,” Davis said.

The foundation’s members argued that its willingness to highlight shortcomings in government policies should not be taken as evidence of political allegiance. They said the organisation also recognises positive action by the Andrew Holness-led Administration and wants improvements to continue.

Youth Policy Committee member Darrell Scott said the foundation is not opposed to acknowledging government initiatives that benefit children, but believes there is a responsibility to identify areas requiring attention.

“So it’s not that we won’t applaud the Government…but I think what we want is the continuation of the good work that the Government has done while also highlighting areas that they may have missed,” he said.

Founded in 2019, Fi We Children Foundation emerged from discussions about what its members saw as a gap between policymakers and the issues that matter to children. Scott said the organisation was established to give young people a greater role in representing children’s interests, rather than leaving decisions entirely in the hands of adults.

He said its work began before it became more visible in public discussions, with an earlier focus on children in rural Jamaica, who the foundation believes are often overlooked in national conversations.

Scott attributed some of the disruption to its activities to the COVID-19 pandemic, while also pointing to the expansion of its team and the increased attention being paid to children’s issues as reasons for its more recent public presence.

The organisation now has an online membership of about 215 people and an executive board of four, according to Youth Policy Committee member and law student Jordaina Denton.

She explained that it has two main membership categories: General membership is open throughout the year, while applications for the Youth Policy Committee are opened once annually. Denton said applicants to the committee are shortlisted and interviewed, with members expected to take a more direct role in leading advocacy on youth issues.

The foundation also runs a programme called Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) in Schools, which seeks to equip students with alternative ways of resolving conflicts without resorting to violence.

Denton said the initiative was developed against the background of violent incidents involving students, including stabbings and physical confrontations in schools.

The foundation also conducts forums involving schools and said it had encountered approximately 10 to 15 schools through its ADR work, although Scott cautioned that the figure was not exact because some schools were reached through forums rather than direct programme activities.

Beyond school violence, the organisation has been working on issues surrounding the National School Nutrition Policy. Scott said it had collaborated with the Jamaica Youth Advocacy Network, UNICEF Jamaica and Heart Foundation to advance discussions about children’s nutrition.

Another initiative, called Eyes on the Budget, focuses on helping young people understand how public money is allocated and spent. The foundation also appeared before Parliament’s joint select committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act, during which members contributed to the discussions.

For the foundation, these projects form part of a wider commitment to children’s rights rather than a series of unrelated activities. Scott said its work is guided by that broad purpose, with particular projects developed to address specific concerns as they arise.

However, while the committee members acknowledged that the organisation’s public image has been shaped heavily by its statements criticising government decisions, Denton disagreed that the foundation is failing to promote its other work

“We do promote that information, so we have it on our Instagram page. And even when we went to Parliament for the joint select committee, we had done a press release on that. So I think that it is not necessarily that Fi We Children is simply opposing, I think people take it that way because…people are drawn to see a more negative view of things rather than to see the work that we do that does commend people and promote our work,” she said.

World.title: Patra: Far from finished
World.content:
Patra ...honoured with the Lifetime Achievement Award by the organisers of the recently concluded Caribbean Music Awards.

Constantly busying herself with ideas of reinvention, Patra was deep in preparations for upcoming interviews when she first received word that she would be honoured with the Lifetime Achievement Award by the organisers of the Caribbean Music Awards (CMA).

In fact, the Queen of the Pack artiste didn’t open the message until days after it was first sent. Still, the delay did little to diminish the emotional impact of the gesture. The news stopped her in her tracks, causing her to reflect on the journey that had brought her to that moment.

“I got very emotional and it put me in a sense of realisation and meditation,” Patra recalled. “I looked back at where I used to be as an artiste and it was very humbling. To be acknowledged by the CMA, it was a beautiful experience for me. I could barely contain myself.”

For an artiste who has spent decades navigating the shifting currents of the music business, the honour represented more than another accolade to add to an already notable résumé. It was a moment to pause and acknowledge the work.

“Going there to pick up the award, healthy, and still being able to do something that I love, was a feeling I still can’t put into words,” she said. “The highlight was when I realised that I really did do a lot to receive this acknowledgement and the moment allowed me to go back and honour that journey.”

Sometimes, she admits, artistes become so consumed with the next show, the next song, and the next move that they fail to fully appreciate what they have already accomplished.

“Sometimes as artistes, we know what we’ve done, the work we’ve put in but sometimes, the reflection really drives that home,” she said.

For Patra, that reflection is particularly powerful because her story is not simply one of success. It is also one of endurance. The little girl from the country who entered contests from school stages to major competitions already had an instinct for performance. But talent alone, she soon learned, would not be enough.

Having entered an industry in which men significantly outnumbered women, Patra was prepared to face anything thrown her way, including pushback. What she experienced, however, was an environment that allowed her to thrive.

“When I started out there were far more males in the industry than there were females. But the way they treated me when I got into the business was remarkable,” she said. “I always wanted to be a superstar and take my country to the world, and they really facilitated my growth. It made me excited getting into this business and I knew it was meant to be,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

That sense of purpose steered her career. Understanding from very early in her journey that surviving in music required more than knowing how to command a stage, the fiery deejay made a deliberate effort to learn the business, including that the often unseen army of people are responsible for bringing music to audiences.

“I made sure to educate myself on the business, and through that process I learnt to care for and appreciate the works of those behind the scenes,” she said.

That education, coupled with guidance from people who genuinely cared about her development, became part of the foundation on which she built her career. And the lessons continued even when she took a hiatus from the active music scene.

Now, Patra says she is ready for a resurgence marked by renewed energy and a different sense of creative possibility.

“I took a break and now I’m ready to get back out there with a new distribution deal through J House and Sony Orchard,” she said. “People haven’t seen anything yet. Patra is warming up, because there are a lot of good things going on.”

The next chapter is already taking shape, with Patra planning to release two albums in the first quarter of 2027, each exploring a different musical direction. One will deliver what she calls her personal “Patra vibes”, while the other will venture into house music.

The sounds may differ, but she insists the woman at the centre of both projects will remain unmistakably Patra.

“It’s going to be two different vibes, but it will still represent me; my image, my sensuality, my attitude, everything,” she said. The projects will also be message-driven and designed to make people feel good, reflecting an artiste who appears increasingly comfortable with the freedom to explore rather than remain confined by the expectations attached to her past.

“I am happy that with these two projects. I get to present myself to the world in the way I see myself with a sense of freedom. Now, I can do more than one genre of music,” she said, teasing that there will also be surprises on both projects.

In the meantime, she is giving fans a taste of the direction ahead with her latest singles, Me So Sexy and No Threat. The latter, she explained, is about reclaiming her individuality while acknowledging those who came before her, while Me So Sexy serves as the single from the J House Vol 1 project. Its accompanying video is also on the way.

There are performances ahead as well, including an appearance on the Rock The Bells Cruise, keeping Patra firmly connected to the live stage that helped establish her reputation in the first place.

World.title: A clearer view of danger
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (right) is greeted by Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda on arrival at the commissioning ceremony for Jamaica’s new Defender S850 Doppler Weather Radar system at Cooper’s Hill, St Andrew, last Wednesday. (Photos: Naphtali Junior)

AFTER years of mechanical setbacks and prolonged interruptions that left Jamaica’s weather monitoring capabilities compromised, the country stepped into a new era of weather forecasting with a fully upgraded Doppler radar system, now operational and promising sharper insight into developing storms, heavier rainfall, and other potentially dangerous weather conditions.

At a cost of US$2.45 million, the Defender S850 Doppler Weather Radar was procured in 2020 under the Improving Climate Data and Information Management Project, with funds from the World Bank through the Climate Investment Fund. Located at Cooper’s Hill in St Andrew, it is expected to significantly strengthen the island’s ability to track weather systems, identify the nature and movement of precipitation, and provide meteorologists with more detailed information to improve forecasts and warnings.

According to Meteorological Service of Jamaica Principal Director Evan Thompson, the system should have initially been commissioned in 2022, following its installation in 2021, but was delayed due to mechanical failure.

“Testing and integration of the radar into the operations of the National Meteorological Centre ensued until the first quarter of 2022 when arrangements were being made for its commissioning on World Meteorological Day 2022. A mechanical failure, however, within the physical infrastructure forced a disruption of the service on March 9, two weeks before the commissioning was supposed to take place, and the radar remained offline through to late 2024,” Thompson told guests at the Radar Commissioning Ceremony and Hurricane Melissa commemorative book launch at the site last Wednesday.

“The rebuilding process resumed in September 2024 and was completed in June of 2025, shortly after the start of the hurricane season. This was timely, of course, in preparation for the development and the passage of Hurricane Melissa. The radar, however, experienced another disruption of service in November of 2025, shortly after the passage of Melissa, and this was not restored until March of this year, with partial functionality. But the comprehensive, full functionality of the radar was completed in September of 2026,” Thompson explained.

Experts describe the Defender S850 Doppler Weather Radar as a stateof- the-art, S-Band, meteorological system manufactured by Enterprise Electronics Corporation. It is engineered specifically for long-range severe weather detection, tracking, and early warning capabilities.

“The range of the radar is 480 kilometres, so it only goes as far as western Haiti; it doesn’t go that far east,” Thompson told the Jamaica Observer when asked whether the technology could detect and analyse weather systems from the time they move off the west coast of Africa, where most atmospheric disturbances that travel towards the Caribbean during the hurricane season originate.

The radar, he added, provides close monitoring over and immediately around Jamaica. He said the Defender S850 is an upgrade from that which was first installed in 1999 — the WSR-88D, which was the first of its kind in the Englishspeaking Caribbean. “It is an upgrade…it has further features, including what we call dual polarisation, so it allows for us to distinguish better between the different things that it is sensing — whether it may be rainfall or hail, or it might be dust particles that it is picking up. It helps us to distinguish better what is it we are identifying from the radar. There are some other features, but it is an upgrade to what we had,” he said.

According to Thompson, the new system is included in the Caribbean Meteorological Organisation (CMO) radar mosaic. “There are a number of radars operating, coordinated by the CMO, so they are operating throughout the region in different countries. Each radar is represented on a website so we are able to track systems moving right through the Caribbean. All of them together — if you show the radar imagery of the Caribbean — you could track systems from one radar to the next, so it allows for us to create that mosaic of all the radars so we can see them all represented in one picture,” Thompson explained.

“Now that we have our radar and it is fully operational, we have included it into that mosaic, so it fills the gap between the Dominican Republic and the Cayman Islands,” he added.

Thompson told the ceremony that the system has undergone several upgrades since its installation in 1999, but the recent upgrade marks a significant milestone for weather forecasting in Jamaica.

“The radar served well through many severe weather systems, including, of course, Hurricane Ivan in 2004, but eventually it experienced many downtimes from ageing parts, with those instances becoming more and more frequent. The time had come during the latter part of the decade to have it totally modernised or replaced. In 2016 the Government launched the Improving Climate Data and Information Management Project (ICDIMP), implemented by the PIOJ [Planning Institute of Jamaica], and this was a project amounting to a cost of about US$6.8 million, but almost half of that went to the radar. That was about US$3 million for a new S-band radar that was part of the project. This current radar was installed as part of that ICDIMP,” he said, adding that the radar station also benefited from the installation of a solar power solution to reduce energy costs, and a water-harvesting solution to ensure consistent provision of water.

The newly installed Defender S850 Doppler radar system was prioritised by the Government to strengthen Jamaica’s preparedness for increasingly intense storms.

In October 2025, as Hurricane Melissa bore down on Jamaica, real-time radar data gave meteorologists a critical, up-to-the-minute picture of the storm’s speed, path, and intensifying strength. The intelligence proved vital, allowing authorities to get ahead of the threat by directing evacuations, mobilising emergency services, and opening shelters before the monster storm made landfall.

“This investment made a major difference. It’s the first time in about seven years that Jamaica was able to rely on some of its own data capacity to forecast what was going to happen,” said Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda.

“For 10 days before the storm actually made landfall the Met Service was able to warn Jamaicans that this was coming without having to solely depend on the National Hurricane Center in Florida — and that makes a massive difference when we’re able to give our citizens early warning,” he added.

Last week, Thompson explained that radar technology gives forecasters lead time, “especially for flash floods on Jamaica’s short-switched rivers that satellite alone cannot give”.

“The radar is essential to our early warning system in Jamaica, facilitating real-time monitoring of precipitation over and around the country, determination of speed and direction of movement of rainfall cells, providing the data for short-term forecasting of severe weather systems, verifying the output of automatic weather stations and manual rain gauges through ground truthing, and being a valuable contributor to scientific evaluation and research,” he said.

Last Wednesday’s ceremony was also used to launch the Hurricane Melissa commemorative book, produced by the Meteorological Service and the Ministry of Water, Environment and Climate Change.

Samuda noted that the book serves as an important documentation for what the country went through, and will be available islandwide.

“It is the Hurricane Melissa – The Jamaican Chronicle.

This knowledge product is not technologically displayed here this afternoon but is important to document the work that the Met Service and, indeed, ODPEM [Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management] would have had to do pre- and post-Hurricane Melissa,” Samuda said.

“When I got assigned to this portfolio I asked for mountains and mountains of documents as we tried to learn the portfolio. Some of the things I asked about was, ‘Where was the chronicle post-Ivan?’ It wasn’t there. There are academic studies on Hurricane Gilbert, but nothing produced by us. So, the Government is documenting the incredibly destructive event so that future generations are, indeed, able to study, learn how we prepared, learn how we recovered,” Samuda said.

World.title: ON THE HORIZON
World.content:
SASHER-GAYE Henry- Wright, the senior Sunshine Girls head coach, says the technical staff will intensify training for the upcoming netball Horizon Series against the England Roses.

Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls and the England Roses are to meet in a four-match series, with the first two encounters set for the Copper Box Arena in London, England, on November 21 and 22. The final two matches are slated for the National Indoor Sports Centre (NISC) in St Andrew, Jamaica, on December 5 and 6.

Henry-Wright said the focus is on addressing areas for improvement and testing player combinations, with an objective to show consistent growth across the four games.

“We are impressed with the ladies who have been selected [for the series], and we’re looking forward now to the few weeks that we have remaining to really intensify the training as much as we can,” Henry-Wright said.

“You know, [we’re] looking at the areas. Really pushing hard in areas that we need some more improvement on, and looking at the combinations — what will work, what we can do differently — heading into this series.

“One of the big things we’re focusing on is improving. We know it’s going to be a keenly contested four matches but we definitely want to improve each game, and we really want to see some growth and improvement throughout all four games,” she added.

The Horizon Series is contested in honour of two netball icons — Jamaica’s Molly Rhone and England’s Jean Hornsby — and has quickly developed into a keen rivalry since its inception in 2024.

That inaugural series produced a classic, with Jamaica claiming a 2-1 victory after one match was tied, underlining the evenly matched nature of the two sides.

Last year, England were declared 2-0 winners of the series after both matches in Jamaica were cancelled due to the devastating passage of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, leaving unfinished business between the teams.

This year’s renewal carries added significance. It is expected to be Jamaica’s final major assignment before next year’s Netball World Cup, and comes on the back of a historic campaign for the Sunshine Girls who captured a silver medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

The coach admitted that naming the final squad was a difficult exercise given the depth of talent vying for positions, but said she is impressed with the group selected and confident in their ability to compete.

“So yes, the team has been named — and you know it was really a tough call to really name this team,” Henry-Wright said.

With the return of veteran shooter Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard, who rejoins the squad after an absence due to pregnancy and childbirth, and a blend of youth and experience throughout the court, Jamaica will be aiming to not only show improvement from game to game but also to reclaim the Rhone-Hornsby Trophy on home soil in December.

World.title: De Wever poised to offer his resignation as Belgian budget talks fail
World.content:
De Wever had ruled out starting the new year with a temporary budget, which would let the government continue with the same budget as last year’s.

Budget talks have been ongoing for weeks, with tensions emerging mostly between the Flemish socialists of Forward and the Francophone center-right Reformist Movement.

The former asked for more contributions from the highest incomes, through taxes, while the latter ruled that out and pushed back against a wider reform of value-added tax.

There were still “far too many taxes on the table,” David Clarinval, deputy prime minister for the Reformist Movement, told reporters when talks broke up. He didn’t rule out discussions resuming today.

Last November, Belgium’s budget talks also went into extra time. On this occasion, De Wever did not tender his resignation, but requested an extension to budget talks from King Philippe. The king granted him an additional 50 days to reach an agreement.

If Belgium is on track for snap elections, the country could lean toward extreme parties, with both the far-right Vlaams Belang and the far-left Workers Party performing well in the polls.

World.title: Has Shabana Mahmood won her immigration tussle?
World.content:
Are domestic political battles about to collide with diplomatic challenges for the prime minister?

As Andy Burnham jets off to the Caribbean, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood prepares to unveil one of the government’s most contentious policies: a major crackdown on legal migration.

A year after the plans were first proposed, Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy look at whether Labour has quashed the internal rebellion and how much influence Angela Rayner has had on the PM’s position.

Plus, as the Commonwealth Summit gets underway in Antigua, the prime minister has issues to address on the international front – from potential reparations for slavery to US and Chinese influence over the Caribbean.

World.title: Canada, coffins and confessionals
World.content:
The jet lag has barely worn off, but Brussels is already grappling with what its new relationship with Canada could actually look like.

After the 48-hour whirlwind EU-Canada summit in Montreal, Prime Minister Mark Carney has given the EU six months to hash out what “associate membership” actually means. On the show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Nick Vinocur unpack the deals struck at the summit and what lies ahead for the relations between the two powers.

Next, after last month’s unwieldy European Council summit drew criticism of its president, Antonio Costa, he’s doubling down on his push to secure a budget by 2027. This week, his head of cabinet Pedro Lourtie will be holding so-called “confessionals” with national governments to get a sense of where they stand.

And finally, Europe’s coffin makers are afraid Chinese competitors could be the death of their business.
