World.title: Allies fear Trump will target NATO in case of midterm loss
World.content:
“Usually what happens to lame duck presidents is a mix of venting frustrations and adventurism in foreign policy,” said one senior European defense official. And attacking NATO “seems to be a consistent part of [the] Trump worldview.”

White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales told POLITICO that “President Trump has done more for NATO than anyone else,” citing his successes in securing agreements by allies to raise defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, bolster U.S. military presence in Greenland, and efforts to end Russia's all-out war in Ukraine.

Yet he “remains firm that our NATO allies should have been there for the United States” over the war in Iran, she said, adding: “The President will never settle for the West’s managed decline and will continue to unapologetically advance our interests at home and abroad.”

Democrats are widely expected to win the House of Representatives and potentially flip the Senate, while Trump’s personal approval ratings have fallen to his lowest on record.

The worries underscore growing transatlantic tensions after a U.S. cutoff of Starlink satellite services for Ukraine and a fresh rapprochement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin weeks before the midterms. Further attacks would deal a fresh blow to NATO, just as Russia steps up its sabotage campaign and so-called hybrid war across Europe.

“He could be very pissed off,” said one of the NATO diplomats. If so, “he’ll be very harsh.”

World.title: EU and Canada’s 6-month test of commitment
World.content:
The test of that plan comes in six months, when the European Commission will meet with the Canadian government to see what progress has been made. One diplomat involved in the talks, granted anonymity to speak freely, said the meeting, which will be held in March before next year’s EU-Canada summit in Brussels, should make clear how far the relationship can develop and whether Ottawa is really on track for associate membership.

In the months ahead, there will be plenty of issues that could distract EU leaders. Governments must negotiate the bloc’s next seven-year budget, amid deep divisions over its size and spending priorities. Plus, a series of elections in some of the EU's biggest countries, including Spain, France, Italy and Poland, will make concentrating on Canada a tall order.

Deal first, definition later

The joint declaration signed in Montreal commits both sides to defining the concept of “associate membership” by their 2027 summit. In the meantime, they have a slate of agreements and work plans to put into practice.

Carney speaks during an interview with POLITICO at the Port of Montreal Tower in Montreal, Canada on Oct. 30, 2026. | Adil Boukind for POLITICO (@adilboukind on IG)

That includes a digital trade agreement and a competition deal signed in Montreal, plus Canada’s participation in the EU’s high-performance computing partnership. They also agreed on a new framework for cooperation between EU border force Frontex and the Canada Border Services Agency. Ottawa said it intends to join the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan facility.

The declaration sets out further work on critical raw materials and energy, including a feasibility study into long-term liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and exploring ways to jointly stockpile strategic resources. It also calls for cooperation on subsea cables, artificial intelligence and research, closer financial links, Arctic security, and disaster response. Canada and the EU will begin talks on deeper Canadian participation in Erasmus+, the EU’s education and youth program.

The summit also saw the launch of the Alliance for the Future, a broader partnership plan that could eventually include Japan, South Korea and Australia. It aims to build resilient supply chains and coordinate on economic security, so partner nations do not inadvertently harm one another with trade measures as they respond to Chinese overcapacity and U.S. tariffs.

World.title: Russian strikes leave thousands without power in Ukraine, says Zelenskyy
World.content:
Zelenskyy’s comments came as Russian authorities reported a “massive” Ukrainian drone strike overnight on an industrial facility in the Nizhny Novgorod region.

“A massive drone attack occurred overnight and this morning in the Nizhny Novgorod region: more than a hundred drones were destroyed,” Gleb Nikitin, the region’s governor, wrote on Telegram on Sunday.

“According to preliminary reports, there were no casualties,” he said, adding that an industrial facility in the Kstovsky district sustained “significant damage.”

“During the restoration process, temporary power outages and reduced hot water and heating services are possible in certain sections of the utility networks supplying residential buildings,” he wrote.

Nikitin did not specify which industrial facility had been attacked. The NORSI oil refinery is located in the region.

On Friday, the local governor of Russia’s Samara region blamed Ukraine for an early morning drone attack that struck an oil refinery in Novokuibyshevsk city.

The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Kyiv agreed to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries until after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump.

Ukraine paused drone strikes on Russian oil refineries for 72 hours when Trump announced an energy ceasefire in October, but the Kremlin continued to bombard Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

World.title: Commission backs Tusk as he vows no compromise in court showdown
World.content:
The Commission said it was closely monitoring developments and, in a carefully worded statement to POLITICO, appeared to show support for Tusk’s position.

“The Polish Constitutional Tribunal needs to be able to function in accordance with the Polish constitution and the case law of the Court of Justice of the EU,” Commissioner for Democracy, Justice and the Rule of Law Michael McGrath said.

“This matters for every Polish citizen, and it is for the Polish authorities to ensure that,” McGrath added, stating that “the Venice Commission has been clear that appointing the new judges lies within the power of the Sejm [Poland’s lower house of parliament].”

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk vowed Saturday night not to back down on the dispute. “In some matters there can be no compromise,” Tusk said in an address to the nation, comparing calls for reconciliation to a thief demanding to keep half the contents of a stolen handbag.

“We have waited too long for the treasure of an independent, democratic Poland to be frightened into retreat,” Tusk said.

The prime minister also targeted Nawrocki, who turned his plane around mid-flight en route to Senegal and returned to Warsaw, where he pushed his way into the Tribunal shortly after midnight Saturday, confronting judges challenging its leadership.

World.title: UK’s future lies in EU, says Rachel Reeves
World.content:
Reeves added that while she believes “Britain’s future lies in the European Union”, it was “incumbent on supporters of our re-entry to make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right.”

Last week, Burnham expressed an openness to restarting free movement between the U.K and the EU. He also said he’d like to see Britain rejoin the bloc in his lifetime — but ruled out a move to reverse Brexit in the current parliament.

At the last election, Labour’s manifesto — which Reeves helped to draw up — said a Labour government would stay outside the EU.

But at the Labour Party’s conference in September, Burnham called for closer links with the bloc.

Reeves’ intervention comes ahead of a leaders’ summit later this month where she said “at a minimum” she hoped to see confirmation of a youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for.

At the Nov. 20 summit, the EU and the U.K. hope to sign off on a set of agreements ranging from trade to climate regulations.

World.title: Ryanair eyes cost cuts as it faces a €2 billion rise in its fuel bill next year
World.content:
Ryanair reported a net profit of €2.15 billion for the period between April and September 2026, the first half of its financial year ending March 2027.

 

The result was 15% below the same period last year.

This came as unhedged jet fuel prices doubled while fares also fell, although passenger numbers increased. The airline is reviewing costs as it prepares for a further rise in its fuel bill next year.

On a per-share basis, the Irish airline's first-half diluted earnings fell 14% to €2.05 per share. In the same period, revenue rose 3% to €10.08bn and passenger numbers grew by 6% to 125.8 million, but fares fell by 4%.

Ryanair said the Middle East conflict had made consumers more hesitant and led them to book later as operating costs increased by 10% to €7.69 billion.

The results reflect only part of the rise in fuel prices as Ryanair has hedged 80% of its fuel needs for the year ending March 2027, using financial contracts to lock in prices in advance.

This has helped protect its earnings, but the price of the remaining 20% doubled.

A €2 billion fuel bill increase

According to Ryanair, its fuel bill could rise by around €2 billion in the financial year ending March 2028, based on current forward prices.

"Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict, we expect jet-fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027," CEO Michael O'Leary said.

O'Leary warned that cheaper fuel hedges would expire ahead of summer 2027, leaving European airlines facing much higher bills.

He also previously warned that European airfares could rise by up to 20% in 2027 in an exclusive interview with Euronews in late October.

However, Ryanair expects higher fares and cuts in competitors' capacity to fall short of fully covering its extra fuel costs.

To address the elevated costs, Ryanair is reviewing possible cost-cutting measures, including temporary pay freezes, lower crew-to-passenger ratios and greater use of AI across operations and support teams.

The airline also announced an €800 million share buyback programme, starting in February 2027 and expected to run for around 10 months, subject to market conditions.

Demand for October–December remains strong, with fares running modestly above last year, but late bookings make the outlook harder to predict.

Ryanair said it was too early to give a full-year profit forecast, citing uncertainty over conflicts, fuel prices, the wider economy and European air traffic control disruptions.

In September, Ryanair announced it would reduce its winter schedule to limit exposure to unhedged fuel costs, cutting its full-year passenger target from 216 million to 214 million.

Ryanair's share price was up by 2% in Dublin in early trading on Monday.

World.title: Prada champions the human touch and not AI slop for their new Christmas campaign
World.content:
As generative AI continues to pollute the internet and advertising, certain luxury houses are betting on human craft when it comes to their Christmas marketing.

 

Call it "effort signaling" all you want; their efforts are to be applauded at a time when cost-cutting initiatives result in mediocre and bar-lowering slop.

One luxury brand choosing to celebrate human creativity this year is Italian fashion house Prada, which has swapped AI-generated dross for traditional, hand-drawn illustration for their new Christmas campaign.

Combining live-action footage with hand-drawn characters, the ‘Drawing Prada: Animated By Hand’ campaign has enlisted veteran animator John Pomeroy to lead a team of artists to bring animated characters and environment to life.

“That sense of touch expresses a fundamental notion of humanity, and a connection with craft that always lies at the very heart of Prada’s approach to creation,” according to a press release.

The campaign, developed under the creative direction of Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons, with Ferdinando Verderi overseeing campaign creative direction, sees each frame drawn by hand and the live-action scenes photographed by Glen Luchford.

Check out the campaign below, which features a cast of celebrity ambassadors including Sadie Sink, Maya Hawke, Chen Haoyu, Luther Ford and Kelvin Harrison Jr.:

Best known for his work at Disney, Pomeroy has contributed to iconic films including the Oscar-nominated Winnie the Pooh and Tigger Too (1974), The Rescuers (1977), Pete’s Dragon (1977) and The Fox and the Hound (1981).

After his departure from Disney, he established independent animation studio Don Bluth Productions, creating films like The Secret of NIMH and The Land Before Time.

He later returned to Disney, where he worked on films such as Pocahontas, Fantasia 2000, Atlantis: The Lost Empire and Treasure Planet. He later worked as an animator on films like Curious George, several Tom and Jerry films, and Space Jam: A New Legacy.

Still from Prada's Christmas campaign 2026 Prada - YouTube

In a behind-the-scenes film accompanying the campaign, Pomeroy explained his commitment to traditional technique.

“I learnt my craft with pencil and paper, through traditional, analogue drawing. We’ve remained faithful to that approach and want to pass it on to future generations,” said Pomeroy.

“There’s a very distinct and purposeful reason to do hand-drawn animation, and that’s to see that there’s value in it and that hand-drawn and handcrafted work is still alive in the world today.”

Prada's ad comes at a time when other brands aren't caring as much. Their 2026 campaign feels like a direct response to those still indulging in a tech which is threatening human creativity and livelihoods.

Unlike Coca-Cola and their AI-generated Christmas s, which faced criticism in both 2024 and 2025 (since the brand did not learn from their mistake the first time around), certain companies are starting to understand how fed up potential consumers are with AI.

More and more people have grown wary of the pervasive tech and there is a growing backlash towards the rise of AI – leading younger, digital-savvy generations to appreciate the value of human creativity while older generations embrace the traditional crafts in a bid to push back against soulless imagery.

Moreover, the "not-made-by-AI" approach has become a massive selling point, and Prada have understood the value of delivering an antidote. Their new campaign has sparked enthusiasm online, with users commenting: "Love it when ads go AI free, much respects to the artists"; "Now this, THIS is how you make an ad"; "Normally not interested in Prada, but I'm reading "Animated by Hand" and I'm in"; and "Such a breath of fresh air seeing something with soul again".

It goes to show that something as simple as hand-drawn illustration can still create enthusiasm.

Your move Coca-Cola. Let's see if a multi-billion company can be bothered to pay real animators this year or if they'll churn out yet another deeply derivative campaign based on the works of artists, used without permission.

World.title: Can the EU’s energy solutions lower your bills? Take our poll
World.content:
EU energy ministers met energy on October 29 and confronted a painful reality: despite massive efforts to wean the bloc off Russian fuel, the EU remains entirely at the mercy of the next global supply disruption.

 

Why? Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it supplied around 45% of the EU’s gas imports, compared with just 12% in 2025. To replace it, Europe has turned to more expensive liquefied natural gas (LNG) from countries such as the US. Meanwhile, the conflict in the Middle East (with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz) is pushing prices higher as Europe competes with Asian countries for alternative imports.

To provide immediate relief to consumers this winter, member states intend to lower utility bills by reducing electricity network charges and cutting state-imposed taxes on power. Additionally, the plan introduces incentives for households and businesses to shift high-energy activities to cheaper, off-peak hours. To secure physical supplies, the plan also mandates stricter coordination of emergency gas stockpiles across member states to prevent regional shortages as temperatures drop.

Can these measures be enough? Are energy bills reaching a breaking point for households? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. The results will be featured across XL's EU-wide coverage, including videos, articles and newsletters, and will help shape our reporting as we examine how Europe can secure its position in the age of artificial intelligence.

World.title: Dutch MP proposes law banning 'harmful addictive design features' on all digital platforms
World.content:
A Dutch MP has proposed a new law banning "the most harmful addictive design features" on digital services, such as infinitive scrolling, autoplay videos, push notifications and manipulative algorithms.

 

Barbara Kathmann, an MP from the Dutch Parliament’s main opposition party, the centre-left Progressief Nederland (PRO), submitted the proposal on Monday 2 November, saying the ban "protects both children and adults".

BigTech platforms are facing mounting global pushback over concerns that their services are designed in harmful ways that encourage addiction and other destructive behaviours. Meta, TikTok and SnapChat, among others, have all been brought to court in recent years by rights groups.

Kathmann is working with parliamentarians across Europe in Germany, France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, Italy, and Portugal, who want to regulate digital platforms and address their alleged harmfully designed services.

"People need to regain control over their own time and attention. Manipulative tricks online can have a major impact on our mental and physical health, brain development and attention span, now and for future generations," said Kathmann.

"The Netherlands must therefore show leadership now and be the first in the world to ban addictive design. We can only stand up to Big Tech’s manipulative tricks if we protect everyone."

The proposed law would subject digital platforms to a "fairness by design" duty of care, requiring them to prove their online services are not addictive and instead make sure their features are designed to be "fair and non-manipulative".

'Addictive algorithms manipulate our minds'

This is not the first time a Dutch politician has submitted a proposal on the topic.

In 2023, a report by Dutch MEP Kim van Sparrentak, also from PRO, was adopted by the European Parliament calling for the European Commission to put forward a proposal for an addictive design ban.

She backed today’s proposal in the Dutch Parliament saying, "With this law, the Netherlands is taking the lead in Europe, and we can finally build a safe and non-addictive internet.

"No self-discipline can beat Big Tech’s addictive tricks. Every day that we fail to take action, we let addictive algorithms manipulate our minds and in the long run our democracies, as they keep offering the most extreme content to keep us hooked.

"And Europe is failing to take action. Companies like Meta are filling their pockets with money earned by exploiting your attention and the way you are wired, whilst the tech lobby is sharpening its knives to water down the rules."

The Commission is due to table a proposal this November under its Digital Fairness Act, with a EU-wide addictive design ban a key measure among several others aimed at enhancing consumer protections in Europe.

The Act is complemented by other EU legislation in the pipeline, such as the EU Kids Act, which aims to protect children online by shifting the burden of responsibility from parents to digital platforms, requiring them to make their services safe by design.

The EU Digital Services Act, which has been in force since 2022, combines several measures requiring very large online platforms (VLOPS) such as Meta and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) like Google to detect, remove and prevent illegal content, hate speech and dangerous products.

World.title: Mbappé’s ‘Chinese dictator’ comment: How do Chinese people react?
World.content:
French football star Kylian Mbappé has apologised after comments about a meme depicting him as Chinese leader Mao Zedong sparked a backlash in China.

 

In a video clip, Mbappé was asked about his favourite meme of himself. He replied that it was “a video someone made of a guy ... I think he was a Chinese dictator”, before an altered image showed his face on Mao’s body.

The controversy has spread across Chinese social media. At least three Chinese companies have terminated brand deals with the footballer, and China's Foreign Ministry has responded to the incident.

In Beijing, some residents said they were unsure what Mbappé had said, while others believe he should apologise again.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV also pulled a Real Madrid La Liga match from its Sunday broadcast schedule following the controversy.

World.title: German MPs and ministers warned iPhones have been targeted by spyware
World.content:
Germany’s digital minister, Karsten Wildberger, has confirmed that members of the Bundestag and the federal government received warnings from Apple that their iPhones may have been targeted by spyware.

 

Speaking on ARD’s Bericht aus Berlin on Sunday, Wildberger said there had been "a notification from Apple that certain devices may have been compromised with so-called spyware".

According to a letter from the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) seen by Wildberger, the alerts began reaching the affected phones on 29 October. They warned that Apple had detected an attack using "mercenary spyware".

Wildberger said the BSI had "reacted super quickly" and written to everyone affected about what to do. He did not say how many politicians had received the alerts, or who they were.

According to Wildberger, the BSI advised those affected to assume - as a precaution - that their device may have been compromised, because the alerts do not show whether an attack succeeded.

Euronews has contacted the BSI for comment.

What is an Apple threat notification?

Apple sends threat notifications when it believes that a user has been individually targeted by mercenary spyware, which it describes as "vastly more sophisticated than regular cybercriminal activity".

Apple says Mercenary spyware is harder to detect and prevent, but the vast majority of users will never be targeted.

The warnings appear on the iPhone’s lock screen and in its settings, and are also sent by email.

According to the BSI, spyware of this kind can give attackers access to messages, including those sent on encrypted apps, as well as to calls, contacts, calendars and location data. It can also switch on a phone’s microphone and camera.

Neither Apple nor the German authorities have said who may be behind the attack.

World.title: Paris riots: France investigates after petrol bomb sets officer on fire
World.content:
France has opened an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces during protests against the rising cost of living in Paris on Saturday.

 

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across France for a third weekend of demonstrations. Clashes erupted in Paris and other cities, with police reporting attacks involving projectiles and incendiary devices.

Dramatic footage circulating on social media shows a police officer performing crowd-control duties when his leg suddenly catches fire after an explosive device goes off at his feet.

Two colleagues struggle to extinguish the flames, while a man in a white T-shirt and straw hat rushes to help. They said they had singled out three individuals dressed in black in the style of Black Block protesters as suspects.

World.title: Serbia remembers 16 victims of Novi Sad railway station collapse
World.content:
Serbia marked the second anniversary of the deadly collapse at Novi Sad railway station, as thousands of students and supporters marched through the rain to honour the 16 people killed.

 

The silent procession ended outside the station, where participants laid wreaths and placed red hearts bearing the victims' names. Others lit candles in their memory. On 1 November 2024, a concrete canopy above the station entrance collapsed in the northern Serbian city, killing 16 people.

The tragedy sparked a student-led movement calling for accountability and an investigation into alleged corruption and negligence during the station's renovation. Thirteen people, including a former government minister, were charged, but no trial has begun.

Sunday's commemoration came just a week after the movement's Student List won Serbia's snap parliamentary election on 25 October, defeating the bloc led by Aleksandar Vučić. Preliminary results gave the students 140 of the 250 seats in parliament.

For those gathered in Novi Sad, the election result has raised hopes that the case will finally progress and those responsible will be held to account.

World.title: Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean
World.content:
The ratification of a maritime agreement between Libya and Turkey is stoking tensions across the eastern Mediterranean. Athens has condemned the deal as illegal, amid wider regional concern over Turkey’s growing influence.

Advertising

On Thursday, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis criticised the deal, which Libya’s eastern-based parliament ratified on 20 October, calling it “blatantly illegal, null and void”. The agreement sets out an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between Libya and Turkey that encompasses the Greek island of Crete.

Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli signed the agreement in 2019, but the rival administration in eastern Libya had refused to ratify it until October.

“I don’t think it’s possible to overestimate its political and symbolic importance. The whole world knows that Turkey has been pursuing this parliamentary ratification,” said Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank.

“People thought that eastern Libya was a reliable friend of the enemies of Turkey, and that the process was going to drag on for several years,” he added.

According to Harchaoui, the ratification is a bold step in Ankara’s broader strategy to assert its influence across the region, known as the Blue Homeland doctrine.

Turkey courts Libya's rival factions in bid to further Mediterranean ambitions

“We should never forget that the exclusive economic zone is a corollary of the Blue Homeland doctrine,” he said. “And the Blue Homeland doctrine is really about nationalism, commitment to projecting Turkish influence across all of Africa, across the sea.”

Divided country

Libya has been divided since Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a Nato-backed uprising in 2011. The Government of National Unity rules the west from Tripoli, while the Government of National Stability holds sway in the east from Benghazi.

Ankara has long backed the Tripoli-based government, but it has recently set out to win over the Benghazi administration, hoping to bridge Libya’s deep divide. Benghazi’s approval of the maritime deal is seen as a direct result of these diplomatic efforts.

“It’s one of the most critical diplomatic achievements recently in the Mediterranean,” said Elem Eyrice Tepeciklioglu, professor of African studies at the Social Sciences University of Ankara. “This agreement is also a reflection of Turkey’s efforts to engage with both parts of the country.”

Tepeciklioglu expects the EEZ to bring economic rewards. “The region covered by the deal has significant energy resources. So it’s important for energy exploration as well,” she said.

Regional resistance

Ankara now faces strong opposition in the region. Greece, Cyprus and Egypt have all condemned the agreement, arguing that it encroaches on their territorial waters, while the European Union and the United States have also voiced concerns.

With vast energy reserves believed to lie beneath the disputed waters, Federico Donelli, professor of international relations at the University of Trieste in Italy, warns that tensions could rise.

Turkey and Egypt turn page on decade of friction with show of friendship

“The more immediate risk is an increase in diplomatic tension and especially competing activities in disputed maritime areas,” he said. “So exploration licences, seismic surveys, naval deployment and even some naval drills could be used to reinforce competing claims, and the possibility of incidents could increase.”

Donelli suggests that Italy, which has close ties to both Turkey and Libya, could play a key role in easing tensions with its fellow EU members Greece and Cyprus. Meanwhile, Ankara is reaching out to Cairo and has invited Egypt to join the maritime pact.

Libya expert Aya Burweila of the Athens-based Center for Hellenic and Mediterranean Studies says the ratification caught Greece off guard.

“For Athens, symbolically, it’s a huge blow. I don’t think they expected it,” she said. “If you see the map, you know, it basically cuts across Crete’s maritime waters.”

Despite Greece’s tough rhetoric, Burweila believes diplomacy can prevail. “It’s [the agreement] more symbolic than anything else, because I don’t see how it can be enforced,” she said. “So I think this is an opening for negotiations with Egypt and Greece and other countries. And I think these talks are already happening between Libya and Egypt.”

France hosts global push to promote stability in Libya, keep elections on track

Israeli concern

The agreement also risks inflaming tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have already been sharpened by Ankara’s support for Hamas and the war in Gaza. Israel is increasingly worried about Turkey’s regional ambitions. In September, Israeli Navy commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel warned of Turkey’s growing assertiveness in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Harchaoui believes Israel’s concerns are likely to grow. “Turkey was able to pull off an extraordinary win. If you look at just the area of influence, it has almost won eastern Libya. Turkey is going to just sell more weapons; it’s going to build more airstrips, so it’s literally expanding… So they [Israel] have to decide: are they going to remain in the rhetorical space or do something about it?”

World.title: For US Democrats, climate policy is now about energy bills
World.content:
Climate change has all but disappeared from Democrats' campaign pitches, replaced by promises to lower electricity bills. But what would the party actually do on climate if it wins control of Congress?

President Donald Trump's administration has gutted US climate policy. Yet even as wildfires, record heat waves and flooding hit communities across the country, Democrats are keeping quiet about global warming on the midterm campaign trail.

Instead, candidates are packaging climate policy as an affordability issue, stressing how Americans are struggling to afford gas, groceries and to insure their homes against climate-fueled weather extremes.

Take Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas, who represents the party's best chance at winning the race in the Republican stronghold in nearly 40 years. Though he makes some mention of climate change on his campaign's "energy and environment" page, that is not his focus.

His pledges center around lowering energy costs, providing emergency relief for spiking utility bills, making data centers pay for their own grid upgrades and growing energy sector jobs.

This aligns with analysis from nonprofit news organization Inside Climate News showing that the Democrats have dramatically reduced mentions of climate change in their press releases and campaign messaging.

The Trump administration has pushed back against renewables in favor of fossil fuels, but rooftop solar is gaining popularity with US homeowners Image: Mario Tama/Getty Images

"We've entered an interesting space where climate policy doesn't need to be called climate policy to be climate policy," Max Frankel, executive director of the SEEC Institute, a nonprofit that helps guide climate policy in Congress, told DW.

What would a Democratic win mean for climate policy?

Most forecasts project Democrats winning the House and a narrow majority in the Senate in the November 3 election. But without control of the White House, passing any legislation will be difficult and almost any climate policy will have to be a bipartisan endeavor, say analysts.

Given that and the Democrats' messaging-shift to affordability over climate, few experts expect a fully resurrected Inflation Reduction Act. Introduced under the Democrats to create incentives for building clean energy projects, the legislation was largely decimated by President Trump's major tax law.

But Democrats may try to bring back some climate-friendly IRA provisions, particularly measures aimed at lowering household energy costs, analysts told DW. Those include incentives for home energy-efficiency upgrades and appliances like heat pumps to replace oil and gas heaters that typically help bring down household energy bills.

Politicians could also expand an IRA manufacturing tax credit for solar, batteries, and critical minerals that largely survived. One bipartisan bill proposes extending it to include nuclear fusion components.

"It's not going to be anything at the scale of the IRA," Adrian Deveny, founder of Climate Vision, a policy firm dedicated to decarbonization, told DW. "It's like singles and doubles as opposed to a home run, which is still worth doing."

A first bipartisan test over building infrastructure

In a rare area of agreement between the parties, some Democrats and Republicans are already backing a reform bill they're hoping to pass before a new Congress is sworn in January.

If enacted, the bill could make it significantly easier to build major infrastructure projects in the US, including long-distance transmission lines that carry electricity between regions but that currently take years to build because of complex permitting rules.

US turns its back on EVs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The biggest beneficiary of building more transmission will be wind and solar power, because the best and cheapest way to generate wind and solar energy tends to be far away from cities," said David Spence, a political scientist at the University of Texas who researches the politics of energy regulation. "And so, they need transmission to get their product to market."

But environmental groups say the bill could also speed up the approval of fossil fuel projects.

If Democrats win big in the midterms there might be some "peeling off their support for that bill because they think they can do better in the next Congress," said Spence.

Looking to the 2028 presidential elections

Major new federal climate legislation is a long shot before the 2028 presidential election. And afterwards it would likely require Democrats winning the White House, the Senate and the House. While no 2028 platforms have been released yet, policy experts expect a few ideas to feature prominently.

One is data centers. Opposition to the energy-guzzling infrastructure being built en masse to power the AI boom is mounting across the country. Half of Americans are now against data centers being built close to their homes, according to a poll from news outlet Politico.

"I'm sure every candidate is going to have a platform with a focus on data center constraints on some level, as a way to address affordability," Deveny, who led negotiations on the IRA, said. "And that's the entry point for climate policy."

There are several ideas currently circulating — including a proposal by Democrats Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to pause data center construction — as well as ending tax breaks for data centers and imposing new taxes on their electricity use.

Wind energy has taken a hit under President Trump, who has incentivized energy companies to cancel offshore wind leases Image: Steve Helber/AP Photo/picture alliance

Democrats may also seek to restore the IRA's clean energy tax incentives. This year, more than 150 legislators co-sponsored the so-called Energy Bills Relief Act designed to reinstate IRA clean energy tax incentives, reform how transmission permits are granted, and make data centers pay for the grid upgrades they need. The bill is unlikely to pass anytime soon but offers a window into what Democrats might support.

"By far, the biggest consensus — to the extent there's anything remotely resembling a consensus — is restoring a lot of the clean energy tax incentives from the IRA," Deveny said. "Not everybody supports that but it is a highly supported idea amongst most congressional Democrats."

Support for other proposals include a new federal program to help insurers cover climate-driven disasters and bring down hefty premiums, as well as so-called climate superfunds. This would require fossil fuel companies to contribute to the costs of damage caused by extreme weather and adapting to the risks of climate change.

Vermont and New York both passed legislation to create funds, although a federal judge blocked New York's.

The 2028 presidential race is expected to begin a few weeks after the midterms end, bringing a fresh round of policy ideas and debates. A new president typically gets to drive the legislative agenda in the beginning of their term if their party also wins Congress.

"As long as the consensus is that clean energy is the cheaper source of energy, and it's going to provide stability over the long term for high energy costs — there's a million ways you can propose solutions through that lens," Deveny said.

World.title: US: Nine killed in Florida jet crash
World.content:
A Learjet plane crashed near a busy road in a residential neighborhood in Palm Beach County, leaving all nine people on board dead and a large crater on ground.

A private jet crashed in a residential area of Cresthaven in the US state of Florida's Palm Beach County on Sunday, killing all nine people on board.

The Learjet 60 business jet nose-dived into the south Florida neighborhood and exploded.

Videos circulating on social media, recorded by people from their vehicles, shows the plane making a loud whooshing sound as it rapidly descends to hit the side of a road and erupts into a large fireball.

The plane's descent in the footage resembled — as Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described — "a missile going down."

A thick plume of black and gray smoke is seen rising against houses, which were narrowly missed.

The crash left a crater on the road, with flames flickering around it.

What do we know about the Florida plane crash?

The plane had departed from Austin-Bergstrom International ⁠Airport in Texas and was bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

It was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 10,660 meters) when the pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation. They requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).

Just moments after, the jet dived steeply, at 10,000 feet per minute initially and then at 20,000 feet per minute to reach up to 30,000 feet per minute — a speed exceeding the plane's design limits — as per air traffic control recording and flight tracking data.

Last words from the cockpit — 'We are out of time'

LiveATC, which provides live air traffic control broadcasts, captured the harrowing final moments of the crash in an audio recording from a Miami air traffic control center.

A person from the plane's cockpit is heard saying "Mayday, mayday, we are descending 10,000 feet per minute."

The person declares an "emergency" just seconds later, urgently reporting a descent of 20,000 feet per minute.

"We're going to crash into ⁠the ground" the voice from the cockpit says and then goes on to report that the descent was at 22,000 feet and the plane was banking 60 degrees.

A scream is heard before the final words from the cockpit — "We are out of time."

Investigation underway

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the crash occurred at 12.50 pm local time and described the incident as a "horrific tragedy."

The cause of the crash and the identities of those on board the plane were not immediately known.

The National Transportation Safety Board has launched a probe into the incident.

There are no immediate reports of anyone on the ground being injured or killed.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at a press briefing that some 600 people were being evacuated from the area and relocated to two ​shelters.

A 34-year-old man accused of having killed two people while racing with his car through a pedestrian zone in the eastern city of Leipzig in May is going on trial on Monday.

The accused has also been charged with 85 counts of attempted murder.

State prosecutors argue that the man planned the attack with the intent of killing people with his car, which reached speeds of up to 90 kmh (56 mph) during the rampage.

A 63-year-old woman and a 77-year-old man were killed in the incident.

The accused is said to have checked into a psychiatric clinic of his own free will a month before the attack and to have been discharged at his own wish a few days prior to it.

However, a psychiatric assessment has found no indications of diminished capacity on his part.

The trial has been scheduled to last until July of next year.

11/02/2026 November 2, 2026 Cyclone Murasu likely to make landfall in Andhra Pradesh

After cyclone Arnab, India is bracing for cyclone Murasu which is moving along the coast of the southeastern state of Andhra Pradesh, packing winds ranging between 100 and 120 kilometers per hour (75 miles per hour).

According to the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD), Murasu is expected to make landfall on Tuesday.

Thousands of people have been evacuated along India's eastern coast. Schools and colleges have been closed as heavy rainfall is expected.

Meanwhile, the IMD has issued an orange alert for six districts and a yellow alert for five districts in the neighboring state of Telangana. An orange alert means heavy rainfall of 11-20 cm.

IMD has also warned of the possibility of Murasu intensifying further into a very severe cyclonic storm before reaching the Andhra Pradesh coastline.

World.title: Kimi Antonelli makes history as youngest F1 champion
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion and Italy's first since 1953 when he finished third in Sunday's thrilling and crash-hit Mexico City Grand Prix.

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.

"I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.

His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

He was then mobbed by his pit crew.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953 Image: Claudia Greco/REUTERS

'An incredible season'

"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old said.

Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

"I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he said. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams."

Antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

Antonelli said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved Image: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.

He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.

After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.

The final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

World.title: South Korea to pour billions into AI
World.content:
President Lee Jae Myung has presented his record-breaking budget proposal for 2027, including major investments in AI and other tech.

South Korea will pour nearly $16 billion on artificial intelligence and semiconductors, South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung said in his annual budget address to parliament.

"We will invest 21.3 trillion won (€14.3 billion, $15.97 billion), nearly twice ​this year's amount, in AI and the three megaprojects of semiconductors, physical ​AI and ‌AI data centres," Lee said on Monday.

He added that 4.7 trillion won will be invested to bolster "frontier AI development projects, with the aim of achieving world-leading performance for our own AI model, a national strategic asset."

South Korea unveils record budget proposal for 2027

The Lee administration has unveiled a record budget proposal for next year, featuring a 12.8% increase in government spending to 820.9 trillion won (€551.5 billion, $615.62 billion).

The proposal needs parliamentary approval, and Lee's party, the Democratic Party of Korea (DPK), currently holds the majority.

South Korea is Asia's fourth-largest economy and home to two of the world's biggest memory chip makers — Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

The AI boom has sent demand for memory chips soaring.

South Korea recorded faster-than-expected economic growth in the third quarter, driven by chip exports and investment.

Exports totaled $930 billion from January to October and are on track to surpass $1 trillion this year, making South Korea the fourth country to achieve the milestone after the United States, China and Germany.

11/02/2026 November 2, 2026 Ukraine says Russia used ceasefire to rearm, rotate troops, Kremlin says 'it's normal practice'

Ukraine's General Staff on Monday blasted Russia's actions during a six-day humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, saying the Kremlin had used the break in fighting to rearm its forces and rotate troops in the front-line area.

In a social media post on X, the General Staff wrote: "Defense Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," adding, "The enemy, by contrast, used the humanitarian pause to improve its positions."

Residents in the Kherson region were warned to be vigilant and told to pay attention to air raid sirens, noting that an intensification of attacks was to be expected after Russia used the brief pause to "strengthen its capabilities."

In Moscow, the Kremlin brushed off the critique, saying Ukraine, "could have used the ceasefire to re-group as well," calling such activity, "normal practice."

World.title: German police investigating after needles found in Halloween candy
World.content:
German police said they received phone calls with reports about sharp objects concealed in Halloween candy.

Needles or other sharp metal objects have been found in sweets that children collected while trick-or-treating for Halloween, German police said Sunday.

Police believe most or all of the objects, which also included metal screws, were placed intentionally to cause harm.

Incidents were reported in Thuringia, Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Lower Saxony, and Rhineland-Palatinate, among other locations, police said.

In one of the cases in the southern city of Nuremberg, police said a child had bitten down on a needle while eating a piece of chocolate. The child was unharmed.

In two separate cases in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg, police said the needles had been concealed as such that they were not visible from the outside.

In several of the cases, police have opened investigations into attempted aggravated assault.

No suspects have been identified.

World.title: Foro World in Progress 2026 de Barcelona, en directo | Sánchez: “Debemos recuperar la confianza en la alta velocidad cuanto antes y cueste lo que cueste”
World.content:
Salvador Illa: “La administración de EE UU es mala, quiere destruir Europa y hay que hacerle frente” | Collboni: “La política tiene que transformar la incertidumbre en confianza” | El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, interviene en la primera jornada

El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha comenzado su intervención en el foro WIP haciendo referencia al accidente ferroviario de Urda. Ha dicho que la principal obligación del Gobierno es “recuperar la confianza quebrada en la alta velocidad cuanto antes y cueste lo que cueste”. Antes, el presidente de la Generalitat, Salvador Illa, ha afirmado con rotundidad que la actual “administración estadounidense “es mala, quiere destruir Europa y hay que hacerle frente”. Lo ha dicho en respuesta a cómo podría Europa estrechar lazos con América Latina con un presidente como Donald Trump que tomaría una mayor influencia europea en el continente como un ataque. Según Illa, el mundo se encuentra entre el fin del orden surgido tras la segunda Guerra Mundial y uno nuevo que no acaba de nacer y en ese contexto, cree que entre Europa y América Latina deben “reforzar las relaciones” a nivel político. Antes, el alcalde de Barcelona, Jaume Collboni, que ha abierto el foro, ha defendido que la política debe servir para transformar “la incertidumbre en confianza” frente a los que “quieren convertir el miedo en división”. En este contexto mundial, entre los grandes avances y promesas de la ciencia y la tecnología y los riesgos catastróficos y vectores de involución, el Foro World in Progress Barcelona (WIP), organizado por el Grupo Prisa (editor de EL PAÍS), busca encontrar claves de progreso, mecanismos de contención del desorden y de los abusos, de promoción de avances compartidos, paz, estabilidad, respeto del derecho internacional y prosperidad.

World In Progress (WIP) es un foro internacional de reflexión y debate organizado por PRISA, EL PAÍS y, como medio colaborador, la Cadena SER. Tiene el apoyo del Ajuntament de Barcelona, Generalitat de Catalunya, Abertis, Fundación la Caixa, Glovo, Iberdrola, Indra Group, Limak, Mango, Moeve, Sabadell, Santander, Telefónica, Veolia y Vueling.

World.title: Jay Kim (The Fork): “Tengo un horno de leña en el jardín y estoy obsesionado con el proceso de hacer pizza”
World.content:
El director general para Iberia de la plataforma de reserva de restaurantes quiere retirarse en España y reconoce que el futuro de sus hijos es lo que le quita el sueño actualmente

Jay Kim nació en Seúl y creció en Nueva York. Estudió ingeniería electrónica, pero en unas prácticas en Intel e IBM se dio cuenta de que su camino profesional pasaba por otros prados. Desde entonces ha ocupado puestos ligados a ventas, marketing y gestión de productos en HP, Lutron y Philips (ahora Signify) y ha vivido en diferentes ciudades y países, como Singapur o Alemania. En 2022 se trasladó a Barcelona como director global de Ventas Centrales de The Fork, la plataforma de reserva de restaurantes, y en 2025 fue nombrado director general para Iberia. No es la primera vez que este amante del café de 54 años, que empieza el día con la preparación ritual de espresso, vive en la capital catalana. Hace más de dos décadas conoció allí a su mujer, y les gusta tanto que jugaron con las palabras Barcelona y catalán para crear los nombres de sus tres hijos adolescentes.

Pregunta. ¿Hay algo que no le guste de la ciudad?

Respuesta. Me gustaba más Barcelona hace 20 años, porque era menos internacional. Quizá auténtica no sea la palabra más adecuada, porque se supone que la ciudad debe ser dinámica y evolucionar, pero por entonces realmente sentía que estaba en un lugar más único. Ahora es tan internacional que la gente me habla directamente en inglés y eso como que le quita un poco el encanto.

P. Ha vivido en distintos lugares. Si tuviera que elegir uno, ¿cuál sería?

R. España, de largo. Estoy planeando activamente establecerme de forma definitiva en España.

P. ¿Le gusta viajar?

R. Sí, sí. Debo decir que viajaba mucho más antes de tener a los tres chicos. Ahora requiere un poco más de logística, así que hacemos un viaje grande al año. Pero no veo la hora de que sean más independientes para que mi mujer y yo podamos viajar más y hacer viajes más espontáneos.

P. ¿Cuál es su próximo gran viaje?

R. Nos gustaría llevar a los niños a Singapur. Allí es donde mi mujer y yo vivimos después de conocernos en Barcelona, antes de tenerlos. El año que viene será nuestro vigésimo aniversario de boda, así que nos gustaría volver con ellos.

P. Su trabajo está ligado a la restauración y la gastronomía, ¿le gusta comer?

R. Por supuesto. Bueno, me pagan por decir esto (ríe)... Bromas aparte, sí, me encanta descubrir diferentes cocinas e ingredientes. Habiendo vivido en diversos lugares y también en ciudades multiculturales como Nueva York o Los Ángeles, estuve en contacto con muchos tipos de gastronomías desde muy joven y eso me ayudó a comprender lo que las hace únicas y a valorarlas más.

P. ¿Qué restaurante le ha dejado huella?

R. Hay tantos que no soy capaz de nombrar solo uno. Pero si alguien está interesado en encontrar un restaurante que realmente le deje un recuerdo imborrable, conozco una app estupenda que puede usar y de la que me encanta hablar.

P. ¿Cuál es su plato favorito?

R. No estoy seguro de poder elegir uno. Pero digamos que si no tengo ganas de pensar qué me apetece comer, mi opción de referencia será un ramen japonés auténtico. Me encanta.

P. ¿Cuál es su magdalena de Proust, ese bocado que lo lleva a un recuerdo?

R. Tendría que decir de nuevo el ramen japonés. Recuerdo haber comido un ramen en Tokio, en un restaurante diminuto, y cada vez que pruebo uno bueno fuera de Japón me transporta de vuelta a ese local donde probé por primera vez el auténtico ramen al estilo Hokkaido.

P. ¿Cocina en casa?

R. Totalmente, me encanta cocinar. Tengo un horno de leña en el jardín y estoy obsesionado con el proceso de hacer pizza: probar diferentes ratios de hidratación y tiempos de prefermentación… Estoy constantemente buscando la combinación perfecta para la mejor masa.

P. ¿Le dedica muchas horas al trabajo?

R. Por supuesto, sí. No sé si sería honesto si dijese que no. La jornada se alarga hasta bien entrada la tarde y la noche.

P. ¿Hay algo que ahora mismo no haga en su día a día que sí le gustaría hacer?

R. Me gustaría poder disfrutar, mejorar e invertir para el futuro. Lo llamo mis tres íes (por las iniciales en inglés). Intento disfrutar de Barcelona todo lo que puedo. Intento mejorar algún aspecto de mi vida. Por ejemplo, estoy retomando el ejercicio. Crecí practicando diferentes artes marciales. Hace unos años empecé a practicar MMA aquí en Barcelona y me encantaba poder entrenar con tipos de mitad de mi edad. Y durante un entrenamiento me rompí el tendón de aquiles. Estuve un año sin poder hacer nada y me lo tomé como una señal de que ya no era tan joven. Ahora hago boxeo con un entrenador personal y podemos adaptar el nivel a mi situación actual.

Y luego está la parte de inversión, cómo puedo aprovechar mi tiempo ahora para que las cosas sean mejor en el futuro. Y ahí es donde intento leer y aprender cosas nuevas. Quizá sea un ejemplo un poco tonto, pero me lo tomo en serio, así que lo incluyó en esta categoría: estoy aprendiendo a jugar al billar. Es algo que ya hacía con amigos, pero me gusta mejorar, así que voy a clases una vez a la semana.

P. Una película, un libro y una canción.

R. Un buen año. Trata sobre un banquero de inversiones en Londres que se hace cargo de la finca de su tío en algún lugar en el sur de Francia y se enamora de la elaboración del vino y del estilo de vida. En cierto modo encaja con mi deseo de encontrar un pueblecito bonito en España y simplemente disfrutar de la vida.

Leo muchos libros. Normalmente tengo tres o cuatro abiertos en mi Kindle. Y leo varios a la vez porque no me gusta terminar uno y luego pasar al siguiente, así que no sé si realmente hay un libro para escoger. Pero no quiero decepcionaros, así que elegiré el que acabo de terminar, la autobiografía de Keith McNally, que fundó muchos restaurantes de éxito en Nueva York y su vida me ha parecido fascinante.

Una canción… Voy a tener que decepcionaros, porque no soy nada de música.

P. Dígame un punto fuerte y una debilidad…

R. Por lo que me dice la gente, tiendo a ser analítico. Intento no sacar conclusiones precipitadas. Y una de mis debilidades sigue siendo que cuando veo las decisiones equivocadas y los errores que cometí me doy cuenta de que han estado motivados o bien por una ambición egoísta o por haber sobrestimado mis capacidades. Mantener eso a raya es algo en lo que puedo seguir trabajando.

P. ¿Hay algo que le quite el sueño?

R. Cuando era más joven, obviamente admiraba a la gente que tenía éxito, pero también los envidiaba. Ahora me doy cuenta cada vez más de que envidio a la gente que tiene hijos a los que les va bien. Lo que realmente me preocupa estos días es el futuro de mis hijos.

P. ¿Algo de ese futuro le inquieta especialmente?

R. Creo que lo que me preocupa es eso, que cada vez es más impredecible. Simplemente deseo que tengan las herramientas correctas para adaptarse a este mundo que cambia tan rápido. Intento exponerlos a muchísimas cosas distintas, a diferentes experiencias de vida, y solo puedo rezar para que los ayuden a estar preparados para el mundo real.

Puede consultar el resto de entrevistas de esta sección aquí.

World.title: No sign of deal on budget ahead of crucial week in parliament
World.content:
Budget talks between the coalition and opposition parties at the weekend have failed to produce an agreement, meaning the plans will go before parliament this week without majority support.

The coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD had hoped to strike a deal with the opposition before the plans are debated this week, but were unable to find a breakthrough despite speaking to three different combinations.

Prime minister Rob Jetten said at his weekly press conference last Friday that he still wanted to come up with an agreement that balanced the demands of left and right-wing parties, while the opposition groups have repeatedly urged him to pick a side.

Jetten appeared to be close to securing the support of the left-wing parties Pro and Volt in September after agreeing to abandon €6 billion of welfare spending cuts. But the cabinet is unprepared to meet the two parties’ other demands to raise wealth taxes to make up the shortfall.

Pro leader Jesse Klaver said after meeting Jetten and other coalition leaders in the Catshuis, the prime minister’s official residence, that “there is no political will to work with us”.

“That’s because the cabinet has chosen to give more money to those with the largest fortunes,” Klaver added.

Abortion and surrogacy

Pro and Volt are the only combination that can offer the three coalition parties the votes they need for a majority in both houses of parliament. Jetten also held a video conference with the leaders of three right-wing parties – the farmers’ party BBB, JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.

The parties have drawn up a laundry list of issues where they want the cabinet to make concessions or block legislation, including reforms to facilitate late-term abortions and surrogacy, which the Bible-belt SGP opposes.

The farmers want agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen to scrap his plans to reduce nitrogen pollution by putting up low-emission zones around protected nature areas and offering buyouts to livestock farmers, but none of the coalition parties are prepared to go back to the drawing board.

The three parties said in a statement that they saw “opportunities to talk further”, but there were no signs of a significant shift in their direction. Jetten said on Friday that it was “not sensible” to make the budget vote dependent on non-financial issues.

A third potential route to a majority in the lower house, via the minor parties ChristenUnie and 50Plus, along with the far-right splinter group of former PVV MPs led by Gidi Markuszower, also seemed doomed after ChristenUnie leader Mirjam Bikker came away from talks saying the process was “not going well”.

“We’re doing things we should have sorted out in August,” Bikker said. “And that’s frustrating”.

Jetten warned at his press conference that opposition parties were jeopardising vital measures to ease the cost of living, such as an extension to the discount on fuel duty, if they voted down next year’s budget.

MPs are due to debate the budget measures on Wednesday, with the votes due to take place on November 12.

World.title: Albert Heijn sister chain hit as fridge hacks spread in Europe
World.content:
Hackers managed to tamper with fridges and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden overnight, including at least 40 branches of Albert Heijn’s sister chain Delhaize, weeks after a similar attack hit hundreds of supermarkets in France.

A Delhaize spokesperson confirmed the hack on Monday morning, newspaper HLN reported, and said shops in both Flanders and Wallonia had been hit.

Delhaize is calling it an “IT incident”. Carrefour said 15 of its Belgian stores had also been hit, Colruyt said five independently run Spar stores had similar problems, and butcher chain De Laet & Van Haver also reported a sudden rise in temperatures.

Delhaize told broadcaster NOS that some of its branches in Luxembourg had also been hit, but did not say how many. The company said it had immediately disconnected the refrigeration systems from the internet.

Some reports showed that fridge temperatures had risen by up to 70°, while RTL Info reported increases to around 15°, mainly in freezers. Store managers got a text message from Delhaize at around 4am warning them of the problem, and some stores brought in refrigerated lorries to save their stock.

Swedish stores hit

In Sweden, supermarket group Ica said a “limited number” of its stores had been affected overnight, and Coop told news agency TT that six of its stores in central Sweden had problems with their refrigeration. One Ica store in southern Sweden said on social media that its fridges and freezers had been set to 50°.

French attack

One month ago on the night of October 11, hackers raised the temperature of refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets, including Intermarché, E.Leclerc and Coopérative U stores, to 50°, destroying fresh and frozen food.

The stores all used equipment from Danish manufacturer Danfoss, which told news agency AFP that most of the affected systems were outdated and no longer received security updates.

It is not yet clear whether the stores hit on Monday use Danfoss systems. In October, RTL Z found that 57 refrigeration systems in the Netherlands could be hacked the same way.

Delhaize and Albert Heijn are both owned by Zaandam-based Ahold Delhaize, which reported a cyberattack to Dutch police in October after shutting down several IT systems. Delhaize told NOS it was investigating whether that attack was linked to Monday’s hack.

World.title: Stroopwafel wars: supermarkets slash prices to 34 cents a pack
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch supermarkets are locked in a price war over stroopwafels, with discount chain Dirk now selling a pack of 12 for 34 cents, Het Parool reports.

That works out at just over 2.8 cents a biscuit, which makes it one of the few food items actually getting cheaper.

Meanwhile, tourists are paying around €13 for a single stroopwafel in central Amsterdam.

In mid-October a pack of Bakker Joop stroopwafels cost 42 cents at Jumbo and 38 cents at Dirk. Albert Heijn was charging 42 cents for a pack of its own brand.

All three have since cut further. Jumbo and Albert Heijn are now at 36 cents, although Albert Heijn’s packs hold only 10 biscuits. That leaves its customers paying the most per waffle, at 3.6 cents each.

Retail expert Paul Moers told the paper that the supermarkets make nothing on the deals, they are so-called “lost leaders” that bring people into the shops, who then inevitably buy other things.

The holdout

Not every chain has joined in. Frisian supermarket Poiesz still charges €1.15 for the same Bakker Joop pack, which earned Moers’ “respect”.

He expects the prices could drop by a few more cents, since the chains are already making heavy losses. Eventually, he said, “the joke will wear off” and the supermarkets will move on to another product.

In Gouda, the stroopwafel’s home town, bakers are unbothered. “It’s comparing apples and oranges,” said Mike van den Berg of Berg’s Bakery and Van Vliet Siroopwafels. “As a baker you have to believe in your product.”

Moers had a final word on the bargain biscuits. They contain no butter, he said, which “says something about how blandening of Dutch taste”.

World.title: Dutch campaigners accuse Philip Morris of heated tobacco fraud
World.content:
A criminal complaint is being filed against Phillip Morris for fraud and forgery. A Dutch anti-smoking foundation says it has falsely presented heated tobacco as less harmful than smoking, and broken the ban on advertising tobacco in the Netherlands.

Stichting Rookpreventie Jeugd, a foundation that campaigns against youth smoking, said on Monday it would hand the complaint to the public prosecution service (OM) in mid-November.

The foundation, chaired by former lung specialist Wanda de Kanter, says Philip Morris backs its claims mainly with its own studies and leaves out worrying findings from independent research. It also accuses the company of illegally promoting heated tobacco through specialist shops.

Cancer charity KWF, the lung and heart foundations, the Antoni van Leeuwenhoek cancer institute and the lung doctors’ association NVALT have pledged to back the complaint.

“Since fines from regulators and settlements with bereaved relatives have not stopped Philip Morris from committing new violations, it is now up to criminal law,” lawyer Sjoerd Lopik said in a statement.

In June, doctors and health groups complained to the advertising watchdog about a Philip Morris campaign that used an AI tool to help people object to tougher EU tobacco rules. The Reclame Code Commissie later ruled that the campaign breached the advertising ban.

The foundation’s previous criminal complaint against tobacco makers, filed in 2016, did not lead to a prosecution. A court ruled that regulating the industry was a matter for the government. The foundation says the new complaint is based on breaches of existing law.

World.title: Big wins for PSV and Twente close gap on leaders Feyenoord
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A late equaliser for Fortuna Sittard in De Kuip proved costly for Feyenoord as PSV and Twente racked up huge victories to move within two points of the Eredivisie leaders.

Feyenoord paid the price for failing to finish off the Limburgers, with Luciano Valente’s 59th-minute goal the only reward for their dominance.

Fortuna equalised with four minutes left when Shiloh ’t Zand, on loan from Feyenoord, was allowed to run through to the penalty area and beat Tjark Ernst with a low shot.

Feyenoord coach Giovanni van Bronckhorst made no effort to hide his disappointment. “We know that Fortuna are the kind of team who can score from the few attacks they have,” he said. “If you don’t score the goals, things like this can happen.”

Second-placed Ajax are a point behind after a narrow win at home against AZ ended an 11-match winless streak against the Alkmaar club, as Tolu Arokodare’s early header proved decisive.

Weghorst bags four

Twente recorded the biggest win of the weekend with a 9-0 demolition of Excelsior in Rotterdam, with Wout Weghorst scoring four times and Sondre Ørjasaeter notching up five assists.

Excelsior collapsed following the fifth-minute dismissal of Nesto Groen for a reckless high challenge. The home side were 5-0 down at half-time, with Weghorst claiming a hat-trick in the opening 33 minutes.

PSV bagged seven goals in a one-sided encounter with bottom club Willem II, with all the goals coming from different scorers including Ricardo Pepi, who came on in the second half after a six-week absence through injury.

Telstar opened up a three-point gap at the bottom over ADO Den Haag with a 4-2 win against Utrecht in a painful return to Velsen-Zuid for Telstar’s former coach Anthony Correia.

ADO went down 1-0 in Zwolle, with PEC’s Dylan Mbayo scoring the only goal with a first-time finish on the stroke of half-time.

The match between Cambuur Leeuwarden and Go Ahead Eagles was suspended in the 82nd minute after visiting fans threw fireworks onto the pitch.

The clubs agreed with the KNVB not to play the final minutes and allow Cambuur’s 4-0 advantage to stand as the final result.

Go Ahead’s director Jan-Willem van Dop said the club would take action against those responsible: “I am ashamed on behalf a small group of supporters who ruined things for the club and a large hare of the fans in the away end,” he said.

World.title: From pickles to magic: 11 great things to do in November
World.content:
It’s November, the quiet before the Christmas cheer storm. But there’s still much non-festive fun to be had, as the list will show.

Make a night of it

It’s Museumnacht in Amsterdam this month. Some 65 museums are keeping their doors open and there is a raft of night-time activities, including Ask an Imam where visitors can discuss matters of faith, a trip on a boat used by refugees, and many more. November 7. Website

Spot the differences

The Frans Hals Museum in Haarlem is planning its own blockbuster exhibition with the succinctly named Hals-Rembrandt, which focuses on the differences and similarities in the styles of the two Dutch 17th-century masters. The museum will open earlier and use time slots to give visitors the opportunity for a proper gaze at the juxtaposed works. From November 6. Website

See ancient Egypt come to life

The Olympisch Stadion in Amsterdam is hosting Tutankhamun – the immersive exhibition, where VR wizardry takes you to the heart of ancient Egypt without getting sand between your toes. It’s a pretty amazing spectacle and children will love it too. From November 6. Website

Spare five minutes

The Orange Theatre Company presents a series of five-minute English language monologues around the theme ‘In the Flesh’ as part of its Tiny Theatre programme. It’s all about desire, so it might get a bit steamy in the Oedipus Brewery in Amsterdam. November 11. Website

Get into a pickle

It’s American Pickle Day on November 14 and Amsterdam, like New York, a traditional pickle city, is getting in on the act. A Big Dill celebrates that history with an exhibition of pickle paintings by New York painter Harvey Herman, himself a member of the Tannenbaum pickle family and a former seller of “pickles for a nickel”, pickle history from both cities and, of course, pickle tastings. It’s on at the st-Art Centre in Amsterdam-West. November 14. Website

Praat Nederlands

People from the Leiden region are invited to join fellow expats/immigrants/internationals struggling to learn the language and speak Dutch all day long. Practise Dutch in “a safe space” to boost your confidence and meet like-minded folk to have a good moan about the pitfalls of this wonderful and useful language. There are activities as well. November 26. Website

Catch Shrek in Amsterdam

Grab your chance to take the nippers to Shrek The Musical, the jolly story of the ogre, the princess and the talking donkey. It’s on at the Amsterdams Theaterhuis and we are including the December dates in case you want to avoid the December festive reservation surge. It’s in English, by the way. November 27-29, December 3-6. Website

Say hi to the Sint at Soestdijk

Sinterklaas is always met with a warm welcome in the Netherlands and that includes a well-deserved stay at the sumptuous, former royal palace Paleis Soestdijk. The Sint will not just be luxuriating in a royal bathtub, of course. The Blue Corridor (the former royal residence) has been turned into a Pieten Palace where Pieten are busy sorting out the presents and poems for December 5. Sinterklaas will make time for children wanting to see him, and they can even take a peek at his bedroom and do lots of activities. Children can bring a drawing to butter the Sint up. November 27, 28, 29. Website

See the seedy side of the Herengracht

The opulence of the houses on Amsterdam’s Herengracht finds its origin in the slave trade. Number 605, now the Willet-Holthuysen museum, named after its last owners who left the double canal house and its contents to the city, is a good example. Previous owners financier Willem Deutz (1697-1757) and merchant Fredrik Berewout (1692-1777) grew massively rich on the profits made from the slave trade, as the current exhibition Plantation along the Canal makes clear. Among the exhibits is a complete inventory of the Jagtlust plantation in Suriname, owned by Berewout, including the names and value of 125 slaves. Until April 4. Website

Find out how it’s done

Abracadabra, at the Jewish Museum in Amsterdam, is a fascinating look at the world of Jewish illusionists around 1900. The “Golden Age of Magic” included such famous names as escape artist Harry Houdini, and Horace Goldin and Okito (the stage name of Dutch magician Theo Bamberg) among others. World-renowned Dutch illusionist and collector Hans Klok became the chosen recipient of Bamberg’s tricks of the trade and decided to share them with the world, along with other magicians’ lore. Klok himself puts in an appearance on video to explain some of the tricks and visitors are invited to have a go as well. Until March 29, 2027. Website

Mind your ankles

Yay! Get your platform shoes on and dance to the music of the 70s at the Wereldmuseum in Amsterdam. There is much more to disco than glitter and glam. Its history is tied up with the emancipation of gays, queers, Latinos and other marginalised groups who created their own fabulous world of music and art. You can bop your way through hundreds of disco tracks, videos, artworks, fashion pieces and design objects, including works by Andy Warhol, Keith Haring, Kwame Brathwaite, Michael Abramson, Meryl Meisler and many others. Until August 22, 2027. Website
