World.title: Fears spread over Gen Z riot plans across NL
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

There are fears that a “Gen Z” protest, inspired by the ongoing unrest that has swept through France and other countries, could hit the Netherlands over the weekend.

A report in AD found that groups on Telegram, Snapchat and other social media platforms are preparing to riot in cities including The Hague, Maastricht and Eindhoven.

While no applications for protest permits have been submitted, police have said they generally monitor online forums for signs of trouble but would not comment on this matter specifically.

The messages, which include calls to loot shopping centres, were enough to prompt school heads to issue warnings to parents in Maastricht. Limburg police backed the warnings, according to local broadcaster L1 News.

Shopkeepers in The Hague have also started boarding up their windows as a precaution, as some messaging groups are calling for gatherings on the Malieveld and attacks on commercial centres nearby, according to Omroep West.

The protests in France, which have spread to Italy and Spain began over education and living standards among young people. Many of the demonstrations quickly descended into serious rioting, often with heavy police response.

There are similar concerns in Germany, where youth groups are preparing to protest over similar issues on Halloween.

World.title: Polish president in physical confrontation with judges amid power struggle at constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis. However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters. On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw. At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors. The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her. Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”. Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”. Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”. ⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94 — Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026 The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal. Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence. At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker. The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners. Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki. Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”. On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki. @PL_2050 na wydarzenia dzisiejszej nocy patrzy z zaniepokojeniem. Przynoszą one Polsce wstyd. Nie przybliżają nas do naprawy tego, co zostało zepsute. Jest dla nas jasne, że Bogdan Święczkowski, wraz z nominatami PiS-u, zrobił z TK karykaturę sądu konstytucyjnego. Sytuacja w… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 31, 2026 Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. His justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, announced on Friday evening that he was seeking to have Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution lifted. On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska. He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”. Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki. “One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. Politicians should not tell them what to do.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Chaos at Poland’s constitutional court as government-backed judges seek to oust chief justice
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki. One of the government-backed judges said that she had suspended the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, from his duties. Police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing Święczkowski from entering the grounds after his supporters had cut through the fence with a power tool. Święczkowski and the opposition claim that an illegal “coup d’état” is underway. Nawrocki, who had been flying to Senegal for a state visit, ordered his plane to turn around and return to Warsaw. Prezes Świeczkowski wraz z grupą posłów przeciął łańcuchy i próbuje dostać się do trybunału konstytucyjnego. Policja nie chce go przepuścić! Przecież to bezprawie! pic.twitter.com/XbIXigwIi3 — Jan Molski 🇵🇱 (@JanMolski) October 30, 2026 The dramatic events follow a years-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. In doing so, he ignored an order by the European Court of Human Rights that the judges be allowed to take up their positions. Święczkowski argued that the ECHR had no authority to issue such a ruling. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 Rumours have long swirled that the government would introduce those judges onto the court by force. PiS supporters have been camped outside the TK grounds for weeks with the aim of preventing that from happening. On Friday evening, large numbers of riot police were deployed around the TK. On the court’s website, a brief statement appeared, saying that a “break in the activities” of Święczkowski and his deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been ordered. The statement did not say who had ordered that break, but it cited article 130 of the law on common courts, under which the president of a court or the justice minister can order an immediate break in a judge’s official duties if they are caught in the act of committing an offence. However, Marcin Matczak, a prominent scholar of constitutional law who was also a critic of PiS’s judicial reforms, wrote on social media, that, while the justice minister exercises oversight over common courts, he cannot do so over the TK. “I consider Bogdan Święczkowski to be the worst person to serve as the president of the TK,” wrote Matczak. “I never thought I’d end up defending him, but this legal basis [for suspending Święczkowski] is nonexistent for a million reasons.” Ze szczątkowych informacji, na jakiej podstawie zawieszono B. Święczkowskiego, wynika, że ma to być art. 19 ustawy o statusie sędziów TK, który mówi, że do spraw nieuregulowanych w tej ustawie stosuje się „przepisy dotyczące praw i obowiązków sędziów SN” i art. 130 ustawy o SN,… — Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) October 30, 2026 Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, issued a statement announcing that he had submitted motions to the TK to waive the immunity from prosecution of Świeczkowski and Sochański. He said that the documents had been “delivered to the longest-serving judge of the Constitutional Tribunal”. That was a reference to Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the TK judges whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. She told state broadcaster TVP that it was she who had issued the order to suspend Święczkowski from his duties. She justified her action by accusing Święczkowski of blocking judges from taking up their positions and of overseeing irregularities in the assignment of judges to cases, reports Polskie Radio. Korwin-Piotrowska’s claim to have the longest tenure among TK judges relates not to her service on tribunal itself, but to the fact that she first began her judicial career in 1995. 🗣️ “Bogdan Święczkowski narusza zasady funkcjonowania TK. (…) Nie było innego wyjścia” – sędzia Anna Korwin-Piotrowska w TVP Info. pic.twitter.com/22FYJJbQAC — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 30, 2026 While the TK website appears to now be under the control of Korwin-Piotrowska, the court’s account on social media service X issued a statement saying that “an unlawful takeover of the TK’s website has occurred”, that “Bogdan Święczkowski remains chief justice”, and that “Korwin-Piotrowska is not a TK judge”. “All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d’état,” it added. Nastąpiło bezprawne przejęcie strony internetowej Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Prezesem @TK_GOV_PL jest nadal Bogdan Święczkowski, a Wiceprezesem Bartłomiej Sochański. Pani Anna Korwin-Piotrowska nie jest sędzią Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Wszystkie osoby uczestniczące w… — Trybunał Konstytucyjny (@TK_GOV_PL) October 30, 2026 The court’s spokeswoman, Weronika Ścibor, told broadcaster Kanał Zero that “seven people elected as [TK] judges this year” had been escorted into the building by officers from the State Protection Service (SOP), a body responsible for protecting state officials. SOP is subordinate to the interior minister. She said they had entered the grounds of the court through a gate that leads from the prime minister’s chancellery, rather than the main entrance from the street where protesters are gathered. Korwin-Piotrowska also confirmed to TVP that she was one of seven judges who were inside the TK on Friday evening. Rzeczniczka Trybunału Konstytucyjnego Weronika Ścibor komentuje sytuację w TK. Według jej relacji siedem osób wybranych na sędziów weszło do budynku w asyście funkcjonariuszy SOP, natomiast wiceprezes Bartłomiej Sochański nie został wpuszczony na teren Trybunału. pic.twitter.com/VwxU4UrYuz — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) October 30, 2026 The developments at the court prompted outrage from the opposition. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński declared outside the court that “as of today, Poland has become a police state, and from there it’s a straight path to authoritarianism, and then to totalitarianism”. Kaczyński called on Nawrocki to return to Poland from his state visit to Senegal and defend the court. The president himself quickly confirmed that he had done so, with flight trackers showing his plane turning around in midair and heading back to Poland. Meanwhile, Zbigniew Kapiński, the chief justice of the Supreme Court – a separate entity from the Constitutional Tribunal – told Kanał Zero that he was “appalled” by what was happening, which was “undoubtedly a coup d’état”. Our most tracked flight right now: A Polish government aircraft en route to Senegal is now returning to Warsaw. https://t.co/YdLhQmV8pl pic.twitter.com/Dz9KPgI3eI — Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) October 30, 2026 Tusk, however, issued a statement on social media defending what was taking place at the TK. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote. “After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland approves first fast-track renewable energy zones
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity. The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures. The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years. Pierwsze #OPRO już są! Sejmik województwa wielkopolskiego przyjął dziś pierwsze w Polsce plany OPRO. Obejmą one ok. 105,4 ha w gminach Lwówek, Rawicz, Słupca i Złotów.🔆 ❓Czym jest OPRO? ✅To Obszary Przyspieszonego Rozwoju #OZE, czyli tereny, na których – już podczas ich… — Marek Pogorzelski (@rzeczni_MKiS) October 26, 2026 Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly. Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days. The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels. Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”. The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly. Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects. EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late. Polish state mining firm JSW, which is the EU's largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland's biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year as it seeks to stem large financial losses https://t.co/EWP3rAVMaH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Poland has long had one of Europe’s most polluting energy sectors. The country still produces around half of its electricity from coal, by far the higher proportion in the EU. However, the share of renewables has grown significantly in recent years. It nearly doubled from 14.7% of the energy mix in 2021 to 29.4% in 2025. Onshore wind was the largest contributor last year, accounting for 14.2%, followed by solar at 12.1% and biomass at 1.8%. Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for just 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. However, another coalition partner, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), says that it will oppose the bill, calling instead for a system allowing taxpayers to allocate part of their taxes to religious institutions of their choice. Senior church figures also say they have not been consulted. 📣 Lewica składa ustawę likwidującą Fundusz Kościelny. Czas na realizację umowy koalicyjnej w zakresie świeckiego państwa‼️ Co zakłada nasz projekt? ⬇️ ✅ Składki na duchownych przestają być w 80 procentach finansowane z budżetu państwa jak dotychczas. 50% składek pokrywać… pic.twitter.com/syqUMdCugr — Lewica (@__Lewica) October 29, 2026 The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings. It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty. Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half. For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.” At least 17.5bn zloty in state funds went to religious bodies from 2021-23, with over 95% going to Catholic organisations, the state auditor has found. In response, the speaker of parliament has proposed measures to reduce and better oversee such spending https://t.co/IN3dpY4La2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 16, 2025 An exception is made in the bill for members of enclosed religious orders and missionaries, who would have their contributions paid in full by their churches. The cost of maintaining historic churches would be covered by the National Fund for the Protection of Monuments, Żukowska explained. Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law. “I would like to remind my coalition partners: our coalition agreement includes a commitment to work toward establishing the principles of a secular state in Poland,” he said, speaking alongside Żukowska. “Our patience is running out”. Ahead of the 2023 election, both the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and The Left pledged to abolish the Church Fund, while the centre-right Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) proposed replacing state funding with voluntary taxpayer contributions. PSL had no equivalent formal party-wide pledge. In 2024, after the coalition came to power, Tusk announced plans to reform the fund and appointed a government working group led by the PSL leader and deputy prime minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The group’s work has since stalled. Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed. Instead, taxpayers should be able to allocate part of their taxes to a religious institution of their choice, a system used in several European countries, to “let the Polish people themselves decide whether or not they want to contribute,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Polsat News. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, a member of Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), said that he supported reform, but criticised The Left for submitting the bill without consulting its coalition partners. A long-term decline in trust in the Catholic church in Poland has accelerated over the last year, with only 35% of Poles now saying they trust the church. Meanwhile, the armed forces now enjoy record-high trust of 94% https://t.co/ErCBE4HwWR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 17, 2025 Religious communities also criticised the proposal for not having been discussed with them in advance. In a press statement sent to PAP, the Polish Episcopal Conference (KEP), the main organ of the Catholic church in Poland, said any solution should comply with the country’s agreement with the Vatican, as well as the constitutional principle that relations between the state and religious communities be regulated by mutual agreement. Bishop Jerzy Samiec, head of the Evangelical-Augsburg Church in Poland, the country’s biggest Protestant body, pointed to the significant costs churches face in maintaining their properties, including care homes and other facilities. The Catholic Church, Poland’s dominant religious institution, has seen a long-term decline in public trust, with only 35% of Poles saying they trusted it in 2025. That has coincided with a series of crises in recent years, in particular over revelations of child sexual abuse by members of the clergy and negligence in dealing with them by the church hierarchy. A variety of surveys, including from the church itself, show that religious attendance and identification have been declining in Poland in recent years. A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself. This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 18, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish opposition leader sparks controversy with speech on potential EU exit talks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, has sparked controversy by appearing to suggest that Poland and some other allied European Union member states could launch the process of leaving the EU if they fail in efforts to reform it. His remarks were condemned by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and other figures from the pro-EU ruling coalition, who have long accused Kaczyński and his national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party of seeking “Polexit” from the EU. However, Kaczyński responded by accusing Tusk of misrepresenting his words, insisting that he wants Poland to reform the EU rather than leave it. Kaczyński pomylił Krynicę z Kremlem. pic.twitter.com/tX0G04krze — Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) October 29, 2026 The comments in question came in an hour-long speech by Kaczyński at the Krynica Forum, an annual conference bringing together leaders from politics, business and civil society, which he used to outline his vision for sweeping reforms of the EU. Repeating his longstanding criticism of Brussels, Kaczyński warned that there had been a “consistent drive to transform the EU into a centralised state” with too much power over national governments. He also called the European Parliament in its current form a “parody”. But soon, said Kaczyński, “a window of opportunity” for reform may appear because “completely different governments could emerge” in Poland, France and Spain, all of which will hold elections within the year. PiS has previously enjoyed close relations with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN) party in France and the nationalist Vox party of Santiago Abascal in Spain. The EU is preparing a "German plan" that would "annihilate the Polish state", said Kaczyński as Poland marks Independence Day. He warned that the incoming opposition government will "strive to implement this plan" and called on Poles to "fight" against it https://t.co/QDbxmiaazJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2023 Kaczyński suggested that Poland, if led by PiS, could work with other like-minded EU governments to push for reform of the bloc by influencing public opinion, identifying breaches of EU treaties, creating a blocking minority in the European Council, and trying to change the EU’s treaties. However, the PiS leader then warned that, “if [those] approaches fail to yield results, the states that want change could conclude a new treaty with the elements we are seeking, but with a delayed entry into force”. Kaczyński then noted that the EU treaties “include provisions specifying the terms under which a state may withdraw from the EU. This all begins with negotiations. And simply begin these negotiations”. “It is a tough approach, a risky one, but the situation is so dire that it is worth employing such a method if all others fail to yield results,” he added. The remarks immediately prompted condemnation from figures in Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused Kaczyński of effectively calling for Polexit – something they have long claimed he wants, even though PiS has not explicitly called for it before. “Jarosław Kaczyński has just announced that Poland should begin negotiations on the terms of its withdrawal from the EU,” wrote Tusk himself on X. “This is, among other things, what the current struggle in Poland is about – a tough struggle. I do not intend to lose it.” “So they do want Polexit after all,” wrote foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Customs borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania…An end to subsidies for farmers and investments…And they swore on their lives that they’d never do that.” In a video published later on Thursday, Tusk declared that next year’s parliamentary elections would help decide “whether Poland remains in the European Union or leaves it”. Jarosław Kaczyński ogłosił właśnie, że Polska powinna zacząć rokowania o warunkach wyjścia z Unii Europejskiej. O taką między innymi stawkę toczy się dziś w Polsce walka. Twarda walka. Nie zamierzam jej przegrać, nawet jeśli nie wszyscy zagrają ze mną. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 29, 2026 Kaczyński responded by saying that “Tusk is lying as usual”. He emphasised that he believes “the EU is needed but it requires thorough reform” so that it “benefits not the elites, but ordinary citizens”. PiS deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek said on Thursday that his party was “considering all scenarios, including the possibility that the EU will kill itself”. However, he added that the priority remained reforming the bloc and “PiS has no plans to leave the EU”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). When PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it regularly clashed with Brussels over a variety of issues, including judicial reform, trade, climate policy, and migration. Since Tusk, a former president of the European Council, took power in 2023, his government has greatly improved relations with Brussels. Tusk jak zwykle kłamie. Najwyraźniej wychodzi z założenia, że dzień bez kłamstwa jest dniem straconym… Unia Europejska jest potrzebna, ale wymaga gruntownej reformy. Kryzys i zapaść w jej obecnym kształcie to efekt rządów Merkel i jednego z jej pomocników, Tuska. Nie ma co się… — Jarosław Kaczyński (@OficjalnyJK) October 29, 2026 Poland has been the largest net recipient of EU funding since joining the bloc in 2004. A study published earlier this year found that the country’s economy is 42% larger than it would have been had Poland not been part of the EU. Opinion polls consistently show a large majority of Poles in favour of remaining part of the EU. However, recent years have seen an uptick in support for Polexit, as well as for anti-EU far-right parties. PiS has increasingly found itself competing against such parties for votes. Regular polling by state research agency CBOS shows that, while opposition to EU membership fell to a record low of 5% in 2022, it has subsequently risen, standing at 14% in the most recent survey. World.title: Polish bishop convicted for failing to promptly report child sex abuse allegations
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In the first ruling of its kind in Poland, a Catholic bishop has been found guilty of failing to promptly inform the law enforcement authorities about allegations of child sex abuse committed by priests under his authority. Andrzej Jeż, the bishop of Tarnów, was handed a non-custodial sentence that will require him to donate 25% of his earnings for two years to a charity that supports victims of child sexual abuse. However, the verdict can still be appealed, and the diocese of Tarnów has already announced that it “disagrees with the court’s ruling” and that an appeal will be filed. Pierwszy taki wyrok w Polsce. Biskup skazany za zwlekanie z powiadomieniem prokuratury o pedofilach w sutannach Ordynariusz tarnowski bp Andrzej Jeż jest pierwszym biskupem oskarżonym o zbyt późne powiadomienie prokuratury o pedofilii w Kościele. I pierwszym, który który został… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 29, 2026 The case relates to alleged abuse by two priests who worked under Jeż’s authority. They can be identified only as Stanisław P. and Tomasz K. under Polish privacy law. In 2022, prosecutors discontinued an investigation into allegations against Stanisław P. because the statute of limitations had expired, despite concluding that he had harmed at least 95 children and committed “sexual acts” against 77 of them over several decades in parishes in Poland and Ukraine. In 2023, prosecutors decided to charge Tomasz K., who allegedly sexually abused children as early as 2018. However, they have been unable to formally present the charges to him because of his poor health, news website OKO.press reported earlier this year. Though Jeż was not accused of complicity in the alleged abuse itself, he was charged under a 2017 law making it a criminal offence not to “immediately notify the authorities” of “credible information” about sexual abuse of minors. The offence is punishable by up to three years in prison. Investigators say that, although an internal church probe into Stanisław P. was initiated in the 2000s and a decision to remove him from the clergy was made in 2013, Jeż only notified the prosecutor’s office in 2020. In the case of Tomasz K., the bishop notified prosecutors only in 2021. In court, prosecutor Marcin Stępień said that Jeż’s failure to report the abuse promptly had allowed the statute of limitations to expire in the case of some of Stanisław P.’s victims. Stępień also noted that the bishop had only come forward with the information when media coverage brought the allegations against Stanisław P. to light, reports broadcaster TVN. A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers. It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026 Prosecutors sought a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for three years, and a fine of 20,000 zloty (€4,550). Jeż, however, denied the allegations against him and sought an acquittal. He argued that he had reported the alleged abuse to the authorities as soon as there was credible information. On Thursday, the court found the bishop guilty, giving him a sentence known as “restriction of liberty” (ograniczenie wolnośći), under which a convict is not imprisoned but required to do some kind of social good. In Jeż’s case, the court ordered that 25% of his salary for two years be donated to the Empowering Children Foundation (Dajemy Dzieciom Siłę), which supports victims of child abuse. He was additionally ordered to pay 20,000 zloty to the Fund for Assistance to Victims and Post-Penitentiary Assistance. In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”. The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up. The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”. In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy. World.title: Turkish engineer creates live 3D pixel map of adopted hometown Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives. The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city. The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London. While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice. Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model. The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users. The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees. Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains. Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly. An observation deck at the top of the EU's tallest building, Varso Tower in Warsaw, has opened to the public. Located 230m up on the tower's 53rd floor, the attraction offers a 360° panorama of Poland's capital.https://t.co/VeEapOmh4s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2025 The result is an incredible level of explorable detail, from major landmarks, such as the communist-era Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower, the EU’s tallest building, down to the seating steps and bars along the Vistula River boulevards. The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves. A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium. I turned Warsaw into a flight sim 🛩️ Take off from Chopin, fly through the ring over the Palace of Culture, then land a UFO inside Stadion Narodowy as the roof opens 🛸 Desktop only for now. Can you land it? 👇 pic.twitter.com/DT2fdk1Vem — Bedirhan (@bedcodes) October 27, 2026 Speaking to Notes from Poland, Yildirim says that he moved to Poland in 2022 to pursue a job in IT before starting his own business. Initially living in Kraków, the country’s second-largest city, he then moved to Warsaw in 2025. Asked what his own personal favourite places in the city are, Yildirim points to Warsaw’s parks, such as Skaryszewski, Pole Mokotowskie and Łazienki. His favourite neighbourhood is Saska Kępa on the right bank of the Vistula. The software engineer adds that his project is an example of how AI can be an “amazing tool to do 90% of the job very quickly”. The remaining 10% of human input “is what keeps it from being ‘AI slop'”. Yildirim says that, without the use of AI, the map of Warsaw he created would have needed an entire team to build over a period of months. World.title: Poland detains Ukrainian accused of arson attack in Romania on behalf of Russia
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained a Ukrainian citizen who is wanted by Romania on suspicion of involvement in an arson attack on a defence company carried out on behalf of Russia. On Tuesday, the Polish police’s Central Investigation Bureau (CBŚP) announced that anti-terrorism officers had detained the man, who can be named only as Artem S. under Polish privacy law, in Warsaw under a European Arrest Warrant issued by Romania. In the early hours of 14 September, a fire broke out in the city of Brașov, Romania, in the immediate vicinity of premises belonging to Carfil, a manufacturer of military equipment. Carfil is a subsidiary of ROMARM, a state-owned defence company. On Monday this week, the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said it had determined that the fire had been deliberately caused by a “sabotage network coordinated from Russia”. It added that “several citizens of former Soviet states who reside in the EU” had been involved in the arson attack. The SRI also revealed that the group’s activities were not limited to Romania. “Its coordinators in Russia had assigned it a wide range of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturing facilities, as well as sites of military and industrial interest.” In a separate statement, Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) confirmed that the suspects were a Ukrainian, who was at large in Poland, and two Belarusians, who had already been detained in Germany, where they “had been preparing to commit similar acts”. Polish broadcaster RMF reports, based on sources, that Artem S.’s role in the Brașov attack was to identify a target and to arrange payment for those involved. A Polish court will now decide whether the 25-year-old should be extradited to Romania. Poland itself has been a primary target for Russia’s campaign of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” in Europe. Many of those detained and convicted have been Ukrainian and Belarusians, though some Polish citizens have also been implicated. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 In some cases, such operatives are amateurs – so-called “disposable agents” – recruited, coordinated and paid through messaging service Telegram. Some have also been pre-existing criminal groups hired by Russia to carry out such tasks. In August, a drone production plant belonging to private Polish arms company WB Electronics was targeted in an arson attack that Poland has blamed on Russia. The following month, a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was likewise hit by an arson attack that Poland blamed on Russia. Two Turkish men were later detained in Germany on suspicion of carrying out the attack. World.title: Sherlock Holmes Exhibition Lets Visitors Play Detective in Prague
World.content:
Visitors can test historical investigative techniques, examine crime scenes and follow clues at a new interactive Sherlock Holmes exhibition in central Prague.

The exhibition, located on the third floor of the Bílá labuť department store, covers more than 2,000 square metres and features over 200 exhibits.

Rather than simply moving between display cases, visitors take on the role of an investigator and work through a series of tasks inspired by the methods used by detectives more than a century ago.



Each visitor receives a detective’s notebook to record observations and clues. The notebook guides them through the exhibition as they investigate evidence, solve puzzles and gradually build their own picture of the case.

One section focuses on the history of criminal investigation around the turn of the 20th century. It includes authentic objects loaned by the Police Museum, ranging from historical fingerprinting equipment and tools used by safecrackers to more disturbing evidence connected with violent crimes.

The exhibition also explores the development of forensic science. Visitors can make footprint impressions, examine insects found at a crime scene, send messages by telegraph and learn how investigators studied bullets and other evidence. Several interactive stations test whether visitors can identify clues and apply the techniques used by detectives of the period.

The literary side of the exhibition looks at the life and work of Arthur Conan Doyle. Visitors can see early editions of the Sherlock Holmes stories and learn more about the author behind one of literature’s most enduring fictional detectives.

A reconstruction of Holmes’s famous Baker Street apartment is among the main attractions. The exhibition then moves into a series of crime scenes where visitors search for evidence and attempt to connect the clues. Some puzzles draw on well-known Sherlock Holmes stories, while others require close attention to details hidden throughout the exhibition.

Period newspapers are also part of the investigation, and visitors are encouraged to look carefully: a coded message may be concealed within the reports.

The final section examines Sherlock Holmes’s lasting influence on popular culture, including books, comics, films and television adaptations. Vintage Sherlock Holmes comic books are also on display.

A scavenger hunt for younger visitors has been added for the current school year, with children asked to find objects hidden throughout the exhibition. The format also works well for school groups, which can divide into smaller teams and compare their discoveries.

Visitors are allowed to take photographs without flash. A full visit typically takes between 90 minutes and two hours, and booking a timed entry is recommended.

Opening hours: Daily from 9 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.

Duration: The exhibition is scheduled to run at least until January 10, 2027.

Admission: Adult tickets start at 380 CZK, while family tickets start at 980 CZK.

World.title: Czech Billionaire Strnad Offers €30 Billion for Ray-Ban Family’s Firm
World.content:
Czech billionaire Michal Strnad has offered €30 billion to acquire Delfin, the investment vehicle of Italy’s Del ​Vecchio family and the key shareholder in eyewear giant EssilorLuxottica.

News of the offer, which was first reported by Italian newspaper Il Domani, comes amid growing tensions within Delfin, whose investment portfolio includes also large holdings in Italy’s ​financial sector.

Il Domani published a copy of a letter dated October 20 ​outlining the offer.



“I am looking for long-term investment opportunities in companies ⁠operating in, or investing in, businesses positioned at the top of their value chain,” ​Strnad said in the letter said, according to the newspaper.

Delfin “perfectly fits my investment approach and ​strategy,” the letter added.

Jan Osuch, a spokesperson for AKIPIA, which oversees some of Strnad’s investment activities outside the defence sector, said the group did not comment “on market speculation or potential business negotiations.”

Strnad earlier ​this year bought a 14% stake in Italian tyre maker Pirelli, opens new tab from China’s ​Sinochem.

Strnad, 34, heads the family’s defence company Czechoslovak Group (CSG) which listed in Amsterdam earlier this year.

Delfin shareholder Leonardo ‌Maria ⁠Del Vecchio, one of the six children of the late Ray-Ban billionaire Leonardo Del Vecchio, confirmed he had been recently informed of an offer for the company received from a foreign investor.

“The work of a lifetime by my father must remain part of ​Italy’s heritage”, he said in a ​statement.

The late Luxottica ⁠founder built his business empire from scratch having grown up in a Milan orphanage.

Delfin’s ownership is divided equally among Del Vecchio’s ​eight heirs: his six children, his widow Nicoletta Zampillo and her ​son from ⁠a previous marriage.

A sale would require a virtually unanimous decision from the heirs, who have become increasingly at odds with one another.

In addition to its stake in EssilorLuxottica, Luxembourg-based Delfin holds stakes in ⁠Italian ​insurer Generali and lenders Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) and ​UniCredit, for a combined current market value of €43 billion.

Delfin declined to comment. A representative for Strnad was not ​immediately available for comment.

World.title: Prague’s Only Christmas MINT Market to Take Place on November 28–29
World.content:
Don’t leave your Christmas shopping until the last minute this year.

On the weekend of 28–29 November, head to Hall 13 at Holešovice Market and discover original gifts directly from the people who made them.

MINT Market will bring together more than a hundred carefully selected brands from across the Czech Republic, offering a relaxed alternative to the pre-Christmas rush in shopping centres.



On Saturday from 10 am to 6 pm and Sunday from 10 am to 4 pm, visitors can look forward to independent fashion, designer jewellery, ceramics, natural cosmetics, illustrations, original accessories and plenty of Christmas gift inspiration.

And, of course, there will be the relaxed and friendly atmosphere that has become an essential part of MINT Market. The event is suitable for all generations and admission is free.

The youngest MINT Market visitors and their families can enjoy the beautiful NOOK Family Lounge, featuring high-quality wooden toys, a creative play area, a quiet zone with books and space to relax, as well as facilities for babies and parents, including a changing table and a peaceful place for breastfeeding.

There will also be Christmas-themed creative workshops.

MINT Market has been active for sixteen years. During that time, it has become an important platform for small and emerging creators, often directly from Prague, who are given the opportunity to present their products to a wide audience.

Residents of Prague and the surrounding area thus have several opportunities each year to purchase quality products that are literally made by their neighbors – locally, sustainably, and with an emphasis on honest craftsmanship.

MINT Market is not just about shopping. Since 2010, the project has been run by a team of people who systematically support small and local brands and are the only ones bringing high-quality Czech design to more than twenty cities across the country.

What started as a small project has gradually grown into a community of more than 1,500 creatives and a platform that has hosted over 450 events and welcomed more than 1.3 million visitors.

World.title: Czech Government Proposes Voluntary TV and Radio Fees Without State Budget
World.content:
People in the Czech Republic could soon be allowed to decide whether they want to pay television and radio licence fees under a new funding model being prepared by the government.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said the Finance Ministry is working on a system that would make contributions to Czech Television (ČT) and Czech Radio (ČRo) voluntary while ensuring the two public broadcasters receive a guaranteed level of funding.

The proposal is expected to be discussed by the coalition council on Monday.



For now, however, the existing system will remain in place. Although the government had initially hoped to introduce changes at the beginning of 2027, Babiš said the legislative timetable makes that unlikely.

Under parliamentary rules, the bill requires a 60-day review period before moving forward. That means its second reading would fall during the Christmas period, delaying further debate until at least January 2027.

The proposed changes have already sparked political and public opposition.

On October 24, the Chamber of Deputies approved in its first reading a proposal to abolish television and radio licence fees. The governing coalition, made up of ANO, SPD and the Motorists party, added the measure to its priority legislative agenda. The vote took place early in the morning after a lengthy parliamentary debate.

Opposition parties have warned that changing the funding system could expose public broadcasters to greater political pressure. Government representatives have rejected those concerns, saying the planned reform does not threaten democratic standards.

Babiš has said the final model must comply with European requirements concerning the independence of public media and predictable funding.

The issue has also prompted demonstrations. On October 25, thousands of people gathered in Prague’s Old Town Square for a protest organised by the Million Moments for Democracy movement.

Participants expressed concern that changes to the financing of Czech Television and Czech Radio could increase political influence over the broadcasters.

World.title: Prague Welcomes a Week of Polish Films and Culture
World.content:
Prague will host a week of Polish cinema and culture from November 9 to 15, as the 3Kino – Polish Film Festival Prague returns for its 13th edition.

The festival will screen 13 feature films representing contemporary Polish cinema, with a program that also includes theater, stand-up comedy, exhibitions, music and events for children.



This year’s festival opens with The Doll (Lalka), directed by Maciej Kawalski. Based on the classic novel by Bolesław Prus, the film is among the most expensive Polish productions ever made and takes audiences to 19th-century Warsaw.

The story explores love, ambition and social divisions, with Marcin Dorociński, one of Poland’s best-known contemporary actors, in a leading role.

Freedom will be the central theme of this year’s edition. The festival will explore the idea through historical events as well as everyday life, personal relationships and decisions that can alter a person’s future.

The program extends beyond the cinema. Visitors can attend theatrical performances, stand-up shows and exhibitions, while this year’s edition will also put a special focus on Poland’s Lower Silesia region.

Among the accompanying events is the opening of photographer Rafał Pawłowski’s exhibition Shadows of Sounds. Another exhibition will mark the 100th anniversary of the birth of Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda, featuring a selection of Polish film posters.

The festival aims to bring Polish culture to audiences across Prague, with screenings and accompanying events taking place at several venues throughout the city.

Ticket sales are now open, and the full program is available on the festival’s official website.

World.title: The intersection of sleek design and modern wellness brands
World.content:
Explore how modern consumer brands are elevating their aesthetic appeal by investing in highly customized and visually striking product hardware.

Discover how deliberate styling and tactile materials redefine daily customer routines.

You probably remember when health tools hid inside bathroom cabinets, kept out of sight because their clunky plastic shells felt purely clinical. Today, wellness tools serve as personal fashion statements that you proudly display on living room tables and office desks.

Modern customers want daily items that mirror their curated tastes and fit their personal spaces. When your brand treats hardware design as an artistic craft, you turn simple wellness routines into meaningful daily rituals.

Why Are Wellness Tools Becoming Lifestyle Statements?

Your customers no longer separate wellness routines from their broader aesthetic choices. They curate their living rooms, nightstands, and carry bags with items that express their taste. When you produce clean hardware with balanced silhouettes, you invite buyers to keep your products in plain view.

Visibility drives regular daily use. A handsome object sitting on a counter prompts natural engagement, while an awkward gadget gets shoved into a dark drawer. By focusing on intentional shapes, you build products that seamlessly merge into home decor.

Thoughtful design also influences how customers perceive product quality and long-term value. Smooth finishes, understated colors, and ergonomic details create a premium experience that extends beyond basic functionality. When wellness tools complement personal spaces and individual preferences, they become desirable everyday accessories rather than purely practical devices.

How Do Color and Material Guide Consumer Choices?

Color establishes an immediate emotional connection with your audience. Earthy neutrals, muted pastels, and soft cream tones communicate calm and relaxation before a buyer even reads your ingredient list. If you choose harsh neon finishes, you risk sending mixed signals about serenity and health.

Material choices reinforce that visual promise. When people lift a device made with weighted aluminum or a soft-touch matte shell, their hands register quality. Thoughtful finishes create an impression of quiet sophistication that plain plastic cannot deliver.

How Do You Align Product Hardware with Brand Identity?

Customers judge your company within seconds of unboxing a new device. When you source sleek empty disposable vape pens that match your signature visual tone, you give customers an experience that feels deliberate and luxurious. That visual harmony bridges the gap between everyday utility and curated luxury. Your audience notices when physical hardware matches the graphic polish of your outer box.

Mismatched components break customer trust. You lose credibility when premium outer cartons hold generic items that clash with your voice. Consistent colors, unified fonts, and matching tactile surfaces establish a unified identity from the moment the package arrives.

Why Does Outer Presentation Drive Buying Decisions?

Your retail box acts as an interactive introduction to your brand story. According to data shared by the Forbes Business Council, roughly 72% of shoppers say that package styling directly impacts their purchasing decisions. That finding confirms that visual presentation carries just as much weight as product features.

Shoppers form split-second opinions based on packaging textures, embossing, and typography. If your exterior box looks rushed, shoppers assume the interior hardware lacks care as well. Investing in bespoke packaging signals that you prioritize quality across every single detail.

What Steps Create a Seamless Product Experience?

Building an unforgettable product requires harmony between visual appeal and reliable mechanics. You need a structured approach that guides your production decisions from concept to final delivery.

Structuring Your Hardware Design Strategy

Practical Manufacturing Benchmarks:

Standardize finish specifications: Pick a distinct surface texture like anodized metal or matte coating across all hardware runs.

Synchronize print colors: Match your Pantone shades across cardboard packaging, printed guides, and physical device shells.

Test hand ergonomics: Check device grip and balance to guarantee that the unit feels comfortable during daily handling.

Following these benchmarks keeps your production tight and reliable. Your buyers receive hardware that looks cohesive, feels comfortable, and performs reliably during routine use.

How Does Responsible Material Selection Support Growth?

Modern consumers care deeply about how companies manage resources. Guidance from the Environmental Protection Agency highlights that analyzing how packaging components are manufactured and discarded shapes sound business investments. When you integrate thoughtful materials into your supply chain, you satisfy conscious shoppers while reducing unnecessary waste.

Sleek presentation does not require excess plastic or non-recyclable wraps. By choosing compact paper boxes and recyclable device housings, your brand displays environmental integrity. Customers respect businesses that balance elegant design with mindful stewardship.

Style and practical functionality walk hand in hand across the modern self-care market. When you treat your hardware as an extension of personal taste, you build genuine customer loyalty that outlasts fleeting market trends.

Focus on thoughtful colors, premium materials, and cohesive packaging to make your brand an unforgettable part of your audience’s daily lives. By consistently delivering attractive designs and dependable performance, you strengthen emotional connections with customers and encourage lasting engagement with your products.

World.title: Czech Citizen Confirmed Dead After High-Speed Train Collision in Spain
World.content:
A Czech citizen has been confirmed among the victims of a deadly train collision in Spain, the Czech Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday.

Spanish authorities identified the victim as a young Czech national who had been travelling on one of the trains involved in the accident near Toledo.

The Czech Embassy in Madrid is in contact with the person’s family and is providing consular assistance, the ministry said.

The collision occurred on Wednesday shortly before 9 a.m. near the town of Urda, in the province of Toledo. Two high-speed trains were involved in the crash, with about 540 people on board.



Sixty-nine people died and around 100 others were taken to hospital, according to the information available from Spanish authorities. Local media reported on Friday that about 40 people remained hospitalized.

Investigators are still examining the circumstances of the crash. According to local reports, one of the trains struck another train that was stationary and may have been travelling at between 160 and 200 kilometres per hour.

The Spanish Foreign Ministry said that more than 40 foreign nationals from at least seven countries were among those killed or injured. The victims included citizens of Mexico, Italy and Japan.

Czech officials had initially said on Wednesday that a Czech citizen might have been aboard one of the trains. Relatives and acquaintances had contacted the ministry’s emergency hotline with concerns about the passenger.

Spain is observing the second day of a three-day period of national mourning following the disaster.

The accident is among the deadliest rail disasters in Europe in recent decades. Earlier this year, another major train accident in southern Spain claimed 46 lives after a train derailed and collided with an oncoming service.

The investigation into Wednesday’s collision is continuing.

World.title: Prague to Begin Winter Maintenance of Roads and Sidewalks on November 1
World.content:
Prague will begin its annual winter road maintenance programme on November 1.

Until the end of March, the Technical Administration of Communications (TSK) will be responsible for keeping roads, sidewalks and other public routes accessible to vehicles and pedestrians.

Maintenance priorities are determined by the importance of individual routes for traffic and local residents. Roads and pedestrian areas are divided into several categories, each with specific deadlines for snow and ice clearance.



Residents can check the designated maintenance routes and the type of work planned for each area through the city’s online Winter Maintenance application (Zimní údržba).

Road maintenance is divided into three priority categories. The first covers 1,399 kilometres of the city’s busiest roads, which must be treated within two to four hours of maintenance crews being deployed.

The second category includes 519 kilometres of roads, with a clearance deadline of 12 hours. The third covers another 346 kilometres, where maintenance must be completed within 48 hours after the first- and second-priority routes have been treated.

Sidewalks, cycle paths and other pedestrian routes follow a separate schedule. The first category includes 1,063 kilometres, which must be serviced within 12 hours. The second covers a further 693 kilometres, with work required by 5 p.m. on the day after maintenance of the first category has been completed.

Altogether, Prague’s winter maintenance programme covers 2,264 kilometres of roads and 1,756 kilometres of sidewalks and other pedestrian routes.

From December 1 to March 31, temporary workers will help clear sidewalks in parts of Prague 6 that are more difficult to reach with standard maintenance equipment.

These include Hanspaulka, Baba, Sedlec, the Šárecké Valley and parts of Ořechovka.

World.title: Halloween horror: nails found in sweets given to children in Hungary
World.content:
A terrifying discovery has shocked families in Gyömrő after nails and other suspicious objects were found hidden inside sweets collected by children during Halloween trick-or-treating. Police have launched an investigation into at least three reported cases.

Nails found in sweet treats given to children during Halloween

Halloween celebrations in the Liget Residential Park in Gyömrő, Pest County, have taken a disturbing turn after several families discovered dangerous objects hidden inside sweets collected by children during the annual trick-or-treating event.

According to an announcement published by the local municipality, a young girl received a sweet containing a nail on the evening of 31 October. Fortunately, she spotted the metal object before eating the treat, avoiding a potentially serious injury.

Nail hidden inside a milk caramel

The municipality said the sweet was particularly suspicious because it had been wrapped in chocolate packaging but actually contained a milk caramel with a sharp nail concealed inside. Officials said the circumstances suggested the act was deliberate. The town administration subsequently filed a police complaint against an unknown perpetrator and urged parents to carefully inspect all sweets collected by their children.

However, the incident may not have been an isolated case. Gyömrő Mayor Szabolcs Kisberk told Hungarian tabloid Blikk that further reports had emerged from the residential community. According to the mayor, at least three separate cases involving suspicious sweets had been identified, writes Blikk.

In addition to the nail hidden in the caramel, another sweet reportedly contained an object resembling a broken plastic screw. A foreign object was also discovered inside a coconut-flavoured sweet. The incidents have raised serious concerns among local families, as Halloween trick-or-treating has become an annual tradition in the residential park, home to several thousand people.

Police investigating suspected attempted grievous bodily harm

The Monor Police Department has launched a criminal investigation against an unknown suspect on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Police confirmed the investigation in response to media inquiries but declined to provide further details, citing the interests of the ongoing inquiry.

The municipality has urged parents to thoroughly examine all Halloween sweets collected by their children, paying particular attention to damaged, unusual or suspicious packaging.

Anyone discovering a potentially dangerous object in a sweet is advised to contact the Gyömrő municipal office and the police immediately. Authorities hope the reported incidents are limited to the local community, but the investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: Fuel prices could soar to terrifying levels in Hungary by the end of the year
World.content:
Hungarian motorists could face another painful blow at the pumps, with diesel prices already exceeding HUF 721 (EUR 1.80) per litre at some petrol stations. As the price of Brent crude oil surges amid escalating conflicts in the Middle East, experts warn that fuel could become up to HUF 100 more expensive by the end of 2026 if tensions persist.

Diesel prices rising again after weeks of stability

After several weeks without significant changes, diesel prices increased twice in Hungary last week, on Wednesday and Friday. The latest increases are largely linked to the rising price of Brent crude, which has climbed above USD 116 per barrel.

According to economist Erik Braun, falling wholesale and retail margins had helped cushion the impact of rising international oil prices in recent weeks. However, these margins have now narrowed so much that they can no longer offset the increases in the global market.

Speaking to ATV’s news programme, Braun warned that if the Middle Eastern conflict does not ease and crude oil prices continue to rise, further increases at Hungarian petrol stations are likely in the coming weeks.

The outlook could be particularly worrying for diesel drivers, with experts warning that the price of a litre of diesel could rise by another HUF 100 by the end of the year.

How much does diesel cost in neighbouring countries?

Fuel prices are also high across much of Central Europe, although the situation varies considerably from country to country.

According to figures reported by ATV, a litre of diesel costs approximately:

Austria: HUF 808

Romania: HUF 736

Slovenia: HUF 712

Slovakia: HUF 708

Croatia currently offers a somewhat cheaper alternative. At EUR 1.80 per litre, diesel there costs roughly HUF 30 less than in Hungary at the current exchange rate.

This has encouraged some Hungarian motorists to combine shopping trips across the border with filling up their tanks, making the journey worthwhile even when travelling primarily for groceries.

Don’t miss this: Hungary reveals plan to revive economic growth and prepare for the euro by 2030

Neighbouring governments intervene to limit fuel costs

Several countries in the region have introduced measures to prevent international oil price increases from being passed on entirely to motorists. In Croatia, fuel prices are reviewed weekly, with the government adjusting excise duties when necessary to limit significant increases. Prices are set every Monday and remain valid for one week.

Romania has also taken action, cutting certain fuel-related taxes by 25% and regulating profit margins in the fuel market. Nevertheless, motorists there are still facing relatively high prices.

One Hungarian driver interviewed by ATV expressed disbelief at the cost of filling up, saying that people who depend on their cars to get to work are finding the situation increasingly difficult.

Austria is also using tax reductions to ease the pressure on motorists, while introducing restrictions on fuel retailers’ margins.

How much more expensive could filling up become?

With Brent crude trading above USD 115–116 per barrel, the direction of international oil prices will remain crucial for Hungarian motorists in the coming weeks. If tensions in the Middle East continue, the pressure on domestic fuel prices could intensify, particularly as petrol stations have increasingly limited room to absorb higher wholesale costs.

World.title: Warning: Lake Balaton could split into three separate bodies of water by the end of the century
World.content:
Lake Balaton, Hungary’s most popular holiday destination, could shrink into three separate areas of open water by the end of the century if no measures are taken to replenish its water supply, according to a worrying climate scenario presented at a conference in Tihany. Experts warn that climate change, persistent drought and construction around the lake could accelerate the deterioration.

Climate model paints worrying picture of Balaton’s future

Hydraulic engineer Bence Fülöp presented research models examining Lake Balaton’s future water levels at a nature conservation conference held in Tihany in early October, Veol reported. According to a 2024 climate model he cited, the lake could face a dramatic deterioration in its water balance during the final third of the 21st century if no additional water is supplied.

Under the model’s pessimistic RCP8.5 climate scenario, the lake could effectively retreat into three larger, separate basins. At a water level of minus two metres, only areas deeper than one metre would potentially remain as open water.

Although this is a probability-based projection under a particularly unfavourable climate scenario rather than a certain prediction, its implications are serious. According to Fülöp, maintaining the lake’s current size towards the end of the century may require substantial and eventually continuous water replenishment if present trends continue.

Even such interventions, however, would not eliminate fluctuations in water levels.

Lake Balaton has already lost significant amounts of water

The warning comes as Hungary’s largest lake has experienced considerable water loss in recent years. During the summer of 2026, its water level fell by 34 centimetres between mid-June and 27 August, dropping from 77 to 43 centimetres on the water gauge.

Other signs of water stress have also emerged around the lake. The water level of Tihany’s Inner Lake (Belső-tó), a separate hydrological system, fell dramatically, exposing large sections of its bed. Mass fish deaths have also been reported in the region.

While the condition of the Inner Lake cannot be used to draw direct conclusions about the future of Lake Balaton, it illustrates the visible consequences of prolonged drought and water shortages in the area.
