Construction around the lake could make matters worse

Fülöp also highlighted the impact of development projects and changing land use around Balaton. According to the engineer, construction can intensify processes already driven by rising temperatures and changing water conditions.

This means that adapting to climate change will require more than technical interventions. Protecting natural areas and introducing nature-based solutions will also be essential, he argued.

The issue is particularly relevant as several settlements around the lake face growing pressure from construction projects, residential developments and the loss of green spaces.

There are already local initiatives aimed at addressing water shortages. Balatonalmádi’s local council, for example, introduced water retention measures during the critical summer shortage, while protests against residential developments in Balatonfüred have also raised concerns about pressure on the water network and disappearing green areas.

World.title: Hungary should look beyond its traditional export markets
World.content:
A trade agreement signed thousands of kilometres from Budapest may carry a lesson worth considering for Hungarian businesses. On October 27, the United Arab Emirates and Canada signed a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement intended to expand trade, investment and cooperation across several strategic industries.

By Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi, MIoL

Hungary was not a party to the agreement, and it would be misleading to suggest that Hungarian exporters will receive any of its preferential trade benefits. Yet the development raises an important question for a country whose prosperity is closely connected to international manufacturing and European supply chains: how prepared are Hungarian businesses for a world in which established commercial relationships can change rapidly?

Hungary has built a substantial industrial economy through its integration into European production networks. Automotive manufacturing, electronics, machinery and related activities have connected Hungarian factories with customers and suppliers across the continent.

These relationships remain valuable. Germany, in particular, is a major destination for Hungarian exports. Data published by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office demonstrate the importance of this commercial relationship and the wider European market.

There is nothing inherently wrong with concentrating business activity where demand, infrastructure and established partnerships already exist. In fact, geographic proximity and participation in the European single market provide Hungarian companies with significant advantages.

The challenge appears when commercial concentration becomes excessive dependence.

A manufacturer that relies on a limited group of customers may experience serious difficulties when orders decline. A supplier whose production schedule depends heavily on one industrial sector may struggle to respond when that industry slows. Even a financially healthy company can face disruption if important transport routes, components or markets become temporarily unavailable.

These are not uniquely Hungarian problems. They are features of an international economy built around highly interconnected systems.

The new UAE-Canada agreement offers an interesting comparison because it illustrates how countries are developing commercial relationships beyond their traditional geographical and economic circles.

The agreement was negotiated in 47 days and is expected to enter into force in 2027, following the required procedures. Once fully implemented, it is expected to reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99 percent of current Canadian exports to the UAE.

Canada is seeking greater access to markets outside its established trading relationships, while the UAE continues expanding its position as an international investment and commercial centre.

For Hungary, the relevant lesson is not the speed of negotiations or the precise terms of the agreement. It is the importance of creating additional economic options before external developments make diversification urgent.

Hungary’s opportunities in this area deserve serious consideration.

The country has industrial capabilities and technical expertise that could be relevant to markets beyond Europe. Hungarian companies involved in manufacturing equipment, food technology, water management, healthcare products, engineering services and specialised industrial systems may find opportunities where international demand matches their capabilities.

If you missed it – Big shake-up for Budapest public transport: capital and suburbs to get one transport system

The Gulf region is one potential area of interest.

The United Arab Emirates already maintains economic relations with Hungary, while the European Union and the UAE have been negotiating a free trade agreement since May 2025. The negotiations cover goods, services, investment and areas of strategic cooperation.

If concluded and implemented, such an agreement could create additional opportunities for businesses across EU member states, including Hungary. However, it remains under negotiation, and companies should not assume that proposed trade provisions are already in force.

That distinction matters.

International commercial opportunities are frequently discussed in terms of political announcements, investment commitments and future projects. Business decisions, however, must be based on conditions that can be verified.

A Hungarian manufacturer considering expansion into the Gulf needs to understand the actual demand for its products, customs requirements, certification standards, distribution arrangements and payment risks. A promising market becomes valuable only when a company can serve it competitively and consistently.

This is particularly important for smaller businesses.

Large multinational corporations often have the financial resources and international networks to explore new markets. Smaller Hungarian manufacturers may possess excellent products but lack the overseas contacts, regulatory knowledge or resources required for expansion.

Chambers of commerce, export-support institutions and industry associations can help bridge this gap by providing reliable market information and facilitating introductions to suitable partners.

Nevertheless, export diversification should not become an exercise in pursuing every available destination.

A company producing highly specialised components for European manufacturers may achieve greater resilience by developing additional customers within the same industry. Another business may benefit more from entering a new geographical market. A third may need to strengthen its supplier network before seeking international growth.

The appropriate strategy depends on the company’s actual vulnerabilities and operational capabilities.

In my view, this is where economic diversification and risk management should become part of the same business discussion.

Governments often evaluate diversification through changes in export destinations or investment flows. These indicators are useful, but businesses also need to examine the reliability of their commercial relationships and their capacity to maintain operations during disruption.

A company with customers in several countries may still depend on a single supplier for an essential component. A manufacturer may gain a new export contract while creating new exposure to currency fluctuations or unfamiliar regulatory requirements.

Diversification does not automatically eliminate risk. Poorly managed expansion can simply replace familiar vulnerabilities with less visible ones.

Hungary also occupies a distinctive position because its businesses operate within the European Union’s trade framework. This provides access to a substantial single market, but it means that international trade negotiations with third countries generally take place at EU level.

Hungarian businesses can still develop new commercial relationships, investment partnerships and export strategies within that framework. The task is to make better use of existing capabilities while identifying opportunities consistent with applicable European trade rules.

The UAE-Canada agreement should therefore be viewed as an illustration of a broader international trend rather than a model Hungary can reproduce directly.

Countries are increasingly reassessing the concentration of their commercial relationships. They are exploring new markets, alternative suppliers and partnerships involving energy, logistics, technology and industrial development.

For Hungary, the important question is how its companies can participate in these changes without weakening the strengths that have supported their existing success.

Read also: Hungary Airlines flight returns to Budapest Airport after mechanical issue in the air

European manufacturing relationships will remain essential. The objective should not be to replace them, but to ensure that Hungarian companies possess enough flexibility to respond when markets change.

That begins with practical decisions: understanding customer concentration, identifying realistic export opportunities, evaluating supply-chain dependencies and investing in the capabilities needed to operate internationally.

A strong industrial economy should not be judged only by how effectively its factories serve existing customers. Its longer-term strength also depends on whether those businesses can adapt when demand shifts and new commercial opportunities emerge elsewhere.

The agreement between the UAE and Canada may not alter Hungary’s trade position directly. But it offers a timely reminder that countries and companies capable of developing credible alternatives are often better prepared for uncertainty than those that discover their dependence only after a disruption occurs.

About the Author

Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi, MIoL, is a UAE-based author and independent researcher specialising in security, risk management, operational resilience and institutional governance. His work examines the relationship between international developments, organisational decision-making and economic resilience.

World.title: Turkish Republic Day in Budapest: Torchlit march celebrates 103 years of the republic – VIDEO
World.content:
Turkish flags, burning torches and a festive celebration brought the spirit of Türkiye’s Republic Day to the streets of the Hungarian capital. Turkish Republic Day in Budapest was marked by a commemorative march and a special ball, celebrating the legacy of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk while highlighting the strong cultural, historical and diplomatic ties between Hungary and Türkiye.

Turkish Republic Day in Budapest brings the community together

Members of Budapest’s Turkish community came together to celebrate the 103rd anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic of Türkiye, established on 29 October 1923.

The celebrations were organised by the Hungarian Turkish Solidarity Network (Macaristan Türk Dayanışma Ağı, MATDA), which held a Republic March through the streets of Budapest.

Carrying Turkish flags and flaming torches, participants commemorated the founding of the modern Turkish republic and honoured its first president, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

According to an Instagram statement shared by MATDA, the procession was followed by a Republic Ball, bringing the community together for an evening of celebration and remembrance.

The organisers expressed their gratitude to the Yunus Emre Turkish Cultural Institute and Asım Öksüz for their hospitality and support, as well as to the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) for helping ensure the event’s safety.

They also thanked the organising team and everyone who participated in the celebrations.

In their message, MATDA emphasised that the ideals of the republic established by Atatürk 103 years ago continue to inspire Turkish communities around the world.

Turkish Embassy in Budapest hosts official Republic Day reception

The 103rd anniversary of the Republic of Türkiye was also celebrated at an official reception hosted by the Turkish Embassy in Budapest.

According to the Embassy’s Facebook post, the event brought together prominent Hungarian officials, diplomats and representatives of the Turkish community. Among those attending were József Jelencsik, President of the Hungarian Parliament’s Hungarian–Turkish Friendship Group, Hungary’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Chief of the Hungarian Defence Staff, and representatives of various government institutions. Members of the diplomatic corps and Turkish civil society organisations were also present. The reception highlighted the diplomatic dimension of the anniversary celebrations and the close relationship between Hungary and Türkiye.

If you missed it: Hungary and Türkiye restart structured diplomatic cooperation after government change

Why 29 October is so important to Türkiye

Republic Day is one of Türkiye’s most significant national holidays, commemorating the proclamation of the republic on 29 October 1923 following the Turkish War of Independence.

As explained in the official history of the Turkish Grand National Assembly, the proclamation fundamentally transformed the country’s political system, with Mustafa Kemal Atatürk becoming the republic’s first president.

The new political order paved the way for sweeping reforms in education, legislation, government and public life, laying the foundations of modern Türkiye.

For Turkish communities living abroad, Republic Day is more than a historical anniversary. It provides an opportunity to celebrate national identity, maintain cultural traditions and strengthen connections between generations.

The Turkish Republic Day celebrations in Budapest reflected these values, bringing a major Turkish national commemoration into the public spaces of the Hungarian capital.

Hungarian–Turkish friendship has deep historical roots

The Budapest celebrations also highlighted the close relationship between Hungary and Türkiye, two countries whose modern friendship has developed despite a complicated shared past.

While Ottoman rule shaped parts of Hungary’s history for approximately 150 years, modern relations have increasingly focused on cooperation, mutual cultural interest and political dialogue.

Diplomatic relations between modern Hungary and the Turkish republic date back to the early years of Atatürk’s presidency. A friendship treaty was signed between the two countries on 15 December 1923, as recorded by Türkiye’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism.

The relationship has strengthened considerably in recent decades.

According to the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Hungary and Türkiye established a strategic partnership in 2013, which was upgraded to an enhanced strategic partnership in 2023.

Both countries are NATO members, while Hungary also maintains observer status in the Organisation of Turkic States, reflecting Budapest’s growing engagement with the Turkic world.

Economic cooperation has also expanded. Turkish official statistics show that bilateral trade reached approximately USD 5.16 billion in 2025, compared with USD 3.95 billion in 2023.

Read also – Türkiye’s road to COP31: From Ankara’s zero-waste ambitions to a greener Black Sea – Video

Cultural cooperation brings Hungary and Türkiye closer

Cultural diplomacy has become another important pillar of Hungarian–Turkish relations.

The year 2024 was celebrated as the Hungarian–Turkish Cultural Year, marking the centenary of the entry into force of the friendship agreement between the two countries.

According to Türkiye’s Directorate of Communications, Hungary organised 160 cultural, artistic and scientific events in 17 Turkish cities during the programme, attracting nearly 1.5 million visitors.

The Yunus Emre Turkish Cultural Institute in Budapest also plays an important role in maintaining these connections by promoting Turkish language and culture among Hungarian audiences.

Events such as the Republic March demonstrate how these bilateral relations extend beyond official diplomacy. They provide opportunities for Turkish residents in Hungary to celebrate their heritage while sharing their traditions with the wider Hungarian public.

The torchlit celebrations in Budapest were therefore not only a tribute to Türkiye’s republican history but also a visible expression of the growing cultural connections between the two nations.

As Türkiye celebrates 103 years of republican history, the Budapest gathering serves as a reminder that national identity and cultural traditions can remain vibrant far beyond a country’s borders.

MATDA shared a video on Instagram capturing the atmosphere of the Republic March and the festivities that followed.

World.title: Inside Esterházy Palace: An exclusive interview about its past, present and future – VIDEO
World.content:
One of Hungary’s most magnificent Baroque landmarks, Esterházy Palace in Fertőd, has witnessed centuries of aristocratic splendour, musical innovation and dramatic historical change. But what does the future hold for this remarkable royal residence? Daily News Hungary visited Eszterháza to speak with the palace’s director about its fascinating past, its role today and the opportunities and challenges ahead.

Often described as the “Hungarian Versailles”, Esterházy Palace is far more than an architectural masterpiece. It is a symbol of Hungary’s cultural heritage, a place closely associated with the great composer Joseph Haydn, and a destination that continues to attract visitors interested in history, art and music.

Esterházy Palace: A brief history of Hungary’s Versailles

Located in Fertőd, close to the Austrian border in north-western Hungary, Esterházy Palace is one of the country’s most impressive historic residences. Its story dates back to the early 18th century, when a hunting lodge was established on the site.

The palace owes much of its present appearance to Prince Nikolaus Esterházy, also known as Miklós “the Magnificent”, who transformed the estate into an extraordinary Baroque and Rococo residence during the second half of the 18th century.

Inspired by the great European royal courts, the prince created a cultural centre renowned for its lavish celebrations, theatrical performances and musical life. The palace even welcomed Empress Maria Theresa in 1773.

One of the most important figures associated with Eszterháza was Joseph Haydn, who worked for the Esterházy family for decades. The composer spent considerable time at the palace, where he directed musical performances and composed works that contributed to his international reputation.

Following the death of Prince Nikolaus in 1790, the palace gradually lost its former prominence. Later periods of revival were followed by the destruction and disruption of the Second World War. Restoration work began in the 1950s, with further major reconstruction projects undertaken in the 21st century.

Today, Esterházy Palace remains an important monument to Hungary’s aristocratic and musical heritage, welcoming visitors to discover its historic interiors, gardens and cultural legacy.

Exclusive interview: Discovering the past, present and future of Esterházy Palace

What does it take to preserve a historic palace while keeping its remarkable story alive for new generations?

The interview brings together three perspectives: the palace’s extraordinary history, its place in contemporary Hungary and the future of this nationally significant landmark.

For international audiences, the conversation offers an opportunity to learn more about a historic destination that may be less familiar than Budapest’s celebrated attractions, but holds an important place in Hungary’s cultural identity.

Eszterháza’s connection with European aristocratic life, classical music and architectural heritage makes it a fascinating subject not only for history enthusiasts but also for travellers seeking to discover another side of Hungary.

Source: Daily News Hungary

Through the interview, viewers can explore the relationship between the palace’s historical legacy and its contemporary role, while gaining a broader understanding of why preserving places such as Esterházy Palace matters.

Watch our exclusive interview from Esterházy Palace

Join Csilla for this special Daily News Hungary interview, filmed at Eszterháza, and discover the story behind one of Hungary’s most remarkable historic landmarks.

The full interview is available in Hungarian with English subtitles.

Whether you are planning a cultural trip to Hungary, interested in the world of the Esterházy family or simply curious about the future of one of Central Europe’s outstanding palaces, this conversation offers a compelling introduction to Eszterháza.

The palace’s history is a reminder that cultural heritage is not simply about preserving beautiful buildings. It is also about keeping alive the stories, artistic achievements and traditions that connect the past with the present – and ensuring they remain accessible to future generations.

World.title: All Saints’ Day in Hungary: Why millions light candles for their loved ones – and how it differs from Halloween
World.content:
Every autumn, cemeteries across Hungary are transformed into seas of flickering candlelight as families gather to remember those they have lost. All Saints’ Day in Hungary, observed on 1 November, is one of the country’s most deeply rooted traditions. But what exactly do Hungarians commemorate, why do they decorate graves with flowers and candles, and how does this solemn occasion differ from Halloween?

What is All Saints’ Day in Hungary?

Known in Hungarian as mindenszentek, All Saints’ Day falls on 1 November and is a national public holiday. Originally a Christian feast honouring all saints, including those without individual feast days, it has also become closely associated with remembering deceased family members.

The following day, 2 November, is halottak napja, or All Souls’ Day, traditionally dedicated to praying for the dead.

Although the two occasions have different religious meanings, they are closely connected in everyday Hungarian life. Many families visit cemeteries on 1 November, while others spread their commemorations across both days.

All Saints’ Day is an official public holiday in Hungary, while All Souls’ Day is not. In 2026, 1 November falls on a Sunday.

Why do Hungarians light candles and decorate graves?

One of the most recognisable Hungarian traditions is visiting the graves of deceased relatives, often travelling considerable distances to return to family burial places.

In the days leading up to All Saints’ Day, families clean gravestones, remove fallen leaves and arrange fresh flowers, particularly chrysanthemums, which have become strongly associated with remembrance.

As darkness approaches, they light candles and small memorial lanterns, known as mécsesek.

The flames traditionally symbolise remembrance, eternal light and hope. According to older folk beliefs, they could also help guide the souls of the departed.

If you missed it: Best Hungarian comfort dishes for cold weather

The result can be an extraordinary sight. Large cemeteries in Budapest and smaller village graveyards alike glow with thousands of lights, creating an atmosphere that is peaceful rather than frightening.

For many Hungarians, the occasion is not necessarily about religion. Even non-religious families maintain the custom as an expression of respect, affection and family continuity.

All Saints’ Day in Hungary. Illustration. Source: depositphotos.com

Forgotten Hungarian folk traditions

Hungarian remembrance customs once extended well beyond the cemetery.

According to the Hungarian National Digital Archive, older folk beliefs held that deceased relatives could return home during this period.

In some communities, families left food, bread or water on the table for visiting souls. Others kept a candle burning at home to welcome the departed.

Certain regions also had traditions of baking special bread or sharing food with those in need.

Although most of these practices have largely disappeared, they reveal how Christian observances became intertwined with Hungarian folk culture over the centuries.

All Saints’ Day vs Halloween: What is the difference?

For foreigners, the proximity of Halloween and All Saints’ Day can be confusing.

Halloween, celebrated on 31 October, combines historical Celtic and Christian influences with modern customs popularised particularly in North America. Today, it is widely associated with costumes, pumpkins, parties and trick-or-treating.

Hungarian All Saints’ Day, by contrast, traditionally focuses on reflection, remembrance and family visits to cemeteries.

Interestingly, the word Halloween derives from All Hallows’ Eve, meaning the evening before All Saints’ Day. The occasions therefore share historical connections despite their very different modern expressions.

Halloween has become increasingly popular in Hungary, especially among younger generations. Costume parties, pumpkin carving and themed events are now familiar features of late October.

Pumpkin carving. depositphotos.com

However, Halloween has not replaced the older traditions. A Hungarian family might attend a Halloween party on Saturday and still visit relatives’ graves on Sunday.

The two customs increasingly coexist, although some Hungarians consider the quieter atmosphere of remembrance more appropriate for this period.

What should foreigners know about All Saints’ Day in Hungary?

Visitors spending early November in Hungary may notice unusually busy cemeteries, flower stalls and an increased demand for candles.

Those wishing to observe the tradition can visit a cemetery respectfully, keeping noise to a minimum and avoiding intrusive photography of grieving families.

Budapest’s historic Fiumei Road Cemetery is particularly notable for its elaborate mausoleums and the graves of prominent figures from Hungarian history.

For foreign residents, understanding All Saints’ Day offers a glimpse into an important aspect of Hungarian culture.

While Halloween often turns the supernatural into entertainment, the Hungarian tradition gives remembrance a visible place in everyday life.

And as thousands of candles illuminate the November darkness, the message remains remarkably simple: those who have died are still remembered by the people they leave behind.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Presidential Election Winner Pledges Reset with Russia
World.content:
Bulgaria’s acting President, Iliana Iotova, cemented a five-year mandate after winning the runoff election on Sunday. Backed by the Progressive Bulgaria government and her former Bulgarian Socialist Party, BSP, Iotova won 57.6 per cent of votes cast against the pro-EU opposition candidate, Andrey Gyurov, on 39.5 per cent. Turnout was low at 29.1 per cent, but higher than the all-time low of 22.98 per cent registered in the first round on October 25.

“People believed in our way of politics, which pledged dialogue, conversations, searching for decisions, coordination,” Iotova said on Sunday evening in a briefing that Prime Minister Rumen Radev also attended and where he answered most of the questions.

“Bulgarians chose the future instead of the past, they chose peace, stability, normalcy”, said Radev, both of them dodging questions on the low turnout.

Iotova built her campaign as “the President of peace”: she has pledged to offer a more balanced attitude towards Russia and be skeptical about further military aid to Ukraine. She has also called for Bulgaria to be less obedient to the EU.

“If you say yes to everything, which was Bulgaria’s case for decades, you are voiceless … but things have changed a lot, times have changed in the EU, too”, Iotova said in a TV debate with Andrey Gyurov.

In an interview on October 30 on YouTube with two pro-Russian commentators, she said: “I don’t see Russia as an enemy state … I hope Russia will take part in Europe’s future security architecture.”

During her campaign, Iotova was criticised, along with Prime Minister and Progressive Bulgaria leader Rumen Radev, for remaining elusive about drone attacks in the Black Sea, including in Bulgaria’s zone, and for a lack of preparedness.

Her Vice will be Kiril Valchev, Director of the Bulgarian News Agency, the country’s official newswire, his nomination raising questions about Bulgaria’s media freedom and political ties.

After her victory on Sunday, Iotova said all the criticism from the opposition had been a form of aggressive political attacking, adding: “But we didn’t allow ourselves this speech of hate.”

Iotova was born in 1964 in Sofia. She worked as a TV presenter and news editor at Bulgarian National Television in the 1990s. Her time there is remembered for a controversy from 1995, when, on air, she prioritized coverage of then-Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov doing a traditional dance, or horo, at a public event instead of covering the death of 14 soldiers during an accident – the case became colloquially known as “the blood horo”.

Iotova’s involvement with the Moscow-aligned Bulgarian Socialist Party started in 1997, first as a head of the party’s press office. She joined the party аs Bulgaria was going through an economic crisis and was pressured by mass protests aimed at Socialist-led cabinets.

Iotova became an MP in 2005, when the BSP clung to power through a coalition with the NDSV, the National Movement for Stability and Progress, the now faded party of former monarch Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha.

She became a Member of the European Parliament in 2007 and again in 2014.

In 2016, she resigned from the EP to become a Vice President when Rumen Radev won his first term.

She remained in position until January 2026 when, following months of speculation, Radev resigned from the Presidency to form his own party, Progressive Bulgaria, which won the April elections. This made Iotova acting President, while Radev became the first politician to have served both as President and Prime Minister.

World.title: Coal Plant Case Against Montenegro Still Open Despite Upgrade
World.content:
Montenegro still faces a possible finding of non-compliance with Energy Community rules over its ageing Pljevlja coal-fired power plant, despite a major environmental upgrade, Adam Cwetsch, head of the Decarbonisation and Governance Unit at the Energy Community Secretariat, has told BIRN.

Montenegro’s only coal-fired power station, Pljevlja Thermal Power Plant remains a major challenge to the country’s green transition. Commissioned in 1982, the plant exceeded its permitted limit of 20,000 operating hours in December 2020, triggering infringement proceedings under the Energy Community Treaty.

In an interview, Cwetsch said the case concerning the plant’s breach of its permitted operating hours remains open.

“Pljevlja power plant has already exceeded the limit that was given to the power plant, which was 20,000 working hours,” he told BIRN.

World.title: ‘Life on Hold’: Poland’s Immigrants Face Years Waiting for Residence Permits
World.content:
Permanent waiting mode

When millions of Ukrainians crossed into Poland after Russia’s full-scale invasion, the voivodeship offices were given breathing room. From April 2022, deadlines in certain residence proceedings were suspended, along with the usual legal consequences of administrative delays. That provision, now Article 100d of the special act on assistance to Ukrainian citizens, however, applies to foreigners of every nationality. Initially intended to expire at the end of 2022, it was introduced under the previous Law and Justice government and repeatedly extended under Donald Tusk’s coalition. It now runs until March 4, 2027.

It is precisely this provision that migrant rights campaigners are now challenging. They acknowledge the solution was indispensable in 2022, but argue that almost five years later it has become part of the problem.

“It was meant to be a temporary measure to help the system cope,” says Vladimir Medvedev, co-founder of Glos Migranta. “It should have been lifted two years ago, yet here we are in 2026, and nothing has changed. The system is still not working.”

Under ordinary administrative rules, foreigners can formally challenge delays. Article 100d, however, suspends the deadlines and restricts those remedies, allowing offices to argue that no deadline has technically been breached even after months or years of waiting.

In May 2025, the Supreme Administrative Court refused to apply the provision to the period after June 2024, finding it incompatible with the constitutional right to a fair hearing. The law nevertheless remains in force. In June 2026, the Interior Ministry acknowledged in a letter to Poland’s Ombudsman that courts would likely decline to apply it in similar cases, but maintained that administrative offices must continue enforcing it.

“The Ministry understands the problem and its causes, but in our view, it is not doing enough to resolve it,” Marcin Kusy, director of its Migrants’ Rights Team at the Ombudsman’s Office, tells BIRN.

Since April 2022, the office has received 1,161 complaints concerning the legalisation of residence, and lengthy proceedings are among the most common problems raised by migrants.

“Unfortunately, we’re not talking about months of waiting, but years,” Kusy says. “The uncertainty alone takes a toll on people’s sense of security.”

There are practical consequences, too. Banks often require foreigners to produce valid residence documents before granting access to services, while proof of a pending application may not be enough. For migrants running businesses, being unable to open a bank account can make it impossible to operate.

“I’ve heard of cases where people’s existing accounts were blocked simply because they didn’t receive their new residence permit in time,” Medvedev says. Some, he adds, have resorted to paying taxes and bills in cash at the post office.

International travel presents another obstacle. A pending residence application may allow someone to remain legally in Poland, but without a valid residence card or visa, leaving the country can mean being unable to return, stuck between countries.

World.title: Exhibition in Kosovo Capital Asks What Antifascism Means Today
World.content:
At the Reporting House Museum, the exhibition moves from the architecture of imprisonment to the ways journalism and personal testimony shape historical memory. The question of who holds the camera and who is seen through its lens is addressed.

It features a painting of a photograph of Albanian migrants arriving in Italy by ship during the exodus that followed the fall of communism in Albania in the early 1990s. The photograph captures an unusual reversal: an Albanian migrant, Armando Lulaj, photographed journalists as they photographed the arriving migrants. Those who were the subjects of the image turned the lens on the people documenting them.

The painting was commissioned by Lulaj, who asked artist Zef Shoshi from the Manifesto Collective to produce what Lulaj described as his “last socialist painting”.

It is displayed above a real human skull, bringing together migration, artistic memory and the physical traces of human life.

“I am glad we made this part of the museum, as the first documentation of the exodus in Albania we have in the museum,” said BIRN Kosovo executive director Jeta Xharra.

Also in Reporting House, ‘A Wall Divides Us’ presents dozens of letters exchanged by Kosovo Albanian activists Xheva Krasniqi-Lladrovci and Fehmi Lladrovci between 1985 and 1990, coinciding with Milosevic’s rise to power in Serbia, growing repression of Kosovo Albanians, and the twilight of federal Yugoslavia.

Lladrovci was imprisoned in the former Yugoslavia for his agitation for Albanian rights. He and Krasniqi-Lladrovci had been engaged for just over a month when he was imprisoned. Their communication continued throughout his detention.

Xharra said it was “rare to find this much passion and political energy within the same letters”, presented publicly for the first time in almost 40 years,

“It particularly impressed me how Xheva was teaching the elderly generation how to read and write [in order to write to their dissident sons in jail] and arguing for more education for young Kosovo Albanian girls who were abandoning school when Milosevic closed Kosovo public schools in 1990.”

Alongside letters, the exhibition includes the red outfit Krasniqi-Lladrovci wore when she got engaged, and the ammunition vest she was in when she was killed in 1998 alongside Lladrovci while fighting Serbian security forces.

From denial to remorse

World.title: Tragedy that Led to Change: Serbia Marks Two Years Since Canopy Collapse
World.content:
Novi Sad, Serbia’s second city, was in shock and mourning on November 1, 2024.

Since Sunday, the grief and anger once so palpable in this Danube city and the country as a whole has given way to hope for a better future and talk of ‘liberation’ following a bruising election defeat suffered by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, at the hands of a student-led protest movement.

On November 1, 2024, Serbia and Novi Sad were firmly under the rule of the SNS and its founder, then President Aleksandar Vucic. At 11.52 that morning, everything changed.

That was the moment the outdoor canopy of Novi Sad’s newly renovated railway station collapsed. Fourteen people, including children, were killed instantly, buried under tonnes of concrete. Three others fought to stay alive, but ultimately only one did not succumb to their injuries, taking the death toll to 16.

World.title: The Anatomy of Forging Freedom: Lessons from Serbia’s Students
World.content:
An avalanche of small acts

Through the same painstaking, often exhausting practice of direct democracy, faculty assemblies distributed quotas to select 250 parliamentary candidates, ensuring representation across the country. Every name then underwent nationwide scrutiny, with faculties able to challenge and collectively veto one another’s choices. Finally, they chose a parliamentary list reflecting the breadth of Serbian life they had encountered on foot, from workers and farmers to academics, doctors and judges: Student List – Students Are Winning.

On September 9, 492 days after the students first called for early elections, Aleksandar Vucic finally yielded and called the vote. Eighteen days later, he resigned the presidency to run for prime minister.

From that moment, the fruits of the students’ long democratic struggle began to show. Student working groups, established months earlier, launched the campaign, backed by a formidable infrastructure of civic self-organisation, with millions of citizens contributing whatever time, skills and resources they could. Recognising the circumstances, most opposition parties stepped aside. By election day, there was hardly a corner of Serbia where students and citizens had not organised to safeguard the vote against fraud and manipulation.

Turnout reached a historic high. The Student List secured 52.71 per cent of the vote against 39.17 per cent for the then-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, winning an outright parliamentary majority. So decisive was the victory that even a regime determined to hold on to power at any cost had no choice but to concede defeat.

At the beginning, these young people had little more than imagination and the stubborn hope that their country could be different. Through two years of determined work, courage and sacrifice, they brought millions alongside them. Most had wanted nothing more than a democratic Serbia, a country where they might finally imagine a future of their own.

And yet, by bringing down a regime that had long fuelled tensions across the Western Balkans, maintained close ties with Putin’s Russia and presented itself to Europe as a guarantor of stability, they accomplished something far beyond a change of government.

They loosened the grip of a politics that had held the region’s future hostage for far too long, inviting the Western Balkans and the EU to finally begin building the future they had spent so many years waiting for.

Milan Vujić currently works at the Erste Foundation in Vienna, and is also a lawyer and former student activist from Novi Sad in Serbia.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: New Rules are Coming for Road Users in Croatia
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – New rules are coming into force for road users across Croatia, with higher penalties and significant amendments to the Road Traffic Act.

The Ministry of the Interior has now released for public consultation a draft of amendments to the Road Traffic Safety Act. Index reports that it will introduce significantly stricter penalties for dangerous behaviour in traffic, new parking rules and easier removal of vehicles by tow truck, as well as special registration plates for taxis and electric cars.

higher fines for those filming and posting dangerous driving

One of the key novelties concerns drivers who film their own dangerous driving in order to post it on social media, which the legislator now treats as a significantly more serious offence. While such behaviour was previously punished as ordinary mobile phone use while driving with a fixed fine of 130 euros, the new proposal introduces fines of 800 to as much as 2,000 euros for anyone who uses a mobile phone or other device while driving to record their own unlawful behaviour and then makes it publicly available. The explanatory notes state that such posts have additional social harm because they encourage others to imitate them and normalise dangerous driving patterns.

police no longer need to attend minor collisions

For the first time ever, the law defines the concept of a “minor traffic accident,” which means an accident involving only material damage that does not impair the technical soundness of essential parts of the car and allows it to be easily removed from the road. Under the new Article 182, police officers are no longer obliged to go to the scene of such an accident if the participants are able to exchange details with each other or complete the European Accident Statement. Drivers who nevertheless refuse to immediately move their cars off the carriageway and continue to block traffic while waiting for the police will be fined 200 euros, whereas the fine until now was 60 euros.

a total ban on parking on squares

The draft also introduces the concept of a restricted traffic zone into the law, together with significantly stricter rules for stopping and parking in city centres. The previous practice whereby drivers, especially delivery vehicles, parked in city squares and pedestrian zones while invoking the rule about leaving a 1.60-metre passage for pedestrians will no longer apply. Article 82 introduces an absolute ban on stopping and parking in squares, in cultural-historical complexes and on surfaces that local authorities have designated exclusively for pedestrians, regardless of how much free space remains. At the same time, the rules for the operation of the tow-truck service are also changing. A tow truck will be legally able to lift an improperly parked vehicle from the pavement if the free passage between the car and any obstacle is less than one metre. An obstacle is no longer considered only a building, but also bollards, waste bins, outdoor café terraces or any other physical obstacle on the sidewalk.

special registration plates for taxis and electric cars

The law also introduces the obligation to issue special registration plates for two categories of vehicles — taxis and electric-powered cars. While in the case of taxis this is about easier control and alignment with market rules, for electric cars the reason is directly linked to the safety of emergency services. Lithium-ion batteries in electric and hybrid vehicles, in the event of a collision and fire, generate extremely high temperatures, release toxic gases and require completely different firefighting tactics from classic petrol and diesel engines. Special plates will enable firefighters, already upon arrival at the scene of a traffic accident, to recognise electric propulsion and immediately apply the appropriate extinguishing and rescue procedure.

World.title: 135 Years of the Zagreb Tram – From Horses to Modernity
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – 135 years is the time period during which the now iconic blue Zagreb tram has snaked through the capital city. From being pulled by horses to new vehicles, let’s look back at the history of what we now know as ZET.

Dubravko Grakalic reports for Index that frequent trams have been circulating Zagreb’s streets for 135 years now. They have become the blue symbol of the city, living history on the rails, and transport without which Zagreb can hardly function, something Zagreb residents felt most clearly during the recent multi-day ZET workers’ strike, which caused days of traffic problems until a court declared it illegal and banned it.

horse-drawn trams named after vineyard pests…

The first tram circled Zagreb back in 1891. It was pulled by horses and was far from the technical modernity we know today. Zagreb’s trams were once yellow and ran on only a few lines through the very city centre. People affectionately called them “konjka” (horse-tram), but also mockingly “filoksera”, after the notorious wine louse (phylloxera) that was ravaging vineyards in those years, because the workers laying the tracks had dug up and torn apart half the city. Before the trams, passengers were transported around Zagreb by omnibuses that resembled stagecoaches from Western films. They ran from the city centre to the bathing spots on the Sava and from the railway station to a few hotels. As ZET explains, “the city fathers in Zagreb began discussing the need to introduce a horse-drawn tram as a means of transport” in 1885.

French engineer Raoul Pierre Alexandre Gautier proposed a contract for the introduction of tram traffic to the Zagreb City Magistrate on the 20th of June 1887. The city municipality accepted his offer and on the 26th of March 1889 issued him a permit to build a tram line on the ground of the city streets. The Association of Engineers and Technicians allowed the construction of a 76-centimetre-wide track, and the Tramway Company, a special private enterprise, began work. The first tram depot was built on the site of today’s Nikola Tesla Technical Museum.

ilica, zagreb’s modern main artery, was dug up

zagreb.hr

The first lines were built from the corner of Ilica and Mandaličina Street to Maksimir, from the corner of Ilica and Frankopanska Street to the Sava Bridge, and from the corner of Ilica and today’s Republic of Austria Street to the Western Railway Station. Construction began in May 1891, and the trams started running a few months later. Historian Lelja Dobronić, in the article “Old Notes on the Zagreb Tram” published in the magazine Kaj, cites a document from the 17th of August 1891: “Since the long-awaited rails from England and the carriages from Graz (in Austria) have finally arrived, Upper Ilica has been being dug up since last Thursday, and from today Frankopanska Street as well, so that the rails can be laid. Certainly by this Sunday the rails will be laid through the whole of Ilica and Jelačić Square. Up to 500 workers are working a day.”

At the time when Zagreb’s trams were pulled by horses, there were ten closed and six open vehicles available, manufactured at the Weitzer factory in Graz. The average speed of the horse-drawn tram cars was 7.5 km/h. Zagreb’s horse-drawn tram also carried passengers in Velika Gorica, where the joint-stock company Horse Railway was founded back in 1907. They had a seven-kilometre line from the railway station, through the centre of Velika Gorica, to Novo Čiče. It was called “konjača.” After 1945 the horses were replaced by a small diesel locomotive.

electrification and expansion

The electric tram started in August 1910, but horse-drawn trams continued to operate for the following year. Zagreb’s trams changed colour in 1923. They became blue instead of yellow, while the vehicles were reconstructed. A new model, the M-24, manufactured in Zagreb and running on the right-hand track, also appeared on the streets. Summer open-air trams soon became available as well. During the time of the Independent State of Croatia (NDH), Zagreb’s trams ran with increasing difficulty because of bombing, and services were suspended in 1944. Traffic resumed after liberation, and in the autumn of 1945 tracks were built through Vodnikova and Mihanovićeva streets. From then on, the tram lines had numbers. In the following years lines were built towards Žitnjak as well as the Mihaljevac–Dolje line. A building for ZET workers was constructed in Puljska Street.

bull, czech and katica…

At the beginning of the 1950s, Zagreb’s residents also received the first domestically produced tram, built in the ZET workshop. It was prototype 101 with 95 passenger seats. This was followed by cooperation with the “Đuro Đaković” wagon factory from Slavonski Brod and the purchase of M-201 vehicles.

The last example of the M-201 tram, nicknamed “Đuro” or “Bik” (Bull), ran until June 2024 on line 9. Its predecessor, the M-24, ran from 1924 to 1977. Today it is used as the Christmas tram. In 1977 Czechoslovak trams from the ČKD-Tatra factory in Prague were purchased. The Czech T4 model trams, known as “Čeh” (Czech), ran for years on lines 4, 6 and 14. Years later the Tatra KT4YU trams, better known as “Katice,” also arrived. An important date in the history of the Zagreb tram was the 25th of November 1979, when the line along Držićeva Street, across the Bridge of Youth, to New Zagreb was opened. That was when the tram crossed the Sava. In 1980 a tram-bus terminal was built at Črnomerec on the site of a former brickworks. In November 1985 the tram also started running across the Adriatic Bridge towards New Zagreb. Further development of ZET includes the abolition of the conductor’s job in 1996 (conductors had been cancelling and selling tickets in the vehicles for 105 years) and the extension of tram routes to Dubec and Prečko.

and then came končar…

Over the last thirty years or so the old trams, Bulls, Czechs and Katicas, have been replaced by trams manufactured at Končar, Zagreb’s technological giant.

“In more than 30 years of operation on Zagreb’s tram network, Končar trams have covered more than 140 million kilometres, confirming their quality, reliability and indispensable role in the lives of Zagreb residents,” Končar told Index. The company had already begun manufacturing electric rectifier stations for ZET back in 1954. “After almost three decades of cooperation on energy infrastructure, ZET and Končar began joint development of tram vehicles. Production of the TMK 2100 series trams began in 1993, and the prototype was presented on the 5th of September 1994 and immediately put into regular service,” the company notes, also recalling the TMK 2200 trams. “From June 2010 a total of 140 TMK 2200 series trams and two shorter TMK 2200-K trams (which carry the designation TMK 2300 in ZET’s fleet) have been produced for Zagreb,” Končar says. The company later also manufactured shorter trams for the Latvian city of Liepāja.

zagreb’s blue trams

In order to fill gaps in the timetable until the delivery of new vehicles, ZET bought 11 used GT6M trams from Augsburg, Germany, at the end of 2023 and during 2024. This sparked lively public debate because of their age and the fact that the passenger areas are not air-conditioned. The newest Zagreb trams, the TMK 2300, have been in service since February 2025, and there will be forty of them. Through their rich history Zagreb’s trams have become the city’s blue symbol, a mark of the development of domestic technology, and an indicator of Zagreb’s expansion ever further from its historic centre. Zagreb is, along with Osijek, the only Croatian city with tram traffic. Trams once also ran in Pula (from 1904 to 1934), Dubrovnik (from 1910 to 1970), and Rijeka and Opatija.

World.title: Zoran Milanović Accuses EU of Wanting to be a Superstate
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – Croatian President Zoran Milanović has accused the EU of wanting to become a superstate, adding that Montenegro, with which Croatia has multiple open issues, is otherwise welcome to join.

President Zoran Milanović stated that Montenegro is welcome to become a full member of the European Union, while at the same time criticising the direction in which the EU is developing. Index reports that the president believes the EU is increasingly trying to become a superstate, whereas it should focus on free trade, freedom of movement and the harmonisation of rules among member states.

Milanović spoke at the 27th Lučindan Gatherings in Zagreb, a traditional meeting of the Montenegrin community in Croatia. The event was also attended by Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović, who is on a working visit to Croatia. The two presidents discussed relations between the two countries and Montenegro’s European future.

“montenegro is welcome to join”

“Montenegro is a candidate for membership of the European Union, it is moving towards the EU and let it come. As far as I am concerned, it is welcome,” Milanović said. Nevertheless, he repeated his criticisms of the European Union, which he believes is exceeding the powers and possibilities on which it was originally founded. In his view, the EU should stick to economic cooperation, free movement and the alignment of rules, rather than striving to create a superstate.

Milanović told Montenegrins that the greatest value they have is their state. He emphasised that Montenegro has realised its statehood and that its future success does not depend exclusively on membership of the European Union. “The greatest thing you have is your state. Montenegro has realised itself, and everything else consists of greater or lesser advances that do not stand in the way of Montenegro being successful, well-governed and relatively prosperous,” Milanović said. He wished Montenegro to continue on its own path and develop as a successful and well-governed state. He concluded his address with verses by the Montenegrin ruler and poet Petar II Petrović Njegoš.

trust between croatia and montenegro must be strengthened

Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović assessed that Croatia and Montenegro are friendly countries and that Montenegro’s membership of the European Union is in the interest of both countries. He stressed that improving relations requires continuing political dialogue and resolving existing open issues.

“It is our shared responsibility to build good-neighbourly relations, foster open dialogue, overcome current challenges and strengthen mutual trust,” Milatović said. He emphasised that a common European future implies political and economic cooperation, mutual respect and a willingness to resolve disagreements. He thanked the Montenegrin community in Croatia for preserving national identity, culture and ties with the home country.

The Lučindan Gatherings are a traditional event dedicated to preserving Montenegrin cultural identity, tradition and ties with Montenegro. They bring together members of the Montenegrin national minority in Croatia as well as representatives of the cultural and public life of the two countries. According to the 2021 census, 3,127 members of the Montenegrin national minority live in Croatia, or 0.08 percent of the total population.

World.title: Before You Apply: The Legal Deadline Blocking Croatian Descendants
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – There is a somewhat unknown legal deadline blocking Croatian descendants from obtaining their Croatian and as such EU passport.

That issue relates to the exact reason your family left the former Yugoslavia, and why exactly this could throw a spanner in the works of your EU future. Let’s turn the clock back to October the 8th, 1991… If you’re exploring your eligibility for Croatian citizenship by descent, you have likely come across a specific date repeatedly, and that date is October the 8th, 1991. In the (often confusing) world of Croatian citizenship law, this is the ultimate historical line in the sand. Under the descent and emigrant pathways of the Croatian Citizenship Act, your ancestor must have left the territory of what is now the recognised territory of Croatia before this exact date to grant you a pathway to a Croatian and therefore EU passport of your own.

For many second- and third-generation descendants of those who left what was then Yugoslavia, this seems straightforward at first glance. They look at their family history, note that their parents or grandparents moved to the United States 1960s, 1970s, or 1980s, and check the box. However, many “DIY applicants” face rejections from the Croatian side of the fence because they fail to realise that the Ministry of the Interior (MUP) enforces strict, hidden caveats regarding why and how your ancestor left when they did. Simply proving your family departed before the clock struck 1991 is not quite enough. To secure your Croatian citizenship, you must prove the exact legal nature of their exit. That is where, quite understandably, many people become unstuck and their citizenship applications get shoved to the back of a shelf somewhere to gather dust.

what exactly does croatia deem to be an emigrant?

The Croatian side evaluates citizenship applications based on a highly specific legal definition of what they deem an emigrant to actually be. Under the law as it stands, an emigrant is someone who left the territory of Croatia with the clear, permanent intention of abandoning their domestic residence and resettling somewhere abroad. Because of this ultra-narrow definition that leaves very little wiggle room, there are two major legal traps that routinely catch DIY applicants by surprise.

the so-called internal migration problem

If your ancestor was born in Croatia but moved to another republic within former Yugoslavia, such as Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or Slovenia, and then moved across the pond to North America, Croatia’s authorities may not view them as a legal emigrant from Croatia because of that, regardless of the fact that they still ended up in the USA. If that person’s initial move was treated as an internal migration within the same federal state, the chain of continuity for Croatian descent can be heavily compromised or, as is often the case, simply rejected outright.

the curse of the Croatian gastarbajteri…

A Monument to Croatian Emigrants – Anglogermantranslations

During the 1970s and 1980s, hundreds of thousands of people left the former Yugoslavia to work abroad as temporary economic migrants, often referred to as gastarbajteri (guest workers). Many of these individuals retained their active residency rights, property registrations, and legal ties to Croatia and as such to Yugoslavia, fully intending to return after a few years. If MUP reviews your ancestor’s file and determines that their departure was legally categorised as a “temporary economic migration” rather than a permanent severance of domestic ties, your application under the emigrant track can be denied.

verifying permanence…

Commons/Bain News Service

When you submit your application to a Croatian consulate, the reviewing officers will thoroughly inspect your paperwork to determine the legal permanence of your ancestor’s departure. A simple plane ticket or family story will not suffice. To build an airtight case, you must present a synchronised paper trail that cross-references multiple things.

The first is what’s known as a foreign naturalisation timeline. This works to document precisely when your Croatian ancestor applied for and received citizenship in their new country, showing a definitive shift in legal allegiance. Then come the international arrival records. These are official historical maritime or flight manifests matching the timeline of their permanent resettlement. Last but not least comes the so-called letter of motivation. This might seem odd, but there should always be an explicit structure built up of your family’s narrative, framing their historical departure to meet the rigid legal thresholds expected by Croatia.

for croatia, the year 1991 represents a minefield in several ways…

Proving the legal nuances of a person’s departure that took place forty or fifty years ago is a massive bureaucratic challenge. It requires a deep understanding of historical (and of course needlessly complicated) Yugoslav exit laws, international naturalisation records, and precise legal phrasing in the Croatian language. This is exactly why the structured service provided by Croatian By Descent is an essential safeguard for diaspora families.

croatian by descent‘s experts understand the complexities of the former state

Rather than treating your citizenship application like a roll of the dice, their team conducts an exhaustive upfront document review. They analyse your family’s specific migration timeline, identify potential legal vulnerabilities in how your ancestors left Yugoslavia, and meticulously format your application package. By coordinating the procurement of records and managing the precise drafting of your legal motivation letter, they ensure that the Ministry views your family’s departure as a definitive, permanent emigration. They handle the heavy administrative legal lifting, protecting your application from common 1991 cutoff traps and turning your family history into a flawless submission package. Outsource the endless guesswork and verify your eligibility with the expert team at Croatian By Descent.

World.title: Dinamo Sack Mario Kovačević After Shock Defeat to Rudeš
World.content:
Dinamo have sacked head coach Mario Kovačević following Saturday’s 1-0 defeat to newly promoted Rudeš in the 12th round of the SuperSport HNL. The Zagreb club, led by Zvonimir Boban, confirmed the decision on Sunday.

B team coach Jerko Leko will take charge on an interim basis, starting with Thursday’s Europa League trip to Sunderland and followed by the league match against Varaždin.

The defeat in Velika Gorica proved the final straw. Junior Fernandes scored the only goal for Rudeš, while Dion Drena Beljo had two goals ruled out, one for offside and one for handball. Dinamo also finished with ten men after substitute Iker Almena was sent off for an elbow to an opponent’s head.

Speaking after the match, the 51-year-old said he understood the supporters’ anger and would not hide behind anyone. “If people are angriest with me, I accept the blame,” he said. Asked whether he still justified Boban’s faith in him, Kovačević pointed to his record over 16 months: a rebuilt squad, a league and cup double, and a solid start to this season. He called the Rudeš result a major slip, said four points in Europe was less than Dinamo had wanted, and insisted the season could still be turned around.

Kovačević took over in June 2025 and led Dinamo in 73 matches, winning 48, drawing 11 and losing 14. Last season he delivered the double, winning the SuperSport HNL and the SuperSport Croatian Cup.

Born in Jablanica, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kovačević played for Varteks, Belišće, Slaven Belupo, Međimurje, Slovenian side Nafta, Nedelišće and Dinamo Tirana before retiring in 2008. He began coaching in 2014 with Međimurje, and went on to work with Varaždin’s youth and senior teams, Polet Sveti Martin na Muri, Podravina Ludbreg, Mladost Ždralovi and Slaven Belupo.

In November 2023, Varaždin announced that Kovačević had been diagnosed with lung cancer. He stayed on the bench until early December before stepping away for surgery, and in late March 2024, he confirmed that the cancer had receded.

World.title: Zagreb Will Remain Directly Connected to Madrid This Winter
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – Zagreb will remain directly connected to Madrid this winter as Croatia Airlines decides to keep the direct link between the two capital cities open outside of summer.

The Spanish capital is one of the largest cities in the EU, a paradise for lovers of food, football, history and the irresistible Mediterranean lifestyle. Madrid, with an average altitude of 650 metres, is the second-highest capital in Europe after Andorra. Lana Mindoljevic writes for Putni kofer that this metropolis is now also available to Croatian travellers over winter. Croatia Airlines is, for the first time, opting to continue running its seasonal route between the Croatian and Spanish capitals even after the end of the summer timetable.

FLIGHTS ARE ON MONDAYS, THURSDAYS AND SATURDAYS, WITH A BREAK DURING PART OF THE WINTER

Direct flights between Zagreb and Madrid will operate until the 16th of January 2027, and then again from the 15th to the 27th of March 2027. In both periods they are scheduled three times a week, on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays. The only period without flights will therefore be from the 17th of January to the 14th of March. For all three days the departure and arrival times are the same. Departure from Zagreb is at 8:25, and the return from Madrid at 12:10. The flight lasts between two hours and 45 minutes and two hours and 55 minutes.

Such a schedule allows, for example, departure on Thursday and return on Monday, with four overnight stays in Madrid. For a shorter break one can combine Saturday departure with return on Monday. The morning flight from Zagreb leaves a good part of the first day for getting to know the city, while on the last day one has to count on leaving for the airport during the morning.

madrid is an excellent winter city break from zagreb

Madrid is an excellent choice for travellers who like to combine art, architecture and good food. The winter months give a special rhythm to the visit: a colder morning can be spent in a museum, the sunny part of the day in a park, and the evening in one of the city taverns. Although we associate Spain with sun and a warm climate, in Madrid in winter you should not expect spring temperatures. A warm jacket and comfortable shoes are a mandatory part of the luggage.

For art lovers the main asset is the famous museum triangle. The ‘Golden Triangle of Art’ consists of three renowned Madrid museums: Museo del Prado, Reina Sofía and Thyssen-Bornemisza, which are home to some of the world’s most valuable art collections. In the Prado one can see Velázquez’s “Las Meninas” (The Maids of Honour), Goya’s “Black Paintings” and Bosch’s “The Garden of Earthly Delights”. The Reina Sofía Museum holds Picasso’s “Guernica”, while Thyssen-Bornemisza offers an overview of European painting through different periods. Instead of trying to see everything in one day, choose the museum that interests you the most and leave it enough time.

THE ROYAL PALACE IN WHICH NOBODY ACTUALLY LIVES

A first visit to Madrid is hard to imagine without the Royal Palace, Plaza Mayor and Puerta del Sol. These places can be connected into a walk through the historic centre, with stops for coffee and exploring the surrounding streets. The Royal Palace is the official royal residence even though no one has lived in it since 1967. It has a huge courtyard and an incredible 3,418 rooms, and today it is used exclusively for state ceremonies. The building is open to the public, and for visitors to Madrid the changing of the guard, which takes place every Wednesday and Saturday, could also be interesting.

TWO FAMOUS SQUARES THAT SHOULD NOT BE MISSED

The famous Puerta del Sol square, translated as the Gate of the Sun or simply ‘Sol’, is an unmissable stop, and on it is the ‘centre of Spain’. Namely, on Sol, in front of the building of the Royal Post Office, there is the well-known plaque that marks ‘kilometre zero’ of all Spanish roads. In the centre of the square there is also a statue of King Charles III, but it is not the most popular statue on the square. It is overshadowed by the statue of a bear standing on its hind legs to feast on the fruits of the madroño tree, a sculpture that essentially symbolises the growth of the city.

Plaza Mayor, a gigantic square in the very heart of Madrid, has always been the centre of events. Kings were crowned there, but heads were also cut off. Today coffee is often drunk and time is enjoyed surrounded by beautiful buildings. This very square is also home to the traditional Christmas market, which has been held there since 1860. For a quieter part of the day there is El Retiro park, one of the favourite city green destinations. Together with the Paseo del Prado area it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage. It is nice to fit it into a day dedicated to museums: after a few hours in front of paintings a walk in the open air will be welcome.

Madrid is also discovered at the table. In the La Latina neighbourhood, especially around Cava Baja and Cava Alta streets, taverns and bars line up where you can try small bites and share several dishes. Croquettes, patatas bravas and potato tortilla are a good start to such a gastronomic tour. For a cold afternoon save a place for churros with thick hot chocolate, one of the recognisable Madrid sweet stops. If you stay in the city over Sunday, you can spend the morning at El Rastro, the famous flea market where clothes, records, antiques and various small items are browsed, and then continue for lunch in La Latina.

the city of football

Madrid is known as a city of football, and many visit it precisely to take a look at some of its famous stadiums. In the case of Real Madrid it is Estadio Santiago Bernabéu, which can hold 81 thousand people, and in the case of Atlético de Madrid Wanda Metropolitano. If you are a football lover, you can opt for one of the guided tours and look at the clubs’ memorabilia, jerseys and trophies in the museums on that topic.

IN DECEMBER MADRID PUTS ON ITS FESTIVE ATTIRE…

A trip in December brings an additional reason to come: illuminated streets, Christmas decorations and the traditional market on Plaza Mayor. A walk through the city then easily turns into an evening tour of festive scenes. For now it is known that Advent begins at the end of November and will last until the end of December, and besides the main location with more than 100 wooden stalls other locations in the city are also decorated.

World.title: Slovenia Wants a Hydropower Plant Next to the Border – Croatia Says No
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – Slovenia wants to construct a new hydropower plant next to the border with Croatia, but Croatia is, so far, totally against the plan.

Croatia currently completely opposes neighbouring Slovenia’s intention to build the Mokrice hydropower plant on the Sava River, which would be located about 450 metres from the Croatian border. Index reports that there is concern that the project could ecologically endanger the Sava as it enters into the territory of Croatia and call into question the supply of drinking water in that area, whose sources also supply Zagreb with water. HRT reports that energy expert Ivica Jakić and director of the Slovenian company HESS Boštjan Pišotek spoke about this topic.

potential problems for croatian drinking water

This is otherwise a hydropower plant that would be the last in a series of six facilities on the lower course of the Sava. Slovenian Minister for the Environment and Spatial Planning Polona Rifelj announced the relaunch of the procedure for deciding on the predominance of the public interest of energy production over nature conservation, reports N1 Slovenia. The Croatian Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition opposes the project due to the possible deterioration of the condition of surface and groundwater downstream of the dam.

The organisations Croatian Society for the Protection of Birds and Nature, CEE Bankwatch Network and Biom have also warned of the risks. According to their claims, existing Slovenian hydropower plants have already reduced the transport of sediments towards Croatia, which has contributed to the deepening of the Sava riverbed and the lowering of the groundwater level in the wider Zagreb area. The associations warn that the construction of HE Mokrice, downstream from the confluence of the Krka River with the Sava, could further worsen the situation and endanger the sources of drinking water for Zagreb. The Croatian ministry also states that the benefits of the project would remain on the Slovenian side, while Croatia would bear the negative consequences. Among the possible impacts, additional erosion of the riverbed, endangerment of fish habitats and protected areas of the Natura 2000 network are highlighted.

slovenia: the project is in line with all rules and regulations

HESS director Boštjan Pišotek said that this is a project that is being developed in accordance with European rules. “Croatia was informed about the procedure from the very beginning, about 15 years ago when the development of the Mokrice hydropower plant project began,” Pišotek said. He emphasised that cooperation with Croatia has several levels and that this resulted in Croatia giving a positive opinion on the placement of the Mokrice hydropower plant in the space. The Slovenian Ministry for the Environment and Spatial Planning earlier stated that Croatia can participate in cross-border consultations and put forward comments, but that it does not have a right of veto on the project. The decision on issuing the permit remains within the competence of the Slovenian authorities, while respecting international and European regulations.

croatia will link up its own system

Energy expert Ivica Jakić explained how the Croatian Multipurpose Hydraulic System Zaprešić would link up with the Slovenian hydropower plant. “The Mokrice hydropower plant must come from the Slovenian side to solve for the Slovenians the problem of soil deepening and the problem of deposits. It is a logical solution that Slovenia is looking for and wants to have,” Jakić said. He added that Croatia will link up with its own system. “It will solve the stabilisation of the water flow and the deepening of the soil. It will help us, but also Slovenia in further regulating the flow of the Sava River through the Croatian part,” Jakić concluded.
