Officials and local fishermen pull a boat ashore at Patakadapalem in SPSR Nellore district on Monday after its engine failed in seas made rough by Cyclone Murasu. All seven fishermen on board were rescued. Special Arrangement https://t.co/FbNW0z6qGQ — The Hindu - Andhra Pradesh (@THAndhra) November 2, 2026

The boat’s anchor snapped, and because of the strong waves, the vessel drifted towards Patakadapalem village in Bogole mandal of the district. The officials of the Fisheries Department and the Marine Police responded immediately.

With the assistance of local fishermen, they initiated rescue efforts. Initially, reaching the boat proved difficult because of the high waves. Ultimately, they managed to bring the boat to the shore at Patakadapalem and ensured that all fishermen were safe.

The District Collector commended the Fisheries Department officials, Marine Police, surveillance personnel and local fishermen for their presence of mind and efforts in saving the lives of the fishermen.

He also advised the local fishermen to remain vigilant when facing adverse weather conditions at sea and to strictly follow the instructions provided by the authorities.

World.title: Union Home Minister Amit Shah in Hyderabad for padayatra
World.content:
Union Home Minister Amit Shah reached Hyderabad to participate in the padayatra to be held in the city on Monday (November 2, 2026), with the slogan ‘Let us safeguard democracy - let us end anarchism’.

Prior to the rally, he along with senior leaders from the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) Telangana unit offered prayers at the Bhagyalakshmi temple near Charminar.

“Reeling from successive defeats in the elections, the Congress Party is now determined by any means to seize power, even if it means murdering democracy through their anarchic actions. To protect our democracy from the Congress Party’s nefarious attempts, I will participate in the grand padayatra titled ‘Let Us Safeguard Democracy - Let Us End Anarchism’ taking place this evening in Hyderabad,” Mr. Shah posted from his account on X.

The padayatra is scheduled to be held from Babu Jagjivan Ram statue in Basheerbagh to MJ Market in the city. Senior leaders from the State BJP unit have earlier inspected the routes. Union Minister for Coal and Mines G. Kishan Reddy, Union Minister of State for Home Affairs Bandi Sanjay, BJP Telangana president N. Ramchander Rao and other leaders from the party would participate in the rally. Hyderabad Traffic Police announced restrictions on major routes in the central part of the city.

World.title: PC Jeweller says SEBI warns promoter, compliance officer over failure to maintain insider-trading database
World.content:
Markets regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has issued an administrative warning letter to PC Jeweller's promoter and managing director, Balram Garg, and its company secretary and compliance officer, Vijay Panwar, the company said in a stock exchange filing on Monday (November 2, 2026).

SEBI cited the violation as "failure to maintain structured digital database in relation to an unpublished price sensitive information relating to business update given by the company for the quarter ended June 30, 2025," according to the filing.

PC Jeweller said it had not maintained the database for the update, which it disclosed to the exchanges on July 3, 2025.

The company said, however, that the trading window for designated persons and their immediate relatives was closed from July 1, 2025, until two days after it declared results for the quarter on August 1, 2025, that is, until August 3, 2025.

SEBI's insider-trading rules require listed companies to maintain a structured digital database of people with access to unpublished price-sensitive information.

World.title: Gatsby Collection’s festive edits explore contemporary menswear and womenswear
World.content:
For generations of Chennai residents, Gatsby Collection has been a go-to destination for tailored suits and fine fabrics. Now, with its Autumn/Winter 2026 collection, Quiet Attraction, and festive collection, Borrowed Light, creative director Heeba Sait brings a contemporary take to menswear and womenswear, exploring the theme of the attraction between two individuals and the warmth of celebrations during festivals.

With Quiet Attraction, Heeba wanted to explore the laws of attraction between two forces, people, and even the universe. The collection unfolds through three phases – polar, shift, and equilibrium, tracing the journey from the initial pull between two people to a relationship that settles into balance. “When two people have just met and are trying to get to know one another, there is a certain draw, a gravity pulling them towards each other. That is the polar phase,” she says.

In the collection, the one-piece collar jacket is among the standouts in menswear. The collar and the shoulders form a continuous construction, without a separate break between the two. Heeba describes it as a “fresh take on a traditional jacket”. The collection also features streamlined jackets with exaggerated sleeve details, structured suits and reversible jackets.

Sculpted jackets

For womenswear, Heeba has experimented with sculpted jackets and tailored trousers with intricate detailing. One of the highlights is a pair of trousers with a waistband that transforms from a cummerbund into a sash with fringe. Another highlight from the collection for women is a one-piece stand-collar tuxedo shirt, paired with corset-inspired high-waisted wide-leg trousers.

The collection also features a sari fall-inspired, hand-dyed Fuji silk off-shoulder corset with a single sleeve, paired with embroidered barrel-leg trousers. The collection uses worsted wool for suiting, jaquard, and silks, and cotton velvet for the evening wear.

Hand-embroidered

The festive collection, Borrowed Light, features cutwork jackets, sheer overlays, foil-printed jumpsuits, and embroidered jackets. Organza, raw silk, jacquard, and sustainable lotus silk form the base of the collection. “Everything is hand-embroidered. There is no machine embroidery being used anywhere,” says Heeba.

One of the highlights is the trousers that are a take on dhoti pants. Heeba wanted to develop an alternative that retained the fluidity of draping without moving away from the brand’s tailoring-led aesthetic. “I wanted a skirt and a pant. How can I stay true to my identity but develop something that is still feminine?” she says. The result is a silhouette that brings together the two forms in a single garment, paired with corsets, bustiers, and structured jackets.

Both collections offer two interpretations of modern dressing, from everyday formalwear to festive occasions.

Collection is available at Gatsby Collection, Khader Nawaz Khan Road and online at gatsby.in. Priced ₹30,000 onwards.

World.title: I was offered ₹5 crore to make someone Iyal Isai Nataka Mandram president: Rajmohan
World.content:
Tamil Nadu Minister for Information and Publicity Rajmohan on Sunday alleged that he was offered ₹5 crore as a bribe to appoint someone as the president of the Iyal Isai Nataka Mandram.

Participating at the Tamil Nadu Day event celebrations at Egmore in Chennai, the Minister said: “I have not revealed this before. [Tamil Nadu Textbook Corporation chief] Layola Mani knows this. A person said, ‘If I am given the post of president of the Iyal Isai Nataka Mandram, I will offer ₹5 crore to Minister Rajmohan’. I smiled and told Layola Mani, even if someone offers ₹500 crore as bribe, I will not give the post to someone who is not suited for it. Without even getting a single rupee from anyone, Pushpavanam Kuppusamy, who is the most suited for the role, was appointed as the president of the association.”

According to him, for the first time in Tamil Nadu, every Minister [in the C Joseph Vijay cabinet] hates bribery and corruption.

Reveal identity: Jayakumar

Meanwhile, AIADMK leader D. Jayakumar questioned the identity of the person who allegedly offered to bribe Mr. Rajmohan and said the person should be prosecuted.

Speaking to reporters, he said: “There is no doubt that Pushpavanam Kuppusamy is the right person for that post. But, who was the one who came forward through [Chairman of the Tamil Nadu Textbook and Educational Services Corporation] Layola Mani to offer ₹5 crore? Should that person not be brought before the law?”

Mr. Jayakumar added: “If Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay was honest, he should name the person and prosecute him.”

World.title: Cyclone Murasu LIVE updates: Odisha expedites evacuation from vulnerable areas as storm intensifies
World.content:
The Odisha government on Monday (November 2, 2026) expedited the evacuation of people from vulnerable areas after Murasu intensified into a severe cyclonic storm in the Bay of Bengal, officials said.

A total of eleven flights arriving and departing from Chennai airport and Ten IndiGo flights scheduled from Gannavaram Airport today (November 2, 2026) have been cancelled due to Cyclone Murasu on Monday (November 2, 2026). According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the system may continue to move northwestwards and cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast, near Ongole, as a Severe Cyclonic Storm with wind speeds of 100 to 110 kmph gusting 120 kmph.

Watch: Days after Cyclone Arnab, Cyclone ‘Murasu’ forms over Bay of Bengal

A deep depression over the Bay of Bengal on Sunday (November 1, 2026) intensified into a cyclone named “Murasu”, which means war drum. The latest storm is set to make landfall on the morning of November 3 between Nellore and Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh.

Chennai and Tiruvallur District Collectors announced that schools and colleges of the districts will be closed on Monday (November 2, 2026) due to heavy rains. An orange alert was announced in six Telangana districts and a yellow alert in five districts in Telangana for November 2.

Also read: A.P. seeks assistance from Tamil Nadu, Karnataka for cyclone power restoration

World.title: Chennai police granted custody of ex-Minister Anbil Mahesh till November 4
World.content:
The Special Court for Cases under the Prevention of Corruption Act in Chennai on Monday (November 2, 2026) permitted the Central Crime Branch (CCB) of the Greater Chennai Police to take former DMK Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi into police custody for interrogation for three days in an alleged multi-crore bribery case involving irregularities in granting various approvals to private schools.

Mr. Poyyamozhi, who served as School Education Minister in the previous DMK Government (2021-26), was recently arrested by the CCB following a complaint by an association of private schools alleging that crores of rupees were collected as bribes for granting permanent recognition to private schools. He is currently lodged in Puzhal Central Prison, Chennai.

Five-day police custody sought

The police, who suspect that bribes of up to ₹400 crore may have been collected, had sought five days of police custody to interrogate him. The court had earlier directed the police to file their response by November 2 to Mr. Poyyamozhi’s bail petition.

Mr. Poyyamozhi was brought from Puzhal prison and produced before the special court judge L.S. Sathyamoorthy on Monday (November 2, 2026).

During the hearing, the Judge questioned the police whether there was any objection to videographing the crucial parts of the interrogation. The police responded saying the entire proceedings could not be video-recorded. The former Minister’s counsel sought video recording of all interrogation proceedings, except the time spent transporting him.

Partly allowing the police plea, the Judge permitted the CCB to interrogate Mr. Poyyamozhi from 1 p.m. on November 2 until 5 p.m. on November 4, subject to conditions.

The police must first take him to the Rajiv Gandhi Government General Hospital in Chennai and obtain a medical certificate confirming he is fit to undergo interrogation. A fresh medical fitness certificate must also be obtained and submitted to the court when he is produced after the completion of the interrogation.

The court permitted a lawyer representing him to remain present during questioning, provided the lawyer stays at a distance where he cannot hear the questions asked or the answers given. The interrogation must be video-recorded.

Permission to meet advocate

The judge also directed the police to allow Mr. Poyyamozhi to meet his lawyer for 10 minutes every evening. The police must not subject him to physical or mental harassment and must produce him before the court in good health after the interrogation.

The police were further directed to strictly comply with the court’s earlier orders concerning his food, medication and other requirements during the custody period. The court will hear his bail petition and plea seeking the return of certain electronic devices seized by police on November 5.

World.title: Andhra goes ahead with Kotia local body polls despite Odisha’s plea in Supreme Court
World.content:
The Andhra Pradesh government and the State Election Commission are making all arrangements to conduct local body elections in the Kotia group of villages on the Andhra Pradesh-Odisha border, despite strong objections from Odisha. The neighbouring State has approached the Supreme Court to stop the election process in the disputed region.

Both the States have been at odds over the jurisdiction of the Kotia group of villages for about seven decades. Both have also been holding local body elections there for many decades. Odisha has objected before: it filed contempt petitions when Andhra Pradesh held polls in the villages in 2021. This time, it filed a fresh contempt petition last month, alleging that the poll notification violates the Supreme Court’s 2006 order directing both States to maintain the status quo. The villages are located 35 km from Salur town of Parvathipuram Manyam district.

Since the court has not passed any order on Odisha’s petition, the Parvathipuram Manyam district administration is making all arrangements to hold elections in places like Ganjai Bhadra, Pagalu Chennuru, Pattu Chennuru, Kurukutti, Sarika, Kotia and other villages on November 5, 2026. The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP), which won the Salur Zilla Parishad Territorial Constituency and all four Mandal Parishad Territorial Constituencies in 2021, is keen to win them again with its spirited campaign in all Kotia villages.

Former Deputy Chief Minister and YSRCP senior leader Peedika Rajanna Dora on Monday alleged that the TDP, JSP and BJP alliance parties colluded with the ruling BJP leaders of Odisha to stop the election process in the Kotia group of villages as they were fearful of defeat there. “Mr. Jagan Mohan Reddy government had won the hearts of Kotia people with its welfare schemes with an aim to get complete jurisdiction rights for AP over Kotia group of villages. The people who benefited from the welfare schemes of Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy will vote for us,” said Mr. Rajanna Dora while speaking to the media in Salur.

The Telugu Desam Party rejected the YSRCP’s allegations and said the TDP and its alliance partners would get an absolute majority in the Kotia villages this time, as was evident from the spectacular response to the TDP’s campaign in those villages. “In spite of the strong objection from Odisha officials, TDP has been campaigning vigorously in all villages. Recently, Odisha officials seized our campaign vehicle. In spite of all hurdles, we are continuing the campaign in those villages,” said TDP Salur mandal president A. Parameswara Rao.

Meanwhile, Parvathipuram Manyam Collector N. Prabhakara Reddy and Superintendent of Police S.V. Madhav Reddy directed all political leaders to be cautious while campaigning in sensitive areas of the AP-Odisha border. They also asked polling officials to take care of ballot boxes, ballots and other polling material while conducting the election process in the Kotia group of villages. The police department is expected to send additional security forces to the Kotia villages to ensure free and fair elections. According to them, there may not be any untoward incidents on polling day as the local body elections were conducted smoothly in 2021.

World.title: US-backed consortium proposes $4.4bn LNG project
World.content:
• Proposal envisages four tanks holding 560,000 cubic metres at Port Qasim in first phase of the $4.4bn plan that also includes a 1,100km upcountry gas pipeline

• Project would charge $4.93 per mmBtu for terminal and storage, $1.91 for transmission over first decade

ISLAMABAD: A private consortium of US companies, backed by the Trump administration, is pushing for an investment of up to $4.4 billion in an integrated liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Pakistan, covering imports, storage, re-gasification, gas transmission and sales to large consumers on a ‘merchant basis’.

The development comes after Energas, an earlier frontrunner consisting of the Lucky Group and QatarEnergy, abandoned a similar project citing fundamental changes in Pakistan’s energy policy and requirements, as well as longstanding unresolved policy and fiscal issues.

The US consortium comprises Global Vision Energy Partners (GVEP) and Khanjee Holdings, both related firms, along with strategic co-investors from other countries and General Mediterranean Holding, a Luxem­bo­urg-based US financial conglomerate.

The sponsors have reportedly sec­ured consent from the Port Qasim Aut­hority for the proposed project site. An application has also been filed with the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) for a provisional licence.

A special purpose vehicle (SPV), a separate legal entity established to hold specific assets and liabilities and isolate financial risks, has been incorporated. Government facilitation has also been conveyed through the Mini­stry of Maritime Affairs and the Mini­stry of Energy’s Petroleum Divi­sion, according to documents seen by Dawn.

The project has been approved for consideration under the US Trade and Development Agency’s (USTDA) project preparation programme. It may also receive partial financing from the US Development Finance Corporation, backed by export credit guarantees from the US Export-Import Bank for technology, equipment and services.

Pakistan currently has no LNG storage facilities, leaving its domestic re-gasified LNG supplies entirely dependent on import supply chains and international energy prices.

The sponsors plan to develop the project in two phases. The first phase will comprise an LNG terminal and storage facility with four tanks and an estimated annual throughput of 35 billion cubic feet (BCF), at a cost of $1.7bn.

The second phase will involve the construction of a 1,100km, 42-48-inch pipeline to transport gas upcountry, with a capacity of around 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (BCFD). This will take the total project cost to $4.4bn.

The government had previously pursued a similar North-South gas pipeline project with Russia.

The proposed venture is being structured as a merchant infrastructure platform to meet domestic regasification requirements while establishing a physical LNG storage and trading hub in South Asia for US and Middle Eastern suppliers.

The consortium is engaging local inve­stors for up to 10 per cent equity participation, with indicative investments starting at $50 million per investor.

The sponsors also expect to attract strategic co-investors, including global energy and infrastructure funds and institutional investors such as Grey Rock Investment Partners, Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co, Blackstone Inc., Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and the Kuwait Investment Authority.

Their participation remains subject to due diligence, investment approvals and definitive agreements. No binding equity commitments have been confirmed so far.

The SPV will develop, own and operate the project as a regional LNG storage, regasification and trading hub, serving Pakistan’s domestic gas market alongside US and Middle Eastern LNG suppliers. The model will not depend on a single government-backed offtake arrangement.

Re-gasification tariffs for the domestic market will be submitted to Ogra for approval, while other commercial services, including storage, tolling and transshipment, will be priced on market-based terms.

The US sponsors consider Port Qasim strategically important because of its existing port infrastructure and marine access for LNG carriers. Its location outside the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most significant energy shipping chokepoints, is another key consideration.

Under the proposed financing structure, the project will have a 70:30 debt-to-equity ratio. GVEP will hold a 26pc stake, followed by General Mediterranean Holding with 24pc, and Khanjee Holdings and strategic co-investors with 20pc each. Local investors will hold the remaining 10pc in the first phase, which is estimated to cost $1.32bn (70pc of the $1.7bn cost).

The final project cost will be determined after the execution of engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contracts and other construction and supply agreements.

The commercial model is expected to combine long-term tolling and storage agreements, transshipment arrangements and take-or-pay commitments where appropriate, with the remaining capacity reserved for merchant activities.

The proposed tolling tariff for the terminal and storage facility is $4.93 per million British thermal units (mmBtu), while the separate transmission tariff is estimated at $1.91 per mmBtu for the first 10 years. These rates are projected to decline to $2.20 and $0.92 per mmBtu, respectively, thereafter.

The LNG terminal and storage facility will have four tanks, each with a capacity of 140,000 cubic metres, providing total static storage capacity of 560,000 cubic metres.

Based on three inventory turnover cycles annually, the facility is expected to handle approximately 35.6BCF of LNG a year, with storage capacity of around 11.9BCF per cycle.

Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

World.title: Lahore's air quality index crosses 530 as pollution reaches hazardous levels
World.content:
LAHORE: Air pollution in Lahore reached hazardous levels on Monday, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) crossing 530 and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations climbing to 343 micrograms per cubic metre. Several other cities in Punjab also recorded extremely high pollution levels, according to air quality monitoring platform IQAir.

At 8am, IQAir recorded an AQI of 535 in Lahore, placing the city in the hazardous category. PM2.5 concentration, referring to tiny particles that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, stood at 343µg/m³.

Air quality had already deteriorated sharply in the early morning, with hourly readings also entering the hazardous range.

Figure shows the top ranked polluted cities according to IQAir on Friday morning. — Screengrab via IQAir

The deterioration was not confined to the provincial capital. IQAir’s live ranking of Pakistani cities on Monday morning placed five Punjab cities among the country’s six most polluted urban centres.

Gujranwala topped the ranking with an AQI of 606, followed by Lahore at 509, Faisalabad and Multan at 310 each, and Sialkot at 260. Peshawar ranked sixth with an AQI of 216.

The readings varied across monitoring updates, with Gujranwala subsequently recording 675 and Lahore 535 in separate hourly updates, highlighting the rapidly changing pollution situation.

Figure shows the top ranked polluted cities in Pakistan according to IQAir on Friday morning. — Screengrab via IQAir

The worsening air quality comes amid a sharp increase in agricultural fire detections across Punjab.

According to an analysis published by environmental monitoring website HamariHawa, Nasa satellites detected 13,241 fire spots in Pakistani Punjab between Oct 1 and 29, compared with 3,158 in Indian Punjab — 4.2 times as many.

Around 92 per cent of the detected fires in Pakistani Punjab were located on farmland and were likely associated with crop-residue burning.

The analysis found that 6,655 fire spots, around half of the monthly total, were detected during the last seven days of October. Oct 29 recorded the highest number of detections, at 1,327.

Okara recorded the highest number of fire spots at 2,144, followed by Gujranwala with 1,011 and Nankana Sahib with 1,003.

The findings point to extensive agricultural burning in the rice-growing belt surrounding Lahore. Smoke from these fires, along with emissions from vehicles, industries and other sources, adds to the regional pollution burden. Weather conditions, including weak winds and atmospheric inversions, can further trap pollutants close to the ground.

Weather factor

Meanwhile, a new analysis by the Pakistan Air Quality Initiative (PAQI) has questioned the extent of improvement in Lahore’s air quality during October, despite government claims that the city experienced its cleanest October in five years.

According to PAQI, average PM2.5 concentrations in October 2026 fell by 27 per cent compared with the same month last year across 26 monitoring sites.

However, after accounting for weather conditions, the improvement was estimated at just four per cent. The analysis attributed a substantial part of the decline to weather conditions, particularly a deeper nighttime atmospheric mixing layer, which allowed pollutants more room to disperse.

The remaining improvement reflected the combined effects of government measures, changes in agricultural burning and other pollution sources. However, the analysis could not establish the individual contribution of each factor.

Despite the decline, PM2.5 concentrations exceeded Pakistan’s prescribed daily limit on every day in October, according to PAQI.

The initiative’s forecast, issued on Nov 1, projected PM2.5 concentrations to rise to 149µg/m³ by Wednesday, Nov 4 — around 49pc above October’s average.

The findings offer a more cautious assessment of the improvement claimed by the provincial government.

Punjab Senior Minister Marriyum Aurangzeb had shared data with Dawn in October showing that Lahore’s average US AQI (PM2.5) stood at 180.5 during October 2026, compared with 204.6 in 2025, 213 in 2024 and approximately 193 to 195 in 2022 and 2023.

Her data showed that October 2026 was the only year among the five in which the city did not record an AQI above 300, with the highest reading standing at 262 on Oct 31.

However, PAQI’s assessment underlines that the improvement was partly weather-driven and that pollution remained above the national health standard throughout the month.

With November bringing a fresh deterioration in air quality, the latest readings and satellite fire detections highlight the continuing challenge of controlling agricultural burning and other sources of pollution across Punjab.

World.title: LHC seeks report from Punjab Home Department on extended detention of Imran's sisters
World.content:
LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday sought reports from the Punjab Home Department on pleas challenging the extension of the detention of PTI founder Imran Khan’s sisters and seeking medical treatment for one of them, Noreen Niazi.

Justice Abher Gul Khan directed the Home Department to submit the reports by 2pm as he heard pleas filed by Noreen’s daughter, Sakeena, and Shahrez Khan, the son of Imran’s second sister Aleema Khan.

Aleema and Noreen, along with their sister Uzma Khan, were detained under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960 in September, as the PTI geared up for a protest march to Islamabad. Their detentions have come amid reports of several PTI leaders and workers being taken into custody ahead of the march planned to demand Imran’s release from prison.

Among them, Aleema was detained on Sept 20 for 30 days and Noreen and Uzma the next day for the same period. Their detention was challenged in the court after the 30-day period lapsed last month, following which the Punjab government informed the court that their detention periods had been extended for another 30 days.

At the hearing today, petitioner’s counsel Rana Mudassar Umar contended that Aleema, Noreen and Uzma’s detentions had been extended “unlawfully”.

He noted that after the completion of the initial 30-day detention period, the Lahore deputy commissioner had issued a notification for its extension.

He claimed that the detained women had also not been allowed to meet their family members or lawyers.

The counsel asked the court to declare the fresh detention notifications “illegal”.

PTI Secretary General Advocate Salman Akram Raja informed the court that Aleema’s driver had also been detained. He requested the court to show leniency towards the driver, saying his family was deeply distressed.

Justice Khan then sought reports from the Punjab Home Department and said he would examine the matter after going through the reports.

Among the three detainees, Noreen had been shifted to the Punjab Institute of Cardiology (PIC) following her deteriorating health, on the recommendation of the doctors of the Kot Lakhpat Jail, where she has been detained.

Later, adviser to the prime minister on political affairs, Rana Sanaullah, had informed the Senate that Noreen was fine after being provided medical treatment in Lahore.

On Friday, the Lahore High Court directed Noreen’s lawyer to file a separate application seeking medical treatment and family meetings for his client.

World.title: Pakistan assumes chairmanship of SCO Interbank Consortium for 2026-27
World.content:
Pakistan has assumed the chairmanship of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Interbank Consortium (SCO-IBC) for 2026-27, the Ministry of Finance said on Monday.

HBL Chairman Sultan Ali Allana has taken over as head of the consortium for the period.

“The development coincides with Pakistan’s chairmanship of the SCO for the same period, reflecting the country’s role in promoting regional trade, investment, financial connectivity and economic cooperation”, the statement said.

The ministry congratulated Allana on assuming the responsibility and reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to strengthening economic partnerships among SCO member states, facilitating cross-border trade and investment, and advancing regional integration and shared prosperity.

The SCO-IBC is a key platform for financial collaboration among SCO member states. It aims to promote sustainable development through cooperation with multilateral institutions, enhance regional trade and investment, and explore new mechanisms for developing transnational mega projects.

Pakistan is also set to host the next meeting of the SCO Council of Heads of State (CHS) after assuming its chairmanship in September. The development marks another step in the country’s growing engagement with the regional organisation, which has expanded its focus from security cooperation to economic development and regional connectivity.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has said Pakistan’s membership of the SCO has evolved from observer status to proactive full membership since 2017, reflecting its commitment to multilateralism and regional cooperation.

He has also described Pakistan’s upcoming chairmanship as a reflection of the confidence reposed in its regional and international leadership.

Pakistan hosted the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Islamabad in October 2024 and is currently chairing the organisation’s Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure for 2025-26.

It also holds the permanent chairmanship of an SCO working group on poverty alleviation, which focuses on improving living standards across the region.

World.title: Bangladesh garment workers protesting for higher wages clash with police
World.content:
Thousands of Bangladeshi garment workers blocked a major highway and clashed with police on Monday, demanding a monthly minimum wage more than double their current pay, as protests spread across industrial hubs.

The South Asian nation of 170 million people is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, manufacturing clothes for some of the largest international brands.

Hundreds of workers in Gazipur, north of the capital Dhaka, blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, vandalising several vehicles, while large groups took to the streets in the Mirpur district, where police dispersed demonstrators with tear gas, AFP reporters saw.

Garment workers gather to protest demanding higher minimum wages in Dhaka on November 2, 2026. — AFP

Angry workers also set fire to a police vehicle.

The protests came despite the government’s announcement on Sunday that it would establish a wage board to review the minimum wage in the vital garment industry, which employs millions of people and generates the bulk of Bangladesh’s export earnings.

However, labour leaders say workers’ grievances extend beyond the formation of the board, citing inflation and rising household expenses.

The protesters demand a 30,000-taka monthly wage, more than double their current pay.

Workers currently earn about 13,000 taka a month, according to Kalpona Akter of the Bangladesh Centre for Workers Solidarity.

Police fired stun grenades and tear gas canisters to disperse crowds in Ashulia, a Dhaka suburb and the site of some of the country’s largest factories.

Police personnel detain a garment worker during a protest demanding higher minimum wages in Dhaka on November 2, 2026. — AFP

“Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up — the government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages,” said Mamum, 28, a factory worker.

Machine operator Sharmin, 24, said: “We keep the wheels of the economy turning. They must listen to us.” Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed warned that the government was taking strong action to stop the protests.

“Those engaging in unlawful activities and conspiracies under the guise of labour movements will be tackled with an iron hand,” he said after meeting industry leaders on Monday.

Police personnel stand guard near the site of garment workers protest demanding higher minimum wages in Dhaka on November 2, 2026. — AFP

However, Ahmed also said earlier Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had instructed officials after hosting an emergency cabinet meeting late on Sunday to “ensure workers’ rights and improve their living standards”.

He said Rahman had told them to make sure production and exports continued “unhindered”.

Bangladesh’s main manufacturer associations for garments and knitwear warned that “prolonged unrest could disrupt production, delay export shipments and affect Bangladesh’s commitments to international buyers”, the state-run BSS news agency said on Monday.

Kamrul Hasan, general secretary of the Ekota Garments Sramik Federation, told AFP some labour leaders had gone into hiding.

“We were not prepared for this unrest either, as the wage board has already been formed,” he said.

“But workers are now protesting over wages and other unresolved issues.”

Police personnel stand guard near the site of garment workers protest demanding higher minimum wages in Dhaka on November 2, 2026. — AFP

In Ashulia, security officers chased protesters as they scattered down narrow side streets, with the choking tear gas drifting into densely packed housing where families often live crammed into single rooms.

“Police fired tear gas shells inside our compound,” said Kamona, 24, who gave only one name.

“We have children, but they don’t care.”

Industry representatives said workers from at least 529 factories in Dhaka and its surrounding industrial areas, including Savar, Ashulia, Jirani and Gazipur, had left their workplaces on Sunday.

World.title: US midterms: Michigan Democrat's endorsement of Republican ruffles critical Senate race
World.content:
A prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, giving President Donald Trump’s Republicans an unexpected boost in ​a critical US Senate race two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.

US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats’ Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly ‌contested race, publicly backed Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.

“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in a video posted to social media.

Hours later at a political rally in Iowa, Trump invited Stevens to join the Republican Party. He told reporters beforehand that he would reach out to her to thank her for the endorsement, which he called “a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country.”

Thirty-five Senate seats and ​all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favored to win a majority of the House and are locked in a ​tight battle for control of the Senate, where the outcome likely will rest with a handful of states, including Michigan and Alaska.

If Democrats take control of the House or ⁠Senate, they could block Trump’s legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities.

The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump’s agenda ​without the aid of Congress, including its tarrif pressure on trading partners.

Michigan rift

Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers came on the day she was scheduled to appear with El-Sayed in a show of party unity. But the planned event unraveled after Stevens called ​on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices.

“That ad was very painful,” Stevens told CNN on Sunday night. “There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in, or this is a campaign you don’t belong in.’”

El-Sayed’s campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said.

Republicans sought to capitalise ​on Stevens’ move. “This is courage in politics in America today,” Rogers said. “When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of ​people, it gets dangerous.”

Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated false claims that El-Sayed is a “jihadist” - attacks that fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans targeting Arab Americans and Muslims.

Stevens’ move did not appear to dent support ‌for El-Sayed. A ⁠New York Times/Siena poll released and partly conducted on Sunday showed the Democratic nominee with a 53 per cent to 42pc lead over Rogers.

A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign said that it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens endorsed Rogers, making it the campaign’s second-best fundraising day since the Democratic primary election in August.

He declined to directly address Stevens’ endorsement on Sunday.

“This race was never about me,” El-Sayed told MS NOW. “It was never even about Mike Rogers. It’s certainly not about Haley Stevens. This race is about the people in the state of Michigan, the people that I’ve gotten to know in their churches and synagogues, in their basements and their living rooms, talking about what they need and deserve.”

A number of ​Stevens’ congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to ​reports from CNN and the Hill, while some voters expressed ⁠disdain.

“Haley Stevens is a traitor,” said Pamela Johnson, 72, after casting her ballot for El-Sayed in Warren, a Detroit suburb.

Alaska Intervention Falters

Also on Sunday, the Trump administration’s attempt to intervene in Alaska’s Senate race faltered when a federal judge dismissed the US Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly ​loses.

The Justice Department argued voters may be confused by the presence of a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr on the same ballot.

The issue has roiled the campaign ​over the last several days after ⁠the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr into the race as a spoiler.

The senator said on Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday’s election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the issue. But Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has suggested he may not certify a victory by Peltola, and the incumbent Sullivan declined to say whether he would support efforts to refuse certification.

He joined his party colleagues in accusing ⁠the other Sullivan ​of trying to confuse voters with his similar name.

“They got the decoy guy on the ballot,” the senator told CNN’s “State of the Union” ​program. “I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery. So what I say to Alaskans is, ‘Don’t let them get away with the tricks.”

Peltola has denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.

World.title: Nine people dead in Learjet crash in south Florida, officials say
World.content:
A Learjet crashed on Sunday afternoon in a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, ‌killing all nine people on board, US transportation officials said.

The private jet had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a statement.

Videos on social ​media showed the jet slamming into the ground next to a road and exploding.

“It was a ​big-time tragedy that happened,” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said at a press conference near ⁠the crash site in Lake Worth Beach.

“When you see that video, it’s a jarring thing. It was like ​a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere.”

The National Transportation Safety Board said it had ​launched an investigation into the crash, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called a “horrific tragedy”.

FAA records list the Bombardier-made Learjet 60’s owner as a Delaware corporation. Canada-based Bombardier said it would fully support the investigation and cooperate as needed.

The crash left a “massive crater” ​by the road near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores ​said at the news conference. About 600 people were being evacuated from the area and relocated to two shelters in the ‌county, ⁠Flores said.

Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area at the time, forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement.

An audio recording from a Miami air traffic control centre posted on LiveATC, a site that broadcasts air traffic control communications, captured the plane’s final moments before the crash in unusual detail.

At first, someone in the plane’s ​cockpit reported to an ​air traffic controller that ⁠they were “managing the ice” but faced “moderate” turbulence and were seeking “better rides”.

Less than a minute later, the person said “Mayday, mayday”, reporting that the plane was suddenly descending at a ​rate of 10,000 feet per minute.

Seconds later, the person said they were declaring ​an emergency, ⁠with the rate of descent accelerating to 20,000 feet per minute.

Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: “We’re going to crash into the ground” before saying that the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the ⁠plane started ​banking.

About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last thing ​heard from the cockpit was a rapidly spoken “We’re out of time”.

Flight tracking website Flightradar24 said data showed the vertical descent rate at ​one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute.

World.title: Laden with eggs, robots race up sacred Chinese mountain
World.content:
Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China’s most famous peaks on Monday, carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organisers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.

For hundreds of years, Mount Tai — the tallest peak in China’s eastern Shandong province — was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors and features prominently in Chinese mythology.

But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.

The Unesco World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.

Over a 3.9-kilometre course with more than 600 metres of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods like fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.

A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology — a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree — completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.

Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.

The fastest humanoid robot — belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue — completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.

Organisers called Mount Tai’s rocky terrain a “natural extreme testing ground” that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.

The race, organised by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
