These demands are reasonable and logical: No final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the US naval blockade is brought to an end, Iran’s demands are respected, and Iran’s legitimate requirements are addressed,” Baghaei said.

On Saturday, Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi as saying that under a deal the Strait of Hormuz could be opened within a two-day timeline rather than within the seven days originally envisaged.

Iran’s initial proposal was rejected by US President Donald Trump.

The latest round of diplomacy comes amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States. Asked about Tehran’s view on the midterms, Baghaei said Tehran did not expect elections to “give birth to a new US.”

Trump has said the United States would not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Senate majority united in stripping 2027 budget bill of ‘corruption-prone items’ – Lacson
World.content:
PING LACSON. Senator Ping Lacson speaks during the Senate plenary debates on the 2026 budget on November 18, 2025.

Senator Ping Lacson says no one will be spared in their bid to 'cleanse' the proposed 2027 budget

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate majority bloc is united in removing “corruption-prone” items from the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said.

“The majority of senators are rallying behind Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito’s efforts to cleanse the 2027 budget of unwarranted, whimsical, and corruption-prone items — all means all!” Lacson said in a social media post.

Over the weekend, Lacson said Ejercito had secured the commitment of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) that it will submit all supporting documents for its infrastructure projects by Tuesday, November 3. Projects without the required documents would be removed from the House-approved version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB).

Budget advocacy groups, including the People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) and BetterGovPH, had flagged nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion with no published project attachments in the HGAB.

A separate Senate review also found that the number of DPWH projects had increased from 11,420 in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) to 16,244 in the House-approved GAB. Of these, 6,271 were new projects introduced by lawmakers without prior vetting by the executive branch.

Lacson also said Ejercito would invite civil society organizations to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the budget, which would be livestreamed to promote transparency.

The Senate will take up the budget bill when plenary sessions resume on November 9, with plenary debates expected to begin on November 23. – Rappler.com

World.title: What does the Million Mask March mean for the Philippines?
World.content:
Hacktivist activity related to the Million Mask March of a given year tends to fluctuate depending on issues brought up or simmering in the interim

MANILA, Philippines – If you see a defaced Philippine government website this early in November, it could be a one-off event, but it also may be a single defacement of many, owing to a movement called the Million Mask March.

The Million Mask March is a worldwide day of protest held on November 5 and is also colloquially known as “Operation Vendetta,” after the movie and British graphic novel V for Vendetta, wherein the main character of the story wears a Guy Fawkes mask.

Originally set up by hacking collective Anonymous, the Million Mask March began in 2012 with the largest events occurring outside the Philippines, such as in London in the United Kingdom and Washington DC in the United States.

The event is usually preceded by hacking activities or online defacements of websites to drum up interest and sentiment in conducting a Million Mask March in a given locality. These defacements and hacks decry a number of issues, such as political corruption, police violence and militarization.

This was most strongly felt in the early iterations of the protest, especially in the Philippines’ 2013 Million Mask March, which saw more than 30 Philippine government websites crashed or defaced.

A video from Anonymous on the affected sites back then apologized for the disruption but called on citizens to join the November 5 protest action. In response, police at the time also took steps to maintain public safety, but also invited protesters in for questioning.

An impactful Million Mask March for 2026?

Activity related to Million Mask March tends to fluctuate depending on the time frame of issues brought up.

While the 2025 Million Mask March was apparently less pronounced and did not receive as much media coverage save for notices in online hacking communities, there’s no telling what might spur on a 2026 protest action.

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) could possibly be in for a long few days of work though, seeing as there is a new DICT secretary, former Social Security System chief Robert Joseph de Claro,.

There also seeming loss of trust in the institution owing to the actions — and resignation — of the previous DICT secretary, Henry Aguda, as regards the temporary banning of Discord and the threat to ban other services that may be responsible for the spread of nihilistic violent extremism.

There’s also the preventive suspension of DICT eGov Undersecretary David Almirol over alleged conflicts of interest in the eGov app and the system’s development, which may bring an opportunity for bad actors or hacker-activists to take advantage of the situation.

Unfortunately, there’s no telling what could spark strong protest actions on November 5 in the Philippines, and it’s just as difficult to determine if an informal Million Mask March is coming this year.

Perhaps it’s better to remember the fifth of November as a day when plans to bring injustices to the forefront of public consciousness comes to a head.

Though in this country, that may as well be any given weekday. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who’s coddling Bato dela Rosa? Not us, says MNLF
World.content:
The Moro National Liberation Front quickly distances itself from the fugitive senator, after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Dela Rosa is being protected by an 'armed group' in Mindanao

If Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is, indeed, hiding in Mindanao, the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) insists they’re not the ones sheltering him.

In a statement, the MNLF denied it is the “powerful armed group” that had been “cuddling” (or shouldn’t that be coddling?) Dela Rosa, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over his alleged role in the bloody drug war of the Rodrigo Duterte administration.

“The MNLF is not cuddling Senator Bato. There is no established formal relationship between Sen. Ronald ‘Bato’ dela Rosa and the MNLF,” the group said in its statement.

Dela Rosa has been out of public view since May amid the ICC arrest warrant.

The MNLF made the statement after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that he had received information that the legislator was being protected by an “armed” group in Mindanao.

Remulla had also warned that attempting a forced arrest on the lawmaker could cost “10,000” lives, to explain why he would rather negotiate the senator’s surrender.

The interior chief did not identify the alleged armed group. The MNLF, however, was quick to distance itself from the speculation, saying the personal ties between former president Rodrigo Duterte and MNLF founder Nur Misuari should not be construed as evidence that the group was hiding dela Rosa.

“The claim that the MNLF may be protecting him is speculation, not a confirmed fact. Reports emphasize that the MNLF is fragmented and that it is uncertain whether the Misuari faction would-or could-shield him from arrest,” the group said.

“So, the accurate answer is: dela Rosa appears to have personal and political connections to figures associated with the MNLF, especially through Duterte’s relationship with Nur Misuari, but there is no verified evidence that he is an MNLF member, ally in an operational sense, or currently being protected by the group,” it added.

Partido Demokratiko Pilipino Lakas ng Bayan, Dela Rosa’s political party, has appealed to the Supreme Court for a swift resolution of Dela Rosa’s case. The senator’s camp also urged the High Court to reverse its earlier ruling and stop the use of an ICC warrant of arrest against him.

But with the senator still nowhere to be found, could his arrest be drawing closer?

The Philippine National Police has intensified its manhunt for its former chief after the one-week deadline for his voluntary surrender lapsed.

Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, who previously called for Dela Rosa’s safe arrest, has a reminder for authorities: Keep their operations under wraps.

“When pursuing a high-profile target or handling a sensitive live case, secrecy discipline is key — unless disinformation is necessary to flush the quarry into the open,” Lacson, a former PNP chief, said in a social media post.

Did Lacson have anyone in particular in mind when he gave the unsolicited advice? – Rappler.com

World.title: Can’t keep up with COP lingo? This list has got you covered
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) This guide to the UN climate summit's terms and acronyms will help you understand the negotiations shaping the world's efforts to address the climate crisis

This story was first published on November 14, 2025. Due to recent events, we are republishing it with updated information.

If this is your first time tuning in to the United Nations (UN) Climate Change Conference or COP, you might be a little lost.

A meeting among world leaders on solving the climate crisis sounds simple enough. That is, until you throw in a bunch of acronyms like NDCs, NAPs, and GST, along with technical terms like carbon markets, climate debt, and concessional finance — all with an extra side of a whole lot of politics.

As world leaders navigate the two-week-long conference’s complicated landscape, everyone else has to make sense of whatever it is that’s coming out of their mouths.

Here’s a list of terms you need to know if you’re tuning in to COP — which you probably should be doing if you care anything about our warming world.

Play Video

United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) – It is a treaty adopted in 1992 to halt climate change. It has since been joined by 198 countries, and is the parent treaty of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol and 2015 Paris Agreement. The ultimate goal of all these agreements is to control greenhouse gas emissions so that we do not end up irrevocably changing our climate to a dangerous degree.

Conference of the Parties (COP) – As a generic term, it refers to the decision-making body composed of the countries who agreed on an international treaty or convention. In the context of the world’s climate agreements, it is an annual summit of countries who signed the UNFCCC, where they decide how to implement their commitments to tackle climate change. During the COP, countries also meet to discuss the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement in conferences known as the CMP and CMA, respectively.

1.5ºC – A tipping point in the Earth’s temperature that triggers irreversible and self-reinforcing changes in the environment, as identified by scientists. These changes include the Amazon rainforest turning into a savanna, melting ice sheets, or dying coral reefs, among others.

35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge – It is a pledge by governments to accelerate the clean energy transition by increasing the share of global final energy consumption met by electricity from almost 24% in 2023 to 35% by 2035.

Action Agenda – A platform for civil society to join voluntary initiatives that will accelerate emissions reduction, boost climate resilience, and support the transition to sustainable economies. It became a part of the COP’s regular program in COP21 back in 2015 as an initiative to expand beyond government negotiations and include people who don’t negotiate during the COP but act to put agreements into practice, like businesses, investors, and local governments.

Adaptation – It refers to preparations made for a warmer world with more heat waves and higher sea levels. They can include strategies like planting trees for shade or safeguarding supplies against extreme weather disruptions. Funding for these strategies is called adaptation finance. (EXPLAINER: A guide to UN climate jargon, from NDCs to ‘unabated’ emissions)

Baku Finance Goal – It is a commitment to channel $1.3 trillion to developing countries each year that will help them implement climate plans. To achieve this goal, developed countries must take the lead in mobilizing at least $300 billion per year for developing countries by 2035. The blueprint to achieve this is called the Baku to Belém Roadmap.

Belem Action Mechanism for a Global Just Transition (BAM) – It is a proposed mechanism that will outline how governments and the private sector can put people at the heart of national and sectoral transitions to renewable energy. This includes job creation, worker training, and strategies to diversify industries into climate planning and investment.

Biennial transparency reports (BTR) – Every two years, countries are required to submit a report on national inventories of their emissions, progress toward their nationally determined contributions, policies and measures, climate change impacts and adaptation, financial and technical support provided or needed, and areas for improvement. The first submission of these reports was in December 2024, which means the second submission period will fall a month after COP31 in 2026 ends.

Carbon credits – The carbon crediting mechanism was established under the Paris Agreement. When countries or companies reduce greenhouse gas emissions, they earn carbon credits that they can sell to other companies. Buying these credits allows companies to comply with their own emissions reduction obligations or meet net-zero targets. The trading systems in which carbon credits are sold and bought are called carbon markets.

Common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR) – Based on a “polluter pays” principle, this idea says that wealthy countries should do more to rein in climate change because they contributed the most emissions historically to the atmosphere.

Climate debt – It is the sum of damages caused by emissions from developed countries on developing countries who do not emit as much yet are the most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.

Climate finance – Funding provided by governments, development banks, private investors, and philanthropies to help countries lower greenhouse gas emissions or adapt to climate impacts. These include renewable energy projects or protection from floods, among others. (READ: What is climate finance and why does it matter?)

Champions – A person acting as a liaison between governments and civil society on behalf of the COP president, specifically working to involve businesses, communities, financial institutions, and other actors who do not negotiate climate agreements but are essential for putting them into practice. There are two types: high-level champions and youth champions. Each champion serves a term of two years.

Climate justice – An idea recognizing that those who contribute least to carbon emissions are paying the highest cost. It means holding responsible countries, corporations, and people that drive the climate crisis.

Concessional finance – It refers to below market rate finance provided by major financial institutions, like development banks and multilateral funds, to developing countries to accelerate development or climate objectives.

COP Truce – It is an appeal to nations to stop military operations during the month of the COP.

Cover decision – A statement outlining the high-level political agreements on key issues. It embodies what the summit has achieved and the broad goals that every country has agreed to pursue. (EXPLAINER: What happens at a COP climate summit?)

Decarbonization – The process of reducing carbon emissions.

Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) – It was established in Article 7 of the Paris Agreement as a goal to enhance a country’s capacity to adapt, strengthen resilience, and reduce vulnerability to climate change. It provides a system for countries to track their adaptation progress and urge them to act on managing climate change risks.

Global Implementation Accelerator (GIA) – It is a “cooperative, facilitative, and voluntary initiative” that aims to speed up programs to keep 1.5°C within reach and support countries in implementing their nationally determined contributions and national adaptation plans. The initiative started at COP30 in 2025 and will continue into COP31. It will focus on specific actions on the ground and the mobilization of all actors.

Global stocktake (GST) – It is a periodical assessment of the collective progress in achieving the Paris Agreement. It takes place every five years, with the first-ever stocktake concluded at COP28 in 2023. This assessment informs the climate action plans of every country.

Green Climate Fund – A fund established under the Paris Agreement to distribute $100 billion in annual climate finance from wealthy nations to help developing countries fund the energy transition and projects for adapting to a warmer world.

High-Level Segment – A part of the COP where national leaders give back-to-back speeches in the venue’s main plenary hall.

Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) – It is the UNFCCC’s main scientific body, where scientists from the countries who signed the treaty work together to release reports every six to seven years detailing global scientific consensus on climate science.

Just transition – A shift from fossil fuels, like coal into renewable energy sources, that looks after those who will be displaced by the energy transition, especially workers. (EXPLAINER: What is just energy transition?)

Kyoto Protocol – A treaty that entered into force in 2005 where industrialized countries agreed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in accordance with agreed individual targets. It only binds developed countries, placing a heavier burden on them because they are largely responsible for the high levels of these emissions in the atmosphere.

Loss and Damage Fund – Loss and damage refers to the negative consequences of climate change, like extreme weather events, rising sea levels, prolonged heatwaves, changes in ocean conditions, and damage to agriculture. They still occur despite mitigation and adaptation efforts, so COP28 approved a fund that will provide financial assistance to nations most vulnerable and impacted by these harmful effects. The Philippines is the host of this fund’s board.

Mitigation – It refers to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions to slow, if not halt, global warming. It is the main focus in the world’s transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources.

Montreal Protocol – It is an international agreement that regulates the production and consumption of nearly 100 man-made chemicals that harm and deplete the ozone layer.

Mutirão Decision – It is the cover decision or final agreement made between countries at the end of COP30 hosted by Brazil. It was a compromise climate deal aimed at boosting finance for poor nations coping with global warming, although it omitted any mention of the fossil fuels driving it. The term “Mutirão” originally comes from the Tupi-Guarani language of Brazil and can be translated as “collective efforts.”

National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) – They are strategies developed by countries, particularly developing nations, to prepare for and respond to the impacts of climate change, such as droughts, floods, and sea level rise. Their main goals are to reduce climate vulnerability, integrate adaptation into public policies, plan actions based on scientific data, and access international climate finance.

Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) – These are pledges by each country on their target amount for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and their plans to adapt to the impacts of climate change. They are submitted every five years to the UNFCCC secretariat, and must represent a progression compared to the previous NDC, reflecting a country’s highest possible ambition.

Net zero – It means releasing no more emissions than can be recaptured by technology, tree-planting, or other means. In short, reaching net zero means greenhouse gas concentrations stop increasing.

Negotiating group – Countries sending delegations are distributed into groups or blocs that work together to represent their common interests in international climate change negotiations. The Philippines is part of the Group of 77 + China — the largest alliance of developing countries that promotes the interests of the Global South — and co-founded (but eventually left) the Like-Minded Developing Countries bloc.

New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) – It is a global climate finance goal set from a floor of $100 billion per year. In COP29 in 2024, they came up with a $300-billion annual target, called the Baku Finance Goal.

Paris Agreement – A legally binding international treaty enacted in 2016 that aims to keep the increase in global average temperature to 2ºC — but preferably 1.5ºC — above levels before the Industrial Revolution. Under the agreement, signatory countries are expected to present their action plan to align with these goals. It also provides a framework for developing countries to receive support from developed countries. (READ: Where are we now on the Paris Agreement, a decade after it was adopted?)

Paris Rulebook – These are the implementation guidelines for the Paris Agreement, laying out the tools and processes for them to fully, fairly, and effectively follow the climate plans outlined in their NDCs. It was completed in COP29.

Phaseout – A gradual reduction in the production and use of fossil fuels.

Santa Marta First Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) – After COP30 omitted a fossil fuel phaseout in its final decision, this conference was held in Colombia in April 2026 and convened a 57-country “coalition of the willing” (excluding China, Russia, the US, and India to prevent the same deadlock that occurred in the previous year’s climate summit). The conference established a voluntary TAFF coordination process and adopted the “Santa Marta Vision” meant to inform the COP31 global fossil fuel roadmap.

Secretariat – The UNFCCC secretariat, also referred to as UN Climate Change, is the UN entity tasked with supporting the world’s response to climate change. It organizes and supports the COP and other negotiations, provides technical expertise and reviews climate change information reported in these negotiations, and maintains a registry for NDCs.

Small Island Developing States (SIDS) – They are a distinct group of 39 states and 18 associate members of UN regional commissions located in the Caribbean, the Pacific, and the Atlantic, Indian Ocean and South China Sea. They face unique social, economic, and environmental vulnerabilities because of their remote geography, such as high import and export costs for goods, irregular international traffic volumes, and a narrow resource base.

The Troika – The host countries of COP28, COP29, and COP30, who said they were collaborating to ensure continuity in organizing the annual UN climate talks. All three countries have economies that rely on fossil fuels.

Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF) – It is a global fund supporting tropical forest conservation that was first announced during COP30.

UAE Consensus – It is a response to the results of the first global stocktake, setting standards for a just transition and goals like tripling renewable energy, halting deforestation, and doubling energy efficiency by 2030.

Unabated emissions – Describes carbon pollution not being captured by new technologies such as carbon capture and storage. – Rappler.com

World.title: 2026 ASEAN Summit: Road closures, alternative routes in Metro Manila
World.content:
ASEAN. Various local government units and other agencies continue cleaning and organizing the area around the Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex in Pasay City in preparation for the upcoming 2026 ASEAN Summit, on October 22, 2026.

To ease traffic congestion during the ASEAN Summit, Malacañang declared November 16 to November 18 as special non-working days in Metro Manila

MANILA, Philippines – Several roads in Pasay City will be closed to motorists during the Philippines’ hosting of the 49th ASEAN Summit from Monday, November 16, to Wednesday, November 18.

The affected roads are mostly near the Philippine International Convention Center, one of the summit’s venues, and the Cultural Center of the Philippines.

The following roads will be affected by the closures:

Pedro Bukaneg Street

Vicente Sotto Street

Buendia Avenue corner Magdalene Jalandoni Street

Diosdado Macapagal Boulevard

J.W. Diokno Boulevard corner Atang Dela Rama Street

Atang Dela Rama Street

The Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said security checkpoints will be set up in the area from October 24 to November 8. The public may still enter during this period, subject to security screening and verification.

From November 9 to 18, the area will be closed to the public. Only authorized personnel and vehicles with valid access credentials will be allowed entry.

Alternative routes

Motorists may take the following alternative routes to avoid the affected roads:

For northbound traffic

For motorists traveling along Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard toward Roxas Boulevard:

1. Turn right to Seaside Boulevard.

2. Turn right to Macapagal Boulevard.

3. Turn left to EDSA.

4. Turn left to Roxas Boulevard.

For southbound traffic

For motorists traveling along Roxas Boulevard toward Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard:

1. Turn right to EDSA.

2. Turn right to Diokno Boulevard.

3. Turn right to Macapagal Boulevard.

The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) also temporarily suspended the issuance of permits for fun runs, motorcades, and other public activities from October 24 to November 20, 2026, in the cities of Manila, Pasay, Parañaque, Makati, and Taguig.

Roxas Boulevard may also be affected by traffic caused by the ASEAN event, Manila Mayor Isko Moreno said. Moreno said some events will also be held in some parts of the city.

To ease traffic congestion, Malacañang declared November 16 to November 18 as special non-working days in Metro Manila.

Other cities in Metro Manila have yet to release a traffic advisory for ASEAN. This story will be updated as information becomes available.

Security measures

The MMDA will be deploying 2,955 personnel for the summit. The Philippine National Police, meanwhile, will deploy 13,868 cops to ensure the security of delegates.

In Makati, the city government banned the use of drones for the whole month of November, as part of safety and security measures for the summit. – Rappler.com

World.title: ASEAN Envoy’s Farce: Humanitarian Aid as Smokescreen for Regime Atrocities
World.content:
Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Special Envoy and Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro has staged a farcical “humanitarian mission” in Taunggyi, a safe city in a military-controlled part of Shan State, where there has been no fighting or war-related destruction since the military coup in 2021.

Meanwhile, her hosts, the Myanmar military junta, continue to send paramotors, gyrocopters and fighter jets to bomb villages, schools, hospitals, markets, Buddhist monasteries and residential houses, killing and maiming women, schoolchildren, babies and displaced civilians.

What Lazaro has done is a grotesque spectacle, a cynical manipulation of humanitarian aid and a shameful betrayal of the people of Myanmar.

Let me be absolutely clear: Lazaro is not an innocent diplomat who has been deceived or manipulated by the junta. She knows perfectly well what is happening in Myanmar. She knows about the daily airstrikes, the massacres of civilians and the deliberate obstruction of humanitarian assistance to communities most desperately in need.

She knows what she is doing. She has willingly played her part in this cynical, carefully choreographed farce.

The purpose of this theatrical humanitarian performance is to manufacture a false image of a cooperative, humanitarian-minded military regime and provide ASEAN with another opportunity to rehabilitate Min Aung Hlaing and lift its ban on the criminal junta’s political representatives attending the bloc’s summits.

The junta decided where Lazaro could go, what she could see and whom she could meet. She was not allowed to meet Aung San Suu Kyi, despite repeated requests from the Philippines. She did not meet representatives of the National Unity Government, ethnic revolutionary organizations, local administrations or the civil society networks delivering humanitarian assistance in areas beyond junta control.

The military controlled the stage. Lazaro knowingly played her assigned role. She happily posed for photographs. And the junta collected the political dividends.

Her photographs from peaceful, junta-controlled Taunggyi are part of a carefully constructed smokescreen intended to conceal the reality of Myanmar: daily atrocities against civilians, relentless aerial bombardment, mass displacement and the systematic obstruction of humanitarian assistance precisely where it is needed most.

I do not object to food reaching people displaced by the junta’s deliberate burning of villages and bombing of towns and cities. Every bag of rice matters to those who receive it.

What is outrageous is that ASEAN’s special envoy has played along with this farce, allowing humanitarian aid to be used as a propaganda instrument to whitewash the very military responsible for creating Myanmar’s humanitarian catastrophe.

What did Lazaro achieve?

No meaningful breakthrough in humanitarian access to resistance-controlled areas, where atrocities continue, hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced, and millions of internally displaced people remain beyond the reach of international aid. No access to Aung San Suu Kyi. No genuine engagement with all relevant stakeholders. No commitment by the military to stop bombing civilians.

Instead, the junta proudly announced that its foreign minister had discussed with Lazaro the restoration of Myanmar’s “original role and rights” within ASEAN.

There it is. The real political dividend of this entire farce.

ASEAN’s own Five-Point Consensus requires an end to violence and engagement with all concerned parties. Yet Lazaro allowed the junta to dictate the terms of her mission, select her interlocutors and exploit humanitarian assistance for its campaign of international rehabilitation.

We should refuse to pretend that this was merely another unsuccessful diplomatic initiative undertaken with good intentions. Lazaro was not simply a spectator in this shameful performance. She was an informed and willing participant. She chose to cooperate in a spectacle that served the junta’s political interests.

She cannot hide behind diplomatic language about dialogue, humanitarian assistance and constructive engagement.

While Min Aung Hlaing’s forces continue their campaign of aerial terror against the people of Myanmar, ASEAN’s special envoy has knowingly helped project an image of his regime as a legitimate and cooperative partner deserving renewed international acceptance.

Instead of exposing and confronting the perpetrators of Myanmar’s humanitarian catastrophe, Lazaro has willingly participated in a performance that helps polish their bloodstained image.

The people of Myanmar do not need ASEAN’s humanitarian theater. They need humanitarian assistance that actually reaches those most in need. They need protection from the military’s relentless airstrikes. They need ASEAN to stop providing diplomatic cover and opportunities for international rehabilitation to those responsible for their suffering.

Igor Blazevic is a senior adviser at the Prague Civil Society Centre. Between 2011 and 2016 he worked in Myanmar as the head lecturer of the Educational Initiatives Program.

World.title: Rakhine Civil Society Urges UN No-Fly Zone as Civilian Deaths Soar
World.content:
Rakhine civil society organizations have urged the United Nations and international actors to declare a no-fly zone over the western state as civilian deaths from regime airstrikes surge to unprecedented levels.

The regime has bombed dozens of civilian targets in the month since a Sept. 28 aerial attack on a busy market killed at least 50 people and drew widespread international condemnation.

The Arakan Civil Society Charitable Organizations (ACSO), an umbrella group of 70 local and international Rakhine groups, is urgently calling on the UN Security Council (UNSC), the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), international governments, and global humanitarian organizations to back their statements with immediate action to prevent further loss of civilian life.

Along with a no-fly-zone, the ASCO is demanding international sanctions to cut off the supply of aviation fuel, weapons and other military equipment that sustain the regime’s aerial campaign.

The appeal follows an escalation in deadly strikes on civilian areas since the market massacre.

“Our local humanitarian workers were on hand to witness the slaughter of children and pregnant women in the Kyauktaw bombing,” an ACSO official told the Irrawaddy, explaining the urgency behind the appeal.

Requesting anonymity for safety reasons, he stated the regime had conducted over 600 airstrikes across Rakhine over the past six months, targeting markets, displacement camps, and monasteries in Thandwe, Ponnagyun, Mrauk-U and Sittwe, and in neighboring Chin State’s Paletwa Township.

Data from the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute, a research body founded by military defectors, shows the regime launched 136 aerial attacks across Rakhine in September alone, leaving 144 civilian casualties — 62 dead and 82 injured. Rakhine logged the highest civilian casualty count in the country, followed by Sagaing with 101 and Magwe (61).

Additionally, the ACSO urged the international community to establish cross-border channels to deliver food, medicine, and basic necessities directly to displaced populations facing severe hardship in war-torn Rakhine.

It also called on the UN’s Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar to document human rights violations and ensure that perpetrators are held accountable through national and international justice mechanisms.

The regime ramped up airstrikes in Rakhine after the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) seized 14 of its 17 townships along with Paletwa during its 2023-2024 offensive. Intense battles continue around the capital Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, home to a China-backed seaport and economic zone, as AA forces push to capture the regime’s last remaining Rakhine strongholds.

On Tuesday, the regime’s key allies — China, Russia, and Belarus — blocked international condemnation over its human rights record at the UN General Assembly.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic push for legitimacy since installing himself as president in April after a widely derided election, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, and India. Critics have condemned the diplomatic thaw as normalizing a regime that is deploying military force to subdue its own population.

“If the international community continues to turn a blind eye to the suffering public, we can only conclude that it lacks any empathy,” the ACSO official said.

World.title: Regime Threatens Migrant Workers in Thailand Over Document Boycott
World.content:
Myanmar regime Labor Minister Maung Myint on Thursday warned that migrant workers who boycott the Certificate of Identity (CI) process in Thailand would be banned from returning home if they failed to apply for the document.

With its CI-issuing centers in Thailand seeing very few applicants, the junta’s Labor Ministry has intensified its threats. Before the regime began enforcing remittance requirements as part of the CI application process, the facilities were regularly overcrowded with thousands of Myanmar migrants eagerly seeking the documents.

Migrants are boycotting the CI process as the cash-strapped junta attempts to wring more money out of them. Workers applying for the document must now prove that they remit at least 25 percent of their wages to Myanmar through official channels, as well as a 2 percent income tax payment. Official channels offer far less favorable exchange rates than unofficial channels.

Fearing their hard-earned wages will fund the regime’s military campaigns against civilians, workers have launched an online campaign demanding the Thai government grant legal stay and work permits without requiring a CI, which serves as an alternative document to the Myanmar passport.

The Thailand Migration Reform group urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the framework based on the Pink Card, an identity card issued by Thailand for undocumented foreigners residing in the country.

Maung Myint said the CI process was “a project implemented in cooperation with the Thai authorities,” adding that migrant workers without a CI or a passport and an Overseas Worker Identification Card (OWIC) “would be undocumented.” He added that they would not be allowed to travel back to Myanmar during their time off.

The regime started operating five CI centers across Thailand on October 14, but they have seen few applicants. Those who have attended have paid the extra cost for the application, while most are holding off to monitor the situation.

The boycott campaign has derailed Maung Myint’s goal of matching last year’s total of US$5.6 billion in remittance inflows in 2026. Thailand hosts Myanmar’s largest migrant population, estimated at approximately 4 million.

Since he was appointed labor minister earlier this month, Maung Myint has been pushing for enforcement of the remittance and tax rules in order to squeeze foreign currency from overseas workers, who have emerged as a major source of foreign currency for the regime amid shortages and international isolation.

On Tuesday, he said that by trying to cut off foreign currency inflows to the regime, the campaign was only “driving the people of Myanmar and migrant workers into ruin, instead of damaging the government.” He said the funds were to be used for fuel and gas imports, a claim he has often made.

He accused the campaign organizers of being “gaslighters,” claiming they themselves hold CIs or passports while urging workers not to apply for them.

“He is just acting like a psycho,” Khin Soe, a board member of the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT), which is organizing the campaign, told The Irrawaddy in response to the minister’s claim. “He may not even understand what he said. He just seems to follow orders from above.”

He added that there would be no reason to oppose the regime, or campaign against the CI process, if its policy benefited workers. “I don’t take [his accusation] seriously,” he said.

An ultranationalist with a military background, Maung Myint is known for spreading hate speech against the Muslim community and slandering the National League for Democracy.

During his election campaign in 2020, when he represented the Union Solidarity and Development Party, a lawsuit was filed against him over his use of an inflammatory song that urged voters to choose the party “to protect race and religion and to drive out a group that destroys the race.”

Winning seats in elections in 2010, 2015 and 2025-26, he has served as a minister and deputy minister in various ministries—including labor and foreign affairs—under successive regimes since 2004.

In his new role as labor minister, Maung Myint has become the face of the regime’s efforts to extract funds from Myanmar workers and their families amid the country’s political and economic crises.

World.title: Big Brother Defends Myanmar Regime at UN, Chinese Aid Shortfall, and More
World.content:
China defends Myanmar regime at UN

The UN General Assembly’s Third Committee devoted its 29th plenary session Tuesday to Myanmar’s human rights crisis, hearing reports from Special Envoy Julie Bishop, Independent Investigative Mechanism head Nicholas Koumjian, and Special Rapporteur Kelley Currie. All three highlighted the war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by the military regime.

Of the 23 countries whose delegates spoke, only Belarus, Russia and China defended the regime. Finding nothing good to say about it either, Beijing instead urged the international community to say fewer bad things. “The international community should focus on helping bridge differences and resolving problems rather than intensifying tensions and aggravating turbulence,” China’s representative said.

Myanmar, after all, is “an important member of the ASEAN family and an equal member of the international community,” he added, voicing support for the regime’s pursuit of a development path “suited to its national conditions and supported by its people.”

Beijing bristled when Currie noted that during Min Aung Hlaing’s first 100 days after declaring himself president, he deployed new coercive surveillance technologies “gifted” by China and Russia to suppress dissent.

China’s representative rejected the allegation, calling it “false information,” and urged Currie to carry out her mandate “objectively and impartially” and avoid spreading “unverified” claims that could mislead the public.

Currie hit back directly: “Countries that are most loudly complaining about interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs are ones that are most actively interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs. Those that are talking most loudly about peace are the ones selling the weapons to Min Aung Hlaing that he uses against his own people.”

She challenged Beijing’s denial, saying she would welcome any evidence refuting that China was selling arms or providing political and economic support to the regime. Currie reminded delegates that under UN procedures, China, Russia and Belarus had been given five days to respond before her October report was published—and none of them had.

She cited the 2023 report “The Billion Dollar Death Trade” by her predecessor Tom Andrews as the proof of her claim. The report found Myanmar’s military imported over US$1 billion in arms and dual use goods since the 2021 coup, with China and Russia identified as top suppliers. Chinese state-linked firms provided raw materials and equipment for Myanmar’s ordnance factories including aircraft parts and explosives precursors used in attacks on civilians.

A milestone for China’s cross-Myanmar pipeline

The Myanmar–China crude oil pipeline has transported more than 100 million metric tons of crude oil since it began operations in 2017, PipeChina announced earlier this week. Stretching 771 km from embattled Kyaukphyu in Rakhine State through northern Shan State to Yunnan Province, the twin oil and gas pipelines are strategic lifelines that reduce Beijing’s dependence on the congested and vulnerable Malacca Strait.

One of China’s four major energy import corridors, the pipelines traverse 22 townships across Rakhine, Magwe, Mandalay and Shan, and today ethnic armed organizations such as the Arakan Army (AA), Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) control substantial sections there.

Myanmar is projected to receive around $1.5 billion annually from the pipelines, though the exact profit structure is unclear. It certainly receives a fixed, annual right-of-way payment of $13.81 million for both pipelines plus $1 per ton of crude transiting through the country—PipeChina reckons at an average rate of 35,000 tons a day, most of it disgorged at Kyaukphyu from the Middle East. PipeChina and CNPC own 51 percent, while state-owned Myanma Oil and Gas Enterprise (MOGE) holds 49 percent.

The gas pipeline, meanwhile, started operation in 2013 and carries output from the offshore Shwe fields, with a a design capacity of 12 billion cubic meters per year. China National Petroleum Corporation holds a controlling 50.9 percent stake and MOGE just 7.365 percent. Sales of natural gas from Shwe to China are estimated to generate around $1 billion annually.

To finance its stakes, MOGE borrowed around $1.5 billion from the China Development Bank at an interest rate of 4.5 percent, according to Sandhi Governance Institute. Nobody knows how much of that has been paid back or ever will be.

Chinese aid bottleneck throttles Myanmar regime’s budget

Myanmar’s military regime faced severe fiscal strain in the 2025–2026 fiscal year when China withheld approval for multiple projects under the Lancang–Mekong Cooperation (LMC) Special Fund. Naypyitaw’s budget deficit shot up amid overspending by ministries and loss‑making state enterprises.

Deputy Planning and Finance Minister Kyaw Htin admitted that the deficit was exacerbated by failure to secure expected grants, project approvals, and technical resources from Beijing. The Ministry of Cooperatives and Rural Development did submit proposals for LMC financing in 2025, but the response was deafening silence. Likewise, the Industry Ministry budgeted for computer hardware and technical equipment for Chinese experts who were to come to Myanmar for a technology transfer, but they never turned up and the equipment was not delivered.

The reasons are shrouded in mystery. In a recent article in regime newspapers, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia claimed China had backed 140 development projects in Myanmar through the LMC Special Fund. In March, Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said the country benefited from 132—worth $38.6 million—since 2017.

Either way it would be the biggest handout to any Mekong country.

Some older Chinese projects are already falling to pieces. Kyaw Htin admitted that power transmission lines from two China‑backed hydropower plants—the 240 MW Dapein Hydropower Station in Bhamo, Kachin State and the 600 MW Shweli 1 Dam in Namhkam Township, northern Shan State—were damaged and could not be repaired due to “security conditions,” depriving the regime of projected electricity revenues.

Russian grant money that had been promised was also not forthcoming, Kyaw Htin said. The rest of the world has suspended official development aid since the 2021 coup.

More trouble in Shan over Kokang ‘Sinicization’

The past two weeks have seen growing tensions between Shan communities and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) that is consolidating its control in territories it has seized over the past three years.

The Shan State Joint Action Committee (SSJAC)—comprising the armed Shan State Progress Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), the civilian Shan Nationalities League for Democracy, and other Shan opposition groups—issued a statement accusing the MNDAA of undermining ethnic rights, erasing Shan cultural heritage, and imposing Chinese language and governance systems there.

The MNDAA rejected the allegations as “baseless” and “politically motivated” and accused the SSJAC in turn of stirring the ethnic pot.

Earlier this month, Shan civil society organizations also released an open letter warning that the MNDAA’s cultural and administrative practices threaten ethnic coexistence and stability on the Chinese border. And in April, Ta’ang civil society groups condemned the MNDAA after it seized Kutkai, where ethnic Ta’ang communities form the majority.

Founded in 1989 from the remnants of the Communist Party of Burma, the MNDAA is rooted in Kokang, an enclave that is 90 percent ethnic Chinese. Once limited to Laukkai and Kongyan townships, the group has expanded its territory west of the Salween River since Operation 1027, and locals report a great deal of painting over of signboards and other attempts to suppress their languages and identities by their brash new masters.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Hosts Russian Mining Billionaire After Approving Gold Ventures
World.content:
Russian mining billionaire Vladislav Sviblov — head of Russia’s Areal Group — met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Wednesday to discuss cooperation in mineral exploration and mining between the two Western-sanctioned actors.

According to regime media, both sides spoke of “mutual trust and friendly relations” between Myanmar and Russia and discussed cooperation in education, science, and technology.

Formerly known as Highland Gold Mining Limited, Areal Group rebranded after expanding beyond precious metals into base, rare, and strategic minerals. Areal and its owner have been under U.S. and EU sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Similarly isolated by international sanctions after the 2021 coup, Min Aung Hlaing and his regime have been courting economic and diplomatic support from Russia.

On the day that Sviblov arrived in Naypyitaw, Myanmar’s Investment Commission approved 16 new investment proposals — including large‑scale gold mining ventures. The green lights came just weeks after Min Aung Hlaing invited investment in Myanmar’s mineral sector at the Russia–Myanmar Economic Forum in August, touting “value‑added mineral products” as a new export base.

Russia’s sanctions‑hit companies have leaned toward Asian markets since 2022, while Myanmar’s regime, starved of foreign currency, is eager to attract Russian capital.

Regime insiders suggest rare earths may have been on the agenda of Wednesday’s meeting, given the presence of natural resources minister Khin Maung Yi, while Sviblov himself spoke on on rare earths at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum in June.

Myanmar boasts rich deposits of the critical minerals, exporting roughly half of the world’s heavy rare earth elements over the border to China.

Meanwhile, the U.S.’s recent reengagement with Naypyitaw has fueled speculation that a global scramble for rare earth resources is driving Washington’s policy recalibration. Regime supporters now boast that the junta has a “rare earth card” to play, pointing to parallel interest from India.

However, almost all of Myanmar’s estimated 600 rare earth mines lie beyond the regime’s control in territory overseen by ethnic armed groups. Despite repeated invitations by the regime and talk of “strategic partnerships,” Russian [mining?] businesses have yet to make any substantial investments in Myanmar.

World.title: ASEAN Envoy Ends Myanmar Trip With No Public Aung San Suu Kyi Meeting
World.content:
YANGON—The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s special Myanmar envoy, Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, wrapped up a two-day visit to the nation Thursday, with no sign of having met detained democratic ex-leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

The Philippines, which currently holds the rotating chair of ASEAN, has repeatedly called this year for access to Aung San Suu Kyi, who has been detained since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

The status of the 81-year-old has long been a sticking point for the 11-nation ASEAN bloc, which has frozen Myanmar’s leaders out of its summits since the putsch.

Lazaro and regime Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe “held substantive discussions on ways to restore Myanmar’s original role and rights within ASEAN,” according to a statement from Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry.

It did not mention any meeting with Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who authorities say is being held at a “designated residence” in the capital Naypyitaw.

The Philippine Foreign Ministry earlier said Lazaro had spent Wednesday in the eastern state of Shan, overseeing humanitarian schemes aiding those displaced in the civil war triggered by the coup.

This year, analysts say authorities have allowed Aung San Suu Kyi increasing—albeit still extremely limited—contact with the outside world in a bid to shake off their pariah status abroad.

Last week, there were two rare updates on Aung San Suu Kyi.

On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.

Her UK-based son Kim Aris was then allowed a 20-minute consular phone call with her last Thursday, their first spoken communication in more than half a decade.

He told AFP his mother sounded “fairly healthy” but he feared she was being used as a pawn to improve the public image of those detaining her.

The Philippines requested “brief access” for Lazaro to meet Aung San Suu Kyi in April, after authorities said she was moved from prison to house arrest.

In August, when she met Myanmar’s senior Red Cross official, they made a renewed call for access.

World.title: Cartoon Campaign Boosts Myanmar Regime’s Hydropower Dreams
World.content:
The military regime has launched a campaign of cheesy cartoons across the propaganda media to push its bid to revive the shelved Myitsone Dam hydropower project.

Regime newspapers started featuring cartoons since Oct. 20, with uplifting messages suggesting the project will deliver 24/7 cheap electricity to households in Kachin State and beyond while boosting domestic industry.

They also lash out at opponents of the harebrained scheme. On Oct. 25, the Kyemon Daily carried a cartoon portraying critics as obstinate and unwilling to assess the project’s pros and cons objectively. The cartoon insisted the dam would cause no suffering, dismissing public concerns as baseless.

Cartoons have long been a propaganda tool for successive juntas, their simplified, condescending messages used to smear civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, ethnic leaders, and Western governments, while glorifying the regimes’ various leaps forward into the past. The habitual public response is to laugh at them.

The project to dam two tributaries to the Irrawaddy River, the N’Mai and Mali, was conceived under dictator Than Shwe. It was suspended in 2011 under President Thein Sein after unprecedented opposition over potential environmental destruction, mass displacement, the sites’ cultural significance for the Kachin people, and lack of transparency.

But now, the regime of Min Aung Hlaing is making relentless efforts to revive the project. Naypyitaw is touting it as a solution to its chronic electricity shortages—even though, under the original contract, most of the power generated by the dams was to have been exported to China.

As part of the new campaign, the regime has been marshalling local populations into a publicity blitz. Regime-appointed Kachin State Chief Minister Khet Htein Nam and the Myitsone Support Committee have staged more than 50 public meetings across the state, often strong-arming locals into attending. Yet executives from the mooted Chinese dam developer have been conspicuously absent.

With the cartoon strips across national newspapers, the campaign is going nationwide.

Officials insist the dam will bring many benefits, particularly to foreign investors setting up factories in Myanmar, and any seismic and environmental risks have been ironed out since the project was first proposed.

Experts warn otherwise. They point out that blocking river flow could allow seawater intrusion into the Irrawaddy delta, damaging agriculture and drinking water supplies. Sudden releases during monsoon season could also cause flash floods downstream.

Amid the revival campaign, resistance remains strong. Civil society groups, ethnic organizations, and ordinary citizens continue to oppose the project.

And a China analyst notes that the supposed Chinese financiers and builders are nowhere to be seen, no feasibility studies are being conducted, and Beijing has anyway long graduated from the need for extra power from the Myitsone project over the last 25 years.

“It’s really just the regime one-sidedly making efforts to revive the project because it sees Myitsone as leverage for political gain,” she said. She also pointed out that Myanmar would likely have to repay heavy costs incurred by the project’s suspension, which the cash-strapped regime can ill afford.

Indeed, during Min Aung Hlaing’s latest Beijing trip, Chinese officials made no mention of the dam, emphasizing instead the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor projects (CMEC) under its sweeping Belt and Road Initiative.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Begins Releasing Rakhine Deportees After Malaysia Pressure
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime has begun releasing hundreds of ethnic Rakhine deported from Malaysia last month after Kuala Lumpur sought clarification on their detention.

The first Rakhine deportees were released on Wednesday, just 48 hours after Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan faced questions about their fate in parliament.

Malaysia deported nearly 1,500 Myanmar refugees and migrants in late September, including over 400 from Rakhine, where the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) has seized 14 of the state’s 17 townships and is now pushing to claim the capital Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, home to a China-backed seaport and economic zone.

While other deportees were allowed to return home on arrival, the ethnic Rakhine were held for interrogation at two military detention centers in Yangon’s Thanlyin and Hlaingthayar. Those with identification cards were allowed to return home starting Wednesday, according to the Khamee Youth Unity Association, citing testimony from a released individual.

The association, which represents an ethnic subgroup of Rakhine, stated that 26 Khamee individuals were among the detainees.

Previous efforts by their families to secure the deportees’ release had fallen on deaf ears, with the regime offering no explanation for their prolonged detention.

“My younger brother was only set free yesterday,” a Khamee man, who requested anonymity due to security concerns, told The Irrawaddy. “I didn’t even know he was among those released.”

He had been seeking his brother’s release since October 21 after being informed of his detention by a regime administrator. He was told the delay was due to incomplete paperwork for a national registration card and smart card.

“Once we sent the complete documentation over, he was released within a week.”

The regime barred ethnic Rakhine from returning to their home state in late 2023 and early 2024 as AA forces made sweeping gains on the western front.

Malaysia sent back 1,479 Myanmar nationals on September 29, in the first phase of a repatriation plan that has drawn heavy criticism from the United Nations refugee agency and international rights groups. Kuala Lumpur claims all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation under the plan to deport 5,000 Myanmar nationals in stages from Malaysia, where over 10,300 others remain in detention.

The United Nations warns that civil war triggered by the 2021 coup makes safe repatriation impossible under international law. Concerns are rising over reports that the regime is forcibly conscripting returnees into the military.

Malaysia has repatriated around 8,000 citizens by air and 1,500 by sea so far this year, according to regime data cited by AFP.

World.title: Kazakhstan Opens Small Modular Reactor Simulator for Nuclear Training
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has opened a training classroom featuring a simulator of the SMR-300 small modular reactor at the Institute of Nuclear Physics in Almaty on Oct. 30 to provide practical training for specialists in the nuclear energy sector.

The training complex was established under the FIRST program, in which Kazakhstan has participated since 2022, becoming the program’s first partner in Central Asia. Launched in 2019 under the U.S. Department of State, the Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology (FIRST) program harnesses the power of the nuclear industry and innovation to expedite deployment of SMRs worldwide.

According to Sayabek Sakhiev, director general of the Institute of Nuclear Physics, the facility builds on the institute’s longstanding work in training professionals for the nuclear industry, reported the Kazinform news agency.

“According to the recommendations of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), specialists with higher professional education for nuclear power plants should be trained on research reactors such as the one at the Institute of Nuclear Physics,” Sakhiev said.

The institute’s training centers have prepared more than 5,000 specialists for Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries. The new facility is also expected to serve as a regional training center.

Based on the SMR-300 simulator, the complex is designed to support educational and practical training in small modular reactor technologies. The equipment has been installed and tested, with the facility intended to help students, young professionals, engineers and researchers develop practical skills.

Asset Makhambetov, deputy chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy, said nuclear energy was becoming a strategic area of the country’s development.

“The significance of the new training complex goes far beyond equipping it with modern technology. It will help improve the knowledge of Kazakh specialists and develop their practical skills,” he said.

The next stage will involve developing training programs, scenarios and practical exercises in cooperation with the simulator’s developers.

More than 1,300 students studying for nuclear sector

Gulzat Kobenova, vice minister of science and higher education, said 12 universities in Kazakhstan train specialists in nuclear energy, including through partnerships with research institutes and foreign universities.

The new classroom will support not only lessons but also research projects, master’s programs, doctoral research and scientific internships.

More than 1,300 students are currently enrolled in relevant programs at Kazakh universities, 96% of whom study under state-funded educational programs, according to Kobenova. The country’s annual demand for new specialists is estimated at approximately 200 to 300 people.

The Institute of Nuclear Physics is also preparing a separate classroom for senior-year students specialising in nuclear energy. The opening of the facility forms part of cooperation between Kazakhstan and the United States on the peaceful use of nuclear energy and the development of modern nuclear technologies.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Samodelkina Finishes Fifth at Skate Canada Grand Prix
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Sofya Samodelkina finished fifth at the Skate Canada Grand Prix, scoring a total of 206.89 points across the short and free programs.

Samodelkina earned 71.84 points for her short program and 135.05 for her free skate, securing a place in the top five among 12 competitors.

Japan’s Mao Shimada won the event with 235.44 points, followed by Estonia’s Nina Petrykina with 221.07. American Isabeau Levito took third place with 212.22, while Japan’s Saki Miyake finished fourth with 210.09.

Samodelkina, 19, has been training in the United States since 2025 under renowned coach Rafael Arutyunyan. She won bronze at the Denis Ten Memorial in Almaty earlier this season.

In a recent online meeting with Kazakh journalists, Samodelkina said her daily routine largely revolves around training, which typically takes six to seven hours a day, including three to three and a half hours on the ice, with the remaining time devoted to physical conditioning, running and walking, reported the Kazinform news agency.

She said Arutyunyan’s experience and attention to detail have changed her understanding of figure skating, including how seemingly small technical issues can affect a jump. According to Samodelkina, one of the defining features of his coaching is his ability to identify details other coaches might overlook.

“You can skate a program perfectly cleanly, and he will point out three things that need to be improved completely. So when a coach like that says ‘well done,’ it means you really have done well,” she said.

Samodelkina also cited American figure skater Nathan Chen, the 2022 Olympic champion and another of Arutyunyan’s students, as an example of the coach’s influence.

“He worked with Rafael Vladimirovich for 12 years, and I don’t have that much time anymore. Rafael Vladimirovich always says: he learned this in 12 years, and your task is to learn it in two years, otherwise you won’t make it in time,” she said.

Samodelkina said she hopes to continue competing through the 2030 Winter Olympics.

“I will definitely keep skating for another four years, and then we’ll see,” she said.

Learning Kazakh and staying connected to home

Despite her demanding schedule in California, Samodelkina said returning to Kazakhstan gives her an opportunity to relax, spend time with loved ones and feel at home. She described California primarily as a place for training, with much of her routine limited to travelling to the rink, practising and returning home.

The skater said she has seen little of California during her two years there because of her training commitments. She usually spends time at home only between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. and rarely gets the chance to go out with friends.

Samodelkina is also studying Kazakh through online lessons. She said representing Kazakhstan at international competitions and carrying the country’s flag have encouraged her to learn more about its language and culture.

Learning the language has not always been easy, she acknowledged, particularly because of differences in pronunciation and sounds that do not exist in Russian. Nevertheless, she continues to study and enjoys using Kazakh to greet supporters and thank them for their encouragement.

Following the Grand Prix events, Samodelkina is expected to return to Kazakhstan to perform in the ice show “Alice in Wonderland on Ice” in Almaty on Dec. 26. She may also compete at the Four Continents Figure Skating Championships, scheduled to take place in Almaty in February 2027.

World.title: OPEC+ Countries Agree to Keep Oil Production Levels Unchanged in December
World.content:
ASTANA – Seven OPEC+ countries, including Kazakhstan, have agreed to maintain oil production levels in December 2026 at the levels set for September, according to a statement published by the organization.

Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman held an online meeting on Nov. 1 to review developments in the global oil market and its outlook. The seven countries had previously announced additional voluntary production adjustments in April and November 2023.

Following the meeting, participants agreed to maintain their September 2026 production levels for December, according to the table published in the organization’s statement. The countries also reaffirmed their commitment to fully comply with the terms of the Declaration of Cooperation, which underpins coordination among OPEC+ members.

The seven countries will continue to hold monthly meetings to review global oil market conditions. Their next meeting is scheduled for Nov. 29.

World.title: Educator Who Changed Kazakh Schooling: Remembering Ybyrai Altynsarin
World.content:
ASTANA – In 1864, a school with just 16 boys opened in Turgai, marking an important step toward expanding secular education across the Kazakh steppe. Its founder, Ybyrai Altynsarin, would become one of the most influential figures in Kazakh educational history, a legacy Kazakhstan honors on the 185th anniversary of his birth on Nov. 2.

Altynsarin’s efforts to expand access to schooling, develop educational materials in the Kazakh language and promote learning among girls transformed education across the Kazakh steppe.

Born on Nov. 2, 1841, in what is now the Kostanai Region, Altynsarin lost his father at an early age and was raised by his grandfather, Balgozhy Zhanburchin. In 1850, he enrolled in a boarding school for Kazakh children under the Orenburg Border Commission, graduating seven years later.

In 1860, he was appointed to establish a primary school for Kazakh children in a small town of Turgai. Despite limited funding and a resistance from local authorities, Altynssrin pursued the project, and the school finally opened on Jan. 8, 1864, with 16 boys enrolled.

Altynsarin was committed not only to teaching but also to improving students’ moral and intellectual development. In a letter dated March 16, 1864, he described his enthusiasm for the work, writing that the boys had learned to read and write in Russian and Tatar within just three months.

Building a modern education system

In 1879, Altynsarin was appointed inspector of schools in the Turgai Region, a position he held until his death. From that position, he helped lay the foundations of a broader and more modern education system, opening four two-class Russian-Kazakh schools across the region and supporting the establishment of vocational, agricultural and girls’ schools, as well as schools for the children of Russian settlers.

He placed particular emphasis on the quality of school facilities and the availability of books. Altynsarin planned to establish libraries for teachers and students at schools throughout the region, raising money for the initiative.

“The purpose of these libraries is not only for students and teachers to use the books,” he wrote, “but also for graduates and literate people in general to have places in the steppe from which they can borrow useful books and guides for further self-education.”

Altynsarin was also a strong advocate for expanding educational opportunities for girls. With his support, a girls’ school opened in Irgiz, followed by similar institutions in Turgai, Kostanai and Aktobe in the years after his death.

Recognizing the importance of teacher training, Altynsarin supported the establishment of a teachers’ school to prepare Kazakh educators. He also promoted libraries at schools, raising funds to provide books and learning materials for both students and teachers. He believed these libraries should serve not only pupils but also people who had completed their studies and wished to continue learning independently.

These efforts reflected his broader vision: an education system supported by trained teachers, accessible learning materials and institutions that could serve the community.

Contribution to Kazakh literature

Beyond his work in education, Altynsarin helped shape the development of Kazakh written literature. He adapted the Cyrillic script for writing Kazakh and translated works by Russian authors, including Lev Tolstoy, Ivan Krylov and Konstantin Ushinsky, making their writings accessible to Kazakh readers.

His own literary works included stories, fables, poems and adaptations of folklore. Among his best-known stories are “The Son of a Rich Man and the Son of a Poor Man,” “Mother and Son” and “The Clean Spring”. Through his writing, he promoted education, ethical conduct and the ideals of enlightenment.

Altynsarin also documented Kazakh customs and traditions as an ethnographer. In 1868, he presented a study of courtship and wedding traditions in the Orenburg region to the local branch of the Imperial Russian Geographical Society. His research combined observations of everyday life with criticism of practices he considered outdated.

A lasting legacy

Altynsarin died at 47 on July 29, 1889, and was buried near his home on the banks of the Tobol River in what is now Kostanai.

His influence extended far beyond the schools he established. Through his textbooks, literary works and efforts to expand access to education, including opportunities for girls, Altynsarin helped make learning more accessible to generations of Kazakh children. He id remembered as one of Kazakhstan’s foremost educators and enlightenment figures, whose belief in learning and the development of local expertise helped shape the country’s modern educational tradition.

World.title: Kazakh Ophthalmologist Puts Down Roots in Hong Kong With Award-Winning Eye-Tech Venture
World.content:
HONG-KONG – Kazakh ophthalmologist Mukhit Kulmaganbetov has spent the past five years building a medical technology career in Hong Kong, developing an award-winning screening device aimed at detecting age-related macular degeneration at an early stage.

Kulmaganbetov, co-founder and chief executive of Entoptica Limited, recently shared his journey in a new promotional video by Hong Kong Talent Engage, saying the city had given him the freedom to pursue both scientific research and entrepreneurship.

“Hong Kong made me fall in love at first sight. Here, I don’t have to choose between being a scientist and an entrepreneur,” he said.

Born into a family of doctors and raised in a rural village in Kazakhstan, Kulmaganbetov said he was inspired from a young age by his parents’ work in communities with limited medical resources.

A personal health scare in 2016, when he faced the possibility of losing his eyesight, pushed him further toward medical research and the study of retinal neurodegenerative diseases including glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration.

“Combining science and technology can allow medical services to reach more people,” he said.

After completing his doctorate in the United Kingdom in 2021, Kulmaganbetov moved to Hong Kong and joined the Centre for Eye and Vision Research, a research collaboration between the Hong Kong Polytechnic University and the University of Waterloo in Canada under the Health@InnoHK cluster.

He later co-founded Entoptica, which developed the Structured Light Observation Perception and Evaluation, or SLOPE, device.

The system uses structured-light and quantum-optics technology to screen for age-related macular degeneration through a quick, non-invasive test. According to the Hong Kong ICT Awards, it is designed to identify signs of the disease before noticeable vision loss occurs and can complete screening in about two minutes without pupil dilation.

Entoptica won the ICT Startup Grand Award at the Hong Kong ICT Awards 2025, while SLOPE also received the ICT Startup (Hardware and Devices) Gold Award.

Kulmaganbetov described the device as a form of “hope,” saying earlier screening could give patients a better chance of receiving treatment before irreversible vision loss develops.

Before moving to Hong Kong, he said he had received opportunities from countries including Britain, Canada, Singapore and Japan, but chose the city for its combination of research, clinical applications, entrepreneurship and international connectivity.

“I came for research, and I stayed because this is where ideas can become reality,” he said. “Hong Kong’s opportunities allow me to bring together medicine, quantum physics and data science. What the city gives us is not only funding, but a complete innovation ecosystem that can turn research into real products and genuinely help patients.”

Kulmaganbetov also described Hong Kong as being well placed to connect researchers with mainland China, Southeast Asia, Europe and the wider international scientific community.

Outside the laboratory, he said he and his wife had embraced local life, from visiting wet markets and trying neighborhood food to hiking and exploring quieter beaches.

He even singled out the Cantonese minibus phrase “m̀h’gōi yáuh lohk” — used to ask the driver to stop — as an essential part of daily life.

“Today, I really can’t think of any reason to leave Hong Kong,” he said.

The article was originally published in the The Standard and is reprinted as part of the partnership between The Astana Times and The Standard media outlets.

World.title: Almaty’s Murals Turn City Walls Into Open-Air Galleries, Reflecting History and Identity
World.content:
ALMATY – From a snow leopard against a mountain backdrop to portraits of celebrated Kazakh artists and scenes inspired by the city’s past, Almaty’s murals have transformed residential facades into an open-air gallery, bringing art into everyday urban life.

The large-scale paintings, created by local and international artists, reflect the city’s cultural heritage, natural surroundings, historical memory and connection to global popular culture. Over the past decade, murals have become a recognizable part of Almaty’s urban identity, turning walls into landmarks for residents and visitors.

Unlike conventional graffiti, murals are often conceived as independent works of public art, designed to interact with their surroundings. They can tell the story of a neighbourhood, celebrate prominent figures, preserve collective memories or introduce artistic interpretations of local traditions.

In Almaty, murals gained particular visibility through international street art festivals held between 2016 and 2019. Artists from Kazakhstan, Belarus, Ukraine and the United Kingdom, among other countries, painted residential buildings, creating works that combine local themes with different artistic styles.

Murals reflecting Kazakhstan’s cultural heritage

One of the most recognizable themes in Almaty’s street art is the relationship between the city and the natural landscape surrounding it.

The mural “Snow Leopard 2.0,” located at 59 Abylai Khan Avenue, was created by the Kazakh art team Neon & Shaman in 2017 for Almaty City Day. The composition depicts a snow leopard against a mountainous backdrop, bringing together two powerful symbols of the region.

The snow leopard represents the wildlife of the surrounding mountains and has become an important symbol associated with Almaty. The mural uses the animal not only as a subject but also as a visual expression of the city’s connection to its natural environment.

Another work inspired by Kazakh traditions is “Berkutchi,” painted by Ukrainian artist Andrii Palval on the facade of a building at 111 Rozybakiev Street during Mural Fest in 2017.

The mural depicts a berkutchi, a traditional eagle hunter. Golden eagle hunting has a long history among the nomadic peoples of Central Asia, making the image a reference to Kazakhstan’s cultural heritage. Palval is known for his portraits and depictions of birds, and the work demonstrates how an international artist can interpret a subject closely connected to local identity.

Historical memory took center stage in “Girl with Petroglyphs,” created by Belarusian artist Alexander Blagiy, known as KONTRA, during Mural Fest in 2019. The composition featured a girl surrounded by imagery inspired by the ancient petroglyphs of Tamgaly, connecting a contemporary figure with the history of the Kazakh steppe.

The work also incorporated references to the Almaty aport apple, another symbol associated with the region. Through these images, the mural linked ancient rock art, local traditions and contemporary life.

However, “Girl with Petroglyphs,” formerly located at the intersection of Kurmangazy and Tulebayev streets, has been covered during facade renovation work. Blagiy expressed regret over the disappearance of the artwork in a social media comment.

“Hello!
