Pashinyan said opposition MPs were “reaping what they sow” because they had so far failed to respond appropriately or condemn the behaviour of their fellow MPs.

“That is how it will always be from now on. Whenever they behave like this, they will get the same response,” he stressed.

“Eradicate violence” — Human Rights Defender

The Office of the Human Rights Defender issued a statement on the parliamentary incident. It said that any acts of violence by public officials, including MPs, help justify violence and lead society to regard it as a normal way to resolve disagreements.

The Human Rights Defender called for an end to:

Behaviour that involves or implies the use of violence.

Any statements that justify violence.

“This incident must be subject to a proper investigation conducted in accordance with established legal procedures,” Human Rights Defender Anahit Manasyan said.

Pashinyan on the brawl in Armenia’s parliament

World.title: Iran's flare gas collection surpasses 17 million cubic meters
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 2. Iran is collecting more than 17 million cubic meters of associated gas from flaring sites per day, according to the country’s Ministry of Petroleum.

The ministry said the achievement, alongside the implementation of several contracts and projects, demonstrates continued progress in the oil sector toward meeting its 2029 development targets and improving the utilization of the country’s hydrocarbon resources.

Collecting and processing flare gas in Iran creates significant opportunities for supplying fuel to the petrochemical industry and manufacturing high-value products. In this context, projects have been identified and contracts drafted, with a focus on private sector involvement. Beyond increasing the capacity for flare gas collection, these initiatives foster investment, generate employment, boost the operations of related industrial enterprises, and contribute to a reduction in environmentally harmful gas emissions.

One such initiative is the commissioning of the Dehloran (NGL 3100) processing plant, a project that involved an investment of 1.1 billion euros. The plant was built to collect and process flare gas produced alongside oil at the Cheshmeh-Khosh, Paydar-e Gharb, Danan, Sarvak, Azar, and Dehloran oil fields. It has the capacity to process 240 million cubic feet (approximately 6.8 million cubic meters) of gas per day. This plant plays a fundamental role in collecting flare gas, gas produced alongside oil, from the mentioned fields and in supplying feedstock to facilities within the petrochemical sector. Under the planned program, nine flares (where flare gas is currently burned off) in the region where these fields are located will be extinguished.

In addition to major processing projects, the Ministry of Petroleum has prioritized the delegation of flare gas collection projects to the private sector. Several work packages have been defined for the collection of flare gas within the operational area of the National South Oil Company. Once the work under these packages is completed, the country’s capacity for collecting flare gas will increase significantly.

According to statistics, work has been completed and facilities have been commissioned for 6 packages within the National South Oil Company’s territory. Work is currently underway on 17 other packages. Furthermore, 16 packages are at the contract-signing stage, while 4 are in the process of being handed over to contractors. The capacity for flare gas collection at the commissioned facilities is reported to be approximately 78 million cubic feet (about 2.2 million cubic meters) per day. Furthermore, upon the full completion of the projects, there will be a total capacity to collect 504 million cubic feet (nearly 4.3 million cubic meters) of flare gas per day.

The ministry noted that the target is to collect 90% of flare gas currently being burned off in the country by the end of 2028.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s oil reserves stand at 6.950 billion barrels, Eni says
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 2. In the region of Russia and Central Asia, Azerbaijan ranks third for the volume of oil reserves as of December 31, 2025, Italian Eni said in its latest report.

Eni estimates that during the reporting period, Azerbaijan’s oil reserves stood at 6.950 billion barrels, unchanged since 2015. Russia comes first in the region with 107.799 billion barrels, followed by Kazakhstan with 29.799 billion barrels.

According to the company, globally, top 3 countries in terms of the oil reserve volume are Venezuela with 303.701 billion barrels as of December 31, 2025, Saudi Arabia with 267.200 billion barrels, followed by Iran, which holds 208.600 billion barrels.

“In 2025, the oil market continued to be dominated by uncertainty and volatility, mainly driven by escalating geopolitical tensions that significantly influenced market dynamics,” said Eni.

The company notes that at the end of 2025, global proved oil reserves exceeded 1.790 trillion barrels, an increase of 0.4% year-on-year.

“Venezuela, Saudi Arabia and Iran continued to hold more than 40% of global reserves. The global reserves-to-production (R/P) ratio fell from 50.2 to 48.9 years, as production growth outpaced reserve additions,” said Eni.

As regards production, the report reveals that output increased by 3.1 Mb/d year-on-year in 2025, reaching 100.4 Mb/d, excluding biofuels and processing gains. Positive contributions came from both non-OPEC countries (+1.8 Mb/d), particularly the United States (+0.8 Mb/d), and OPEC (+1.3 Mb/d), following the completion of the planned unwinding the production cuts agreed in 2024.

World.title: YouTube leads Azerbaijan’s social media market with 40.49% share in October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 2. YouTube had the highest market share (40.49%) among social media platforms in Azerbaijan for October 2026.

This was reflected in the Global Stats Statistics Center’s report.

During the reporting month, YouTube’s usage share increased by 18.93 percentage points from the previous month.

Facebook ranked 2nd. The platform’s market share in Azerbaijan fell by 10.31 percentage points in October to 26.95%.

X (formerly Twitter) secured the 3rd position with a 10.12% market share. The platform’s figure decreased by 0.9 percentage points compared to the previous month.

Instagram settled in 4th place. The platform’s market share stood at 7.3%, down 5.02 percentage points month-on-month.

The 5th position was taken by Pinterest with a 6.38% market share. Its share decreased by 1.31 percentage points in October compared to the previous month.

LinkedIn claimed the 6th position. The platform’s market share in Azerbaijan stood at 5.66%, up 0.47 percentage points month-on-month.

Reddit ranked 7th with a 2.58% share. The platform’s market share fell by 2.18 percentage points compared to the previous month.

Thus, the top three social media platforms in Azerbaijan by market share in October were YouTube, Facebook, and X.

Facebook leads globally

According to global figures, Facebook also had the top market share worldwide in October 2026.

The platform’s global market share dropped by 0.35 percentage points from the previous month to 70.97%.

YouTube ranked 2nd worldwide with a 7.85% share. Its global market share grew by 0.6 percentage points month-on-month in October.

X secured the 3rd position. The platform’s global market share stood at 7.64%, up 0.22 percentage points from the previous month.

Instagram settled in 4th place with a 6.19% market share. Its figure decreased by 1.2 percentage points month-on-month.

Reddit ranked 5th with a 3.35% share. Its global market share increased by 0.93 percentage points during the month.

The 6th position among social media platforms worldwide was taken by Pinterest with a 3.22% market share. The platform’s figure declined by 0.16 percentage points in monthly terms.

LinkedIn ranked 7th with a 0.58% market share. Its global figure decreased by 0.03 percentage points in October.

World.title: Kazakhstan attracts over $30B in CAREC investment since 2005
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 2. Kazakhstan has attracted more than $30 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) from countries participating in the Central Asia Regional Economic Cooperation (CAREC) program since 2005, while trade with these countries reached $8.8 billion in 2025, up 14.4% year-on-year, according to the Kazakh government.

This was stated by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin at the opening of the Second Tianshan Forum for Central Asia Economic Cooperation.

Zhumangarin identified expanding mutual trade, developing transport and logistics links, and attracting high-quality investment as key areas of cooperation under the CAREC program.

"Our common task is not only to increase trade volumes, but also to consistently remove barriers, simplify trade procedures, develop e-commerce, and expand entrepreneurs' access to the markets of neighboring countries," he said.

Another priority is the development of transport infrastructure. Kazakhstan is expanding the capacity of its transport corridors, modernizing its railway and road infrastructure, and developing multimodal transportation.

To accelerate cross-border shipments, it is also necessary to ensure the compatibility of transport systems, digitize border procedures, and reduce cargo transit times, Zhumangarin said.

Investment cooperation is another important component of the regional agenda. Kazakhstan's investments in CAREC countries have exceeded $4 billion. More than 28,000 enterprises from countries in the region and over 2,500 joint ventures are registered in Kazakhstan.

According to the deputy prime minister, it is important not only to increase investment volumes but also to channel funds into establishing new production facilities, introducing modern technologies, raising labor productivity, and manufacturing higher value-added products.

Kazakhstan is interested in expanding cooperation with international financial institutions in transport and logistics, industry, agriculture, energy, and digital infrastructure.

Other issues on the regional agenda include the digitalization of trade and logistics, climate change, and the rational use of water resources.

The second Tianshan Forum is being held in Almaty on November 2-3 under the theme "Strengthening Resilient Connectivity and Quality Investment in Central Asia." The forum is organized by the CAREC Institute and Kazakhstan's Ministry of National Economy, with the Asian Development Bank participating as a strategic partner.

Around 400 participants are attending the event, including representatives of CAREC member countries' governments, international financial institutions, development organizations, businesses, and expert communities.

World.title: Childcare centre, supervisor fined over toddler's death
World.content:
A Darwin childcare centre and its supervisor have been convicted and fined for offences related to the tragic death of a toddler three years ago.

Warning: This article contains content some readers may find distressing.

Ebony Thompson was just 22 months old when she was found by a staff member hanging from a loop-top fence in a "blind spot" at the Humpty Doo Community & Child Care Centre on August 31, 2023, after being left unsupervised in the playground.

Last year Northern Territory Coroner Elisabeth Armitage found Ebony had been trapped in the fence for at least four minutes after trying to lean over it to see into the centre's chicken coop.

She found the toddler's death had been preventable.

Ebony Thompson died after becoming trapped in a fence at the Humpty Doo Community & Child Care Centre in 2023. (Supplied)

The childcare centre pleaded guilty in October to inadequately supervising children and inadequately protecting children from harm and hazards.

Supervisor Casandra Harris, who was not rostered to work or present on the day, pleaded guilty to a charge of inadequately protecting children from harm.

On Monday, Ebony's family members, wearing her favourite colour, purple, filled out the gallery of the Darwin Local Court to hear Judge Stephen Geary's final deliberation.

Ebony Thompson became trapped after trying to lean over the fence to see into the centre's chicken coop. (Supplied: NT Courts)

Judge Geary said it was clear a lack of supervision and "failure to take every reasonable precaution" was central to Ebony's death.

Childcare centre guilty of supervision breach before death A Humpty Doo childcare centre has pleaded guilty to inadequately supervising children and inadequately protecting children from harm following the death of Ebony Thompson.

"No educator was in a position to see if the children were in a blind spot, no walk-throughs or checks of the yard were conducted … and no written policy was formulated requiring a walk-though of the yard," he said during sentencing.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, Ebony's parents said that "not a single moment goes by that we don't feel Ebony's absence".

"She brought happiness to everyone she knew," they said.

Failure to address blind spot

Judge Geary said there had been four incidents related to a lack of supervision at the childcare centre prior to Ebony's death, which had been investigated by childcare regulator Quality Education and Care NT.

He said the centre made changes following the regulator's inspection, including to its supervision methods and headcounts, but "nothing was changed in respect to the blind spot".

The regulator did not identify any potential risks or hazards in its inspection, Judge Geary said.

The Humpty Doo Community & Child Care Centre is located about 37 kilometres south-east of Darwin. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

"The blind spot was never really addressed or considered by anyone despite it being a high-risk area," he said.

"I want to be clear, I'm not associating blame to the regulator or Kidsafe, but their involvement may have indirectly contributed to the centre and Ms Harris letting their guard down somewhat on safety."

Judge Geary said his reasoning focused heavily on general deterrence and the welfare of future children.

The court heard there were four other incidents at the childcare centre before Ebony's death. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

He found Ms Harris was less culpable than the childcare centre and told the court she had no prior convictions and was not working on the day of the incident.

"I've read the references provided on her behalf and she's clearly a very caring childcare supervisor … I also note her distress … her role in the matter is something she will have to live with for the rest of her life," Judge Geary said.

" If one of the roles of a judge is to try and deliver some kind of justice to the victim or their family, I can't do that today. "

Judge Geary noted that childcare centre and Ms Harris had entered early pleas and applied a 25 per cent discount to the sentence for each of their offences.

He said the maximum penalty for each offence at the time of the incident was $50,000 for the childcare centre and $10,000 for an individual.

The childcare centre was fined a total of $42,000, while Ms Harris received a $2,150 total fine.

Judge Geary said since Ebony's death, the centre had installed a gate to prevent children having access to the blind spot, and added that the childcare centre had fully cooperated with the regulator.

World.title: More than 400 jobs to be affected under Mater Pathology changes
World.content:
Mater has outsourced its pathology services in a move that will affect more than 400 staff.

The announcement was made today, just a month before Christmas.

The healthcare provider has blamed rising costs, saying Medicare subsidies have not kept pace with increasing financial pressures over the past decade.

Mater says the transition to external pathology providers will affect more than 400 part-time, full-time and casual employees over the next 12 to 18 months.

A spokesperson said the change will have no affect on patients. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

More than 100 positions will be lost in the next two months, with most of the remaining positions ending in 2027.

Under the new model, pathology services at Mater's Brisbane and Springfield hospitals will be delivered through specialist providers, including Sullivan Nicolaides Pathology and Pathology Queensland.

The change will not affect Mater hospitals in Townsville, Mackay, Rockhampton, Bundaberg or the Gold Coast, which already rely on external pathology service providers.

A Mater spokesperson said the decision would have "no impact on the high-quality care Mater patients receive".

"The pathology model Mater is adopting is used by private hospital operators across Australia and will allow more resources to be directed to the clinical care of our patients.

"We are deeply grateful to our Mater Pathology people," the spokesperson said.

"This decision is not a reflection on their capability, professionalism or commitment."

World.title: One-year-old dies in house fire south of Perth
World.content:
A one-year-old child has died in a house fire in Western Australia's South West, with authorities investigating the cause of the blaze.

Firefighters extinguished the fire at the home in Collie, 200 kilometres south of Perth, on Sunday afternoon, before the child's body was located.

Police said several people were inside at the time of the fire but managed to escape safely.

Firefighters were called to extinguish the blaze at about 2:30 pm on Sunday. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

Arson Squad officers are yet to determine the cause of the blaze.

But a WA Police spokesperson said the child's death was not being treated as suspicious and that a report would be prepared for the coroner.

Community members have left flowers and messages of support for the family on the front lawn of the property.

World.title: Cats' rise well overdue as AFLW finals loom
World.content:
Co-captain Nina Morrison has always felt Geelong had the potential to be among the AFLW's best teams.

And she is not surprised by teammate Georgie Prespakis's rise to super stardom that has helped remove Geelong's underachievers tag and catapult the Cats to new heights.

Geelong has thrived under former Melbourne mentor Mick Stinear this year and will face the Demons in Saturday's qualifying final at Princes Park.

The Cats (11-1) are the highest-scoring regular-season AFLW team of all time and only finished second behind North Melbourne on percentage.

"We've been disappointed the last couple of seasons, to be honest, about where our performance has been," Morrison said.

"I feel like I've always looked at the group that we've had and the list profile and thought that we could be playing better footy.

"So in that sense, I would look at our performance and it doesn't feel like it's come out of the blue.

"We've probably just unlocked a few things that were already there and it's just about being able to do that all together and at the right time."

Georgie Prespakis is one of the superstars of the AFLW. (Getty Images: AFL Photo/Michael Willson)

Explosive midfielder Prespakis, the runner-up in the 2025 AFLW best and fairest, has gone to another level.

The 23-year-old has averaged 30.6 disposals, 8.1 clearances and eight score involvements.

"She's put in a body of work off-field as well to get herself in the right mindset coming into games to be able to perform well," Morrison said.

"She's obviously a star of the competition and I stand back in awe sometimes at the things she's doing on-field.

"She's an amazing player but her ability to bring her teammates into a game has always been a strength, but [she's] riding the ebbs and flows of that a bit better this season.

"To be someone that can do such incredible things but then also be such a great teammate has been her real growth this year."

Saturday will be the first time Stinear leads Geelong against Melbourne.

Tyla Hanks and Melbourne's impressive midfield will pose a tough test for the Cats. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Wiltshire)

Morrison, who will play her 75th game, played down how much his inside knowledge could help against a star-studded midfield led by Kate Hore, Tyla Hanks and Olivia Purcell.

"We haven't played them, clearly, this year so I'm looking forward to the challenge of going up against one of the best mids in the comp, just seeing how we stack up against them," Morrison said.

"Obviously they're a pretty well-rounded team and Mick will know them pretty well as well.

"I'm sure he'll have some little things that we can draw on but I think a big focus for us over the course of the year has been how we focus on us and do us well. I'm sure that'll be no different this week."

Morrison insisted having to play at Princes Park instead of home ground Kardinia Park — booked out for a dirt bike event — was not on players' minds.

World.title: Woman feared for life during indecent assault in Geraldton
World.content:
A woman who was kicked in the head during the course of an indecent assault in Geraldton, WA, says she was convinced her attacker was going to kill her.

This report contains descriptions of an indecent assault that some readers may find distressing.

Teahl Taylor, 29, said she had been out with friends but split from the group and was walking along Chapman Road in an "emotional state" sometime after 10pm on Saturday night.

She said a man near the public toilets at AJ's Cafe on the Foreshore said something to her as she walked past.

"It was something like, 'Hey what are you doing?'" Ms Taylor said.

The woman says she was brutally assaulted while walking along Chapman Road in the Geraldton suburb of Beresford. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

"I ignored him completely and kept walking."

She said she walked another 100 metres before realising the man was following her.

"I go to wipe my cheek, and my tears away, and look over my shoulder as I'm doing so, and he's standing right over my right-side shoulder within arms' reach," Ms Taylor said.

"[I was] terrified. Absolutely terrified."

She said she yelled "what the f***?" and tried to distance herself, but the man "king hit" her in the back of the head.

"As I'm falling to the ground he's trying to grab my butt, I'm turning around and kicking him," Ms Taylor said.

"He's gone in and grabbed my crotch and he's dragging me along the pavement. I’m kicking and screaming.

"He literally jumps back, spins around, like, spun on the spot, and boots me in the head."

Ms Taylor said the man, thinking she was unconscious, laughed, put his hands on his head and said, "You're gonna be fun, alright".

"I just thought in my head, 'This man is going to kill me,'" she said.

Ms Taylor yelled her own name out while she was being assaulted, in a bid to attract attention and hopefully humanise herself in the eyes of her attacker.

"I wanted him to know who I was," she said.

Desire to keep other women safe

Ms Taylor said she managed to break free, towards lights and jumped in front of a car.

The driver stopped to help her and briefly searched for the man before taking her to hospital.

Ms Taylor took to social media to warn other women in the city and because she wanted to ensure the man was caught.

She said she was usually highly vigilant about safety at night.

"I was so emotional at the time, I kind of had a moment of weakness and in that moment of weakness he got me," Ms Taylor said.

“I’m sick of it. I’ve healed myself from previous incidents.”

A WA Police spokesperson confirmed the attack was reported at about 1:15am on Sunday and was under investigation.

The attacker is described as being aged in his 40s and approximately 180 centimetres in height. He was wearing dark clothing, including a dark cap or hood.

Anyone who witnessed the incident or saw a person matching that description in the area is urged to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Charity 'heartbroken' by theft of Christmas toys, shoes
World.content:
An Adelaide children's charity says it has been left "heartbroken" by the theft of thousands of dollars worth of donated items intended for vulnerable families as Christmas presents.

Puddle Jumpers said thieves had targeted a Brompton facility being used as a temporary storage site, weeks after its op shop on Port Road at Hindmarsh was gutted by a suspicious fire.

SA Police has confirmed it is investigating the Brompton break-in, which it said occurred in the early hours of October 28.

The charity estimates $23,000 worth of goods were stolen, including Nike shoes. (ABC News: Bethanie Alderson)

In a post on social media, Puddle Jumpers said it was "absolutely gut-wrenching" to discover that "toys put aside for Christmas presents" had been stolen.

"After losing our Hindmarsh op shop to fire, we have been working so hard to keep going," it said.

"To now face another devastating loss is horrible.

" Our volunteers give so much of their time and hearts, and our community keeps showing up for us. This has left us feeling sick, exhausted and deeply saddened. "

Puddle Jumpers says the Brompton site was targeted last week. (ABC News: Bethanie Alderson)

Puddle Jumpers CEO and founder Melanie Tate estimated the value of the stolen goods was about $23,000, but described the theft as a "far greater loss than just the monetary value of those items".

"Seventy-eight pairs of shoes have been taken, [including] brand new Nike shoes," she said.

"Brand new Christmas items that would have gone to vulnerable children and families were stolen from us.

"We're working with kids living in cars, we're working with families who don't have enough food to eat, we're working with children who work in out-of-home care.

"It's the children and families who are going to miss out. That's the really sad and hard part."

Melanie Tate described the theft as "devastating" and "heartbreaking". (ABC News: Bethanie Alderson)

Ms Tate said the owners of the storage facility had alerted her to the theft on Friday, but she suspected the site had been targeted multiple times.

"The disaster unfolded when we realised, looking back from the camera footage from the owners, that they [the thieves] had actually been here … three or four times that week," she said.

"Today, we've come back here and realised that more has gone over the weekend."

Puddle Jumpers' Port Road op shop was gutted in September by a blaze that is being treated by police as suspicious.

Puddle Jumpers' op shop on Port Road at Hindmarsh after a suspicious fire in September. (891 ABC Adelaide: Bobby Macumber)

At the time, police said a pair was seen "fleeing on foot towards the city along Port Road", and today confirmed investigations were ongoing.

Ms Tate said the charity was exploring options for a new site.

World.title: Logan community gathers to remember drive-by shooting victim
World.content:
The Logan community has gathered together for a silent reflection following the death of a young woman from a drive-by shooting.

Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau, 19, from Jimboomba, was shot in the head and neck at Fitzys Loganholme on October 24 and died in hospital days later.

A woman lays flowers at the base of a tree in Mandew Park. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

Three men aged between 27 and 38 were also shot during the attack, when at least six bullets were fired from a car into a crowd of people gathered outside the hotel.

Members of the community were invited to Mandew Park in Brisbane's south on Monday evening to pay their respects.

Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau died in hospital after the shooting. (Supplied)

Bouquets of flowers and messages were left at the base of a tree while members of the public stood in silence.

Logan Mayor Jon Raven was among those who paid tribute with flowers.

A fundraiser to support Ms Schuster-Togiatau's family has raised more than $76,000 since it was launched last week.

A fundraiser for the shooting victim's family has raised more than $76,000. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

Police are yet to identify those involved in the shooting but have confirmed they are following several lines of inquiry.

Detective Inspector Ian Galpin confirmed last week that more than 80 detectives were involved in the investigation.

World.title: Male nurse charged with raping three elderly women faces court
World.content:
An elderly woman allegedly raped by a nurse at hospital in Brisbane's south has since died, a court has heard.

She is one of three elderly women that 42-year-old Jeremy David Pearce is accused of raping between 2020 and 2024. It is not alleged that her death was connected with the alleged incident over which Mr Pearce has been charged.

Mr Pearce was arrested in the south-west suburb of Riverhills on November 5, 2025, and charged with two counts of rape for assaults that allegedly occurred at Greenslopes Private Hospital in 2020 and 2024.

At the time, police urged anyone with information or interactions of a similar nature to come forward.

The court heard Greenslopes Private Hospital investigated a complaint against Mr Pearce in 2020. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The court heard Mr Pearce was then given an additional rape charge, for an offence that occurred sometime in 2021.

On Monday, his committal hearing in the Brisbane Magistrates Court commenced.

At the outset of the hearing, the court heard one of the elderly victims had died.

Prosecutor Patrick Bates told the court that the committal hearing should continue today, noting the age and the emotional toll of the court proceedings of the other complainants.

" They are deeply concerned by the court process. They've already jumped that hurdle by attending court today. "

Mr Pearce was placed behind a privacy screen, shielding him from the two surviving complainants as they were cross-examined in closed court.

Jeremy David Pearce appeared in Brisbane Magistrates Court on Monday. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Hospital investigation

When court reopened, several of Mr Pearce's colleagues were cross-examined about events surrounding some of the alleged offending at the private hospital.

The court heard one complainant was "shocked" and "upset" and had some trouble recounting the alleged incident.

Male nurse charged with rape Police allege the 41-year-old committed the offences against two women in their 80s in 2020 and 2024 at a hospital in Brisbane's south.

Earlier in the hearing, the court also heard that a complaint about Mr Pearce was investigated by the hospital in 2020.

"That matter did not proceed as a police complaint at that time, that matter was investigated internally by the hospital and the matter was dismissed, or unsubstantiated," defence barrister Kim Bryson told the court.

"It was only in 2025, some five years later, that police made contact with [the complainant]."

The part-heard committal hearing was adjourned until January, and Mr Pearce remains on bail.

World.title: Crisafulli makes case for re-election against One Nation in Queensland regions
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland government Crisafulli makes case for re-election against One Nation in Queensland regions William Davis November 2, 2026 — 9:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. As the federal LNP makes a dramatic gamble to ward off One Nation in the Queensland regions, state leader David Crisafulli says his government has demonstrated it is working effectively on behalf of voters two years into its four-year term. On Monday federal Nationals leader Matt Canavan confirmed a bid to switch from the Senate to the lower house, setting up a showdown with Pauline Hanson’s insurgent populist party in the Rockhampton-based seat of Capricornia where he lives. Premier David Crisafulli at the Queensland Media Club. AAPIMAGE Asked shortly after the announcement if he believed it could provide a blueprint to his own MPs on how to counter One Nation at the 2028 Queensland election, Crisafulli talked around the question. “What we’re doing in Queensland I hope shows what a good, united, disciplined government looks like,” he told reporters in Hervey Bay.



“Our focus is always on making sure that there’s a future for agriculture and tourism and mining, and new opportunities in advanced medical research and education. Related Article Exclusive

Resolve Political Monitor ‘Not landing many blows’: New polling to heap pressure on Miles’ leadership “We want to see people moving to the state. We want people to be able to afford a home.” Polling conducted exclusively for this masthead and published in October showed One Nation just three percentage points behind Labor on primary votes, with the government on 32 per cent, opposition on 24 per cent, and Hanson’s party on 21 per cent. Among women, One Nation narrowly outperformed Labor and was nine percentage points behind the LNP, despite having no leader in the state, or existing members of parliament.



Crisafulli added on Monday he was banking on voters believing he and his government had demonstrated integrity during their first term. “We’re doing everything we said we would do, and I just hope in some way that maybe that’s something that people will look at,” the premier said. As One Nation have surged in the polls across Australia, Queensland Labor has attempted to frame them as an extension on the LNP. “The next election will be a fight between Labor and a far-right coalition of the LNP and One Nation swapping preferences and hoping to govern together,” leader and former premier Steven Miles told the party’s annual conference earlier this year. At the time, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie ruled out a potential preference deal or coalition with One Nation, saying he believed the LNP could expand its majority at the next state election.



The rise of One Nation has also led some to question if Crisafulli will walk away from his promise to reintroduce optional preferential voting – as One Nation could take more votes from his party more than the Greens could take from Labor – though he has said this will not happen. World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service Little fanfare as state-run water body lands well-connected new chief Matt Dennien November 2, 2026 — 9:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: Sunwater quietly names a former ministerial office figure as its next chief executive, a top seat-filler moves to Trade and Investment Queensland, and triple-bunking is coming to a prison near you. For all the Crisafulli LNP’s crowing about delivering a fresh start with a broom through various government boards, it seems the renewal narrative hasn’t been taken up with as much verve by some of those bodies themselves. Fresh from government-owned energy corp Stanwell’s quiet loss of a chief executive, regional water provider Sunwater is the latest state entity to see some big news without sharing it too widely. Newly announced Sunwater chief executive, James Benjamin, started on Monday after stints most recently in Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie and Water Minister Ann Leahy’s offices. But they’re not the only links raising eyebrows. Sunwater The water body, whose board is led by Newman-era deputy premier Jeff Seeney and former LNP state executive member John Cotter, lost its chief executive in May after leaks emerged the board had urged government to dump its Paradise Dam rebuild plans.



David Hourigan, a senior state and federal public servant quickly emerging as a go-to seat-warmer (more on that later) for the LNP, was parachuted into the $900,000-plus job in an interim capacity while external recruitment was carried out. Word reached the Circus tent late last month that none other than Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie’s recent deputy chief of staff, James Benjamin, had emerged as Sunwater’s new permanent leader – and got his knees under the desk on Monday. But you wouldn’t know this unless you were particularly plugged in, or judiciously refreshing the Sunwater website. While there was a media statement with quotes from Seeney uploaded there late last week, it – like the Stanwell news – doesn’t appear to have been sent any wider. We haven’t got a response from Sunwater as to why. We don’t suggest Benjamin is not qualified for the role, but Circus does hear his background and well-established links to the government have raised some eyebrows.



This background goes beyond a six-year stint he did at south-east state-run water operator Urban Utilities, and previous roles in various iterations of the state’s energy department. Related Article Public service Ex-deputy premier and chief spinner reunite around regional water cooler It also includes the six-month stint in Bleijie’s office, which ended in September, and his time as an adviser to Water Minister Ann Leahy shortly after the 2024 election – a role his wife, now out of the office, then held until his new role firmed up. This was glossed over in the board’s statement as Benjamin having been “most recently, a key adviser to Queensland government ministers”. For three years prior, he was the chief executive at Initiative Capital – the Cotter-founded venture capital firm behind the dumped Urannah Project featuring a dam, renewable energy hub and irrigation scheme west of Mackay.



Asked if Cotter had any role in the recruitment process now bringing Benjamin to Sunwater, and whether the pair have any ongoing conflict of interest management measures in place, a Sunwater spinner did not give a direct answer. “Benjamin’s appointment was made following a comprehensive, external, merit-based process in accordance with government-owned corporation policy requirements,” the spokesperson said. “In making the appointment Sunwater has followed full, independent advice provided by the Queensland Integrity Commissioner.” Trade and Investment Queensland also quietly gets new (temporary?) boss Back to Hourigan, the former Newman-era Department of Premier and Cabinet deputy director-general who was pulled back into Queensland government circles after the 2024 election to serve as interim chief of the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority.



After a brief break following that seven-month stint, he was then handed the five-month interim gig steering Sunwater. But handing over those reins hasn’t meant he can hang up his boots just yet. Posting on (where else but) LinkedIn on Sunday, Hourigan said he had now been tapped for another interim role as chief executive of the state’s global business cheerleading agency, Trade and Investment Queensland. David Hourigan appears before an estimates hearing in July while interim Sunwater chief executivel. Queensland Parliament “Whiplash moment – finished up my interim CEO role with Sunwater last Friday and will now be starting my next Interim CEO role at Trade and Investment Queensland this Monday. Retirement goes on hold a little longer,” he quipped. “Special thanks to the board, executive leadership team and all the staff at Sunwater for the help and support. This was genuinely one of the best jobs I’ve had and I really enjoyed my five-month stint as they searched for, and found, their permanent CEO.



“Bit of a change to go from the company supplying water to farmers, industry and communities right across regional Queensland to leading the Queensland government team that promotes all our international trade and attracts investment into the state.” “Variety is the spice of life.” We’ll say. We wondered if the LNP-refreshed board had given Labor-appointed Justin McGowan his marching orders two years into a five-year contract. But on this occasion, Circus has been told McGowan continues in the role, and is simply on leave until “the New Year”. “The TIQ Board has appointed David Hourigan as Acting CEO from today (Monday 2 November), on an interim basis,” a TIQ spokesperson said in a statement. “The TIQ Board Chair, the Hon. Will Hodgman AC, announced the interim appointment to TIQ Staff on Thursday 29 October. TIQ’s website reflects this interim appointment.”



Why that vacancy couldn’t be filled by someone in TIQ is anyone’s guess. Another curiosity is the use of the word “interim”, which sure carries a different weight than “acting” to describe someone temporarily filling a role. An opposition-era David Crisafulli and Laura Gerber on the 2024 election trail in Cairns. Matt Dennien Minister, department go to ground after ‘triple-ups’ briefing concession Premier David Crisafulli uses a simple proposition to answer the concerns raised about his government’s hardline bail changes passed by parliament last week. “I’d rather have more crooks in a cell and less in your loungeroom,” Crisafulli told parliament back in August – a line he’s repeated countless times when questioned about already strained prison, youth detention and police watch house capacity.



Now the cabinet figure in charge of both youth and adults prisons, Laura Gerber, has made a frank admission in response to a backbencher’s softball in question time last week. Related Article Public service Youth justice critics lose funding for bail support work “One of the first briefings I received when I became the corrections minister was that Corrections was planning triple-ups as a result of the previous Labor government’s failure over a decade to deliver the infrastructure needed to keep up with the prison population,” Gerber said, seemingly referencing her incoming ministerial brief. “This is the data I received. After Labor’s decade of decline, prison numbers increased 54 per cent but cell capacity increased only 15 per cent. That is the reason we are in this situation now.” Neither the Department of Corrective Services nor Gerber’s office would share this data with us, or tell us when such a drastic measure might be required. No on-the-record response could be provided, with a suggestion that this would be prevented by the cabinet confidentiality of the former Labor government.



While extra beds have been added to cells statewide to partially boost capacity, this does nothing to alleviate pressures on staffing, and the logistics of managing more people in a space built for less. The whole situation has fostered an energy among stakeholders – from staff in the detention space to their unions, and the legal and rights sector – of waiting for a looming summer storm. Summer being the key word. One source with knowledge of the matter tells Circus the expectation was for triple-bunking to start in some locations within two-to-three months – even before the passage of the new laws. Buckle up. P.S. While somewhat outside the usual spirit of this column, we had to highlight the weekend work of resident Schrinner LNP council administration ratbag, Ryan Murphy.

“Sorry, Mary Carde, but I think your ‘lawn prawns’ (C8) are isopods (which have seven pairs of legs) and are a different classification order of Crustacea than prawns, (decapods, which have ten pairs of legs),” says fellow Queenslander, John Glaister of Buderim. “They could also be amphipods. Gee whizz, as a former crustacean biologist, pointing this out has made all those years of tagging prawns worthwhile!”

Andrew Cohen of Glebe senses an opportunity: “Yummy! Lawn prawn salad, green Thai curry lawn prawns, lawn prawn cocktails, or perhaps just throw some on the barbie?”

“I just read David Baird’s item about uptick and downtick (C8),” says Tim Crawshaw of Kenthurst. “It reminded me of the rarely heard expression ‘tickety-boo’. Maybe as people experience a downtick due to cost of living pressures and Trumpian wars, we can have an uptick in expressions like ‘tickety-boo’ to bring a smile to people’s faces?”

Peter Miniutti of Ashbury notes that “Charles Davies-Scourfield flags the over-abundance of doublebarrelled names in the Greens (C8), but this is run-of-the-mill and plain-ordinary compared to the New Zealand Warriors who boast an eight-fold of such-like in their NRL squad.”

And while David Prest of Thrumster points out that “in the armed services, anyone with a hyphen in their name is known as ‘two dads’,” Peter Thornton of Killara thinks “the solution for Mr Shoebridge is a hyphen as his name is already two words. Shoebridge = Shoe-Bridge!”

World.title: Former Bachelor star Sam Wood to appeal bail decision
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland courts Former Bachelor star Sam Wood to appeal bail decision Julius Dennis November 2, 2026 — 8:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Former reality TV star and fitness influencer Sam Wood has filed an appeal to the decision denying his bail. Wood, 46, has been held on remand since his arrest on October 3, when police alleged he had strangled and assaulted his wife Snezana while on holiday in Noosa, on the Sunshine Coast. Sam Wood and his wife Snezana met on the Bachelor. Channel Ten The former Bachelor star was denied bail by a magistrate days later, and transferred to a prison in Brisbane. He was denied bail again last Friday, this time in the Supreme Court.



In his ruling, Justice Patrick McCafferty said Wood had had several drinks at dinner, before an argument about Snezana wanting to pack their bags broke out. McCafferty said Wood had allegedly become angry. “An argument commenced, not with [Snezana] but the other person [daughter Eve Markoski Wood] who was a witness to the events,” he said. “That is said to have, according to the witness, to involve ... saying she and the witness can ‘both die, I’m going to send you back to your family’.” Wood allegedly came at Eve, before Snezana intervened.



The couple went back to their room, and Eve alleged she could hear her mother’s voice become muffled and described hearing gasping. Snezana alleges her husband grabbed her by the throat, and she was unable to breathe. “[Snezana] ended up on the floor. The applicant was still holding her throat, and the complainant alleges was choking her,” McCafferty said. Wood’s lawyers appealed McCafferty’s decision to deny bail on Monday. They will argue not enough consideration was given to how long Wood could spend in prison before his trial, that the decision was unreasonable or unjust, and that McCafferty failed consider if proposed bail conditions would reduce the risk of reoffending, and failed to give reasons for why they would not.



The appeal could be held as soon as Friday, November 6. With Cloe Read Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Inside the Democrats’ embarrassing and potentially costly Michigan meltdown
World.content:
The relationship between Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed shattered in part because of Israel, but also because of their sensitive egos and hurt feelings. The split had been months in the making.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Detroit: The last straw for Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens came on Saturday afternoon. She was on the cusp of appearing at a unity event with Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated her in an August primary and became Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee. Several powerful intermediaries had been trying to broker peace between the former rivals, who were sparring over El-Sayed’s strong criticisms of Israel. But after Stevens issued a hostile statement on Friday morning calling upon El-Sayed to condemn an ad made by a supportive political action committee and make other concessions, he stepped before reporters and said what his campaign had been signalling privately: he no longer wanted Stevens to join him at a Detroit church on Sunday. Haley Stevens speaking alongside Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers (left) after a church service in Detroit on Sunday. AP Photo/Jose Juarez It was one thing not to be welcomed by El-Sayed’s Senate campaign. It was quite another for him to say so in public. So Stevens on Sunday did what she had been telling everyone she would not do. She endorsed former congressman Mike Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent in a race critical to control of the Senate. “Abdul made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn’t need me there, that he didn’t want me there,” Stevens said while standing next to Rogers outside a black church in Detroit, where they had just attended the Sunday service.



“I did endorse the Democratic nominee, and he chose to close this campaign by saying I wasn’t welcome. I’ve never been invited to a campaign event. That’s fine. You know, he’s busy. He’s running all around.” Stevens’ extraordinary declaration and church appearance with Rogers were a stunning denouement of her weeks-long feud with El-Sayed, who narrowly defeated her in the Michigan Senate primary. Throughout their evident tension this northern fall, she insisted she was a team player and a good Democrat who would grit her teeth and back El-Sayed while working hard for other party members on the ticket. Related Article Analysis

US midterms ‘Despicable betrayal’ reopens a Democratic Party wound that won’t heal Costly drama for Democrats? Their dispute is deeply personal, involving slights between two mercurial millennial politicians of sizable egos quick to take offence. El-Sayed, supremely confident, did not wish to give an inch to a defeated rival. Stevens, still absorbing her primary loss, eventually felt scorned by his campaign’s failure to include her in events or reach out for her views, and embarrassed to be told to stay away. But the breach also represents a major fissure coursing through the Democratic Party about what its relationship with Israel and Jewish donors should be. El-Sayed, if he wins on Tuesday (US time) and enters the Senate in January, would be the most anti-Israel US senator since the formation of the Jewish state 78 years ago.



For now, the collapse of the Stevens-El-Sayed alliance has created an embarrassing and potentially costly drama for Democrats in a race that holds Republicans’ best chance of flipping a Senate seat. Stevens faced a swift backlash Sunday from her party, which was caught off-guard by her defection. “It’s just really unfortunate given the stakes that this has turned into such a spectacle because of one person,” said Lonnie Scott, a veteran Michigan Democratic operative. “It is definitely not ideal that we’d be talking about Haley Stevens three days out from an election.” This account of their split is based on interviews with more than a dozen people involved in or briefed on talks with El-Sayed’s camp and Stevens’ team, some of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations, as well as public remarks from El-Sayed, Stevens and Rogers. Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said he was unbothered by Haley Stevens’ defection. Julia Demaree Nikhinson A unity breakfast, and then nothing more Days after El-Sayed won a bitter primary race against Stevens in August that centred on disagreements over Israel, they appeared together at a unity breakfast. Stevens gave him a hug. And that was about it. Since then, El-Sayed’s campaign hired a handful of Stevens’ campaign staff members, but he had next to no communication with her, according to Stevens and two others with knowledge of their relationship. She was never invited to campaign with him, nor were her thoughts solicited about how to proceed.



At times, other Democrats tried to include her in the campaign. In mid-September, Ray Wert, whose wife, Mallory McMorrow, had run in the Democratic Senate primary but finished a distant third, texted Stevens. He had a request. Wert, who is active in Democratic circles, wanted to publish an opinion essay in Stevens’ name attacking Rogers in a Jewish news outlet. Stevens was initially receptive, according to screenshots of texts Wert provided to The New York Times. “I really like what you wrote,” she messaged to Wert on September 20. Loading Wert replied, “I hope I captured your voice.” “You did,” she replied. “So nice.” In late September, Stevens was suggesting edits to the essay over text. But something seemed to change at the end of the month. “Pls hold for now,” she wrote on September 30, without elaborating. “I love you all but cannot move forward with this right now.”



At the root of the disagreement between Stevens and El-Sayed was US policy on Israel. El-Sayed has emerged as one of the Democratic Party’s leading critics of Israel. Stevens, who is not Jewish, once said, “I see Israel in my dreams” at a Hanukkah service. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which supported her in the primary, spent at least $US30 million ($43 million) attacking El-Sayed during the primary and began spending more starting in October. Related Article US election Can a left-wing Muslim win the Midwest? Or are Democrats about to make a big mistake Stevens’ fiance is Jewish and is an AIPAC donor. She said in an interview on Friday that she was considering converting to Judaism. The El-Sayed campaign believed no amount of acquiescence to Stevens would be sufficient, according to one of his campaign officials. So when she began to issue demands late last month that he disavow an ally’s online ad that she viewed as antisemitic, El-Sayed at first did not budge. She became increasingly critical of him in her cable television appearances. He tried to ignore her. By last Wednesday, Stevens said she would not be campaigning with El-Sayed. That day, her fiance, Jason Turkish, endorsed Rogers. He said El-Sayed would make the world less safe for Jews, and that he hoped Stevens would run for the Senate again in the future. Congressman James Clyburn of South Carolina, a Democratic powerbroker and mentor to Stevens in the House, was privately growing nervous that Stevens might pull her support from El-Sayed and back Rogers. In the eyes of some Democrats, it was time for an intervention.

World.title: My suburb is a flirty extrovert, even with those who can’t pronounce it properly
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The American tourist joined the queue at the 333 bus stop at Bondi Junction railway station. “Will this bus take me to the world-famous Bondy Beach?” he asked me. It wasn’t so world-famous, apparently, that he could pronounce it correctly. “Yes,” I confirmed, “this one goes to Bond-eye Beach.” Perhaps he’d thought it was named after Alan “Bondy” Bond, the Ossie famous for stealing the America’s Cup (among other things). So I told the American where he could get off. Rather, as we boarded the bus (standing room only because it was a Saturday), I asked the driver to alert this newcomer when he should alight: on the hill at the southern end of the beach, just before Notts Avenue, the address of the Bondi Icebergs, the essential starting point for a first-timer. Bondi Beach at sunrise. Steven Siewert Bondi Beach sunbakers. Flavio Brancaleone A blood moon rises from North Bondi. Flavio Brancoleone The Strip off for Skin Cancer installation by photographer Spencer Tunick. Flavio Brancaleone A Bondi Beach Christmas. Flavio Brancaleone



Bondi Pavilion Steve Christo Noah’s Backpackers at South Bondi. Flavio Brancaleone Bondi Beach’s Festival Of The Winds. Sitthixay Ditthavong It was one of those shimmering autumn days – cobalt-blue sky over indigo ocean, “diamonds scattered out to sea”, as Richard Clapton sings in Capricorn Dancer. I’d already taken it all in with my morning beach walk and dip, so I knew the American was in for a treat. “You’re about to witness Bondi at its flirty best,” I told him. He frowned: “Flirty?” “You’ll see,” I assured him. “But you should also know that there’s much more to Bondi than its world-famous beach.” And yet the beach does steal the show. “It’s an extrovert,” I said. “It’s the flirty, giggly exhibitionist of Sydney’s beaches.” Again, he frowned. Again, I said: “You’ll see. Anyhow, that’s the way we like it.”



The Bondi Icebergs pool. Andy Wills Note that this conversation happened last year, long before the December 14 atrocity that cast a pall over the famous beach and its well-earned reputation as a place for frivolity, as a refuge from seriousness and sadness. “I gather you’re a local,” the American said. “Almost,” I replied. “Forty years, with a year off for good behaviour. Now, are you thirsty?” He looked at me warily. It was early in the day for a session. Was I a pathetic, lonely drunk, desperate for company? Or, worse, was I a sweet-talking confidence man plotting to lead him into an alley and mug him? He seemed disappointed, though, when I said my stop was only minutes away, several before his. I would have to leave him, not only with his belongings but with riding instructions. Bondi at sunset. John Tanner Watermelon time. Andy Wills



First, find a perch on the balcony at the Bondi Icebergs – the everyman club, not the (fine) Dining Room and Bar next door, unless you’re hungry enough to test the greenback against the Australian peso. From here, imbibe the Bondi postcard, from the lap swimmers in the Icebergs pool and the sun worshippers on its deck to the full canvas of the beach and its dazzling speckles of humanity and the white trails of surfers carving its waves. Then, backtrack up Notts Avenue and find the steps to the sand and kick off your shoes and, after noting the rock-dwelling yogis at the south end, stroll the shoreline and dodge the acrobatic ball kickers and the splishy-splashy toddlers and the guitar strummers and the parade of fabulous abs and barely-bikinis, all the way to the north end. Here, get wet. You must. Locals at the open-air gym. Steven Siewert If still thirsty, cross the road to the North Bondi RSL, the northern bookend of Bondi’s beachside clubs, and perch on its balcony. Or, across the road from the North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club, you’ll find lifesaving coffee at Porch & Parlour, the proprietor of which, Louise Shaw, while working as a barista to fund her university studies, travelled to Indonesia for field research on the supply chain of specialty coffee from farm to cup. See – you’re just 30 seconds from the sand and already frivolous Bondi is capable of a cerebral conversation. Next, return to the beachfront and its promenade for the sheer spectacle: the calisthenics musclemen defying gravity and human limitation on the parallel bars in the outdoor gym; the Sydney Handstand Club (on Saturdays), whose members apparently include a look-Mum-no-hands subset of synchronised somersaulters; the Bondi Pavilion for its less athletic but equally sea-salted throng of everyday people; and back at the south end, the Bondi Skate Park for more exhibitionists, the aerial acrobats.



The no-hands somersaulters of the Sydney Handstand Club. Andy Wills Getting air at the skate park. Andy Wills But now, you must – must – leave the beachfront. If there’s no time for anything else, a first-timer should climb Bondi’s ascending anterior artery, Hall Street, the heart of the suburb for those of us who live here. Do not pass the Gertrude & Alice Cafe Bookstore. Another American visitor, Oprah Winfrey, didn’t miss it last December and called it the best bookshop in Australia. One of her favourite American authors, Ann Patchett, also visited and went one better: best in the world. American author Ann Patchett (right) with Australian writer Meg Mason at Gertrude & Alice. James Brickwood Among my family’s six Bondi addresses was the happiest of dead-end streets, Cox Avenue, the cul-de-sac of which abutted Hall Street. The only sensible way out to buy a loaf of bread was on foot. That could become a one-hour, five-conversation expedition, as it might in the chatty main street of any decent country town. Back home: “You forgot the milk.” So off I’d trot for another hour. I should have told the American to stroll from Cox to Forest Knoll, another glorious dead end around the corner, and climb its precipitous stairs to Francis Street, then cross to the magical pedestrian lane that connects to Edward Street. Stop in the lane! Here, admire its outdoor gallery of artworks, as I did last month when I discovered an old Bondi friend, Greg Perano, tending to the “exhibition”. I’d been impressed to learn about 35 years ago that Greg was an early percussionist with Australian band Hunters & Collectors. I was more impressed now by his devotion as a Bondi citizen: he had created this gallery with another local, Rex, who named the lane Fredward. Greg Perano in “Fredward” Lane. Rick Feneley

World.title: Find out how your neighbours voted in 2022 – and what it means for this election
World.content:
Use our interactive map to search any polling booth in Victoria, as we analyse how the results from 2022 may shape this year’s election.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victoria is a very different place than it was in 2022. At the last state election, Labor was returned to power in a thumping “Danslide”, as Jess Wilson entered the parliament as a first-term Liberal MP. In the four years since, Labor has been knocked off course by scandal after scandal, its approval rating has plummeted, and three premiers have led the state. Polls suggest the party will be banished to the opposition benches – and replaced by a government led by Wilson. Daniel Andrews celebrates his 2022 election victory. Getty Images For all of this change, however, the results in 2022 hinted at the trends now shaping the upcoming state election campaign: the warning signs for Labor in its heartland, the unexpected rise of One Nation, and the potential weakness of the Liberal Party in traditional blue-ribbon seats. If you scroll to the bottom of this article, you can search for your own local polling station to see how your neighbours voted last time. Across schools, community halls and sporting clubs, The Age has analysed the results from every polling booth in 2022 to investigate what they might mean for the results on November 28. Worries in Labor’s northern heartland



Labor’s red wall in the northern suburbs began crumbling four years ago. While the Daniel Andrews-led government was convincingly re-elected, the party suffered large two-party preferred swings to the Liberals in Thomastown (11.2 per cent), Mill Park (13.5 per cent), Broadmeadows (14.8 per cent) and Greenvale (13.3 per cent). At the Bethal Primary School booth in Greenvale, Labor’s Iwan Walters – who ultimately won the seat – suffered a whopping 33.2 per cent swing against him. This benefited the Liberals, but also conservative independent Fatma Erciyas, Family First Victoria and the Victorian Socialists. Greenvale is a culturally diverse area and large numbers of voters have Turkish, Lebanese, Iraqi and Italian heritage. In 2026, it is being targeted by Liberal candidate Jim Overend, who has served on Hume City Council for the past six years and ran a small business. Early signs of the orange wave



One Nation was a barely visible political force in 2022, winning just 0.22 per cent of the statewide primary vote. But in the seat of Morwell, about 150 kilometres east of Melbourne, the party pulled 6.1 per cent of the vote, an early signal of Pauline Hanson’s political potency in regional communities. At the Traralgon South Community Hall, 8.4 per cent of voters gave their vote to One Nation. The booth is close to the Hazelwood coal-fired power station, a cornerstone of the local economy which closed in 2017 and resulted in hundreds of job losses. The electorate is one of the most disadvantaged in Victoria – the suburb of Morwell recorded an 11 per cent unemployment rate at the 2021 census, more than double the state average. One Nation’s vote is currently strongest in regional and rural electorates, and among older, non-university educated voters. The Age’s latest Resolve Political Monitor has the party polling with a primary vote of 23 per cent in Victoria, which could result in a significant presence in both the lower and upper house. Casey Murphy, the party’s Morwell candidate, previously ran for One Nation in a supplementary election in the Gippsland seat of Narracan in early 2023. Teals targeting blue-ribbon seats



After the success of the so-called teal independent movement at the federal election in May 2022, a host of Climate 200-backed independents ran in the Victorian state election that November. Although none were elected, several managed to put a dent in the support for major party candidates, and are running again in 2026. Though Jess Wilson won the blue-ribbon seat of Kew at her first state election of 2022, the Liberal Party’s primary vote dropped by 5 per cent. At the Canterbury Girls Secondary College booth, Wilson’s 44.6 per cent primary vote was down 7 per cent on her party’s performance in 2018, as teal candidate Sophie Torney pulled in 25 per cent, ahead of Labor and the Greens. Torney, who has since served as Boroondara mayor, is again challenging Wilson, this time with triple the financial backing compared to the $115,000 she raised in 2022. Wilson, of course, has seen her public profile grow markedly since she became opposition leader late last year. Changing tide in the west



In 2022, the Liberal Party gained significant ground in Melbourne’s western suburbs for the first time – a momentum they will be hoping to build on to prise some electorates out of Labor’s hands later this month. The city’s west is home to many migrants and lower-socioeconomic residents – demographics which have traditionally supported Labor. But the Liberals, as well as independents, fared better in 2022. The introduction of One Nation and The West Party – a group of locals running on a platform of community issues – further threatens Labor’s grip. Melton, Werribee and Sydenham are all considered in play for conservative parties this time around. In Sydenham, Labor suffered a massive 17.5-percentage point drop in its 2022 primary vote, almost triple the statewide swing of 5.8 per cent. At the Sydenham-Hillside Primary School booth, Labor’s primary vote plummeted by 20.9 percentage points compared to 2018, as the Liberal primary vote inched up and voters moved to other options including Family First and the Victorian Socialists. Veteran MP Natalie Hutchins is not recontesting the seat this year, while concerns over data centres in the electorate are a further headache for Labor.

World.title: Crisafulli makes case for re-election against One Nation in Queensland regions
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland government Crisafulli makes case for re-election against One Nation in Queensland regions William Davis November 2, 2026 — 9:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As the federal LNP makes a dramatic gamble to ward off One Nation in the Queensland regions, state leader David Crisafulli says his government has demonstrated it is working effectively on behalf of voters two years into its four-year term. On Monday federal Nationals leader Matt Canavan confirmed a bid to switch from the Senate to the lower house, setting up a showdown with Pauline Hanson’s insurgent populist party in the Rockhampton-based seat of Capricornia where he lives. Premier David Crisafulli at the Queensland Media Club. AAPIMAGE Asked shortly after the announcement if he believed it could provide a blueprint to his own MPs on how to counter One Nation at the 2028 Queensland election, Crisafulli talked around the question. “What we’re doing in Queensland I hope shows what a good, united, disciplined government looks like,” he told reporters in Hervey Bay.



“Our focus is always on making sure that there’s a future for agriculture and tourism and mining, and new opportunities in advanced medical research and education. Related Article Exclusive

Resolve Political Monitor ‘Not landing many blows’: New polling to heap pressure on Miles’ leadership “We want to see people moving to the state. We want people to be able to afford a home.” Polling conducted exclusively for this masthead and published in October showed One Nation just three percentage points behind Labor on primary votes, with the government on 32 per cent, opposition on 24 per cent, and Hanson’s party on 21 per cent. Among women, One Nation narrowly outperformed Labor and was nine percentage points behind the LNP, despite having no leader in the state, or existing members of parliament.



Crisafulli added on Monday he was banking on voters believing he and his government had demonstrated integrity during their first term. “We’re doing everything we said we would do, and I just hope in some way that maybe that’s something that people will look at,” the premier said. As One Nation have surged in the polls across Australia, Queensland Labor has attempted to frame them as an extension on the LNP. “The next election will be a fight between Labor and a far-right coalition of the LNP and One Nation swapping preferences and hoping to govern together,” leader and former premier Steven Miles told the party’s annual conference earlier this year. At the time, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie ruled out a potential preference deal or coalition with One Nation, saying he believed the LNP could expand its majority at the next state election.



The rise of One Nation has also led some to question if Crisafulli will walk away from his promise to reintroduce optional preferential voting – as One Nation could take more votes from his party more than the Greens could take from Labor – though he has said this will not happen. Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: Sunwater quietly names a former ministerial office figure as its next chief executive, a top seat-filler moves to Trade and Investment Queensland, and triple-bunking is coming to a prison near you. For all the Crisafulli LNP’s crowing about delivering a fresh start with a broom through various government boards, it seems the renewal narrative hasn’t been taken up with as much verve by some of those bodies themselves. Fresh from government-owned energy corp Stanwell’s quiet loss of a chief executive, regional water provider Sunwater is the latest state entity to see some big news without sharing it too widely. Newly announced Sunwater chief executive, James Benjamin, started on Monday after stints most recently in Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie and Water Minister Ann Leahy’s offices. But they’re not the only links raising eyebrows. Sunwater The water body, whose board is led by Newman-era deputy premier Jeff Seeney and former LNP state executive member John Cotter, lost its chief executive in May after leaks emerged the board had urged government to dump its Paradise Dam rebuild plans.



David Hourigan, a senior state and federal public servant quickly emerging as a go-to seat-warmer (more on that later) for the LNP, was parachuted into the $900,000-plus job in an interim capacity while external recruitment was carried out. Word reached the Circus tent late last month that none other than Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie’s recent deputy chief of staff, James Benjamin, had emerged as Sunwater’s new permanent leader – and got his knees under the desk on Monday. But you wouldn’t know this unless you were particularly plugged in, or judiciously refreshing the Sunwater website. While there was a media statement with quotes from Seeney uploaded there late last week, it – like the Stanwell news – doesn’t appear to have been sent any wider. We haven’t got a response from Sunwater as to why. We don’t suggest Benjamin is not qualified for the role, but Circus does hear his background and well-established links to the government have raised some eyebrows.



This background goes beyond a six-year stint he did at south-east state-run water operator Urban Utilities, and previous roles in various iterations of the state’s energy department. Related Article Public service Ex-deputy premier and chief spinner reunite around regional water cooler It also includes the six-month stint in Bleijie’s office, which ended in September, and his time as an adviser to Water Minister Ann Leahy shortly after the 2024 election – a role his wife, now out of the office, then held until his new role firmed up. This was glossed over in the board’s statement as Benjamin having been “most recently, a key adviser to Queensland government ministers”. For three years prior, he was the chief executive at Initiative Capital – the Cotter-founded venture capital firm behind the dumped Urannah Project featuring a dam, renewable energy hub and irrigation scheme west of Mackay.



Asked if Cotter had any role in the recruitment process now bringing Benjamin to Sunwater, and whether the pair have any ongoing conflict of interest management measures in place, a Sunwater spinner did not give a direct answer. “Benjamin’s appointment was made following a comprehensive, external, merit-based process in accordance with government-owned corporation policy requirements,” the spokesperson said. “In making the appointment Sunwater has followed full, independent advice provided by the Queensland Integrity Commissioner.” Trade and Investment Queensland also quietly gets new (temporary?) boss Back to Hourigan, the former Newman-era Department of Premier and Cabinet deputy director-general who was pulled back into Queensland government circles after the 2024 election to serve as interim chief of the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority.



After a brief break following that seven-month stint, he was then handed the five-month interim gig steering Sunwater. But handing over those reins hasn’t meant he can hang up his boots just yet. Posting on (where else but) LinkedIn on Sunday, Hourigan said he had now been tapped for another interim role as chief executive of the state’s global business cheerleading agency, Trade and Investment Queensland. David Hourigan appears before an estimates hearing in July while interim Sunwater chief executivel. Queensland Parliament “Whiplash moment – finished up my interim CEO role with Sunwater last Friday and will now be starting my next Interim CEO role at Trade and Investment Queensland this Monday. Retirement goes on hold a little longer,” he quipped. “Special thanks to the board, executive leadership team and all the staff at Sunwater for the help and support. This was genuinely one of the best jobs I’ve had and I really enjoyed my five-month stint as they searched for, and found, their permanent CEO.



“Bit of a change to go from the company supplying water to farmers, industry and communities right across regional Queensland to leading the Queensland government team that promotes all our international trade and attracts investment into the state.” “Variety is the spice of life.” We’ll say. We wondered if the LNP-refreshed board had given Labor-appointed Justin McGowan his marching orders two years into a five-year contract. But on this occasion, Circus has been told McGowan continues in the role, and is simply on leave until “the New Year”. “The TIQ Board has appointed David Hourigan as Acting CEO from today (Monday 2 November), on an interim basis,” a TIQ spokesperson said in a statement. “The TIQ Board Chair, the Hon. Will Hodgman AC, announced the interim appointment to TIQ Staff on Thursday 29 October. TIQ’s website reflects this interim appointment.”



Why that vacancy couldn’t be filled by someone in TIQ is anyone’s guess. Another curiosity is the use of the word “interim”, which sure carries a different weight than “acting” to describe someone temporarily filling a role. An opposition-era David Crisafulli and Laura Gerber on the 2024 election trail in Cairns. Matt Dennien Minister, department go to ground after ‘triple-ups’ briefing concession Premier David Crisafulli uses a simple proposition to answer the concerns raised about his government’s hardline bail changes passed by parliament last week. “I’d rather have more crooks in a cell and less in your loungeroom,” Crisafulli told parliament back in August – a line he’s repeated countless times when questioned about already strained prison, youth detention and police watch house capacity.



Now the cabinet figure in charge of both youth and adults prisons, Laura Gerber, has made a frank admission in response to a backbencher’s softball in question time last week. Related Article Public service Youth justice critics lose funding for bail support work “One of the first briefings I received when I became the corrections minister was that Corrections was planning triple-ups as a result of the previous Labor government’s failure over a decade to deliver the infrastructure needed to keep up with the prison population,” Gerber said, seemingly referencing her incoming ministerial brief. “This is the data I received. After Labor’s decade of decline, prison numbers increased 54 per cent but cell capacity increased only 15 per cent. That is the reason we are in this situation now.” Neither the Department of Corrective Services nor Gerber’s office would share this data with us, or tell us when such a drastic measure might be required. No on-the-record response could be provided, with a suggestion that this would be prevented by the cabinet confidentiality of the former Labor government.



While extra beds have been added to cells statewide to partially boost capacity, this does nothing to alleviate pressures on staffing, and the logistics of managing more people in a space built for less. The whole situation has fostered an energy among stakeholders – from staff in the detention space to their unions, and the legal and rights sector – of waiting for a looming summer storm. Summer being the key word. One source with knowledge of the matter tells Circus the expectation was for triple-bunking to start in some locations within two-to-three months – even before the passage of the new laws. Buckle up. P.S. While somewhat outside the usual spirit of this column, we had to highlight the weekend work of resident Schrinner LNP council administration ratbag, Ryan Murphy.
