“Sorry, Mary Carde, but I think your ‘lawn prawns’ (C8) are isopods (which have seven pairs of legs) and are a different classification order of Crustacea than prawns, (decapods, which have ten pairs of legs),” says fellow Queenslander, John Glaister of Buderim. “They could also be amphipods. Gee whizz, as a former crustacean biologist, pointing this out has made all those years of tagging prawns worthwhile!”

Andrew Cohen of Glebe senses an opportunity: “Yummy! Lawn prawn salad, green Thai curry lawn prawns, lawn prawn cocktails, or perhaps just throw some on the barbie?”

“I just read David Baird’s item about uptick and downtick (C8),” says Tim Crawshaw of Kenthurst. “It reminded me of the rarely heard expression ‘tickety-boo’. Maybe as people experience a downtick due to cost of living pressures and Trumpian wars, we can have an uptick in expressions like ‘tickety-boo’ to bring a smile to people’s faces?”

Peter Miniutti of Ashbury notes that “Charles Davies-Scourfield flags the over-abundance of doublebarrelled names in the Greens (C8), but this is run-of-the-mill and plain-ordinary compared to the New Zealand Warriors who boast an eight-fold of such-like in their NRL squad.”

And while David Prest of Thrumster points out that “in the armed services, anyone with a hyphen in their name is known as ‘two dads’,” Peter Thornton of Killara thinks “the solution for Mr Shoebridge is a hyphen as his name is already two words. Shoebridge = Shoe-Bridge!”

Former reality TV star and fitness influencer Sam Wood has filed an appeal to the decision denying his bail. Wood, 46, has been held on remand since his arrest on October 3, when police alleged he had strangled and assaulted his wife Snezana while on holiday in Noosa, on the Sunshine Coast. Sam Wood and his wife Snezana met on the Bachelor. Channel Ten The former Bachelor star was denied bail by a magistrate days later, and transferred to a prison in Brisbane. He was denied bail again last Friday, this time in the Supreme Court.



In his ruling, Justice Patrick McCafferty said Wood had had several drinks at dinner, before an argument about Snezana wanting to pack their bags broke out. McCafferty said Wood had allegedly become angry. “An argument commenced, not with [Snezana] but the other person [daughter Eve Markoski Wood] who was a witness to the events,” he said. “That is said to have, according to the witness, to involve ... saying she and the witness can ‘both die, I’m going to send you back to your family’.” Wood allegedly came at Eve, before Snezana intervened.



The couple went back to their room, and Eve alleged she could hear her mother’s voice become muffled and described hearing gasping. Snezana alleges her husband grabbed her by the throat, and she was unable to breathe. “[Snezana] ended up on the floor. The applicant was still holding her throat, and the complainant alleges was choking her,” McCafferty said. Wood’s lawyers appealed McCafferty’s decision to deny bail on Monday. They will argue not enough consideration was given to how long Wood could spend in prison before his trial, that the decision was unreasonable or unjust, and that McCafferty failed consider if proposed bail conditions would reduce the risk of reoffending, and failed to give reasons for why they would not.



The appeal could be held as soon as Friday, November 6. With Cloe Read Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Major parties take voters for granted
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Major parties take voters for granted November 2, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. TRUST Re Australians have lost trust in politicians and decry not having a voice (″⁣Trust in politicians plunges″⁣, 2/11).

The ready-made ideological blueprints of major parties diminish the importance of citizens in the political process. Having gained our vote, we can disappear.

As a volunteer for a community independent, I feel empowered. It can be hard work but purposeful. It’s not for everyone.

Regular electorate consultations, opinions sought in pursuit of true representation in policy formulation and constant direct community engagement allow voices to be heard.

There’s no caucus, federal council or ″⁣supreme″⁣ leader or factional appeasement, just a contract between the local member and constituents.

Being heard doesn’t guarantee a win, but community independents chisel away with political integrity and transparency, demonstrating common sense and intelligent concern for the future of Australia, its people and environment. They offer a freshness of ideas based on our ideas. A replication of the work of Helen Haines, Monique Ryan, Allegra Spender and other independents is my hope for better politics in Victoria and the restoration of trust.

Jennifer Quigley, Balwyn Integrity reveals itself

Even a poorly educated individual can see when two essential ingredients in a politician are missing. Trust and integrity are not hard to see when they are present, but stand out like a flashing light when they are not.

Bill Howard, Essendon



Election promises mean little

The article ″⁣Trust in politicians plunges″⁣ should be no surprise to anyone, including politicians. Yet, the politicians on the campaign trail keep promising more and more without any financial detail of the promises.

The electorate is well aware of the struggles entailed in the cost of living, mortgage rates and the level of state debt. However, political candidates continue with promises of new services that either can’t. or won’t, be delivered.

Peter Roche, Carlton Ask a public servant

During 36 years in parliament and in senior cabinet roles including a brief period as prime minister, Sir John McEwen had a personal secretary. When he needed information to form an opinion, he asked the public service.

Alan McLean, Queenscliff What does our future hold for those in control?

I’m getting on a bit, so I guess I should be voting on the basis of what I can get out of the government in the next 10 years or so.

But that’s not what is happening. Instead, I am thinking of what the future holds for those who come after me – my children and their children – and what legacy current politicians will deliver for the future.

I would like to hear Jess Wilson tell me what sort of state or country she would like to be living in when she is my age, 40 years from now. She will probably be there to experience it, so it is well worth her thinking about it. Will it be a place where gas is still burned, coal is still mined, and renewable energy is minimised? Will it be a place where railways have not been built, people still live on the streets, free education is a distant memory and politics is full of hate, fear and division?

Where Indigenous people have still not been recognised as the true custodians of the land they have lived on for the last 60,000 years?

Tim Shirley, Benalla THE FORUM Wilson’s culture wars

In recent policy announcements, Jess Wilson has confirmed that she will abolish our treaty with Indigenous people, remove the payroll tax from exclusive private schools, and make it difficult for citizens in this state to express their political and social concerns through rallies.

This indicates, should she become premier, that she will not be governing for all Victorians and that, contrary to her protestations, she is deeply engaged in the culture wars.

In another area, she will abolish the emergency services and volunteer fund which replaced the fire services property levy. If elected, does this mean that the old tax will be re-introduced, or will the money required for those services be magically created out of thin air, or come from cuts to other services such as health and education?

Graeme Gardner, Reservoir



Boomer myth

Contrary to your Letters correspondent’s (2/11) claim of mortgage-belt families struggling while their parents are mortgage-free, ABS data show the Boomer generation has been far from universally cocooned in property ownership.

As of 2021, the generational proportion of renters for the Boomers, Gen X (born 1965-1980) and Millennials (born 1981–1996) was 30.2, 34.6 and 43.1 per cent respectively.

Home ownership data indicate that, when aged 25 to 39 years, 65.4per cent of Boomers owned a home outright or had a mortgage. For Gen X, the comparable figure is 61 per cent and for Millennials, 54.6 per cent.

In terms of disadvantage, older women are today’s fasting growing homeless demographic, with 80per cent of unpartnered women retiring in poverty. They overwhelmingly worked in lower-paid, frequently downsized, service-delivery echelons, with time out to raise families, and contributed up to half of Australia’s annual GDP through unpaid domestic and voluntary work.

In all, universal Boomer wealth is a myth. The factual profile is far more nuanced, irregular and lopsided, particularly in terms of gender.

Barbara Chapman, South Yarra RBA puzzle

I can’t understand why, when the Reserve Bank of Australia uses it seemingly only tool against inflation, the extra money mortgage holders have to pay goes straight into the banks’ coffers.

What exactly have they and their shareholders done to deserve such a massive increase in their profits? How can they possibly justify it? Perhaps they could come to an agreement with the government to funnel some of this enormous windfall into something fairly non-inflationary that benefits the community such as preventative healthcare, early intervention family and youth support or making childcare more affordable to free up carers to enter the workforce.

Paul Sands, Sunbury What stops the nation?

In the 2026 Melbourne Net Zero Cup, the One Nation entry has bolted to the front, but with no long-term strategy. Previous champion Labor is struggling, with extra weight added from Queensland coal and North West Shelf gas.

The once competitive Liberals have neglected net zero followers, with many other fans switching to One Nation. The Green competitor has a strong net zero diet, but still cannot use it to join the pack.

With no consistent stayer, the net zero race is fading dangerously.

John Hughes, Mentone Feeling lucky

First, it was nuclear weapons that were going to end humanity, then Y2K, then climate change, then Donald Trump, and now AI. Since the first four have failed to bump us off, why should we think AI will be any more successful? Fifth time lucky perhaps?

Greg Hardy, Upper Ferntree Gully Risk calculation

Surely, the outstanding abilities (so-called) of AI can sort out the problem of emergencies being allowed in the Melbourne Cup.

Alex Risk, Geelong West



Progressive group think

Your correspondent’s letter (″⁣The Forgotten Lesson″⁣ 1/11) in response to antisemitism envoy Jillian Segal’s latest proposals in her updated report, states quite rightly that none should have to demonstrate political conformity to retain public support.

It would have been so gratifying, if that civil right and its underlying philosophy could have been extended to Jewish academics, students, writers, entertainers, health practitioners, educators and employees who, since October7, 2023, have been held personally responsible for the actions of the Israeli government and often exhorted to make public their allegiances.

Jewish singers and artists who have had their gigs and exhibitions cancelled, writers told that there are no safe spaces for Zionists, a Jewish academic barricaded into his office by anti-Zionist students, and Israeli and Jewish speakers who have been de-platformed – all under suspicion of supporting the existence of the Jewish state, and punished by an ″⁣institution″⁣ on that presumption, or for simply being Jewish.

The Jewish philosopher Hannah Arendt would have seen current progressive social justice advocates and far left academia as the circles of group think that they have become, as they themselves seek to suppress any independent judgement and dissenting opinion in relation to Israel and Gaza.

I do not know if Segal’s proposals are right, but the behaviours and language of so-called progressive social justice advocates, who fail to afford Jewish Australians the rights they claim for themselves, have indeed contributed to the breakdown of Australia’s social cohesion.

Ruth Freedman, Murrumbeena Segal overreach

Everything Jillian Segal recommends in her Report to Combat Antisemitism (30/10) proposes shrieks of challenging Australia’s democratic norms and principles – be it what can or should be available in the arts and theatre, what is not OK in protests, freedoms of movement, how universities deal with protests relating to Israel, the terms upon which people get visas to enter Australia, cancelling visas of those in Australia and the vetting of what the ABC and SBS show or publish.

Jeffrey Loewenstein, Brighton East Home birth right

It’s ironic that Brittany Busch highlights the trauma faced by many birthing women, with a disturbing figure that ″⁣suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in Australia″⁣ (″⁣Bethany thought only veterans and first responders got PTSD. Then she gave birth″⁣ 1/11). A Senate inquiry started Monday (2/11) hearing submissions into women’s health with a focus on postpartum care.

How about the politicians in Canberra recognise that a lot of postpartum trauma is caused by a lack of choice and a lack of continuity of care in how and where women give birth? The federal government could fix one problem straight away.

On January 1, proposed changes to professional indemnity insurance for private midwives will result in many women no longer having the choice to birth at home with a midwife, and many midwives will be leaving the profession as a result.

There will also be more women opting for a ″⁣free birth″⁣ if home birth supported by a midwife is unavailable to them.

Rallies in every state this month will culminate in a ″⁣Grandmother of All Rallies″⁣ on the steps of Parliament House, Canberra, on November 24. Home birth is not for everyone, but these rallies are about the rights of women to have choices about where and how they birth.

Helen Larkin, Ocean Grove Halloween unhinged

Your correspondent (Letters, 2/11) rightly questions a violent costume associated with Halloween. At a local shopping centre hosting a Halloween event, I saw a young boy bedecked inside a contraption that looked like a bundle of dynamite sticks. Just in case anyone missed the message, it was clearly labelled in large letters: TNT. I also saw a child fully clad in black, wearing a balaclava and a backpack that appeared to contain knives or guns or perhaps both – hopefully fake.

What parents buy such costumes and allow their kids to wear them?

Overseas we have wars, and locally we have terrorism, firebombings, and violent attacks. Horror costumes and horror movies mock the suffering of so many people and have the potential to de-sensitise vulnerable elements of our community to real-world pain, mutilation, and consequences.

Joan Reilly, Surrey Hills Motorcycle awareness

Now that ″⁣Motorcycle Awareness Month″⁣ for car and truck drivers is over, we could have ″⁣Motor Vehicle Awareness While we Weave in and out of Traffic on the Freeway at Double the Speed Limit Month” for the motorcyclists.

Pamela Whiting, Southbank



Horses for courses

Re “The price of Victoria Barracks is much higher than $200 million” (30/10). I can understand why many have deep emotional and historical reasons for maintaining the status quo Victoria Barracks in Melbourne.

How that works with the needs of a 21st century defence force, however, escapes me. Even more puzzling is why outdated, hugely expensive to run and no longer fit for purpose buildings should be handed over to the arts as museums or performance spaces, irrespective of the lack of suitability, high operational expenditure, and the need for additional safety and audience amenities, renders me despairing of commonsense.

Horses for courses, for the ADF and the arts.

Alison Fraser, Ascot Vale AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Test cricket

An addition to the MCG Test tea break menu: Cape Town Crumble.

John Rosenbrock, Mount Martha After Australia’s lamentable third Test (and series result), perhaps it’s time for new selectors who actually reward effort and performance (Scott Boland) and opt to discard non-performing players.

Dorothy Galloway, Mentone



Australian Test effort at Newlands: defeat from the jaws of victory.

Graeme Rose, Wangaratta Pat Cummins needs a well-earned rest and should be replaced by Scott Boland for the Tests against NZ. Travis Head should be appointed captain with Alex Carey as his deputy in the interim.

Paul Chivers, Box Hill North Furthermore

Does the letter writer (2/11) complaining about the conditions facing the mushroom lady consider the misery she heaped upon her victims and the effects it still has on those still living?

Michael McKenna, Warragul How many advisers does it take to provide sound advice on the AUKUS dud deal? Apparently more than the 20 staffers advising Defence Minister Richard Marles. A poor return on taxpayers’ money.

Angela Smith, Clifton Hill During the COVID lockdowns, a daily highlight was Patrick Stewart reading his way through Shakespeare’s sonnets. A great memory!

Chris Watson, Ivanhoe



Because I love winning, I have either an each-way or a safe place bet on the entire field in the Melbourne Cup race, and that way I can always say ″⁣I backed the Cup winner″⁣! At least I get most of my money back, and if an outsider gets up, maybe a few quid extra. Simple pleasures.

Tris Raouf, Hadfield Finally

No DA on Saturdays? Oh, David, your supercallifragilistic-expialidociousness will be sorely missed.

Raeleene Gregory, Ballarat East The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Inside the Democrats’ embarrassing and potentially costly Michigan meltdown
World.content:
The relationship between Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed shattered in part because of Israel, but also because of their sensitive egos and hurt feelings. The split had been months in the making.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Detroit: The last straw for Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens came on Saturday afternoon. She was on the cusp of appearing at a unity event with Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated her in an August primary and became Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee. Several powerful intermediaries had been trying to broker peace between the former rivals, who were sparring over El-Sayed’s strong criticisms of Israel. But after Stevens issued a hostile statement on Friday morning calling upon El-Sayed to condemn an ad made by a supportive political action committee and make other concessions, he stepped before reporters and said what his campaign had been signalling privately: he no longer wanted Stevens to join him at a Detroit church on Sunday. Haley Stevens speaking alongside Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers (left) after a church service in Detroit on Sunday. AP Photo/Jose Juarez It was one thing not to be welcomed by El-Sayed’s Senate campaign. It was quite another for him to say so in public. So Stevens on Sunday did what she had been telling everyone she would not do. She endorsed former congressman Mike Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent in a race critical to control of the Senate. “Abdul made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn’t need me there, that he didn’t want me there,” Stevens said while standing next to Rogers outside a black church in Detroit, where they had just attended the Sunday service.



“I did endorse the Democratic nominee, and he chose to close this campaign by saying I wasn’t welcome. I’ve never been invited to a campaign event. That’s fine. You know, he’s busy. He’s running all around.” Stevens’ extraordinary declaration and church appearance with Rogers were a stunning denouement of her weeks-long feud with El-Sayed, who narrowly defeated her in the Michigan Senate primary. Throughout their evident tension this northern fall, she insisted she was a team player and a good Democrat who would grit her teeth and back El-Sayed while working hard for other party members on the ticket. Related Article Analysis

US midterms ‘Despicable betrayal’ reopens a Democratic Party wound that won’t heal Costly drama for Democrats? Their dispute is deeply personal, involving slights between two mercurial millennial politicians of sizable egos quick to take offence. El-Sayed, supremely confident, did not wish to give an inch to a defeated rival. Stevens, still absorbing her primary loss, eventually felt scorned by his campaign’s failure to include her in events or reach out for her views, and embarrassed to be told to stay away. But the breach also represents a major fissure coursing through the Democratic Party about what its relationship with Israel and Jewish donors should be. El-Sayed, if he wins on Tuesday (US time) and enters the Senate in January, would be the most anti-Israel US senator since the formation of the Jewish state 78 years ago.



For now, the collapse of the Stevens-El-Sayed alliance has created an embarrassing and potentially costly drama for Democrats in a race that holds Republicans’ best chance of flipping a Senate seat. Stevens faced a swift backlash Sunday from her party, which was caught off-guard by her defection. “It’s just really unfortunate given the stakes that this has turned into such a spectacle because of one person,” said Lonnie Scott, a veteran Michigan Democratic operative. “It is definitely not ideal that we’d be talking about Haley Stevens three days out from an election.” This account of their split is based on interviews with more than a dozen people involved in or briefed on talks with El-Sayed’s camp and Stevens’ team, some of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations, as well as public remarks from El-Sayed, Stevens and Rogers. Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said he was unbothered by Haley Stevens’ defection. Julia Demaree Nikhinson A unity breakfast, and then nothing more Days after El-Sayed won a bitter primary race against Stevens in August that centred on disagreements over Israel, they appeared together at a unity breakfast. Stevens gave him a hug. And that was about it. Since then, El-Sayed’s campaign hired a handful of Stevens’ campaign staff members, but he had next to no communication with her, according to Stevens and two others with knowledge of their relationship. She was never invited to campaign with him, nor were her thoughts solicited about how to proceed.



At times, other Democrats tried to include her in the campaign. In mid-September, Ray Wert, whose wife, Mallory McMorrow, had run in the Democratic Senate primary but finished a distant third, texted Stevens. He had a request. Wert, who is active in Democratic circles, wanted to publish an opinion essay in Stevens’ name attacking Rogers in a Jewish news outlet. Stevens was initially receptive, according to screenshots of texts Wert provided to The New York Times. “I really like what you wrote,” she messaged to Wert on September 20. Loading Wert replied, “I hope I captured your voice.” “You did,” she replied. “So nice.” In late September, Stevens was suggesting edits to the essay over text. But something seemed to change at the end of the month. “Pls hold for now,” she wrote on September 30, without elaborating. “I love you all but cannot move forward with this right now.”



At the root of the disagreement between Stevens and El-Sayed was US policy on Israel. El-Sayed has emerged as one of the Democratic Party’s leading critics of Israel. Stevens, who is not Jewish, once said, “I see Israel in my dreams” at a Hanukkah service. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which supported her in the primary, spent at least $US30 million ($43 million) attacking El-Sayed during the primary and began spending more starting in October. Related Article US election Can a left-wing Muslim win the Midwest? Or are Democrats about to make a big mistake Stevens’ fiance is Jewish and is an AIPAC donor. She said in an interview on Friday that she was considering converting to Judaism. The El-Sayed campaign believed no amount of acquiescence to Stevens would be sufficient, according to one of his campaign officials. So when she began to issue demands late last month that he disavow an ally’s online ad that she viewed as antisemitic, El-Sayed at first did not budge. She became increasingly critical of him in her cable television appearances. He tried to ignore her. By last Wednesday, Stevens said she would not be campaigning with El-Sayed. That day, her fiance, Jason Turkish, endorsed Rogers. He said El-Sayed would make the world less safe for Jews, and that he hoped Stevens would run for the Senate again in the future. Congressman James Clyburn of South Carolina, a Democratic powerbroker and mentor to Stevens in the House, was privately growing nervous that Stevens might pull her support from El-Sayed and back Rogers. In the eyes of some Democrats, it was time for an intervention.

World.title: My suburb is a flirty extrovert, even with those who can’t pronounce it properly
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The American tourist joined the queue at the 333 bus stop at Bondi Junction railway station. “Will this bus take me to the world-famous Bondy Beach?” he asked me. It wasn’t so world-famous, apparently, that he could pronounce it correctly. “Yes,” I confirmed, “this one goes to Bond-eye Beach.” Perhaps he’d thought it was named after Alan “Bondy” Bond, the Ossie famous for stealing the America’s Cup (among other things). So I told the American where he could get off. Rather, as we boarded the bus (standing room only because it was a Saturday), I asked the driver to alert this newcomer when he should alight: on the hill at the southern end of the beach, just before Notts Avenue, the address of the Bondi Icebergs, the essential starting point for a first-timer. Bondi Beach at sunrise. Steven Siewert Bondi Beach sunbakers. Flavio Brancaleone A blood moon rises from North Bondi. Flavio Brancoleone The Strip off for Skin Cancer installation by photographer Spencer Tunick. Flavio Brancaleone A Bondi Beach Christmas. Flavio Brancaleone



Bondi Pavilion Steve Christo Noah’s Backpackers at South Bondi. Flavio Brancaleone Bondi Beach’s Festival Of The Winds. Sitthixay Ditthavong It was one of those shimmering autumn days – cobalt-blue sky over indigo ocean, “diamonds scattered out to sea”, as Richard Clapton sings in Capricorn Dancer. I’d already taken it all in with my morning beach walk and dip, so I knew the American was in for a treat. “You’re about to witness Bondi at its flirty best,” I told him. He frowned: “Flirty?” “You’ll see,” I assured him. “But you should also know that there’s much more to Bondi than its world-famous beach.” And yet the beach does steal the show. “It’s an extrovert,” I said. “It’s the flirty, giggly exhibitionist of Sydney’s beaches.” Again, he frowned. Again, I said: “You’ll see. Anyhow, that’s the way we like it.”



The Bondi Icebergs pool. Andy Wills Note that this conversation happened last year, long before the December 14 atrocity that cast a pall over the famous beach and its well-earned reputation as a place for frivolity, as a refuge from seriousness and sadness. “I gather you’re a local,” the American said. “Almost,” I replied. “Forty years, with a year off for good behaviour. Now, are you thirsty?” He looked at me warily. It was early in the day for a session. Was I a pathetic, lonely drunk, desperate for company? Or, worse, was I a sweet-talking confidence man plotting to lead him into an alley and mug him? He seemed disappointed, though, when I said my stop was only minutes away, several before his. I would have to leave him, not only with his belongings but with riding instructions. Bondi at sunset. John Tanner Watermelon time. Andy Wills



First, find a perch on the balcony at the Bondi Icebergs – the everyman club, not the (fine) Dining Room and Bar next door, unless you’re hungry enough to test the greenback against the Australian peso. From here, imbibe the Bondi postcard, from the lap swimmers in the Icebergs pool and the sun worshippers on its deck to the full canvas of the beach and its dazzling speckles of humanity and the white trails of surfers carving its waves. Then, backtrack up Notts Avenue and find the steps to the sand and kick off your shoes and, after noting the rock-dwelling yogis at the south end, stroll the shoreline and dodge the acrobatic ball kickers and the splishy-splashy toddlers and the guitar strummers and the parade of fabulous abs and barely-bikinis, all the way to the north end. Here, get wet. You must. Locals at the open-air gym. Steven Siewert If still thirsty, cross the road to the North Bondi RSL, the northern bookend of Bondi’s beachside clubs, and perch on its balcony. Or, across the road from the North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club, you’ll find lifesaving coffee at Porch & Parlour, the proprietor of which, Louise Shaw, while working as a barista to fund her university studies, travelled to Indonesia for field research on the supply chain of specialty coffee from farm to cup. See – you’re just 30 seconds from the sand and already frivolous Bondi is capable of a cerebral conversation. Next, return to the beachfront and its promenade for the sheer spectacle: the calisthenics musclemen defying gravity and human limitation on the parallel bars in the outdoor gym; the Sydney Handstand Club (on Saturdays), whose members apparently include a look-Mum-no-hands subset of synchronised somersaulters; the Bondi Pavilion for its less athletic but equally sea-salted throng of everyday people; and back at the south end, the Bondi Skate Park for more exhibitionists, the aerial acrobats.



The no-hands somersaulters of the Sydney Handstand Club. Andy Wills Getting air at the skate park. Andy Wills But now, you must – must – leave the beachfront. If there’s no time for anything else, a first-timer should climb Bondi’s ascending anterior artery, Hall Street, the heart of the suburb for those of us who live here. Do not pass the Gertrude & Alice Cafe Bookstore. Another American visitor, Oprah Winfrey, didn’t miss it last December and called it the best bookshop in Australia. One of her favourite American authors, Ann Patchett, also visited and went one better: best in the world. American author Ann Patchett (right) with Australian writer Meg Mason at Gertrude & Alice. James Brickwood Among my family’s six Bondi addresses was the happiest of dead-end streets, Cox Avenue, the cul-de-sac of which abutted Hall Street. The only sensible way out to buy a loaf of bread was on foot. That could become a one-hour, five-conversation expedition, as it might in the chatty main street of any decent country town. Back home: “You forgot the milk.” So off I’d trot for another hour. I should have told the American to stroll from Cox to Forest Knoll, another glorious dead end around the corner, and climb its precipitous stairs to Francis Street, then cross to the magical pedestrian lane that connects to Edward Street. Stop in the lane! Here, admire its outdoor gallery of artworks, as I did last month when I discovered an old Bondi friend, Greg Perano, tending to the “exhibition”. I’d been impressed to learn about 35 years ago that Greg was an early percussionist with Australian band Hunters & Collectors. I was more impressed now by his devotion as a Bondi citizen: he had created this gallery with another local, Rex, who named the lane Fredward. Greg Perano in “Fredward” Lane. Rick Feneley

World.title: EV registrations up 174.1% on a year ago
World.content:
Electric vehicle registrations rose sharply last month compared to one year ago, according to Motor Trade Association (MTA) data.

The MTA said registrations of plug-in hybrids and battery electric vehicles (BEVs) reached 3317 in October 2026, up 174.1 percent on October 2025.

The monthly total of light vehicle registrations rose 11.5 percent on October 2025 to 23,289, the second-highest monthly total of 2026 behind September.

Spokesperson Larry Fallowfield said some of the increase for EVs was registrations catching up with sales from when petrol prices first started surging in March.

"When the Iran conflict started there was a bit of panic and not enough stock to meet demand.

"But there's growing reports and belief that higher fuel prices aren't just a spike, they'll be around for a while yet, and that's clearly influencing buyer behaviour."

World.title: Local iwi trust takes over troubled Pahīatua Medical Centre
World.content:
Iwi trust buys Pahīatua Medical Centre

Ownership to change hands immediately

Move welcomed by locals, staff who stepped down likely to return

An under-pressure lower North Island medical clinic has a new owner - a decision that's allowed locals to breathe a sigh of relief.

On Monday, it was announced Ngāti Kahungunu ki Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua Trust had bought the Pahīatua Medical Centre from the Tararua Health Group, which is owned by Omnihealth.

This follows a period of turmoil at the centre, including staff resignations, due to overwork and safety concerns.

Audio player for " Pahiatua Medical Centre bought by local iwi amid turmoil " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2302711%2Flocal-iwi-trust-takes-over-troubled-pahiatua-medical-centre

Pahiatua Medical Centre bought by local iwi amid turmoil Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Here to provide healthcare, not make money

Iwi trust chairman Hayden Hape said it saw a need in the community and acted. The trust had raised the possibility of iwi taking over the centre during a public meeting in September.

Hape said he was now telling medical centre staff that they would be part of a new culture.

"We want them to fall in love with what they've dedicated their lives to do - being nurses and practitioners.

"They have the passion to take care of the community, but unless they take care of themselves, they're unable to deliver that to the community."

Iwi trust chairman Hayden Hape says workers who resigned from the centre, such as Mark Emmerson, right, are welcome to return. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

The clinic has more than 4500 patients on its books and is the only general practice in the town. The closest major centres are Palmerston North, a 40-minute drive away, and Dannevirke, 30 minutes.

Hape reassured patients they would be well cared for.

"The value is in the people here," he said. "Ngāti Kahungunu is not here to make money out of health.

"We're here to deliver healthcare that the community can connect to. They can see themselves in it and they get the service that's deserved, without having to go outside the district."

The iwi trust also ran Dannevirke clinic Te Kahu Hauora. Hape said it had created a good environment there and wanted to do the same in Pahīatua.

Seven staff, including a doctor and nurses, recently resigned from the Pahīatua Medical Centre, saying they wouldn't be back, if Omnihealth, which owns the Tararua Health Group, remained in charge.

Health NZ is reviewing Omnihealth operations in the Tararua District and last month took over the running of the Dannevirke Community Hospital.

Hape said the trust would keep their jobs open, if they wanted to return, and employ all existing staff.

One of the first six who left - registered nurse Mark Emmerson - told RNZ on Monday he would return.

"I've signed a contract with Kahungunu," he said. "The other five of us who resigned initially are in negotiations for their contracts.

Raymond Hira says the community would be buggered without its medical centre. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

"They'll be receiving their contacts shortly. Things will certainly be different now.

"Omni had a lot of trouble recruiting staff, which certainly compounded the workload.

"Now Kahungunu, I think, are able to attract good-quality staff who want to work in the community and who want to support the community."

'About time'

Pahīatua residents spoken to by RNZ welcomed the change in ownership, which took effect immediately.

Raymond Hira had just hitchhiked to the town from nearby Woodville for a medical appointment.

"The fact that the local iwi has stepped in to buy it is plainly a win-win," he said. "At least it's going to remain open for the community.

"Without it, we'd totally be buggered."

Barbara Duckett was relieved to hear of the change.

"It's about time, I think. I've use my medical centre for years.

"The staff have been wonderful and you couldn't ask for better staff.

"I'm sorry that some of them have left. Please come back," she said of those who resigned.

District mayor Scott Gilmore says local ownership is important to residents. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

John Chapman said he attended the public meeting where Hape floated the idea of iwi ownership and said he supported it, especially if it improved services.

"It seems to be a long waiting period to get in."

Another resident, Julie, said she wanted to know more about the new owner and its motivations, but echoed Chapman's concerns about access to care.

"You can't get in for love nor money," she said. "There are a lot of people who are very sick and can't see somebody straight away.

"I've got things that I know I need to get checked out, but I just know I won't get in, so I just don't."

Tararua District Mayor Scott Gilmore said the news was positive, especially after the recent uncertainty.

"It has been really clear that local ownership has been a real priority for people, so it's really pleasing to see this solution come to pass."

Iwi offer best solution - former owner

Tararua Health Group director Mark Wills said the iwi approached it with an offer.

John Chapman attended a recent public meeting about the centre. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

"We considered that in the context of all that's been going on. and thought this is the best solution in terms of ensuring a long-term continuous service there and consolidation of services in the Pahīatua area."

RNZ asked if that was an admission the Tararua Health Group wasn't running the medical centre as well as it should.

"No, that's not at all," Wills said. "It's really just, obviously, there was a loss of some staff, which has been highly publicised, but we were focused primarily on what we can do to ensure the strongest service for the patients going forward.

"This opportunity presented to us was something that we gave serious consideration to and it resulted in us then deciding to sell the Pahīatua Medical Centre to the iwi."

Details of the sale were confidential, he said.

Wills didn't have exact staffing figures, but said it was operating with a "reasonable" number, as per the plan that we developed with [primary health organisation] the PHO to ensure that the services were being delivered to the Pahīatua community".

"We are committed to supporting Ngāti Kahungunu ki Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua through the transition and ensuring continuity of care for patients."

Health NZ central regional director for planning, funding and outcomes Geoff Gwynn said the PHO had been providing onsite support at the medical centre for the past month. It would continue to support the transition to the new owner.

World.title: Review finds no evidence of anti-forestry bias at Gisborne District Council
World.content:
An independent review into Gisborne District Council's regulatory approach to the forestry industry has found it has "acted diligently and in good faith".

The review, released Monday, was commissioned by the council three months ago amidst criticism from industry players and central government that it was being too tough on forestry companies.

It was undertaken by a three-person panel, led by former National MP Chris Finlayson, KC.

Of particular concern was the council's use of enforcement orders - a tool under the Resource Management Act that regulatory bodies can apply to the Environment Court to use to instruct a respondent to carry out certain actions.

Foresty Minister Todd McClay raised concerns about the orders, and previously said the industry had come to him saying it faced decisions it considered "unworkable and costly" and were considering whether to remain in the region.

However the review found the council was following proper legal process, and the use of enforcement orders had improved forestry practises. The 80-page report provided a thorough analysis of the council's processes, framed by the panel's remit to examine whether these were fit-for-pourpose, reasonable and proportionate to the scale of risk faced by the region.

'GDC is anti-foresty... empty rhetoric'

At the outset, the panel addressed what it stated were "extravagant statements" made to it during its inquiry.

These statements included "GDC [Gisborne District Council] is anti-forestry"; "Forestry does not have a future in Tairāwhiti"; "Forestry companies don't concern themselves with environmental matters".

The panel unpacked these statements as examples of empty rhetoric or hyperbole.

For example, it pointed out that all companies it had spoken to for its inquiry had an appreciation of the environment and the need for their practises to address environmental concerns.

In total, the panel spoke with 12 representatives from six forestry companies. It also spoke to five industry bodies, as well as contractors and logging operators, and owners of Māori land forestry blocks and companies. These made up more than 100 interviews conducted for the review, with technical experts, and representatives from local councils as well as central government agencies included.

In regard to the council's relationship with the forestry industry, the panel stated that at no time had it discerned an "anti-forestry bias".

It stated that it was clear that the council and the forestry industry recognised the importance of commercial forestry to Tairāwhiti, and that the council had specific responsibilities to manage the impacts of that on the environment and community through a competent and transparent regulatory system.

Consenting process on-track

The panel found, overall, the council's consenting process was "generally very sound".

It highlighted two instances which raised concerns over its internal processes. The first was a job  for a compliance officer who "could stand up" to the forestry. The  was published on the council's website earlier this year. The second was the inclusion of enforcement orders as a KPI in the council's revised forestry strategy.

In the first instance, the job  was taken down promptly and was found not to have been properly advertised. The panel said it was important the council avoided "this kind of misstep which conveys the wrong impression".

In the second instance, the panel made a similar observation, cautioning against the kind the wrong impression of impression that could result from a KPI around enforcement orders.

It also looked at the quality of communication throughout the consent process, and time frames for consent applications - which had been highlighted by some forestry companies as cumbersome.

The panel did not find major problems with the timeframes in Gisborne District Council's consenting process, and noted delays were often due to applicants and the need for more information.

It went on to say that "a number of submitters" complained about the amount of requests for further information from the council, however "those requests could be lessened if applicants took more care to address fundamental matters and presented their applications in a coherent and logical manner".

It also noted the problem appeared to be more widespread than in Tairāwhiti, with other councils indicating they struggled with the "low standard of many forestry consent applications".

Despite that, the panel also found Gisborne District Council wasn't without fault. It stated it needed to be "clear, concise and consistent" in its communications with applicants, however "some emails we read dealing with these issues are hardly models of clarity and GDC needs to lift its game".

Enforcement orders "costly" but shown to work

The inquiry also delved into the council's use of enforcement orders.

In the past three years, seven enforcement orders have been issued by the Environment Court directing companies to clean up forestry blocks in Tairāwhiti. Just last week, Summit Forests NZ was officially ordered to clean up a forestry block on the East Cape described by experts as "one of the worst" ever seen.

The panel found enforcement orders had "been more effective at shifting behaviour than previous approaches" when it came to improving forestry practices. However, they were a costly and time-consuming process for the council, which was already struggling to manage demand on its resources and staff.

The panel also stated that naming company directors in enforcement orders had been a top concern when it met with forestry company representatives.

On this, it acknowledged the seriousness of naming individuals and that it was step "which should not be taken lightly". It also found that the council had had "experienced considerable improvement in compliance" since it had begun doing so.

It also noted the council did not have a blanket approach to automatically naming company directors.

Government criticism of Gisborne council 'unfair'

Overall, the panel found the council's approach to the forestry industry had been justified and was proportionate to the risks associated with the geological characteristics of the region, such as the susceptibility of land to erosion.

It also highlighted that forestry practises had improved, though more work needed to be done.

Alongside this, it examined the role of central government in forestry in Tairāwhiti, and its decisions to weigh in on the council's approach to the industry.

Notably, the same week the council announced it had commissioned its independent review into consenting and compliance practises in August, the government appointed "a facilitator" to advise it directly on what was happening with the forestry sector in the region. Minister for Regulation David Seymour also contacted the council in May warning it's approach was potentally risking [investment by forestry companies.

On this point, the panel was clear central government had behaved improperly.

"It is unfair for the Crown to criticise GDC [Gisborne District Council] as it has in recent times," it said.

It also called on central government to address shortfalls in regulatory settings and legislation like the Resource Management Act that was adding to gaps and confusion around the consent process.

In regard to the management of slash, it stated "any uncertainty could be overcome by a conseting process which clearly covers slash discharge".

The Crown must come to the table

Chairperson Chris Finlayson directly addressed the importance of support and engagement from the Crown for the future of forestry and land sustainability in Tairāwhiti following the release of the report. This was particularly important as forests planted in the wake of 1988's Cyclone Bola were due to be harvested within the next five years.

"The Crown has known about the land-use challenges facing Tairāwhiti for decades and played a significant role in establishing the forestry landscape we see today," Finlayson said.

"It cannot now expect council, the forestry industry and local communities to resolve these complex and longstanding issues on their own. The scale of the challenge demands national leadership, appropriate investment and a coordinated approach to land-use transition.

"Central government must take responsibility for the policy settings, resources and solutions that sit within its control," he said.

Gisborne Mayor Rehette Stoltz said the panel findings confirmed the council's approach to forestry had been justified, but acknowedged it could also make improvements in areas like communication with consent applicants.

"The findings provide assurance that the fundamentals of our regulatory approach are sound," she said.

World.title: More mental health patients allowed community leave at time of murder - inquest
World.content:
An increasing number of patients at Christchurch's Hillmorton Hospital were given community leave around the time a woman was murdered by one in the street, an inquest has heard.

Laisa Waka Tunidau was stabbed to death by Zakariye Mohamed Hussein outside her Sockburn home in June 2022.

Hussein was jailed for life, with a 13-year non-parole period, in November that year, and had previously been jailed for more than six years for kidnapping, stabbing and intimidating people across Christchurch in March 2012.

At the time of Waka Tunidau's death, Hussein was allowed to leave Hillmorton Hospital on unescorted community leave.

An inquest into the death resumed in Christchurch on Monday in front of coroner Alexandra Cunninghame.

More than 20 doctors, psychologists, psychiatrists and nurses who were part of Hussein's care were due to give evidence during the inquest.

Coroner Alexandra Cunninghame RNZ / Nate McKinnon

A former senior nurse, who worked within Hillmorton's forensic mental health unit during Hussein's stay, gave evidence during the opening day of the inquest's second phase.

The nurse, whose identity was suppressed, was asked about community leave procedures at Hillmorton, after another witness previously said during the inquest's first phase that abandoning leaves would ease pressure on staff.

"Something I noticed being different to when I was [at Hillmorton during earlier years] was that the number of people that had leaves and the number of leaves we had to accommodate had increased in the years that I returned there in recent years," they said.

They later explained to lawyer for registered nurses Rebecca Scott that a "culture of making an effort to give people leave" had increased.

The court heard that community leave was largely determined by adequate staffing levels, which had improved by 2022.

They were also asked about regular multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings, where different healthcare specialists came together to review a patient's care and progress.

The inquest previously heard that case managers didn't always attend these meetings, including those on Hussein's file.

Christchurch's Hillmorton Hospital. RNZ/LouisDunham

Lawyer Kiri Rademacher asked the witness whether this was still the case or whether there had been changes.

The nurse said it was "tricky" with shift work to ensure case managers could attend every meeting.

Counsel assisting the coroner Lucy Kenner also asked about how information was reviewed, when a patient had requested community leave.

The nurse said clear guidelines around what documents and notes were reviewed when considering a community leave request weren't stipulated.

Health NZ forensic mental health nursing director Patsy Tarrant began her evidence on Monday afternoon.

The first phase of the inquest heard that police emailed Hillmorton Hospital staff in February 2022 to say they intended to arrest and charge Hussein, and sought assistance to ensure it was not too disruptive.

The coroner heard the process took some time, partly because police were under the impression that Hussein was in a secure unit and would not be released into the community.

The inquest resumes on Tuesday.

World.title: Millie Moon nappies told to investigate after complaints of rashes
World.content:
Consumer NZ says the country is not acting strongly enough to protect babies from potentially unsafe products.

The Ministry for Business, Innovation, and Employment (MBIE) confirmed on Monday it had received five reports about Millie Moon nappies, with the complaints referring to a "rash/blisters forming" after using them.

It comes after the Consumer Product Safety Commission in the US received hundreds of complaints about Millie Moon nappies.

MBIE declined to be interviewed but said it had told the nappy business, which was part of the Zuru Edge group, to investigate and that it expected a product to be recalled if it was not safe.

Audio player for " Nappy business warned of potential recall after complaints of rashes " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2303272%2Fmillie-moon-nappies-told-to-investigate-after-complaints-of-rashes

Nappy business warned of potential recall after complaints of rashes Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

Consumer NZ's head of research, Gemma Rasmussen, said currently the onus was on businesses to ensure products are safe.

She said that while some products targeted at under-threes, including cots and nightwear, had mandatory product safety standards around them, the vast majority did not.

"In New Zealand, we have a reactive product safety system. What tends to happen is that an issue occurs and then there is a sort of reaction, which to our mind is a really dangerous product safety system.

"We are missing in action when it comes to children and babies."

She said there were more products than ever coming onto our shores and being sold in stores, and that came with a higher level of risk.

"I think that the government should be placing more focus on reviewing what these products are that are coming in, particularly for children, because waiting for harm to occur is not a great model."

Milly Moon did not respond to RNZ's request for an interview.

But in a statement on social media, the company said its independent testing found no issues.

"Our diapers and training pants passed every test conducted as part of our independent investigation. No harmful bacteria were detected in the samples tested, and the products met the requirements assessed under the US Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act (CPSIA).

"We worked with six independent laboratories to test our diapers and training pants, including batches linked to complaints.

"We have also investigated whether unintended substances could have been introduced through raw materials, manufacturing processes, processing aids, adhesives or other product components.

"Based on the investigations and testing completed to date, we have not identified a product-related cause for the reported reactions."
