World.title: Why Netball NZ pulled the plug on Mowbray-Williams deal
World.content:
Netball New Zealand says key elements of a proposed private domestic league changed from the original terms agreed with investors Anna Mowbray and Ali Williams, ultimately prompting its board to pull the plug on the deal.

RNZ revealed on Friday Netball NZ had abandoned plans to privatise the elite competition, just eight weeks after signing a non-binding term sheet with the high-profile couple.

The collapse of the deal has blindsided players already facing months of uncertainty over their professional futures, but the national body says it is already working on an alternative pathway to ensure an elite domestic competition can go ahead in 2027.

Mowbray and Williams said they were devastated by the decision, claiming they had been given no explanation for Netball NZ's decision to walk away.

Audio player for " Netball NZ says it has a plan B after plug pulled on privately run league " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/sport/2302596%2Fwhy-netball-nz-pulled-the-plug-on-mowbray-williams-deal

Netball NZ says it has a plan B after plug pulled on privately run league Checkpoint Download MP3 10m

However, speaking to RNZ on Monday, Netball NZ chief executive Jennah Wootten said it had become clear that, "despite throwing everything we could at this negotiation process", an agreement could not be reached.

She said the "principles and objectives" Netball NZ had established at the beginning of the process, and which were reflected in the term sheet, needed to remain central to any final agreement.

"A number of the things that I talked about when the term sheet was signed in regards to features of the likely future arrangement had shifted," Wootten said.

"Some of those shifts were okay and some of those shifts the Netball New Zealand board felt comfortable with, but others the board did not feel comfortable with."

Asked if she believed Mowbray and Williams had breached the spirit of the initial agreement, Wootten responded:

"I do genuinely believe we all went into this process in good faith and we were all genuinely optimistic about what we thought we could achieve together. Sometimes over time and when you get into these detailed negotiations, things can change. And I respect that they had views and perspectives that they felt really strongly about, but so too did Netball New Zealand."

Mowbray and Williams emerged as potential saviours of the sport's elite competition earlier this year, offering a lifeline with a proposal to establish a privately owned franchise league.

Originally pitched for 2028, the plan was accelerated to allow a minimum five-team competition to launch in 2027. The proposed league was intended to bring much-needed private investment into a competition Netball NZ could no longer afford to run in its existing form.

After weighing up its options, Netball NZ announced at the beginning of September that it had selected the Mowbray-Williams proposal as its preferred option, with the parties signing a non-binding term sheet.

At the time of the announcement, Netball NZ said the investors would hold the licence for the competition and its franchises, while the national body would retain a governance role on the board established to oversee the new league.

The parties were then expected to work towards a long-form agreement covering franchise licences, the competition window, league format, and commercial and broadcast arrangements.

Wootten declined to elaborate on the specific areas of disagreement, pointing to confidentiality agreements in place. But she said the board had a responsibility to put the future of the sport, its participants and players ahead of the difficulties involved in ending negotiations.

"Ultimately that was all about ensuring the strong, safe future of netball in this country and you've got to make these decisions with the best long-term interests of the sport and the participants and the players at the heart."

Anna Mowbray and Ali Williams emerged as potential saviours of netball's elite competition earlier this year. RNZ

RNZ has sought comment from Mowbray and Williams on Netball NZ's characterisation of negotiations. A spokesperson for the Mowbray said the couple were not available for an interview on Monday.

However, in a statement released to media on Friday, the high profile couple, who own a 15 per cent stake in A-League club Auckland FC, said the news came out of the blue.

"Ali and I gave this everything. Our time, our money and our hearts. We did it because we've seen what a team can do for a community. With Auckland FC we've watched families come together, kids find heroes and a city find its voice. This was our chance to do that for netball, for women's sport, at a scale this country has never seen," the statement read.

"Yesterday that ended with an email. No reason. No call."

Wootten clarified she had written to Mowbray and Williams on Thursday outlining the position of the board and informing them that Netball NZ was not able to proceed any further with negotiations. In the email, Netball NZ invited the couple to sit down with them the following morning to discuss the decision and the "next steps", including how the decision would be communicated to the players.

However, news of the proposed private league's collapse was leaked to media before Netball NZ had a chance to tell players.

"In the confidential correspondence, we were really clear that we wanted together to be engaging with the players and we wanted to be speaking with our stakeholders in a really coordinated way. The players should have heard this news from us directly," said Wootten.

"It is enormously regrettable that that information ended up being leaked and that players found out about the development as they did."

Midcourt star Peta Toeava is one of the players left in limbo by Netball NZ's decision to pull the pin on plans to privatise the elite domestic league. Aaron Gillions / www.photosport.nz

Another blow for players

For players, the collapse of the deal marks another emotional twist in a prolonged period of uncertainty about their futures.

Just as it appeared elite netball had been thrown a lifeline through the Mowbray-Williams proposal, the sudden reversal has left them back where they started - with no certainty over what next season will look like.

The uncertainty is particularly acute for some of New Zealand's leading players, with several current Silver Ferns still without contracts for next season.

They include Peta Toeava, Martina Salmon, Parris Mason and injured defender Catherine Hall. Several recent internationals, including Phoenix Karaka, Maia Wilson and Michaela Sokolich-Beatson, are also uncontracted.

Netball NZ Players Association boss Pippa Moore warned the prolonged period of uncertainty was taking a major toll on player welfare.

She said the organisation has seen a significant increase in players seeking mental health support and financial assistance.

"There's a number of players that we're really concerned about and I think this will just add to it. So that will be our number one focus at the moment," said Moore.

"People have been holding out for [the new league]. We've been waiting all year, and then we deliver the good news that someone's coming in to save the day and now that's just been ripped away from them leading into Christmas. And there's no suggestion of anything else at this point."

Wootten said the distress and uncertainty it has created among the players is deeply regrettable.

She said her priority was now connecting with those most affected and reassuring them the decision had been made with their best interests, and those of the sport, at heart.

"They are phenomenal athletes. They are phenomenal New Zealanders and we know how important it is that we're creating an elite pathway in Netball New Zealand that they feel excited and positive about.

"So I am really looking forward to connecting with them and having these conversations and ensuring that the pathway forward is one that they understand and one that they feel positive about."

Netball NZ says it has an advanced alternative plan for an elite domestic competition in 2027. © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

Back to square one

Netball NZ says it is already working on an alternative pathway for 2027, revisiting an option it explored earlier this year before settling on the private investment proposal.

Wootten said the organisation had been working with zones and teams over the weekend to reassess the options, building on work that began several months ago.

"We have progressed relooking at that to see what options we have for 2027, and [we're] looking forward to sharing more details in the coming weeks," she said.

Asked if Netball NZ were working on the alternate plan while still negotiating with private investors, Wootten responded:

"No we weren't. It was only when we believed that we were not able to conclude negotiations with Anna and Ali that we started looking at what this option could be. We were absolutely invested in trying to make this deal work and every endeavour was given that way right to the last minute."

Wootten would not offer any details of the competition model it was exploring, or how far advanced the organisation was in discussions with broadcasters and sponsors.

"I'm not going to explore details publicly before I've spoken to the players and those that are most directly impacted," she said.

She also could not offer any guarantees there will be an elite domestic league next season.

World.title: Base jumper pleads guilty after getting stuck on side of Auckland hotel
World.content:
A base jumper who became stuck on the side of an Auckland hotel by his parachute has pleaded guilty to two charges of criminal nuisance and agreed to pay $22,000 in reparation.

Ilies Nait El Cadi, a 22-year-old from Belgium, initially faced two charges of burglary but these were amended to the less serious charges in Auckland District Court today.

His lawyer, Deborah Reid, said that he was sorry for his behaviour and would pay $22,000 reparation.

She asked that he be discharged without conviction.

Judge Brooke Gibson said before allowing this, he wanted to see that the money had been paid.

Nait El Cadi's lawyer asked that the matter be stood down while her client transferred the funds. Judge Gibson allowed this, however, after an adjournment t of 20 minutes or so, Deborah Reid said Nait El Cadi had only been able to access $1000.

The case was adjourned until Thursday.

According to the agreed summary of facts, on 28 September, Nait El Cadi gained unauthorised access to the Auckland central's Seascape Building on Customs St East, which was at the time a construction site.

He jumped the front fence and security hoardings and gained access to the stairwell, from where he made his way to the top floor.

According to the summary, the building contained numerous hazards which, if they fell, could endanger the lives of pedestrians on the footpath below.

The instagrammer launched himself off the building and after releasing his parachute, landed at the intersection of Anzac Ave and Beach Rd.

In a second incident, Nait El Cadi gained entry to the Indigo Hotel in the CBD, which is close to 150m tall, and made his way to the roof. He again launched himself off and released his parachute, but this time the parachute became stuck about halfway down the building and he had to be rescued.

About 20 or 30 FENZ staff attended the incident and the area below had to be cordoned off before FENZ officers smashed their way through a window on Level 23 and he was rescued. FENZ said the rescue came with a price tag of some $20,000.

Defence lawyer Deborah Reid said her client was sorry for his behaviour and will in the future be more mindful of the laws of countries he travels.

World.title: Usyk's path to global dominance goes through Gatton
World.content:
Oleksandr Usyk has earned a tongue-in-cheek invite to resume his cruiserweight career in Gatton after the boxing great's plan to return to the division set him on a path for David Nyika.

The Ukrainian (25-0) unified the cruiserweight division before wiping the floor of his heavyweight rivals, beating Anthony Joshua, Tyson Fury and Daniel Dubois twice in the last five years.

The 39-year-old now wants to return to the cruiserweight ranks and sweep the belts again in one final act, with the vacant IBF title his first target before a date with current WBO and WBA champion David Benavidez (32-0).

Benavidez will fight Michal Cieslak for the WBC belt next month.

New Zealand Olympian David Nyika, based in the rural Queensland town of Gatton under trainer Noel Thornberry, is the IBF's number one-ranked fighter.

A potential title fight has been put on hold until the organisation's legal dispute with fellow Queensland-based champion Jai Opetaia is resolved.

Opetaia, who brutally knocked out Nyika to retain the IBF and The Ring belts in January last year, had his IBF status stripped when he debuted for rebel league Zuffa Boxing this year.

Jai Opetaia knocked David Nyika out when they met in January, 2025. (AAP Image: Dave Hunt)

Usyk's plans have put a spanner in the works for Opetaia, who is eyeing off a heavyweight cameo against Deontay Wilder next month before a potential unification clash with Benavidez next May.

Opetaia could still win back his IBF strap in the courtroom and earn a date with Usyk he has coveted since they competed at the 2012 London Olympics when the Australian was barely 17.

Opetaia exacts brutal toll in knockout, with heavyweight domination in his sight Jai Opetaia is the only man who can challenge heavyweight champion Oleksandr Usyk says promoter Eddie Hearn, after the IBF and Ring champion exacted the toll of trying to match it with boxing's best from David Nyika.

But even then Nyika remains the mandatory opponent and would command step-aside money for the Opetaia-Usyk fight to proceed.

"We'd have to sit down and come to an agreement, but we'd enforce his mandatory for sure if we were to stand aside," Thornberry told AAP on Monday.

Thornberry trained and managed former world champion contender Alex Leapai out of his Gatton boxing shed and has regularly held fight nights at the town's Shire Hall.

With Saudi powerbroker Turki Alalshikh backing Usyk, Thornberry joked that he could pencil in an upgrade to the venue as part of the fight contract.

Oleksandr Usyk (right) won the undisputed IBF, IBO, WBA, WBC and WBO world heavyweight titles. (Getty Images: Richard Pelham)

"I've reached out to Usyk's management, they know we're certainly interested," Thornberry said.

"I'm sure they see David as a good way back in, but it's a great opportunity for David and he said he'd take it in a heartbeat.

"And, historically, no-one goes well when they come back in weight."

Oscar De Le Hoya lost to Manny Pacquiao, who went up two classes, when he dropped down in weight for their 2008 clash, while Antonio Tarver got the better of Roy Jones Jnr in a three-fight saga between 2003–2005.

Usyk showed off his slimmed-down physique at Canelo Alvarez's Saudi Arabia win on the weekend, but Thornberry reckons the jury is out.

"They come back down and go, 'Oh shit, this is a different algorithm to what I was accustomed to,'" he said.

"So let's see."

AAP

World.title: Wanderers' chair calls out 'totally unacceptable' fan treatment by police
World.content:
Western Sydney chairman Paul Lederer has slammed the "totally unacceptable" treatment and over-policing of Wanderers' supporters this season and vowed to seek answers from police.

The Red and Black Bloc (RBB), Western Sydney's active supporter group, staged a silent protest against over-policing in the opening 20 minutes of Saturday's goalless draw between the Wanderers and Macarthur at Campbelltown Sports Stadium.

The RBB, who also held banners that read "Stand Up For Fans. Not Police Demands" as a message to the Australian Professional Leagues (APL), said they had been directed by NSW Police to surrender their drums, megaphone and banners two hours before kick-off.

Macarthur coach and former Socceroo Sasa Ognenovski and his Wanderers' counterpart Ufuk Talay backed the fans, and Lederer joined them on Monday, releasing a lengthy statement.

Ufuk Talay (right) and Sasa Ognenovski were both sympathetic to the fans' cause. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

"Since the beginning of the season, we have witnessed repeated issues surrounding the treatment of our supporters. The events of this weekend have brought those frustrations to a tipping point," Lederer said.

"The treatment of our members and fans has been totally unacceptable. Enough is enough.

"The RBB are an integral part of our club which we are extremely proud of. That will never change, and we will continue to stand behind the positive contribution they make to the Wanderers and football in this country.

The fans who care the most The Red and Black Bloc are the most controversial sports fans in Australia, but the game they love is struggling.

"Our supporters should never be made to feel like second-class citizens simply because they choose to support a football club.

"We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for equal treatment and common sense.

"For too long, our supporters have faced excessive policing, policing that you as members and fans pay for."

Lederer pointed to hundreds of fans being withheld from entering the Sydney derby for up to 30 minutes and the presence of up to 20 public order and riot squad officers behind the Wanderers' supporter bays in Campbelltown.

"This only adds to the feeling of intimidation experienced by the families that largely make up our supporter base," he said.

"This level of treatment is neither reasonable nor proportionate, and there is no justification for a riot squad presence at our football matches."

Wanderers' fans, pictured here in round one's Sydney derby, have been backed by their chairman. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Lederer stressed the club did not condone anti-social behaviour, but said most of Western Sydney's fan base were not a problem and should be treated with "the utmost respect".

"As chairman, I have a responsibility to protect the future of the Western Sydney Wanderers. That means standing up for the people who give this club life," he said.

"I will not accept our members and fans being treated as though their passion makes them any less deserving of respect. Neither will this club.

"We will continue to raise our concerns directly with NSW Police, the A-Leagues and relevant stakeholders, seek clear answers and push for fair, consistent and respectful treatment."

Lederer also thanked the Wanderers' fans.

"You have never stopped standing up for this club," he said.

"And as your chairman, I want you to know that we will never stop standing up for you."

AAP has contacted the APL and NSW Police for comment.

AAP

World.title: Big is beautiful as Australia's first UFC champion finally comes home
World.content:
It has taken more than a decade, but Rob Whittaker, Australia's first-ever UFC champion, is finally coming home.

The UFC light-heavyweight has been confirmed for the promotion's next card in Sydney on February 7, where he will face Uzbekistan's Bogdan Guskov in his first hometown fight in over 12 years.

Whittaker can barely recall his last effort in the Harbour City, when he knocked out American Clint Hester in 2014.

It came so early in his career it was closer to his Padstow products days as a Railcorp electrician than a world champion.

"It's hard to remember, to be honest. So much has happened since. I've ridden the rollercoaster," said Whittaker.

Rob Whittaker last fought in Sydney in 2014. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Josh Hedges )

"My friends and family can all be there. They can be a part of the whole journey without having to spend a billion bucks to be there.

"But I hope things settle down. I'm going to have to stop replying (to people asking for tickets).

"It'll be good to be home after so long. You normally have to travel so far to put on a show."

Putting on a show far and wide has been second nature for Whittaker during his long career with the UFC.

Since that night in Sydney, all but one of his UFC losses have come against future or reigning world champions, confirming his status as one of Australia's top combat sport exports.

The 35-year-old snuck in a few fights on home soil, but the last was in 2019 when he lost the middleweight title against Israel Adesanya in Melbourne in front of over 57,000 fans, still the biggest crowd in UFC history.

The crowd won't quite be the same at the Sydney SuperDome for this card, headlined by rising Perth lightweight Quillin Salkilld's bout with Benoit St Denis, but Whittaker — a father of three sons and three daughters — is just happy he can take his kids to work.

Rob Whittaker recently broke a two-fight losing streak. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Ed Mulholland )

"Last fight, my two eldest could come. This time it might be my three eldest. They loved it last time, and I loved having them be a part of it," said Whittaker.

"They get to see their old man work for a living. I'm sure half the time they think I'm unemployed.

"I love fighting. I don't think there's a cooler way to earn money if we want to keep it real basic, and I'm good at it as well. I'm earning a trade, and I'm going to keep doing it."

The fight will be Whittaker's second since moving from middleweight (83.91kg) to light-heavyweight (92.99kg).

After a third-round knockout win in his division debut over Nikita Krylov in July, he has plenty of confidence after snapping a two-fight losing streak.

Whittaker was wary of the power difference against bigger fighters, but after a strong start, where he left Krylov with a broken jaw, bigger has become beautiful.

Rob Whittaker has bulked up from middleweight to light-heavyweight. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Ed Mulholland )

"I'm definitely more confident in my ability to zip and zag and my ability to land power, to be faster, to have the confidence to shoot when I feel it, to have confidence in my instincts again," said Whittaker.

"I can eat for fuel, I don't need to starve myself, and that makes living — especially with a family and heaps of kids — much more enjoyable.

"But it's a slippery slope, because after a fight I can get really stuck in.

"Light-heavyweight eating is different to middleweight eating, let me tell you."

Guskov has a strong track record with 15 knockouts from his 18 wins, but Whittaker is confident he has the experience to outpoint the 34-year-old.

"He's a big, rangy guy. He hits hard, he's finished a lot of people, but there's nothing he brings to the table that I haven't seen in my years in the game," said Whittaker.

"There's nothing he brings to the table that I think I can't beat."

World.title: Australian batting 'stronger' despite repeat South Africa collapses
World.content:
Coach Andrew McDonald says Australia's batting is in a better place now than before the South Africa tour, despite admitting the team underperformed in the 2-1 series loss.

Players began flying out of South Africa on Sunday and Monday, with Australia to now turn its focus to a home series against New Zealand and a tour of India that starts in January.

There remains an ongoing sense of frustration about the way the South Africa tour ended, with McDonald lamenting several missed opportunities to clinch the series.

That includes letting South Africa off the hook with the ball in Gqeberha and Cape Town, while nightmare collapses in both those Tests also hurt.

Australia has been 4-95 or worse in 14 of its past 25 Test innings, with that brittleness exposed again as the team slumped to 8-62 on the series-deciding day five in Cape Town.

But Australia's coach pointed to the performances of Cameron Green, Matt Renshaw and Josh Inglis as reasons for legitimate positivity, with the latter two scoring centuries.

Josh Inglis scored a superb century in Cape Town. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

"If you look at the batting unit, I think we walk away in a stronger position," McDonald said.

"For Josh Inglis to step up at late notice [in Cape Town] … he's been a batter that's been carried around with us for a while; it's exciting.

"Albeit there's a lot of negativity floating around at the moment, it's exciting to see him and Cameron Green and even Matthew Renshaw."

McDonald also admitted selectors would have some decisions to make "around the age profile of that team", with 23-year-old Cooper Connolly playing his second Test in Cape Town and Sam Konstas firing in the Sheffield Shield.

Selections and strategy in the spotlight After a disastrous series loss to South Africa, Australian cricket faces some tough decisions.

"It's still a very good cricket team with a lot of very good players in there, and down the path they will be acknowledged as legends of the game," McDonald said of the current side.

"So we've got to balance that out with who comes in, what the next decisions are.''

Beyond the obvious turning points, McDonald pointed to Australia's inability to build a big first-innings lead in Cape Town after starting day three at close to parity with four wickets down as a big moment in the series.

But he stressed that not all fault lay with the batters, after the bowlers failed to put a final nail in South Africa on day four in Cape Town.

Australia has now lost three of its past five Tests, with the back-to-back defeats in Gqeberha and Cape Town the first successive failures since the 2023 Border-Gavaskar Trophy.

The defeats have cost Australia the number one spot in the rankings, ahead of a nine-month period that includes the away Border-Gavaskar Trophy and Ashes series.

Still, McDonald pointed to Pat Cummins's 60 per cent win rate as skipper and the fact it was one of the highest among all Australian captains.

"We've underachieved here," McDonald said.

"It feels as though it's hard to win on the road. That's the greatest challenge, and that's where we will be critiqued.

"And we're incredibly frustrated that we weren't able to execute this tour after being 1-0 up."

AAP

World.title: West Coast Eagles star suffers brutal injury news
World.content:
West Coast could be without midfielder Ella Roberts for the entire 2027 AFLW season after scans confirmed the superstar had ruptured her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

Roberts, 21, suffered the right knee injury when she planted her leg in an attempt to change direction in the first quarter of Saturday's loss to Hawthorn, the Eagles' final game of the campaign after failing to make finals.

The midfielder immediately went down and had to be assisted from the field.

The Eagles confirmed on Monday that Roberts had torn her ACL and would need a knee reconstruction.

Given the typical 12-month recovery from that surgery, Roberts will be racing the clock to feature at all next year.

"We are all saddened by the injury sustained by Ella," West Coast AFLW boss Michelle Cowan said.

"Our priority is to arrange surgery as soon as possible and ensure she receives the very best care and we will wrap our arms around her throughout this journey.

"She is a true professional and we have every confidence she will approach her recovery with the same diligence and determination, fully supported by our medical team."

Roberts, who can play both midfield and forward, is one of the most talented players in the game and has kicked 20 goals in 55 games since her 2022 debut.

She is a two-time All-Australian and won the Eagles' best and fairest award in 2024 and 2025.

Roberts averaged 21.7 disposals and five clearances this year as West Coast finished 13th.

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: NZ duo on brink of history as Lebanon goes into folklore
World.content:
The group stage of the Rugby League World Cup is in the books after a remarkable double-header to finish things off.

Lebanon's golden-point win over France and Tonga and Samoa's epic showdown were both classics, giving the tournament the close finishes that have been in short supply.

With Australia, New Zealand, Tonga and Samoa progressing to the semifinals, here are the quick hits from the final round of matches.

1. Was this the last World Cup for the old Kumuls?

Gairo Voro is one of several Papua New Guinea players with a big future. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

No country in rugby league will see the sport transform in their nation from this World Cup to the next like Papua New Guinea.

The entry of the PNG Chiefs to the NRL in 2028, with their near-limitless resources and game-bending salary cap concessions, will change the game in the land where they love it most.

So long as the Chiefs fulfil their promise of creating strong pathways for local talent to make it to the top level, it has the potential to change the national side forever.

England's World Cup fate is resting on a miracle After a scratchy win over Papua New Guinea, England's Rugby League World Cup needs a miracle to stay alive.

The prospect of talents like five-eighth Gairo Voro, who scored a sharp solo try, or winger Dudley Dutoi, who got the better of England star Dom Young, getting regular NRL football is a tantalising one.

The two were among Papua New Guinea's best in a spirited defeat, and from the Highlands to the islands of New Britain there can be so many more like them.

PNG's improvement over the past decade has been steady, but it is about to hit overdrive. This game against England might be the last dance for the Kumuls as we've come to know them.

2. The New Zealand duo closing in on history

Casey McLean seemingly cannot stop scoring tries for New Zealand. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It was another Kiwi romp as New Zealand punished a Fiji side that struggled to backup from last week's fine performance against Australia, but amid the near-endless tries and ill-tempered flare-ups, Casey McLean and Jamayne Isaako continued their march towards history.

Isaako scored 26 points from a try and 13 goals from as many attempts to go with his 38 points against the Cook Islands the weeks before, and the winger is closing in on Shaun Johnson's all-time Kiwi pointscoring record.

The former Dolphin has 215 points from his 17 Tests, just 10 shy of Johnson's mark, and could claim top spot as early as the World Cup final if the points continue to flow for Stacey Jones's side.

McLean has more work to do to run down Manu Vatuvei as the nation's highest-ever try-scorer, but he is making a cracking pace.

In just seven Tests, McLean has scored 15 tries to sit in equal-eighth spot on the all-time list. Every other player around him had at least 20 caps, and Vatuvei took 29 to collect his 23 tries.

The second four-try haul of his budding career means that at just 20, McLean is odds on to become New Zealand's Test try-scoring king sooner rather than later.

3. Are Australia still the favourites?

Australia has done enough to qualify for the semifinals. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

The Kangaroos are one of only two unbeaten sides heading into the knockout phase, but their hold on favouritism is shaky at best.

Their brilliant win over New Zealand in the tournament opener had more than a few elements of fortune in their favour, especially the two length-of-the-field intercept tries that kept them in the game early on.

They scratched their way past Fiji and romped home against the Cook Islands since, looking short of their best in both performances.

While they are always a threat, it feels as though all four nations in the semifinals are in with a chance of lifting the trophy rather than it being Australia's birthright.

Kevin Walters has a big decision to make at halfback between Tom Dearden and Sam Walker but seems to have settled on Reece Walsh as his custodian, and after the Broncos playmaker laid on five tries in this 66-6 mauling to go with his game-changing plays against the Kiwis, it's hard to argue.

4. Lebanon-France is what the World Cup can be

Abbas Miski's miracle try was one of the moments of the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

After a tournament filled with blowouts, the epic finish between France and Lebanon shows what's possible when things line up right at the World Cup, as two winless teams desperate to restore some pride played out a classic.

This was two teams of similar skill levels in front of a rowdy and emotionally invested crowd at a venue that accentuated at least one of the fan bases.

That's a simple recipe to follow, and while you won't always be rewarded with the epic finish of this golden point thriller, a new format that keeps teams like this together and therefore produces more of these match-ups is a must for 2030.

When that next tournament rolls around, plenty of tales from this game will be told, from Cesar Rouge's game-winning field goal controversially chalked off the board to Lebanon's remarkable extra-time try to Abbas Miski.

That score put the tragedy of French fullback Arthur Mourgue, a mad genius who doesn't always nail the genius part, into World Cup folklore after his remarkable field goal sent the game to extra time before a maniac kick inside his own 20 fell for the Cedars's winning try.

5. The veteran Tonga cannot do without

Tui Lolohea had another role to play in another epic win for Tonga. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Amid a match with a galaxy of stars that promised a glorious future for Samoa and Tonga, Tui Lolohea seemed the odd man out.

The Tongan veteran was the only player in the game who doesn't ply his trade in the NRL, and given his mercurial career, he might have seemed a weak link for the Mate Ma'a.

But after 12 seasons in the red jersey, Lolohea has proven himself an invaluable part of their rise to the top of Test football, and while they have more talent at their disposal than ever before, they always come back to him when it counts.

Along with Jason Taumalolo, Lolohea is the only man to have played in each of Tonga's most important wins over the past decade and always seems to defy critics when it matters most.

He is older and slower, but he always gives Tonga what they need — the 31-year-old, who currently doesn't have a club for next season, set up a try for Jojo Fifita with a clever floating pass and held up well in defence under heavy pressure from Samoa, who clearly targeted the former Huddersfield Giant.

With Latu Fainu fit and Talatau Amone in the squad, Tonga are not short of options in the halves, but Lolohea rewarded coach Kristian Woolf's faith yet again, as he always seems to do when it matters most.

World.title: Large crocodile spotted near future Olympic rowing course
World.content:
The sighting of a saltwater crocodile near the proposed 2032 Olympic rowing precinct in Rockhampton is under investigation, while Rowing Australia says it is a "shock" and a wake-up call.

North Rockhampton Golf Club alerted members at the weekend when the crocodile, estimated to be up to 3 metres long, was spotted near the 11th hole.

The sighting was within a few kilometres of the Fitzroy River precinct earmarked for rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The selection of Rockhampton as the home of the Games' rowing has been questioned by some. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

On Monday, a spokesperson for the Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation (DETSI) said the sighting was not reported to the department, but was now under investigation.

Speaking in Hervey Bay on Monday morning, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli played down concerns about the crocodile and expressed confidence in Rockhampton's ability to host the Olympic rowing events.

"Many, many decades of success prove that it's a world-class venue," he said.

"It's a magnificent community and they'll do it very, very well."

David Crisafulli has backed Rockhampton's rowing venue amid renewed crocodile concerns. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Rowing Australia life member Ray Ebert said the sighting was a wake-up call for those involved in planning the 2032 Olympic rowing events on the Fitzroy River.

"It's a bit of a shock to me," Mr Ebert told ABC News Breakfast on Monday.

"I've been saying that the crocodiles are the least of our problems. I'm going to admit to something that none of the politicians have admitted to: maybe I was wrong."

Mr Ebert pointed to previous crocodile sightings in the area, including two reported in December 2024, involving animals measuring about 2.5 metres and 1 metre.

Loading...

He said the latest sighting raised questions about how authorities would manage crocodile risks around the proposed rowing venue.

"It's not the crocodiles that you can see that I would be worried about. It's the ones that I can't see," he said.

Mr Ebert questioned whether the Queensland government was taking the issue seriously enough and said the sighting could prompt further questions about the venue's suitability and safety.

Rowing venue scrutiny

State and national rowing regattas have been held on the Fitzroy River and the venue has also been used by Australian rowing teams for pre-Olympic training camps over the years.

In September, Mr Crisafulli announced the Rockhampton venue had passed an independent technical assessment "with flying colours" to host rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.

It came after months of fierce debate over the Fitzroy River's suitability, including its status as a crocodile habitat.

The Rockhampton rowing facility has hosted multiple events. (Supplied: Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club)

International sporting bodies are now awaiting the next phase of venue planning, which include technical details and confirmation of service levels and facilities needed for Olympic and Paralympic competitions.

Queensland Opposition Leader Steven Miles said the sighting highlighted the need for the Crisafulli government to release the technical report underpinning Rockhampton's selection as an Olympic rowing venue.

Mr Miles said the report should outline how crocodile risks would be managed during the Games, arguing its release would help address concerns about the Fitzroy River.

A sign at the North Rockhampton Golf Club warns visitors of crocodiles on the course. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

University of Queensland crocodile expert and emeritus professor Craig Franklin was more critical of the decision to hold Olympic rowing on the Fitzroy River.

He described it as a political decision rather than one based on common sense, saying he would go so far as to call it "foolish".

On September 19, a saltwater croc was spotted upstream from the Rockhampton rowing course, according to the Queensland government's official sightings dashboard.

There have been two further sightings since that were reported closer to the proposed venue.

Croc expert supports removal

Reptile expert John Lever, who owns Koorana Crocodile Farm near Rockhampton, said the animal was likely to be a male saltwater crocodile and estimated it was "up to three metres" long based on the photograph of the sighting.

Mr Lever said wildlife rangers would likely need to assess the animal's behaviour before a decision was made about whether it should be removed.

Koorana Crocodile Farm owner John Lever. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

The area is not currently classified as a Category A zone, where crocodiles are automatically targeted for removal.

However, Mr Lever said he believed crocodiles spotted in the vicinity of the planned Olympic venue should be dealt with.

"With the Olympics coming up, my take on this would be that any crocodile seen in that area should be removed," he said.

"But that's not up to me to do that, it's up to the government."

A DETSI spokesperson said the Queensland Crocodile Management Plan was reviewed every year.

The Fitzroy River has faced intense scrutiny since its selection as an Olympic venue. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Mr Lever said heavy rainfall in central Queensland last week may have stimulated the animal's activity.

"There's crocodiles, of course, in the Fitzroy [River], we all know that, so a sighting is not uncommon," he said.

"This is the mating season. Males and females are both moving around looking for mates."

World.title: Bancroft reaches acceptance over Test recall chances after 'dejection'
World.content:
Cameron Bancroft says his passion to return to the Australian Test side has faded as the national team scrambles for a solution to its batting woes following a disastrous Cape Town collapse.

Australia returned to Cape Town last week for the first time since the infamous 2018 sandpaper scandal that saw Bancroft banished from Test selection.

As the national side capitulated in the series decider, Bancroft recorded his 34th first class century and 15th in seven years, hammering 186 for Western Australia against South Australia in the Sheffield Shield at Adelaide Oval.

Strategy, succession planning needed for Australia after Cape Town collapse After a disastrous series loss to South Africa, Australian cricket faces some tough decisions, writes Russell Jackson.

"I'm definitely not as feverish now about my opportunities to play at that level," Bancroft told ABC Sport's Summer Grandstand.

"I'm fully accepting of the fact that the likelihood is that I won't play at that level again. If an opportunity came I'd be very grateful and I'd take it, but I'm at peace with playing at the level and the opportunity I had there."

Despite being the leading run-scorer in the 2022/23 Shield season and second in the 2023/24 campaign for WA, Bancroft wasn't selected for the Test series against the West Indies and Pakistan that summer, with selectors opting for David Warner to complete a retirement tour and then trialling Steve Smith in the opener position.

Bancroft revealed he still isn't quite sure why he wasn't picked despite his strong domestic form.

"It's a great question. I'm not sure … it just didn't go my way," he said.

Cameron Bancroft has remained a prolific run scorer at the Sheffield Shield level but remains out of favour with the Australian selectors. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

"Naturally you feel a bit of dejection. It did bring me down for sure. When you want something so badly and you feel like you've given 100 per cent and it's not quite enough; naturally you feel those emotions.

"The reasons why you play and enjoy the game get questioned. A big part of my own career is finding peace with that."

The Australian men's side has now had nine different opening combinations in their past 19 Tests and is facing a race against time to find a solution, with a home series against New Zealand in December and overseas tours of India and England in 2027.

Bancroft believes the national team is lacking chemistry due to the inconsistent nature of the top order.

You can have your say on the Summer of Cricket every weekend at 1pm EDT by calling 1300 558 222 to speak to the ABC Sport team on Summer Grandstand.

"There's no doubt continuity is something that has been lacking a little bit," he said.

"From the outside there's lots of changes and thoughts and theories. It's probably something that hasn't been figured out or solved yet."

Tech.title: Jackery made its portable power stations even smaller
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Jackery announced a new portable power station that uses the safer and longer-lasting lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries the company first introduced in 2023. But what makes the new Explorer 100D stand out is that it’s Jackery’s smallest power station to date, measuring only 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighing just 1.87 pounds. Its size and 96Wh (30,000mAh) of battery capacity means you can squeeze it into your carry-on and power multiple devices during a long flight.

The Jackery Explorer 100D will be available starting November 15th through Walmart for $99. The power station is already available from Costco if you don’t want to wait, but only in a two-pack for $179.99. You can definitely find smaller and cheaper 30,000mAh portable chargers, but the LFP cells in the 100D are “engineered for up to 8 years of regular use,” according to Jackery, with a 3,000 charge cycle lifespan, so it should easily outlast competing products that use more common lithium-ion battery cells.

Image: Jackery

Although the 100D is considerably smaller and lighter than Jackery’s other portable power stations, the company still includes an integrated handle and offers an optional shoulder strap for carrying it around. On the front, you’ll find a pair of 140W USB-C ports, plus an additional 18W USB-A port, but the 100D maxes out at 158W of total output, so power delivery across the ports will be reduced when all three are in use. If you need to charge it, can’t find an outlet, and managed to find room to also pack a solar panel, the 100D supports up to 100W of direct solar input, which will charge it back up to 80 percent capacity in about an hour and a half.

Tech.title: NASA hopes the commercial space industry can help save Hubble
Tech.content: “Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible … If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.”

Tech.title: Flock keeps ignoring requests to cancel its contracts
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

While more cities are canceling their contracts with Flock Safety, just as many are discovering how difficult that can be in some instances. Plymouth, Minnesota’s city council voted to terminate its contract with Flock in September, but failed to respond to the city’s request. For over a month, the cameras remained up, and the city had received no acknowledgment from the company. So, Police Chief Eric Fadden took matters into his own hands and physically disconnected the cameras.

“After hearing nothing for more than a week, I directed our staff to disconnect the power cords from the cameras in order to be sure that they are not functioning or recording plates,” Fadden told The Drive.

Roughly 20 miles up the road, Dayton, Minnesota, is having its own issues with Flock. In this instance, the company acknowledged the city’s request and said it would take up to 60 days to remove the equipment. Despite this, Flock reconnected two cameras within the city limits without authorization, and following a specific request from the local police not to complete the work order.

Dayton’s local government posted on Facebook:

On September 17, 2026, the Police Department was made aware of a maintenance work order produced by Flock. The City notified Flock on September 18, 2026, that the program was on hold, and no work orders were to be completed. Unfortunately, the City’s direction was not followed, and the camera was placed back into service without authorization.

Flock spokesperson Andrew Smith told The Verge, “We are proud of the impact our technology has had in Plymouth. We respect the city’s decision and are working with the customer to have the cameras removed.”

This follows a similar ordeal in Illinois, where the company refused to take down cameras and uncovered cameras at Elgin Community College after the administration sought to cancel its contract.

Update November 1st: Added comment from Flock.

Tech.title: Apple’s HomeView could add security camera features
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Reddit user pdfu found hints hidden in the HomeView 27.2 code that Apple could be adding security camera features to its smart home hub. The strings describe a security camera mode with motion detection, live streaming, and recording options, as well as privacy functions. According to pdfu, there is a setup page that even explicitly reads: “Your HomeView can be used as a security camera with HomeKit Secure Video.”

Supposedly, the video feeds will only be visible to members of the home, and will both show an indicator light and play a sound when either someone is watching the camera feed or when it starts to record. Home members will also get a notification anytime settings are changed for the Secure Video mode. It will also include customizable options for what to detect, stream, or record, based on whether you’re home, away, or asleep.

Some wondered why Apple did not allow HomeView to double as a security camera at launch, and the company hasn’t said anything to suggest the features are coming. But, considering how central privacy is to Apple’s marketing, the company may be waiting to fine-tune those features before launch.

Tech.title: A fully playable version of Portal prequel F-Stop leaked
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Leakers have pieced together a playable version of the canceled Portal prequel F-Stop. Most of the assets came from the massive 12-terabyte leak that dropped this August. That didn’t include the game’s source code or map data, but those final pieces apparently hit the Valve Cut Content Discord this week, allowing a nearly complete version to be pieced together.

Some dialog and elements of F-Stop eventually found their way into Portal 2. But it differs dramatically from the mainline Portal games in that it’s built around a camera mechanic that lets you capture an item by taking its picture and place it elsewhere using the resulting Polaroid-like photos. It’s not unlike Viewfinder in that way.

The game is short, with videos showing off its full campaign all clocking in at under an hour. That’s not terribly surprising, though. F-Stop was developed as part of the “Directed Design Experiments,” a three-month period in 2007 when Valve broke into five teams to build new video game experiments.

Tech.title: North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist
Tech.content:
North Korea Responsible for $6 Billion+ Binance Attack

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026. The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as “TraderTraitor.”

The FBI, together with partners at the USSS and IRS-CI, has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH). It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages.

Tech.title: HomePod Mini 2 first look: Three things I love and one disappointment
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When I first heard about the new $149 HomePod Mini 2 at Apple’s Welcome Home event last month, I was disappointed. It’s been six years since Apple launched its entry-level smart speaker, and all it got in the second gen was a chip bump, some color glowy stuff, and better AirPlay? For $50 more than the original, which launched at $99, Apple didn’t even upgrade the sound system. It felt like the company phoned this one in.

Now that I’ve got my hands on a couple and set them up in my home office, I’m more enthused. The Mini 2 is so much faster than the first-gen Mini, playing music in a few seconds and responding to smart home commands just as quickly. If you’re fed up with standing over your HomePod waiting for it to finally do what you asked, then that alone is worth the upgrade.

Here are my three favorite features of the new Mini 2 after spending a couple days with it, and my one big disappointment.

Siri is much snappier and much less chatty

The biggest upgrade for the Mini 2 is Siri AI, but that isn’t available yet. Apple says it’s coming “later” in a software update. However, the basic smart voice assistant has definitely improved. Siri on the Mini 2 is much snappier than on the first-gen Mini, regularly responding in under three seconds. This is thanks to a newer, faster processor (the S10, up from the S5) and Wi-Fi 6E support (up from Wi-Fi 4).

When I asked Siri to play Taylor Swift, a song started in a couple of seconds. It correctly told me who won this year’s World Series in under two seconds, and turned off the light or opened the shades in under three seconds.

That’s a huge improvement over the up to 10 seconds I often have to wait for Siri to get things done on the first-gen Mini. However, asking something harder, like who will win the US midterm elections, still brings up the familiar offer to look at some web results on my iPhone. As I said, Siri AI isn’t here yet.

The other new behavior I am really enjoying is that when I ask Siri to perform a smart home action, such as open the shades or turn on the lights, instead of “OK, Jen,” or “One sec,” followed by a wordy confirmation of the action that I often get on the first-gen Mini, the Mini 2 just does it and doesn’t talk back. It’s not silent for every action, but it’s quiet enough to be a noticeable improvement.

This Mini is gorgeous in green and sounds great

The green color is divine. This is the prettiest small smart speaker I’ve seen — and I’ve tried them all.

Yes, Amazon’s Echo Dot Max’s purple is fun, the Google Home Speaker’s pale green is elegant, but Apple’s deep green is seriously sophisticated. It’s a color that fits in really well in various places around my home, and I’m so glad the company finally released a green option. It’s a big improvement over the slightly garish yellow and orange of the prior-gen Minis and the best of the new colors.

The Mini in green. Other than the color, it looks identical to the first-gen speaker. It comes with a power brick and a color-matched fabric cord. The cord is very pale green, practically white. The base now has an embossed logo instead of a painted one.

I saw all the colors in person at Apple’s Welcome Home event, and while the pink is pretty, it’s very pale, and the blue is functionally identical to the first-gen blue, maybe a shade lighter. While a lot of folks will be happy with black (don’t get white unless you plan to dust it regularly), the green is my new go-to.

Two green HomePod Mini 2s look so good on the walnut Nanoleaf monitor stand I’m testing; it’s like my office got an instant upgrade. And while Apple didn’t update the speakers in the Mini 2, it’s still a very good speaker for its size, doing a fine job with Bad Bunny’s bass and delivering clear mids and vocals. While $300 is steep for computer speakers, two as a stereo pair in my office definitely delivered on room-filling sound.

You can finally disable touch

A few weeks ago I fumbled for my phone on my nightstand and accidentally hit the top of my HomePod Mini, blaring music in the bedroom at 3AM. My husband was not happy.

Sound Glow illuminates the top of the Mini in colors that match the album art. It only works with Apple Music and Apple Podcasts.

A new setting in the Home app now lets you lock the Mini’s top controls. This goes for all HomePods, old and new, and it’s a major quality-of-life upgrade. How often do you intentionally touch the top of your HomePod? I bet far less often than accidentally!

The other new trick for the top of the HomePod is Sound Glow. This makes the LEDs display colors that match the album art of the song you’re playing (it’s also backward compatible with the first-gen Mini and the second-gen HomePod). It’s neat, but only works with Apple Music and Podcasts and is so subtle that I don’t feel it adds much to my music-listening experience.

A stereo pair of Minis sounds very good. Here they’re pictured on Nanoleaf’s new monitor stand, which has built-in LED lighting.

Signature feature fail

Beyond the speed improvement, the other new feature I was excited about is the HomePod Mini 2’s ability to be the default speaker for your Mac using what Apple calls “a responsive and persistent AirPlay connection.” This creates a wireless point-to-point connection between the computer and the HomePod.

You can pair a single speaker or a stereo pair to your Mac, and the feature also works with the second-gen HomePod. (Two or four HomePod Mini 2s can also now be part of a surround sound setup using the new Apple TV 4K.)

Disappointingly, I couldn’t get the Mac speaker set up to work. I have the required hardware: a Mac that supports Wi-Fi 6E, running the public release of macOS 27.2 (a Mac Mini M4), and HomePods on HomePod Software 27.2. But the Sound pane in my Mac’s settings didn’t offer an option to set a HomePod via AirPlay as the default sound output.

The Mini showed up and connected like any other AirPlay speaker, with the same flaws as regular AirPlay — occasional artifacting, drop-offs, and some lag with notification sounds — along with the Mac defaulting to its built-in speakers when the computer restarts, or anytime I activate Siri on the HomePod. I also tried with a stereo pair of Minis, but they also played over regular AirPlay.

The chip bump and speed improvements make this a bigger upgrade than it initially seemed

According to a 9to5Mac’s hands-on, when the persistent AirPlay is enabled, the HomePod Mini should show up as a default system output device in the System Information, and there should be an option to enable it under “Play sound effects through” in the Sound pane in System Settings, but neither was there for me. I have seen other reports of the same issue.

I tried resetting both HomePods completely after they updated to 27.2 out of the box (I was on the HomePod Software betas, but 27.2 is now in general release), and the feature still isn’t working. I reached out to Apple, but the company hasn’t responded to my requests yet; I’ll update this article if I hear back or find a solution.

There’s more to come

I’ve only been testing the Mini 2 for two days, and while the real test will come when it gets its Siri AI upgrade, the chip bump and speed improvements make this a bigger upgrade than it initially seemed. Apple does need to work on the Mac pairing feature; it has a lot of potential, but based on my struggles here, it feels unfinished.

I plan to do a full review once Siri AI launches, and of course compare it to Apple’s big new smart home release: the upcoming $299 Apple HomeView smart display. It is also a Home hub, but the screen gives it more functionality. At $149, though, the Mini 2 is now the cheapest way to get an Apple Home hub with Thread and Matter support.

Tech.title: New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the biggest game releases of the year, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepbackhere.

How it started

The two biggest games of 2026 are set to launch just a few weeks apart in November.

On the one side you have the behemoth that is Grand Theft Auto VI, an experience 13 years in the making, and the sequel to one of the best-selling games in history. Its predecessor, GTA V, has sold a staggering 230 million copies since it launched in 2013, and was re-released across three generations of consoles. Developer Rockstar is a pioneer in the realm of open-world games, dating back to GTA III, and the scale and ambitions of those worlds have steadily grown since then. With GTA V and later Red Dead Redemption 2, the studio’s ideas reached a new level of realism. And the sixth GTA looks poised to eclipse them both, which has created an unprecedented level of demand.

Analyst firm Circana estimates that 29 percent of gamers in the US intend to buy the game, with demand so large it could boost flagging console sales. “Many consumers who have yet to upgrade to a current-generation console may choose to purchase a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series specifically to play the title,” analyst Mat Piscatella says in a statement. GTA VI’s reach is so vast that almost every other major game launched early to avoid it.

The one exception is Nintendo. The company’s tentpole release for the holidays, and its next major exclusive for the Switch 2, is a lavish remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

The release is notable for a few reasons. For one thing, it’s an attempt from Nintendo to modernize one of the most influential and beloved games in its long history. The original Ocarina of Time was the world’s first introduction to a 3D iteration of Hyrule, which, in turn, made it an early glimpse at what was possible in three-dimensional spaces, laying a blueprint for countless games that came afterward. Nintendo has since expanded on that, turning Switch-era adventures Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom into wide-open adventures designed for player creativity. They went on to become some of the best-selling games for Nintendo’s most successful console.

These aren’t just two blockbuster games – they’re two series with the pull to make this a real cultural moment, akin to “Barbenheimer” but for video games. They’re the kind of launches that make it onto Saturday Night Live and have NBA players worried.

It’s just too bad about the rest of the industry.

How it’s going

These major November releases are something of a mirage, two outliers that stand out amid the wreckage that is the rest of the video game industry. While there have been plenty of major releases and great games this year, the main theme of 2026 has been just how dire things have become. Layoffs, studio closures, unpopular business models, the ever-looming threat of AI, and massive increases in hardware costs have combined to create an ominous cloud over the medium.

What happens next

It’s not all doom and gloom. There have been rare success stories, where studios like FromSoftware and Remedy have managed to carve out a sustainable existence in a turbulent field. But for the most part, the established norms that have been part of the blockbuster games industry for years are going away. Big games are too expensive to make, hardware is too expensive to buy (and the cost is only going up), and somewhere, something has to give.

It’s tempting to look at Zelda and GTA as answers to these problems. After all, if Nintendo and Rockstar are doing so well, there must be a solution out there. But they’re also two very specific cases that are essentially impossible to replicate. Nintendo maintains ownership over all aspects of its platform, from the hardware to the games, and it has taken a careful and largely risk-averse approach that has allowed it to weather the current storm and create a growing entertainment empire. Rockstar, meanwhile, is the rare example of being too big to fail. GTA V was so massive for so long — Circana says it was among the top 20 best-selling games in the US for 13 straight years — that it allowed the studio to build up both an unprecedented amount of anticipation and, it seems, a game big enough to match it.

In that way, Zelda and GTA are throwbacks to a time when major games were sure bets. Their duelling releases are fascinating both because these games are so impactful, but also because, with all of the impending upheaval, the industry might never see a moment like this again.
